papers.abstract: Predicting where to grasp and how to move is fundamentally a geometry problem. Vision-language models treat it as language generation instead. They tokenize spatial coordinates into text and decode them autoregressively. This mechanism ignores spatial structure and truncates continuous precision. Errors compound across coordinate tokens during decoding. In this paper, we show that compact off-the-shelf VLMs with 0.5-2B parameters already encode rich spatial information in their intermediate hidden states. Autoregressive decoding is the dominant bottleneck for trajectory prediction, while affordance prediction depends additionally on feature depth and decoder architecture. We expose the latent spatial information with a lightweight, geometry-compatible prediction head that attaches to a frozen backbone. It reads features from an intermediate hidden layer, conditions a learned query on the task instruction and refines it via cross-attention over the visual tokens to regress affordance boxes and trajectory waypoints directly as continuous values, without modifying the backbone. We evaluate on ShareRobot-Bench and AGD20K. Our 2B variant reduces trajectory error by over 60% and improves ShareRobot-Bench affordance mAP by 85% relative to the autoregressive baseline. It approaches RoboBrain on trajectory prediction (0.251 vs 0.191 DFD) at 3.8x higher throughput. These results demonstrate a favorable accuracy-efficiency trade-off for instruction-conditioned 2D geometric prediction.
authors: Akila Ayanthi, Darshana Priyasad, Tharindu Fernando, Dimity Miller, Sridha Sridharan, Clinton Fookes, Peyman Moghadam
bullets: Problem: Tokenizing coordinates as text loses continuous spatial precision and causes autoregressive error accumulation.
Method: Attach a lightweight head to a frozen VLM, using intermediate features, instruction-conditioned queries, and cross-attention to regress boxes and waypoints directly.
Contribution: Separates geometric prediction from language decoding without modifying the VLM backbone.

Results: On ShareRobot-Bench and AGD20K, the 2B model reduces trajectory error by over 60%, improves affordance mAP by 85% relative to the autoregressive baseline, and achieves 3.8× higher throughput than RoboBrain while approaching its trajectory performance.
Scope: Affordance prediction also depends on feature depth and decoder architecture.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Architecture overview. A frozen VLM processes an RGB image and task instruction; hidden states from an intermediate layer are passed to a lightweight geometric prediction head. A DETR-style transformer decoder, conditioned on the instruction via the final text token hidden state, refines a learned query against the visual memory tokens. Two independent FFNs decode the query into continuous outputs: affordance boxes (L1+GIoU loss) and trajectory waypoints (L1+startpoint+endpoint loss). No gradient flows into the VLM.

Figure 1. Accuracy, efficiency, and model size. Each bubble represents a model; bubble size encodes the number of active parameters. Color denotes model family: LLaVA-OV, Qwen2-VL, RoboBrain. Dashed arrows indicate improvement over the corresponding base VLM. (Top) Trajectory prediction DFD (↓) vs. inference speed (FPS on H100) on ShareRobot-Bench-Trajectory. (Bottom) Affordance mAP (↑) vs. inference speed (FPS on H100) on AGD20K. Our method outperforms both base VLMs, approaches larger-model accuracy, and retains favorable parameter and inference efficiency.

Trajectory DFD on ShareRobot-Bench-Trajectory and affordance mAP on AGD20K across all language-model layers for Qwen2-VL-2B and LLaVA-OV-0.5B, compared against the base VLM and LoRA fine-tuned autoregressive baselines. Colored markers indicate the selected layer used in the final model.

The visualizations in the first three rows demonstrate that our geometry head effectively generates end-effector manipulation trajectories based on the observation and task instruction. The fourth row presents some failure cases arising from object-localization errors or insufficient spatial understanding.

The visualizations in the first three rows demonstrate that our geometry head effectively generates affordance boxes based on the observation and task instruction. Figure 6. Efficiency–performance trade-off across layers on Qwen2-VL-2B for the trajectory prediction task.

Figure 7. Predicted waypoint heatmaps over the test set, visualizing how endpoint supervision shapes the spatial distribution of trajectory predictions. (a) Ground-truth distribution: waypoints are broadly spread, reflecting the spatial diversity of manipulation trajectories in the dataset. (b) Zero-shot Qwen2-VL-2B baseline: predictions collapse to the image boundaries, confirming that vanilla autoregressive generation fails to produce spatially meaningful trajectories. (c) Geometry head without endpoint supervision: predictions collapse to a single central region, as the uniform L1 objective is minimised by regressing toward the dataset mean. (d) Geometry head with endpoint supervision: the distribution recovers spatial diversity matching the ground truth, demonstrating that boundary supervision forces input-specific localization rather than dataset-level averaging.

papers.selection_reason: Decodes geometry directly from VLM hidden states for robot affordance and trajectory prediction, avoiding autoregressive tokenization.
papers.title: Decoding Geometry, Not Tokens: Efficient VLMs for Robot Affordance and Trajectory Prediction
papers.tldr: A lightweight geometry-aware head unlocks spatial information already present in compact VLMs, enabling faster and more accurate continuous robot affordance and trajectory prediction than autoregressive coordinate decoding.

papers.abstract: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) devices allow human experts to demonstrate tasks for robot learning without teleoperating physical robots. Using these demonstrations as training data still requires a consistent hardware setup, calibration, and data processing. We present UMI-Live, a full-stack open-source bimanual UMI system for in-the-wild data collection. We design our custom UMI-Live hardware to integrate camera and LiDAR--inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power, without external tracking equipment or calibration within the collection environment. We implement a simple user interface for recording data while an asynchronous pipeline performs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets. We also release software that supports dual-YAM teleoperation and VLA policy training and inference. We validate UMI-Live data quality by fine-tuning $\pi_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct2, achieving success rates of 10/10 and 8/10, respectively on a bimanual pick-and-place task. Furthermore, we release 40 hours of UMI-Live data across three tasks, and complete hardware designs, software, and reproduction guides at our $\href{https://umi-live.github.io/}{\text{project website}}$.
authors: Govind Velamoor, Adrian Lin, Sam Jung, Spencer Mateega, Brandon Y. Yang, Amish Sethi
bullets: Integrates cameras, LiDAR-inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power into custom wearable hardware.
Provides a simple recording interface with asynchronous SLAM reconstruction and dataset generation.
Supports dual-YAM teleoperation plus VLA policy training and inference.
Validated on a bimanual pick-and-place task with 10/10 success for π₀.₅ and 8/10 for MolmoAct2.
Releases 40 hours of data across three tasks, alongside hardware, software, and reproduction guides.

figures.caption: Figure 6: Data collection and processing in UMI-Live. (a) Each gripper i ∈ {L,R} records wrist images Ii, LiDAR data Pi, and IMU data U i. (b) Raw episodes R(e) are processed in parallel to estimate jaw widths wi t, reconstruct poses T i t , and align the streams. (c) We assemble demonstration trajectories T (e) with wrist images, 14-dimensional bimanual states, and task instructions into dataset D. Training samples use observations ot = (ILt , I R t , gLt , g R t , ℓ) and query-relative action chunks At ∈ RH×20, as defined in Appendices E and F.

Figure 7: Handheld collection and physical robot evaluation. (a) Wrist-camera views at two moments in a UMI demonstration collected at a different location and under different lighting from the robot evaluation, brightened for display. papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) can condition robot actions on generated visual futures, but this additional context is neither cost-free nor uniformly beneficial. We examine what a predicted future actually changes: the action delta $\Delta a$ between the future-conditioned and future-free execution paths of the same model. Under a shared WAM checkpoint, this delta barely shifts average benchmark success ($+0.8$ points on LIBERO, $-0.8$ on RoboTwin~2.0), while generating visual futures increases inference latency by 1.7--1.9$\times$. These aggregate metrics conceal a concentrated failure mode that we term \emph{future-induced negative transfer}: while predictive deltas benefit long-horizon tasks ($+2.4$ points on LIBERO-Long) and remain negligible on most routine manipulations, they induce severe degradation on precision tasks---with \emph{Press Stapler} and \emph{Place Can Basket} losing 54.0 and 34.0 points, recurring as top failure modes across independently trained WAM variants. We introduce \textbf{Utility-WAM} for in-place correction of future-conditioned control. Its primary learning component is a residual adapter that repairs future-induced velocity deltas under a frozen shared WAM by aligning them with ground-truth dynamic guidance and penalizing excess error beyond the future-free baseline. The adapter selectively eliminates the majority of severe task drops (reducing losses to 6.0 and 14.0 points) while preserving long-horizon foresight. To eliminate superfluous video computation, a lightweight pre-generation gate reuses counterfactual action outcomes to selectively bypass video generation on 75.5\% of RoboTwin queries, cutting latency by 38\% while improving average success to 93.3\% on RoboTwin~2.0 and 98.9\% on LIBERO. On physical bimanual manipulation across three real-world tasks, Utility-WAM succeeds in 53 of 60 trials, compared to 43 for FAST-WAM.
authors: Feihong Zhang, Xi Lin, Yulong Shi, Zuxing Lu, Yanghong Mei, Zhaopeng Gu, Tingyu Yuan, Zihao Liang, Yinuo Wang, Zhaowen Li
bullets: Future-induced action changes provide little average benefit and can severely hurt precision tasks, despite helping long-horizon tasks.
A residual adapter repairs future-conditioned velocity changes against dynamic guidance while preserving the shared WAM and its foresight.
A lightweight gate bypasses video generation for 75.5% of RoboTwin queries, reducing latency by 38%.
Utility-WAM reduces major task losses, reaches 93.3% success on RoboTwin 2.0 and 98.9% on LIBERO, and succeeds in 53/60 real-world trials versus 43/60 for FAST-WAM.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Utility-WAM repairs future-induced action changes before allocating future-generation compute. Stage 1 trains a shared WAM with matched future-free and future-visible action paths. Stage 2 freezes the WAM and trains a residual adapter on self-generated future features, using beneficial ground-truthfuture velocity deltas and the future-free path as supervision. These two stages establish the core correction method. Stage 3 reuses the adapter’s paired final-action outcomes to train a gate. At inference, the gate runs before video generation: it either executes the future-free path and skips that compute, or invokes future generation and the corrected future-conditioned path. papers.abstract: We present SONIC-K1, to our knowledge the first open-weights whole-body motion tracker for the Booster K1 humanoid, obtained by adapting the SONIC framework to this smaller robot. The policy is trained from scratch on a single shared GPU with a small fraction of the compute reported for SONIC. In MuJoCo simulation, it tracks nearly all held-out motion clips and performs well on external benchmarks under SONIC's success criterion. On the real K1, it tracks upper-body and slow motions, while stepping and turning remain less reliable, and simulation experiments show a sensitivity to action latency. These results show broad motion-tracking capability on a modest training budget and point to quantitative hardware evaluation as the main next step. Code, policy weights and evaluation tools are publicly available.
bullets: Targets whole-body motion tracking on the smaller Booster K1 humanoid.
Trains the policy from scratch using a single shared GPU and substantially less compute than the original SONIC work.
Tracks nearly all held-out motion clips in MuJoCo and performs well on external benchmarks under SONIC’s criterion.
On the real robot, upper-body and slow motions work reliably, while stepping and turning are less reliable.
Simulation reveals sensitivity to action latency; code, weights, and evaluation tools are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Learning-based traffic signal control (TSC) has achieved promising performance, but most methods rely on structured traffic states that must be estimated from sensor observations in real deployments. Visual TSC learns signal decisions directly from images, yet existing methods depend on fixed roadside cameras and remain tied to specific intersection configurations and visual domains. UAVs offer on-demand bird's-eye-view (BEV) observations that jointly capture intersection topology and traffic dynamics, making them a promising sensing platform for visual TSC. We present BEVLight, a generalizable TSC framework that directly maps BEV observations to signal actions. BEVLight grounds visual features onto individual lanes and composes them along the junction topology into movement and phase representations, allowing a shared policy to score candidate phases across heterogeneous intersection layouts and signal plans. To train the policy, we develop a web-based virtual teleoperation platform and collect over 5K human control decisions together with their underlying traffic states. Simulator-provided traffic states first supervise lane- and movement-level representations, after which human phase selections and rankings supervise the phase scorer. Re-rendering the recorded trajectories under diverse appearances preserves both forms of supervision and encourages robustness to visual changes. Closed-loop experiments demonstrate zero-shot generalization across traffic demands, signal plans, and intersections: BEVLight reduces average waiting time by 7--9\% relative to perception-to-control visual baselines and matches or outperforms structured-state RL controllers that receive ground-truth traffic states, achieving the lowest waiting time in 12 of 16 scenarios. An offline study further shows that BEVLight transfers to real UAV observations without target-domain adaptation.
authors: Maonan Wang, Yuxin Cai, Junming Liu, Zhengyan Huang, Yi Yu, Ding Wang, Yifeng Zhang, Yirong Chen
bullets: Addresses the dependence of existing visual traffic signal controllers on fixed cameras and specific intersection layouts.
Maps visual features to lanes, movements, and phases, then uses a shared policy to rank candidate signal phases across layouts and plans.
Trains with over 5K human control decisions, simulator traffic-state supervision, and appearance-diverse trajectory re-rendering.
Closed-loop tests show 7–9% lower average waiting time than visual baselines and the lowest waiting time in 12 of 16 scenarios.
Transfers to real UAV observations in an offline study without target-domain adaptation.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic tasks are commonly decomposed into semantic subgoals to simplify planning. However, subgoal progress in LLM-based planning is typically inferred implicitly from interaction histories. Inaccurate estimates can misguide execution and allow local errors to propagate. To address this, we propose ProLoop, a Progress-Aware Closed-Loop framework that derives explicit subgoal progress from structured relations between desired and execution states. A learned State-Relation Monitor assesses these relations, which are then aggregated into subgoal progress as ongoing, deviated, or completed. The resulting progress guides execution adaptation, enabling reliable progress-aware control throughout execution. Experiments on AgentBoard ALFWorld and a real-world robotic platform show that ProLoop improves success rate by 12.94% overall and by 15.46% on Hard tasks, while reducing environment interactions by 32.3%.
authors: Runxin Zou, Qingmiao Liang, Jiatao Zhang, Xinyan Lv, Liangyu Qie, Meiyi Bu, Wei Song, Shiqiang Zhu
bullets: Implicit progress estimates from interaction histories can cause planning errors to propagate.
A learned State-Relation Monitor compares desired and execution states to classify subgoals as ongoing, deviated, or completed.
These progress assessments guide execution adaptation throughout task completion.
Experiments in ALFWorld and on a real-world robotic platform report 12.94% higher overall success, 15.46% higher success on Hard tasks, and 32.3% fewer environment interactions.

Fig. 4. Representative ALFWorld executions with ProLoop. Ongoing progress allows execution to continue without additional intervention, deviated progress triggers targeted correction, and completed progress enables subgoal transition and memory update.

papers.abstract: Fine manipulation requires robots to recognize when a grasped object makes or changes contact with its environment, yet such extrinsic contact is not always directly observable from vision or local contact geometry. Force and torque signals carry this information, but also vary with object weight, grasp configuration, and robot motion, leaving it unclear whether they can provide a reusable representation of physical state. Here we show that bilateral six-axis force/torque histories can be pretrained as a semantically structured physical representation by aligning them with a frozen language space using supervision generated from simulated pick-and-place interactions. On unseen objects in simulation, the learned representation supports text-prototype readout of robot action, object weight, and grasp interaction. In real-world placement, unlabeled calibration enables contact and support-state recognition without updating the encoder, outperforming a vertical-force sign-reversal rule baseline. For connector insertion, an event absent from pretraining, low-rank adaptation improves data-efficient learning over training from scratch. These results show that force/torque histories can support both direct readout of known physical states and efficient adaptation to new extrinsic-contact events.
authors: Kazuki Takahashi, Hiroaki Murakami, Ryota Sakuma, Mitsuhiro Kamezaki, Matthew Ishige, Yoshihiro Kawahara
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of inferring environmental contact from vision or local geometry alone, given force/torque variation from weight, grasp, and motion.
Pretrains six-axis force/torque histories by aligning them with a frozen language space using simulated pick-and-place supervision.
Supports text-prototype readout of robot action, object weight, and grasp interaction on unseen simulated objects.
Enables unlabeled real-world calibration for contact and support-state recognition, outperforming a vertical-force sign-reversal baseline.
Low-rank adaptation improves data-efficient learning for connector insertion, an event not included during pretraining.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies increasingly learn from data collected across diverse tasks and embodiments, yet typically assume a single controller for each robot. This assumption limits transfer because different controllers can assign different physical meanings to the same action and may require different strategies to complete a task. We study how to transfer robot data across both embodiments and controllers without allowing conflicting action interpretations to interfere with learning. Our setting spans six controller types as well as variations in controller gains and compliance. We propose a framework that encodes behavioral interaction under a controller through examples of commanded actions and the resulting robot motions. A transformer context encoder summarizes these interactions, allowing a single policy to adapt in context. Across real-world experiments, our method improves average success by 33 percentage points over naive data pooling, achieves 50\% success on unseen controller modes and 52\% on unseen controller gains, and transfers to tasks with limited controller-specific data. On contact-rich tasks such as USB insertion and surface wiping, behavioral interaction context enables the policy to adapt not only its actions but also its strategy. Our results provide a path toward generalist robot policies that can leverage data collected across diverse action interpretations. For more information, visit \href{https://controller-transfer.github.io}{https://controller-transfer.github.io}.
authors: Jonathan Yang, Chelsea Finn, Dorsa Sadigh
bullets: Addresses conflicting action meanings across robot embodiments, controller types, gains, and compliance settings.
Uses a transformer context encoder to summarize commanded actions and resulting motions, enabling in-context policy adaptation.
Evaluated across six controller types and real-world tasks, including USB insertion and surface wiping.
Improves average success by 33 percentage points over naive data pooling; reaches 50% success on unseen controller modes and 52% on unseen gains.

papers.abstract: Lattice-type modular reconfigurable robots rearrange standardized modules across tasks. Dedicated transport robots reduce module weight and cost by eliminating module level reconfiguration actuators. But existing systems use low capacity connections or internal fastening robots that occupy space for functional components. This paper presents CuBot-STT, which integrates module transport, interface locking, and release in one external robot. Cubic modules provide structural support and $24\,\mathrm{V}$ power distribution. On each face, a gear transmission converts one external input into motion of four helical locking points, preserving internal space. The robot uses alternating foot support, a gripper for module handling, and a tightening head for interface actuation. The controller coordinates two-foot support and module locking through continuous constraint transfers. The planner decomposes relocation costs into an analytical lower bound and a residual learned through expert-guided, goal conditioned Q-learning. Contact face $A^*$ search expands relocation sequences into robot primitives satisfying connectivity, asymmetric manipulation, and foot stance constraints. Experiments demonstrate normal and tangential interface capacities of $300\,\mathrm{N}$ and $490\,\mathrm{N}$, electrical continuity across six modules, and autonomous reconfiguration of an 11-module lattice. Planning benchmarks show superior search efficiency over analytical guidance and bidirectional heuristic search, with generalization beyond training lattice sizes without fine-tuning.
authors: Chongxi Meng, Da Zhao, Yanmin Zhou, Runjie Shen, Zhipeng Wang, Bin He
bullets: Combines module transport, interface tightening, and release in one robot, avoiding internal fastening mechanisms.
Uses cubic modules with face-mounted gear transmissions that actuate four helical locking points from one external input while distributing 24 V power.
Coordinates alternating foot support, gripping, tightening, and constraint transfers for stable manipulation.

papers.abstract: Legged robots have demonstrated advanced capabilities across a wide range of real-world tasks, yet much of this progress concerns the robot controlling only itself. Once the robot is coupled to an external object -- particularly an underactuated one -- the dynamics of the combined assembly become more complex. Towing a wagon is a common practical scenario, where coupled dynamics make reliable navigation challenging. This difficulty is amplified in confined spaces, where collision-free navigation requires finding a narrow set of feasible paths under strict real-time constraints. To address this, we propose a navigation framework that combines Conditional Flow Matching (CFM) with Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control over a learned Forward Dynamics Model (FDM). The CFM model mitigates the initialization problem of MPPI and accelerates its convergence, while MPPI with the FDM recovers feasible solutions beyond the CFM model's training distribution by iterative refinement. We integrate the framework into a full-stack navigation system for RAIBO-Wagon, a quadruped towing a custom wagon, and validate it in real-world outdoor experiments on 15 m-long courses through confined spaces, with all sensing and computation performed fully onboard. The system achieves an 85% success rate across 40 trials, towing a total load of up to 40 kg -- nearly 100% of RAIBO's body weight.
authors: Insung Yang, Eunchae Kim, Jungwoo Hur, Seunghun Jeon, Donghyuk Choi, Jemin Hwangbo

papers.abstract: While frontier vision-language models demonstrate strong capabilities in user interface (UI) navigation, their high inference costs prohibit everyday use. Conversely, smaller models trained via supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or offline reinforcement learning often memorize static trajectories, leading to brittle execution and an inability to recover from errors. To address these limitations, we propose a novel online reinforcement learning framework that trains UI navigation agents directly on live iOS applications. Our framework decouples the agent into two specialized components: a Planning agent and a UI Grounding model. We rely on an LLM-as-a-Judge to provide comprehensive reward signals, combining dense, step-level feedback to evaluate intermediate progress with a terminal reward for overall task completion. To effectively leverage this dual reward structure, we optimize the agent using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with step-level advantage estimation. Furthermore, we introduce GiGPPO, a novel neighbor-conditioned value estimation method that improves critic stability by leveraging reward signals from visually similar states across concurrent trajectories. To support this online training paradigm at scale, we introduce an efficient infrastructure that orchestrates hundreds of concurrent virtual iOS devices. Evaluations on rigorous benchmarks, including UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld, demonstrate that our online RL trained agents substantially outperform both SFT and terminal-only RL baselines while accelerating training convergence. Notably, our 8B RL agents achieve nearly a sevenfold improvement over the SFT baseline in out-of-distribution generalization to Android environments, while outperforming Gemini-3.5-Flash and tying with Gemini-3.1-Pro on real iOS applications.
authors: Peitong Duan, Khashayar Gatmiry, Jeffrey Nichols, Samy Bengio, Emmanuel Abbe
bullets: Addresses brittle trajectory memorization and high inference costs in UI navigation.

Uses LLM-based dense step rewards plus terminal task-completion rewards, optimized with PPO and step-level advantages.
Introduces GiGPPO, which stabilizes value estimation using rewards from visually similar states in concurrent trajectories.

Evaluations across UINavBench, iOSWorld, and AndroidWorld show stronger performance than SFT and terminal-only RL baselines, including nearly sevenfold OOD improvement for 8B agents on Android and competitive results on real iOS apps.

papers.abstract: Trajectory-level GRPO is a common approach for training multi-step GUI agents, but repeatedly rolling out complete trajectories from the task root can be inefficient: task-level rewards provide coarse supervision over which intermediate decisions require improvement, while already-mastered prefixes are repeatedly re-executed before reaching difficult states. We introduce a two-stage adaptive training framework that jointly addresses where to learn and how far to roll out. We first construct reusable intermediate checkpoints from successful expert trajectories and select informative pivots using action disagreement, which measures uncertainty directly from sampled GUI actions. Stage I performs one-step RL at these pivots to improve uncertain local decisions. Stage II then progressively expands policy responsibility through adaptive Local, Suffix, and Root training according to task progress. Recoverable checkpoints enable repeated training from intermediate states without replaying the preceding trajectory. Across MobileGym and CUA-Gym-Hub, our method reduces environment interaction by 56-61% relative to Vanilla GRPO while improving task performance, demonstrating that jointly allocating training across states and rollout ranges can substantially improve GUI-agent RL efficiency.

bullets: Addresses the inefficiency of replaying full trajectories from the task root and the coarse supervision of task-level rewards.

papers.abstract: Learning task progress from robot demonstrations provides a practical way to construct dense shaping rewards for robotic reinforcement learning. A common approach uses normalized demonstration time as progress labels, implicitly assuming monotonically increasing task progress. During policy exploration, however, actual task progress can stall or even regress. Such models may mistake regressions for progress, assigning positive shaping rewards to actions that cause progress loss. Real suboptimal and failed executions offer corrective experience, but assigning absolute progress values to their states is difficult. Our key observation is that stalls, regressions, and recoveries establish local relative progress relations even when absolute progress is unknown. We introduce Event2Reward, which uses normalized temporal labels to anchor the progress scale and these within-trajectory relations to constrain local changes, combining absolute and relative progress supervision. Its progress predictions serve as potentials for reward shaping. We curate an event-annotated dataset from approximately 100K raw real-robot execution records, covering successful, suboptimal, and failed executions, without requiring framewise absolute progress labels. Under the same training budgets, Event2Reward improves average policy success by 18.16 percentage points over a baseline using only sparse task rewards across 40 tasks in four LIBERO suites. On real robots, average success after 30 minutes of wall-clock training reaches 60.0% on three precise insertion tasks and 90.0% on three object manipulation tasks, exceeding the sparse-reward baseline under the same budget by 36.7 and 23.3 percentage points, respectively. Ablation studies further show that absolute progress supervision and relative progress relations are complementary, with joint supervision yielding better downstream policy learning.
authors: Junnan Nie, Zitian Fan, Jiachen Zhang, Junyi Lao, Likui Zhang, Chenghao Liu, Xiaoyang Lu, Yunbo Wang, Yixue Zhang, Linbo Zhai, Jiayi Li, Mengzhe Wang, Xichang Wu, Bin Wang, Chang Liu, Tianle Zhang, Songfang Huang

papers.abstract: Experience can help embodied agents turn high-level plans into grounded actions, but transferring it across tasks remains challenging: previously effective strategies may be inapplicable to the current state or fail to produce their intended outcomes. We present EmbodiExp, a framework for constructing transferable experiences and composing them online during embodied task execution. Our key observation is that tasks often share subgoals whose completion can be assessed independently of overall task success. We therefore introduce an outcome-grounded subgoal experience that specifies a subgoal, applicability conditions, an adaptable policy, and a verifiable outcome. During execution, applicable experiences guide action generation, while verified outcomes can establish the conditions required by subsequent experiences, enabling online composition. Subgoal-level outcome attribution further enables failure utilization: failed trajectories can still contribute verified local successes and condition-specific guidance on actions to avoid. Experiments on multiple embodied benchmarks under a fold-based protocol with frozen experience banks demonstrate the effectiveness of EmbodiExp.

bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring strategies across tasks when applicability and outcomes vary by state.

Demonstrates effectiveness across multiple embodied benchmarks with frozen experience banks under a fold-based protocol.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video has emerged as one of the most scalable sources of data for learning generalizable manipulation priors. Yet, despite its growing use in pretraining robotic policies, it has been underutilized as a validation tool for physical intelligence, a key component of which is understanding where to make contact with an object to achieve an intended interaction. We present EgoContact, a large-scale egocentric dataset for evaluating the generalizability and precision of learned manipulation priors through future contact-point prediction. EgoContact contains 22.5K manually verified interaction events, each with a pre-contact observation, semantic intent, and pixel-precise contact locations. We find that current methods often struggle to predict precise interaction contacts and sometimes fail to localize the target object in diverse, in-the-wild scenes, even when allowed multiple predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the usefulness of EgoContact's annotated interactions for robotic manipulation: simply using EgoContact as the memory bank of an existing affordance-transfer policy improves grasp success from 14.2% to 31.2% in simulation and from 16% to 58% on a real robot.

papers.abstract: Operational strategies for long-horizon robotic tasks require reliable evaluation to determine whether execution is progressing, stalling, regressing, or recovering from errors. Yet real- world robot datasets that capture error recovery and provide frame-level error annotations remain scarce. To address this gap, we introduce and open-source ReSTEP, a dataset of 3,156 episodes across two manipulation tasks with semantic stage labels and frame-level er- ror annotations. ReSTEP supports training and benchmarking progress monitors through successful execution, mistakes, and recovery. Existing progress estimators can struggle to distinguish visually similar task stages and maintain temporally consistent predictions while responding to genuine setbacks. We therefore propose REMORA, an online progress esti- mator that combines recurrent visual memory, distributional prediction, and causal peak selection. Memory retains execution history to help resolve visual ambiguity, while distribu- tional prediction represents alternative progress hypotheses and causal peak selection tracks a supported hypothesis over time. Together, these components enable consistent progress tracking that remains responsive to errors and recovery. Experiments on both ReSTEP tasks demonstrate that REMORA outperforms the state-of-the-art SARM baseline in progress ac- curacy and temporal consistency.

papers.abstract: As a representative form of embodied robotic interaction, aerial grasping requires close coordination between the aerial platform and manipulator. Most existing systems perform aerial grasping with static or slowly moving targets under fixed scenarios. Dynamic and precise grasping across different conditions introduces additional challenges, including target motion, localization drift, dynamic coupling, and external disturbances. In this work, we present CAPTURER, a dexterous aerial manipulator for centimeter-level grasping across diverse environments. To achieve the challenging goal, we first develop an onboard perception system for state estimation and target detection. Drift correction and global pose transformation are introduced to improve target localization during flight. A cooperative motion planner is proposed to coordinate the mobility of the aerial platform with the dexterity of the manipulator according to the relative target state. To maintain grasping accuracy under disturbances, we design a disturbance-rejection controller to compensate for dynamic coupling, model uncertainty, and external disturbances. The capability of CAPTURER is validated through indoor and outdoor experiments with both static and moving targets. The results demonstrate that CAPTURER achieves centimeter-level grasping accuracy for a marker pen measuring only 1.5 cm in diameter at flight speeds exceeding 1.5 m/s.
authors: Meng Wang, Jindou Jia, Sicheng Zhou, Zeshuai Chen, Kexin Guo, Xiang Yu, Lei Guo

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of CAPTURER workflow. Body: CAPTURER integrates onboard perception, cooperative motion planning, and anti-disturbance control within a unified framework. Perception: The perception module combines visual–inertial state estimation, target detection, drift correction, global pose transformation, motion prediction, and active target search to provide consistent robot and target states. Planning: Based on the relative target state, the cooperative planner generates coordinated motion references for the aerial platform and manipulator while accounting for the predicted platform attitude and their different motion characteristics. Control: The dynamic controller reconstructs and compensates the strong coupling effects induced by manipulator motion and employs residual observers to handle model uncertainty and external disturbances. The resulting framework supports indoor and outdoor grasping of stationary and moving targets using onboard sensing and online replanning. More details, including CAD models and source code, are available on the Project Site.

papers.abstract: Learning from offline datasets is limited in scalability, as collecting new experience is often costly or unsafe in the real world. World models offer an alternative way to generate new experience through a learned dynamics model, yet learning policies in latent space is limited due to compounding errors in imagined rollouts. To this end, we propose using the world model as a local transition generator, leveraging critic guidance to choose actions inside that model to generate synthetic experiences. We study action refinement methodologies, introducing Critic-Guided Synthetic Experience (CGSE) generation in world models. Specifically, CGSE augments an existing offline dataset by sampling candidate actions using an offline policy and refining each to maximize a first-order approximation of the $Q$-function within a trust region. We then use a frozen latent world model to imagine the future state given each updated action, and use the critic to choose the best one, appending this synthetic transition to the replay buffer. Our method requires no additional real-environment interaction or test-time planner, as it generates synthetic experience offline using the world model. On three OGBench manipulation tasks, CGSE improves an offline policy by a relative improvement of $7.1\%$ on the average success rate.
authors: Jorge de Freitas, Christos Ziakas, Alessandra Russo
bullets: Addresses limited scalability and safety of collecting new offline experience, while reducing errors from long imagined rollouts.

Augments the replay buffer offline, requiring neither further environment interaction nor a test-time planner.
Improves average success rate by 7.1% relatively across three OGBench manipulation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: CGSE transition generation in world model. Starting from an offline latent z0, the fixed BC-flow actor samples N candidate first actions and FMQ-style guidance applies a one-step trustregion critic-gradient refinement to each candidate. The refined candidates are rolled out under fψ, scored with Qϕ, and the best branch supplies only its first action a∗ and first model successor z′ψ = fψ(z0, a ∗). The resulting synthetic transition (z0, a ∗, z′ψ) is appended to the replay buffer.

papers.abstract: Collecting naturalistic human manipulation demonstrations with accurate contact force and hand pose is essential for robot dexterous manipulation policy and foundational world model learning - yet no existing wearable platform provides both calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a form factor that preserves natural manipulation behavior. We present Tactus, a textile-integrated sensing glove that co-optimizes three design pillars: (1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5 mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies, and (3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable. Tactus includes a documented calibration pipeline for cross-glove consistency and per-session calibration for subject-dependent correction. To enable objective comparison, we introduce standardized benchmarking protocols for tactile force regression and hand pose estimation, and apply them to Tactus and two commercially available tactile gloves - to our knowledge the first quantitative cross-platform evaluation of this kind. Tactus resolves a minimum detectable force of 0.59 N at 95% confidence, 1.6 - 2.7x lower than the commercial baselines, and with 0.87 cross-participant consistency, while our pose tracking sustains 11.0 mm fingertip keypoint relative error during manipulation, when occlusion is heaviest. We show that these combined signals support object property estimation, slip detection, and representative recording of hand-object interaction - yielding demonstration data with the fidelity required for contact-aware manipulation policies and world models.

papers.abstract: Controlling continuum robots' shape to operate in confined, enclosed environments is challenging, since it cannot rely on external observation. Existing embedded shape sensing methods, although they can provide shape reconstruction, are insufficient to enable real-time shape control due to limitations in reconstruction accuracy, computational speed, and compatibility with shape-state representation. In this work, we present an embedded shape-sensing framework that uses readily available IMU and actuator feedback to reconstruct the continuum-robot shape with a neural network, providing accurate shape feedback at $400~\mathrm{Hz}$ for physical closed-loop control. We systematically investigate four key reconstruction design choices: shape-state representation, network architecture, training objective, and sensing inputs, through more than $5{,}000$ trained models on one- and three-segment continuum robots. The selected framework achieves global shape errors of $0.9\%L$ and $1.7\%L$ (of the robot length) for the one- and three-segment systems, respectively. In closed-loop control, one-segment tip tracking achieves a $6.1\%L$ error and three-segment shape control achieves a $2.3\%L$ global shape error, whereas IMU--PCC reconstruction using the same uncompensated measurements fails. Enclosed-space experiments further demonstrate operation without external observation. These results provide a practical framework for translating readily available embedded sensing into high-rate feedback for continuum robot closed-loop control.
authors: Jiahe Wang, Sultan Haidar Ali, Eric Weissman, Jiefeng Sun
bullets: Addresses shape-control challenges when external observation is unavailable.
Reconstructs robot shape from IMU and actuator feedback at 400 Hz for real-time control.

Reports reconstruction errors of 0.9%L for one segment and 1.7%L for three segments; closed-loop errors are 6.1%L for one-segment tip tracking and 2.3%L for three-segment shape control.
Demonstrates enclosed-space operation, while same-input IMU–PCC reconstruction fails in closed-loop control.

papers.abstract: Modern robot learning systems feed on high-quality demonstration data, and their performance hinges on coverage. Without good coverage, small errors compound and the policy can quickly go into out-of-distribution states from which it cannot recover. Yet there is no principled way of collecting high-coverage data, and data collection often relies on heuristic instructions to human operators. Purely online reinforcement learning (RL) explores at the cost of safety and sample efficiency, while DAgger-style interventions require the policy to fail by chance before a human can correct it. In this paper, we ask instead whether we can modify how the robot behaves during data collection to collect more useful data. We propose Data Inoculation (DI), a shared-control framework in which a human provide closed-loop teleoperation commands while a residual policy perturbs these commands. The residual policy is trained online, on the growing dataset, with the same reward-maximizing objective later used for policy extraction, so its perturbations steer data collection toward the deviations a policy trained on the data would make. These perturbations expose the robot to a wider range of states, while the human's continuous corrections provide recovery demonstrations, "inoculating" the dataset against the learner's future mistakes while the human remains in control. On three challenging real-world robotic tasks, DI consistently improves or matches the success rate of policies trained with both behavioral cloning and offline RL, showing DI as an effective data collection strategy for improving downstream policy performance.
authors: Qiyang Li, Zhiyuan Zhou, Charles Xu, Sergey Levine
bullets: Addresses poor state coverage and compounding errors in demonstration-based robot learning.
Uses shared control: a human teleoperates while an online-trained residual policy perturbs commands toward likely future mistakes.
Continuous human corrections provide recovery demonstrations while perturbations expand the collected state distribution.
Across three real-world tasks, policies trained with behavioral cloning and offline RL consistently improved or matched performance using DI-collected data.

papers.abstract: Catching arbitrary objects requires generalization to novel projectiles and real-time adaptation to unpredictable contact dynamics under noisy visual observations. This paper presents Catch It All!, a sim-to-real catching framework for humanoid robots that generalizes and adapts to unseen objects with variable physical properties for underhand and overhand catches, using only one egocentric camera. We learn policies which generalize to unseen objects with varying geometry, deformability, elasticity, and physical properties. Effective grasps which adapt real-time to object poses and shapes are learned through careful grasp reward design. We provide safety-aware curricula which enable safe, high-frequency action execution near hardware limits, including wrist torque limits as low as 5 Nm. We validate our system by deploying zero-shot on a Unitree G1. With only one egocentric camera, Catch It All! successfully performs underhand and overhand catches on 9 unseen objects not seen during training, including low-rebound plushes, semi-deformable toys and chip bags, and rigid-elastic objects with high rebound on contact.

papers.abstract: Radio-frequency (RF) sensing enables robot ego-motion estimation in darkness, smoke, and fog, yet RF odometry remains challenging because multipath and moving reflectors make cross-frame matching highly ambiguous. Existing methods often rely on auxiliary inertial sensors or ground-truth pose supervision. We present RFWalk, a self-supervised, RF-only odometry framework that models dense correspondences across range-azimuth frames as random walks on a space-time graph and learns them from unlabeled sequences through temporal cycle consistency. To rule out correspondences that are cycle-consistent but physically implausible, we introduce a Doppler consistency loss that constrains correspondence-induced motion using radial velocity measured by the RF sensor itself. Ego-motion is then recovered through robust $\mathrm{SE}(2)$ registration that suppresses uncertain correspondences and those arising from independently moving objects. Without pose labels or auxiliary sensors, RFWalk remains competitive with supervised baselines in static scenes and reduces absolute trajectory error by 58% in dynamic scenes with moving pedestrians.
authors: Kunzhe Song, Jialuo Du, Jingkai Lin, Huacheng Zeng
bullets: Addresses ambiguous RF frame matching caused by multipath and moving reflectors.
Models dense range-azimuth correspondences as random walks on a space-time graph.
Uses temporal cycle consistency and a Doppler consistency loss without pose labels or auxiliary sensors.
Recovers ego-motion via robust SE(2) registration that downweights unreliable and independently moving-object correspondences.
Remains competitive with supervised baselines in static scenes and reduces absolute trajectory error by 58% in dynamic pedestrian scenes.

papers.abstract: Anticipating the motion of nearby objects is critical for safe and efficient robot navigation. Without a proper understanding of what may move, a robot may plan overly conservative, inefficient trajectories to guarantee safety, or it may be overly risky, resulting in unacceptable collisions. While tracking and predicting the motion of known objects has seen significant progress, little research addresses how a robot should adapt online to novel objects, including anticipating how one object may move another (e.g., a person operating a forklift to move a pallet). To enable this capability, we propose a meta-learned graph neural network that leverages a semantic, geometric, and relational history of objects to accurately predict, from a few online observations, when objects will begin to move in new environments. We demonstrate that our method, which is trained only in simulation, accurately anticipates the motion of objects unseen at training time, transfers to hardware without any fine-tuning, and outperforms a vision-language model and a class-frequency baseline in both simulation and hardware experiments. Our method's accurate prediction enables collision-free traversals in a closed-loop navigation simulation, while remaining within four seconds of the fastest, collision-prone planner.
authors: Mason Peterson, Gage MacLin, Camilla Tabasso, Jonathan P. How, Joshua Migdal, Tye Brady, Taskin Padir
bullets: Targets open-world motion anticipation, including one object causing another to move.
Uses semantic, geometric, and relational object histories in a graph neural network with meta-learning.
Trained only in simulation, it transfers to hardware and handles objects unseen during training without fine-tuning.
Outperforms a vision-language model and class-frequency baseline in simulation and hardware experiments.
Supports collision-free closed-loop navigation while staying within four seconds of the fastest collision-prone planner.

papers.abstract: Reliable obstacle avoidance is essential for safe quadrotor flight in unknown environments, yet conventional frame-based cameras remain challenged by motion blur, limited dynamic range, and latency under fast motion. Event cameras, with sub-millisecond latency, high dynamic range, and negligible motion blur, offer a promising alternative, but leveraging them for closed-loop control remains difficult. Existing approaches either adopt cascaded architectures that first estimate depth and then map it to control commands, introducing error propagation, or achieve end-to-end control through costly offline pretraining before online fine-tuning can even begin. We address these challenges with a CUDA-based event simulator that exploits GPU parallelism to render events efficiently within the training loop, integrated into a differentiable simulation pipeline that enables direct gradient backpropagation through the differentiable physics model, improving sample efficiency. This allows us to train an end-to-end policy that maps event frames directly to control commands, without intermediate depth estimation. We validate our approach through zero-shot real-world deployment on a quadrotor, achieving robust obstacle avoidance in both odometry-assisted and odometry-free settings, including under low-light conditions where conventional cameras typically fail.
authors: Chenlu Shou, Yunfan Ren, Jiaxu Xing, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses motion blur, limited dynamic range, and latency in frame-based obstacle avoidance for fast quadrotor flight.
Uses a CUDA-based event simulator integrated with differentiable physics to backpropagate through the training loop.
Learns an end-to-end policy mapping event frames directly to control commands, avoiding cascaded depth estimation.
Demonstrates zero-shot real-world deployment in odometry-assisted and odometry-free settings, including low light.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: System Framework Overview. The simulator renders a grayscale frame from each quadrotor state, and two consecutive frames are used to compute the event frame. The event frame is fed into a differentiable policy consisting of a CNN and a GRU, which predicts an action. The differentiable point-mass dynamics model then propagates the current state forward using this action. A loss is computed based on the resulting state and action, and the corresponding gradients are propagated backward through the entire differentiable pipeline to update the policy.

papers.abstract: Lane-changing (LC) maneuvers are highly challenging vehicle interactions, with substantial implications for traffic safety and efficiency. Developing effective LC strategies for connected and automated vehicles in mixed traffic is complicated by the uncertainty associated with surrounding-vehicle behavior and the computational burden of embedding realistic prediction models within optimization schemes. To capture these complex interactions while retaining tractability, this study proposes a data-driven optimization framework that embeds neural network (NN) surrogates for safety and lateral comfort within a B\'ezier-curve-based trajectory planner. Specifically, the safety cost during the LC process is quantified via a surrogate composed of an input convex recurrent neural network (ICRNN) encoding the planned trajectory, a fully input convex neural network (FICNN) embedding the LC duration, and a partially input convex neural network (PICNN) decoder fusing them with historical traffic states; separately, another FICNN surrogate approximates the optimal lateral comfort cost as a function of the LC duration. Both surrogates are embedded via linear programming (LP) formulations, avoiding the binary variables required by conventional mixed-integer programming (MIP) approaches for NN-embedded optimization. We further theoretically establish their exactness at optimality and extend the framework to problems with additional analytical objective terms and multiple surrogates. Experiments on a hybrid dataset combining real-world and simulated trajectories demonstrate that the proposed method achieves surrogate accuracy competitive with unconstrained baselines while substantially improving optimization efficiency over conventional MIPs. Closed-loop simulations further show that the proposed planners markedly reduce the weighted planning cost and consistently outperform baseline methods.
authors: Yuanxiang Yang, Yu Liu, Fabricio Oliveira, Yu Han, Claudio Roncoli
bullets: Addresses safety, lateral comfort, uncertain surrounding-vehicle behavior, and the computational cost of NN-embedded optimization for connected automated vehicles.
Uses ICRNN, FICNN, and PICNN surrogates to model safety from planned trajectories, lane-change duration, and historical traffic states; a separate FICNN models lateral comfort.
Embeds the surrogates through linear programming, avoiding the binary variables required by conventional mixed-integer formulations.

Experiments show competitive surrogate accuracy, substantially better optimization efficiency than conventional MIPs, and lower weighted planning cost than baseline planners in closed-loop simulations.

papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning (RL), temporal reasoning is essential for estimating the density of future outcomes under a policy's occupancy measure. While self-predictive representations have been a dominant paradigm for occupancy density estimation, we find that they yield surprisingly poor estimates. On the other hand, generative occupancy models can produce remarkably accurate samples from the occupancy measure. Yet, they cannot easily recover occupancy densities, limiting their use for control despite their expressivity. In this paper, we propose Geometric Time Score Estimators (GTSE), a framework that bridges the two paradigms by learning occupancy density estimators along probability paths. We analyze how GTSE implicitly induces better occupancy estimators through improved representation learning and show how to directly extract self-predictive representations from this framework. Through experiments across several locomotion and manipulation tasks, we show that GTSE improves performance over state-of-the-art methods by $2\times$ to $6\times$ in goal-conditioned RL settings, and that the representations learned using our framework transfer effectively to downstream RL tasks. Website: https://aravindvenu7.github.io/website/gtse/
authors: Aravind Venugopal, Grace Liu, Jeff Schneider, Benjamin Eysenbach
bullets: Self-predictive representations can estimate future occupancy densities poorly, while generative models produce accurate samples but do not readily provide densities for control.
GTSE learns occupancy density estimators along probability paths, connecting the strengths of both paradigms.
The framework improves representation learning and enables direct extraction of self-predictive representations.
Experiments on locomotion and manipulation tasks report 2×–6× better performance than state-of-the-art methods in goal-conditioned RL.
Learned representations transfer effectively to downstream RL tasks.

papers.abstract: Embodied instruction following in interactive environments requires agents to interpret natural language commands and complete long-horizon tasks. Existing planners either rely on large labeled trajectories, or use few-shot and zero-shot LLM prompting that produces a whole plan in a single serial reasoning process. These approaches depend on linguistic common sense, commit to a plan from the initial instruction, and only update after failures, which weakens robustness and state awareness. We present AtomTree, a hierarchical framework for state-aware task planning with LLMs. AtomTree incrementally builds a tree of subgoals and actions, where the LLM decides at each step, from the current symbolic state, whether to further decompose or to output a grounded low-level action. A lightweight memory module summarizes past outcomes for reuse in later decisions. When a low-level action stalls, AtomTree triggers hierarchical backtracking replanning to return to the parent node and regenerate the subtree plan from the latest state, preventing continued drift along an incorrect trajectory. In zero-shot evaluation on the ALFRED benchmark, AtomTree outperforms prior LLM-based planners. Project page: https://zhaihaotian.github.io/atomtree-website/.
authors: Haotian Zhai, Tianming Sha, Junnan Li
bullets: Addresses the brittleness of one-shot, serial LLM plans for long-horizon interactive tasks.
Builds a hierarchical tree of subgoals and actions, deciding at each step whether to decompose further or issue a grounded low-level action.
Uses symbolic state updates and lightweight memory to inform subsequent planning decisions.
Performs hierarchical backtracking and replanning when an action stalls, regenerating plans from the latest state.
Outperforms prior LLM-based planners in zero-shot evaluation on ALFRED.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of our hierarchical planning framework for embodied instruction following. Given a task instruction and the current visual state, our method recursively decides whether to decompose the current goal into finer-grained subgoals or execute it directly. This process incrementally builds an explicit hierarchical goal tree, shown in the upper-right panel, where higher-level goals are progressively refined into executable actions. In contrast, we compare against two representative paradigms: (1) a fully supervised end-to-end EIF model trained on the full dataset, and (2) an LLM-based method using retrieved few-shot examples. While these baselines may produce incorrect action sequences, our method maintains a structured tree-based plan and performs step-by-step decomposition conditioned on the current state and memory, enabling more accurate long-horizon reasoning and execution.

Fig. 3: Overview of our state-aware decision prompt. The prompt summarizes the role and mission, decision options, input information, available atomic actions, global rules, output format, and a small set of decision-guiding examples. Given the current subgoal together with the current state and memory, the LLM predicts whether to decompose the goal into subtasks or execute it directly.

Fig. 4: Qualitative comparison with and without memory. Without memory, the model predicts an incorrect subgoal after picking up the cleaned lettuce, whereas AtomTree correctly predicts the next subgoal as navigating to the fridge.

Fig. 1: Error analysis on the Valid Seen split of the ALFRED benchmark with respect to ground-truth PDDL plan length, showing that for FLARE, a state-of-the-art few-shot method, incorrect-plan errors dominate overall and become the primary failure mode for long-horizon tasks (PDDL length > 7).
Fig. 5: Comparison between a few-shot baseline and AtomTree on a multi-instance task.

We annotate each method by its evaluation setting, publication venue, and whether it is explicitly state- and history-aware. For methods that do not report results on certain splits or metrics, we mark them as “N/A”. Results marked with an asterisk (*) are produced by [13].

TABLE II: Ablation of ATOMTREE on ALFRED validation splits. “Hier.” enables hierarchical planning with Decompose and a subgoal tree. “Memory” adds the state&history memory mt = (St, Ht). “Replan” enables hierarchical backtracking replanning. We report SR on Valid Seen and Valid Unseen.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in off-road terrain is commonly achieved using hierarchical control and planning architectures that rely on explicit cost maps and one-way information flow from a high-level planner to a low-level controller, decoupling planning from the true execution cost experienced during control. We propose a hierarchical planning and control framework in which information flows bidirectionally, allowing the low-level controller to guide trajectory selection at the planning level. The highest level of the hierarchy is a Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control-style planner that determines optimal trajectories and passes these waypoints to a pretrained low-level reinforcement learning (RL) controller. Rather than drawing from an explicit cost map, our MPPI planner leverages the value function of the RL controller as an implicit cost representation. In this formulation, MPPI serves as a trajectory exploration mechanism, while the low-level controller's value function guides the search. To account for the distribution shift seen by the value function between training and evaluation, we propose an online policy evaluation process that adapts the value function to unseen driving experiences, and we demonstrate this adaptation in unseen off-road simulation environments. We evaluate our approach in a high-fidelity off-road driving simulator across a range of challenging terrain conditions and compare its performance against a baseline MPPI controller. The results demonstrate that our method achieves safer and more effective navigation to goal locations while eliminating the need for explicit cost maps and enabling tighter coupling between planning and control.
authors: Anoushka Alavilli, Raymond Song, Guanya Shi, Jeff Schneider
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between high-level planning and low-level execution in hierarchical off-road navigation.
Uses MPPI to explore trajectories, with the pretrained controller’s value function guiding trajectory selection.
Applies online policy evaluation to adapt the value function to unseen driving experiences and distribution shift.
Evaluated in a high-fidelity off-road simulator across challenging terrains against a baseline MPPI controller.
Reports safer, more effective goal-directed navigation while removing the need for explicit cost maps.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of our value-guided planning framework. We pre-train RL policies to provide both an actor πθ(s) and a value function Vϕ(s). MPPI samples candidate trajectories and evaluates them using a cost that combines goal progress with the negative value estimate, treating −Vϕ(s) as a control-aware cost. The selected trajectory is executed by the policy, and the resulting experience can be used to update the value function online. This enables planning to be guided by the expected performance of the controller without requiring an explicit cost map.

Fig. 3: Comparison of pitch and vertical jerk violations across all 64 evaluation trajectories for the MPPI baseline ((A), (B)), our algorithm ((C), (D)), and our algorithm with online adaptation ((E), (F)). Panels (A), (C), and (E) show pitch violations exceeding 0.4 rad (22.9◦), while (B), (D), and (F) show vertical jerk violations exceeding 10e−2 m/s3. The violations are colored by their severity and are no more than 0.7 rad. and 2 m/s3 for pitch and jerk respectively. The MPPI baseline includes an explicit pitch cost term, whereas our method is trained with a jerk penalty in the reward function. When divided into equally-spaced buckets of low, medium, and high violation severity, the MPPI baseline recorded 317, 51, and 19 jerk violations and 84, 0, and 0 pitch violations, respectively; ours recorded 22, 1, and 0 jerk violations and 11, 1, and 0 pitch violations; and ours with online adaptation recorded 31, 0, and 0 jerk violations and 1, 1, and 3 pitch violations.

Fig. 2: Comparison between baseline MPPI, our algorithm, and our algorithm with online adaptation. All trajectories were unseen during training. In (A), our method incurs damage midway through the trajectory, while the online adaptation variant avoids this region through online updates alone, without any prior knowledge that this region would cause damage. In (A), (B), and (E), the baseline MPPI algorithm becomes stuck and is unable to complete its planned route. In (C), our algorithm demonstrates its ability to follow existing trails, which provide safer traversal than off-trail terrain. In (D), our algorithm with online adaptation reaches the maximum time limit and does not complete the trajectory.

Fig. 4: (A) Visualization of training data coverage and evaluation start–goal waypoints. (B) Trajectories traversed by the online adaptation variant of our algorithm, colored by the incurred reward as defined in Eq. 1. (C) and (D) show value estimates of the traversed terrain during execution for our algorithm without and with online adaptation, respectively. These value maps can be interpreted as implicit cost maps over the visited regions. After online adaptation, regions associated with lower reward decrease in value (i.e., appear lighter), reflecting updated terrain estimates. Despite this, the algorithm continues to favor on-trail paths, as they are predicted to have higher value than off-trail terrain. All colorbars are scaled between the 10th and 90th percentiles of the plotted values.

TABLE I: Comparison of navigation performance and terrain interaction metrics across methods. Each algorithm is evaluated on 64 randomly sampled start–goal pairs, all unseen during training. Episodes terminate after a maximum of 50 seconds (250 control steps) and are marked as failures if the goal is not reached within this budget (denoted “timeout”). Other episodes terminate with the vehicle stuck (on a steep slope, for example), and these failures are denoted “stuck.” Reported values reflect trajectory statistics aggregated over all trials; lower values in Z-axis motion and orientation indicate smoother traversal. Note: p10 and p90 represent the 10th and 90th percentile of values, respectively.
TABLE II: Hyperparameters used in all implementations. PPO policy training is performed using the standard StableBaselines3 implementation [6].

papers.abstract: Post-training quantization (PTQ) reduces the memory footprint of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but lowering bit widths while maintaining task performance remains challenging. Existing work has used sensitivity estimates from calibration data to assign bit widths to different model components. However, using task success directly to guide mixed-precision allocation is underexplored because closed-loop evaluations are costly and the effect of quantizing one component depends on the precision of other components. To this end, we propose \textbf{QbD-VLA}, a task-guided mixed-precision quantization method that uses task success from short closed-loop evaluations to assign weight and activation bit widths while accounting for interactions between model components. Experiments covering four VLA models and all four LIBERO suites show strong task performance at average precisions of approximately 4 bits for weights and fewer than 6 bits for activations. On SIMPLER, the gain over uniform quantization is small. On a Franka Research 3 robot arm, simulation-selected allocations show no detected success-rate loss on X-VLA but fail on $\pi_{0.5}$. These findings support using task success to guide mixed-precision VLA quantization, while highlighting the need for real-world evaluation before deployment. Code is available at \href{https://github.com/jiuyixu25/QbD-VLA}{\texttt{github.com/jiuyixu25/QbD-VLA}}.
authors: Jiuyi Xu, Xiao Hu, Meida Chen, Song Wang, Yang Ye, Yangming Shi
bullets: PTQ can reduce VLA memory use, but selecting low bit widths without harming task success is difficult.
QbD-VLA guides per-component weight and activation precision using task success and accounts for interactions between components.
Across four VLA models and all four LIBERO suites, it maintains strong performance at approximately 4-bit weights and fewer than 6-bit activations on average.
On SIMPLER, it provides only a small gain over uniform quantization.
Simulation-selected precisions showed no detected loss for X-VLA on a Franka Research 3 arm but failed on π₀.₅, motivating real-world validation.

papers.abstract: Future planetary rovers will traverse steep, deformable terrain where slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation can threaten mobility. Although simulation can capture some wheel-soil effects, unmodeled deformable-terrain phenomena create sim-to-real gaps requiring deployment-time adaptation. Yet, rover operations leave little room for extensive trial-and-error. We introduce TERRA (Targeted Exploration for Reward-Relevant Adaptation), an online adaptation framework that efficiently seeks deployment data exposing task-relevant model errors and corrects them. TERRA adapts a simulation-trained world model with a reward-weighted prediction loss and trains a loss predictor to estimate where future performance-relevant errors are likely to occur, using this signal to guide exploration during MPC. In simulation, TERRA reaches approximately 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution pretraining conditions, outperforming exploration baselines in reward, completion time, and energy to first success. On the ERNEST rover, TERRA recovers coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five real-world trials. Project website: https://terra-explore.github.io
authors: Jacob Levy, Arthur Bouton, Tristan D. Hassler, Hari Nayar, David Fridovich-Keil
bullets: Addresses sim-to-real gaps from unmodeled slip, sinkage, and terrain deformation while limiting costly trial-and-error.
Uses a reward-weighted loss to adapt a simulation-trained world model online.
Trains a loss predictor to identify likely future performance-relevant errors and guides MPC exploration toward them.
In simulation, reaches about 90% slope-climbing success within five trials under severe out-of-distribution conditions.
On the ERNEST rover, restores coordinated active-suspension locomotion on a deformable Mars-simulant slope within three to five trials.

papers.abstract: Autonomous far-range rocket landing is a challenging control problem because navigation, descent-rate regulation, attitude management, and fuel use must be coordinated in the presence of uncertain atmospheric and vehicle dynamics. This paper presents a curriculum-driven proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework for three-dimensional rocket landing in a stochastic environment incorporating altitude-dependent aerodynamic drag, wind shear, temporally correlated turbulence, discrete gusts, uncertain propulsion and aerodynamic parameters, thrust-vector misalignment, engine lag, actuator-gain variation, noisy observations, and command latency. Learning is organised into far-range approach, soft descent, and integrated landing stages. Policy transfer, critic warm-up after reward changes, rehearsal of earlier tasks, and progressive expansion of weather severity are used to support learning across these coupled phases. Across 100,000 evaluation episodes, the policy achieves 96,656 successful landings, corresponding to a success rate of 96.656\% and a 95\% Wilson confidence interval of 96.543--96.766\%. Success decreases from 98.84\% under zero-disturbance conditions to 88.07\% in the highest weather-severity band. Successful touchdowns exhibit small miss distances and low residual horizontal and vertical velocities. An exploratory logistic-regression analysis identifies mean wind speed as the strongest measured correlate of success, with initial distance, initial altitude, initial vertical velocity, and wind-shear exponent also associated with outcomes. The results quantify both the effectiveness of the learned policy over the evaluated disturbance distribution and the degradation that occurs under severe compound atmospheric conditions.
bullets: Addresses coordinated navigation, descent-rate, attitude, and fuel control for far-range landing under stochastic disturbances and model uncertainty.
Uses staged learning for approach, soft descent, and integrated landing, with policy transfer, critic warm-up, rehearsal, and progressively harsher weather.
Evaluated over 100,000 episodes: 96,656 successful landings, with success ranging from 98.84% in calm conditions to 88.07% under the most severe weather.
Successful landings generally have small position errors and low residual horizontal and vertical velocities.
Mean wind speed is the strongest measured correlate of success in an exploratory logistic-regression analysis.

Although the schematic includes the label “6-DoF”, the simulation model used in this study approximates three-dimensional translation and commanded pitch/roll attitude dynamics; it is not a validated full six-degree-of-freedom aerodynamic vehicle model.

papers.abstract: Smart wheelchairs are robotic devices that gather information from the surroundings and allow people to safely drive through various environments. They usually rely on the interpretation of high-level user's intentions, typically decoded through human-robot interface (HRI) or brain-machine interface (BMI). However, navigating in an unknown environment and accurately understanding user commands remain significant challenges. Misinterpretation of commands or the environment can lead to user frustration, distrust of the system, or even unsafe situations. In this paper, we present a novel Multi-Layer Navigation System (MLNS) for a smart wheelchair that enables navigation in unknown environments while interpreting and safely contextualizing user's intentions even in the case of limited and faulty commands. The stack relies on a Virtual Sensors-Driven Potential Fields (ViSPF) method for obstacle detection that accounts for the wheelchair's actual size, a Model Predictive Control (MPC) module for trajectory generation, and an open-vocabulary computer vision algorithm for target identification. Finally, a system based on Priority Queue (PQ) was implemented for target selection. We validated our system on a real smart wheelchair with experiments involving 10 participants without disabilities, including scenarios with faulty input interfaces. The results demonstrate the robustness and effectiveness of our system in real-world environments, proving its potential for practical applications in assistive technologies.
authors: Piero Simonetto, Anna Polato, Francesco Pasti, Muhammad Rameez ur Rahman, Sebastiano Vascon, Nicola Bellotto, Emanuele Menegatti, Stefano Tortora, Luca Tonin

Validated on a real smart wheelchair with 10 participants, including faulty-interface scenarios, demonstrating robust real-world operation.
