papers.abstract: The growing volume of end-of-life products has intensified the need for automated disassembly, yet hook-type connections remain challengin: their orientations vary, they deform under load, and their geometry is hidden, so vision alone cannot identify a feasible non-destructive disassembly direction. This work proposes a constraint-aware reinforcement learning framework that infers feasible extraction directions online from contact forces. The policy is trained in a robot-agnostic, object-centric simulation on a simplified peg-in-hole pair and deployed zero-shot on a physical robot, where it transfers to real connections with unseen, multi-stage constraint structures. Because instantaneous contact forces are noisy and locally ambiguous, the policy is coupled with a particle filter belief that provides the policy with temporally integrated directional information and reduces redundant exploratory motion. The approach is validated on four real-world tasks, from peg-in-hole pairs to the inner propeller and front cover of an end-of-life air-conditioning unit. The full method achieves success rates of 100%, 100%, 90%, and 75% with the highest path efficiency on every task, and raises the success rate on the air-conditioning cover from 45% to 75% relative to a policy trained without the belief. These results indicate that force-driven reinforcement learning can enable disassembly without product-specific models or demonstrations.
authors: Nadeen Elhadad, Takuya Kiyokawa, Kensuke Harada
bullets: Addresses hook connections whose orientations, deformation, and hidden geometry make vision-only disassembly unreliable.
Uses object-centric reinforcement learning with contact-force sensing and a particle-filter belief to integrate directional evidence over time.
Trained on a simplified peg-in-hole simulation and deployed robot-agnostically without product-specific models or demonstrations.
Validated on four real tasks, achieving success rates of 100%, 100%, 90%, and 75%, with the highest path efficiency in each.
The belief component improved air-conditioning-cover success from 45% to 75% and reduced redundant exploration.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of the proposed framework. Left: During training, the SAC policy receives state observations and belief estimates and is shaped by a multi-component reward. Center: The particle filter maintains a belief over the feasible extraction direction, updated from force-motion observations (Section III-C). Right: During deployment, a single-system condition is adopted where the gripper and grasped object are assumed to move as a rigid composite body and the wrist-measured forces equal the constraint force on the object [18]. Using proprioceptive information, force sensor data, and particle filter belief specifics, the policy drives a Cartesian impedance controller on the physical robot.

Fig. 2: Training Environment: Simulated contact interaction under misaligned and aligned extraction actions. When the commanded action direction (cyan arrow) deviates from the groundtruth extraction axis (left), the peg engages the surrounding constraint geometry, producing visible contact forces (gold contact markers). On the other hand, when the action direction is more aligned to the groundtruth axis (right), contact decreases until it disappears at complete alignment. This illustrates that contact forces carry direct information about the feasible motion direction, which the proposed method exploits during learning.

The front cover is retained by two asymmetric constraint mechanisms: two downward-facing hooks on the left edge and two lip-type fasteners on the right edge. papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn to predict representations rather than pixels, offering a compact way to model how visual scenes evolve. We ask whether this predictive objective improves closed-loop control when a vision-language-action (VLA) policy already uses V-JEPA features. We call our JEPA-conditioned flow policy family SaiVLA-JEPA. It combines a vision-language model with a diffusion transformer action expert and receives features from a frozen V-JEPA encoder. Two lightweight auxiliary heads predict future representations during training and are omitted at inference, leaving the action sampler unchanged. We compare policies without JEPA features, with current JEPA conditioning, and with additional future supervision on 10,030 paired LIBERO-Plus episodes. Current JEPA conditioning reaches about 82.5% success versus 71.6% without JEPA, while future supervision provides no detectable aggregate gain at the evaluated training budget. We separately evaluate SaiVLA-JEPA-TCA, which adapts latent context, and SaiVLA-JEPA-TPA, which adapts selected parameters. The context-retry gain is a system-level result under a larger attempt budget; parameter adaptation shows no consistent advantage over the frozen policy and target controls. These results motivate assessing latent-prediction objectives through paired closed-loop rollouts rather than latent loss alone.
authors: Rufeng Xiao (VLA Research Team, Synthoid.ai), Ruihao Xiao (VLA Research Team, Synthoid.ai), Wei Chen (VLA Research Team, Synthoid.ai), Xinhai Sun (VLA Research Team, Synthoid.ai)
bullets: Evaluates whether predicting future latent representations improves closed-loop VLA control.
SaiVLA-JEPA combines a vision-language model, diffusion-transformer action expert, and frozen V-JEPA features.
Two auxiliary future-prediction heads are used only during training and do not alter inference-time action sampling.
On 10,030 paired LIBERO-Plus episodes, current JEPA conditioning achieves about 82.5% success versus 71.6% without JEPA.
Context retry can improve system-level performance under a larger attempt budget, while parameter adaptation shows no consistent advantage.

figures.caption: Figure 1: SaiVLA-JEPA architecture and its FutureJEPA training variant. Current images feed the frozen VJEPA and VLM encoders; projected JEPA tokens join the native prefix and action tokens in the repeated DiT action expert, while VLM features enter through per-block cross-attention and robot state is encoded separately. Four Euler evaluations produce a 16-action chunk. For FutureJEPA, JEPA-token hidden states from the shared DiT trunk feed residual heads at offsets 4 and 16, supervised by detached targets from a frozen V-JEPA encoder. This auxiliary branch is absent at inference. CurrentJEPA omits future supervision; BaseFlow also omits JEPA conditioning.

Figure 2: SaiVLA-JEPA-TCA context pathway. The frozen SaiVLA-JEPA policy applies the context adapter at each of four Euler evaluations using fixed e = [m; u]. After every executed four-action window, a frozen observer computes a latent prediction loss and two gradient steps update only m and u for the next action chunk. The initial attempt uses zero context and defers fitting until it ends. On failure, m is retained with decay or evidence gating while u is cleared. Network weights remain frozen online.
Figure 3: Success and cost under bounded retries. Left: cumulative success with up to five attempts, compared with the one-attempt baseline. Right: mean cumulative environment steps per case.

papers.title: SaiVLA-JEPA: Evaluating Future Latent Prediction in JEPA-Conditioned VLA Control

papers.abstract: Behavior Cloning (BC) of expert controllers for multiscale dynamical systems is challenging: state variables evolving at widely separated timescales induce highly nonlinear couplings that a shared latent space may fail to adequately represent, degrading closed-loop generalization. We propose Structured Representation Learning for Behavior Cloning (SRLBC), an architecture designed to leverage the physical knowledge of multiscale systems in which slow state variables, fast (stiff) state variables, and predictable exogenous inputs evolve at different timescales. On 500 long-horizon roll-outs of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) load-following benchmark -a high-dimensional, stiff industrial system with challenging safety constraints -and across 20 training seeds, separated embeddings systematically outperform shared embedding baselines on cumulative cost, imitation accuracy and constraint satisfaction. The resulting standalone policies approach NMPC closed-loop performance at a computational cost 15 times lower on average. Since standalone policies still leave a few percent of trajectories infeasible, we embed the learned policies in a safety-augmented approximate NMPC framework, in which the optimizer is only called when the predicted input sequence is not certified as safe. This yields controllers still 6.8 times faster than the NMPC controller on average, with a feasibility (i.e., constraint satisfaction) of at least 99.8% for all architectures, SRLBC retaining the lowest closed-loop cost. Under distribution shift, standalone BC policies degrade sharply: SRLBC degrades the least, and once safety-augmented, it retains a feasibility above 98% with the lowest closed-loop cost. Beyond the quantitative results, Jacobian-based sensitivity analysis shows that the resulting controller relies on a sparse and less redundant set of latent features, each attributable to a single group of physical variables, and aligned with the physical timescale decomposition of the system.
authors: Perceval Beja-Battais (CB), Alain Grosset{\^e}te (CB), Nicolas Vayatis (CB)
bullets: Shared latent spaces struggle with nonlinear coupling in multiscale dynamical systems, motivating timescale-aware representation learning.
SRLBC separates embeddings for slow states, fast stiff states, and predictable exogenous inputs.
On a PWR load-following benchmark, separated embeddings improve cumulative cost, imitation accuracy, and constraint satisfaction over shared-embedding baselines.
Standalone SRLBC policies approach NMPC performance at 15× lower average computational cost; safety-augmented policies are 6.8× faster while achieving at least 99.8% feasibility.
Under distribution shift, standalone policies degrade, but SRLBC degrades least and retains over 98% feasibility when safety-augmented.

papers.selection_reason: Behavior-cloning architecture with separated timescales is technically transferable to robot learning and control.
papers.title: Accelerating Nonlinear MPC by Behavior Cloning with Separated Timescales: Application to Nuclear Reactor Load-Following
papers.tldr: SRLBC accelerates behavior-cloned nonlinear MPC for nuclear reactor load-following by separating representations across physical timescales while preserving safety through selective optimization.

papers.abstract: Robotic grasping relies on large manually annotated datasets, which are costly to create. We introduce a straight-skeleton-based algorithm for generating two-finger grasp keypoints and identifying regions suitable for stable, feasible grasps. Our automated pipeline produces consistent grasp annotations without human intervention. We also propose the Skeleton-based Generative Grasp Convolutional Neural Network (SkelGG-CNN), a 4-DoF architecture that learns geometric grasp features from skeleton-based guidance. To extend auto-labeling to 6-DoF grasping, we develop a generalized quasi-3D skeletonization algorithm that operates directly on point clouds. Using automatically generated 4-DoF labels, SkelGG-CNN achieves accuracies of 95.42%, 96.55%, and 97.1% on Jacquard V1, Jacquard V2, and Cornell, respectively. On the GraspNet novel split, 6-DoF auto-labeling achieves an average precision of 18.33, comparable to state-of-the-art model-based approaches. In simulation, the 6-DoF method achieves success rates of 98.4% on Dex-Net and 89.1% on EGAD!. Real-world experiments with a Delta parallel robot show success rates of 97.4% on single household objects and 95.0% in cluttered scenes, outperforming state-of-the-art methods without domain adaptation. The 4-DoF pipeline adapts across environments and produces annotations approaching human-level precision, enabling efficient training of lightweight models on small datasets. The generalized 6-DoF method provides scalable, geometry-aware annotations for cluttered 3D scenes.
authors: Ali Sabzejou, Farbod Azimmohseni, Mehdi Tale Masouleh, Ahmad Kalhor
bullets: Generates two-finger grasp keypoints and stable, feasible grasp regions using straight-skeleton geometry.
Introduces SkelGG-CNN, a skeleton-guided 4-DoF model, and a generalized quasi-3D skeletonization method for point-cloud-based 6-DoF labeling.
Reports 4-DoF accuracies of 95.42%–97.1% across Jacquard and Cornell, and 6-DoF average precision of 18.33 on the GraspNet novel split.
Achieves simulated 6-DoF success rates of 98.4% on Dex-Net and 89.1% on EGAD!, with real-robot success rates of 97.4% on single objects and 95.0% in clutter.
The approach supports small-dataset training and cluttered 3D scenes, with scope demonstrated on the reported benchmarks and a Delta robot.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the proposed method. The pipeline begins with the simulation environment, where RGB-D images are captured from a set of 3D meshes sourced from the Dex-Net dataset. The subsequent stages show the details process of the straight skeleton-based grasp pose estimation algorithm. After this process, the generated grasp poses are used to create the SkelGG-CNN model labels. The skeleton heatmap is generated during the polygon offsetting phase of the algorithm, adding geometric features to the model.

Figure 8. Overview of the generalized 6-DoF skeleton-based auto-labeling pipeline. (Left) The input object point cloud is partitioned into overlapping horizontal cross-sections (80% overlap) orthogonal to the z-axis. (Center — upper path: 3D skeletonization) Each slice is processed with a Laplacian contraction skeletonization; skeleton points within a slice are connected using a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) and then linked to nearest neighbors in adjacent slices to produce a compact 3D skeleton graph that captures the object’s volumetric structure. (Center — lower path: 2D polygon approximation and initial centers) Each cross-section is projected to 2D and approximated with an alpha-shape polygon; a straight skeleton computed on this polygon yields initial central grasp centers. (Right) Candidate skeleton-node pairs are sampled and refined by traversing the 3D skeleton (depth-first search) from these initial centers; at each candidate pair a local plane is fitted to neighboring skeleton edges and the antipodality of the planes is evaluated as the grasp quality measure. (Far right) Top-scoring pairs are selected and visualized as final 6-DoF gripper poses superimposed on the original point cloud.

papers.selection_reason: Geometry-aware auto-labeling and learning for robotic grasping; fits manipulation and 3D perception.
papers.title: Skeleton-Guided Geometry-Aware Auto-Labeling for Robotic Grasping: From 4-DoF Learning to 6-DoF Execution
papers.tldr: A geometry-aware skeletonization pipeline automatically generates grasp labels for 4-DoF and 6-DoF robotic grasping, enabling accurate and scalable learning without manual annotation.

papers.abstract: To solve problems in 3D space rather than merely describe images, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) need 3D spatiotemporal reasoning: reconstructing 3D geometry from occluded 2D views, anticipating physical dynamics, and executing precise, closed-loop actions. Prior studies test passive VQA on static images or symbolic planning, requiring no execution or supplying privileged coordinates while ignoring collision, statics, and timing. We introduce SpaceAct, an interactive benchmark evaluating 3D spatiotemporal reasoning via closed-loop physical action and active perception, with SAPA, a Spatiotemporal Active-Probing Agent framework. Built on interlocking bricks and mechanical puzzles, it has 108 verified instances across 36 task families in six categories, without privileged coordinates, and diagnostic modes (+plan, +state, no-camera, blind, L7 levers). In brick-bridging or aperture-threading, models rotate the camera to resolve occlusion, read in-scene rulers, output 6-DoF poses under swept-collision and statics checks, and self-correct via split-screen rollback feedback (dynamic tasks freeze time during deliberation and give five strobe frames). Across 10 frontier MLLMs on the 44 hardest instances, scores span 4.8-79.1 (seven solve at most 27.3% of 6-DoF tasks); for the top three, a reference plan (+plan) closes 44% of the gap while leaving collisions at 5.2 per episode, whereas adding exact 3D state (+state) closes 90% and cuts collisions to 0.5; for four others, +plan lifts the mean score from 10.9 to 35.3 and +state to 81.8; and 46% of failures are collision or observation loops. SpaceAct and SAPA advance evaluation to closed-loop physical interaction, showing that even with a valid plan, MLLMs remain bottlenecked by 3D visual grounding and action refinement, while offering a testbed for active multi-view exploration and explicit 3D grounding.
authors: Chenglong Shi, Zekai Yuan, Yue Song, Jon Pu, Will Wu
bullets: Benchmarks 3D spatiotemporal reasoning through active perception and physical action rather than passive image question answering.
Includes 108 verified brick and mechanical-puzzle instances across 36 task families, with no privileged coordinates and diagnostic settings for planning, state access, vision, and control.
SAPA uses camera rotation, in-scene measurement, 6-DoF action output, collision/statics checks, and feedback-based self-correction.
Across 10 MLLMs, performance ranges from 4.8 to 79.1; many models solve few 6-DoF tasks, and 46% of failures involve collision or observation loops.
Providing exact 3D state greatly improves performance and reduces collisions, while reference plans help less, highlighting 3D grounding as the main bottleneck.

figures.caption: Figure 4: The SpaceAct task suite and the SAPA active-perception agent. (a) The six task categories contain 36 task families and 108 verified instances in total (44 in the main matrix). (b) At each turn, the input comprises actively acquired RGB observations with rulers, task rules, the available tools, and a dynamic memory (a bounded history window plus a persistent note). A single MLLM call per turn jointly performs 3D localization (𝒢vis), physics identification (ℐphys), multi-step planning (𝒫plan), and frame-aware control (ℰctrl), returning a JSON response with a rationale, a memory update (note), and 1–5 tool calls; the four capabilities are a diagnostic decomposition, not four separate calls. The tool calls execute sequentially in swept substeps of at most 0.05 stud or 0.5°, without a motion planner, under collision/topology and static-equilibrium checks, and the simulation clock is frozen while the model deliberates. (c) Observations are RGB images with rulers and no coordinates; dynamic tasks provide five frames from the same viewpoint at 0.25-s intervals. The first violation truncates execution and skips the remaining calls, returning a 1280 × 640 split-screen rollback view (left: the violating contact; right: the last valid state). (d) The diagnostic conditions grouped by the operator of Eq. (3) that they replace or stress.

Figure 2: SpaceAct's four design principles (conceptual illustration). Active 3D grounding: the agent reads in-scene rulers and moves the camera to resolve occlusion, with no privileged coordinates. Physics-constrained action: the full swept motion path is checked for collisions and structures for static equilibrium, without a motion planner. Controlled-time dynamics: simulation time pauses while the model deliberates and during camera actions, and advances only with timed physical actions; five sameview frames expose the motion. Controlled failure diagnosis: split-screen rollback feedback pairs the contact with the last valid state, and separately run +plan and +state conditions isolate the bottleneck.

Figure 3: Inputs of the three controlled-diagnostic conditions (schematic), each run separately on the same instances. All conditions share the RGB observation, task and rules, history, and note; the model generates every action, and all actions run under the same execution protocol. +plan adds a reference high-level plan (turns and regions; distances are left to the model). +state supplies the reference plan as well, plus the coarse layout as text and the exact 3D pose of the payload at every turn.

Figure 9: Failure modes of the 227 unsolved batched-protocol episodes with complete trajectories, broken down (a) by category and (b) by model (number of unsolved episodes in parentheses). Each episode receives a single signature in the priority order defined in Section 6.6.

papers.selection_reason: Benchmarks closed-loop physical action, active perception, and 3D spatiotemporal reasoning in MLLMs; directly targets embodied VLA and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: SpaceAct: Benchmarking 3D Spatial and Temporal Reasoning via Closed-Loop Action and Active Perception
papers.tldr: SpaceAct shows that MLLMs struggle with closed-loop 3D physical reasoning, especially visual grounding and precise action refinement, even when given valid plans.

papers.abstract: When a person declined our robot's invitation to play, Alice turned her shoulder away and said "No worries, it's all good." Only after a brief pause did she drive off. The words and gestures were plausible but their order changed the message. In another episode, Alice informed a host that his visitor had arrived---while the visitor stood right beside him. Both came from a three-year ROS 2 HRI consortium that integrated large language and vision models as they emerged. Today's foundation models give robots broader capabilities to perceive their surroundings, reason about situations and generate behavior. Yet capability alone does not ensure that a changed situation shapes the action that reaches a person. Evidence may never be acquired, or a purpose or constraint may fail to survive planning and execution. A system may even report Success when an action no longer serves its intended purpose. Drawing on the consortium's engineering experience, we develop five design lessons about attention, knowledge, commitments, embodied timing and action authority. We then introduce TRACE, a lightweight review that changes one interaction premise, follows it to a decision or enforcement boundary, and produces an actionable architecture finding. A bounded analysis of a published LLM-generated behavior-tree system illustrates how an available clarification mechanism can go unused. The engineering lesson is to preserve accountability boundaries, not the computational pipelines that once exposed them.
authors: Eliahu Khalastchi (The College of Management Academic Studies)
bullets: Real HRI failures included poorly ordered speech and gestures, and announcing a visitor who was already present.
The authors identify five design lessons: attention, knowledge, commitments, embodied timing, and action authority.
TRACE reviews what happens when one interaction premise changes, tracing its effects to a decision or enforcement boundary.
A bounded analysis shows that an available clarification mechanism in an LLM-generated behavior tree may go unused.
The central engineering lesson is to preserve accountability boundaries rather than merely reusing computational pipelines.

papers.selection_reason: Design lessons for foundation-model robots in physical HRI; relevant to embodied agents despite being a lessons/analysis paper.
papers.title: When "No Worries" Went Wrong: HRI Lessons for Foundation-Model Robots
papers.tldr: Foundation-model robots can produce plausible but socially wrong behavior when situational evidence, intent, timing, or constraints are lost between perception and action.

papers.abstract: Quadrupedal manipulators can extend their workspace through whole-body interaction, but task-planning agents' capabilities remain limited by their available controllers. We present ELEVATE, a framework that uses persistent failures during task-program refinement to identify and acquire missing whole-body control capabilities. When these failures suggest a missing physical capability, a coding agent formulates and iteratively refines a reinforcement-learning problem, specifying behavior-specific rewards, curricula, and termination conditions. Validated controllers are added to the capability library and composed with existing controllers to retry the task. Starting from a single pretrained loco-manipulation controller, ELEVATE autonomously acquires controllers for wall-supported elevation, supported manipulation, and wall descent across a sequence of seven simulation tasks. These controllers are reused in subsequent reaching and object-manipulation tasks. On the five tasks beyond the initial controller's workspace, ELEVATE achieves mean success rates of 98.4%-100% across five independent runs, while coding-agent baselines with a fixed controller library fail to complete these tasks. The synthesized task programs, together with the acquired controllers, also transfer to a physical quadrupedal manipulator without real-robot training or fine-tuning, achieving 18/20 successes in rack retrieval and 16/20 in floor-to-rack placement. Videos and demonstrations are available at https://agentic-quad-elevate.github.io/public/.

papers.title: ELEVATE: Agentic Controller Acquisition from Task Failure for Quadrupedal Manipulation
papers.tldr: ELEVATE autonomously expands a quadrupedal manipulator’s controller library when task failures reveal missing whole-body capabilities, enabling successful simulation and real-robot manipulation beyond its initial workspace.

papers.abstract: Discretizing continuous actions into discrete skills using methods like VQ-VAE has emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation. However, quantization errors yield a suboptimal distribution for the skill prior, degrading its performance. While reinforcement learning offers a path for refinement, its direct application faces unstable encoder updates and a granularity dilemma in importance sampling. To address these challenges, we introduce Cascaded Skills Optimization (CSO), a two-stage post-training framework. First, Rejection-Sampling Supervised Fine-tuning aligns the model's observation-to-skill mapping with the distribution of successful online trajectories via supervised fine-tuning. Second, with the observation encoder frozen, Skills Policy Optimization computes an independent, clipped importance ratio for each complete skill, enabling stable and efficient updates. With a lightweight QueST-style policy, CSO raises overall LIBERO success from 80.1% to 97.5%, improves performance on RoboTwin2.0, and achieves 61.0% success across five physical single-arm tasks. Additional comparisons with FAST, discrete BEAST, and fixed-buffer IQL further validate the effectiveness of our two-stage post-training strategy.
authors: Zhiyuan Xiang, Xiang Deng, Wanjie Tao, Xu Chen, Zhao Jielun, Weili Guan
bullets: Addresses performance degradation from quantization errors in learned skill priors.
Uses rejection-sampling supervised fine-tuning to match observation-to-skill mappings with successful online trajectories.
Freezes the observation encoder and applies clipped, skill-level importance ratios for stable policy optimization.
Raises LIBERO success from 80.1% to 97.5%, improves RoboTwin2.0 performance, and reaches 61.0% success across five physical single-arm tasks.
Evaluations against FAST, discrete BEAST, and fixed-buffer IQL support the effectiveness of the two-stage strategy.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The architecture and data flow of our proposed CSO framework. Stage 2 (SPO): With the encoders now frozen, the policy collects groups of trajectories. The SPO algorithm then updates the skill prior with a skill-level policy gradient based on terminal group-relative advantages.

papers.abstract: Reliable box manipulation requires successful placement without damage, which depends on maintaining sufficient contact force without excessive loading. We hypothesize that per-finger force feedback improves manipulation reliability relative to open-loop finger commands. To this end, we present Finger External-Force Estimation from Proprioceptive SignaLs (FEEL), an uncertainty-aware residual method that estimates per-finger external force magnitude from proprioceptive histories. Our method combines a calibrated virtual-spring estimate with a residual distribution predicted by a Mixture Density Network (MDN) and requires no dedicated contact sensors during deployment. The estimated force is used for continuous per-finger adaptation, while predictive uncertainty is evaluated as an empirical signal of ambiguity in proprioceptive force estimation. Across ten fingers and contact forces spanning 0-20 N, our method achieves a mean RMSE of 0.251 N, reducing the error by 92.8% relative to the virtual spring and by 9.4% relative to an end-to-end MDN. In box pick-and-place, force adaptation maintains task success at 10/10 and increases both damage-free outcomes and reliability from 7/10 to 10/10. The project page is available at https://finger-force-estimation.pages.dev/

Improves box pick-and-place reliability and damage-free outcomes from 7/10 to 10/10.

papers.abstract: Zero-shot vision-and-language navigation (VLN) requires an agent to use past observations without navigation-specific training. We study what information an 8B-scale navigation system should retain and how it should be organized for subsequent decisions. Our agent combines instruction progress, hierarchically compressed observation history anchored to poses, and accumulated geometry in complementary task, temporal, and spatial memories. An 8B observer summarizes observations, and an 8B reasoner uses the memories to select waypoint intents or request additional views, a geometric controller executes the selected targets. A semantic information perspective motivates the distinction between retaining evidence, making it accessible to the reasoner, and acquiring further observations. On R2R-CE val-unseen, the complete system achieves the highest among the evaluated Qwen3-based zero-shot baselines. Removing temporal memory reduces SR and sharply increases average path length from 16.9 to 39.1m, removing the spatial-map and planning component reduces SR as well. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that our zero-shot method achieves higher success rates than the post-trained baseline in both corridor and office environments, suggesting better transfer to the evaluated real-world settings. As a complementary evaluation, LAW2 uses paired instruction interventions to examine behavioral responses, instruction following ability beyond endpoint success. These results support preserving task progress, observation history, and geometry in structured memory for zero-shot navigation with smaller open models.

Real-world tests on Unitree Go2 show higher success than a post-trained baseline in evaluated corridor and office settings; LAW2 probes instruction-following behavior beyond endpoint success.

papers.abstract: Compositional diffusion planners have demonstrated remarkable success on long-horizon diffusion planning by sampling short trajectories, namely chunks, and composing them into a long trajectory. However, averaging overlapping chunks can induce the mode-averaging problem, resulting in discontinuous trajectories. Several works aim to address this problem, whereas a non-negligible portion of plans remains infeasible. In this work, we propose Selective Compositional Diffuser (SCD), handling this problem by measuring reachability. To this end, we present a self-supervised learning method for the reachability classifier. This is trained on offline data and generated chunks jointly to address potential distributional mismatch, while reducing the bias inherited from the generated data. Based on this, we construct a graph whose edge costs represent whether consecutive chunks are reachable, and traverse the graph to find effective yet efficient routes. Lastly, we generate bridging trajectories and refine the composed trajectory for smooth transitions. We evaluate our method on OGBench stitching tasks. It practically reduces incompatible mode compositions and the mode-averaging problem compared to the studied baselines. Across tasks, SCD improves success rates, reaching state-of-the-art results on HumanoidMaze-Large and Giant tasks.
authors: Chanyoung Park, Youngjoong Kim, Jaesik Park

papers.abstract: Embodied systems can update policies, world models, skills, and executable programs from deployment experience, allowing one interaction to benefit later tasks. When a system also revises and reuses its data-acquisition, feedback, or learning procedures, experience changes the process that produces capability, introducing recursive self-improvement. This paper surveys research in physical AI through the connection between persistent capability and its improvement process. We first explain the functional distinction between learner updates and improvers, then compare policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable harnesses. These approaches connect to revisions of curricula, rewards, and research programs in different ways. Contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs determine whether the resulting gains accumulate during continued deployment. An L0-L3 rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation, persistent capability gain, inherited process revision, and verified improver gain. Representative benchmarks and within-study contrasts relate these distinctions to existing results. We further propose common-data and interactive comparisons that evaluate reference and revised improvers from shared learner starts, separating the use of experience from its acquisition. This perspective connects the diverse methods, physical operating conditions, and evaluation evidence, underpinning embodied RSI. A comprehensive list of studies in this survey is available at https://github.com/nkd-lkz/physical-ai-rsi-survey.
authors: Xiaofeng Han, Kaize Luo, Zenghuang Fu, Zichong Zhu, Zhe Feng, Changwei Wang, Rongtao Xu, Weiliang Meng, Xiaopeng Zhang
bullets: Distinguishes ordinary learner updates from improvers that revise data collection, feedback, or learning procedures.
Reviews policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable learning harnesses.
Identifies contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs as factors governing whether gains persist during deployment.
Introduces an L0–L3 rubric spanning task-local adaptation to verified improvement of the improver itself.
Proposes common-data and interactive comparisons to separate learning from experience from improving how experience is acquired.

figures.caption: FIGURE 1. Overview of the review framework for recursive self-improvement in physical AI. (a) Conceptual distinctions among programmed robots, learned policies, persistent self-improvement, and recursive improvement. (b) Physical experience and feedback support capability updates, while system-generated process revisions are retained and reused to govern later learning. (c) Persistent artifacts can modify the learner, the improver, or both. (d) The evidence rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation (L0), persistent capability gain (L1), inherited process revision (L2), and verified improver gain (L3). L3 requires greater subsequent gains from shared learner starts under matched resource budgets and independent tests. The levels specify evidence requirements for individual claims. Comparisons are schematic, and robot scenes are illustrative renderings.

FIGURE 3. Evidence requirements across a declared reset boundary. Episode context c, retained learner state x, and improvement procedure ϕ have different persistence roles. L0 describes task-local changes that reset; L1 concerns retained capability gains in later independent attempts. L2 requires a system-generated process revision to be inherited and used in a later learner update. L3 requires greater subsequent gains under shared learner starts, matched resource budgets, and independent tests. The diagrams illustrate the criteria and corresponding evaluation conditions.

FIGURE 5. Four carriers of persistent physical experience. Policy and value updates change parameters and action selection; world models retain predictive structure learned from observed transitions; indexed memory and skill libraries support retrieval and composition; programs and harnesses retain changes to execution logic, illustrated by a recovery branch. Each panel exposes the retained representation and its later use. A program change is classified by its functional role in execution or in producing later updates.

FIGURE 6. Fixed-model planning and model–policy co-improvement. The fixed-model planner evaluates imagined action alternatives and executes a selected action while retaining model parameters. In the coupled loop, real transitions train the model, the updated model generates imagined trajectories for policy learning, and the updated policy collects further physical experience. Solid and dashed paths distinguish physical and model-generated experience. The observed–predicted offset is schematic; coupling alone does not establish inherited revision of the improvement procedure.

papers.selection_reason: Survey connecting persistent capability, world-model updates, memory, and recursive self-improvement in embodied physical AI.
papers.title: Recursive Self-Improvement in Physical AI: Mechanisms, Evidence, and Evaluation
papers.tldr: This survey frames embodied recursive self-improvement as systems that improve both their capabilities and the processes used to acquire those capabilities, and proposes ways to evaluate it.

papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning seeks to learn decision policies from previously collected data, but deployment environments may differ from the domains in which the data were collected, and logged variables may omit confounders that affected both historical actions and outcomes. We study offline policy learning under the joint challenges of domain discrepancy and unmeasured confounding, where multiple heterogeneous source datasets provide complementary information about a target domain. We develop a causally adjusted transportability framework combining transportability theory with instrumental variables, negative controls, and proxies to identify target-domain causal quantities. For confounded contextual bandits, identification reduces to systems of bridge-function integral equations, enabling minimax estimation from finite samples. Confidence sets for the identified quantities are then used for pessimistic policy optimization, yielding CAT-CCB. We extend the framework to episodic confounded Markov decision processes, where complementary sources identify target reward and transition mechanisms under structural and completeness conditions. Under Gaussian dynamics and linear function approximation, this yields CAT-CMDP. We establish high-probability finite-sample suboptimality guarantees that quantify the effects of approximation, estimation, source-to-target shift, offline coverage, and sample size. For bounded finite-dimensional linear classes, the contextual-bandit guarantee recovers the standard $\widetilde{\mathcal O}(N^{-1/2})$ rate. Numerical experiments support the effectiveness of the framework for learning target-domain policies from heterogeneous confounded data. Together, the results provide a principled approach when no single source dataset suffices for causal identification and policy optimization.
authors: Junyi Liao, Hangqi Ren, Zhuoran Yang
bullets: Addresses offline reinforcement learning with both source-to-target domain discrepancy and unmeasured confounding.
Uses transportability theory with instrumental variables, negative controls, and proxies to identify target-domain causal quantities.
Develops bridge-function integral-equation methods and pessimistic policy optimization for confounded contextual bandits (CAT-CCB).
Extends the framework to episodic confounded MDPs under structural and completeness conditions, including Gaussian linear dynamics (CAT-CMDP).
Provides finite-sample suboptimality guarantees and numerical evidence, with performance depending on approximation, estimation, shift, coverage, and sample size.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires instruction-consistent planning and reliable execution under collision constraints. Yet many hierarchical approaches optimize the planner while keeping execution fixed. We introduce MATCH, a framework that jointly learns a language-conditioned planner and a goal-conditioned primitive-action executor. An execution-aware topological graph represents start-dependent execution options and integrates executor value estimates with realized outcome memory, enabling the planner to select execution requests and refine their targets through bounded continuous offsets. A transition-aware dense macro reward balances ordered progress along the reference route against execution residual, encouraging executable requests without substituting local success for instruction following. A staged curriculum culminates in synchronized on-policy updates, with the executor learning on planner-generated requests and the planner adapting its requests to the executor's current behavior. With 0.5B parameters, MATCH achieves state-of-the-art performance on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks. Preliminary real-robot deployments further demonstrate its practical potential.
authors: Shuhao Ye, Yufei Wei, Demao Wang, Shichao Zhai, Rong Xiong, Yue Wang

papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) typically mitigates distribution shift by imposing divergence constraints on the action distributions of the learned and behavior policies. However, this paradigm cannot ensure the underlying dynamic consistency structure: even minor action deviations can lead to drastically different transitions, inadvertently driving the agent away from the offline dataset. To address this, we explore policy constraints through their induced state-consequence distributions rather than relying on pure action-distribution matching. Nevertheless, directly enforcing such consequence-aware constraints is computationally intractable without access to the true underlying dynamics model. To bypass this issue, we propose Structural Behavior Regularization (StBR), which replaces the intractable objective with a closed-form latent divergence. Structuring this latent space to reflect transition dynamics renders the latent divergence a theoretically bounded surrogate for the true consequence-distribution divergence. By regularizing the learned policy with this latent divergence, StBR adaptively tightens the behavior constraint in dynamics-sensitive regions, effectively preventing deviations outside the offline dataset. Empirically, we demonstrate that StBR achieves superior performance across diverse offline RL benchmarks.
authors: Wen Jiang, Ke Jiang, Xiaoyang Tan
bullets: Action-distribution constraints may fail when small action changes cause large transition differences and dataset departure.
The method, Structural Behavior Regularization (StBR), uses a closed-form divergence in a dynamics-structured latent space.
This latent divergence provides a theoretically bounded surrogate for the intractable true consequence-distribution divergence.
StBR adaptively tightens constraints in regions sensitive to dynamics, helping keep learned behavior within the offline data distribution.
Experiments report superior performance across diverse offline RL benchmarks.

papers.abstract: We demonstrate the first zero-shot sim-to-real transfer for a surgeon-robot collaboration task in open surgery: retractor take-over. A robot arm takes a retractor from the surgeon's hand and preserves retraction at handoff, using a policy trained only on simulated demonstrations, without human demonstrations or real-world fine-tuning. Imitation learning from real demonstrations is limited by collection and labeling costs, and by performance degradation when the environment changes. Our framework, SimRetract, generates simulated demonstrations designed for transfer: the policy observes masked instrument images and grasp geometry, learns to recover from off-nominal states, and acts with margin for execution drift. Deployed zero-shot, it grasps the retractor in 90% of 50 surgeon-defined phantom presentations and preserves retraction at handoff in 78%. Results on unseen retractors suggest potential for generalization to instruments with similar grasp geometry. Across ten policy configurations and 1,200 simulated and real trials, we localize the sim-to-real gap to components: in simulation, grasp rates across ablations span 80-96%, while on the real robot removing the instrument mask alone drops performance to 22% grasped and 12% held. Transfer-oriented design thus makes zero-shot sim-to-real transfer feasible for a surgical assistance task without human demonstrations. Code is available here: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/simretract-58D2.
authors: Xucheng Wang, Zhizhou Yang, Sung Eun Kim, Romain Hardy, Michael P. Sampson, Aakash Reddy, Ankit Pal, Xiaoman Zhang, Luyang Luo, Pranav Rajpurkar

Results on unseen retractors indicate potential generalization to instruments with similar grasp geometry; performance depends strongly on instrument masking.

papers.abstract: Mobile manipulator robots rarely reposition their base during manipulation, because doing so requires real-time knowledge of how well the arm can reach its surroundings among obstacles. Reachability maps (RMs) encode this knowledge, but existing methods are slow, coarse (typically 5 cm), or ignore real obstacles. This article asks whether a neural network can predict an obstacle-aware RM at 2 cm resolution from a live depth camera, on embedded hardware, fast enough for online use. We present HERON, a 3D U-Net trained on RMs computed with the GPU-accelerated inverse kinematics of cuRobo, first on synthetic scenes and then on real depth data, and deployed on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT and INT8 quantization. HERON predicts the RM of a 2.56 m cube around the arm in 115 ms on average, for a measured system rate of 8.57 Hz, close to the 10 Hz update rate of the obstacle map, whereas computing the same map with cuRobo takes about 90 min. Against the cuRobo ground truth, 95% of the voxels lie within 1 class out of 51 with the FP32 model and within 3 classes with the INT8 model, with a Pearson correlation of 0.99 and a quadratic weighted kappa above 0.9. Accuracy degrades mainly at the workspace boundaries.
authors: G. Dupoiron, F. Michaud, J. P. Roberge
bullets: Targets the need for base repositioning during manipulation by estimating arm reachability around obstacles.

Trained on cuRobo-generated maps from synthetic and real scenes, then optimized with TensorRT and INT8 quantization on a Jetson AGX Orin.
Runs in 115 ms on average (8.57 Hz), compared with about 90 minutes for direct cuRobo computation.
Matches cuRobo closely: Pearson correlation is 0.99; accuracy mainly degrades near workspace boundaries.

papers.abstract: Robot imitation learning uses demonstrations from operators of varying skill, but selecting training data remains challenging. Existing methods score demonstrations using smoothness, diversity, or estimated influence on policy performance, but differences in selection and evaluation protocols make it difficult to determine whether they outperform simple baselines. We introduce \textbf{CuraEval}, a framework combining mathematical analysis of demonstration scores with controlled comparisons against fixed size-matched random subsets and full-data training on mixed-skill robomimic data using Diffusion Policy and BC-RNN. We show that the evaluated PSD score depends only on episode length and squared position magnitudes, and produces nearly the same ranking as episode length on \textit{square} ($\rho=0.999$). With Diffusion Policy, selecting the shortest 50\% of demonstrations improves \textit{square} success from 70.7\% under random selection to 76.5\%. Compared with random selection, our adapted geometric-entropy LOO selector reduces success at 25\% retention from 94.7\% to 74.0\% on \textit{can} and achieves 41.7\% on \textit{square}, below the mean success rates of all three independently sampled random subsets (59.8--62.5\%). On the same 3 \textit{square} Diffusion Policy training seeds, length-based selection at 75\% retention improves success over full-data training from 76.7\% to 86.7\% under the original protocol, but lowers it from 80.5\% to 79.5\% after checkpoint reporting, rollout count, and evaluation seed change jointly. No evaluated curated condition significantly outperforms full-data training after Holm correction, although confidence intervals still permit useful gains. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/CuraEval.
authors: Jiuyi Xu, Meida Chen, Yang Ye, Yangming Shi
bullets: Evaluates demonstration scores on mixed-skill robomimic data using Diffusion Policy and BC-RNN, with size-matched random and full-data baselines.
Finds the PSD score is determined by episode length and squared position magnitudes, ranking nearly identically to episode length on square.
Selecting the shortest 50% improves square success from 70.7% to 76.5% versus random selection under one setup.
An adapted geometric-entropy leave-one-out selector can substantially underperform random subsets, reaching 41.7% on square at 25% retention.
After correcting evaluation conditions and multiple comparisons, no curated setting significantly beats full-data training.

papers.abstract: Behavior Cloning has demonstrated promising generalization capabilities for robotic manipulation in terrestrial environments. However, marine visual distortions and dynamic currents create a severe domain shift that remains a key bottleneck in adapting generalist architectures to underwater field manipulation. To address this, 1616 episodes of underwater manipulation data were collected in calm and turbulent waters and were used to train 14 generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (DynamicVLA) with varying proprioception observation configurations. Across three tasks on 1260 gradable on-hardware rollouts in a pool, 10 models outperformed the baseline, with the highest-performing model achieving a 93.3% overall success rate, including partial successes. Results are also introduced from a case study evaluating the performance of a single-task Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) and a generalist VLA (SmolVLA) policy for two tasks in marine archaeology and conservation: grasping and mooring. Experiments are performed on an ROV on and around the WWII wreck Coralita X127 and at Manoel Island Marina, Malta. Across 748 collected episodes and 508 gradable on-hardware rollouts, the ACT policy substantially outperformed SmolVLA (47.9% vs. 7.9% pooled success rate), earning a 66.7% success rate on the most successful task at the marine archaeological site. To enable further contributions to embodied intelligence in marine field robotics, the BLUEMBODIED KIT used to collect data, train models, and deploy policies on the ROV has been open sourced.
authors: Greta Perez-Haiek (New York University), Luca Macesanu (New York University), Kevin Angers (New York University), Mohammed Imam (New York University), Timothy Gambin (University of Malta), Christopher Clark (New York University)
bullets: Marine visual distortions and currents create a major domain shift for terrestrial-trained manipulation policies.
The study collected 1,616 underwater episodes to train 14 generalist VLA models with different proprioception inputs.
In pool experiments, 10 models beat the baseline; the best reached 93.3% overall success, including partial successes.

papers.abstract: Robot-learning studies often compare position and velocity actions as though each label identified a single experimental treatment, yet the label alone does not determine what the robot executes. Before affecting robot motion, bounded policy output passes through filtering, physical scaling, reference construction, feedback, timing, and effort limits. We study how these omitted properties affect attribution under one shared learner and training budget. Across three contact-rich Factory tasks (PegInsert, GearMesh, and NutThread), we compare five joint-space interfaces, with ten independently trained policies per condition. We first remain within the same position-feedback law and vary the executed interface: substituting only the physical action scale as the directly modified component changes sample-median evaluation success by 0.645-1.000 across tasks, while removing an exponential moving average produces task-dependent changes. We then move to a cross-law comparison and choose a velocity scale that exactly matches the position interface's local raw-torque command gain. This calibration raises the sample median on GearMesh and NutThread, with no median change on PegInsert. Yet clear residual sample-median gaps remain on PegInsert and GearMesh, while the NutThread interval includes zero. Thus, even this explicit equality leaves feedback and held-action dynamics unmatched and does not establish position-velocity trained-outcome equivalence. Action-interface comparisons should therefore report the executed pathway and state the physical quantity they match.
bullets: Studies five joint-space interfaces across three contact-rich Factory tasks using one learner, shared training budget, and ten policies per condition.
Within the same position-feedback law, changing only physical action scale alters median success, while removing smoothing has task-dependent effects.
Calibrating velocity scale to match position-interface local torque gain improves median success on two tasks but not the third.
Residual performance gaps remain, showing that matching one gain does not establish position–velocity equivalence.
Comparisons should report the full executed action pathway and the physical quantity being matched.

papers.selection_reason: Directly studies action-interface effects in contact-rich robot manipulation learning.
papers.title: Same Label, Different Interface: Beyond Action-Space Labels in Robot Learning
papers.tldr: Action labels alone do not define robot behavior: physical scaling, filtering, feedback, and timing can substantially change learning outcomes, so position–velocity comparisons require explicit interface matching.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning holds the promise of robots that learn manipulation skills from interaction alone, without pretrained priors or demonstration data. In practice, on-policy methods such as PPO routinely stall on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks: dense reward shaping carries the policy through stages, yet stitching them together and discovering sparsely rewarded events rarely succeeds. We trace this failure to the missing action discrimination in state-value credit assignment: a state-value critic judges progress only by episode outcomes, so when the policy converges to a partial solution all outcomes coincide, and improvement stops because no action can prove better than another. We therefore extend PPO with an action conditioned value critic which, can compare the executed action with alternatives sampled at the same state and aid the learning signal. Combined with Generalized Advantage Estimation and a bound on exploration noise, we show how the extended algorithm escapes the plateau and completes precise peg insertion within a training budget where PPO with identical exploration fails.
authors: Giovanni Minelli, Giulio Turrisi, Lorenzo Amatucci, Victor Barasuol, Claudio Semini
bullets: On-policy RL methods can stall when dense rewards support partial solutions but fail to encourage rare, precisely sequenced events.
The issue is attributed to state-value credit assignment, which cannot discriminate among actions once outcomes become similar.
The proposed PPO extension compares executed actions with alternatives sampled at the same state using an action-conditioned value critic.
Combined with Generalized Advantage Estimation and bounded exploration noise, it escapes a plateau and completes precise peg insertion where matched-exploration PPO fails.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Normalized training reward on the multi-stage peg-insertion task (5 seeds); horizontal bands mark the reward level of each completed stage. PPO (blue) stalls mid-task without reaching insertion; PPO+GRPO, using grouprelative action credit (yellow), escapes the plateau and converges to consistent insertion.
Figure 1. Task scene with detail of the contact-rich insertion stage: the peg, grasped and transported, must be aligned with and inserted into a tight-fitting hole.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an action-conditioned value critic for PPO to escape local minima in contact-rich manipulation, directly relevant to robot learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Learning from Relative Action Credit for Escaping Local Minima
papers.tldr: An action-conditioned critic helps PPO distinguish better from worse actions and escape plateaus in long-horizon robotic manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Humanoid controllers often require task-specific training despite sharing the need for balance and whole-body coordination. We present Metatron, a promptable whole-body execution layer combining a generative base policy with a programmable skill layer. The base policy receives partial goals, collectively called a prompt, that can combine timed body-part targets, velocity commands, and style cues. It produces diverse whole-body motions consistent with these goals. Training combines motion capture, synthetic recovery trajectories, and retargeted scene-interaction motions. After training, the policy is frozen. Stateful programs called skills express task intent as prompts at each control step, drawing rough geometric sketches that the policy turns into coordinated movement. Skills are ordinary code, refined by coding agents that analyze motion data and fit compact rules without task-specific policy training. On the physical Unitree G1, one frozen checkpoint supports walking, recovery, teleoperated object pickup, and sitting on furniture. Comparative evaluations show higher reaching success and push robustness than the tested reference-tracking pipelines. The same recipe produces climbing and acrobatics on a simulated character. Metatron enables coding agents to turn learned motor capabilities into new skills through code, without further policy training.
authors: Chen Tessler, Yifeng Jiang, Alec Otto, Yi Shi, Umar Iqbal, Gal Chechik, Xue Bin Peng
bullets: Addresses the need for separate training for humanoid tasks requiring balance and whole-body coordination.
Combines a generative base policy with programmable, stateful skills that issue prompts containing body targets, velocity commands, and style cues.
Trains on motion capture, synthetic recovery, and retargeted scene-interaction motions, then freezes the policy.
Demonstrated on a Unitree G1 for walking, recovery, object pickup, and sitting; evaluations report higher reaching success and push robustness than tested reference-tracking pipelines.
Also produces climbing and acrobatics in simulation, while remaining scoped to the demonstrated robot and simulated-character settings.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can learn to follow execution preferences, such as where to grasp an object or how to move around an obstacle, from demonstrations annotated with preference labels. Providing these annotations for every new task, however, is costly. We study whether learned preference control can transfer to new tasks whose demonstrations contain the desired behaviors but lack preference annotations. We find that a policy trained with preference annotations can follow preferences on a new task before adaptation but achieves limited task success. Fine-tuning on target demonstrations without these annotations improves task success while weakening preference control. Motivated by this finding, we introduce Self-Labeled Preference Transfer (SPT). SPT jointly trains a shared vision-language backbone for preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition on annotated source demonstrations. It then freezes the recognizer to preserve its cross-task preference recognition capability and uses it to self-label target demonstrations for policy fine-tuning. Across five types of execution preferences in simulation, the recognizer achieves 96.4% accuracy, and SPT reaches 84.8% preference following and 89.2% task success, compared with 59.4% and 88.0% for naive finetuning. We further extend to multiple preferences, achieving 93.8% preference following compared with 42.5% of baselines. In real-world experiments, SPT increases preference following from 52.5% to 92.5% relative to naive finetuning across two task transfers. These results show that SPT can support preference adaptation across tasks and objects while maintaining success, without additional manual preference annotations.
authors: Kaiwen Hong, Shaoting Peng, Xiangyu Zeng, Pengcheng Wang, Boyuan Tian, Haonan Chen, Yifan Zhu, Yixiao Wang, Katherine Driggs-Campbell
bullets: Preference annotations are costly, and naive fine-tuning on unlabeled target demonstrations improves task success but weakens preference control.
SPT jointly learns preference-conditioned action prediction and preference recognition from annotated source demonstrations.
It freezes the recognizer and uses it to self-label target demonstrations for preference-aware policy fine-tuning.
In simulation, SPT achieves 84.8% preference following and 89.2% task success, outperforming naive fine-tuning on preference following.
Across multiple preferences and two real-world transfers, SPT maintains strong preference following without additional manual annotations.

papers.abstract: This paper presents a two-stage learning framework for versatile and agile humanoid locomotion that couples online reduced-order model (ROM) reference generation with whole-body tracking control. In the first stage, we train a command-conditioned whole-body reference generator using single rigid body dynamics combined with full humanoid kinematics. In the second stage, the frozen ROM policy is rolled out online to generate references for training a whole-body tracking policy on the full-order dynamics model. Learning a kino-dynamically consistent reference generator in the simplified ROM space enables us to generate references over a broad command space and over multiple locomotion strategies using a single unified framework. We demonstrate the approach on a Unitree G1 humanoid robot, achieving longitudinal velocities from -2.0 m/s to 2.8 m/s, lateral velocities up to +-1.0 m/s, angular velocities up to +-3.0 rad/s, one-legged hopping, and continuous transitions across the commands, all using one unified reference policy and one whole-body tracking policy.
authors: Adrian B. Ghansah, Yujin An, Jeeseop Kim, Soon-Jo Chung
bullets: Addresses broad-command humanoid locomotion across multiple strategies with a single framework.
Trains a command-conditioned reference generator using single rigid body dynamics and full humanoid kinematics.
Rolls out the frozen reduced-order policy online to train a whole-body tracker on full-order dynamics.
Demonstrated on a Unitree G1 with fast multidirectional motion, one-legged hopping, and continuous command transitions.
Reported capabilities include -2.0 to 2.8 m/s longitudinal, ±1.0 m/s lateral, and ±3.0 rad/s angular velocities.

papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) enables teams of agents, such as robots and autonomous vehicles, to learn coordinated behavior, but what such teams learn is largely determined by their reward function. Because task success alone provides too little guidance for learning, intermediate rewards are usually designed by hand, and this effort must often be repeated whenever the environment or the team changes. Large language models (LLMs) can automate the effort by writing reward functions as code, yet the resulting rewards are typically designed and tested in a single setting. To enable their reuse across settings, GARDEN (Generalist Autonomous Reward Design through Evidence Navigation) is proposed, in which one reward program is developed for a family of related scenarios and transferred, unchanged, to scenarios that were not available during its design. During development, environment code, training records, and agent behavior are investigated by an LLM reward engineer, and draft rewards are tested in trial training runs, while the learning algorithm and the rule for selecting the final reward are held fixed. On unseen scenarios of the Overcooked and SMAX benchmarks, task returns were increased by 58.2% and 52.5% over the default rewards on two kitchen layouts, and the mean win rate in two combat scenarios was raised from 51.0% to 89.9%. Under matched candidate and probe budgets, this exceeded the 84.2% and 79.2% obtained with fixed diagnostic feedback and Eureka-inspired reward reflection. These results show that a single autonomously engineered reward can be reused effectively across related cooperative scenarios.
bullets: Addresses the repeated manual design of intermediate rewards when environments or agent teams change.
An LLM reward engineer examines environment code, training records, and agent behavior, then tests draft rewards through trial training runs.
The final reward and learning algorithm are selected using fixed procedures, enabling unchanged transfer across scenarios.
On unseen Overcooked and SMAX scenarios, GARDEN substantially improved task returns and win rates over default rewards and outperformed compared reflection-based methods.
The approach is scoped to families of related cooperative scenarios; the abstract does not establish generalization beyond them.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for general-purpose household robotics. However, inference and data-collection strategies that have been deployed in smaller-scale settings do not necessarily generalize to large-scale, diverse task suites. To address this gap, we conduct a systematic, paired evaluation of previously proposed inference and data-collection strategies across all 100 tasks. Our evaluation uses a fine-tuned $\pi_{0.5}$ model based on the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge winner, which achieves a Q-score of 0.39 on the public test set. These results show that proposed strategies do not transfer uniformly to new environments and tasks. Project page, videos, and detailed analysis: https://rubenhammele.github.io/behavior2026
authors: Ruben Hammele, Samira Huber, Mohammad Nazeri, Amirreza Payandeh, Alexandyr T. Card, Aaron Nguyen, Anuj Pokhrel, Daeun Song, Xuesu Xiao, S\"oren Pirk
bullets: Evaluates previously proposed inference and data-collection strategies systematically across all 100 BEHAVIOR-1K tasks.
Uses a fine-tuned π₀.₅ model based on the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge winner.
Reports a Q-score of 0.39 on the public test set.
Finds that strategy effectiveness varies across environments and tasks.
Provides detailed analysis and supplementary materials on the project page.

papers.abstract: Scaling visual reinforcement learning (RL) with GPU-accelerated simulation is computationally expensive due to rendering and visual-policy inference costs. Consequently, two-stage teacher--student distillation is commonly used to train visual policies, but introduces an imitation gap. In this preliminary study, we introduce \echomethod{}, \textbf{a single-stage off-policy RL framework that scales experience collection without proportionally increasing visual computation}. Through \textbf{inverse distillation}, a state-based auxiliary policy imitates the evolving visual policy and collects inexpensive, unrendered experience. Echo leverages this experience for off-policy value learning, directly improving the visual policy through a shared privileged critic. We instantiate \echomethod{} with FastTD3 and evaluate it on three visual control tasks and two dexterous manipulation tasks in Genesis. Relative to \sdpgmethod{} under the evaluated configurations, Echo reduces time to reference returns by an average of \textbf{60\% across the three locomotion tasks} and \textbf{56\% across both hand tasks}, while improving peak mean returns by \textbf{62\% and 12\%}, respectively. Both hand tasks also achieve higher mean returns at matched simulator-transition budgets. These initial results suggest that scaling off-policy experience is a promising approach to efficient direct visual RL.
bullets: Addresses the rendering and visual-policy inference costs of scaling visual RL, while avoiding the imitation gap of teacher–student distillation.
Uses inverse distillation: a state-based policy imitates the evolving visual policy to gather inexpensive unrendered experience.
Applies the experience through off-policy value learning with a shared privileged critic to improve the visual policy.
In Genesis experiments, Echo reached reference returns 60% faster on locomotion and 56% faster on dexterous manipulation tasks than the evaluated baseline.
Peak mean returns improved by 62% on locomotion and 12% on hand tasks; results are preliminary and limited to five tasks.

papers.abstract: Robots, autonomous vehicles, and consumer 360{\deg} cameras use fisheye lenses for wide fields of view (FoVs). Simulation-ready digital twins require photorealistic rendering across the full FoV and an aligned collision mesh. However, prior fisheye Gaussian Splatting methods only rasterize up to 180{\deg} and do not produce meshes, while Gaussian surface reconstruction methods assume pinhole training images. We present GOFish, the first 3D Gaussian Splatting surface reconstruction method to train directly on fisheye images, rasterize FoVs beyond 180{\deg}, and extract an aligned mesh from the same scene. Calibrated densification recovers the surface across the entire FoV, while Calibrated Mip Filtering and Wide-Angle Appearance Modeling keep pixel blur and lens falloff out of the scene and mesh. Across the 200{\deg} FIORD and 205{\deg} FullCircle benchmarks, GOFish improves PSNR over the best prior method by 2.28 and 1.97 dB, respectively. It also outperforms fisheye rendering baselines within their own FoVs and achieves the highest mesh F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set. Together, the Gaussian scene and mesh form a LiDAR-free, simulation-ready digital twin that renders in real time, ray traces the full FoV, and provides collision geometry.
authors: Allen Tu, Meher Gitika Karumuri, Shifan Zhu, Hailing Wang, Yen-Liang Lin, David Held, Matthias Zwicker, Tom Goldstein
bullets: Addresses fisheye reconstruction beyond 180° while producing collision-ready geometry.
Uses calibrated densification for full-FoV surface recovery.
Applies calibrated mip filtering and wide-angle appearance modeling to separate blur and lens falloff from the scene and mesh.
Improves PSNR over the best prior method by 2.28 dB on FIORD and 1.97 dB on FullCircle.
Achieves the highest reported mesh F-score on FIORD and the main ScanNet++ set, while supporting real-time rendering and full-FoV ray tracing.

papers.abstract: Humans navigate their environment based on their vision system, anticipating how the ground will respond before committing to a step. Self-supervised learning could provide legged robots the same ability, but the supervisory signal is typically chosen on intuition, and its effect on what the model learns is rarely examined. We present Terrain-Aware COntact Supervision (TACOS), which proposes a meaningful and consistent footstep instability score, based on the residual of a factor graph in legged state estimation. It projects the continuous score into preceding images to supervise a dense visual predictor. We propose two variants, a hard score that exploits hindsight and a causal soft score available immediately. Both metrics are compared against state-of-the-art alternatives in two independent evaluations that share no data or labels. On 1716 manually annotated contacts, both variants outperform every evaluated alternative at detecting instability and ranking its severity, improving pooled severity ranking by 28 % over the strongest baseline. On three outdoor test runs, our metric also trains the most accurate visual predictor, improving rank correlation by 58 % over the strongest alternative, and by a further 25 % when supplemented with onboard context. In a real-world experiment over a 50 m forest trajectory, the trained predictor handles non-geometric terrain properties such as mud and vegetation, while stepping around geometric obstacles like fallen branches. Code is available for reproducibility at https://github.com/norlab-ulaval/TACOS.
authors: Jean-Michel Fortin, William Larriv\'ee-Hardy, Gabriel Jeanson, Olivier Gamache, Daniele De Martini, Fran\c{c}ois Pomerleau, Philippe Gigu\`ere
bullets: Defines a consistent footstep instability score from the residual of a legged-robot factor graph.
Projects the score into preceding camera images to train a dense visual instability predictor.
Provides a hindsight-based hard score and an immediately available causal soft score.
Both variants outperform evaluated alternatives for detecting and ranking contact instability; the best predictor improves rank correlation further with onboard context.
In a 50 m forest test, the predictor responds to mud and vegetation while avoiding geometric obstacles such as fallen branches.

papers.abstract: The rapid progress of software engineering agents drives interest in applying them to open-ended problems such as GPU kernel optimization. However, we find that existing coding agents converge to local optima on real-world, expert-written kernels (e.g., FlashInfer). We introduce Evolving Agent Teams, a multi-agent framework that escapes such local optima. It features (1) a central supervisor that diagnoses each local optimum and restructures a team of agents; and (2) a persistent file system that comprises a learning document, an evolution history, and per-team artifacts, grounding restructuring with accumulated experience. Under a matched token budget, Evolving Agent Teams consistently outperforms strong coding-agent baselines. With an extended token budget, Evolving Agent Teams generates a CUDA kernel that reaches 1.2x mean speedup over the production FlashInfer MLA paged decode kernel from scratch and wins on 36 of 47 production workloads from FlashInfer-Bench (0.86-0.99x on the remaining 11). It also demonstrates superior performance on tasks such as KDA prefill on AMD MI350X (3.01x over vLLM) and NVIDIA B200 (3.44x over FlashKDA), MoE expert-offload serving on Apple silicon (30.3 tokens/s decode for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next in MLX 4-bit on a 48 GB M4 Pro), and RoboDojo robot manipulation (62.1 on held-out seeds vs. 55.3 for the best leaderboard entry). Code is available at https://github.com/caoshiyi/EAT.
bullets: Existing coding agents often stall at local optima on expert-written, real-world kernels such as FlashInfer.
A central supervisor diagnoses stagnation and reorganizes agent teams; a persistent filesystem stores learning documents, evolution history, and team artifacts.
Under matched token budgets, the framework consistently outperforms strong coding-agent baselines.
With more compute, it achieves a 1.2× mean speedup over FlashInfer’s production MLA paged-decode kernel and wins 36 of 47 FlashInfer-Bench workloads.
The approach also shows strong results on AMD/NVIDIA kernel tasks, Apple-silicon MoE serving, and RoboDojo manipulation.

papers.abstract: Multi-objective reinforcement learning is a fundamental problem for modern AI, with applications spanning post-training, reasoning models, and robotic control. A central challenge is to learn policies that balance competing objectives, such as helpfulness versus honesty in safety and alignment, or speed versus energy in robotics. The optimal policy can vary sharply with objective-weighting combinations, and the extent of this variation depends crucially on the degree of conflict among objectives, making per-preference policy learning sample-inefficient. In this paper, we introduce objective-conflict coefficients and derive near-optimal regret bounds for online settings using this measure, thereby quantifying the impact of misalignment on learning efficiency. Then, we design routed ensemble policy learning, an algorithm that maintains a small set of basis policies and dynamically routes trajectories to the policy with the highest potential reward. Finally, we consider trajectory selection as another approach to mitigate objective conflict, and design a kernel surrogate trajectory attribution algorithm that estimates how feedback signals from a set of trajectories influence policy learning on other trajectories. The kernel can capture nonlinear interactions such as synergy and antagonism between trajectories. We evaluate our approach across diverse environments and benchmarks: routed ensembles improve average performance by 4.3% over baselines for online environments from Meta-World and MO-Gymnasium, and kernel surrogate attribution improves correlation with leave-one-out analysis over existing baselines by 50%. When applied to trajectory selection, kernel-based attribution yields a 27% improvement in reward over baseline attribution methods.
bullets: Introduces objective-conflict coefficients and derives near-optimal online regret bounds that relate learning efficiency to objective misalignment.
Proposes routed ensemble policy learning, which maintains a small set of basis policies and routes trajectories to the most promising policy.
Develops kernel surrogate trajectory attribution to model nonlinear synergy and antagonism among trajectories and guide feedback selection.
Across Meta-World and MO-Gymnasium online benchmarks, routed ensembles improve average performance by 4.3% over baselines.
Kernel attribution improves leave-one-out correlation by 50% and produces a 27% reward improvement for trajectory selection over baseline attribution methods.
