papers.abstract: Endowing robot policies with anticipatory capabilities has proven effective in improving control performance. However, existing methods predominantly rely on explicit supervision derived from future observations, in either pixel or latent space, at the cost of additional architectural and computational complexity. Departing from explicit future supervision, we ask whether such foresight can be elicited directly from the action signal. To this end, we propose \textbf{AdaPolicy}, an \textbf{A}ction-\textbf{d}riven \textbf{a}nticipatory policy framework that shapes future-aware representations via cascaded next-chunk prediction. Specifically, an Online Action Head jointly produces the current action chunk and an evolved latent state. Building on this state, a cascaded Unrolled Action Head forecasts the next chunk, and the resulting loss flows back through the evolved state to instill implicit foresight into the online policy. Importantly, this training-only unroll requires no future-observation encoding, keeping AdaPolicy lightweight to train with zero inference-time overhead. Experiments on MetaWorld, RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and real-world deployments demonstrate consistent gains across diverse settings, including up to $14$ percentage points on millimeter-precision tasks such as earphone assembly and shoelace threading. More details and visualizations are available at \href{https://teee111.github.io/AdaPolicy/}{https://teee111.github.io/AdaPolicy/}.
bullets: Addresses the complexity and computational cost of methods that use explicit future observations for foresight.
Uses an Online Action Head to predict the current action chunk and evolve a latent state.
A cascaded Unrolled Action Head predicts the next action chunk, with its loss shaping future-aware representations.
The training-only unroll requires no future-observation encoding and adds zero inference-time overhead.
Demonstrates consistent gains across simulation and real-world settings, including up to 14 percentage points on millimeter-precision tasks.],

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) are becoming increasingly important and useful for embodied intelligence, as they enable robots to anticipate the consequences of candidate actions before interacting with the physical environment. However, underwater robots are usually subject to passive dynamics, such as inertia, buoyancy, hydrodynamic drag, and persistent drift, which can continue to affect the vehicle even after an action is completed. Existing WAMs, which primarily predict action-conditioned visual observations, are not explicitly designed to capture such passive motion dynamics. In this paper, we present AquaWAM, the first World Action Model designed for underwater embodied agents. Instead of predicting future images, AquaWAM models both action-conditioned and passive physical dynamics, including the thruster dead band, the inertial glide that outlasts each command, and ambient currents. Specifically, it senses through the DVL, IMU, pressure sensor and joint encoders, while cameras supply only semantics for understanding goals and target pose. By modeling compact navigation states rather than high-dimensional visual observations, AquaWAM substantially reduces the model size and computational cost compared with conventional WAMs. Experimentally, AquaWAM achieves a 72.6% task success rate across 20 underwater tasks on the USIM benchmark, outperforming existing methods while making action decisions 2.7x faster than U0 on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. Our model also remains effective when some onboard sensor measurements are unavailable. For example, without DVL velocity measurements, our method still achieves a 61.6% success rate, compared with 39.4% for U0.
bullets: Addresses inertia, buoyancy, drag, thruster dead bands, drift, and currents that conventional visual WAMs do not explicitly capture.
Uses DVL, IMU, pressure, and joint-encoder data for compact navigation-state prediction, while cameras provide semantic and target-pose information.
Achieves 72.6% success across 20 USIM underwater tasks and makes decisions 2.7× faster than U0 on a Jetson AGX Orin.
Maintains robustness under missing DVL velocity measurements, achieving 61.6% success versus 39.4% for U0.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of AquaWAM. Cameras supply the goal and the object pose; the predictor imagines each candidate two seconds ahead and executes the first 0.5 s of the best.

Figure 1: Motivation for a dynamics-aware World Action Model. Many existing World Action Models primarily predict future observations in video space, without explicitly modeling underwater vehicle dynamics. However, underwater motion is often strongly affected by passive physical factors such as buoyancy, drag, currents, and residual momentum, causing the vehicle state to continue evolving even after a control command is issued. Ignoring these dynamics can lead to inaccurate predictions of where and how the vehicle will move.

papers.selection_reason: World action model for underwater robots modeling action-conditioned and passive dynamics; directly relevant to embodied navigation and interactive world models.
papers.title: AquaWAM: A Dynamics-aware World Action Model for Underwater Embodied Agents
papers.tldr: AquaWAM models both commanded actions and persistent underwater dynamics to enable faster, robust world-action planning for underwater robots.

papers.abstract: As robots transition from structured factory settings into homes, they are required to interact with an ever-increasing variety of objects. Many tasks require grasping, and often it is not sufficient to just pick up the target object. Consider a task like "pouring coffee" --- to facilitate the subsequent pouring, the robot should grasp the mug by its handle. Existing learning-based approaches for grasping either find robust and collision-free grasps that are largely agnostic to the task (e.g., picking up the mug by its rim), or leverage foundation models to propose task-appropriate grasp locations that lack fine-grained physical grounding (e.g., reaching for and missing the handle). In this work, we bridge these approaches with a real-to-sim-to-real framework. Based on a single RGB-D observation, we construct a digital twin of the environment, query a large foundation model to propose grasps that align with the object's affordances and task description, and then optimize the proposals to ensure robustness and plausibility before executing the result on the real robot. Our key insight is that the grasp proposals of the foundation model should be regarded as semantic priors that serve as seeds for local, gradient-free optimization. We leverage Bayesian optimization with Thompson sampling to draw batches of nearby poses, which are subsequently evaluated in parallel under domain-randomized physics rollouts. The resulting grasp is both task-oriented and physically feasible for execution by the robot arm. Our full zero-shot real-world transfer only takes a few minutes and improves task-oriented grasping success by up to 33% as compared to other state-of-the-art pipelines. Our code is available here: https://github.com/VT-Collab/GraspTwin/
bullets: Addresses the gap between task-agnostic robust grasps and semantically appropriate but physically imprecise foundation-model proposals.
Builds a digital twin from a single RGB-D observation and uses the task description and object affordances to generate grasp priors.
Refines these priors with gradient-free Bayesian optimization using Thompson sampling and parallel domain-randomized physics rollouts.
Transfers the optimized grasp to a real robot in a few minutes without task-specific training.
Improves task-oriented grasping success by up to 33% over other state-of-the-art pipelines in real-world experiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of GraspTwin. (Left) We convert from real to sim by constructing a digital twin from an RGB-D image of the robot’s environment. We estimate the scene objects θ̂ and identify θ̂1, the target object for grasping. (Middle) We then render the target object θ̂1 from multiple perspectives, and use a VLM conditioned on the task τ to select task-oriented grasp positions P(i) VLM and an approach direction RVLM. (Right) These proposals become the initial guesses for localized grasp optimization. We simulate grasp poses T in the digital twin with object perturbations ∆θ. Batch Bayesian optimization with Thompson sampling enables parallel evaluations for gradient-free optimization. The minimum-cost grasp pose T∗ is executed by the real robot.

Fig. 1. We present GraspTwin, a zero-shot method for identifying grasps that are both task-oriented and physically feasible. Given a single RGBD image of the scene, GraspTwin constructs a digital twin. Within that digital twin we query foundation models to propose grasps that facilitate the downstream task. These semantically-aware grasps seed local optimization while enforcing physical constraints (e.g., unintended collisions) and domain randomization. The resulting grasp pose is then executed by the real arm.

papers.title: GraspTwin: Zero-Shot Task-Oriented Grasp Optimization via a Digital Twin

papers.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-powered multi-robot systems are vulnerable to semantic manipulation: an accepted false world-state claim can trigger a fleet-wide behavioral cascade, causing unnecessary replanning, increased path costs, congestion, or apparent mission infeasibility. Conditioning on a successful manipulation, we propose an active verification framework that contains its downstream effects before they propagate across the fleet. A dedicated verification module generates a structured Verify-Adapt-Hold plan: selected robots inspect consequential regions, a limited subset provisionally adapts when necessary, and the remaining robots retain their trusted plans. We evaluate the framework in a multi-robot transportation environment using injected false obstacle claims across different impacts and team sizes. Evaluation measures cascade containment, Sum-of-Costs, makespan, and coverage ratio. Results show that treating post-compromise verification as a team-level planning problem, rather than a binary trust decision, effectively limits the cascading physical consequences of semantic manipulation.
bullets: False claims can trigger fleet-wide replanning, congestion, higher path costs, or apparent mission failure.
The framework creates a structured Verify-Adapt-Hold plan: some robots inspect, a limited subset adapts, and others keep trusted plans.
It is evaluated in multi-robot transportation scenarios with injected false obstacle claims across varying impacts and team sizes.
The approach measures cascade containment, Sum-of-Costs, makespan, and coverage ratio.
Results indicate that team-level post-compromise planning contains physical consequences more effectively than a binary trust decision.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the proposed framework: A malicious input leads the compromised operator O to accept fake obstacles X and propose them as an occupancy set, which is never written to the trusted map. The verification module V , reasons over available physical evidence to produce a Verify–Adapt– Hold assignment (with Rest reserved for the close step). The initial call assigns every robot a verify, adapt or hold role and later calls reassign only the robots that triggered an event. A space-time A∗ planner executes the assignment.
Fig. 4: Sum of costs and Makespan variations across different scenarios and team sizes.

Fig. 1: (a) Under Naive Replan, all robots treat the false obstacle claim X as blocked and replan, propagating route changes even to robots whose paths do not intersect X . (b) Under Verify–Adapt–Hold, a selected robot verifies the claim from a stand-off, threatened robots provisionally adapt around unresolved claimed cells, and unaffected robots retain their trusted trajectories until physical evidence resolves the claim.

papers.title: Containing Behavioral Cascades from Manipulated Claims in LLM-Powered Multi-Robot Systems
papers.tldr: An active team-level verification strategy limits how false world-state claims spread through LLM-powered robot fleets after a successful manipulation.

papers.abstract: Humanoid hands require tactile feedback across the whole finger, not just the fingertip, to grasp and manipulate objects properly. Vision and proprioception alone cannot reliably provide this information, particularly when the hand's own fingers occlude the camera's view of the grasp. We present a low-cost tactile array for a humanoid finger, made from Velostat and conductive tape. The fingertip carries seven contact points including a 2x3 matrix wrapped across its front, left, and right faces, and a separate contact point at the tip. The proximal and middle phalanges each carry a single front-facing contact line. We measure the sensor's hysteresis and recovery time after release, through repeated loading and press-release tests. We also test a compliant, 3D-printed contact structure with a gap and a bump, inspired by similar designs in prior work, and show it cuts recovery time by 74% compared to a flush-contact baseline. We then show the sensor can produce distinct activation patterns for different contact geometries (flat, edge, corner) at the fingertip, and that it registers contact across all three phalanges during a grip. Finally, we discuss the limits of our fabrication changes and point to software-based compensation as a promising way to more directly fix the remaining hysteresis in the future.
bullets: Addresses the need for whole-finger tactile feedback when vision is occluded during grasping.
Uses conductive-tape and Velostat sensing: a multi-point fingertip array plus contact lines on the middle and proximal phalanges.
Characterizes hysteresis and recovery through repeated loading and press-release tests.
A compliant 3D-printed contact structure reduces recovery time by 74% versus a flush-contact baseline.
Detects distinct fingertip signatures for flat, edge, and corner contacts and registers contact across all phalanges during gripping.

papers.abstract: Autonomous navigation in previously unseen environments requires effective perception, persistent environmental representation, and collision avoidance while maintaining progress toward a goal. Existing perception-based methods often rely on prior maps or short-horizon observations, limiting their ability to exploit previously observed structure. We propose a memory-aware multi-sensor navigation framework that integrates LiDAR and RGB perception, online distance-field representation learning, and a stage-adaptive Modulated Control Barrier Function Quadratic Program (MCBF-QP). The framework persistently represents static infrastructure while tracking dynamic obstacles, enabling the MCBF-QP controller to exploit previously observed geometry for obstacle circumvention and adapt its safety constraints and guidance to local conditions. Experiments in complex indoor and outdoor environments demonstrate improved navigation efficiency and goal-reaching performance while maintaining collision avoidance in narrow passages and around dynamic obstacles.
bullets: Targets limitations of prior-map dependence and short-horizon perception in unseen environments.
Fuses LiDAR and RGB data with online distance-field representation learning.
Separately preserves static infrastructure while tracking dynamic obstacles.
Uses a stage-adaptive Modulated Control Barrier Function Quadratic Program for safe, context-aware control.
Experiments in complex indoor and outdoor settings show improved efficiency and goal reaching while avoiding collisions in narrow and dynamic scenarios.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed memory-aware multi-sensory perception and navigation framework, integrating onboard state estimation, dynamic obstacle detection, online environment representation learning, and stage-adaptive MCBF control for safe and live navigation in previously unmapped environments.

papers.title: Memory-Aware Multi-Sensor Perception for Efficient and Safe Navigation in Dynamic Environments
papers.tldr: A memory-aware LiDAR–RGB navigation framework persistently models environments and adapts safety control to navigate efficiently and collision-free around static and dynamic obstacles.

papers.abstract: Policies trained with imitation learning can accumulate errors over time, causing the robot to drift outside the training distribution. Existing methods mitigate this covariate shift by collecting additional data where the policy fails or is likely to fail. The first places the robot in unsafe conditions and the second requires choosing an appropriate noise distribution to collect new expert demonstrations under that noise. We propose Policy-Calibrated DAgger, a method that makes use of the properties of recent generative policies to estimate the policy's noise offline by using its own predicted action distribution. We measure a diffusion policy's spread of predicted actions at observations along the expert trajectory and measure its closed-loop error relative to a recorded trajectory. To address issues with measuring error in a multimodal action space, we guide the policy towards the trajectory during closed-loop control through partial denoising, and use properties of a diffusion model to unnormalize the measured error as if we did not guide it. We experiment in a scenario where a robot is tasked to reach an engine lever in a cluttered and narrow environment and show results in a 3D photorealistic simulator and a 2D planar reacher environment. We show that our method surpasses policies trained with dataset aggregation without noising and matches the performance of the best noise level in hindsight, without requiring a sweep over noise levels.
bullets: Imitation policies can accumulate errors and drift outside the expert-data distribution.
The method measures predicted-action spread and closed-loop error along expert trajectories using a diffusion policy.
Partial denoising guides rollouts toward the reference trajectory, enabling error estimation in multimodal action spaces.
Experiments in photorealistic 3D and 2D reaching environments show performance better than non-noised dataset aggregation and comparable to the best noise level selected in hindsight.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Our method augments the data collected during a DAgger-style data collection loop. The policy at data collection round k is trained on the base dataset D0, aggregated intervention data D1 . . .Dk and noised intervention data D̂1 . . . D̂k. To generate policy-calibrated noised intervention data: (a) We sample the policy open loop at every other timestep along the expert trajectory to estimate Σ̂t. (b) We sample blended trajectories between the policy and expert with partial denoising to estimate W . (c) We combine (a) and (b) to compute the policy noise per timestep Σα t . (d) We average the per-timestep Σα t across all data to obtain the pooled Σ̄α. In this example, the per-timestep ellipsoidal noise estimates average to become more isotropic. We sample states and corrective action pairs within this local area around the expert intervention.

Fig. 1: Our method estimates policy error while tracking a trajectory by making use of the probabilistic properties of generative policies. By sampling along pre-recorded expert data and making use of the model’s noise schedule to undo the normalizing effects of partial denoising towards the expert distribution in closed-loop control in simulation, we can estimate the policy’s noise with respect to the expert data. We can sample targeted recovery trajectories within this policy-calibrated noise distribution to reduce covariate shift between the policy’s visited states and the expert data.

Fig. 5: We evaluate our method in two cluttered goalreaching tasks with narrow passageways, where the robot often must untangle its links to make progress towards the goal. The 3D photorealistic physics simulation recreates our real mockup. We run ablations on the 3-link planar robot.

papers.title: Policy-Calibrated DAgger: Offline Calibrated Noise Injection for Imitation Learning
papers.tldr: Policy-Calibrated DAgger estimates an effective noise level from a diffusion policy offline, avoiding unsafe data collection and noise sweeps while improving imitation-learning robustness.

papers.abstract: Robust control under delayed sensory feedback remains a key challenge in both robotics and neuroscience. Classical cerebellar models explain delay compensation through forward prediction but fail to account for fast online corrections and rapid adaptation observed in biological systems. We propose a cerebellum-inspired control framework that combines multiplexed predictive representations with internal feedback. By jointly encoding kinematic variables and task-relevant error signals, the model enables accurate online correction despite delayed feedback. Furthermore, incorporating feedback within the cerebellar loop significantly accelerates adaptation, reducing learning time by an order of magnitude. Our results show that single-signal predictions are insufficient under delay, while multiplexing and feedback together provide a unified mechanism for online control and rapid learning.
bullets: Addresses robust control and biological motor learning with delayed feedback.
Jointly encodes kinematic variables and task-relevant error signals for online correction.
Adds internal feedback within the cortico-cerebellar loop to accelerate adaptation.
Finds that single-signal prediction is insufficient under delay, whereas multiplexing plus feedback supports both control and rapid learning.
Scope: focuses on a cerebellum-inspired framework for delayed-feedback motor control.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Multiplexed representations are required for robust online error correction. (A) Experimental reaching behavior: Hand trajectories across three learning phases: baseline (initial 30 trials), early adaptation (first 10 perturbation trials), and late adaptation (final 30 trials of a 150-trial epoch). Trajectories are colorcoded by target direction. Data adapted from [20]. (B) Single-variable predictive models: Model predictions on the test set across all phases. Performance is invariant regardless of whether the cerebellar (cb) module predicts velocity, position, or position error independently; notably, single-variable models fail to exhibit corrective re-aiming. (C) Multiplexed model: When the cerebellum integrates velocity, position, and position error, the system successfully reproduces the characteristic re-aiming behavior observed during early biological adaptation. (D) Direct feedback baseline: Performance in the absence of the cerebellar module, where control is driven exclusively by the delayed position error signal, resulting in systematic instability and poor target acquisition.

Fig. 1. Model architecture and learning mechanism. (A) Schematic of the proposed cortico-cerebellar model. (B) The cerebellar module learns through temporally specific, error-driven plasticity consistent with experimental observations. In particular, the discrepancy between the cerebellar prediction c and delayed behavioral variables (120 ms) drives synaptic updates via climbing fiber signals at the parallel fibre–Purkinje cell synapses.

Fig. 4. Cortical dynamics under different feedback architectures. (A) Model variant with both cerebellar feedback and direct delayed sensory input to the RNN. (B) Average change in RNN activity across time, computed from population activity r(t) obtained by averaging hidden-unit activity across neurons and trials; and comparison with experimental recordings [20]. Neural population activity is obtained by averaging firing rates across neurons, and both model and data are aligned to movement onset (Go cue) for temporal comparison.

Fig. 3. Error-driven adaptation dynamics. (A) Model architecture with delayed sensory feedback to the cerebellum. (B) Take-off angle error across baseline (white) and adaptation (blue) phases. (C) Task error (endpoint angular error) during early (first 10 trials) and late (last 30 trials) adaptation, comparing models and experimental data.
Fig. 5. Error-dependent feedback dynamics and adaptation performance.

Table 1. Performance of different cerebellar prediction and sensory feedback architectures across adaptation stages. Results are averaged across 3 seeds. Takeoff error is reported in angular deviation (deg), while task error is decomposed into directional and lateral components relative to the movement trajectory (cm). Values are reported as mean±std.

papers.title: Error- and Prediction-Driven Motor Learning in the Cortico-Cerebellar Loop
papers.tldr: A cerebellum-inspired controller combines multiplexed predictions with internal feedback to correct actions under delayed sensory feedback and learn much faster.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) leverage large-scale vision-language pretraining for semantic robot control, but often lack explicit foresight into how robot actions change the scene. World-Action Models (WAMs) address this limitation by conditioning policies on predicted futures, yet existing approaches typically rely on computationally expensive video generation with substantial pixel-level redundancy. We present LaWAM, a Latent World Action Model that exposes predictive dynamics to robot policies through compact latent visual subgoals instead of reconstructed future video. At the core of LaWAM is a latent-action-conditioned Latent World Model (LaWM). We obtain LaWM by training a latent action model in the latent space of a pretrained vision foundation model and repurposing its forward decoder to predict future observation features for scene evolution. LaWAM then conditions action generation on these predicted latent visual subgoals to enable dynamics-aware robot control. LaWAM achieves state-of-the-art or competitive success rates (SRs) across LIBERO (98.6% SR), RoboTwin (91.22% SR), and real-world manipulation tasks while retaining low-latency inference. LaWAM runs in 187 ms per action-chunk prediction and achieves up to 24x lower wall-clock latency than pixel-space WAMs.
authors: Jialei Chen, Kai Wang, Kang Chen, Shuaihang Chen, Feng Gao, Wenhao Tang, Zhiyuan Li, Weilin Liu, Zhuyu Yao, Boxun Li, Yuanbo Xu, Chao Yu
bullets: Addresses the limited action foresight of vision-language-action models and the computational cost of pixel-space world-action models.
Learns a latent action-conditioned world model in the latent space of a pretrained vision foundation model.
Uses predicted future observation features as compact visual subgoals for action generation.
Achieves strong performance on LIBERO, RoboTwin, and real-world manipulation tasks, including 98.6% and 91.22% success rates on LIBERO and RoboTwin.
Provides low-latency inference at 187 ms per action chunk, with up to 24× lower wall-clock latency than pixel-space WAMs.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of LaWAM. Stage 1 learns a latent-action-conditioned world model from visual transitions: an inverse-dynamics encoder infers latent actions, and the decoder is retained as LaWM to predict future observation features. Stage 2 integrates LaWM into a VLA policy: latent-action distillation teaches the policy to drive LaWM, whose predicted latent visual subgoal is passed to an Alternate-DiT action expert for subgoal-conditioned action generation.

papers.title: LaWAM: Latent World Action Models for Efficient Dynamics-Aware Robot Policies
papers.tldr: LaWAM enables dynamics-aware robot control by conditioning policies on efficiently predicted latent visual subgoals instead of costly future video.

papers.abstract: Agile robots require spatiotemporal intelligence to interpret scenes, reason about interactions, and anticipate future events. Yet it remains unclear how well foundation vision models support these capabilities, particularly from a moving egocentric camera, which is a natural view for robots. To investigate this, we collect an annotated tennis dataset and train a suite of vision models on spatiotemporal tasks. Our dataset contains egocentric video synchronized with five allocentric videos, estimated global positions, labeled contact times, and annotated stroke types. We then evaluate seven prediction tasks from egocentric images: 2D ego player and 3D ball localization, future player and ball trajectories, forehand or backhand stroke anticipation, time to the next ego player ball contact, and 3D ball position at that contact. We compare image encoders, video encoders, and vision-language models with jointly trained prediction heads. The best performing models achieve mean current-frame localization errors of 0.14 m for the ego player and 0.54 m for the ball, future forecasting errors of 0.34 m for the ego player and 0.91 m for the ball over 1.1 s, and a mean contact-time prediction error of 0.14 s. Auxiliary depth information substantially improves 3D ball localization, suggesting that inferring metric depth remains a challenge. Longer image histories do not improve ball forecasting, indicating that representations exploit scene context rather than rely solely on inter-frame motion. Finally, we propose a conditional diffusion model to generate whole-body kinematic tennis motion from vision encoder predictions on egocentric video at real-time rates, adapting movements as predictions are refined. These results move towards a deeper understanding of how foundation vision models can support real-time dynamic robots using egocentric video.

papers.abstract: Imitation policies that reliably execute most of a manipulation trajectory can still fail in localized regions requiring last-mile precision. Updating the full policy or exploring residual actions everywhere treats this local failure as a global learning problem. We introduce Adaptive Residual Correction (ARC), a lightweight post-training module that uses reinforcement learning (RL) to learn a residual correction on top of a frozen policy while using sparse human corrections to structure autonomous exploration. Rather than treating human corrections as imitation targets, ARC uses pre-intervention states to determine 'when' residual control should become active and correction geometry to determine 'where' in residual action space autonomous refinement should explore; task reward determines 'what' residual is ultimately executed. Across three precision-manipulation tasks on a real robot, ARC improves average task success from 33.3% to 75.0%. The human corrections define task-dependent 2-3 dimensional subspaces of the seven-joint residual space that retain 96.0-97.7% of squared correction magnitude. Together, these results show that sparse human corrections can localize and constrain autonomous post-training without requiring the observed correction itself to serve as the final action target.
authors: Anukriti Singh, Maxime Caniot, Pratap Tokekar, Firas Abi-Farraj
bullets: Addresses localized manipulation failures without retraining the full policy or exploring residual actions everywhere.
Learns a residual correction on top of a frozen policy, using human interventions to identify when correction activates and where exploration should occur.
Uses task reward—not the observed human action—as the final criterion for selecting residual behavior.
On three real-robot precision-manipulation tasks, average success rises from 33.3% to 75.0%.
Human corrections define 2–3D task-dependent subspaces capturing 96.0–97.7% of squared correction magnitude.

papers.abstract: Failure diagnosers for robot manipulation are increasingly vision--language models (VLMs), trained and evaluated on single-arm failures produced by perturbing a successful demonstration. Bimanual tool use adds failures of other kinds: a tool that slips out of its socket while still held, two correct gestures made at different times, and attempts that fail for two reasons at once. On a simulated bimanual tool-use task whose failure causes are read from the recorded trace, we measure what each sensing channel lets a diagnoser tell. The tool's slip is read on the tool hand; which hand was late is read on both arms, while a sensor on one hand reads its own hand's delay and at most part of the other's; and whether a late attempt was also pushed too weakly is not identifiable from passive sensing when the tool hand is late. Within two attempts, a repair policy that escalates when the cause is not identifiable repairs as many failures as one told the true cause. A VLM's internal state carries the late hand almost perfectly, along a direction no closer to the one its answer reads than a random one; whether the answer reports it depends on the wording of the question.
authors: Baptiste Bonin, Caro Strickland, Audrey Durand
bullets: Bimanual tool use introduces slips, timing mismatches between hands, and failures with multiple simultaneous causes.
Tool slips are detectable from the tool hand; identifying which hand was late generally requires observations from both arms.
A single-hand sensor may detect its own delay and only part of the other hand’s, while passive sensing cannot distinguish weak force from lateness when the tool hand is late.
An escalation-based repair policy matches oracle-cause performance within two attempts, despite ambiguous diagnoses.
The VLM internally represents which hand was late, but whether it reports that information depends strongly on question wording.

papers.title: Which Hand Was Late? Diagnosis for Robot Failure Recovery in Bimanual Tool Use
papers.tldr: Diagnosing bimanual robot failures requires sensing both arms and carefully phrased questions, but escalation can recover failures even when causes are ambiguous.

papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion in confined spaces requires continuous height adaptation across multiple locomotion modes, yet most existing approaches remain limited to height-adjustable bipedal walking. We present REACH, an RL-based hierarchical framework that enables a Unitree G1 humanoid to traverse height-constrained environments through variable-height bipedal walking and crawling. The learned policies regulate body height over complementary command ranges of 1.27--0.50m in bipedal locomotion and 0.50--0.20m in crawling, extending traversal beyond the clearance limits of crouched walking. To address contact-rich crawling dynamics, we employ a history-conditioned latent representation that captures terrain and interaction context from proprioceptive observations. A bidirectional transition policy further connects crouched bipedal locomotion and crawling across large kinematic and contact discontinuities. These skills are integrated with a LiDAR-based planner that converts point clouds into collision-free three-dimensional paths and locomotion commands, including proactive height targets. Real-world experiments demonstrate accurate height and velocity tracking, robust terrain traversal, reliable mode transitions and confined-space traversal with the proposed pipeline. Code and videos are available at https://aislab-sustech.github.io/REACH/.
authors: Shengzhang Xu, Yuning Guo, Weiyi Hu, Yifeng Xu, Zhongyu Li, He Kong
bullets: Addresses the limitation of bipedal systems that cannot traverse spaces below crouched-walking clearance.
Uses hierarchical reinforcement learning with history-conditioned latent representations for contact-rich crawling.
Employs a bidirectional transition policy to connect crouched walking and crawling despite major kinematic and contact changes.
Combines learned locomotion skills with LiDAR-based 3D planning and proactive body-height commands.
Real-world experiments show accurate tracking, terrain robustness, reliable mode transitions, and confined-space traversal.

papers.abstract: Multimodal intelligence can be viewed as human-guided co-evolution between worlds and agents through interaction. However, scaling this process faces two bottlenecks: constructing heterogeneous, verifiable environments is costly, and manual Harness iteration cannot keep pace with growing task diversity and complexity. A key insight is that tasks with different modalities and surface forms can share the same underlying capability requirements. We therefore introduce The Trinity, a recursive self-improvement framework coupling world generation with Harness evolution through three roles: Creator, Explorer, and Evolver. Drawing on verified execution trajectories, Evolver shifts the basis of task organization from surface categories to shared requirements, reorganizing the original task tree into a hierarchical capability tree. We introduce Capability-Driven Real2Sim2Real: for heterogeneous tasks at the same node, Creator abstracts their common requirements into simplified, verifiable simulated worlds for capability learning, while evaluation on original tasks measures transfer. Along this capability tree, Explorer progressively evolves reusable capability modules through selective inheritance, forming a Harness tree whose validated updates accumulate across iterations within a fixed topology. The resulting Harnesses specialize in different capabilities, motivating a Capability-Aware Harness Router that uses public task information to select compatible module configurations from the tree. Our evolved Harnesses improve mean performance by 34 points across 28 training benchmarks and 26 points across 18 unseen benchmarks, including two real-world embodied tasks.

Builds a hierarchical capability tree and a Capability-Aware Harness Router to select compatible module configurations.

papers.selection_reason: Recursive self-improvement framework for multimodal agents with world generation and capability learning, evaluated on real-world embodied tasks.
papers.title: The Trinity:Capability-Driven Recursive Self-Improvement for Multimodal Agents
papers.tldr: The Trinity enables recursive self-improvement for multimodal agents by organizing tasks around shared capabilities and jointly evolving simulated worlds and reusable Harness modules.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models offer a scalable alternative to costly real-world interaction for improving robot policies. However, existing world-model-based methods largely treat world models as forward-only surrogates of the physical environment, leaving untapped a capability no physical environment affords: rewinding to past decision points to explore counterfactual futures. We introduce Rollback, a policy improvement paradigm that turns world models from passive simulators into counterfactual engines: it rolls back to critical decision points, branches into alternative actions, and contrasts their outcomes to attribute success to individual decisions. This concentrates imagination where it matters most and distills counterfactual outcomes into fine-grained, action-level supervision without a separately learned value model. We build a scalable training system that unifies distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution, forming a self-reinforcing cycle: real-world experience continually sharpens the world model, and a sharper world model in turn drives further policy improvement. We term the world-model side of this cycle test-time physics grounding, a capability that hand-built physics simulators lack: while the world model serves as the training environment, real transitions from the policy it trains correct its dynamics through a lightweight LoRA pipeline. Experiments on three challenging real-world tasks show that Rollback improves success rates over the strongest baseline by an absolute 10.67%, 11.11%, and 11.85% on block extraction, ball tossing, and tabletop curling, respectively, while achieving more stable improvement throughout training. Although initialized from teleoperated demonstrations far below human level, Rollback surpasses the average success rate of human players on both ball tossing and tabletop curling within 8 hours of training.
authors: Jiayi Luo, Yang Zhang, Liliang Chen, Nan Wang, Chen Gao, Boxiang Qiu, Zhuoxuan Li, Baorui Peng, Chuankang Li, Yuxiang Yan, Si Liu, Qingyun Sun, Shuicheng Yan, Maoqing Yao, Jianxin Li, Guanghui Ren
bullets: Addresses the limitation of forward-only world models, which cannot identify which decisions caused success or failure.
Rolls back to critical points, branches over alternative actions, and converts outcome comparisons into fine-grained action-level supervision without a separate value model.
Combines distributed world-model search with asynchronous real-robot execution in a self-reinforcing training cycle.
On three real-world tasks, it improves success rates over the strongest baseline by 10.67%, 11.11%, and 11.85% absolute.
Surpasses average human success on ball tossing and tabletop curling within 8 hours, despite starting from below-human teleoperated demonstrations.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Rollback. (a) Experience-backtracking tree search restores cached world-model contexts to explore informative branches without regenerating shared prefixes. The world model predicts both multi-view observations and the robot’s proprioceptive state. (b) Tree-structured value estimation aggregates downstream outcomes into relative action-quality labels for policy training without an additional value model. (c) World model–policy co-evolution continually incorporates real trajectories to refine the world model through test-time physics grounding (LoRA SFT followed by DMD) while the policy keeps improving.

Figure 3: Rollback training infrastructure. The cloud runs tree search on GPU workers, stores real trajectories and tree supervision in the Experience Fabric, and trains the policy and the world model in parallel. Edge sites run policy inference for their robots, buffer trajectories for upload, and cache policy snapshots. Robots send observations to their edge site and execute the returned actions. Policy snapshots are sent to search workers and edge sites; world-model snapshots are sent only to search workers.

Figure 1: From real-world interaction to learning in world models. (a) Real-world RL incurs costly physical interaction. (b) Forward-rollout world-model RL spends much of its interaction budget on less informative exploration. (c) Our proposed Rollback enables high-value exploration and dense supervision through experiencebacktracking tree search, while real-world feedback refines the world model.

Figure 4: Training process of Rollback. The robot continually executes the latest policy and uploads real trajectories Dreal. The policy is continually updated with tree supervision Dtree from rollback search, while the world model is repeatedly adapted to real trajectories via LoRA SFT and DMD; each search tree uses the latest versions of both.

papers.abstract: General-purpose embodied intelligence requires robots to coordinate diverse skills over long horizons, track task progress, and recover from failures. Specialist policies alone do not ensure task-level reliability, while powerful multimodal agents rely on costly reasoning and external experience that compact models struggle to reproduce. We introduce OmniBrain-0, a lightweight unified embodied agent that coordinates manipulation and navigation through a shared high-level decision model, integrating task understanding, planning, progress tracking, and feedback-driven recovery. Our progressive training framework combines embodied pretraining, domain-specialized agent distillation, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD). It distills powerful teachers' interaction experience into manipulation and navigation experts, then consolidates their decision capabilities into OmniBrain-0. Unification therefore occurs within the learned decision model rather than only at the tool interface. We further introduce Rubric-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement (RSI), a data flywheel in which a Meta-Agent turns execution evidence into refined rubrics, step-level reminders, and verified trajectories for domain-expert updates before their reconsolidation into OmniBrain-0 through MOPD. We evaluate OmniBrain-0 on LIBERO-Pro, LIBERO-Plus, RoboCasa365, RoboTwin 2.0, and R2R-CE Val-Unseen, as well as multiple real-world manipulation tasks. OmniBrain-0 combines strong cross-domain task performance with substantially lower inference and execution overhead than its closed-source teacher, demonstrating efficient transfer and consolidation of embodied capabilities into a compact unified agent.
bullets: Targets reliable long-horizon robot behavior, where specialist policies and costly multimodal agents have limitations.
Uses a shared high-level decision model for task understanding, planning, progress tracking, and feedback-driven recovery.
Trains progressively through embodied pretraining, agent distillation, and multi-teacher on-policy distillation to consolidate domain expertise.
Introduces Rubric-Guided Recursive Self-Improvement, which converts execution evidence into rubrics, reminders, and verified trajectories for iterative updates.
Evaluated across simulated manipulation, navigation, and real-world manipulation tasks, showing strong cross-domain performance with lower inference and execution overhead than its teacher.

papers.abstract: Collecting tactile demonstrations on robots is costly and slow, motivating the use of lower-cost human tactile gloves for scalable data collection. However, human capacitive/piezoresistive gloves and robotic tactile sensors differ fundamentally in transduction principle, sensor layout, spatial resolution, and dynamic response, making alignment of raw sensor channels ill-posed. To address this problem, we present TACROSS, a scalable system for learning from human touch and transferring it to robots that bridges this heterogeneity by aligning tactile streams at the level of contact events rather than raw sensor values. The hardware component of TACROSS integrates a piezoresistive glove with five layers and a cost of USD 10.86 with 285 sensing points. To align contact semantics, we design canonicalizers and residual adapters that map heterogeneous signals into a shared tactile latent with 256 dimensions via a temporal Transformer with attention across fingers. We further introduce a robot-grounded policy learning scheme in which robot demonstrations provide the sole source of ground-truth action supervision, while human demonstrations support tactile representation learning and provide confidence-weighted auxiliary supervision through valid retargeted hand targets. We evaluate our system on four contact-rich manipulation tasks. Compared to conventional teleoperation, our proposed system achieves a 3.5-fold efficiency improvement while reducing demonstration acquisition equipment cost by 95.7%. We will open-source the TACROSS hardware and software system and publicly release a tactile dataset comprising over 150 hours of recordings. Project page: https://tacross-touch-project.github.io/.
bullets: Addresses the costly, slow collection of tactile robot demonstrations and the mismatch between human gloves and robotic tactile sensors.
Uses a $10.86 five-layer glove with 285 sensing points, canonicalizers, residual adapters, and a 256-dimensional temporal Transformer tactile latent.
Learns robot policies with robot demonstrations as the only ground-truth action supervision, while human data aids tactile representation learning and auxiliary supervision.
Evaluated on four contact-rich tasks, achieving 3.5× higher efficiency and 95.7% lower demonstration-equipment cost than conventional teleoperation.
Plans to release the hardware, software, and a tactile dataset with over 150 hours of recordings.

papers.abstract: Learning contact-rich dexterous manipulation from human demonstrations provides a scalable source of interaction data, yet transferring such skills to robots remains challenging due to unreliable human--robot correspondence. Existing human-to-robot transfer methods typically rely on visual appearance or motion similarity, which may associate similar motions with different contact states and force patterns. Tactile dynamics provide interaction-aware cues to distinguish manipulation processes with similar motions but different contact states. We introduce tactile-guided optimal transport (TacOT), a framework for human-to-robot contact-rich manipulation. TacOT leverages action--tactile dynamic time warping to identify human--robot demonstration correspondences with consistent interaction dynamics and uses these correspondences to guide soft optimal transport alignment in a shared policy representation space. This enables human demonstrations to provide contact-rich supervision for robot policy learning without requiring predefined frame-level human--robot pairing. Across four real-world dexterous manipulation tasks, TacOT improves closed-loop success rates over action-guided OT by up to 17 points on in-distribution tasks and 20 points under targeted human-to-robot out-of-distribution transfer. Further analyses show that tactile-guided correspondence selects demonstration pairs with more consistent contact dynamics and produces latent representations that better reflect interaction-state evolution. These results demonstrate that tactile dynamics provide an effective semantic signal for establishing reliable human-to-robot correspondence in contact-rich dexterous manipulation.

papers.abstract: When rewards are sparse, reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) often uses hints or intermediate guidance to generate more successful rollouts. This enrichment biases policy-gradient updates unless corrected via importance weights, but existing methods omit correction or truncate importance weights in order to avoid the high variance of correction. It thus remains unclear what exactly is gained or lost in RLVR by correcting enriched rollouts. We show, mathematically, that omitted or truncated correction implicitly reweights the defined reward, and we decompose the resulting gradient error into scale, rotation, and variance to explain their distinct effects on learning. To make correction practical, we develop a novel sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) weight correction mechanism that, under stability and particle-order assumptions, tempers the exponential compounding of standard correction variance over the length of a sample to an additive accumulation. We then apply our analysis of enrichment to interpreting the results of a fine-tune of Qwen3-1.7B on a sparse band of OpenMathReasoning, establishing a concrete mechanism of how enrichment, both corrected and uncorrected, helps avoid collapse in sparse domains. Our main contribution is to understand, in general, how enrichment and correction can affect training, as opposed to claiming that either mode of operation is superior to unenriched RL.
bullets: Omitting or truncating importance correction implicitly changes the effective reward and biases policy-gradient updates.
The resulting gradient error is decomposed into scale, rotation, and variance effects.
A sequential Monte Carlo correction mechanism changes standard variance growth from exponential compounding to additive accumulation under stability and particle-order assumptions.
Analysis of a Qwen3-1.7B fine-tune on sparse OpenMathReasoning shows how corrected and uncorrected enrichment can help prevent collapse in sparse domains.
The work explains these mechanisms rather than claiming enrichment or correction is universally superior to unenriched RL.

papers.abstract: Most current grasp synthesis systems are trained offline and remain fixed during deployment. While this works well when deployment conditions resemble the training data, performance can degrade when robots encounter conditions they have not seen before, such as unfamiliar objects. In this work, we present a continual-learning framework for single-view 6-DoF grasp synthesis for a parallel-jaw gripper in cluttered scenes. Rather than finetuning a large parametric model, our method adapts through memory in a learned embedding space: grasp outcomes update future grasp scores, while optional user demonstrations are recalled and transferred to new scenes as additional candidate grasps. We evaluate our method in simulation and in extensive real-world experiments comprising over 1500 grasp trials. We show that our method matches the performance of existing 6-DoF grasping baselines even before adaptation, improves online on unseen objects from categories absent or underrepresented during training, and supports long-horizon continual learning with limited forgetting. In real-world experiments, our method reaches over 90\% success rates on several challenging object categories after only 50 online grasp attempts. Videos and code at https://giuschio.github.io/cl_grasping/.
bullets: Addresses performance degradation when deployed robots encounter objects or conditions unlike offline training data.
Uses a learned embedding-space memory to update future grasp scores from grasp outcomes and transfer recalled user demonstrations as candidate grasps.
Targets parallel-jaw grasping in cluttered scenes from a single view.
Evaluated in simulation and over 1,500 real-world grasp trials.
Maintains baseline-level performance before adaptation, improves on unseen objects, and supports long-horizon learning with limited forgetting.

papers.title: Continual Learning for 6-DoF Grasp Synthesis via Experience and Demonstrations
papers.tldr: A memory-based continual-learning framework adapts single-view 6-DoF grasp synthesis to unfamiliar objects using grasp outcomes and optional demonstrations, achieving over 90% success on several challenging categories after 50 online attempts.

papers.abstract: General Purpose Service Robot (GPSR) tasks, as defined in the RoboCup@Home benchmark, require robots to interpret diverse natural language commands and generate multi-step action sequences in real home environments. Conventional Single Prompt (SP) approaches suffer from context bloat and the "Lost in the Middle" phenomenon, leading to unreliable task planning. We propose an LLM chaining architecture that separates instruction classification and action generation into two specialized stages, reducing per-inference prompt length by approximately 45% while improving planning consistency. We evaluate our method using 100 randomly generated GPSR commands across three language models spanning local open-source and frontier cloud deployment contexts. Results show consistent planning improvements over SP across all models, with gains of up to +37 percentage points on local models. Further, real-robot execution experiments on the Toyota Human Support Robot (HSR) reveal that planning success alone does not guarantee task completion, with 6 of 10 tasks completing successfully and execution-layer failures identified as the primary remaining bottleneck.
bullets: Targets unreliable multi-step planning for General Purpose Service Robot tasks caused by prompt bloat and the “Lost in the Middle” effect.
Uses two specialized LLM stages: instruction classification followed by action generation.
Reduces per-inference prompt length by approximately 45%.
Evaluation on 100 generated GPSR commands across three language models found consistent planning improvements over single-prompt prompting, with gains up to 37 percentage points on local models.
In 10 Toyota HSR robot trials, 6 tasks completed successfully; execution-layer failures were the primary remaining limitation.

papers.abstract: Cross-embodiment learning has shown that a single model, such as a vision-language-action (VLA) model, can learn state representations and manipulation skills that can be applied across heterogeneous robots to accomplish various tasks. We hypothesize that the same holds for safety enforcement. The reasoning required to satisfy a safety constraint, such as detecting an obstacle, recognizing that it should be avoided, and selecting a safe abstract action, is largely shared across robots. What differs across embodiments is how the abstract safe action is realized: morphology, kinematics, and dynamics determine which actions are safe and feasible. Consequently, the same action can be safe for one robot and unsafe for another. This is especially important for generalist manipulation policies that operate in a common end-effector action space without explicitly capturing how safety depends on the robot's morphology and kinematics. We propose embodiment-conditioned safety filtering, in which a Hamilton-Jacobi reachability-based value function and its corresponding safety-maximizing policy are shared across robots. Using a morphology-aware latent representation of the robot and its environment, we perform Hamilton-Jacobi reachability analysis directly in latent space so that the learned safety concepts can generalize across embodiments while remaining explicitly conditioned on each robot's morphology and kinematics. We evaluate our approach across five bimanual robot embodiments and five manipulation tasks with whole-body collision-avoidance constraints. Our results show that a single policy, jointly trained across five manipulation tasks and four embodiments, exhibits zero-shot generalization to a held-out embodiment, reducing the nominal policy's collision rate. They also show that training using more embodiments improves generalization.
bullets: Safety reasoning can be shared across robots, but safe action execution depends on each robot’s morphology, kinematics, and dynamics.
The method performs Hamilton–Jacobi reachability analysis in a morphology-aware latent space.
A shared safety value function and safety-maximizing policy are conditioned on the robot and environment.
Evaluations cover five bimanual embodiments and five manipulation tasks with whole-body collision constraints.
Joint training across tasks and embodiments generalizes zero-shot to a held-out embodiment and reduces nominal-policy collisions; more embodiments improve generalization.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) achieves strong performance in sequential decision-making but remains brittle under dynamic uncertainty and distributional shifts. Robust Adversarial Reinforcement Learning (RARL) improves robustness via worst-case perturbations, but existing approaches frequently suffer from unstable optimization and degraded value estimation. In particular, overly aggressive adversaries can drive the agent toward uninformative failure states, while adversarial perturbations amplify disagreement between double critics and introduce biased value targets. We propose a unified framework, RACER (Risk-sensitive robust Adversarial critic ConsistEncy-regularized Reinforcement learning), that revisits adversarial RL from a risk-sensitive perspective. First, we introduce a state-dependent adversarial objective that adaptively regulates perturbation strength, suppressing harmful disturbances while preserving informative exploration. Second, we propose critic consistency regularization to reduce disagreement between Q-value estimators and stabilize learning. Comprehensive experiments on challenging continuous control benchmarks demonstrate that RACER consistently improves performance, robustness, and training stability over strong robust RL baselines.
bullets: Targets brittleness in RL caused by dynamic uncertainty, distribution shifts, and adversarial perturbations.
Uses a state-dependent adversarial objective to limit harmful disturbances while preserving informative exploration.
Adds critic consistency regularization to reduce disagreement between Q-value estimators and stabilize value targets.
Experiments on challenging continuous-control benchmarks show improved performance, robustness, and training stability over robust RL baselines.

papers.abstract: Action-chunked vision-language-action (VLA) policies improve inference efficiency, but limited feedback within committed action chunks can lead to accumulated execution errors. Residual adaptation can correct such deviations without retraining the VLA; however, existing corrections are typically optimized for reference-action consistency without explicitly considering their downstream consequences. To address this limitation, we present Cerebellum-Inspired Consequence-Aware Residual Governance (CereVLA), a unified framework that integrates lightweight residual refinement and predictive consequence evaluation into frozen VLA execution. Corrective actions are first generated by flow-based residual refinement, and their short- and interval-horizon consequences are then evaluated by a recurrent state-space model and a history-aware classifier. Residual corrections predicted to be unfavorable are selectively suppressed by a lightweight governor. Comparisons with state-of-the-art methods on LIBERO-10 and LIBERO-GOAL demonstrate the effectiveness of CereVLA. On SO-101, CereVLA increases task success from 57.5% to 90.0% and reduces mean control steps by 19.6% among successful trials, relative to the frozen SmolVLA baseline.
bullets: Addresses error accumulation caused by limited feedback during committed action chunks.
Uses flow-based residual refinement with short- and interval-horizon consequence prediction.
A recurrent state-space model and history-aware classifier evaluate correction outcomes.
A lightweight governor selectively suppresses unfavorable residual actions.
On SO-101, success rose from 57.5% to 90.0%, while mean successful-trial control steps fell by 19.6% versus frozen SmolVLA.

papers.abstract: An animal with a weakened limb does not necessarily switch its gait, instead it unloads the affected limb, re-coordinates the remaining limbs, and scales its response with injury severity. This graded adaptation allows locomotion to persist despite partial loss of limb strength, rather than requiring a discrete transition between healthy and failed. Inspired by this behavior, we propose SG-CPG, a central pattern generator (CPG) for quadruped locomotion under continuous actuator degradation. SG-CPG preserves a frozen healthy CPG policy and introduces two severity-driven gates: a residual gate that re-coordinates all four legs and an amplitude gate that progressively shortens the weakened leg's stride as degradation increases. We emulate progressive degradation through two mechanisms: lowering the joint torque ceiling (ceiling mechanism) and scaling its low-level controller gains (gain mechanism), representing distinct forms of actuator weakening. Our simulations on a Unitree Go2 show that SG-CPG maintains a trot gait with 100% survival across an omnidirectional command schedule under 95% joint strength loss while tracking commands within 8%. Under a lowered torque ceiling, removing either severity path, the residual's severity observation or the amplitude gate, raises clipping at the weakened joint from 4.4% to 13.6% and 26.3% of steps at an 80% loss. On a real Go2, SG-CPG survives 28 of 29 forward and turning trials with up to 93% calf torque degradation. These results show that severity-gated adaptation can extend a healthy locomotion policy to progressive actuator degradation without treating the fault as a discrete failure.
bullets: Motivated by biological injury adaptation, the method avoids forcing a discrete healthy-to-failed gait transition.
It freezes a healthy CPG policy and adds a severity-driven residual gate for whole-body re-coordination plus an amplitude gate that shortens the weakened leg’s stride.
The approach models degradation through reduced joint torque ceilings or low-level controller gains.
In simulation, the Go2 maintained a trot with 100% survival under 95% joint-strength loss and command tracking within 8%.
Real-robot trials survived 28 of 29 forward and turning tests with up to 93% calf-torque degradation; scope is demonstrated on the Unitree Go2.

papers.abstract: We present and tackle two problems associated with deploying Foundation Models (FMs) on Embodied Agents performing navigation: 1) Training bias in FMs leading to poor personalization in unseen environments, and 2) Limited FM context length hindering success, especially on long horizon tasks. Our solution for the former involves priming the FM with human-habit data mined from the scene and our solution for the latter involves active memory management via a novel `memory head' augmentation. We first present a taxonomy of existing literature on FM-based Embodied Navigation, and highlight these limitations. We then present our approaches, Transit-Aware Planning (TAP) and MemCtrl to address the limitations. With TAP, we present real-world results in a lab environment with a Turtlebot for personalized target finding that shows an average improvement of 18% over a non-TAP baseline. On MemCtrl, we report a 6% average improvement across various embodied tasks, with 20% on long instruction subsets, all while using nearly half the context used in the baseline model. Motivated by these result, we present our stance the deployability of FM-based embodied agents in real-world environments, and highlight open research directions.
bullets: Targets poor personalization in unseen environments and context-length limits on long-horizon navigation.
Transit-Aware Planning (TAP) primes models with human-habit data mined from the scene.
MemCtrl adds a memory head for active context management.
In a Turtlebot lab setting, TAP improves personalized target finding by 18% over its baseline.
MemCtrl improves embodied-task performance by 6% overall and 20% on long-instruction subsets while using nearly half the baseline context.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Taxonomy: We consider 3 classes of FM-based methods for Embodied Navigation. The gray boxes indicate the classical pipeline. 1) FM as a Perceiver (in red) takes the input observation and instruction and produces semantic groundings to be used by a planner. 2) FM as a Planner (in blue) uses the outputs of a perception module to produce subgoals or sequences. 3) FM as a policy goes directly from the input to action.

Fig. 3:Real-world Experiment: We create a simulation of our lab environment and define DOMs for priming FM-based TAP agents. The first phase involves gathering images from the scene and constructing a topological scene graph (in blue). The graph is then converted to a Dynamic Object Map (DOM) that models the object dynamics, which is then used to train a transit model T for the transit-aware agent (TAP). Finally, we transfer this to the real-world for personalized assistance. Please refer to the video attached for more visuals. Table 2 presents our results in this environment.

Fig. 7:Base Performance on EB-Habitat: Here, we compare the performance of GPT-4o vs Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Ins, with various memory augmentations. The green box around the image indicates successful task completion, while the red box indicates otherwise. The images are agent observations. Note GPT-4o takes more steps to complete the task. On the other hand, µ boosts the performance of a significantly weaker model, and in this scenario, even doing it quicker with µRL. Grayed out images indicate discarded memories.

Fig. 4: MemCtrl (µ): We present MemCtrl, a novel memory filtering scheme to improve decision making performance on small MLLMs tackling embodied tasks. Our approach proposes a trainable memory head (green box) that learns to actively filter out redundant observations on-the-go. This form of active filtering aims to alleviate issues inefficient retrieval from stored observations, while also enabling scalable deployment on FMs as a detachable memory head.

Fig. 6: Context Growth: MemCtrl (in blue) shows for lesser memory usage and better performance over a baseline Memo-style (in red) approach that stores the entire history as context. These results are on the EB-Habitat environment with Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Ins augmented with an offline supervised µ, using GPT-4o data.

Fig. 2: Finding Portable Objects: Objects at home move over time. Modelling these movements in simulation would help with personalized inference during deployment. In this figure, an embodied agent is tasked with finding a wallet that changes positions between 9:00 and 9:20. Pwallet represents the transit route of the wallet. The Transit-Aware Planner (TAP) is learns routines on ‘real2sim’ data which primes the FM-based navigation agents with these routines for temporally informed decision-making.

Fig. 8: Long Horizon performance on EB-Habitat: We notice that on long horizon tasks, the expert tends to end the task early by hastily assuming that it is done (finishing after placing one plate instead of all plates). Memory heads highlight unique performance improvements, with µRL exhibiting a more exploratory nature by continuing to place new objects at the right counter, and µExpert being more exploitative by repeating the same activity over and over, with a single plate. Investigating this is part of a future study. Note: Grayed out images indicate discarded memories.

Fig. 5:MemCtrl Variants: We experiment with 3 variants. The simple case acts as a non-trained baseline, where the MLLM is directly queried about storage. In the offline supervised case, µ is first pretrained using expert answers from a high performing, expert MLLM (GPT-4o here). This trained binary classifier then acts as a head on top of the MLLM backbone. In the Online RL case, we train the memory head online as a policy network. We use a sparse reward on task success and a dense reward on action success. Note that MemCtrl is trained as a detachable head that takes the latent MLLM embeddings as input.

Table 3: MemCtrl Results: We augment Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Ins with the 3 variations of MemCtrl on 5 subsets of EB-ALFRED and EB-Habitat [45] across 3 trials. Note the improve performance overall of adding the memory head µ. In particular, we note superior performance on long context and complex instructions, which tend to be long horizon where memory is particularly useful.

Table 1:Object Transit Scenarios: Portable targets transition in a topological graph under structured scenarios inspired by human habits. In the random case, the portable objects can move to any room at any time during each episode. In the routine cases, the rooms that the target objects can travel to are fixed.

Table 2: Real World SR: We report average success rates for finding portable objects in our lab environment over 50 episodes. Note the improved performance of the TAP-LLM approach over a vanilla LLM scheme ( [13]). Transit awareness helps improve performance in the routine cases, where paths have structure.

papers.selection_reason: Fits embodied navigation with foundation models and active memory management for long-horizon tasks.
papers.title: Deploying Foundation Models for Embodied Navigation
papers.tldr: The paper improves foundation-model-based embodied navigation by addressing personalization bias and limited context through habit-aware planning and active memory control.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have made substantial progress in robotic manipulation, but their generalization remains constrained by the diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Human videos provide much broader behavioral and environmental experience, while learning from them faces a fundamental trade-off between scalable data and explicit action grounding. We introduce ThinkWorld, a VLA learning framework that grounds action reasoning in world dynamics and strengthens it through reinforcement learning with world imagination. ThinkWorld represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD), a sequence of discrete motion tokens that captures the intermediate dynamics connecting the current world to a future state and serves as a common action representation across embodiments. We first initialize CoD with action-labeled demonstrations, then predict the future induced by each CoD and reinforce those whose predictions better match the observed outcome. This enables videos without action annotations to provide direct supervision from observed state transitions, allowing human and robot experience to refine the same reasoning space. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate effective human-to-robot transfer and strong generalization to unseen tasks and environments.
authors: Chaehyun Kim, Chi-Pin Huang, Jisoo Kim, Min-Hung Chen, Yu-Chiang Frank Wang, Seungryong Kim, Fu-En Yang
bullets: Addresses limited diversity and coverage of action-labeled robot demonstrations.
Represents each action thought as a Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) linking the current state to a future state through discrete motion tokens.
Initializes CoD from labeled demonstrations, then reinforces chains whose predicted futures match observed outcomes.
Uses unlabeled human videos as supervision through observed state transitions, aligning human and robot experience in one reasoning space.
Simulation and real-robot experiments show human-to-robot transfer and generalization to unseen tasks and environments.

figures.caption: Figure 2: ThinkWorld architecture and training stages. In stage (a), supervised fine-tuning (SFT) tokenizes robot actions and annotated human hand motions into a unified discrete motion space to ground Chain-ofDynamics (CoD) reasoning, while CoD-conditioned imagination predicts the future visual feature. In stage (b), reinforcement learning (RL) uses the alignment between imagined and observed futures as a scalable reward for CoD reasoning over human and robot videos, strengthening action reasoning without motion annotations and improving guidance for continuous control.

Figure 7: Effect of Chain-of-Dynamics (CoD) on future prediction. We compare future DINO predictions under generated, shuffled, empty, and no-CoD conditions against the current and future ground-truth features. The generated CoD captures the future-state structure, whereas the other variants largely remain similar to the current state and fail to reflect the expected future change.

papers.abstract: Dexterous manipulation with multi-fingered hands is the next frontier of robotics, yet learned hand skills remain limited to simple grasps or basic repeated motions, such as rotating an object. As robots attempt more demanding in-hand maneuvers, safety, such as not dropping the object, becomes critical, yet it is rarely measured. We study in-hand object pose reaching, a task that demands diverse and difficult grasps: moving an object to almost any position and orientation within reach of the fingers, at any wrist orientation, through long sequences of consecutive goals. We present a recipe for training such policies for a LEAP hand in simulation without human data, built on a range of insights, from diverse resets and goals via generated grasp datasets to an adaptive friction curriculum. With careful system identification, the policies transfer zero-shot to the real hand, using either motion capture or a single wrist-mounted depth camera, and prove remarkably capable and robust. On top of the task policy, we add a learned residual safety filter with adjustable conservativeness, letting us tune the balance between performance and safety and greatly reduce object drops. In 13.3 hours of real-robot evaluation over 4,800 unseen goals across 4 objects and diverse wrist orientations, the state-based policy reaches 95.2% of goals within 2 cm and 0.4 rad, and the filter cuts its drops by 75% while still reaching 91.5% of goals. The policies can also spin a lightbulb held in an arbitrary pose, reach out-of-distribution goals, withstand fast arm motion and perturbations, and, needing only a wrist camera, serve as portable skills such as screwing in a lightbulb. We release the full recipe as a platform for studying performance, reliability, and safety in high-dimensional dexterous systems. Videos and more are available at https://ian-chuang.github.io/dexsafe/.
authors: Ian Chuang, Hiya Shah, Vamsi Chilamkur, Iman Soltani, Claire Tomlin
bullets: Targets diverse, long-horizon object position and orientation goals under arbitrary wrist orientations.
Trains a LEAP-hand policy without human data using generated grasp resets and goals, adaptive friction curricula, and system identification.

Across 4,800 unseen goals, the state-based policy reaches 95.2% within 2 cm and 0.4 rad; safety filtering reduces drops by 75% while retaining 91.5% goal success.
Demonstrations include lightbulb spinning, out-of-distribution goals, fast arm motion, perturbation recovery, and portable camera-based screwing skills.

papers.abstract: Scientific discovery often begins with an unexpected observation that prompts a new research question. In a world with altered physical laws, can large language models (LLMs) notice unexpected behavior, such as heavier objects falling more slowly, and discover the law through experiments without being told what to investigate? To evaluate this ability, we introduce LongChang, an automated framework that creates simulated worlds with altered physics, where one or more laws differ from ordinary physics. The evaluated LLMs act as explorers, manipulating objects and building tools to investigate their own questions without research tasks or hints about these laws. Separate LLM agents generate and review scenes, review tool designs, and evaluate reports for correctness and experimental support using the altered physical laws and exploration records. These records guide scene evolution for further exploration, allowing the full cycle to run without human intervention. Among 12 LLMs, GPT-6-Astra achieves a discovery rate of 16.7%, while the other 11 score 0%. The exploration records reveal uninvestigated anomalies and only partial identification of the altered physical laws.
authors: Zhen Yang, Wen Wang, Xander Xu, Ying-Cong Chen
bullets: Creates simulated worlds where one or more physical laws differ from ordinary physics.

Separate agents generate and review scenes, tools, and scientific reports, using exploration records to evolve experiments.

Exploration records showed that agents often noticed anomalies but only partially identified the underlying laws.
