papers.abstract: Supernumerary robotic fingers augment human dexterity by enabling a single hand to perform complex "hold-and-manipulate" tasks that typically require bimanual coordination. However, existing devices are often hindered by bulky hardware that limits interaction to large objects and rely on explicit hand motion triggers that lack environmental context. To address these challenges, we present EgoThumb, a fully open-source, vision-driven supernumerary robotic thumb. EgoThumb features a compact, dual tendon-driven finger whose actuation is relocated to the forearm, reducing distal weight while enabling precise active joint control. The system utilizes a visual imitation learning policy that maps egocentric images from a palm-facing camera directly to continuous joint positions. By implicitly decoding human intent from visual cues capturing both the hand and the object of interest, EgoThumb achieves robust autonomous manipulation and strong generalization across diverse users and environments. All hardware designs and software implementations are fully open-sourced at https://ego-thumb.github.io.
authors: Jianyu Hou, Jiawei Fu, Weikang Wan, Minghui Jiang, Jiajun Li, Hao Su
bullets: Addresses bulky supernumerary fingers and hand-motion triggers that limit object interaction and environmental awareness.
Uses a compact dual tendon-driven finger with forearm-mounted actuation for lower distal weight and precise joint control.
Maps palm-facing camera images directly to continuous joint positions through visual imitation learning.
Infers user intent from the hand–object scene to support autonomous manipulation across users and environments.
Hardware designs and software are fully open-sourced.

papers.abstract: AI agents have made substantial progress in domains where they have a non-trivial amount of time to deliberate between actions, such as mathematics, software engineering, and performing tasks on desktop applications. It is less clear how such models fare in settings that demand real-time interaction, such as playing a video game or operating a physical device. In these settings, the environment state may evolve as the agent is reasoning, or even as the underlying model is performing a forward pass. To gain insight into the real-time interaction capabilities of vision-language agents, we introduce Gym-Anything-RT. Our key idea is to construct visual minigames that demand a portfolio of capabilities required for interactive real-time settings. Gym-Anything-RT uses an agentic pipeline to automatically generate such environments based on a taxonomy of six capabilities required for real-time interaction, including the ability to perceive the environment and act under an evolving environment state. A key feature of Gym-Anything-RT is that it allows for controlled comparison of real-time interaction capabilities: we can run the same minigame in real time, or pause or slow down the environment to relax the requirement for real-time actions. We use Gym-Anything-RT to construct 100 real-time minigames and evaluate AI agents on them. We find large capability gaps in real-time interaction. For example, GPT-6 Astra (xHigh) achieves a pass rate of only 9.0% on the real-time minigames, which rises to 75.0% when the environment is paused. We also identify intriguing behaviors by the most powerful frontier agents: for instance, when given the ability to write code, these agents write code that bypasses the need to perceive and act in real time. We publicly release Gym-Anything-RT and the generated minigames to spur further research on AI agents in real-time interactive settings.

papers.abstract: Threading a quadrotor through a moving narrow gap is a demanding test of agile flight, requiring centimeter-level spatial alignment and precise temporal execution. We address this challenge using a control policy that operates directly on onboard visual and inertial measurements to output collective thrust and body-rate commands. The task is difficult because success lies on a thin feasible manifold: small errors in timing, position, attitude, or visual observability cause collision. Prior planning and learning methods rely on privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation; learning dynamic narrow-gap traversal directly, from scratch, remains open. We introduce a differentiable moving-gap formulation that gates centering, alignment, and smooth collision terms by signed distance to a time-varying gap plane, turning a sparse traversal event into a dense pathwise objective. We integrate this formulation into a visual-feature-to-command policy trained in one stage from random initialization, without a teacher, planner, or distillation. We validate our approach in both synthetic and real-world experiments. In controlled benchmarks, we demonstrate that pathwise gradients significantly outperform score-function gradients for precision-critical tasks, yielding a 99.3% success rate in simulation after only a few minutes of training on a single GPU. Furthermore, the policy transfers directly to a real quadrotor, successfully crossing a dynamic narrow gap from varied initial conditions using onboard sensing and inertial measurements, achieving an 80% success rate over 10 physical trials.
authors: Riccardo Bianco, Yunfan Ren, Jiaxu Xing, Davide Scaramuzza
bullets: Addresses precise timing, alignment, and collision avoidance when flying through moving narrow gaps.

Trains a visual-feature-to-thrust/body-rate policy in one stage without privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation.
Pathwise gradients outperform score-function gradients in controlled precision-critical benchmarks.
Achieves 99.3% simulation success and 80% success across 10 real-world trials from varied initial conditions.

papers.abstract: Manipulation policies are evaluated predominantly by binary task success, which cannot tell whether the commanded gesture is the one the object's kinematics admit. We introduce Constraint-Referenced Strategy (CRS), which projects the commanded end-effector twist onto the object's joint axis, separating progress along the joint from off-constraint waste. CRS requires a joint model and a joint-following scripted controller derived from it, but no recorded demonstration or learned judge. On 74 simulated articulated objects, success registers three transfer failures as lower rates but attributes none, while the two CRS channels give each a distinct signature. A door-trained behavior-cloning policy opens drawers in 59 of 110 episodes, and in these passes it commands about $40\times$ the off-axis rotation of a drawer-trained policy's passes ($1.27$ vs.\ $0.032$~rad/s). Relative to a scripted controller scored with the same axis, CRS verdicts are unchanged under joint-axis errors up to $30^\circ$; absolute thresholds tolerate about $8^\circ$.
authors: Baptiste Bonin, Caro Strickland, Audrey Durand
bullets: Binary task success cannot distinguish kinematically valid gestures from inefficient or invalid commands.
CRS projects the commanded end-effector twist onto the object’s joint axis, producing progress and off-constraint motion signals.
It uses a joint model and a model-derived scripted controller, without demonstrations or a learned evaluator.
Across simulated articulated objects, CRS differentiates transfer failures that success rates only aggregate.
Its verdicts remain stable with joint-axis errors up to 30°, while absolute thresholds tolerate about 8°.

papers.abstract: Event cameras offer low latency, high dynamic range, and milliwatt-level power consumption, making them ideal for agile robots such as tiny drones navigating through cluttered environments. However, existing simulators generally render photorealistic images before converting them into events, making large-scale reinforcement learning prohibitively slow. We propose an analytic event simulator that exploits what event cameras fundamentally measure - moving contrast edges - to synthesize event streams directly from scene geometry and ego-motion without visual rendering. Our simulator generates a 64x64 event observation in 17 microseconds on a single GPU - over 400x faster than a state-of-the-art rendering pipeline - enabling end-to-end reinforcement learning for goal-directed obstacle avoidance to converge in under 30 minutes - three orders of magnitude faster than training on rendered events. Policies transfer zero-shot to physically based event simulations (ray-traced Isaac Sim). Our policy reaches 83% success in cluttered courses unseen during training (mid-difficulty, traversability probability approx. 0.57), at 2.4 m/s average goal velocity, and retains 70% in a simulated texture-dense indoor hall. Furthermore, we quantized the policy to a 1.2 MB int8 network running fully onboard a 56-gram Crazyflie equipped with a Prophesee GenX320 event camera and an OpenMV N6 microcontroller board. Without any fine-tuning, external processing, or positioning, the policy achieves an average success rate of 82% (5/5, 5/6, 4/6 flights) across three real-world obstacle courses of increasing difficulty. Code: https://github.com/tudelft/rendering-free-event-nav
authors: Dequan Ou, Austin Lopez, Quentin Missinne, Christophe De Wagter, Guido C. H. E. de Croon
bullets: Generates event streams directly from scene geometry and ego-motion, avoiding photorealistic image rendering.
Produces 64×64 event observations in 17 μs on a single GPU, over 400× faster than a rendering-based pipeline.
Enables obstacle-avoidance policies to converge in under 30 minutes and transfer zero-shot to ray-traced simulation.
Achieves 83% success in unseen cluttered simulated courses and 70% in a texture-dense indoor hall.
A quantized 1.2 MB policy runs onboard a 56 g Crazyflie, reaching an average 82% success rate across three real-world courses.

papers.abstract: A joint of pipe run into the hole swings from the elevator over the well and strikes a fixed stabbing guide at whatever speed the swing has. StabBot, a robotic stabbing system, predicts the swing and meets the pipe at its own speed. A pendulum Kalman filter tuned from the pipe tally tracks the joint in stereo images. A six-axis arm with an open V-shaped roller head closes in at matched velocity, confirms the last millimetres by touch, aims the pin over the box when the elevator hangs off centre, and follows the block down with lateral compliance. A ResNet-18 keypoint network locates the pipe, pin nose and box mouth in 3-D, and a residual reinforcement-learning policy refines the capture. On 200 paired random jobs with nine sizes from 2-3/8-in. tubing to 20-in. casing, StabBot seated every joint with the pipe touching only rollers, against 74% for a conventional fixed guide. Median contact speed fell from 18.4 to 2.3 cm/s and median peak head-pipe force from 11.3 to 1.4 kN, and the force was lower in all 200 jobs (Wilcoxon $p < 10^{-30}$). The network locates the pipe with 0.4-mm median error in 2.3 ms per stereo pair. With the network in the loop, success stayed at 100% under 20 mm of added noise, 300-ms delay, 85% frame loss, 20-mm calibration offset, 20-cm elevator offset and 40-cm swings. All results come from a 1:4 Froude-scaled MuJoCo model and are reported at full scale.
authors: Mohamed Ashraf Mostafa, Taher El-Fakharany, Samir Khaled
bullets: Addresses pipe stabbing when swinging joints strike a fixed guide at uncontrolled speeds.
Combines a tally-tuned pendulum Kalman filter, ResNet-18 3-D keypoints, touch confirmation, compliant following, and residual RL.
Seated 100% of 200 simulated jobs across nine pipe sizes, versus 74% for a conventional fixed guide.
Reduced median contact speed from 18.4 to 2.3 cm/s and peak head-pipe force from 11.3 to 1.4 kN.
Maintained 100% success under substantial simulated noise, delay, frame loss, calibration, elevator-offset, and swing disturbances.

papers.abstract: In smart factory environments, passive entities such as humans and movable obstacles may interfere with autonomous robot operations, posing significant safety risks. Detecting potential conflicts between robots and entities outside their field-of-view (FoV) is therefore of paramount importance. However, conventional passive object detection systems rely on sensors such as LiDAR, radar, or cameras, which operate under direct line-of-sight (LoS) and are limited by obstacles and occlusions. To overcome these limitations, integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) enables environmental perception via the communication infrastructure thanks to cooperation among distributed wireless devices. In this paper, we propose a framework for passive entity sensing beyond the robot's FoV that relies solely on distributed channel measurements from the communication infrastructure to perform risk-aware classification. These measurements are embedded into high-dimensional representations using hyperdimensional computing (HDC), enabling robust and scalable learning without explicit channel reconstruction. Numerical simulations based on a commercial ray tracer and ROS-based validation in realistic smart factory scenarios demonstrate improved safety and enhanced path planning with up to 89% accuracy under severe occlusions, while maintaining low computational complexity.
authors: Placido Mursia, Marco Rossanese, Francesco Devoti, Adrian Lendinez Ibanez, Lanfranco Zanzi, Xi Li, Xavier Costa-Perez
bullets: Addresses robot safety risks from humans and obstacles hidden by occlusions in smart factories.
Uses distributed communication-channel measurements rather than direct line-of-sight LiDAR, radar, or camera sensing.
Maps measurements to high-dimensional representations with hyperdimensional computing for risk-aware classification without reconstructing channels.
Validated through ray-tracing simulations and ROS-based smart-factory scenarios.
Supports safer path planning under severe occlusions, with scope demonstrated in simulated and realistic validation environments.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot control requires integrating distributed camera views while predicting separate action sequences. Most vision-language-action and world-action models target one robot. Combining multiple views alone does not establish spatial correspondence between them. World Dreamer v5-lite is a multi-robot world-action model built around a shared world state for robot-specific action prediction. Calibrated features from a pretrained video encoder populate this state in workspace coordinates; its spatial size remains fixed as views are added. A vision-language model provides scene context and one query per robot. The queries read the shared state and exchange pose-aware information, while their action streams remain separate. Masked-view cooperative training withholds selected camera views from both visual branches while retaining all action targets. This encourages the use of observations shared by other robots. Pretraining uses more than 10,000 hours of trajectories from 20 simulated robot types, RoboFactory, and real robots. On RoboFactory, World Dreamer v5-lite achieves 74.0% mean success, 23.7 percentage points above the strongest evaluated baseline. Across four real-robot tasks, it reaches 78.8% mean success, a margin of 13.8 points. It also reaches 58.08% overall on RoboCasa365.
authors: Guoning Wu (World Agents), Zijian Cai (World Agents), Yuhang Zhang (World Agents), Ying Liu (World Agents), Yongbin Zheng (World Agents)
bullets: Addresses the challenge of integrating distributed camera views while predicting independent action sequences for multiple robots.

Masked-view cooperative training encourages robots to use observations available from other robots.
Reports 74.0% mean success on RoboFactory, 78.8% across four real-robot tasks, and 58.08% overall on RoboCasa365.

The video strip depicts a temporal window: observed video latents are encoded and combined with camera geometry to build the shared world state ϕ; future latents supply training supervision only. The Action Decoder uses the VLM outputs, ϕ, proprioception, and multi-robot noisy actions to predict a flow velocity for each robot.

papers.abstract: As egocentric video becomes increasingly available for embodied learning, an important research question is how to turn this low-cost, scalable source of data into robot manipulation capabilities. Egocentric videos naturally provide rich context for high-level task understanding, while real-robot demonstrations with wrist observations and action annotations provide supervision for fine-grained action alignment. We present Ego-CEVR, a data-native framework for hierarchical visual representation learning that assigns distinct learning objectives to global and interaction representations. The global module learns object relations, task state, and temporal progress through future prediction on egocentric video. The Interaction module interprets wrist observations in global context and learns local alignment and contact cues through robot action supervision. Separate residual paths expose both representations to the action policy, preserving direct access to task context alongside fine-grained execution information. Ego-CEVR supports independent pretraining of its global video module on large-scale human egocentric videos and videos from diverse robot embodiments, without requiring robot action labels or paired wrist observations.
authors: Keru Zhou, Zhirui Fang, Xinrun Xu, Yaopeng Lou, Zeyuan He, Zihao Zhu, Xinze Niu, Chen Wang, Tianfu Li, Samith Va, Bin Qian, Junwei Li, Wenjia Ding, Yicheng Xu, Chang Zhou, Ziwei Wang, Li Liu, Xiu Li, Maoqing Yao

Provides separate residual paths so policies retain both task context and fine-grained execution information.
Enables independent pretraining of the global video module without robot action labels or paired wrist observations.

papers.abstract: Medium altitude, long endurance unmanned aerial systems such as Shahed-type strike drones are an unanswered threat in modern conflicts. Conventional air defense systems are too expensive to provide a feasible large-scale solution. Quadcopter interceptors are a cheap, battle-proven alternative, but their extremely limited flight time restricts them to low altitude targets at short range, whereas fixed-wing platforms have the endurance to reach higher altitude targets from longer distances. However, such interceptors are still operated manually. Recent developments in learning-based controllers show potential for automation. In this work, a fixed-wing interceptor is presented that is controlled by a neural network that maps filtered monocular vision observations directly to actuator commands. The policy was trained in a custom Python environment using reinforcement learning and proximal policy optimization. The policy was then deployed on a fixed-wing platform and tested in real interception scenarios. As a baseline, two classical guidance controllers were also developed and tested in simulation. The policy is able to intercept targets both in simulation and in real flight. In simulation, the policy outperforms the classical controllers under most conditions. The interceptor was ultimately successfully validated in real flight by intercepting maneuvering fixed-wing targets. This novel system shows the potential of artificial intelligence for autonomous control of fixed-wing interceptor drones.
authors: Daan van Hamersveld, Ewoud Smeur, Iurii Kriachko

Outperforms two classical guidance controllers under most simulated conditions.

papers.abstract: Deep Reinforcement Learning remains difficult to interpret and align due to the black-box nature of neural networks. While (neuro-)symbolic approaches improve transparency by incorporating symbolic reasoning, applying them directly to low-level actions results in overly complex, unreadable policies. We introduce NEXUS, a hierarchical RL framework that resolves this tension by combining neural skills with symbolic meta-policies. By shifting transparent reasoning to high-level skills rather than atomic actions, NEXUS drastically reduces symbolic complexity without sacrificing environment performance. Object-centric observations enable high-level reasoning and the design of reward functions and meta-policies by interaction with LLMs. We demonstrate that NEXUS agents learn disentangled skills, are interpretable regarding high-level goals, are better aligned to goals described in the game manual, less prone to reward hacking and more robust to game simplifications than deep RL. Finally, we isolate and evaluate the impact of different meta-policy architectures (neural, symbolic, neuro-symbolic) on environmental return and aligned task performance.

papers.abstract: Objective: This study aims to determine whether a hip-exoskeleton policy trained in simulation, by co-adapting with a musculoskeletal human model under a metabolic-energy reward, reduces the metabolic cost of walking in new users without per-user tuning, and how mechanical-power shaping affects the learned assistance. Methods: We developed MARL-Exo, a multi-agent reinforcement learning framework in which a full-body human model (304 muscle actuators; randomized anatomy, gait, and speed) and a bilateral hip-exoskeleton policy are trained concurrently in two stages. The exoskeleton observes only delayed hip kinematics and its past commands; its reward includes muscle metabolic power from a physiologically based energetics model, alone (Metabolic) or with mechanical-power shaping (Metabolic + Power). The Metabolic policy was deployed and tested without retraining in eight healthy adults walking at 1.25 m/s, using indirect calorimetry. Results: In simulation, the Metabolic policy reduced modeled muscle metabolic power by 13.8% relative to no-device walking, versus 8.8% for Metabolic + Power. On hardware, MARL-Exo reduced net metabolic rate by 18.3 $\pm$ 6.6% relative to Passive in all eight participants. Relative to No-Exo, the mean reduction was 7.4 $\pm$ 10.0%; six participants more than offset the 13.1% device-wearing penalty, walking up to 24.2% below their No-Exo cost. Conclusion: A metabolically informed policy co-adapted in simulation transferred to users without per-user tuning and consistently reduced the metabolic cost of walking with the device, while explicit power shaping reduced the simulated benefit. Significance: Unlike per-user human-in-the-loop optimization, this approach yields a single population-level controller and allows assistance objectives to be screened in simulation before human testing.

papers.abstract: Robot policy evaluation often relies on a binary success signal for task completion. In real-world deployment, however, desired execution behaviors are also defined by quality attributes such as execution speed and motion smoothness, which need to be dynamically controlled according to task requirements. To address this, we introduce Quality-Controllable Policy (QCP), a robot policy that enables inference-time control over both individual quality attributes and their combinations. To extend the controllable quality range beyond initial demonstrations, we further propose an iterative hindsight relabeling loop: QCP collects online rollouts under target quality labels, adds successful trajectories to the dataset, relabels the accumulated trajectories in hindsight according to their measured quality, and fine-tunes the policy. Experiments on Robomimic and RoboEval demonstrate that QCP consistently improves both task execution quality and success rates across iterations, producing successful rollouts that exceed the quality of the initial demonstrations. Finally, we validate QCP on real-world manipulation tasks, where controlling speed increases throughput in conveyor operations and controlling transport stability improves success when carrying wine glasses, demonstrating that quality-controllable policies yield practical gains in physical deployment.

papers.abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but their understanding of physical dynamics remains limited. Video world models can capture scene dynamics, yet generating future videos introduces high latency into the control loop. We introduce PDRVLA, whose lightweight Physical Dynamics Module extracts physical tokens from vision--language features to condition action generation without online video generation. The module learns through direct prediction of future RGB, depth, and optical-flow features, with auxiliary supervision through a frozen pretrained video world model. Training relies entirely on publicly available data, expanded through human-to-robot synthesis, subtask annotation, and embodied chain-of-thought (ECoT) annotation. Across four simulation benchmarks, PDRVLA achieves success rates of 99.3% on LIBERO, 89.9% on LIBERO-Plus, 93.6% on RoboTwin~2.0, and 81.5% on SimplerEnv. Ablations show improved future prediction with world-model supervision and evaluate how subtask conditioning, future object-pose supervision, and ECoT training affect action success.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models integrate high-level reasoning with low-level action execution for end-to-end robotic control. However, most VLA models target static manipulation in unconstrained environments, overlooking spatial constraints and dynamic obstacles. Fine-tuning VLAs on obstacle-avoidance data is a straightforward solution, but collecting such data is costly, especially for dynamic scenarios, and may degrade their original task capabilities. To address these limitations, we propose VLA-Stem, a lightweight, reinforcement-learning-based safety mechanism for VLA systems. Without fine-tuning the underlying VLA policy, VLA-Stem converts its action chunks into motion references and uses trajectory-level guidance to preserve their spatial intent while allowing flexible motion and timing adjustments. Conditioned on these references, robot proprioception, and local obstacle information, the Stem policy adaptively modifies execution at inference time, preserving the original task intent while enabling responsive adaptation to spatial constraints and dynamic obstacles. For robust and sample-efficient training, we combine teacher-student distillation with curriculum learning. We evaluate VLA-Stem on reference following, static spatial constraints, and dynamic obstacle avoidance. Across six constrained simulation settings, VLA-Stem achieves 52.8% average collision-free task success versus 23.7% for the strongest safety baseline, while preserving base-policy performance in obstacle-free settings; real-world experiments further show consistent collision reductions under static and dynamic obstacles. These results demonstrate that VLA-Stem couples high-level VLA task intent with rapid, reflex-like responses to immediate physical risks, providing a brainstem-inspired mechanism for robust robot execution.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. VLA-Stem pipeline. The teacher policy takes as input the trajectory sequence produced by the base VLA policy, robot proprioception, and obstacle information, and additionally leverages privileged task information about the target object to accelerate training. Finally, the teacher policy is used to distill a student policy, removing the dependence on task-specific privileged information at deployment.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a promising paradigm for scalable robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on success-only behavioral cloning leaves them brittle; lacking corrective training signals, minor execution errors rapidly compound into unrecoverable, out-of-distribution failures. To address this limitation, we propose Adaptive Failure-Informed Learning (AFIL), an end-to-end framework that leverages failure trajectories as adaptive negative guidance for diffusion- and flow-based VLA policies. AFIL uses a pretrained VLA to generate failure rollouts online, avoiding the need for handcrafted failure-mode design or human-in-the-loop recovery. It then jointly trains Dual Action Generators (DAGs) for successful and failed behaviors while sharing a common vision-language backbone, enabling efficient failure-aware policy learning with limited parameter overhead. During sampling, the failure generator adaptively steers action generation away from failure-prone regions and toward more reliable success modes, with guidance strength determined by the per-diffusion-step distance between success and failure distributions. Experiments across in-domain and out-of-domain robotic manipulation tasks, covering both short- and long-horizon settings, show that AFIL consistently improves task success rates and robustness over existing VLA baselines, demonstrating its effectiveness, efficiency, and generality.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies form structured internal representations of traffic, ego behavior, and road constraints. These representations offer a monitoring interface for anticipating failures, complementing risk signals from trajectories, controls, and manually designed features. We introduce the Structured Representation Probe (SRP), a lightweight monitor that reads actor, ego, and map representations from a frozen policy. SRP learns a separate linear risk direction for each source and aggregates element scores through cardinality-normalized log-mean-exp pooling, retaining sensitivity to salient evidence while reducing dependence on token count. Event-window supervision links the readout to upcoming hard failures, and auxiliary event type heads jointly train the source directions across failure modes. Online alerting uses a single generic score without modifying the driving policy. Bench2Drive experiments on DriveTransformer, UniAD, and VAD show higher frame-level PR-AUC and ROC-AUC than the evaluated runtime baselines. On DriveTransformer at a horizon of 2 seconds, ROC-AUC reaches 0.833 versus 0.715 for temporal consistency, with 2.67% readout runtime overhead. The trained probes also retain the ability to distinguish impending failures on new routes.
authors: Jiawei Liang, Tianrui Lou, Le Yang, Xianghao Jiao, Wei Wang, Xiaochun Cao
bullets: Addresses the need for risk monitoring that complements trajectory-, control-, and hand-crafted-feature-based signals.
Reads actor, ego, and map representations, learning source-specific linear risk directions and combining element scores with cardinality-normalized log-mean-exp pooling.
Uses event-window supervision and auxiliary event-type heads to train a single generic online alert score without changing the driving policy.
On Bench2Drive with DriveTransformer, UniAD, and VAD, SRP outperforms evaluated runtime baselines; for DriveTransformer at a 2-second horizon, ROC-AUC is 0.833 versus 0.715 for temporal consistency.
Adds 2.67% readout runtime overhead and retains failure-discrimination ability on new routes.

papers.abstract: Human-robot collaboration requires partners to coordinate interdependent contributions toward a shared goal. Joint Action theory provides concepts for understanding this coordination, but how these concepts are instantiated and combined across empirical research remains fragmented. We conducted a systematic review following PRISMA 2020, identifying 83 empirical papers published between 2021 and 2026. Through theory-driven framework analysis, we organized the literature into nine constructs across three capacities: Representation, Prediction, and Integration. We analyze how these constructs are distributed and co-occur across studies, revealing where empirical evidence concentrates and where it is absent. By mapping empirical HRC research onto a unified Joint Action framework, this review offers a coherent overview of HRC studies, identifies gaps in current evidence, and provides guidelines for future research.
authors: Chengwen Zhang, Jianyang Wang, Chang Liu, Yukun Wang, Yuan Xu, Zhoutong Ye, Jie Cai, Chun Yu, Yuanchun Shi
bullets: Reviews 83 empirical papers published between 2021 and 2026 using PRISMA 2020.
Applies theory-driven framework analysis to identify nine constructs across Representation, Prediction, and Integration.
Examines how constructs are distributed and co-occur across studies.
Finds that empirical evidence is unevenly concentrated, with gaps in several areas.
Provides an integrated overview and guidance for future HRC research.

papers.abstract: The vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action model (WAM) communities debate whether control policies should inherit pretrained knowledge from vision-language models or from visual generators. The debate, however, bundles three separable choices: backbone initialization, the objective applied to future observations, and whether the machinery for that future loss is kept at inference. A gap between a VLA and a WAM therefore cannot simply be attributed to any one of them. We show that decoupling these choices yields a common framework for both families, which we term Just Action Model (JAM): a pretrained visual backbone with an action expert, trained with an action loss and a foresight loss. The foresight loss trains current-observation features to predict frozen encodings of the recorded future through a prediction head discarded after training, so no visual generation is involved in either training or inference, and the backbone can be chosen freely. We first compare objectives within fixed policy architectures, then evaluate the foresight recipe across backbone families. The resulting JAM policies outperform their matched FastWAM and ImageWAM counterparts on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and achieve similar or slightly higher success rates on RoboTwin. Compared with FastWAM, JAM improves the success rates from 97.0%/55.3%/91.2% to 98.2%/64.5%/91.4%, respectively. With cached foresight targets, JAM reduces estimated online training FLOPs per sample per update by 73% relative to FastWAM. Our results show that future supervision improves control without visual generation or additional inference machinery, and strong foresight performance is attainable with either generator-initialized or vision-language backbones. Project Page: https://y0uroy.github.io/JAM
authors: Yonghao Yu, Lang Huang, Runyi Li, Toshihiko Yamasaki
bullets: The paper disentangles three factors often conflated in VLA–WAM comparisons: backbone initialization, future-observation objectives, and inference-time future-loss machinery.
JAM combines a pretrained visual backbone, an action expert, an action loss, and a foresight loss predicting frozen future-observation encodings.
Its foresight prediction head is discarded after training, avoiding visual generation during both training and inference while allowing flexible backbones.
JAM outperforms matched FastWAM and ImageWAM policies on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, and matches or slightly exceeds them on RoboTwin.
Cached foresight targets reduce estimated online training FLOPs per sample per update by 73% versus FastWAM.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles in enclosed spaces such as tunnels and mines rely on range maps that smoke, dust and fog make inaccurate. Conformal prediction calibrates a keepout around the mapped walls that covers the true unsafe set at a chosen probability. Typically an unmodified planner treats the keepout as an inflated obstacle, and nothing ensures that the vehicle can stop before the keepout as it moves when sensing degrades. In narrow passages this margin and the planner's buffer close the route, and existing remedies recover reach by relaxing the coverage level. This paper conditions the conformal margin on a label-free severity estimate to hold coverage near its target as degradation varies. A planning and control layer enforces one braking-distance condition on the keepout at plan time and at every command, takes the measured tracking residual as its only margin and never alters the keepout. The keepout is validated on ground-robot smoke recordings and the closed loop in simulated quadrotor flights in a foggy tunnel against the standard deployment. In closed-loop simulation the proposed system substantially reduces entries into the calibrated keepout and reaches numerically more goals than the deployment pattern in both calibration regimes, an observed gain of 3.2 percentage points pooled whose per-regime confidence intervals include zero. The per-class keepout holds its coverage near the target on held-out recordings.
bullets: Problem: Inaccurate range maps and planner buffers can make narrow passages impassable, while standard deployment does not ensure stopping before moving keepouts.
Method: Condition the conformal keepout margin on a label-free severity estimate and enforce a braking-distance constraint during planning and every control command.
Design: Use measured tracking residuals as the only additional margin and never modify the calibrated keepout.
Evaluation: Validate keepout coverage on ground-robot smoke recordings and test closed-loop navigation in simulated quadrotor flights through a foggy tunnel.

Result and scope: The system reduced keepout entries and reached numerically more goals than the standard deployment; the pooled gain was 3.2 percentage points, but per-regime confidence intervals included zero.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies demonstrate remarkable semantic generalization, yet remain highly vulnerable to out-of-distribution (OOD) visual shifts during execution. While existing test-time methods attempt to suppress spurious visual cues, they fundamentally overlook the rich, uncorrupted kinematic priors embedded in the policy's own training experience. We introduce Retrieve to Act (R2A), a test-time scaling framework that formulates OOD robustness purely as a geometric motion primitive retrieval problem. R2A bypasses fragile visual features by structuring successful training demonstrations into an offline spatiotemporal motion primitive graph. During inference, a query-dependent Graph Neural Network dynamically localizes the robot's ongoing execution within this graph, retrieving structurally compatible future motion primitives. These retrieved geometric priors are then seamlessly harmonized with the frozen VLA's predicted actions via a learned, dimension-wise gating mechanism, adaptively rectifying erroneous spatial trajectories while preserving the policy's local reactivity. Extensive experiments across three state-of-the-art VLA architectures, GR00T N1.7, $\pi_{0.5}$, and StableVLA, demonstrate that R2A consistently and significantly enhances robustness against diverse contextual perturbations. R2A achieves absolute success rate improvements of up to +12% in simulation benchmarks (LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin2.0-Plus) and +40% in real-world deployments, without requiring any finetuning of the base policies. Project page: https://retrieve2act.github.io/r2a/
authors: Pham Tri Quang, Bao-Ngoc Dao, Minh Duc Nguyen, Duc-Duy Nguyen, Hung T. Ho, Linh Dang Le, Trong-Bao Ho, Thien-Loc Ha, Tan Q. Nguyen, Tuan Dam, Vu N. Duong, Daniel Sonntag, Ngan Le, Khoa D. Doan, Jan Peters, An Thai Le, Duy M. H. Nguyen, Vien Anh Ngo
bullets: Targets VLA vulnerability to out-of-distribution visual perturbations while preserving local action reactivity.
Builds an offline spatiotemporal graph of successful training motion primitives.
Uses a query-dependent GNN to localize execution and retrieve structurally compatible future primitives.
Combines retrieved motion priors with frozen VLA predictions through learned dimension-wise gating.
Improves success rates by up to 12% in simulation and 40% in real-world deployments across three VLA architectures, without base-policy finetuning.

papers.abstract: Humanoids and other legged robots operating in complex environments must remember information that leaves their field of view and only becomes relevant much later. Reinforcement learning policies address this using memory networks such as LSTMs that are trained end-to-end with the policy to memorize such task-relevant aspects. Yet, such architectures often fail to preserve sufficient information over long horizons. In this work, we propose a network architecture based on Hadamard memory that specifically targets robot navigation. Our Local Spatial Matrix Memory (LSMM) enables RL agents to store generic task-relevant information at specific, position-based memory cells, enabling flexible and spatially grounded memorization. We evaluate LSMM on the task of autonomous maze exploration, where it matches the maze coverage of strong recurrent and finite-history baselines while being the only architecture that remembers the maze layout, reducing the reconstruction error threefold.
authors: Leon Magnus, Nico Bohlinger, Jan Peters, Oleg Arenz
bullets: Long-horizon navigation requires remembering information beyond the robot’s current field of view.
The proposed Local Spatial Matrix Memory (LSMM) stores task-relevant information in position-based memory cells.
LSMM is evaluated for autonomous maze exploration against recurrent and finite-history baselines.
It matches baseline maze coverage and is the only evaluated architecture to remember maze layout, reducing reconstruction error threefold.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for long-horizon agents relies on feedback from sequences of interactions, making credit assignment to individual actions difficult. Existing methods such as GiGPO compare actions at shared states to compute relative advantages, but estimate each action's value from a single sampled continuation. The resulting local credit remains sensitive to decisions made later in the trajectory. To address this problem, we propose ConCal (Continuation Calibration), a recursive continuation-value estimator that incorporates continuation evidence already present in a rollout batch. ConCal matches visits from the same task by their incoming state-action-state transitions, combines shared continuation evidence with each visit's own transition estimate, and propagates calibrated values backward to refine earlier action-value estimates. This reduces dependence on individual sampled continuations and mitigates local credit distortions without additional rollouts. Held-out return diagnostics show lower error in within-group value differences and higher agreement with reference action orderings than estimates based on individual continuations. With Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, ConCal improves success rates over GiGPO by 3.39 and 5.86 percentage points on ALFWorld and WebShop, respectively. Our code is available at https://github.com/Yingjian-Chen/ConCal.
authors: Yingjian Chen, Lang Zhou, Zixin Zhao, Pingfan Li, Weishi Zheng, Zhilin Zhao
bullets: Targets local credit distortion caused by estimating each action from only one sampled continuation.
Matches same-task visits through shared incoming state-action-state transitions to reuse continuation evidence.
Recursively propagates calibrated values backward to refine earlier action-value estimates.
Held-out diagnostics show lower within-group value-difference error and better agreement with reference action orderings.
Improves success rates over GiGPO by 3.39 percentage points on ALFWorld and 5.86 points on WebShop with Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of ConCal. (1) ConCal matches visits across same-task rollouts by their preceding state, executed action, and current state to identify shared continuation evidence (Left). (2) It recursively combines continuation evidence from matched visits while retaining each visit’s own transition contribution, producing calibrated continuation values for action evaluation. At each recursion depth, all visits are updated using successor estimates from the previous depth (Right). (3) Each action is evaluated using its immediate reward and its actual successor’s calibrated continuation value. The resulting action values are compared within state groups to obtain local advantages, which are combined with episode-level advantages for PPO updates (Bottom).

papers.selection_reason: Action-value calibration for long-horizon RL is a general credit-assignment technique transferable to embodied robot policy learning.
papers.title: Action-Value Calibration via Continuation Sharing for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: ConCal improves long-horizon reinforcement-learning credit assignment by sharing and recursively calibrating continuation values across matching transitions, yielding better value estimates and higher task success without extra rollouts.

papers.abstract: We trained four widely used imitation-learning policies, ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$, on nested subsets of 12, 25, 50, 100 and 200 teleoperated demonstrations of one pick-and-place task with distractor objects, using one fixed training recipe per policy. Every trained model was then run on a physical SO-101 arm on a fixed set of object placements: 1,340 scored episodes in 126 blocks. ACT, trained from scratch, rose from 1 success in 40 episodes at 12 demonstrations to 37 in 40 at 100. $\pi_{0.5}$ with its action expert fine-tuned was the best policy when data was scarce (16 of 40 at 12 demonstrations, 28 of 40 at 25) and then stayed near 70%; from 100 demonstrations ACT was ahead, by a margin this study does not fully resolve. SmolVLA and Diffusion Policy peaked near 50%, and both were affected by a failure to start: SmolVLA's arm never started moving in 47% of episodes, and Diffusion Policy hardly ever started until an idle lead-in was trimmed from the demonstrations. For $\pi_{0.5}$ the fine-tuning recipe mattered more than the amount of data: low-rank adaptation succeeded in 4 of 110 episodes, against 130 of 200 for action-expert fine-tuning. From the joint and camera recordings we place every episode on a four-stage ladder (started, reached the ball, carried it, delivered it) and show that for ACT more data moves failures from reaching, to grasping, to none, while the failures $\pi_{0.5}$ retains are in grasping. We also measure how weak a ten-episode block is as a measurement (the same checkpoint tested twice differs by 2 successes in 10 on average), separate seed-to-seed variation from that noise, and audit the human scoring against the recordings. Training length was fixed within each recipe, so the amount of data and the number of times it was seen change together; we state which conclusions survive that confound and which do not.
bullets: The study compares ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA, and π₀.₅ using 12–200 demonstrations for one distractor-heavy pick-and-place task.
π₀.₅ performs best with 12–25 demonstrations, whereas ACT improves sharply with more data and reaches 37/40 successes at 100 demonstrations.
SmolVLA and Diffusion Policy peak near 50%; startup failures substantially limit both, especially SmolVLA.
For π₀.₅, action-expert fine-tuning is far more effective than low-rank adaptation under the tested recipes.
A four-stage failure analysis shows ACT’s errors shift from reaching toward grasping as data increases, while π₀.₅ mainly retains grasping failures.

papers.selection_reason: Empirical scaling study of imitation-learning policies on a physical robot; directly relevant to robot manipulation and policy learning.
papers.title: From 12 to 200 Demonstrations: How ACT, Diffusion Policy, SmolVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ Scale on a Low-Cost Arm
papers.tldr: On a low-cost arm, imitation policies scale very differently with demonstrations: π₀.₅ leads with scarce data, while ACT becomes strongest from 100 demonstrations onward, with evaluation noise and training confounds limiting some conclusions.

papers.abstract: Reliable real-time 3D object detection based on LiDAR and camera data is critical for safety in autonomous driving, where systems must accurately perceive their surroundings with minimal latency. Many state-of-the-art systems achieve high-quality detection results but fail to meet real-time constraints, limiting their practical use. To address this challenge, we propose FastBEVFusion, a simple, fast, and robust fusion system for 3D object detection. Based on modality-specific features, FastBEVFusion projects these features into semi-aligned modality-specific BEV spaces, without relying on a computationally intensive and potentially error-prone depth estimation. Given these BEV spaces, we propose a light-weight, soft, and dynamic fusion module based on cross-attention, which adapts dynamically to the scene context and enables feature fusion across the entire BEV spaces. Experiments on the complex nuScenes dataset show that FastBEVFusion outperforms state-of-the-art real-time systems, and achieves over 50 FPS without deployment libraries. Additionally, our system shows strong robustness to calibration errors, making FastBEVFusion a powerful 3D object detection system for real-world applications.
authors: Tom Sanitz, Emre G\"ulsoylu, Simone Frintrop, Christian Wilms
bullets: Targets the latency and reliability challenges of real-time multimodal 3D detection for autonomous driving.
Projects modality-specific features into semi-aligned BEV spaces without computationally expensive depth estimation.
Uses lightweight cross-attention for scene-adaptive fusion across the full BEV representation.
Evaluated on nuScenes, it outperforms state-of-the-art real-time systems and exceeds 50 FPS without deployment libraries.
Shows strong robustness to calibration errors, supporting practical real-world use.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of our FastBEVFusion. Multi-view image data is encoded and projected into an image BEV space using a uniform depth distribution to ensure low latency (color-coded in shades of green for different views). During training, an additional 2D object detection head is added. In parallel, the LiDAR point cloud is encoded into a LiDAR BEV space. The semi-aligned BEV spaces are then fused in our light-weight fusion module using on a single attention block exploiting the semi-aligned nature of the BEV spaces (see Fig. 3 for details). Based on the resulting fused BEV space, a detection head generates multi-modal 3D object detections.

Fig. 1. Results of real-time capable 3D object detection methods on the nuScenes dataset. Here, the two versions of our proposed FastBEVFusion based on different backbones offer the best detection quality and latency. Table I presents detailed results. Some latencies are estimated (see Sec. IV).

Fig. 4. Qualitative results of TransFusion-L [1] and our FastBEVFusion in three scenes of the nuScenes dataset. Only one of six views per scene is presented for brevity. Detected objects are color-coded by predicted classes: blue (pedestrians), orange (cars), and red (trucks).

Fig. 3. Detailed view of our light-weight fusion module based on a single multi-head attention block. The modality-specific BEV spaces are encoded and downsampled, before being tokenized and enriched with positional encodings. Subsequently, one multi-head attention layer is applied with tokens from image features as keys/values and tokens from LiDAR features as queries to efficiently learning a soft and dynamic fusion exploiting the semi-aligned nature of the features. Finally, an MLP is applied and a skip connection from the original LiDAR BEV space is added, before upsampling the features, yielding the fused BEV space. Note that we omit typical normalization steps in Transformers for brevity.

Fig. 5. Visualization of the attention scores in image BEV space (heat-map in right parts) given a feature from the LiDAR BEV space (position marked in left parts) as a query in our cross-attention fusion module. All figures show BEVs with the vehicle in the center.

papers.title: FastBEVFusion: Simple Multi-Modal Fusion for 3D Object Detection at 50 FPS

papers.abstract: Coronary guidewire navigation during percutaneous coronary intervention requires continuous interpretation of vessel anatomy, guidewire position, and target stenosis under two-dimensional X-ray fluoroscopy. While existing approaches commonly address vessel segmentation or device localization as separate tasks, a robotic system requires a more structured perception of the coronary scene to support downstream navigation. In this work, we present a simulation-driven framework centered on a Multi-Task Coronary Perception Network (MCP-Net) for robotic guidewire navigation, integrating coronary vessel segmentation, vascular topology extraction, and roadmap generation. Starting from three-dimensional coronary CT angiography, we generate simulated fluoroscopy images containing vascular structures, simulated guidewires, stenotic lesions with varying severity, and diverse vascular geometries, together with simulation-derived ground truth. MCP-Net jointly performs coronary vessel segmentation, guidewire-tip localization, and stenosis localization from a single fluoroscopic frame. These predictions are subsequently converted into a structured vascular graph containing centerlines, bifurcations, endpoints, branch directions, and branch angles. By associating the predicted stenosis with this graph, the framework generates a roadmap from the automatically selected graph root toward the target lesion. The results demonstrate that the proposed framework can jointly recover coronary perception targets and transform them into an interpretable vascular representation suitable for downstream robotic navigation.
authors: Sahar Nasirihaghighi, Tianyuan Wang, Kenan Niu, Stefano Stramigioli
bullets: Addresses the need for structured, continuous coronary-scene understanding beyond separate vessel segmentation or device localization.
Uses simulated fluoroscopy generated from 3D coronary CT angiography, including vessels, guidewires, stenoses, and varied geometries.
Jointly predicts vessel segmentation, guidewire-tip location, and stenosis location from a single X-ray frame.
Transforms predictions into a vascular graph with centerlines, bifurcations, endpoints, branch directions, and angles.
Generates an interpretable roadmap from a selected graph root to the target lesion; evaluation is demonstrated in simulation.

The predicted vasculature is converted into a structured centerline graph and combined with the predicted stenosis target to generate a navigation-oriented roadmap.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) incorporate the prediction of future observations into robot policy learning. However, most WAMs build on billion-parameter vision-language or video-generation backbones, which incur high training cost and inference latency. In this letter, we present GAWM (Geometry-Aware World Model), a compact multi-task WAM that predicts future observations in the latent space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder. GAWM compresses the features of each camera view into a small set of tokens. A lightweight predictor, conditioned on the task rather than on actions, forecasts these tokens at two future horizons. The forecast is supervised with the dense patch features of future frames, which requires it to encode the spatial layout of the future scene. An action decoder directly regresses a chunk of future actions from the current and predicted tokens. With fewer than 100M parameters and no robot or video pretraining, GAWM outperforms billion-parameter WAMs on RoboTwin 2.0 and performs comparably to billion-parameter VLAs on LIBERO. On a dual-arm robot, it achieves lower action-prediction error on held-out demonstrations than a fine-tuned billion-parameter VLA, with substantially lower inference latency. Ablation studies show that the latent world model substantially improves performance when training data or training time is limited. Code is available at https://github.com/gaoxiang12/ga-wm.
authors: Yang Liu, Xiaoli Liu, Liuzhao Li, Yuduo Song, Muyuan Liu, Xiang Gao
bullets: Addresses the high training cost and inference latency of large world-action and vision-language models.
Predicts future multi-view observations in the latent space of a frozen DINOv3 encoder using compact tokens.
Forecasts task-conditioned future tokens at two horizons and uses dense future-frame patch features to preserve scene geometry.
Directly predicts chunks of future robot actions from current and predicted latent tokens.

Uses fewer than 100M parameters, requires no robot or video pretraining, and performs strongly across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and a dual-arm robot; benefits are especially pronounced with limited data or training time.

papers.title: GAWM: A Compact Latent World-Action Model for Multi-Task Robot Manipulation

papers.abstract: Image-goal navigation (ImageNav) requires an agent to reach a location specified by a goal image in an unknown environment. For drones, this task demands exploration, goal- directed navigation, and collision avoidance under limited onboard computing resources. Existing aerial ImageNav methods are built on single-view observations, requiring additional rotation and exploration to search for goal-relevant cues outside the field of view. In this paper, we present Omni-IGN, a fully onboard ImageNav system that integrates quad-fisheye perception, an attention-based reinforcement learning (RL) policy, and a collision-aware safety layer. The policy adaptively fuses goal-relevant features across multiple views to provide directional guidance for continuous navigation. The quad-fisheye RGB images support both ImageNav and obstacle avoidance without a dedicated depth sensor. On Habitat benchmarks, Omni-IGN achieves the best performance among continuous-action baselines. Moreover, flight tests in IsaacSim validate the effectiveness of integrating learning-based depth estimation with the action safety layer for collision avoidance. Finally, real-world experiments demonstrate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer without any fine-tuning or external localization. The code and model checkpoints will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Zichen Yan, Rui Huang, Shenao Wang, Yucong Wang, Nuthasith Gerdpratoom, Lin Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limited field of view, exploration, and collision-avoidance challenges in aerial ImageNav.
Combines quad-fisheye RGB perception, attention-based reinforcement learning, and a collision-aware safety layer.
Adaptively fuses goal-relevant features across multiple views for continuous directional navigation.
Achieves the best performance among continuous-action baselines on Habitat benchmarks.
Demonstrates collision avoidance in IsaacSim and zero-shot sim-to-real transfer in real-world experiments.

papers.abstract: Maintaining contact in non-prehensile manipulation requires more than nominal friction cone feasibility: a force barely inside the cone and one well inside it are both feasible, but they provide different margins against slip and contact loss. This paper uses signed friction distance to measure friction margin in force space and derives a task-adaptive margin from the force correction needed to balance pivot moment deviations in bimanual tilting. The resulting contact margins are embedded in a sequence of second-order cone programs (SOCPs), each giving a globally optimal contact force solution at a tilt angle. The optimizer balances the object about an environmental pivot while keeping robot and pivot contact forces away from the nominal friction boundary. Optimizer-level results show interpretable force redistribution and adaptation to object property changes. Real-world experiments demonstrate successful execution under object property variations and model mismatch, while fixed margin and no-margin comparisons illustrate the importance of adapting the margin to task demand. These results support signed friction distance margins as a force planning mechanism for maintaining contact in bimanual non-prehensile manipulation. Project page: https://keeping-contact.github.io/
authors: Qian Ying Lee, Lin Yang, Domenico Campolo
bullets: Signed friction distance distinguishes barely feasible contact forces from forces with greater slip and contact-loss margin.
The margin is adapted to the force correction required to balance pivot-moment deviations during tilting.
A sequence of SOCPs computes globally optimal contact forces while balancing the object about an environmental pivot.
Results show interpretable force redistribution and adaptation to object-property changes.
Real-world experiments succeed under property variation and model mismatch; fixed- and no-margin comparisons highlight the value of adaptation.

papers.abstract: Learning from experience is essential for building the next generation of agents that continually expand their capabilities. Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already internalize rich world knowledge, yet this knowledge is rarely leveraged to drive policy improvement through online interaction. Realizing this potential efficiently remains challenging, as policy updates shift the agent's interaction distribution, requiring the world model to adapt accordingly, while continually updating large pretrained models is computationally expensive. To address this challenge, we introduce Dwell, a model-based reinforcement learning (RL) framework that reframes a VLM as a recurrent latent transition operator, endowing it with the ability to predict, adjust, and act in latent space. Leveraging the VLM's own representations and its dual role as both world model and policy, the agent continually learns from real interactions to anticipate and evaluate action outcomes, and from latent imagination to improve its behavior. Across five interactive visual environments, Dwell achieves the strongest overall performance among trainable methods while substantially reducing the compute required for imagination, showing that effective world models for VLM agents need not reconstruct the future; they need to predict futures that are useful for action. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/Tom111-lhx/Dwell
authors: Haoxi Li, Sikai Bai, Jianfei Ma, Qinglin Hou, Xiaocheng Lu, Tao Han, Jie Zhang, Song Guo
bullets: Addresses the challenge of efficiently adapting pretrained VLM agents through online experience without continually updating large models.

Combines real-interaction learning with latent imagination to anticipate action outcomes and improve behavior.
Achieves the strongest overall performance among trainable methods across five interactive visual environments.
Substantially reduces imagination compute and suggests useful world models need not reconstruct full futures.

papers.abstract: Real-to-Sim-to-Real (Real2Sim2Real) enables structured world representations for planning, interpretability, and safe execution. Most existing approaches rely on passive perception, which creates real2sim gaps due to imperfect observation. Inspired by how humans perceive actively through actions, we propose ActiveAlign, a framework that leverages active perception to align the Real2Sim2Real gap from interactions. ActiveAlign introduces two complementary modules: (i) ActiveAlign-Waving, which performs hand-eye calibration by exploiting active hand motions and differentiable rendering, and (ii) ActiveAlign-Touching, which refines object alignment through tactile feedback to achieve millimeter-level precision. Together, these capabilities enable strong real2sim alignment. We demonstrate that ActiveAlign-Waving can be used to curate simulation environments for open-sourced uncalibrated robot manipulation datasets, and demonstrate on a real Unitree G1 robot that ActiveAlign enables fine manipulation of millimeter-scale objects such as pressing buttons and moving sliders.

ActiveAlign-Touching refines object alignment with tactile feedback to millimeter-level precision.
Demonstrations include curating simulation environments from uncalibrated manipulation datasets and fine manipulation on a real Unitree G1 robot.
The system handles millimeter-scale tasks such as pressing buttons and moving sliders.

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models may generalize across tasks and embodiments, but their actions still depend on sensors that can fail. When the policy is frozen or inaccessible, can an external monitor diagnose and repair corrupted inputs without access to its internals? We test a structured surrogate that separates periodic gait from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair around a frozen locomotion policy. On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis raises walking success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reaches 382/640, with no triggers in 64 held-out fault-free episodes. A matched boosted-tree surrogate predicts clean actions similarly well but yields no detected repair improvement over no repair. Separate fits improve walking on Go1 and ANYmal C, although phase-aware gradients perform better. Evidence remains limited to one policy and a partly screened simulated fault suite; robot foundation model and hardware validation remain open.
authors: Marc Ziegler, Batu \"Ozen, Sami Mentes, Thomas Waschulzik, Alois Knoll
bullets: Addresses sensor corruption when the robot policy is frozen or inaccessible.
Separates periodic gait dynamics from sensor-dependent corrections to guide input repair.
On simulated Go2, offline diagnosis improved success from 259/640 to 429/640 episodes; online repair reached 382/640.
Produced no false triggers across 64 held-out fault-free episodes; a matched boosted-tree surrogate showed no repair benefit.
Separate surrogate fits helped Go1 and ANYmal C, while phase-aware gradients performed better.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) learn representations for robot control by coupling future visual prediction with action generation. Successful manipulation depends primarily on how the robot and task-relevant objects evolve, whereas future-video prediction must also reconstruct the appearance and background of the entire scene. We therefore propose Trace-WAM, which augments video-action learning with future 3D motion prediction as an auxiliary objective. This objective supervises temporal point correspondence together with image-plane displacement and depth change, directly describing the interaction dynamics and spatial changes involved in manipulation. To this end, we adopt a three-branch Mixture-of-Transformer (Tri-MoT) architecture to jointly learn video prediction, motion prediction, and action generation. The motion expert predicts future trajectories from current visual features, allowing motion supervision to shape the representations used for action generation. Because the action expert does not consume predicted trajectories, inference retains the current-observation policy path: a single visual forward pass followed by action denoising. Experiments on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus demonstrate strong in-distribution performance and out-of-distribution generalization, with particularly clear gains over Fast-WAM under limited demonstrations and distribution shifts.
authors: Xu Hu, Changjie Wu, Linzhe Shi, Hang Zhang, Chen Yang, Lingjun Zhang, Guowen Zhang, Mu Xu, Junran Peng, Qing Li, Zhaoxiang Zhang
bullets: Targets a key mismatch in WAMs: whole-scene video prediction may underemphasize robot-object interaction dynamics.
Adds auxiliary supervision for temporal point correspondence, image-plane displacement, and depth change.

Keeps the action policy conditioned only on current visual observations, requiring one visual pass followed by action denoising.
Experiments on RoboCasa-GR1, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus show strong in-distribution performance and improved generalization, especially with limited demonstrations and distribution shifts.

papers.abstract: Generative planners are often evaluated by the trajectories they can generate, although closed-loop driving ultimately depends on the single candidate committed to control. We identify this mismatch as the sample-to-execution gap and show that improving proposal quality alone can worsen the executed decision. Here, we introduce ExecDiffuser, a recurrent proposal-to-execution framework that couples candidate generation, trajectory selection, and subsequent replanning through shared execution semantics. Intent-Guided Diffusion Proposal (IGD) assigns hypothesis responsibility and shapes trajectories with execution-conditioned supervision. Execution-Grounded Selection (EGS) learns a candidate-conditioned publication utility, commits one trajectory to control, and returns it as context for the next planning cycle. Across nuPlan, InterPlan, and NAVSIM, ExecDiffuser achieves leading closed-loop performance against strong state-of-the-art baselines. Under a unified five-seed protocol, it obtains an average score of 85.62, improving over Diffusion Planner and FlowDrive by 4.02 and 1.31 points, respectively. On NAVSIM, it achieves 92.6 PDMS under the official evaluation pipeline. Matched counterfactual analysis further shows that ExecDiffuser more reliably converts strong candidates into committed decisions, while prefix interventions confirm that this advantage persists after physical execution and subsequent replanning.
authors: Shuo Pei, Bosun Liang, Saihui Zha, Chen Sun, Huachun Tan, Yong Wang
bullets: Identifies a sample-to-execution gap: better generated proposals can still lead to worse committed actions.
Combines intent-guided diffusion proposals with execution-grounded candidate selection.
Feeds the committed trajectory back into subsequent replanning through shared execution semantics.
Reports leading closed-loop performance across nuPlan, InterPlan, and NAVSIM, including an average score of 85.62 and 92.6 PDMS on NAVSIM.
Counterfactual and prefix analyses indicate more reliable conversion of strong candidates into executed decisions.

papers.abstract: Humanoid parkour requires robots to reason about future footholds and whole-body motions over highly discontinuous terrain. We revisit the information asymmetry in asymmetric actor-critic learning for perceptive humanoid locomotion: the critic exploits privileged simulator signals during training, whereas the deployable actor operates solely from onboard perception. We argue that the key is not exposing privileged information to the actor, but learning a deployable approximation of it to narrow the information gap between training and deployment. We present HC2Robot, a deployable perceptive humanoid parkour framework consisting of a Predicted Foresight Module (PFM) and a Hyper-Connection (HC) Transformer. PFM predicts from deployable observations the policy-conditioned timing, location, and support quality of each foot's next touchdown event, converting privileged supervision into a deployable latent representation that provides the actor with predicted touchdown information without privileged runtime sensing. The HC Transformer further enhances temporal reasoning through learnable multi-stream routing, while a future motion prediction head provides short-horizon motion priors for regularization. Across stairs, gaps, high platforms, and slopes, HC2Robot achieves a mean simulated traversal success rate of 97.60% and consistently higher safe foothold rates than strong perceptive locomotion baselines, supporting improved traversal performance and geometric foothold support under deployable sensing.
authors: Wenhao Xu, Yanheng Mai, Yifei Fu, Nan Zheng, Yanbo Zhou, Zirui Huang, Mingsheng Ling, Xinjue Wang, Renjing Xu
bullets: Addresses the training–deployment information gap in asymmetric actor–critic learning without giving privileged runtime signals to the actor.
Uses a Predicted Foresight Module to estimate each foot’s next touchdown timing, location, and support quality.
Employs a Hyper-Connection Transformer for multi-stream temporal reasoning and a future-motion head for short-horizon regularization.
Across stairs, gaps, high platforms, and slopes, reports a 97.60% mean simulated traversal success rate and higher safe foothold rates than perceptive locomotion baselines.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video generation models encode rich priors about physical interactions, but leveraging them for robot control typically requires either resource-intensive video generation at test time or action heads trained from scratch that do not fully utilize the pretrained backbone. We introduce Tokenizing Actions as Video Patches in a Shared Transformer Policy (TAPESTRY), a world action model that repurposes a pretrained video diffusion transformer into a robotic policy without requiring video generation at inference. Our key idea is to treat robot actions as single-patch tokens in the video model's latent space. A lightweight linear projection maps each action timestep to the patch dimensions of the pretrained VAE, and the resulting tokens are processed by the same patchifying layers and transformer backbone used for video. The shared backbone is optimized through three diffusion objectives sampled per minibatch element: Video diffusion uses VAE latents from robot and human videos to establish dynamics priors. Joint video+action diffusion trains on robot demonstrations using a coupled diffusion timestep and an asymmetric attention mask. Action-only diffusion denoises actions conditioned on clean image latents. At test time, the model generates a compact action token sequence in a single DDIM step from pure noise, producing smooth action chunks at 84 ms per action chunk on consumer hardware and avoiding the cost of full video generation. Across simulation benchmarks and real-robot experiments, TAPESTRY achieves strong performance with substantially lower inference cost than comparable joint video--action policies. More information can be found at https://tapestry-wam.github.io.
authors: Jeremy A. Collins, Seungjae Lee, Rachanon Wachakorn, Krishnan Srinivasan, Animesh Garg, Vitor Campagnolo Guizilini, Paarth Shah
bullets: Avoids costly video generation at test time and avoids training a separate action head from scratch.
Maps each action timestep into the pretrained VAE’s patch space, then processes actions with the shared video patchifier and transformer backbone.
Jointly trains video diffusion, video–action diffusion, and action-only diffusion objectives to combine visual dynamics priors with robot demonstrations.
Generates smooth action chunks in one DDIM step, achieving 84 ms per chunk on consumer hardware.
Shows strong results in simulation and real-robot experiments with substantially lower inference cost than comparable joint video–action policies.

papers.abstract: We fine-tuned a separate $\pi_{0.5}$ policy for each of the five tasks in the MetaFine Open Competition, with a task-specific training mixture and number of actions executed per prediction. Training started from the official demonstrations and expert procedures. Local evaluation exposed recurring grasping, pushing, and insertion failures. We addressed them by revising the demonstrated motions and by adding expert continuations from states the policy reached, while keeping nominal demonstrations in training. Checkpoints were compared on every instruction, so that a gain on one instruction could not hide a loss on another. Our submission, MAI, ranked first overall with a score of 96.66.

papers.abstract: Self-driving laboratories (SDLs) are laboratory systems that couple experimental planning, automated execution, and measurement feedback in a closed loop. Integrating flexible robot control with the typed application programming interfaces (APIs) and continuous measurements exposed by laboratory instruments remains an execution-interface challenge. To address this challenge, we propose a traceable framework comprising four components: LAM (Lab Action Model), OpenSDL, Safe-SDL, and L3-Bench. LAM is a proposed measurement-conditioned policy architecture that extends vision-language-action paradigms to generate both continuous robot trajectories and typed instrument API calls. OpenSDL is an execution substrate with an initial control implementation, designed to map role-level operations to heterogeneous devices, coordinate execution, and record timestamped causal events. The proposed Safe-SDL runtime gate combines pre-dispatch schema and resource checks with signal temporal logic monitoring during execution, including extended waiting periods. L3-Bench (Level-3 Laboratory Benchmark) specifies an episode-level evaluation protocol covering physical outcomes, timing, reproducibility, safety violations, and fault recovery. Together, these components provide an end-to-end design for linking hybrid action generation, monitored device execution, measurement feedback, and experimental evaluation, addressing coordination and traceability challenges in SDL workflows.
authors: Zihan Zhang, Zeyu Wu, Xin Zhang, Mingyu Luo, Haohui Que, Tong Zhu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of integrating flexible robot control with typed instrument APIs and continuous measurements.
LAM generates measurement-conditioned continuous robot trajectories alongside typed instrument API calls.
OpenSDL coordinates heterogeneous devices, maps high-level operations to execution, and records timestamped causal events.
Safe-SDL combines pre-execution schema/resource checks with runtime signal-temporal-logic monitoring.
L3-Bench evaluates physical outcomes, timing, reproducibility, safety violations, and fault recovery.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the L3-Bench evaluation protocol. Left: adaptive dilution, measurement-conditioned titration, and fault injection with recovery define three scenario families. Two baselines—a vision-only single-arm policy and LAM without measurement tokens—are compared with the full LAM × OpenSDL framework under nominal, measurement-shift, device-transfer, and fault-injection conditions. Center: initialization comprises profiling, matching, activation, and configuration, followed by on-the-fly schema, safety, and replay-readiness checks of manifest and ledger completeness. The safety-gate ablation is restricted to simulation or risk-assessed hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) evaluation. Right: liquid separation/heating and delay/high pressure illustrate task and condition metadata; the evaluated scenario families are defined on the left. Complete episodes are scored, with batch-level clustering for bootstrap confidence intervals. Primary endpoints are normalized physical yield Y , temporal safety violation rate SVR, and operational time cost C; diagnostic measures include mass-transfer error ∆m, temperature-control error ITAE, makespan, and recovery. Photographs illustrate the laboratory scenarios; check marks and miniature plots indicate protocol requirements and metric types.

Figure 1: LAM architecture for measurement-conditioned hybrid laboratory control. Task language, RGB/RGB-D observations, robot proprioception qt, and time-stamped instrument telemetry Mt enter a multimodal context builder comprising a visionlanguage-model (VLM) backbone and a telemetry encoder. Typed measurement tokens retain device roles, units, sampling times, and data-quality information within the shared context. A continuous action head generates robot-trajectory chunks, a discrete function-calling head generates typed instrument application programming interface (API) calls, and an optional dynamics head predicts the next measurement state Mt+1. The execution layer connects the arm controller and the signal temporal logic (STL) safety monitor with event logging to the OpenSDL bus. Parallel dispatch coordinates compatible actions, while updated observations and confirmed execution events supply feedback for subsequent decisions.
