papers.abstract: This paper presents an approach to achieve side-by-side autonomous motion with a pair of personal mobility vehicles (PMVs). Given a global path, two PMVs plan cooperatively so as to hold a social formation that lets the passengers hold a conversation, while keeping the ride safe and smooth. Each vehicle runs its own sampling-based model-predictive planner; the planners exchange nothing but the odometry each vehicle could observe of the other, and the joint decision is expressed as a pair of utility matrices over pairs of candidate trajectories, resolved by a common rule. The behavioural parameters are fitted by inverse reinforcement learning from 409 minutes of driving by ten pairs of people in human-driven PMVs in an indoor environment, and the lanes the pair can use are derived offline from the corridor itself rather than fixed by hand. A safety layer the cost cannot override executes a move only if the vehicle can still brake clear, measured from its whole body, and a vehicle that is stuck reverses along its own path and continues. In closed-loop simulation over 24 runs in the conditions the drivers were recorded in and 24 in four generated obstacle layouts, no vehicle entered a wall or a cone. The pair holds conversational formation for 60.5 and 68.9 percent of the time among obstacles (anticlockwise and clockwise) and 81.2 and 91.5 percent in a clear aisle, against the drivers' 34.0 and 36.0 percent, and 52.9 and 56.0 percent, and it matches their speed. It keeps one lateral formation where the drivers alternated between a close diagonal and a wide abreast one, and it varies far less. Experimental results are based on a differential drive kinematic simulator running on ROS 2.
bullets: Uses inverse reinforcement learning from 409 minutes of driving by 10 human pairs to fit cooperative behavioral parameters.
Each vehicle runs a sampling-based model-predictive planner and exchanges only observable odometry with its partner.
A common utility-matrix rule coordinates trajectory choices, while corridor-derived lanes and a non-overridable braking-based safety layer support navigation.
In simulation, no vehicle collided with walls or cones across 48 closed-loop runs, and conversational formation was maintained more often than by human drivers.
The system matched driver speed but used a more consistent lateral formation; evaluation was limited to a differential-drive kinematic simulator in ROS 2.

papers.abstract: Flow-based policies for language-conditioned multi-task manipulation commonly share a single $\textit{Gaussian}$ source prior and a common linear transport path across tasks. However, reliably executing multiple tasks with distinct motion requirements remains challenging for a shared policy. We introduce $\textbf{TOPS}$ ($\textbf{T}$ask-$\textbf{O}$riented $\textbf{P}$riors and $\textbf{S}$chedules), which adapts the flow source prior and interpolation schedule to each task without modifying the network architecture. TOPS first constructs multimodal task sources from reverse-mapped expert action sequences, allowing language instructions to select where generation begins. Guided by source-target covariance mismatch, it then slows the transition toward expert actions early in denoising and accelerates it later along directions requiring expansion. Under a $\textit{Gaussian}$ endpoint model, our analysis shows that this schedule adjustment can lower an upper bound on velocity-prediction risk. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and CALVIN demonstrate improved performance across in-distribution, perturbation and cross-environment settings, alongside better data efficiency. Using one integration step, TOPS raises LIBERO-10 success from $53.44\%$ to $69.67\%$ compared with ten-step Standard Flow Matching (FM), while reducing inference time to approximately one-sixth of the baseline. TOPS also yields consistent gains when transferred to the large-scale flow-based $\pi_{0.5}$ policy across all four evaluated settings. Real-world experiments further demonstrate improved task success, including an increase from $20\%$ with standard FM to $80\%$ with TOPS on the upper-drawer opening task.
authors: Tuo An, Chuhao Zhou, Jiahua Dong, Jingliang Li, Jiaqi Bai, Jindou Jia, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Shared Gaussian priors and transport paths struggle with tasks requiring distinct motion patterns.
TOPS builds multimodal, task-specific source priors from reverse-mapped expert actions, selected through language instructions.
It adapts denoising schedules using source–target covariance mismatch, slowing early transitions and accelerating later expansion directions.
The method improves performance across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, CALVIN, transfer to π0.5, and real-world manipulation settings.
On LIBERO-10, one-step TOPS reaches 69.67% success versus 53.44% for ten-step Standard Flow Matching, with roughly one-sixth the inference time.

papers.abstract: Bimanual robot manipulation plays an important role in real-world robotic applications, but the high cost of collecting bimanual demonstrations limits the scalable development of bimanual policy learning. Meanwhile, existing single-arm manipulation data are difficult to directly transfer to bimanual systems due to the Single-to-Dual gap in action spaces, coordination requirements, and arm-side spatial preference. To address this issue, we propose RoboSTD, a zero-shot Single-to-Dual data construction method for bimanual robot learning. RoboSTD first applies sagittal-plane mirroring to observations, proprioception, and actions to construct executable contralateral pseudo-demonstrations. It then uses an LLM to generate structured spatio-temporal coordination constraints that guide the reconstruction of pseudo-bimanual supervision across workspace regions and task stages. We evaluate RoboSTD on the AgileX ALOHA platform in both RoboTwin simulation and real-world settings. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of RoboSTD for bimanual policy learning. Without requiring additional bimanual demonstrations, RoboSTD increases the average number of collected cups to 2.11x that of the single-arm baseline in the cup collection task. Project page: https://huahungy.github.io/RoboSTD/
authors: Hongyu Wu, Chong Liu, Shaoxuan Xie, Shaqi Luo, Hanyu Feng, Shihan Wu, Guocai Yao
bullets: Addresses the high cost of collecting bimanual demonstrations and the Single-to-Dual gap in action spaces, coordination, and arm-side preferences.
Mirrors observations, proprioception, and actions across the sagittal plane to create executable contralateral pseudo-demonstrations.

Evaluated in RoboTwin simulation and on a real AgileX ALOHA platform.
In cup collection, it collects 2.11× as many cups as the single-arm baseline without additional bimanual demonstrations.

The same sign-assignment principle applies consistently across the illustrated robot morphologies. The assignment is determined by the reflected joint-axis relation and the robot mounting configuration, rather than by the joint name itself.

Fig. 3. Overview of RoboSTD. (a) Inputs include single-arm demonstrations, robot geometry, and task context. (b) Sagittal-plane mirroring jointly transforms observations, proprioception, and actions to generate contralateral pseudo-demonstrations. (c) An LLM infers arm assignments, precedence, and conflict constraints. (d) These constraints guide the composition of original and mirrored skills into pseudo-bimanual supervision.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) leverage pretrained video generative models for robotic control by jointly predicting future visual observations and actions. The visual prediction objective plays a key role in adapting pretrained video representations to the target robot domain. Yet standard visual prediction inherited from video pretraining treats all visual regions uniformly, despite their differing relevance to robotic control. We therefore investigate the spatial allocation of visual supervision in WAMs and show that focusing supervision on dynamic regions can substantially improve policy performance. Building on this finding, we introduce Motion-Guided Asymmetric Prediction (MoGAP), which augments WAM training with motion-focused visual prediction. MoGAP allocates noise asymmetrically across regions, training the model to reconstruct more heavily corrupted dynamic regions using less corrupted static regions as context. MoGAP is trained alongside standard video-action prediction through a training-only auxiliary prediction path within the shared video diffusion backbone. It uses motion cues derived directly from training videos, requiring neither an external teacher nor additional modalities. Across robot manipulation benchmarks and WAM architectures, MoGAP consistently improves policy performance, increasing success rates on the GR-1 tabletop benchmark from 38.8% to 47.5% for Fast-WAM (Wan2.2-5B) and from 52.3% to 62.3% for Cosmos3-Nano.
authors: Taeyoung Kim, Junyoung Sung, Heeseung Kwon, Minseop Kim, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: WAMs benefit from allocating more visual supervision to regions that move and matter for control.
MoGAP applies asymmetric noise: dynamic regions are more corrupted, while static regions provide context for reconstruction.
It adds a training-only auxiliary prediction path alongside standard video-action prediction, using motion cues from training videos without extra modalities or teachers.
Across manipulation benchmarks and WAM architectures, MoGAP improves success rates, including GR-1 gains from 38.8% to 47.5% and 52.3% to 62.3%.

papers.abstract: Enabling a humanoid to interact naturally with human partners requires preserving not only individual motions but also the spatial, semantic, and contact relationships underlying the interaction (i.e., hugging, dancing, hand-shaking, etc.). Furthermore, a practical solution should generalize across various humanoid embodiments with distinct morphologies and kinematic constraints. To tackle this challenge, we propose HumiTransfer, a mimetic embodiment transfer framework that converts in-the-wild human-human interaction videos into physically plausible human-humanoid interactions. HumiTransfer first reconstructs 3D human motion with consistent foot-ground contact, then transfers one participant to a target humanoid embodiment via interaction modeling, using weighted joint-relative directions and anatomical offsets to prioritize interaction-critical inter-body relationships, while post-retargeting optimization enforces balance, contact, and collision avoidance. Subsequently, we apply HumiTransfer to 1,200 in-the-wild videos, producing approximately 500,000 frames of diverse interactions for the 26-DoF Unitree R1 Edu and the 23-DoF HighTorque Mini-hi humanoid robot, resulting in our HumiMimic dataset. Across both robots, HumiTransfer achieves superior motion fidelity, preserves inter-body relationships, and maintains contact accuracy compared with existing baselines. Moreover, we demonstrate that HumiMimic supports motion generation methods for synthesizing interactive humanoid motions following a human partner. Finally, our real robot deployments confirm the physical executability of the transferred motions in real-world settings.
authors: Nghia Le (Hann), Khang Nguyen (Hann), Ba Long Tran (Hann), Thi Quynh Nhu Pham (Hann), Binh Nguyen (Hann), Tuong Do (Hann), Erman Tjiputra (Hann), Hoan Nguyen (Hann), Tung D. Ta (Hann), Baoru Huang (Hann), Hai-Nguyen (Hann), Nguyen (Hann), Anh Nguyen
bullets: Addresses natural human-humanoid interaction across robots with different morphologies and kinematic constraints.
Reconstructs 3D human motion with foot-ground contact, then retargets one participant using interaction-aware joint directions and anatomical offsets.
Post-retargeting optimization enforces balance, contact, and collision avoidance.
Generates the HumiMimic dataset from 1,200 videos, covering about 500,000 frames for two humanoid platforms.
Experiments and real-robot deployments show improved motion fidelity, inter-body relationship preservation, contact accuracy, and physical executability over baselines.

papers.abstract: Handheld data-collection interfaces such as the Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) allow manipulation demonstrations to be gathered in the wild without a robot in the loop, but the quality of the resulting action labels is bounded by the accuracy of vision-based localization. Existing systems recover end-effector pose from monocular visual-inertial odometry, which is subject to scale ambiguity and drift, or delegate tracking to closed-source modules and external infrastructure that reintroduce cost and setup burden. We present OpenJaws, a fully open hardware and software framework for sensorized UMI that improves localization and simplifies deployment across robot platforms. OpenJaws pairs a modular, 3D-printed gripper exposing a standardized ISO adapter with a low-cost stereo camera to recover metric camera trajectories. We further introduce UMI-Loc-Bench-v1, a benchmark quantifying real-world localization accuracy for handheld data-collection devices, and show that stereo localization substantially outperforms monocular alternatives. Finally, we demonstrate that policies trained on data collected with OpenJaws can be deployed on a real robot across multiple tasks. Hardware, software, and data are released under a commercially permissive license. Code, data, and videos are available at https://open-jaws.github.io/
authors: Adithyavairavan Murali, Yash Oza, Karanbir Chahal, Neel Jawale, Silas De Vries, Hesam Rabeti, Erwin Coumans, Balakumar Sundaralingam, Stan Birchfield
bullets: Addresses scale ambiguity and drift in monocular UMI localization, while avoiding closed-source tracking systems and external infrastructure.
Combines a modular 3D-printed gripper with a standardized ISO adapter and a low-cost stereo camera.
Introduces UMI-Loc-Bench-v1 for evaluating real-world localization accuracy of handheld data-collection devices.
Reports that stereo localization substantially outperforms monocular alternatives.
Demonstrates robot policies trained with OpenJaws-collected data across multiple real-world tasks; hardware, software, and data are openly released.

papers.abstract: Decision models offer fast choices over sup- plied alternatives, while general-purpose large language models interpret open-ended tasks through flexible generation and reasoning at the cost of sequential decoding. Many work- loads expect a generative backend to determine what can be done and therefore provide no well-defined candidate list. We bridge this in- terface gap with a small candidate formalizer trained on offline teacher-generated lists. The formalizer constructs explicit, validated alter- natives from task context, and a frozen deci- sion model selects an entry. A motivating com- parison with official TypeSafe Jev-1.13.0 on 200 CALVIN-D test episodes reports 11% suc- cess with generic motions versus 46.5% with DeepSeek V4 Flash pose candidates. Sepa- rately, a six-arm privileged-state evaluation on 1,011 CALVIN-D validation annotations finds that a locally deployed decision model can achieve at most 52.6% task success rate with the fine-tuned formalizer, compared with 11.8% without it, and the end-to-end latency is kept to 2.09 s, whereas Qwen3.5-27B is 3.67 s with the exact experiment setting.
authors: Chengxuan Pei, Ziyao Wang, Teng Mei, Zhe Li
bullets: Addresses the interface gap between generative language models and decision models that require explicit candidate lists.
Trains a formalizer on offline teacher-generated lists to construct validated alternatives from task context, while keeping the decision model frozen.
In CALVIN-D evaluations, formalization improved reported task success from 11.8% to 52.6% in a privileged-state setting.
A motivating comparison reported 46.5% success with pose candidates versus 11% with generic motions.
End-to-end latency was 2.09 s, compared with 3.67 s for Qwen3.5-27B under the stated experimental setting.

papers.abstract: To generate landmark-based route instructions, models must understand both map geometry and human landmark preferences. Although large language models (LLMs) show great abilities in language tasks, the best way to structure map data for these models is not yet established. This paper proposes a structured text representation for landmark selection tasks in route navigation, utilizing SVG format to encode spatial features. The structured text maintains a geometric connection with rendered map images, allowing language models to directly access spatial and semantic data. Using a new dataset created from human-written route descriptions and OpenStreetMap data, we evaluate models on two tasks: landmark selection at turns and around destinations. Experiments with five LLMs show that the proposed structured text input performs as well as or better than image-based PNG inputs. In addition, task-specific fine-tuning enables smaller local LLMs to effectively leverage map layouts to achieve high selection accuracy. These results demonstrate that structured text is an efficient and lightweight interface for spatial reasoning in human-oriented navigation.
authors: Mifu Matsumoto, Yuki Nakanishi, Tomoya Hashiguchi, Hiroaki Ohshima
bullets: Addresses the challenge of representing map geometry and semantic information for landmark-based route instruction generation.

Across five LLMs, structured text performs as well as or better than PNG map inputs.
Task-specific fine-tuning allows smaller local LLMs to use map layouts effectively.

papers.abstract: Humans are dexterous, but traditional data collection paradigms such as teleoperation, kinesthetic teaching, and wearable exoskeletons force humans to act through the robot embodiment, bottlenecking their dexterity. Retargeting can avoid this. However, existing methods purely translate kinematics and ignore the real-world contact dynamics essential for task success. We present CARD: Contact-Anchored Retargeting for Dexterous Manipulation, a simulator and object-free framework that retargets human demonstrations to robot actions by explicitly preserving contact force targets. CARD unifies human data sources including video, motion capture, and tactile gloves via a shared hand--contact representation and generates explicit contact force targets in addition to kinematics. To maintain these contact targets during hardware open-loop replay, CARD also introduces a tactile tracking controller. For video which does not contain an explicit tactile source, we present Vid-HACO, our video-to-contact model that sets a new state of the art. Across our video, glove, motion-capture data and the GRAB dataset, CARD maintains contact on $43$--$78\%$ of contact frames, while kinematic and object-aware retargeting methods maintain contact on $<10\%$ and $22.5\%$ of the frames respectively. Further, integrating our formulation into physics-based retargeting improves strict task success from 12\% to 32\% on GRAB dataset. Finally, we show that our tactile tracker is critical to reproduce demonstrated forces during hardware replay. These results establish that contact preservation via CARD is a scalable interface for transferring human dexterity to robots.
authors: Cunxi Dai, Botao He, Francois R Hogan, Wei Pan, Rao Fu, Wen-Han Hsieh, Ruoshi Liu, Jitendra Malik, Guanya Shi, Akash Sharma
bullets: Addresses the failure of kinematics-only retargeting to preserve the contact dynamics needed for successful manipulation.
Uses a shared hand–contact representation for video, motion capture, and tactile-glove data, generating both robot actions and contact-force targets.
Introduces Vid-HACO for inferring contacts from video and a tactile tracking controller for hardware open-loop replay.
Maintains contact on 43–78% of contact frames, compared with under 10% for kinematic and 22.5% for object-aware retargeting.
Improves strict task success on GRAB from 12% to 32% when integrated with physics-based retargeting; hardware results show tactile tracking is essential for reproducing forces.

Joint and contact force targets are replayed by a tactile tracking controller (Sec. 3.4) on hardware.

papers.abstract: We present CPG-ENN, a trainable quadruped locomotion framework that combines explicit neural coordination with learned motion realization. A symmetry-based eight-neuron central pattern generator (CPG) supplies gait rhythms, while a pretrained, leg-shared execution neural network (ENN) maps rhythmic signals and trajectory parameters to joint-angle references without online inverse kinematics. A single feedback policy modulates six physically interpretable trajectory variables. The controller tracks planar velocity and yaw-rate commands across walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk without gait-specific learned controllers or transitionspecific rewards. Simulation yields 99.39% transition success across all 20 directed gait pairs and all source-target speed combinations from {0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0} m/s. Ablations show high cross-gait transition feasibility without transition exposure; exposure mainly refines gait acquisition and velocity transients. Comparisons with AllGaits and Walk These Ways demonstrate accurate gait-speed regulation, and Unitree Go2 experiments validate five gaits and their transitions.
authors: Xiyan Liu, Yide Liu, Guoyong Mao, Shaoxing Qu
bullets: Targets robust velocity and yaw-rate control across walk, trot, pace, bound, and pronk.
Uses an eight-neuron CPG for gait rhythms and a pretrained leg-shared ENN to generate joint-angle references.
A feedback policy adjusts six physically interpretable trajectory variables.

Experiments on a Unitree Go2 validated all five gaits and their transitions; transition exposure mainly improved gait acquisition and velocity transients.

papers.abstract: Differences in musculoskeletal morphology challenge policy reuse across individual models. Here we present MyoAcross, a framework that combines individual musculoskeletal model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning and virtual model augmentation to enable muscle-driven reference-motion tracking without individual fine-tuning. Across 31 held-out individual models, MyoAcross achieves 99.24% completion and reduces tracking error by 22.60% relative to an unconditioned multilayer perceptron. Policy reuse extends to models of 22 held-out individuals constructed from single-image shape estimates, measured height and body mass, and, with asymmetry augmentation, to models with unilateral lower-limb shortening. Comparisons with measurements from 120 additional individuals show agreement in vertical ground reaction force waveforms and channel-dependent agreement between simulated muscle activations and electromyography. These results establish a common control framework for comparative simulations of movement across individual musculoskeletal models.
authors: Bozhao Wang, Yinglei Zhu, Zhengqing Li, Zhiyuan Zhang, Weiming Kang, Yiheng He, XinJun Liu, Senhao Hou, Huichan Zhao, Xiaoqiang Tang
bullets: Addresses policy reuse challenges caused by differences in musculoskeletal morphology.
Combines individualized model construction, morphology-conditioned policy learning, and virtual model augmentation.
Achieves 99.24% completion across 31 held-out models and reduces tracking error by 22.60% versus an unconditioned MLP.
Generalizes to single-image-based models and models with unilateral lower-limb shortening.
Simulations agree with measured ground-reaction forces and show channel-dependent agreement with electromyography.

Retargeting the source motions to each model produces 9,024 reference motions. c, Skeletal measurement fitting error across the 141 models. A morphology encoder maps model-derived morphology features to a learned morphology representation, which conditions the actor and critic through feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM). The actor generates muscle excitations, and training uses proximal policy optimization (PPO).

In b, d and e, points represent individual subjects. papers.abstract: Humanoid behavior foundation models (BFMs) provide reusable whole-body motion priors: given a kinematic reference, they generate coordinated joint commands for motion replay, teleoperation, and VLA control. However, trained primarily on flat-ground motion, BFMs lack an explicit mechanism to adapt foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing to local terrain. Many terrain-aware BFM approaches address this limitation by retraining or fine-tuning the tracker together with perception, incurring substantial data and computation costs while coupling ordinary tracking to the perception pathway. To bridge this gap, we propose GRAFT, a geometry-aware residual adaptation framework for frozen behavior trackers. GRAFT preserves the BFM parameters and motion-reference interface, while a lightweight adapter adds terrain-conditioned corrections only to lower-body execution targets. The adapter is trained with task and foot-geometry rewards, regularized to suppress unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distilled from privileged terrain observations to onboard depth. Because the frozen BFM already provides whole-body reference tracking and nominal locomotion, GRAFT reduces terrain learning to a focused execution-adaptation problem. We instantiate the framework on four frozen trackers and evaluate stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation. We further validate it through real-world deployment on a Unitree G1, where the adapted SONIC tracker traverses terrain with onboard depth and unmodified references.
authors: Liang Li, Guoyao Zhang, Xingyu Chen, Sikai Wu, Qianyang Wu, Yuhang Lin, Renjing Xu, Mingliang Zhou, Diyun Xiang
bullets: Targets missing terrain adaptation in flat-ground-trained behavior foundation models, especially foot placement, swing clearance, and contact timing.
Adds a terrain-conditioned residual adapter that modifies only lower-body execution targets while preserving the frozen tracker and reference interface.
Trains with task and foot-geometry rewards, suppresses unnecessary corrections on flat ground, and distills privileged terrain information to onboard depth.
Evaluated on four frozen trackers across stairs, gaps, and platforms in simulation.
Demonstrated real-world terrain traversal on a Unitree G1 using the adapted SONIC tracker, onboard depth, and unmodified references.

papers.abstract: Low-cost arms such as the SO-101 have become the most common entry point to robot learning, yet no released policy performs spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks on them out of the box, and existing SO-101 benchmarks run only on physical hardware with simple tasks and few held-out objects. We introduce SO-101 Bench, a simulated benchmark for language-conditioned spatial manipulation built on an Isaac Lab digital twin of a real SO-101 setup. It has four tasks scored as five families, 138 objects in seen, unseen-instance and unseen-class splits, 916 evaluation episodes with subsets for held-out appearances, rotate-to-fit planning and occlusion memory, and 3,629 simulated demonstrations on which every learned policy is fine-tuned under an equal compute budget. The twin ranks policies as the real robot does: five policies trained without real data, four VLAs and an LLM agent, keep their exact ranking when the same weights run on the physical arm in an unseen environment with unseen objects (Spearman rho = 1.00, MMRV = 0.000), although simulation overestimates success. Across nine VLAs and world-action models, the best learned policies score near 61%, with spatial placement, unseen object classes and rotate-to-fit planning remaining open. An LLM agent that writes code and hands grasping to a learned policy scores 83.2%, and an ablation shows that this lead comes from the choice of harness and the choice of language model.
bullets: Targets low-cost SO-101 arms, addressing the lack of accessible benchmarks for spatially constrained, language-conditioned tasks.
Provides four tasks across five evaluation families, 138 objects, seen/unseen splits, 916 episodes, and simulated demonstrations in an Isaac Lab digital twin.

Best learned policies achieved about 61%, while an LLM code-writing agent paired with a learned grasping policy reached 83.2%.
Spatial placement, unseen object classes, and rotate-to-fit planning remain open challenges.

papers.abstract: Perceiving human body motion is critical for multimodal systems that understand and assist people. Yet current evaluations of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) largely focus on objects, scenes, and coarse actions, leaving their ability to reason about the body itself poorly assessed. This is especially challenging from the egocentric perspective, in which the body is only partially visible and motion must be inferred from occluded and temporally distributed cues. We introduce SOMA, a benchmark for fine-grained body-motion understanding from egocentric video, comprising 1,632 human-verified questions across three capability axes: body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning. We evaluate 37 leading closed-source, open-source, and specialized egocentric MLLMs, complemented by an extensive human evaluation. We find that humans also find this task difficult from video alone (68.5% accuracy), yet clearly outperform the strongest MLLM (Qwen3.6-27B), which reaches 50.0% zero-shot accuracy. Our error analysis shows that MLLMs often misread the wearer's own body, misjudge events in time, and are prone to biases such as favoring the right hand or under-counting repetitions. To narrow the gap to human performance and support further progress, we introduce a training dataset of aligned video, body motion, and language supervision, and a multimodal baseline that jointly learns from these modalities. By identifying common failure modes and missing capabilities in current MLLMs, we hope SOMA will inspire future research on body-motion understanding and multimodal reasoning. Full benchmark, training data, and code will be released at: https://cnai.epfl.ch/soma
authors: Matea Tashkovska, Na\"el Ouerghemi, Haozhe Qi, Alexander Mathis
bullets: Introduces 1,632 human-verified questions spanning body configuration, motion dynamics, and temporal reasoning.

Finds recurring errors in interpreting the wearer’s body, temporal events, repetition counts, and hand-side biases.
Provides aligned video–body-motion–language training data and a multimodal baseline to support future research.

papers.abstract: Robotic agents operating in real-world environments must adapt continuously from a stream of multimodal demonstrations, often under constraints that preclude storing or revisiting past data. In this replay-free, single-pass lifelong imitation learning setting, sequential updates can progressively distort the representation space, making expert-based approaches particularly sensitive to routing interference, causing expert selection to degrade over time. We propose HIDRA, a structured routing framework that mitigates this issue through a hierarchical dual-attention mechanism, which decouples instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement. To further stabilize routing under representation drift, HIDRA introduces a key-level geometric regularization that enforces both alignment within tasks and separation across tasks. The resulting approach enables reliable expert selection while supporting an expandable set of experts for continual adaptation. We evaluate HIDRA on several LIBERO benchmark suites, including more challenging variants with heterogeneous task sequences and paraphrased language instructions. Our approach consistently outperforms both replay-free and replay-based baselines, improving AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting, with stronger gains under high interference and language variation. The code is available at: https://github.com/yfqi/HIDRA.
authors: Fanqi Yu, Matteo Tiezzi, Cigdem Beyan, Tommaso Apicella, Vittorio Murino
bullets: Targets sequential learning from multimodal demonstrations without storing or revisiting past data.
Uses hierarchical dual attention to separate instruction-level expert retrieval from context-dependent refinement.
Adds key-level geometric regularization to align representations within tasks and separate them across tasks.
Supports an expandable expert set for continual adaptation and reliable expert selection.
On LIBERO suites, including heterogeneous and paraphrased tasks, it improves AUC and forward transfer while maintaining low forgetting; gains are stronger under interference and language variation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of HIDRA. A frozen pretrained multimodal policy produces an instruction query qinst and a context query qctxt . These drive a two-stage hierarchical dual-routing attention mechanism. Stage I performs instruction-level retrieval via qinst to select an anchor expert j∗ and an instruction candidate set Sj∗ over task-level keys {kinsj }. Stage II then uses qctxt to perform context-level refinement within Sj∗ using context keys {kctxj }, producing fused routing scores and selecting the active experts. Key-space regularization (Reg.) promotes intra-task compactness and inter-task separation, enabling stable and interference-resistant expert selection as new task-specific experts are introduced during replay-free lifelong adaptation.

papers.abstract: Monocular outdoor navigation requires robust camera motion estimation and a dense, navigable map, where 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM serves this task through an explicit differentiable parameterization and closed-form projection. However, typically, the geometry is recovered by associating 2D pixels with 3D points, so a modular SLAM system absorbs tracking error into the map, leading to cascading degradation. To address these gaps, we present SG^2SLAM, which couples streaming spatial geometry with a ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel. Streaming spatial geometry replaces the per- frame cross-dimensional correspondence with a chunk-level metric prior that supervises tracking and mapping from one source. A ray-conditioned kernel extends each primitive with a viewing-direction subspace that senses the monocular camera viewpoints. The joint optimization over spatial geometry and poses ensures a globally consistent map and trajectory outcome. Experiments on the KITTI and Waymo Open datasets show that our SG^2SLAM surpasses the per-frame association baselines in the monocular outdoor navigation task. Code will be made publicly available upon acceptance.
authors: Ziang Guo, Didar Seyidov, Yixiao Zhou, Xuefeng Zhang, Ali Alridha Abdulkarim, Chen Min, Zufeng Zhang, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Addresses cascading map degradation caused by absorbing monocular tracking errors into the map.
Uses chunk-level streaming spatial geometry as a metric prior to supervise both tracking and mapping.
Introduces a ray-conditioned 3DGS kernel that models viewpoint-dependent information.
Jointly optimizes geometry and poses to produce globally consistent maps and trajectories.
Outperforms per-frame association baselines on KITTI and Waymo Open datasets.

The chunk fusion is solved over the spatial geometry and poses via a global joint graph.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms have been observed to lose the ability to adaptively learn from new data, a phenomenon termed Loss of Plasticity (LoP). While many metrics have been shown to correlate with it, the causal mechanisms and the geometric conditions from which it can arise have not been clearly identified. We analyze LoP in Proximal Policy Optimization with isotropic Gaussian policies, the state-of-the-art formulation for many continuous action spaces in RL. We report multiple metrics which characterize the effect that the policy standard deviation $\sigma$ has on LoP, and we also suggest related explanations for the effectiveness of widely adopted LoP mitigation techniques. We observe a significant effect of $\sigma$ on the extent of LoP, and accompany this with both theoretical and experimental supporting arguments. Our experimental validation consists of LoP benchmark evaluations against standard baselines as well as real-world policy deployment on a 7-DoF robotic arm.
authors: Andrea Vasco Grieco, Evelyn D'Elia, Edoardo Caldarelli, Raffaello Camoriano
bullets: Analyzes loss of plasticity (LoP), where RL agents become less able to learn from new data.

Connects the findings to why commonly used LoP mitigation techniques may be effective.
Validates the analysis on LoP benchmarks and through deployment on a 7-DoF robotic arm.

papers.abstract: Navigation vision-language-action (VLA) policies repeatedly invoke costly semantic reasoning even when the next command remains unchanged. Command reuse can reduce computation but risks missing instruction-dependent turns or stops. We introduce ASPEN, an event-triggered scheduler based on command persistence prediction: estimating whether the frozen base policy would reissue its previous command. A lightweight multimodal predictor combines temporal observations, language instructions, execution history, and cached VLA confidence. At eligible command boundaries, sufficient predicted persistence permits command reuse. Otherwise, ASPEN triggers fresh semantic reasoning from the VLA. Evaluated with frozen NaVILA on cross-dataset RxR-CE val-unseen, ASPEN reduces VLA calls by 9.5% and estimated inference time by 8.1%, including scheduling overhead. It maintains comparable navigation performance and preserves identical baseline action sequences on 92.1% of episodes.
bullets: Targets redundant semantic reasoning in navigation VLAs when the next command is likely unchanged.
Uses a lightweight multimodal predictor over observations, instructions, execution history, and cached VLA confidence.
Reuses commands when predicted persistence is sufficient; otherwise triggers fresh VLA reasoning.
With frozen NaVILA on RxR-CE val-unseen, reduces VLA calls by 9.5% and estimated inference time by 8.1%.
Maintains comparable navigation performance, with identical baseline action sequences in 92.1% of episodes.

papers.abstract: Complex whole-body loco-manipulation requires executing diverse maneuvers, such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion, within a single long-horizon task. While performing simple pick-and-place behaviors is well-established, scaling to complex, long-horizon tasks remains difficult. Currently, this challenge is addressed by relying on human motion data and correspondingly humanoid platforms, which limits platform independence and introduces substantial data processing overhead. Instead, we extend proximal policy optimization (PPO) to train a single policy for multi-phase tasks across diverse robotic hardware, leveraging prior task structure to shape behavior. Our method adapts PPO using a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated reward functions, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to guide exploration. To support varied hardware, we employ a decoupled hierarchical control architecture that separates lower-level balancing dynamics from high-level phase execution. We demonstrate multi-stage loco-manipulation skills on hardware on both the Unitree G1 and a Boston Dynamics Spot equipped with a manipulator arm, and validate our design choices through ablations. Our approach enables the acquisition of complex loco-manipulation behaviors purely through environment interaction while directly incorporating high-level task structure into policy learning.
authors: Simone Manni, Annika Wollschl\"ager, Dario Bellicoso, Abel Gawel, Marco Hutter, Simon Le Cleac'h, Jan Br\"udigam
bullets: Targets long-horizon tasks combining maneuvers such as crouching, grasping, and locomotion.
Uses a phase-conditioned critic, phase-gated rewards, and a multi-phase reset curriculum to structure exploration.
Employs decoupled hierarchical control, separating low-level balance from high-level phase execution.
Demonstrates multi-stage skills on Unitree G1 and Boston Dynamics Spot with a manipulator arm.
Ablation studies validate the proposed design choices.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of the phase-conditioned PPO framework. An environment state machine segments the task into phases (ψk) via local success conditions (e.g., distance d and phase-specific thresholds ϵ). To tackle exploration bottlenecks, a multiphase curriculum initially resets episodes into later stages before progressively shifting back to the initial phase as training advances. The actor outputs delta actions updating command targets ct, while an auxiliary head enforces phase internalization via cross-entropy loss (LCE) against the true environment phase. The critic conditions value estimation on state st and phase one-hot encoding ek, combining a base value Vbase with phase-specific residual heads. These are constrained by Lreg to keep the main learning burden on the base head. Finally, task rewards are dynamically gated based on the active phase ψk and combined with rewards for forward phase transitions and penalties for backward regression.

Fig. 5: Algorithmic Ablation Study on Spot and G1: Task success rate across training steps on (a) spot tire rolling and (b) g1 push two boxes, comparing our method (Ours) against baseline architectures (MLP, Multihead), an unguided variant (No phase prediction), and execution without multi-phase episode initialization (Initial phase reset). Solid curves and shaded regions denote the mean and variance across 3 random seeds, respectively. (c) Spot Phase Analysis: Evaluation of phase-prediction accuracy across 1,000 successful episodes of spot tire rolling task. Because individual phase durations vary across rollouts, evaluation episodes are temporally anchored at phase transitions with intermediate timesteps linearly warped to uniform phase durations. The top plot shows that the auxiliary head’s online phase predictions tightly track the ground-truth phase steps with minimal variance, while the bottom plot highlights the object-to-goal distance as a proxy for task progression.

Fig. 2: Overview of the low-level whole-body policy. The policy commands leg and waist joints to execute stable locomotion, low crouching, and crouch-walking. Training stability is achieved via inverse kinematics (IK) keyframe initializations that spawn the robot in valid postures, coupled with a feasibility-constrained command space. For standing environments, this region is bounded by the convex hull of admissible IK keyframes, whereas for dynamic environments, the feasible command envelope dynamically contracts as target tracking velocity increases.

Fig. 4: Hardware deployment of the g1 lift box task using onboard state estimation and ArUco marker detection. The right panel shows the Unitree G1 humanoid executing the lift, while the insets display the state estimation visualization (top-left) and the onboard first-person camera view tracking the ArUco marker (bottom-left).

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) offer a promising framework for embodied intelligence, yet mainstream approaches remain centered on video foundation models or vision-language models. Even when geometric features extracted by 3D models such as VGGT are incorporated, they are typically passed into a video model or VLM that serves as the primary backbone, leaving 3D geometry as an auxiliary input or prediction target rather than the native foundation for world modeling. We present E0.5, a geometry-native world-action model built directly on 3D foundation models. E0.5 introduces two key innovations. First, it adopts a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone, making 3D geometry the native representation for both world modeling and action prediction. Second, it explicitly predicts future 3D states together with actions, enabling the model to capture geometric world dynamics beyond action-only modeling or future video prediction. Experiments on RoboTwin 2.0 first demonstrate the effectiveness of E0.5 without embodied-data pretraining, achieving success rates of 89.90\% and 50.09\% under clean and randomized settings, respectively. Building on these results, we further pretrain E0.5 on more than 160k robot trajectories from AgiBotWorld-Beta, jointly learning robot actions and future geometry within the pretrained 3D foundation. This embodied pretraining improves mean real-world manipulation success rates by approximately 15 and 7 percentage points on AgileX Piper and Zerith H1, respectively. Together, these results demonstrate the potential of geometry-native foundations to acquire robot interaction knowledge and transfer it to physical manipulation. E0.5 embodies this geometry-native approach as a member of the VWA family of world-action models.
authors: Era AI Lab Team, Jianhao Lai, Zhihao Zhan, Zhiquan Liao, Qichang Li, Shubin Chen, Zhiyuan Liu, Hongsen Lei, Jianman Lin, Xiaoxin Lin, Ke Gong, Baiyue Gu, Shiming Chen, Junlin He, Longqi Yang, Junrong Xiao, Haolin Luo, Xiaojuan Su, Jianfeng Li, Yu Luo, Xu Sun, Likui Zhang, Jusheng Zhang, Qinhan Lyu, Tianshui Chen, Liang Lin, Guangrun Wang
bullets: Targets the limitation of video- or vision-language-centric world-action models, where 3D geometry is auxiliary rather than foundational.
Uses a 3D foundation model as the primary backbone for both world modeling and action prediction.
Predicts future 3D states alongside actions to model geometric world dynamics.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces a geometry-native world-action model predicting future 3D states and actions, spanning Embodied AI, World Models, and 3D Foundation Models.
papers.title: E0.5: From Reconstructive to Future-Predictive 3D Foundations for Robotic World-Action Modeling

papers.abstract: Autonomous vertical landing of reusable launch vehicles is a critical yet formidable challenge in aerospace engineering, primarily due to highly nonlinear dynamics, stringent precision require- ments, and inherent environmental uncertainties. While reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising alternative to traditional model-based control, existing approaches frequently rely on flat training paradigms and highly simplified initial conditions, drastically limiting their real-world applicability. This paper proposes a comprehensive curriculum-driven deep reinforcement learning framework designed to master both far-range navigation and precision landing. By employing a three-stage curriculum augmented with a critic warm-up procedure and a rehearsal mechanism to prevent catastrophic forgetting, alongside a high-dimensional observation vector utilizing a full 3 X 3 rotation-matrix, the agent is trained to navigate from an initial horizontal distance of 1,000 to 1,500 units vastly farther than prior benchmarks before executing a soft touchdown. Crucially, we intro- duce a redesigned reward function that reduces unnecessary computational overhead and addresses limitations of earlier formulations, including poorly calibrated reward components and potentially conflicting optimization objectives. The redesigned function bounds the per-step reward magnitude by (O(1)), while its progress term accumulates the total distance closed over the trajectory. The available 100,000-episode results report a 99.98% success rate for the proposed policy and 68.31% for the baseline under the evaluation conditions. In the evaluation, the proposed policy retained 69.1% of its initial fuel capacity and achieved a mean final distance from the pad centre of 7.07 units, compared with 13.10 units for the baseline. Landing visualizations are available in Video 1 and Video 2.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of combining long-range navigation with precision vertical landing under nonlinear dynamics and uncertainty.
Uses a three-stage curriculum, critic warm-up, rehearsal to limit catastrophic forgetting, and observations containing a full 3×3 rotation matrix.
Introduces a bounded, computationally simpler reward function whose progress term tracks cumulative distance closed.
Under the reported evaluation, the policy achieved 99.98% success versus 68.31% for the baseline.
The proposed policy retained 69.1% initial fuel and had 7.07 units mean final pad-distance, compared with 13.10 units for the baseline.

papers.abstract: Image quality assessment (IQA) underpins embodied imaging pipelines by judging whether visual quality satisfies downstream tasks, yet most existing methods learn task-agnostic scores aligned with generic human ratings on static benchmarks. This objective mismatches embodied and interactive settings, where image adequacy depends on task goals, context, and action requirements that shape an agent's decisions. We argue that IQA should shift from score regression to goal-conditioned judgment defined by embodied task utility. To this end, we propose an MLLM-based embodied IQA agent framework that reasons about task requirements, grounds quality evidence, and produces decision-facing assessments. A compact VisDrone evidence study shows that conventional perceptual metrics and generic MLLM-based IQA scores are weak proxies for downstream VLM task success, while a task-conditioned utility score better predicts whether visual input supports the target task. These findings support a task-utility-oriented reframing of IQA for embodied, explainable, and decision-aware visual perception.
authors: Jirong Zha, Yanwei Liao, Yemin Wang, Xiangmin Yi, Siqi Peng, Yingfeng Chen, Chen Gao, Xinlei Chen
bullets: Existing task-agnostic IQA scores can mismatch the needs of interactive agents, whose decisions depend on goals, context, and actions.
The paper proposes an MLLM-based embodied IQA agent that reasons over task requirements, grounds quality evidence, and produces decision-facing judgments.
A compact VisDrone study finds conventional perceptual metrics and generic MLLM-IQA scores are weak proxies for downstream VLM task success.
Task-conditioned utility scores better predict whether visual inputs support the target task.
The proposed reframing targets embodied, explainable, and decision-aware visual perception.

papers.abstract: Direct-policy World Action Models (WAM) have demonstrated the benefits of decoupling action generation from explicit future visual prediction for efficient inference in autonomous driving and embodied control. However, they still require tens of denoising steps to achieve competitive action quality, incurring substantial latency and hindering real-time deployment. Simply reducing the number of denoising steps will collapse the nonlinear multi-step denoising trajectory into coarse updates, substantially degrading action quality. To reduce the denoising steps while enabling real-time action generation, we present an effective world action model with one-step action generation, namely OSWAM, for autonomous driving and embodied control. We argue that it is the absence of structured action priors in random noise initialization that forces direct-policy WAMs to recover coherent action sequences through iterative denoising. Hence, we construct imagination tokens to initialize the diffusion process, providing physical priors and action-conditioned representations. We further introduce privileged information distillation with future conditioning to enhance future-aware action generation. As a result, OSWAM can efficiently and effectively generate high quality actions in just one diffusion step. Our experiments demonstrate that OSWAM achieves comparable or even better results in both autonomous driving and embodied control than direct-policy WAM and Joint-WAM that require tens of steps. It obtains approximately $3\times$ speedup over direct-policy WAM baselines and supports real-time compiled inference with latency as low as 40ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 GPU. The project page is available at https://gwenzhang.github.io/OSWAM/
bullets: Direct-policy world action models typically need tens of denoising steps, limiting real-time deployment.
OSWAM uses imagination tokens to provide physical priors and action-conditioned representations at diffusion initialization.
Privileged information distillation with future conditioning improves future-aware action generation.
Experiments report comparable or better performance than multi-step direct-policy and Joint-WAM baselines, with about 3× speedup and latency as low as 40 ms on an NVIDIA RTX 5090.
The abstract evaluates autonomous driving and embodied control, without specifying broader domains or limitations.

papers.abstract: A robot policy needs to understand what a task is asking for in a scene, and how to move the robot to accomplish that task. To achieve these two skills, we introduce Zero-real Agent Policy (ZAP), a recipe that teaches a small off-the-shelf vision-language model to control a robot via a simple tool harness. We use a pretrained 27B parameter model to bootstrap world understanding and reasoning, followed by supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks to teach it how to move the robot. Without observing real-world robot data during training, ZAP reaches 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra in our harness and outperforming the MolmoAct2 VLA (33.3%), while running 3x faster and 17x cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. Furthermore, ZAP also generalizes to an unseen embodiment as well as new objects, goals and strategies never seen during training. On a single-arm Franka, ZAP reaches 55.9% on RoboLab-120, 4.9 percentage points ahead of the leading VLA/WAM baseline.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining task understanding with robot motion control without real-world robot training data.
Uses a pretrained 27B vision-language model, then supervised fine-tuning and GRPO on simple simulated tasks via a tool harness.
Achieves 96.7% success on real-world tasks, matching GPT-6 Astra while running 3× faster and costing 17× less.
Generalizes to unseen embodiments, objects, goals, and strategies; reaches 55.9% on RoboLab-120, 4.9 points above the cited VLA/WAM baseline.
Scope: results are reported for the described harness and selected real-world benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Robotic missions involving spatially distributed tasks often require jointly selecting rewarding locations and planning feasible motions under limited travel budgets. This paper proposes Reward-Guided RRT*, a new sampling-based framework that constructs a budget-feasible mission through a sequence of locally joint task-selection-and-motion-planning stages, evaluated directly in the continuous state space, without requiring a precomputed task-transition graph. The method incrementally builds a mission using reward-guided RRT* searches, while a return-feasibility procedure ensures that each selected task can be visited without violating the mission budget. Experiments with increasing obstacle complexity and number of tasks show solutions comparable to VNS-PRM* while requiring substantially fewer sampled states. We also extend the framework to Dubins steering and evaluate it in CoppeliaSim with a scaled car-like robotic platform, demonstrating its ability to incorporate vehicle kinematic constraints.
bullets: Builds missions incrementally through locally joint task-selection and motion-planning stages.
Uses reward-guided RRT* without requiring a precomputed task-transition graph.
Applies return-feasibility checks to ensure selected tasks remain within the mission budget.
Achieves solutions comparable to VNS-PRM* with substantially fewer sampled states in experiments.
Extends to Dubins steering and demonstrates operation with a car-like robot in CoppeliaSim.

papers.abstract: Quadrotor controller comparisons commonly report a single tracking error, although the resulting ranking also depends on tuning effort, reference information, actuator prediction, optimizer fallback, and command timing. We quantify these effects for cascade PID, hover LQR, boundary-layer sliding-mode control (BL-SMC), linear MPC with LQR fallback (LMPC-F), a preview-enabled LMPC-F, and a geometric $SO(3)$ controller on a common nonlinear plant with rotor gyroscopic coupling, motor lag, and saturation. A primary study (556 episodes at 50~Hz) combines matched twelve-candidate tuning, 400 paired evaluation episodes, and a 48-cell MPC factorial; a confirmation study (1462 episodes) repeats the evaluation on 50 fresh realizations with tuning budgets of 12, 24, and 48 candidates. A matched twelve-candidate tuning protocol changed the mean-RMSE ordering obtained with the fixed baseline settings, moving BL-SMC from last to first; the new ordering recurred on the fresh realizations, and a 48-candidate budget left it unchanged. Reference preview substantially reduced MPC tracking error and, on the figure-eight task, removed fallback activity. On an abrupt step, the outcome depended on the interplay between fallback policy, predictor, and actuator authority. Command timing also changed the outcome: replaying measured command-call delays terminated three of four nominal MPC configurations on a desktop computer and all four on a Raspberry Pi~5, whereas capping the solver at 100 iterations removed every deadline miss in the tested nominal timing profiles. Controller rankings therefore depend not only on tracking accuracy but also on the tuning protocol, reference information, fallback behavior, and implementation timing. We propose a reporting checklist covering tracking accuracy, tuning effort, completion and failure rates, fallback activity, applied-input variation, and command timing.
bullets: A matched 12-candidate tuning protocol changed the baseline RMSE ranking, moving BL-SMC from last to first; this ordering persisted on fresh realizations and with 48 candidates.

On abrupt steps, performance depended on the interaction among fallback policy, actuator prediction, and actuator authority.
Measured command delays caused most or all tested nominal MPC configurations to miss deadlines, while a 100-iteration solver cap removed deadline misses in tested profiles.
The study recommends reporting tracking accuracy alongside tuning effort, completion/failure rates, fallback activity, input variation, and timing.

papers.selection_reason: A reproducible simulation study analyzing how tuning and fallback policies affect quadrotor controller comparisons, providing a reporting checklist.
papers.title: How Tuning, Reference Preview, Actuator Modeling, and Fallback Policies Change Quadrotor Controller Comparisons: A Reproducible Simulation Study
papers.tldr: Quadrotor controller rankings can change substantially with tuning, reference preview, fallback design, actuator modeling, and command timing—not tracking error alone.

papers.abstract: Learning generalizable humanoid loco-manipulation remains bottlenecked by costly real-world demonstrations. Simulation provides a scalable alternative, but requires visually faithful, physics-ready scenes and executable whole-body motions. We present Zero-HLM, a real-to-sim-to-real framework that transforms smartphone captures and simulated source demonstrations into scalable training data for humanoid loco-manipulation. Gaussian-guided agentic real-to-sim reconstruction aligns visual and physical scenes; motion-environment co-adaptation uses rollout feedback to correct whole-body references and interaction geometry. We generate 4,800 physically validated demonstrations for zero-shot transfer across three Unitree G1 tasks. Simulation-trained GR00T N1.7 achieves 66.7% mean full-task success, versus 46.7% with real-data training. On generalized configurations, expanded simulation training raises pooled success from 23% for base-trained real-data policies to 69%, without additional real demonstrations. Project page: https://young-bit.github.io/zero-hlm/
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited scalability of collecting real-world humanoid demonstrations.
Uses Gaussian-guided agentic real-to-sim reconstruction to align visual and physical environments.
Applies motion-environment co-adaptation with rollout feedback to refine whole-body motions and interaction geometry.
Generates 4,800 physically validated demonstrations for three Unitree G1 tasks.
Simulation-trained GR00T N1.7 reaches 66.7% mean full-task success and 69% pooled success on generalized configurations.

papers.abstract: Animals have a remarkable capacity for autonomy---driven by intrinsic motivation---without external sensory cues or extrinsic objectives, yet the computational mechanisms behind this ability largely remain a mystery. We combine whole-brain recordings in the fruit fly (Drosophila melanogaster), which reveal neural representations of spontaneous exploratory decisions more than 10 seconds in advance, with a neuromechanical digital twin to test whether optimizing intrinsic goals yields realistically embodied artificial agents that quantitatively match fly behavior and internal representations of future volitional action during exploration. Our hierarchical policy selects from a discrete library of low-level motor primitives, consistent with ethological theories of behavioral syllables. We train agents without external reward using 20 intrinsic motivation algorithms spanning curiosity, entropy, and competency methods. The agents are evaluated in a virtual tethered-ball assay modeled on the fly experiment, comparing spontaneous locomotor statistics and internal representations and decoding future turn direction from kinematics and neural activity on the same timescales observed in flies. DIAYN, a hierarchical competency algorithm learning discrete policies that maximize behavioral entropy and the separability of induced sensory observations, achieves the strongest joint behavioral and neural prospective coding performance relative to flies. Its learned policies closely capture individual variability in fly exploration strategies, suggesting that this diversity serves to maximize state-space coverage at the population level. DIAYN's latent activity also closely captures the sum-difference rule for interhemispheric encoding of kinematics in biological flies. These results establish hierarchical, intrinsically motivated agents as a powerful framework for reverse-engineering animal autonomy.
bullets: The study investigates how animals generate autonomous exploratory actions without external rewards or sensory cues.
Whole-brain recordings show that future spontaneous decisions are represented more than 10 seconds before action.
A neuromechanical Drosophila digital twin uses hierarchical policies that select discrete low-level motor primitives.
Among 20 curiosity-, entropy-, and competency-based methods, DIAYN best jointly matched fly behavior and prospective neural coding.
The model also reproduced individual exploration variability and a biological interhemispheric kinematic encoding rule.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Agent Architecture Overview. (a) The FlyGym simulator provides visual, proprioceptive, and olfactory observations from a biomechanically realistic fly body. Modality-specific CNN and MLP encoders embed these observations into a shared representation ϕt, which is provided to the actor–critic and intrinsic drive module. When applicable, the policy is additionally conditioned on a sampled skill z. The intrinsic drive module computes an intrinsic reward from the encoded state transition and selected action. The actor outputs a categorical distribution over discrete motor primitives, while the critic estimates the state value. The policy selects a new motor primitive every 100 ms. (b) Locomotor primitives are translated into joint-level commands by a low-level central pattern generator (CPG) controller, while grooming is executed using a kinematic replay. These motor commands are applied within the FlyGym physics simulation, which is integrated with a timestep of 100µs. Thus, each policy action is executed for 1,000 physics steps before the next action is selected.

Figure 1: Environment Overview. (a) The fly policy is trained in an environment with obstacles and multiple odor sources. (b) The policy is then evaluated in a tethered-ball environment where the fly is head-fixed. The angular and forward velocities are read from the ball, analogous to the biological experiment of Brezovec et al. (2023). (c) The policy receives olfaction as a weighted sum of intensities sampled at the antennae and maxillary palps. (d) The policy’s proprioceptive input comes directly from NeuroMechFly and includes joint angles, joint velocities, and body-frame gravity, height, and linear and angular velocities. (e) Vision is also provided to the policy by simulating the ommatidia mapping of pale and yellow type cells to pixels.

Figure 4: Turning Bias. (a) Distribution of turning bias across evaluation rollouts for each method. Points indicate individual rollouts, with the mean and range shown for each method. DIAYN produces a broad distribution of turning biases spanning more of the fly-to-fly variability than the other evaluated methods. Methods with a rollout containing no turns or turns in only one direction are excluded because log(NR/NL) is undefined for those rollouts. (b) Virtual x-y trajectories integrated from the ball state of the nine flies and the nine DIAYN evaluation skills drawn from a common origin.

Figure 3: Turn-direction decoding from neural and behavioral data. Prospective coding is quantified as balanced accuracy in predicting future left/right turns. (a,c) Neural (a) and behavioral (c) prospective coding in the fly and models using elastic-net logistic regression in the −15 to −8 s window. (b) Neural and behavioral decoding before (−15 to −8 s) and during (−0.4 to +0.4 s) turns. (d) Behavioral versus neural prospective coding. The dashed line defines the fly’s behavioralto-neural accuracy ratio, which DIAYN closely matches. (e) Models with no turns or only one turn direction, precluding stratified cross-validation.

Figure 5: Low-dimensional internal structures relate to ω and v. (a) Reconstructed from Brezovec et al. (2023), the IPS of the fly brain has an interhemispheric relationship of z-scored activity that is correlated with angular (interhemispheric difference) and forward velocity (interhemispheric sum). (b) As a functional analogue of the bilateral supercluster pairs in Brezovec et al. (2023), we use PCA to find principal components in the network activation of the LSTM layer of the Actor in the policy whose difference correlates with angular velocity and whose sum correlates with forward velocity. This structural relationship appears in DIAYN’s Actor LSTM layer (b) but, does not appear in (c) the randomly initialized DIAYN model. (d) We rank each IDM by the mean of the squared Pearson correlations of its angular and forward heatmaps with the fly’s. Higher is a closer match.

papers.abstract: Large-scale vision, language, and video pretraining has substantially improved the perception and generalization capabilities of robotic manipulation models, but action generation for complex dexterous manipulation remains constrained by the scarcity of robot demonstrations. Limited robot demonstrations must be used to learn both action representations and task-conditioned action distributions, making it difficult to adequately learn action representations and, in turn, limiting the ability of downstream generative models to generate complex dexterous actions. To address this limitation, we propose ARPG (Action Representation Pretraining and Generation), which explicitly separates action representation learning from action generation: we first pretrain an action representation encoder on large-scale human manipulation data. We then freeze the encoder and train a compact generative backbone (130M parameters) to learn task-conditioned action distributions in the encoder's representation space. Experimental results show that ARPG achieves state-of-the-art performance on the DexJoCo benchmark and improves the average success rate on bimanual dexterous manipulation from 10.1% for $π_{0.5}$ to 44.7%. Scaling experiments further show that broader coverage of human manipulation behaviors effectively improves downstream performance. These results indicate that action representation pretraining provides an independent scaling dimension for improving complex dexterous manipulation capabilities.
bullets: Problem: Scarce robot demonstrations must support both action-representation learning and task-conditioned action generation.
Method: Pretrain an action encoder on human manipulation data, freeze it, and train a compact generative backbone in the learned representation space.
Result: ARPG achieves state-of-the-art performance on DexJoCo and raises average bimanual dexterous-manipulation success from 10.1% to 44.7% versus π₀.₅.
Scaling human behavior coverage further improves downstream manipulation performance.
Scope: The approach targets complex dexterous and bimanual manipulation, with results indicating action pretraining as an independent scaling dimension.

papers.abstract: Scaling vision-language-action (VLA) models is constrained by scarce action-labeled demonstrations and incompatible control spaces across robot embodiments. We present RynnVLA-Latent, a framework that turns heterogeneous interaction videos into scalable supervision for robot policy pretraining. At its core, RynnLAM learns continuous, 3D-grounded latent actions from visual transitions without requiring native robot controls. By combining residual future-feature prediction, camera-compensated 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling, RynnLAM encourages representations that capture control-relevant motion rather than appearance changes alone. We apply RynnLAM to 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, producing 745.52M latent-action descriptors. RynnVLA-Latent then learns to predict latent-action chunks from visual observations and language through flow matching, before adapting its pretrained backbone and action expert to embodiment-specific robot actions. The resulting 4B policy achieves 98.8% success on LIBERO, 84.7% on LIBERO-Plus without benchmark-specific adaptation, 51.9% average success across five VLABench tracks, and 88.6% average success on the RoboTwin 2.0 bimanual benchmark. It also achieves the highest observed success rates among the compared methods on six real-world manipulation tasks across dexterous-hand and mobile-gripper platforms. Together with representation ablations and data-scaling results, these findings demonstrate the potential of latent-action supervision for scaling robot policy learning beyond native action-labeled data.
bullets: Addresses scarce action-labeled demonstrations and incompatible control spaces across robot embodiments.
RynnLAM learns continuous latent actions from visual transitions using future-feature prediction, 3D-flow supervision, and camera-motion decoupling.
Pretrains on 30.1K hours of human, robot, and simulation videos, generating 745.52M latent-action descriptors.
A 4B policy predicts latent-action chunks from vision and language before adapting to robot-specific actions.
Reports strong results across LIBERO, VLABench, RoboTwin 2.0, and six real-world manipulation tasks, with scaling and ablation evidence supporting latent-action supervision.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Architecture of RynnLAM and comparison with existingmethods. (a) Conventional latent action models compress a frame transition into a single latent representation and reconstruct the future observation conditioned on the source frame. (b) RynnLAM factorizes transition information into motion tokens zmt , an action latent zat , and a camera latent zct . The three components are trained through complementary objectives: feature-space reconstruction, 3D dynamic-flow prediction, and relative camera-pose estimation, respectively. This factorization encourages the action representation to capture physical scene dynamics while encouraging camera ego-motion to be represented separately.

Figure 1 Overview of the RynnVLA-Latent pretraining corpus. We aggregate approximately 30.1K hours from 25 datasets, comprising 16.63M episodes and 3.057B frames. Human video and real-robot video each contribute approximately 40% of the duration, with simulation accounting for the remaining 20%. The figure summarizes source composition, dataset contributions by duration, and object and action vocabulary from public tasks.

Figure 4 Two-stage training pipeline ofRynnVLA-Latent. (a) Latent-action pretraining. RynnLAM provides shared transition descriptors for human and heterogeneous robot videos. The policy predicts these descriptors from observations and language. (b) Robot post-training. Both the pretrained RynnBrain backbone and action-expert trunk are reused. The output projection is retargeted to native robot actions, and proprioceptive state is introduced. Post-training adapts the pretrained policy to the target control space without adding a separate latent-to-action decoder.

Figure 2 Data curation pipeline. The video data is collected from diverse sources and partitioned into short clips during data preprocessing. Each clip undergoes a multi-modal annotation process: (1) Video Captioning: Qwen3-VL (Bai et al., 2025) generates detailed natural language descriptions of the video content; (2) Optical Flow Estimation: DPFlow (Morimitsu et al., 2025) computes dense per-frame motion fields; (3) Depth Estimation: Depth Anything 3 (Lin et al., 2025) produces monocular depth predictions.

Figure 6 Latent-action similarity visualization. We retrieve the nearest neighbors of several query latent actions across the multi-embodiment corpus and display the corresponding video frames. The displayed high-similarity neighbors exhibit related motion patterns across different embodiments and visual domains, providing a qualitative illustration of cross-domain transition similarity.

Figure 8 Scaling of latent-action pretraining. We pretrain RynnVLA-Latent-2B and RynnVLA-Latent-4B with 10%, 30%, 50%, 70% and 100% of the latent-action pretraining corpus, and evaluate the resulting policies on LIBERO-Plus (Fei et al., 2025). Both models achieve their highest success rates with the full corpus, although improvements are not strictly monotonic across all data fractions.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have recently achieved remarkable success in motion tracking. However, during real-world deployment, robots inevitably encounter dynamics gaps arising from either extra physical disturbances or inaccurate simulation modeling, resulting in a significant training-deployment gap. Therefore, effectively leveraging real-world data to fine-tune policies represents the crucial last mile for robust deployment. To bridge this gap, we propose HumanoidNDM, an online fine-tuning framework for humanoid motion tracking driven by a real-world-trained neural dynamics model. First, in the data collection stage, we introduce a low-frequency reference perturbation method with an adaptive intensity mechanism, balancing deployment feasibility and exploration efficiency. Second, for the model training stage, we train a robust history-based, proprioceptive neural dynamics model in Euclidean space by incorporating differentiable forward kinematics, eliminating the reliance on costly motion capture systems. Finally, in the policy fine-tuning stage, we directly fine-tune the policy via backpropagated model gradients, achieving high data efficiency. Through physical validation on the Unitree G1 robot, we demonstrate that HumanoidNDM enables rapid real-world adaptation to various perturbations, representing the first online, MoCap-free fine-tuning framework for humanoid tracking policies.
bullets: Addresses the training–deployment gap caused by unmodeled disturbances and inaccurate simulation dynamics.
Collects feasible exploration data using low-frequency reference perturbations with adaptive intensity.
Learns a robust history-based proprioceptive neural dynamics model with differentiable forward kinematics, avoiding motion capture.
Fine-tunes the tracking policy directly through backpropagated model gradients for high data efficiency.
Physical validation on a Unitree G1 shows rapid adaptation to various real-world perturbations.

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a command-aligned sampling distribution that incorporates navigation commands directly into the exploration process to improve the efficiency of sampling-based motion planning for quadcopters in three-dimensional environments. Inspired by the Language-Aided Subset Sampling Motion Planner, this paper extends command-aware subset sampling to aerial systems. Subset sampling is generalized to command-aligned regions, enabling structured 3D exploration while preserving probabilistic completeness. Natural language instructions are grounded into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware geometric constraints using a prompt-based large language model for entity extraction and instruction validation. Extensive simulations in complex environments demonstrate that the proposed method generates collision-free, consistent trajectories while significantly reducing sampling effort compared to uniform RRT-based planners.
bullets: Targets inefficient exploration in sampling-based drone planning for complex 3D environments.
Converts natural-language instructions into yaw-conditioned and altitude-aware geometric constraints.
Uses command-aligned subset sampling to structure exploration while preserving probabilistic completeness.
Simulations produce collision-free, consistent trajectories with reduced sampling effort versus uniform RRT-based planners.
