papers.abstract: Successful tool-use trajectories are not necessarily useful supervision. Even successful interactions may underrepresent multi-step dependencies or contain actions that are unjustified by the information visible to the agent at decision time. We identify two coupled requirements for effective trajectory supervision: compositional coverage, so that important observation-action dependencies are represented, and decision grounding, so that each supervised action is supported by the learner-visible interaction history. We introduce Trajectory2Gym, which constructs executable interactions around under-supported compositional structures and derives supervision only from grounded decisions in their realized executions. Structural-support selection allocates the resulting experience, while parent-normalized supervised fine-tuning preserves the semantic interaction as the unit of training weight. This reframes trajectory generation as the deliberate construction of learnable interaction experience, rather than the collection of successful trajectories. Across five Qwen3 scales, Trajectory2Gym improves Tau1, Tau2, and BFCL at every tested scale, increasing the equal-weight three-benchmark mean by 16.9-29.8 percentage points. The gains are strongest in stateful and multi-turn interaction, where later decisions depend on earlier observations and feedback. Our results suggest that scaling tool-use agents depends not only on collecting more successful trajectories, but on constructing interactions whose dependencies are represented and whose decisions are learnable from the agent's visible history.
bullets: Successful trajectories can still provide weak supervision when multi-step dependencies are missing or actions are unsupported by visible information.
The method builds executable interactions around under-supported observation–action structures and supervises only decisions grounded in their realized histories.
Structural-support selection allocates experience, while parent-normalized fine-tuning keeps each semantic interaction as the training unit.
Across five Qwen3 scales, it improves Tau1, Tau2, and BFCL, with the largest gains in stateful and multi-turn tasks.
The study argues that learnable interaction construction matters more than simply collecting additional successful trajectories.

papers.abstract: We present MOTIO, an agentic skill-engineering system that turns ordinary human-action videos, reality-grounded 3D assets, motion references, and reusable robot skills into executable humanoid loco-manipulation programs. Through in-context task and contact reasoning, an agent constructs staged robot-native interactions and improves them using physics execution, multi-frame feedback, and human validation---without task-specific teleoperation or robot demonstration collection. Agentic 3D supplies metric product and environment assets, while existing whole-body, inverse-kinematics, and dexterous-hand interfaces realize the programs. Across 33 timestamped first approvals, the median recorded agent-turn time is 97.0 minutes and request-to-approval duration is 2.80 hours. Simulation-side layout and object variation prepare a long-horizon bottle-disposal skill for a continuous 101.75-second physical G1 execution in a scanned office; physical refinement reduces screw-tightening thread residual by 76.0%. Agent-generated skills additionally supervise BC/DAgger distillation into one shared reference policy, completing 18 simulated tasks under the same checkpoint without inference-time expert intervention. Project page: https://iiiiqiiii.github.io/motio/
bullets: Uses in-context task and contact reasoning to build staged, robot-native interactions.
Improves programs through physics execution, multi-frame feedback, and human validation.
Combines metric 3D assets with whole-body, inverse-kinematics, and dexterous-hand interfaces.
Demonstrates a 101.75-second physical bottle-disposal task and reduces screw-tightening thread residual by 76.0%.
Generated skills can supervise BC/DAgger distillation into one policy that completes 18 simulated tasks without inference-time expert intervention.

papers.abstract: Force-sensitive manipulation requires contact and load information that is not provided explicitly by visual observations. We present CW-WAM, a world action model that jointly predicts video, motion, and contact wrench. Inspired by hybrid motion-force control, it contains a unified interaction module that treats both motion and contact wrench as modeling targets and predicts time-aligned motion-wrench chunks as control references. A pair-causal attention mechanism structures the motion-wrench dependencies, while a long fixed-length wrench memory retains past interaction information. The predicted wrench chunk acts as a force reference for a 20-Hz outer-loop admittance controller within a slow-fast control system that maintains force feedback and smooth motion between model queries. CW-WAM improves contact prediction and increases the insertion success rate from 25% to 70% for square pegs with 1-mm clearance per side and from 40% to 95% for power adapters, compared with WAM without wrench input. It also improves lifting-height accuracy across different loads. Our framework with an admittance controller reduces force-reference RMSE from 4.8 to 2.7 N for peg insertion and from 2.0 to 1.3 N for wiping, respectively, with smaller force fluctuations during successful execution. Project website: https://cw-wam-project.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit contact and load information in visual observations.

Compared with WAM without wrench input, insertion success rises from 25% to 70% for square pegs and from 40% to 95% for power adapters.
Reduces force-reference RMSE from 4.8 to 2.7 N for peg insertion and from 2.0 to 1.3 N for wiping, while improving lifting-height accuracy across loads.

papers.abstract: Among on-policy deep reinforcement learning methods, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) has become the de facto standard, due to its consistently strong empirical performance across diverse application domains. However, on-policy methods are inherently sample inefficient: fresh data collected under the current policy is used for just a few updates before being discarded. Off-policy methods avoid this inefficiency via experience replay, achieving notable sample efficiency gains, but at the cost of training instabilities or extensive tuning. This motivated the rise of hybrid strategies that augment PPO with off-policy data reuse. Existing sample-reuse variants of PPO demonstrated improved sample efficiency over vanilla PPO, yet a systematic study of when reuse helps, in which scenarios, and to what extent remains missing. In this work, we study the effectiveness of sample reuse in PPO by instantiating two variants within a multiple importance weighting framework. Both retain the core PPO mechanics, reusing only samples from a window of recent iterations, thereby isolating the effect of data reuse from other factors. The variants, termed wPPO-U and wPPO-BH, employ vanilla importance weights or balance-heuristic-corrected ones, respectively. For both, we derive policy improvement lower bounds providing theoretical grounding for their respective losses. We use them to empirically study when and how data reuse improves sample efficiency or final performance of PPO across continuous control tasks.
bullets: Introduces two PPO reuse variants within a multiple-importance-weighting framework: wPPO-U and wPPO-BH.
Reuses samples only from a window of recent policy iterations to isolate the effect of data reuse.
Uses vanilla importance weights in wPPO-U and balance-heuristic-corrected weights in wPPO-BH.
Derives policy-improvement lower bounds to theoretically support both objectives.
Evaluates when and how reuse affects sample efficiency and final performance across continuous-control tasks.

papers.abstract: Large-scale manipulation demonstrations are essential for learning robust visuomotor policies, yet real-world data collection is expensive and difficult to scale. Simulation offers a promising alternative, but physical and visual discrepancies can limit the transferability of synthetic data, particularly for manipulation with soft grippers. We present PhyVisGen, a physically and visually high-fidelity framework for scalable robotic manipulation data generation. On the physical side, PhyVisGen introduces an arm-gripper coupling method based on the Incremental Potential Contact (IPC), enabling high-fidelity soft contact throughout complete manipulation trajectories. On the visual side, it combines real-scene reconstruction with real-time path tracing to generate visually realistic observations while preserving captured scene appearance. Quantitative evaluations demonstrate the physical and visual fidelity of PhyVisGen. Policies trained exclusively on synthetic manipulation demonstrations achieve 65-95% success across five real-robot tasks, without real-robot demonstration data or policy fine-tuning.
bullets: Addresses the cost and scalability challenges of collecting real-world robotic manipulation data, especially with soft grippers.
Uses Incremental Potential Contact (IPC) for high-fidelity arm–gripper coupling and soft-contact simulation across complete trajectories.
Combines real-scene reconstruction with real-time path tracing to produce realistic observations while preserving scene appearance.
Quantitative evaluations show high physical and visual fidelity.
Policies trained only on synthetic data achieve 65–95% success across five real-robot tasks without policy fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Closed-loop evaluation of surgical robots requires tissue that deforms, can be grasped and lifted, and reproduces the anatomy in which the robot will operate. We present a simulator in which this tissue is reconstructed from a fixed-view RGB-D recording of the surgical field, composited to remove the instruments, closed into watertight volumes and tetrahedralised; the pipeline was applied unchanged to three specimens of two species (thirteen organs, 146,061 tetrahedra, no inverted elements). For one specimen, the organs are placed in a bimanual cell in which two Franka FR3 arms operate motorised instruments through 6 mm trocars. The core contribution is the numerical and contact design that keeps this cell stable: implicit integration, simulation meshes separate from collision meshes, numerical guards, and a grasp constraint captured at the live tissue pose. In 45 repeated grasp-lifts, a friction grasp held the tissue in 0 of 15 trials and each constraint grasp in 13 of 15; on displaced tissue, a rest-pose constraint produced one-step snaps of up to 17.8 mm, which live-pose capture eliminates. Against the recording, front-surface depth error is 1.33 to 1.41 mm, organ silhouette IoU is 0.80, and in five grasp-lifts reproduced from video the landmark displacement RMSE is 11.8 mm against 14.2 mm for a static prediction. Biofidelity is not claimed; the environment is intended for closed-loop feasibility, safety, contact and policy screening.
bullets: Reconstructs watertight, tetrahedralised organs from fixed-view RGB-D recordings with instruments removed, applied to 13 organs across three specimens and two species.
Uses implicit integration, separate simulation and collision meshes, numerical safeguards, and grasp constraints captured at the live tissue pose for contact stability.
Constraint grasps succeeded in 13/15 trials, while friction grasps succeeded in 0/15; live-pose capture removes displacement-induced snaps up to 17.8 mm.
Simulation matched recordings with 1.33–1.41 mm front-surface depth error and improved landmark displacement RMSE from 14.2 mm to 11.8 mm versus a static prediction.
Designed for feasibility, safety, contact, and policy screening; the authors do not claim full biofidelity.

papers.abstract: Prioritized experience replay (PER) improves sample efficiency by replaying high-priority transitions, usually according to absolute temporal-difference error. In stochastic environments, PER can distort the distribution of realized outcomes replayed from transitions with the same state-action pair. We call this within-group self-selection. We quantify the resulting changes in within-group outcome frequencies and mean Bellman targets. We decompose PER into between-group allocation and conditional sibling selection, and derive fixed-buffer corrections that preserve current group-level priority mass: SAMPLE selects a group through PER and trains on a uniformly sampled sibling; AVG averages sibling Bellman targets; and MODEL samples from an empirical full-outcome model. In exact state-action environments with rare high-magnitude outcomes, sibling-aware replay improves learning efficiency over PER, although matched parameter sweeps show that tuning can narrow some gaps. In MinAtar, approximate VQ-VAE groups with SAMPLE mitigate degradation under mean-preserving reward tails in four of five games. Sibling-aware replay thus retains the focus on high-priority state-action regions while recovering their empirical outcome frequencies.
bullets: PER can overselect particular stochastic outcomes among transitions sharing a state-action pair, distorting outcome frequencies and Bellman targets.
The paper separates PER into group-level allocation and conditional sibling selection.
It proposes SAMPLE, AVG, and MODEL corrections that preserve group-level priority mass while restoring or modeling sibling outcomes.
In exact state-action settings, sibling-aware replay improves efficiency for rare high-magnitude outcomes; in MinAtar, approximate SAMPLE mitigates degradation in four of five games.
Benefits depend on tuning and the quality of approximate state-action grouping.

papers.abstract: The paper proposes a novel data-driven framework for designing and training a feedback linearizing controller by explicitly incorporating relative degree based conditions into the learning process. This enables the conventional feedback controller components to be replaced by neural Lie derivatives, thereby facilitating a fully data-driven feedback linearization framework. Furthermore, practical closed-loop stability is established by deriving sufficient conditions under which bounded identification errors lead to bounded tracking errors. The derived theoretical results are validated through their application to an armature controlled DC motor.
bullets: Targets fully data-driven feedback linearization without requiring conventional analytical controller components.
Incorporates relative-degree conditions directly into neural controller training.
Uses neural Lie derivatives to construct the feedback-linearizing controller.
Derives conditions showing bounded identification errors yield bounded tracking errors, supporting practical closed-loop stability.
Validates the theoretical results on an armature-controlled DC motor.

papers.abstract: Simulation-trained humanoid proprioceptive odometry faces two transfer challenges: training trajectories generated by specific robot control policies intended for deployment cover only a limited range of motions, while sim-to-real mismatch can make unconstrained predictions unreliable. We address both with Prior-Informed Odometry from Human-Motion Tracking (PRIMO). On the data side, we generate odometry supervision by having the humanoid track diverse retargeted human motions in simulation, decoupling supervision from the deployment policies and broadening the training motion distribution. On the model side, a Prior-Informed estimator uses physics- and symmetry-informed priors to structure velocity and rotation prediction and a coarse raw-context pathway to preserve sensor context alongside encoded features, thereby strengthening sim-to-real generalization. Under a unified real-robot protocol, PRIMO reduces mean error by 31.6%-61.7% relative to the strongest evaluated external baseline in each domain-metric comparison. Across two locomotion-policy revisions, policy specialists exhibit symmetric crossover, whereas Tracking-Locomotion training reduces mean opposite-policy simulation error by 86.8%-94.6%. On real dynamic motion, Tracking-Locomotion training reduces mean error by 69.2%-81.7% relative to training on the union of both deployment policies. Across the tested motion compositions, the Prior-Informed estimator consistently lowers mean trajectory errors relative to its Unconstrained counterpart in both simulation and real-robot evaluation. Code is available at https://github.com/Agibot-Spatial-Intelligence/PRIMO.
bullets: Addresses limited training-motion coverage and sim-to-real mismatch in simulation-trained humanoid odometry.
Generates supervision from diverse retargeted human motions, decoupling training from deployment-policy trajectories.
Uses a Prior-Informed estimator with structured velocity/rotation prediction and a raw-context pathway.
Reduces mean error by 31.6%–61.7% versus the strongest evaluated external baselines under a unified real-robot protocol.
Tracking-Locomotion training and the Prior-Informed estimator consistently improve simulation and real-robot performance across tested motions.

papers.abstract: Low-cost planar air-bearing testbeds have matured into a standard proxy for free-flying spacecraft GNC, but they remain largely thruster-only and are rarely equipped for contact-rich, inertia-coupled manipulation. Building on the open-source ATMOS testbed, we contribute a reaction wheel and two force/torque-sensed robotic arms (LEVION) with interchangeable end-effectors, integrated as first-class control actuators through a unified ROS 2 abstraction layer. On top of the software stack we build a reinforcement-learning training environment and digital twin, and a controller that exploits these added degrees of freedom, letting classical optimal controllers and learned policies be swapped on the same hardware without modification. We validate the integrated system, PINGU, across four benchmark tasks: point-to-pose navigation (classical LQR vs. sim-to-real PPO), dynamic disturbance rejection under arm-induced center-of-mass shifts, reaction-wheel momentum stabilization, and force-controlled docking. The results show that these additions extend an ATMOS-class emulator into the contact-rich regime and bridge classical optimal control and reinforcement learning on one reproducible platform.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of thruster-only planar spacecraft testbeds for inertia-coupled manipulation and contact-rich operations.
Integrates a reaction wheel and two force/torque-sensed robotic arms with interchangeable end-effectors through a unified ROS 2 interface.
Provides a reinforcement-learning environment and digital twin supporting interchangeable classical optimal controllers and learned policies.
Validates the system on navigation, disturbance rejection, momentum stabilization, and force-controlled docking tasks.
Demonstrates an ATMOS-class emulator extended into the contact-rich regime on a single reproducible platform.

papers.abstract: We present Elevator-VIGS, a visual-inertial 3D Gaussian Splatting SLAM system that keeps tracking and mapping through elevator rides. Inside a moving elevator, the two sensors are in conflict. The camera sees only the robot's motion relative to the elevator, while the IMU senses that motion plus the elevator's motion relative to the world. This conflict is challenging for existing visual-inertial estimators. If vision dominates, the estimator tracks only the robot's motion within the elevator and misses the elevator's rise, and if the conflict remains, the estimator diverges. We observe that the conflict comes from forcing both observations into a single coordinate frame. We instead estimate the robot's pose in the elevator's coordinate frame, and the elevator's motion relative to the world as a per-keyframe transport state, the elevator's rise and vertical velocity, within dense visual-inertial bundle adjustment. Elevator-VIGS detects rides zero-shot with a vision-language model and a depth network, and constrains the transport state at the departure and the arrival. We record real-world and simulated elevator sequences. On these sequences, Elevator-VIGS achieves state-of-the-art tracking and rendering performance. On four elevator-free public benchmarks it keeps the state-of-the-art performance of VIGS-SLAM. Project page: https://ruizhou-cn.github.io/elevator-vigs/.
bullets: Addresses the conflict between camera observations of robot-relative motion and IMU measurements that also include elevator motion.
Estimates robot pose in the elevator frame while modeling elevator transport—rise and vertical velocity—per keyframe.
Detects elevator rides zero-shot using a vision-language model and a depth network.
Constrains transport at elevator departure and arrival within dense visual-inertial bundle adjustment.
Reports state-of-the-art tracking and rendering on elevator sequences while retaining VIGS-SLAM performance on elevator-free benchmarks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: System overview. Elevator-VIGS takes RGB frames and IMU readings as input, tracks the camera online and trains a Gaussian map in parallel, extending VIGS-SLAM with the components outlined in red. Each keyframe, selected by optical flow and initialized through IMU preintegration, holds VIGS-SLAM’s 15-dimensional state of pose, velocity and bias together with its disparities. In the frontend, a ConvGRU refines the dense visual correspondences iteratively, and visual-inertial bundle adjustment optimizes the sliding window at every new keyframe. The ride detector ❺ arms on a semantic and a geometric cue from the RGB frames, and the IMU detects the departure and the arrival within the armed window. From the departure until the fold, each keyframe’s position and velocity decompose into an elevator-frame part and the transport state ❶, the elevator’s rise and vertical velocity. The solve then widens to 17 dimensions, the departure and arrival constraints ❷ constrain the transport state, and the update projection ❸ preserves the transport state through every optimization. Once the keyframes from the elevator leave the sliding window, the deferred fold ❹ writes the rise into the poses and returns them to the world frame. The mapper initializes Gaussians from each new keyframe’s depth and refines the map with color and depth rendering losses. Loop closure proposes keyframe pairs from optical flow, a same-floor gate ❻ rejects pairs on different floors, and each detected loop triggers pose-graph bundle adjustment and a Gaussian update.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving maps current observations directly to future trajectories, yet those trajectories must remain valid as the scene evolves. Future state modeling aims to address this temporal mismatch, but general representations often contain information unrelated to ego planning and affect trajectory generation only through auxiliary supervision, static conditioning, or proposal evaluation. We propose FeasibleFlow, a one-step end-to-end generative framework that jointly transports a configuration-space feasibility field and multimodal ego trajectories. Our Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow uses the pathwise Jacobian-vector product in the MeanFlow identity to incorporate field evolution into trajectory transport. Because safety feedback is sparser than progress feedback, we further introduce the Anchor-relative ranker (ARR) and Pareto-ReinFlow to balance safety and progress in candidate selection and generation, respectively. Experiments on the NAVSIM benchmark demonstrate the strong performance of FeasibleFlow and validate both the joint transport of feasibility and trajectories and the proposed safety-first mechanisms.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between static observations and trajectories that must remain valid as scenes evolve.
Introduces Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow to couple feasibility-field evolution with trajectory transport via a pathwise Jacobian-vector product.
Uses Anchor-relative ranker and Pareto-ReinFlow to prioritize sparse safety feedback while balancing safety and progress.
NAVSIM experiments demonstrate strong performance and support the value of joint feasibility–trajectory transport and safety-first mechanisms.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overall architecture and training pipeline of FeasibleFlow. Field and action states are transported by the Asymmetric Joint MeanFlow, and the Anchor-relative ranker (ARR) selects the final candidate through its Imitation ranker and Outcome ranker. (b) Pareto-ReinFlow uses the frozen ranker to select a reference trajectory, evaluates exploratory trajectories by their relative safety and progress, and updates only the online action MeanFlow.

papers.abstract: Many everyday tasks require controlling contact force as well as motion. On a humanoid, this force must often be coordinated across both hands and the whole body, and cannot be specified by kinematic trajectories alone. Therefore, we present FLORE, a framework for learning force-reactive humanoid loco-manipulation. We collect robot-free demonstrations using two force-sensing UMI-style handheld grippers for hand motion and contact wrenches, and wearable trackers for body motion. A force-reactive diffusion policy takes vision, proprioception, and measured wrenches as input, then predicts actions and per-hand force commands. A hybrid compliance whole-body controller with force tracking executes these commands while maintaining balance: an integral of the force error measured by real force/torque (F/T) sensors lets each hand track force accurately along the commanded direction and remain compliant along the others. In simulation, the controller tracks per-hand force commands of varied magnitude and direction, with little loss in whole-body motion accuracy. Across three contact-rich tasks on the robot, the force-reactive policy succeeds in 80% of rollouts, compared with 26.7% for a position-only policy trained on the same demonstrations and executed by the same controller. For more details, please visit our website: https://louis-leee.github.io/FLoRe/.
authors: Sihang Li, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Charlie Cheng, Ruihan Yang, Chen Feng, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi

papers.abstract: This paper proposes a smooth analytic gradient for frictional contact and applies it to policy learning and contact-implicit trajectory optimization for legged locomotion. The exact contact sensitivity is available in closed form but describes changes within the current contact mode, providing no first-order information toward neighboring contact modes. The proposed gradient replaces this sensitivity only in the backward pass, leaving the hard-contact forward solve unchanged and the realized rollout feasible. A central-path relaxation of the de Saxc\'e-corrected second-order-cone complementarity problem for Coulomb friction smooths the conditions defining the separating, clamping, and sliding modes. The relaxed sensitivity is evaluated at a point on the central path obtained by a Newton iteration initialized from the hard-contact solution. The sensitivity remains continuous through contact-mode transitions and converges to the exact sensitivity as the relaxation vanishes. Using 100,000 samples and less than 2 min of training on a desktop PC, policy learning with the proposed gradient produces a policy that transfers to hardware without fine-tuning. On hardware, the robot under a trotting policy withstands pushes and traverses debris and slippery ground. In trajectory optimization, the proposed gradient reaches contact-rich solutions missed by exact and Signorini-relaxed gradients. Project page: https://diffcontact.github.io
authors: Gijeong Kim, Seungbin Oh, Dongyun Kang, Hae-Won Park
bullets: Addresses the lack of first-order information when frictional contacts transition between modes.

With 100,000 samples and under 2 minutes of desktop training, the learned policy transfers to hardware without fine-tuning.
Hardware and trajectory-optimization demonstrations show robustness to pushes, debris, slippery ground, and contact-rich solutions missed by baseline gradients.

papers.abstract: Frontier multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can control robots without robot-specific training, but how their capabilities compare and interact with post-trained vision-language-action (VLA) and world action model (WAM) policies across manipulation demands remains to be thoroughly evaluated. In this report, we evaluate GPT-6-Astra on EBench as the core of an agent that controls a robot through an agent harness under the same visual and proprioceptive observation protocol as post-trained policies. We study two agent configurations: direct control, in which the agent generates waypoint commands directly, and harness with policy, in which it can also invoke a post-trained VLA or WAM policy for action execution. Under direct control, the agent achieves competitive overall performance relative to post-trained policies. It leads on short-horizon tasks and exhibits the least performance variation across generalization dimensions, whereas it underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon tasks, tabletop manipulation, and high-precision contact-rich tasks. In the harness with policy, invoking a post-trained VLA or WAM combines the complementary strengths of both components, raising overall task success to the level of the strongest compared post-trained policies while substantially reducing token cost. However, performance remains below the per-task upper bound of the standalone components due to suboptimal policy invocation, fixed-instruction execution without subgoals, and grasp disruption when the agent resumes control. Overall, our study characterizes the capability boundary of a frontier MLLM agent and suggests directions for improving future agent harness design. Project page: https://internrobotics.github.io/EBench-Astra-Tech-Report/
authors: Yifei Yao, Yude Zou, Guanbo Jiao, Xing Gao, Ning Gao, Yukai Wang, Jiantong Chen, Zihou Zhu, Xinyu Li, Ningyu Yan, Shuai Wang, Jianming Ma, Haoyu Guo, Weinan Zhang, Chunhua Shen
bullets: GPT-6-Astra is evaluated as a robot-control agent under the same visual and proprioceptive observations as post-trained policies.
Direct control performs competitively, especially on short-horizon tasks and across generalization dimensions.
It underperforms post-trained policies on long-horizon, tabletop, and high-precision contact-rich manipulation.
A harness that invokes VLA or WAM policies combines complementary strengths, reaching the strongest standalone policies’ overall success level with lower token cost.
Remaining gaps stem from suboptimal policy invocation, fixed instructions without subgoals, and grasp disruption when control returns to the agent.

papers.abstract: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown impressive capabilities in high-level reasoning and task planning for robots. However, specialized domains remain a challenge for VLMs' image interpretation and grounding abilities. We introduce TrySee, a modular closed-loop robot task planning pipeline integrating general-purpose VLM reasoning with domain-specific perception and established robotics components. The system consists of an inherently reactive cyclic planning pipeline, augmented with domain-specific modular vision preprocessing, to provide online grounding. Finally, a dynamic preprocessing selection mechanism contributes to the scalability of the pipeline. The system requires neither VLM fine-tuning nor end-to-end demonstrations and adapts through replaceable perception modules and motion planning. The approach is evaluated on planning tasks across 5 widely different domains, including a real-world robot disassembly task. The field tests in a brownfield environment demonstrate the approach's practicality in integrating VLM planning into specialized robotic systems with limited domain-specific training data.
authors: Elias Hofele, Thomas Trapp, David Timmermann, Tristan Schnell, Georg Heppner, Arne Roennau
bullets: Targets weak VLM image interpretation and grounding in specialized robotic domains.
Uses a reactive cyclic planning pipeline with online grounding and dynamically selected vision preprocessing.
Requires neither VLM fine-tuning nor end-to-end demonstrations.
Evaluated across five diverse domains, including real-world robot disassembly.
Field tests indicate practical integration in brownfield settings with limited domain-specific data.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are widely adopted for reflective error correction in task planning; however, existing approaches primarily rely on autonomous exploration, rendering them prone to accumulating erroneous experiences during early interactions with new environments. To address this limitation, we propose the Flexible Instructional Scaffolding Reflection Framework (FISRF), an agent--mentor architecture that estimates the robot's Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD) in task planning and adaptively selects reflection strategies and mentor guidance, thereby facilitating the accumulation of effective error-correction experience. Experiments in ALFWorld and on real-world robotic platforms demonstrate that FISRF reduces the average number of error-correction rounds by 37% and redundant reasoning by 25.1%, while improving the overall task success rate by 8%. Project webpage : https://fisrfplanning.github.io/
authors: Qingmiao Liang, Jiatao Zhang, Runxin Zou, Yufan Song, Wei Song, Yuhua Zheng
bullets: Targets the tendency of autonomous exploration to accumulate incorrect experiences in new environments.
Uses an agent–mentor architecture to estimate the robot’s Zone of Proximal Development (ZPD).
Adaptively selects reflection strategies and instructional guidance for error correction.
Experiments in ALFWorld and on real robots reduce error-correction rounds by 37% and redundant reasoning by 25.1%.
Improves overall task success by 8%.

The resulting reflections and planning trajectories are stored in a memory module for long-term retrieval.

papers.abstract: Robot corrections allow people to adjust a robot's behavior, but a single correction changes many features. Also, preferences about object attributes and relationships between objects cannot be expressed by moving the robot. We propose environment edits as a complementary form of feedback. The robot's motion is held constant as the human edits the scene, so the only explanation for the edit is the moved object. We introduce Feature Learning from Environmental and Robot-Relational Edit Traces (FERRET), which learns preferences from both robot and environment corrections. We show that environment edits are able to disambiguate features and learn preferences that robot corrections alone cannot.
authors: Isaac Ngui, Courtney McBeth, Nancy M. Amato
bullets: Robot corrections can change multiple features at once, making preferences ambiguous.
They cannot directly express preferences about object attributes or inter-object relationships.
FERRET learns preferences from both robot corrections and environment-edit traces.
Keeping robot motion fixed makes the edited object the likely cause of the feedback.
Experiments show environment edits disambiguate features and reveal preferences that robot corrections alone miss.

papers.abstract: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) is an important means for loop closure detection in visual Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM). While state-of-the-art VPR and SLAM approaches excel in urban and feature-rich natural environments, the vast and feature-poor environments of extraterrestrial surfaces like on the Moon or Mars pose severe challenges for existing approaches. This paper presents a novel benchmark, VPR-Space, to evaluate VPR capabilities on extraterrestrial surfaces. There are three contributions: (1) We collected sixteen VPR database-query datasets based on existing data from Space Analog Domains (SAD), terrestrial environments that resemble properties of the Moon or Mars. The collection includes a range of challenges regarding environment, viewpoint change, and illumination conditions. (2) To address the ill-posed nature of VPR, we propose a novel approach to generate the ground-truth information in VPR benchmarks. Instead of defining that a query and datbase image show the same place if and only if their camera poses are within fixed position and viewing direction thresholds, we propose to make the decision dependent on whether the match would be valuable in the downstream SLAM task. To avoid the overhead and restrictions of evaluating VPR in-the-loop within SLAM systems, we provide VPR ground-truth (GT) matrices based on the performance of an ensemble of state-of-the-art Relative Pose Estimators (RPE). Under this GT we require a VPR method to identify exactly those image pairs for which a subsequently applied RPE is expected to provide a valuable pose estimate in a SLAM context. (3) We evaluated nine state-of-the-art VPR approaches. The results show considerable room for improvement and indicate directions for future research. We provide a pre-release version of the dataset on github: $\texttt{https://github.com/rfechner/VPR-Space}$
bullets: Introduces 16 database–query datasets from terrestrial Space Analog Domains, covering environmental, viewpoint, and illumination variation.
Defines matches by whether a relative pose estimator can produce a useful pose for downstream SLAM, rather than by fixed pose thresholds.
Provides ground-truth matrices derived from an ensemble of state-of-the-art relative pose estimators.
Evaluates nine state-of-the-art VPR methods and finds substantial room for improvement.
Offers a pre-release dataset and evaluation resources via GitHub.

papers.abstract: This work explores a multimodal approach to the alignment of the behavior of open-ended learning autonomous robots with human purposes through the use of large language models as cultural enablers. While autonomous robots can generate their own skills and goals through interaction with the environment, they often lack mechanisms to ensure that these remain relevant and aligned to those of human users. The proposed approach makes use of the general and cultural knowledge contained in LLMs and VLMs to establish a multimodal interactive alignment process in which human purposes, expressed in natural language, are transformed into motivational components of a robot architecture in the form of robot missions and drives that guide the behavior of the robot. The system is structured into three layers for semantic alignment, mission generation, and drive modeling. This design enables a bidirectional interaction loop: human inputs define high-level purposes, robots expand them into executable missions making use of multimodal information relayed by LLMs and VLMs, and feedback maintains alignment with human intent. Experiments in simulation and with a physical robot demonstrate that the process produces valid missions and behaviors, supporting effective human-agent alignment in interactive scenarios with autonomous robots.
authors: Diana Cerdas-Vargas, Alejandro Romero, Richard J. Duro
bullets: Addresses the challenge of aligning robots’ self-generated skills and goals with human purposes.
Uses natural-language human input, along with cultural and multimodal knowledge from LLMs and VLMs.
Organizes alignment into semantic alignment, mission generation, and drive modeling layers.
Supports a bidirectional loop in which robots turn purposes into executable missions and use feedback to preserve alignment.
Simulation and physical-robot experiments produced valid missions and behaviors in interactive scenarios.

papers.abstract: Efficient robotic data collection remains a major bottleneck for vision-language-action (VLA) policy learning, especially for tasks requiring accurate end-effector positioning and camera-action alignment. This challenge is particularly severe in electronic-waste disassembly, where robots operate in cluttered assemblies of densely packed, visually similar components. Full digital-twin simulation is difficult because many parts are thin, reflective, or mechanically complex, making accurate object-level meshes and contact models difficult to obtain. In this work, we focus on pre-contact reaching and propose a 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS)-based data generation pipeline for wrist-camera VLA adaptation. Our method reconstructs the real workspace with 3DGS and renders diverse wrist-camera observations from robot-aligned poses. These observations are paired with smooth, structured reaching trajectories to provide robot-aligned visual-action supervision for VLA fine-tuning. We further augment the VLA policy with an instruction-conditioned reach verifier that estimates target proximity and provides reliable termination before physical interaction. Experiments in motherboard disassembly demonstrate precise VLA-based reaching using wrist-camera observations alone, without an external side-view camera. With $\pi$0.5, 1,500 generated trajectories achieve 80.0\% precise-reaching success across three targets, compared with 58.7\% using 150 teleoperated demonstrations, while requiring less than 10 minutes of active human capture. Project website: https://001-wang.github.io/PrecisionReach-GS/
bullets: Targets efficient data collection for cluttered, visually similar e-waste disassembly scenes where accurate simulation is difficult.
Reconstructs the real workspace with 3DGS and renders wrist-camera observations from robot-aligned poses, paired with smooth reaching trajectories.

On motherboard disassembly, 1,500 generated trajectories achieved 80.0% precise-reaching success across three targets, versus 58.7% from 150 teleoperated demonstrations.
Demonstrates wrist-camera-only reaching without an external side-view camera, using less than 10 minutes of active human capture.

papers.abstract: Expressive robot motion positively impacts human-robot interaction by improving user engagement, likability, or task performance. We present a novel approach to automatically generate and modulate complex, expressive full-body gesture sequences from a multimodal (text, audio, video) context description. Based on a unified mathematical implementation of the Principles of Animation using Dynamic Movement Primitives, we use multimodal foundation models to generate such sequences along with parametric motion variations that are highly context-aware. This method extends the state of the art in terms of flexibility and generality by being interpretable, composable, and working across different robot morphologies. Moreover, we integrate the system into a continuous control framework and leverage knowledge distillation to learn a much smaller model, significantly improving token efficiency and system latency. Results from a user study with a human-like platform indicate that participants judged our system's motions to be better aligned with the interaction context than motions produced under a non-modulated or API-level condition. We also demonstrate how the system generates expressive motion for robots with different kinematics, showcasing its versatility. Paper webpage: https://gen-mod-expressive-motion-behavior.github.io/.
authors: Till Hielscher, Fabio Scaparro, Kai O. Arras
bullets: Uses text, audio, and video context to generate and modulate full-body gesture sequences.

Demonstrates expressive motion generation across robots with different kinematics.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies and language-model agents provide complementary capabilities, but completing a task also requires adapting their use to the consequences of physical interaction. We study execution as a locus of adaptation: feedback guides the current action and supplies evidence for revising subsequent decisions under fixed model weights. We introduce RoboDoctor, a training-free framework that connects diagnosis, grounded action, and persistent experience across three revision targets. The harness allocates control between policy and agent; intervention determines when to assist while preserving useful policy behavior; and operation refines physical methods through observed effects. Linked experience records retain the reason for a decision, the attempted method, its outcome, and conditions for reuse. On a curated archive of 54 RoboDojo-Sim task entries, RoboDoctor achieves a five-dimension mean score of 57.10, with a native success rate of 49.44%. Recorded interactions illustrate strategy changes, selective correction, and grasp revision. These findings characterize execution-time adaptation in the evaluated system; controlled trials remain necessary to isolate the contribution of cross-episode experience.

papers.abstract: Coordinating many miniature robots in a confined arena, with no leader, central planner, or global map, is a core challenge for swarm robotics. As the swarm grows denser, collision avoidance becomes the limiting factor, and the number of safely coexisting robots depends on the formulation of the inter-robot safety constraint. We present a distributed predictive flocking controller in which each robot solves its own nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) problem, optimizing swarm cohesion and alignment costs, inter-robot and obstacle safety, and a task objective, while exchanging only predicted trajectories with local neighbors. Within this generalized controller architecture, solved in real time, we compare six barrier and control-barrier-function (CBF) safety formulations on a digital twin of an open-source vibration-driven bristlebot in a $0.64\,\mathrm{m^2}$ arena. A look-ahead discrete-time CBF performs best overall, with the fewest collisions and the widest inter-robot margins across nearly every swarm size tested. We deploy it on phototaxis, phototactic orbiting, and cohesion without a stimulus tasks, using swarm sizes starting from ten robots and up to the geometric packing limit. The swarm holds well: collisions stay low in small swarms, rising steeply as the packing limit approaches, while coordination and cohesion degrade gently rather than collapsing. The swarm is found not to trade safety for order, keeping both across the confined arena, with local alignment high at every swarm size.
authors: Prajol Shrestha, Siddhant Mohapatra, Filip Novkoski, Julian Oelhaf, Nicolas Vandewalle, Ana-Sun\v{c}ana Smith, Andreas Maier
bullets: Targets leaderless swarm coordination without a central planner or global map, where dense packing makes collision avoidance the key challenge.
Each robot independently solves an NMPC problem using local neighbors’ predicted trajectories while optimizing cohesion, alignment, safety, and task objectives.

Six barrier and control-barrier-function safety formulations are compared in a digital twin; the look-ahead discrete-time CBF yields the fewest collisions and widest inter-robot margins across nearly all tested swarm sizes.
Experiments cover phototaxis, phototactic orbiting, and cohesion without a stimulus, from ten robots to the arena’s geometric packing limit.
Collisions rise sharply near the packing limit, but coordination and cohesion degrade gradually; local alignment remains high, indicating safety and order are maintained together.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied navigation may be interrupted by a higher-priority instruction before the current task sequence is complete. The agent must finish its current atomic task, execute the inserted task, and resume the remaining sequence from the updated environment state, where its viewpoint and available navigation candidates may have changed. To evaluate this capability, we introduce PIFR benchmark, a novel task for runtime task preemption and resumption in embodied navigation. PIFR includes single, repeated, and nested interruption settings,with stage-specific metrics for inserted-task completion, resumption of the original task, and completion of the full sequence. Evaluations show that recovery performance varies across interruption conditions, while aggregate success can obscure differences in interruption handling and resumption. We further propose a lightweight candidate-ranking baseline to improve target re-grounding after interruption. Together, PIFR and the baseline provide a systematic framework for studying interruption handling and task recovery in long-horizon embodied navigation.
authors: Zerun Liu, Lechao Cheng, Yimin Liu, Shengeng Tang, Yaxiong Wang, Zhun Zhong
bullets: Targets runtime preemption and resumption when higher-priority instructions interrupt an unfinished navigation sequence.

Finds that recovery varies by interruption condition and that aggregate success can hide these differences.
Provides a lightweight candidate-ranking baseline for re-grounding navigation targets after interruption.

papers.abstract: Training robotic manipulation policies in simulation is widely adopted due to safety and cost efficiency; however, tasks involving obstacles remain under-performing and often converge slowly under Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL). To address this challenge, we propose a task decomposition framework for DRL that integrates Transfer Learning (TL) with Reward Redesign (RR) to improve learning efficiency and robustness in obstacle environments. The TL strategy selectively transfers only the first-layer critic parameters across structurally related tasks, since that layer captures general state--action representations while deeper layers encode reward- and obstacle-specific value geometry; RR decomposes tasks into staged sub-objectives to provide denser optimization signals. Experiments on the PyBullet Panda platform show consistent gains in obstacle settings. On Push with obstacle, our method achieves $0.83 \pm 0.05$, outperforming the strongest baseline (Truncated Quantile Critics (TQC), $0.77 \pm 0.06$) by approximately $7.8\%$. On Slide with obstacle, performance reaches $0.95 \pm 0.02$, exceeding Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) ($0.84 \pm 0.06$) by about $11\%$ success rates. In addition to higher final performance, forward transfer reduces convergence time by up to $70\%$ in obstacle tasks, and RR shortens sparse-reward Pick-and-Place training from roughly $0.75$M to $0.20$M steps ($\approx73\%$ reduction). The best policy is deployed on a real Franka Emika FR3 robot as a qualitative feasibility demonstration.

papers.abstract: Existing manipulation data collection methods typically offer either accurate robot-state acquisition through kinematic-chain-based teleoperation or convenient, portable operation through vision-based approaches. We present DEX-PHD, a portable handheld device that combines these advantages for dexterous manipulation by integrating a dexterous robot hand, continuous per-finger control, and multimodal logging. The system records proprioceptive information, fingertip contact data, and wrist-camera video, while the operator directly controls the robot hand through joint-level mapping. Its untethered design enables data collection across diverse environments. We demonstrate DEX-PHD on contact-rich tasks requiring coordinated multi-finger manipulation and deploy the collected demonstrations through open-loop replay on a physical humanoid robot. The results show that open-loop replay preserves the main temporal patterns of finger motion and task-relevant contact. Therefore, DEX-PHD provides a practical platform for portable, multimodal dexterous manipulation data collection.

papers.abstract: Data-enabled predictive control has recently emerged as a promising control paradigm, enabling a transparent optimal-control formulation without the need to learn an explicit dynamics model. This paper presents a number of extensions paving the path towards its use in real-time robotics tasks. Following recent work, we utilize a nonlinear predictor based on Gaussian kernels to represent the relationship between input and output data. We propose a damped Gauss-Newton method that enables real-time control by efficiently exploiting the least-squares structure of the control problem. In addition, we introduce a hybrid buffer management strategy that incorporates informative online data while retaining relevant offline data, allowing the predictor to account for changes in the dynamics. We demonstrate the tracking performance and computational suitability of the proposed method in MuJoCo using a Franka Research 3 arm pushing a block across surface, without prior knowledge of its changing friction values.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving models perform well on standard benchmarks but collide frequently in safety-critical scenarios. We present a failure-mode analysis on NeuroNCAP which shows that 95.9% of DiffusionDrive's collisions are planning failures despite reliable detection, pinpointing the bottleneck in planning rather than perception. We attribute this to a fundamental data imbalance, as safety-critical interactions are rare in real driving logs, so planners are hardly ever trained on them. We close this gap with a novel model-aware framework that generates safety-critical training scenes against a specific planner. Each planner is attacked at the bird's-eye-view (BEV) level through a differentiable surrogate distilled from its own planning head. This keeps the expensive video renderer out of the attack loop. We extract 50 scenes per planner, each pairing an attack with a safe escape trajectory that serves as the fine-tuning label. A fully automated quality-diversity search generates both the attacks and the escapes, so that their variety is not specified by hand. Only these scenes are rendered to fine-tune the planner, which reduces the computational cost significantly. Fine-tuning on these scenes roughly halves the closed-loop collision rate of two planners on NeuroNCAP (SparseDrive 28.0% to 12.2%, DiffusionDrive 37.5% to 19.2%) while largely preserving normal driving. A cross-planner transfer experiment shows that the gain comes from targeting the specific planner. Each planner improves most on the scenes generated against itself, and DiffusionDrive fine-tuned on SparseDrive's scenes retains only 6.7 of its 18.3-point collision-rate reduction.
authors: Khaled M. Seyam (University of Stuttgart, Germany), Julian Wiederer (Mercedes-Benz AG, Germany), Samar Fathalah (University of Stuttgart, Germany), Markus Braun (Mercedes-Benz AG, Germany), Bin Yang (University of Stuttgart, Germany)
bullets: NeuroNCAP analysis attributes 95.9% of DiffusionDrive’s collisions to planning failures rather than perception.
The method attacks each planner through a differentiable surrogate distilled from its planning head, avoiding video rendering during search.
Automated quality-diversity search generates 50 attack scenes per planner, each paired with a safe escape trajectory for fine-tuning.
Fine-tuning roughly halves collision rates for SparseDrive and DiffusionDrive on NeuroNCAP, from 28.0% to 12.2% and 37.5% to 19.2%, respectively.
Cross-planner transfer is limited, indicating that targeting the specific planner is important; scope is demonstrated on two planners and NeuroNCAP.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot teams executing predefined missions must adapt to runtime changes and sustain mission management despite robot failures. This paper proposes MATE-BT (Mission, Allocation, and Task Execution with Behavior Trees), a hierarchically decentralized framework that separates mission execution, allocation, and task execution. An active onboard leader manages mission progression and team-level task assignment, with authority transferable to another leader-capable robot after failure. Interchangeable decentralized methods resolve target assignments, while each robot adapts its local behavior through planning and acting with behavior trees. Webots simulations and real-robot experiments demonstrate mission continuity despite new targets and robot failures, including active-leader failure. In the physical experiments, all MATE-BT computation runs onboard. Hardware-in-the-loop resource measurements further support onboard execution on Jetson Orin Nano and Raspberry Pi 5. By updating only the affected layers without full-plan regeneration, MATE-BT maintained a response time of approximately 130 ms with 30 robots and 120 targets. Comparisons of four target-assignment plugins reveal scenario-dependent trade-offs between mission completion time and total travel distance.
authors: Sunbeen Lee, Hoseon Gi, Jik Hur, Inmo Jang
bullets: Separates mission progression, task allocation, and local task execution into distinct layers.
Uses an onboard active leader whose authority can transfer after leader failure.
Combines interchangeable decentralized target-assignment methods with behavior-tree planning and action.
Webots and real-robot experiments demonstrate mission continuity under new targets and robot failures.
Maintained approximately 130 ms response time with 30 robots and 120 targets; assignment methods showed scenario-dependent travel-time trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Vision-language navigation (VLN) requires an embodied agent to follow language instructions through 3D environments. Maintaining persistent episodic memory remains a challenge for VLM-based streaming agents in long-horizon navigation. We present MEMVLN, a streaming episodic memory framework that maintains a bounded bank of compressed perceptual features annotated with timesteps and action-derived relative poses, and produces compact memory tokens via cross-attention. We pair the proposed memory with a frozen pretrained geometry encoder. To learn the memory module, we design a masking-based trajectory summarization task with multi-granularity sub-trajectory decomposition, encouraging route reconstruction exclusively from episodic memory. Under navigation training restricted to the official R2R/RxR trajectories, MEMVLN achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics on standard VLN-CE benchmarks. Long-horizon analyses further characterize when episodic memory is useful. For physical evaluation, we collect 30 instruction-conditioned episodes in one physical scene, use 24 as demonstrations for post-training, and hold out six for testing. On the held-out episodes, MEMVLN improves success over the VLM baseline from 17% to 40%, and post-training further raises it to 47%.
authors: Yan Wang, Jiangyong Huang, Baoxiong Jia, Siyuan Huang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of retaining useful past observations during long-horizon VLN.
Stores compressed perceptual features annotated with timesteps and action-derived relative poses, then converts them into memory tokens via cross-attention.
Uses a frozen geometry encoder and a masking-based, multi-granularity trajectory summarization task to train the memory module.
Achieves state-of-the-art performance on most reported metrics across standard VLN-CE benchmarks under R2R/RxR trajectory restrictions.
In a physical-scene evaluation, success improved from 17% for the VLM baseline to 40%, and to 47% after post-training.

papers.abstract: Estimating forces acting on Deformable Linear Objects (DLOs) is challenging due to their underactuated nature. However, reliable contact estimation is crucial to precisely control them and enable safe manipulation tasks. Differently from the various approaches presented in the literature, this work adopts a probabilistic formulation where the DLO state and sensor data are related through conditional distributions. In particular, factor graphs are used to determine the magnitude, direction, and location of a 3D force acting on a DLO, while simultaneously reconstructing its shape. Since DLOs are not actuated and are typically thin, like cables and wires, strain gauges and actuation readings are usually impractical. Therefore, to overcome this issue, this work is tested using one type of sensing information only, thus developing a generic technique suited for a wider variety of tasks. Realistic tests are performed by introducing noise into the measurements while the DLO follows a prescribed path in the presence of external forces that are accurately estimated.
authors: Annika Delucchi, Vincenzo Di Paola, Bruno Marco Quadrelli, Matteo Zoppi
bullets: Addresses reliable contact-force estimation for underactuated DLOs such as cables and wires.
Models the DLO state and sensor observations through conditional probability distributions.
Infers force magnitude, direction, and location alongside DLO shape.
Designed to avoid impractical strain-gauge or actuation measurements by using one sensing type.
Realistic noisy-measurement tests show accurate force estimation as the DLO follows a prescribed path under external forces.

papers.abstract: Agentic embodied intelligence plays a foundational role in open-ended, dynamic physical environments. Rather than treating policy learning as an end-to-end mapping from instructions to actions, recent studies reveal that embodied systems depend not only on pre-trained foundation models, but also on harness. Prior approaches largely treat rollouts as static logs for post-hoc reflection, producing harness updates without autonomously testing and refining them through subsequent embodied interaction. To address this challenge, we propose VISTA, a meta-agent framework that transforms post-hoc rollout reflection into active self-exploration for embodied harness improvement. Specifically, VISTA maintains a harness graph that records the lineage of proposed harnesses, which enables the meta-agent to retrieve prior hypotheses, build on effective mechanisms, and avoid repeatedly exploring failed directions. Each iteration begins from a retained harness version and its execution evidence. Rather than directly committing an update from these historical trajectories, the meta-agent actively explores in the environment. It autonomously generates new rollouts, probes execution failures and recovery behaviors, and iteratively modifies the harness based on the resulting evidence. The refined harness is then evaluated afresh and added to the harness graph. We evaluate VISTA on the LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin benchmarks. Experimental results demonstrate that VISTA progressively improves task success and is more rollout-efficient than static reflection, achieving higher success rates with fewer simulator rollouts.
authors: Zhang Zhang, Shengjun Zhang, Simin Huang, Min Chen, Chong Xia, Xin Fei, Yueqi Duan
bullets: Addresses the limitation of static, post-hoc rollout reflection, which updates harnesses without autonomously validating them through interaction.
Maintains a harness graph to track version lineage, reuse effective mechanisms, and avoid repeated failed explorations.
Generates rollouts, probes failures and recovery behaviors, and iteratively updates the harness based on execution evidence.
Evaluated on LIBERO-Pro, RoboCasa, and RoboTwin, where it progressively improves task success and is more rollout-efficient than static reflection.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of VISTA. The meta-agent develops an embodied harness from versioned implementations and multimodal execution evidence. Within a development iteration, it interleaves code revision, active exploration, and autonomous candidate testing. After submission, the frozen candidate undergoes a separate autonomous evaluation under the declared development conditions. The selection rule determines whether it replaces the incumbent; both promoted and rejected versions remain in the history. The inner loop acquires evidence and refines a candidate, while the outer loop selects and retains harnesses across development iterations.

Figure 1 VISTA actively explores the environment to improve embodied-agent harnesses. Starting from an initial harness, a meta-agent inspects prior execution evidence, proposes revisions, and actively interacts with the environment to test hypotheses and refine candidate harnesses before formal evaluation.

Figure 5 A representative harness development process on Goal-t09. The initial harness achieves 0.0% success. The first development round adds lift verification, a bounded re-localization and grasp retry, and an explicit transportand-release procedure, improving performance to 56.3%. Analysis of the remaining failures then leads to a revision of the lift-state interpretation and release behavior, after which the final harness achieves 100.0% in autonomous evaluation.

papers.abstract: World models are emerging as a fundamental component of policy learning for real-world agents, enabling agents to predict future world states and plan actions within a learned representation of the dynamic environment. Existing approaches, however, often model appearance, metric geometry represented by projected LiDAR depth, and ego motion either partially or independently, overlooking the fact that these modalities are different projections of a shared underlying world state. This separation can lead to information loss and cross-modal inconsistency, ultimately limiting downstream performance. Motivated by this unified view of the world, we propose DriveUniTok, a unified multimodal tokenizer for driving world-action models (WAMs) that encodes these modalities in a single decodable continuous latent. We freeze DriveUniTok and adapt a pretrained diffusion model, DriveUniWAM, to predict future unified latents; the tokenizer then decodes them into future appearance, projected LiDAR depth, and ego trajectories. Experiments on NAVSIM demonstrate that our unified design achieves better future prediction and planning performance at lower downstream computational cost than separate-stream alternatives. With reinforcement learning post-training, DriveUniWAM achieves a PDMS of 91.54, reaching state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated WAM-based planners.
authors: Jingbo Xu, Hanchao Leng, JiaHui Huang, Hanbing Li, Jingwei Zhao, Kuiyuan Yang, Chen Gao, Guang Chen, Hangjun Ye, Yong Li
bullets: Addresses information loss and cross-modal inconsistency caused by modeling driving modalities separately.

With reinforcement-learning post-training, DriveUniWAM reaches a PDMS of 91.54 and state-of-the-art performance among evaluated WAM planners.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can select among discrete candidates for pick-and-place manipulation or generate continuous action chunks for motion control. Improving both forms of decision making through a common mechanism while retaining the capabilities of a pretrained policy is an important adaptation problem. Inspired by Jev's structured, probabilistic decision interface, we propose JevVLA, a lightweight energy-based adaptation framework for VLA policies. JevVLA instantiates this inspiration by modeling the relative quality of action proposals: with the base policy frozen, it learns a differentiable scalar energy conditioned on observations, task context, and actions, using execution feedback, expert corrections, or demonstration-derived preferences. JevVLA uses this single learned action preference function in two ways: its values compare discrete candidates, while its action gradients correct continuous actions or guide their generation. Candidate selection and continuous control thus share one trainable decision core. Each benchmark uses independently trained weights and fixed input/output encodings, while retaining the same core network with approximately 80,000 trainable parameters. On the held-out test sets, JevVLA improves task success over the respective matched base-policy controls by 1.28, 2.31, 1.60, 1.52, and 1.28 percentage points on MetaWorld MT50, VIMA, LanguageTable, LIBERO Plus, and CLIPort, respectively. These results support the feasibility of a lightweight, Jev-inspired energy model for adapting both discrete action selection and continuous action guidance. The JevVLA implementation will be open-sourced at https://github.com/ZJU4EmbodiedAI/JevVLA.
authors: Wei Wang, Wenqiao Zhang, Zheqi Lv, Zheng Dong, Yingjie Niu, Jiaqi Zhu, Jun Xiao, Chao Li, Yueting Zhuang
bullets: Addresses adaptation of VLA policies while keeping the pretrained base policy frozen.
Learns an action-quality energy from execution feedback, expert corrections, or demonstration preferences.

papers.abstract: Dynamic target tracking requires a mobile robot to maintain target visibility while navigating obstacles with smooth, feasible controls. Online trajectory optimization explicitly encodes these objectives but requires repeated numerical solving, whereas waypoint-based neural policies separate geometric prediction from control execution. We introduce LECO, a framework that transfers tracking optimization into offline learning of a direct-control policy. LECO predicts control sequences and maps them to trajectories through a differentiable kinematic model, allowing trajectory-level objectives to directly guide control learning. A decaying expert-guidance curriculum initializes effective tracking behavior and progressively shifts learning toward these task objectives. At deployment, a predictive safety lock checks short-horizon obstacle clearance and invokes a classical planning and control fallback when the predicted motion is unsafe or the target prediction is invalid. Across three simulated obstacle densities, LECO reduces root-mean-square linear jerk by 14.1--31.2\% relative to the best competing method for this metric and achieves the highest tracking success rate, with per-cycle computation times of 4.25--5.63\,ms. Experiments on two robot platforms further demonstrate tracking through indoor narrow passages and outdoor forest environments. These results demonstrate that learning direct control from optimization enables smooth and robust dynamic target tracking.

papers.abstract: Grasping is a foundational capability in robotic manipulation. Scene-level 6-DoF grasp synthesis relies on point clouds for metric geometry, yet real-world point observations are often noisy, incomplete, and over-smoothed. RGB images provide object-region, boundary, and appearance cues, yet two bottlenecks limit their effective use in scene representation and local grasp reasoning. We present MMGNet, a Multi-Modal Grasp Synthesis Network that addresses these bottlenecks through hierarchical image-to-3D feature injection and rotational graspness modeling. Hierarchical injection integrates multi-scale image features throughout 3D representation formation, while the rotational graspness jointly predicts the grasp approach direction and in-plane rotation before organizing local image-informed features through grasp-shaded grouping. Ablation studies show that these two modules provide complementary gains. MMGNet achieves a mean AP of 60.34 on GraspNet-1Billion with RealSense, surpassing all compared methods. In real-world experiments with adversarial grasp objects, MMGNet improves the grasp success rate over AnyGrasp by 8.46 percentage points. \emph{Code, models, and data will be released upon publication.}
authors: Rui Cao, Jia-Hui Pan, Yichuan Li, Yunfan Yu, Chi-Wing Fu, Jiangliu Wang, Yun-Hui Liu
bullets: Addresses incomplete, noisy, and over-smoothed point clouds by incorporating complementary RGB cues.
Injects multi-scale image features throughout 3D representation formation.
Jointly predicts grasp approach direction and in-plane rotation, then organizes local features via grasp-shaded grouping.
Achieves 60.34 mean AP on GraspNet-1Billion with RealSense and improves real-world grasp success by 8.46 percentage points over AnyGrasp.
Ablations indicate the two proposed modules provide complementary gains.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Illustration of MMGNet. Rotational graspness prediction then scores joint view–in-plane rotations at candidate grasp centers. Based on the selected rotations, grasp-shaded grouping aggregates local image-informed features within the corresponding gripper frames. Finally, the operation head predicts the remaining depth-wise grasp scores and gripper widths to produce the final 6-DoF grasps.

papers.abstract: This paper studies UAV swarm search in GNSS-denied maritime environments, where inter-UAV ranging drives cooperative localization and uncertainty propagates along the multi-hop reference chain, affecting connectivity, collision avoidance, and search effectiveness. We propose an uncertainty-aware control barrier function (CBF) framework approximating cascading localization covariance through Fisher information matrices. First, the cascading covariance model captures how ranging noise and neighbor uncertainty accumulate along the localization chain. Second, uncertainty-tightened CBFs incorporate the covariance model and its rate into margins for connectivity maintenance and collision avoidance, with conditional invariance and graceful-degradation bounds. Third, a hierarchical Voronoi-target strategy with formation keeping supports efficient forward-looking coverage. The distributed controller is validated with a standard unbiased extended Kalman filter in the loop. The framework is demonstrated on several polygon shapes and swarm sizes from 6 to 30 sUAVs. An estimator-in-the-loop run completes the search in 302.5 s, 20 Monte Carlo deployments confirm repeatable completion with all local QPs feasible and containment in at least 98.97% of UAV-frames, and six MBZIRC runs provide estimator-in-the-loop evidence. The source code is publicly available.
authors: Siyuan Yang, Junning Lyu, Xiaoyu He, Lakmal Seneviratne, Shaoming He
bullets: Addresses cascading inter-UAV localization uncertainty in multi-hop GNSS-denied swarm operations.
Uses Fisher-information-based covariance approximation to model uncertainty propagation along reference chains.
Tightens control barrier function constraints for connectivity maintenance and collision avoidance, with graceful-degradation guarantees.
Combines hierarchical Voronoi targeting with formation keeping for forward-looking coverage.
Demonstrations with 6–30 UAVs, Monte Carlo deployments, and MBZIRC runs show feasible control and robust search containment; source code is available.

papers.abstract: Human behaviour models are increasingly used to provide simulated human interactions for training robots via reinforcement learning (RL). Existing approaches primarily evaluate these models according to how closely their generated behaviours resemble real human data, while their usefulness as training partners is less commonly assessed. This creates a potential objective mismatch: a model that performs well according to behavioural evaluation metrics may not necessarily provide useful training experiences for downstream robot policy learning. Across two human-robot interaction (HRI) domains, highway driving and object handover, we evaluate different types of human behaviour models using common generative-model evaluation metrics. We consider multiple human trajectory representations and compare the resulting evaluations with the downstream performance of RL policies trained using the corresponding models. We find that existing behavioural evaluation metrics do not consistently predict downstream policy performance across domains and trajectory representations, while their evaluations are sensitive to the choice of trajectory representation. We also show that even when the true testing behaviour distribution is known, training against a different distribution may yield better downstream performance than training directly against the true distribution.
authors: Haoyang Jiang, Dana Kulic, Michael Burke, Pamela Carreno-Medrano
bullets: The paper identifies an objective mismatch between generative behaviour quality and downstream RL training utility.
It evaluates human behaviour models in highway driving and object handover HRI domains.
Common behavioural metrics are compared across multiple human trajectory representations and against RL policy performance.
Metric rankings vary with trajectory representation and do not consistently predict downstream policy performance across domains.
Training on a distribution different from the true testing behaviour distribution can sometimes produce better policies than training directly on the true distribution.

papers.abstract: Cities must coordinate domains like infrastructure, mobility, environmental management, emergency response, and public services as conditions evolve. An urban Spatio-Temporal Intelligence (STI) system helps the city monitor citywide states, analyze problems, plan and execute interventions, and adapt through feedback, making urban governance more timely, effective, and transparent. Recent urban twinning and agentic AI techniques provide foundations for such systems. From a twin-agent perspective, this survey takes a system-level view of how these disparate techniques can be coherently integrated into an urban STI system. Specifically, we review how the twin reconstructs and represents a persistent, information-enriched urban environment, and how the agent understands the twin via interfaces, reasons over it, acts reliably, and continuously evolves with the city. Built upon this synthesis, we summarize a two-loop blueprint, where an inner agent loop for grounding, reasoning, and verification, and an outer system loop linking data, twin, agentic action, feedback, and update. We then use this to structure an STI research agenda and show how a shared prototype supports diverse urban domains.
authors: Zhen Dong, Haiping Wang, Wei Tu, Yuan Liu, Bing Wang, Xuan Sun, Jinzhou Cao, Ronald Clark, Zhiheng Fu, Mohammed Bennamoun, Danfeng Hong, Yuanzheng Cui, Gemine Vivone, Pedram Ghamisi, Bisheng Yang, Qingquan Li, Deren Li
bullets: Motivates STI systems that coordinate infrastructure, mobility, environment, emergencies, and public services as conditions change.
Reviews how an urban twin can reconstruct and represent a persistent, information-enriched environment.
Examines how agents interface with the twin, reason over urban states, act reliably, and evolve through feedback.
Introduces a two-loop blueprint: an inner loop for grounding, reasoning, and verification, and an outer loop connecting data, twin, action, feedback, and updates.
Uses the framework to organize a research agenda and describe a shared prototype spanning diverse urban domains.

Leaf labels summarize closely related technical topics.

Fig. 7. Strategies for embedding information in an urban twin. Inside-out methods lift or learn semantic features from reconstruction signals, whereas outside-in methods ground external fields, attributes, and relations on twin carriers.

Fig. 9. Urban agent systems organized by task. Analysis and planning transform urban evidence into analytical results and plans; interaction and control apply decisions to environments; mobility prediction and urban simulation model individual futures and collective dynamics.
