papers.abstract: Visual captures provide detailed scene appearance, but converting them into interactive simulation environments requires object reconstruction, physical modeling, and correction of intermediate errors. We present SceneAgent, an agentic pipeline that coordinates these steps through simulator-based visual inspection and repair. The pipeline processes 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), photogrammetry, LiDAR captures, AI-generated 3DGS scenes, and 4D videos of dynamic scenes, and combines object segmentation, physical parameter estimation, part decomposition, articulation, and deformable simulation. To support policy learning, SceneAgent generates diverse object variants ("digital sisters") and scripted demonstrations. On a cluttered bin scene from GraspClutter6D, SceneAgent raises F1 at 1 cm for every coding agent with scorable outputs both with and without its skills, and its reconstructions are better than SimFoundry: all agent configurations exceed SimFoundry's F1 score, with a best of 60.75% versus 6.9%. On three dynamic scenes from 4DCodeBench, SceneAgent raises the mean dynamic IoU of Gemini 4 Argon from 0.86% to 99.09%. We further demonstrate diverse simulated interactions and preliminary policy transfer to a real robot.

papers.abstract: Vision--language--action (VLA) models increasingly run on edge devices aboard robots, where inference latency constrains closed-loop robot control. However, it remains unclear how to design VLA models, their inference software and edge hardware so that robots can run VLA inference in real time. Most VLA models report only task success, while prior studies cover limited action-generation strategies, divide inference into at most three stages, and lack comparisons of inference optimizations on the same models.benchmarking 18 open VLA models across released and alternative backends on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395, with a seven-stage inference breakdown. Our study reveals three insights. First, action-generation strategy matters more than model size. It dominates 14 of 19 Jetson configurations, latency varies by $82\times$ on Jetson and $157\times$ on AMD, and parameter count explains at most 15% of latency variance. Models that generate long action chunks in a few flow-matching steps keep up with control, whereas token-by-token decoding does not. Second, kernel fusion with 4-bit weights helps most, running $\pi_{0.5}$ and GR00T N1.7 2.6--2.9$\times$ faster than PyTorch with \texttt{torch.compile}, but it exists for only these two models and only on the Jetson. Optimization also moves the time to the stages it shortens least, as CPU preprocessing grows from 12\% to 39\% of the GR00T N1.7 call. Third, after optimization, memory bandwidth limits only the stages that process few tokens on the Jetson, such as the denoising steps, whereas software limits all other stages, from unfused kernels to serial preprocessing on the host CPU. Overall, low-latency edge VLAs should use few action-generation iterations, inference software should extend kernel fusion and low-bit weights to more models and platforms, and edge hardware needs high memory bandwidth and a fast host CPU.
authors: Borui Xu, Hongshi Tan, Wenqi Jiang, Bingsheng He, Ming Wu, Jason Zeng, Michael Heinrich
bullets: Benchmarks 18 open VLA models across multiple backends on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Thor and AMD Ryzen AI Max+ PRO 395, using a seven-stage latency breakdown.
Action-generation strategy dominates latency in most Jetson configurations; long action chunks with few flow-matching steps are more control-friendly than token-by-token decoding.
Kernel fusion with 4-bit weights substantially accelerates the two supported models on Jetson, while optimization shifts bottlenecks toward CPU preprocessing.
After optimization, memory bandwidth limits selected Jetson stages, whereas software inefficiencies constrain other stages across the pipeline.
The study recommends few-step action generation, broader low-bit kernel fusion, high-memory-bandwidth hardware, and faster host CPUs.

papers.abstract: Safe household navigation requires robots to regulate clearance and speed according to what an obstacle is and how close it is, without unnecessary conservatism. Yet existing evaluations do not test whether semantic safety distinctions are reflected in continuous motion. To that end, we introduce OSMA-Bench, an Obstacle-Conditioned Safe Motion Adaptation Benchmark built on spatially matched scenario sets that differ only in obstacle type. We also propose the \emph{Semantic Sensitivity Index} (SSI), which measures whether clearance and distance-dependent speed and smoothness follow the caution ordering of obstacles. Evaluating VLM-based and vision-language-action (VLA) policies on the benchmark, we find that neither consistently adapts its motion to obstacle safety, even with explicit safety prompts. Our analysis shows that the policies can correctly distinguish obstacles by safety relevance but fail to reflect this distinction in the motion parameters or actions they produce. For VLM-based policies, which recognize the obstacle and then generate a navigation program, adding an explicit parameter-inference step between these two stages improves adaptation. These findings expose a gap in \emph{semantic-to-motion grounding}, highlighting the need to translate semantic caution into appropriately safe motion.
authors: Hyunwoong Bae, Jisu Han, Jiyeon Choi, Dohoon Kim, Taesup Moon
bullets: Introduces OSMA-Bench, using spatially matched scenarios that vary only by obstacle type.
Proposes the Semantic Sensitivity Index (SSI) to measure obstacle-conditioned clearance, speed, and smoothness.
VLM and VLA policies inconsistently adapt motion to obstacle safety, even with explicit safety prompts.
Policies distinguish obstacles semantically but fail to reflect that distinction in motion parameters or actions.
For VLM-based systems, inserting an explicit parameter-inference step improves motion adaptation.

papers.abstract: Assistive agents in shared-control settings face a dual challenge: acting proactively to align with the human's intentions while remaining legible enough for the human to comprehend and fluently respond in real time. We present Dream2Assist, a model-based reinforcement learning framework for tightly-coupled shared decision making that addresses both sides of this challenge. Our approach extends a recurrent state-space world model with intent inference, enabling an assistive policy trained via fictitious co-play to anticipate and support discrete human objectives without overriding human agency. Beyond the computational framework, we describe the full deployment pipeline needed to translate a world-model-based policy into a safe, human-centered system in a resource-efficient way. Crucially, we address the sim-to-real-human gap via policy down-selection and reward restructuring within an iterative human-machine interface design. We validate the framework through three human-subjects studies and a preliminary on-vehicle deployment spanning two qualitatively distinct domains: high-speed racing (N=30) and urban driving with richer intent structure (N=10). Our results demonstrate that intent conditioning yields measurable improvements in torque alignment and collision rate. We surface key design insights and practices for deploying learning-based assistive agents in safety-critical, real-time human-robot teaming.
authors: Jonathan DeCastro, Thomas Balch, Emily Sumner, Deepak Gopinath, Laporsha Dees, Patricio Reyes Gomez, Elliot Weiss, Megan Applegate-Kenton, Todd Rowell, John Leonard, Avinash Balachandran, Guy Rosman
bullets: Targets the challenge of proactive yet understandable assistance in tightly coupled human–vehicle control.
Extends a recurrent state-space world model with human-intent inference and trains the assistive policy through fictitious co-play.
Includes a deployment pipeline with policy down-selection, reward restructuring, and iterative human–machine interface design to address the sim-to-real-human gap.
Validated in three human-subject studies and a preliminary on-vehicle deployment covering high-speed racing and urban driving.
Intent conditioning improved torque alignment and collision rate; the work also reports deployment insights for safety-critical human–robot teaming.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) have significantly improved robotic manipulation, yet deploying robots in the open world demands a higher level of autonomy beyond executing predefined tasks. Robot agents offer a promising paradigm for this transition, integrating task discovery, contextual reasoning, physical execution, and adaptive recovery into a closed interaction loop. However, existing benchmarks largely evaluate isolated capabilities, failing to capture the complexity of open-world robot autonomy. We introduce RobotAgentBench (RAB), a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating robot agents in realistic, open-world household environments. Through an agent-assisted, human-in-the-loop real-to-sim pipeline, RAB constructs 50 diverse household layouts with interactive objects and physically grounded tasks, encompassing 90 atomic tasks, 18 short-horizon tasks, 8 long-horizon tasks, and 4 open-ended scenarios. RAB provides a multi-level evaluation of robot agent capabilities: (1) task-level assessments systematically examine five complementary dimensions: task discovery, context reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and robustness; (2) scenario-level evaluation assesses how agents integrate these capabilities to autonomously fulfill high-level user needs. Furthermore, RAB enables systematic comparisons of standalone VLA/WAM models and diverse robot agent architectures under a unified planning-execution-verification framework. Extensive experiments reveal substantial gaps between manipulation and autonomy, demonstrate the advantages of agentic architectures and recursive self-improvement, and highlight the remaining challenges toward open-world robot autonomy.
authors: Lingjun Mao, Jinglin Cao, Lukun He, Wenpeng Xu, Yuchen Yan, Hengyu Jin, Zijun Zhang, Jinzhou Tang, Songyao Jin, Ziche Liu, Yifei Shao, Junbo Huang, Fang Nan, Ruobing Han, Ziqiao Xi, Ziming Xu, Shuang Liang, Sibo Zhu, Wenyi Wu, Xinyue Wang, Yiming Huang, Xinkai Zou, Gao Zhu, Kun Zhou, Biwei Huang
bullets: Addresses the gap between benchmarks for isolated robot capabilities and the integrated demands of open-world autonomy.
Introduces 50 diverse household layouts with interactive objects and physically grounded tasks across atomic, short-horizon, long-horizon, and open-ended scenarios.
Evaluates five task-level abilities: task discovery, contextual reasoning, manipulation, failure recovery, and robustness.
Measures scenario-level autonomy, including how agents combine these capabilities to satisfy high-level user needs.
Experiments show a substantial manipulation–autonomy gap, benefits from agentic architectures and recursive self-improvement, and persistent challenges for open-world deployment.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) combine future-video prediction with robot action learning, yet improvements in task success alone do not reveal how predictive supervision manifests in execution behavior or whether its benefits persist under task and environmental shifts. We conduct controlled future-video prediction loss ablations within FastWAM and OpenWAM, keeping model architecture, initialization, robot training data, and training steps fixed within each model family. Under clean conditions on seen tasks, predictive supervision increases success rates by 24.38 and 72.91 percentage points, respectively. Trajectory clustering further reveals higher success rates within several coarse trajectory clusters, including cases where cluster frequencies change little, indicating that the gains are not solely reflected in changes in the prevalence of trajectory patterns. However, these benefits do not consistently persist under distribution shifts: improvements on unseen tasks vary across models and tasks, while both models exhibit low success rates under the evaluated environmental randomizations, without a consistent advantage from predictive supervision. We further introduce future-video prediction as an auxiliary training objective for $\pi_{0.5}$, where a lightweight Transformer predictor used only during training increases success from 82.94% to 89.19%. These findings support future-video prediction as effective auxiliary supervision for action learning, while distinguishing improved execution on familiar tasks from reliable transfer and showing that such gains need not rely on a large pretrained video diffusion transformer (DiT) in the evaluated setting.
authors: Hanwen Cui, Yuanyuan Li, Qing Guo, Zhida Zhang, Chao Chen, Xi Chen, Jie Cao
bullets: Controlled ablations in FastWAM and OpenWAM isolate future-video prediction while holding architecture, initialization, data, and training steps fixed within each family.
Predictive supervision substantially improves success on clean, seen tasks: +24.38 and +72.91 percentage points in FastWAM and OpenWAM, respectively.
Trajectory analysis suggests gains reflect better execution within existing trajectory patterns, not only shifts in which patterns occur.
Under unseen tasks and environmental randomizations, improvements are inconsistent or absent, with both models performing poorly in the evaluated shifts.
Adding a lightweight training-only Transformer predictor to π₀.₅ raises success from 82.94% to 89.19%, showing that large pretrained video diffusion models are not required in this setting.

papers.abstract: Quadrotor trajectory tracking under unmodeled disturbances often relies on online residual adaptation, but short out-domain residuals can corrupt the learned disturbance model when constant-step updates treat every residual gradient uniformly. We propose Dual Gradient Consensus (DGC), an adaptive-learning method for mixed in-domain/out-domain disturbances that retains the random Fourier feature model, offline BPTT policy, and least-squares adaptation of a prior domain-adaptive residual policy (DAPL) while modifying the online update step size. DGC compares each residual gradient with long- and short-term gradient memories, classifies the current adaptation regime, and uses a confidence map to suppress unreliable updates while recovering adaptation after persistent domain shifts. We evaluate DGC in numerical quadrotor trajectory tracking under four residuals that mix an in-domain component with short out-domain events. Compared with $L_1$-augmented MPC, RFF-based MPC, constant-step DAPL, and a frozen-parameter baseline, DGC achieves the lowest mean position RMSE in all four cases.
bullets: Targets corruption of online disturbance learning caused by treating all residual gradients equally.
Retains DAPL’s random Fourier feature model, offline BPTT policy, and least-squares residual adaptation.
Compares current gradients with short- and long-term memories to classify adaptation regimes.
Uses a confidence map to suppress unreliable updates and recover after persistent domain shifts.
In numerical tests with four mixed disturbances, DGC achieved the lowest mean position RMSE among the evaluated baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of Dual Gradient Consensus for online adaptive learning under mixed in-domain/out-domain disturbances. Center: Long-Term Gradient (LTG) and Short-Term Gradient (STG) memories classify gt into four regimes; only (0, 1) hands LTG over to STG. Right: a confidence map sets the step length of the (α̂, σ̂) update on mixed in-domain/out-domain residuals. Bottom: the applied learning step size remains high in-domain, drops on transients, and recovers after a completed domain shift.

Shaded bands mark impulse intervals. Controllers: MPC (L1-E), MPC (RFF), DAPL, DAPL (w/o σ, α update), and DGC (ours).

papers.abstract: We introduce PhysLadder, a hierarchical Sim-Real benchmark for evaluating physical interaction capabilities in contact-rich manipulation. Its 16 household tasks span three cumulative levels: contact selection and geometric alignment (L1), force regulation within sustained contact (L2), and coordinated contact reconfiguration and force regulation (L3). Each task is instantiated in physically and visually matched simulated and real-world environments, with shared task definitions and success criteria. We evaluate GPT-6 Astra zero-shot with three trials per task in each environment. Real-world success rates decline from 80.0% at L1 to 47.6% at L2 and 0.0% at L3, with corresponding simulation rates of 66.7%, 47.6%, and 0.0%. Ten of the 16 tasks have identical success counts across environments; the remaining six differ by one success out of three trials. Across both environments, recurring difficulties in spatial reasoning, contact selection, force regulation, and coordination often prevent local physical progress from accumulating into task completion. These findings characterize Astra's observed capability boundary across increasing interaction demands and, for this model, support matched simulation as a repeatable, scalable testbed for studying the sustained, coordinated physical interactions that limit reliable manipulation.
authors: Haibao Yu, Jiaqi Meng, Zijian Zhang, Bowen Jing, Lei Yang, Yue Hu, Chenchen Ge, Yiming Hou, Chenbo Xin, Dawen Ye, Haifang Qin, Jin Li, Weitao Zhou, Jianing Qiu, Jiankai Sun, Dandan Zhang, Zaiqing Nie, Ping Luo, Ding Zhao
bullets: PhysLadder is a hierarchical Sim-Real benchmark with 16 household contact-rich manipulation tasks across three cumulative difficulty levels.
Tasks progress from contact selection and geometric alignment (L1), to sustained force regulation (L2), to coordinated contact reconfiguration and force regulation (L3).
Astra’s real-world success rates were 80.0% (L1), 47.6% (L2), and 0.0% (L3); simulation rates were 66.7%, 47.6%, and 0.0%.
Simulation and real-world outcomes closely matched: 10 of 16 tasks had identical success counts, while the other six differed by one success in three trials.
Recurring limitations involved spatial reasoning, contact selection, force regulation, and coordinating local progress toward task completion.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are increasingly used for robot manipulation because they map camera images and a language instruction directly to actions. Robots that cannot be tethered to a workstation, such as mobile manipulators and humanoids, must run them on onboard embedded boards, where the prefill latency of the language backbone grows with the hundreds of visual tokens processed at every control step. To meet real-time limits, training-free accelerators recompute only a subset of the visual tokens and skip the rest, either by pruning them or by reusing their cached key-value (KV) states. The two options save nearly the same computation, yet existing methods apply only one of them to every skipped token. Through a token-level diagnostic, we show that which option keeps the action closer to full recomputation depends on the token's drift, the change in its shallow-layer value since its cache was computed. On both backbones tested, reusing tokens below a drift threshold was no worse than pruning them, whereas beyond it, reuse yields up to 4.4x the action error of pruning; the same diagnostic calibrates this threshold per backbone. Building on this finding, we propose TRIAGE, which deems a cache valid when its drift is below this threshold and it is not too old. TRIAGE recomputes a fixed budget of tokens, prioritizing important tokens with invalid caches, reuses every other token with a valid cache, and prunes the rest; prune-only and reuse-only methods are the two extremes of this partition. Because the budget fixes the number of recomputed tokens, it directly sets the prefill latency. On LIBERO and SimplerEnv, TRIAGE stays within 3 pp of full recomputation in average success rate while cutting prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin by up to 48%, and with only 7% of visual tokens recomputed, it beats the strongest baseline by 24.4 pp on LIBERO-Object.
authors: Sooyoung Kwon, Carlee Joe-Wong, Kyunghan Lee
bullets: Targets onboard VLA inference, where processing hundreds of visual tokens causes high prefill latency.
Finds that reuse is effective for low-drift tokens, while pruning is preferable for high-drift tokens.
Uses a calibrated drift threshold and cache age to classify tokens as reusable, invalid-and-recompute, or prune.
A fixed recomputation budget directly controls latency.

On LIBERO and SimplerEnv, remains within 3 percentage points of full recomputation while reducing Jetson AGX Orin prefill latency by up to 48%; with 7% of tokens recomputed, it exceeds the strongest LIBERO-Object baseline by 24.4 points.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of TRIAGE. Shallow layers mark each token as important (blue) and its cache as invalid (red). The budget B goes to important, invalid tokens first; every other token is reused if valid and pruned otherwise, so B alone sets the prefill latency.

Fig. 5. TRIAGE lies on the Pareto frontier in every setting. Success rate versus prefill latency on a Jetson AGX Orin (top) and an RTX 3090 (bottom), averaged over the LIBERO suites or the SimplerEnv settings; dashed: Pareto frontier. No baseline is both more accurate and faster.

Fig. 1. Recompute only what neither reuse nor pruning can handle. Blue: important tokens; red: tokens changed since frame t−1 (stale caches). Reuse-only recomputes every changed token (18) and prune-only every important token (17). TRIAGE recomputes only tokens that are both (7), reuses valid caches, and prunes the rest.

Fig. 2. Drift decides between reuse and pruning. (a, b) Reuse − prune action error ∆ (Eq. (2), ×10−3) versus drift of the probed tokens on LIBERO-Spatial; blue region: reuse is better. papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models map a language instruction and the current observation directly to actions, without checking whether the instruction has been completed. For long-horizon tasks, a single failed step therefore goes unnoticed and leaves the whole task unfinished. Such failed episodes, however, often end with the task partially complete. Moreover, the unfinished steps are reusable atomic skills that recur across demonstrations. A failed attempt can thus be recovered by composing with atomic skills. We propose RoboDuo, a closed-loop dual-system framework that uses code as the interface between a coding agent and two VLAs. The agent writes a program that lets a full-task VLA attempt the whole task and checks whether it is complete; on failure, an atomic VLA finishes the remaining steps. Since the agent emits no actions and only decides which VLA for execution, RoboDuo wraps an existing full-task VLA without updating its weights. To train the atomic VLA and the coding agent with the completion-checking ability, we build LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge from a single set of LIBERO demonstrations. RoboDuo consistently improves X-VLA and $\pi_{0.5}$ on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, with the largest gains on long-horizon tasks, and recovers failed rollouts of a frozen full-task VLA on a real robot.
authors: Jie Wang, Bo Zhang, Renzhi Lu, Jianyu Chen
bullets: Addresses unnoticed failures in VLAs that can leave long-horizon tasks incomplete.
Uses code to coordinate a full-task VLA, a completion checker, and an atomic-skill VLA in a closed loop.
The coding agent selects which VLA executes actions and does not require updating the full-task VLA’s weights.
Introduces LIBERO-Atomic, LIBERO-Code, and LIBERO-Judge, built from existing LIBERO demonstrations.
Improves X-VLA and π₀.₅ on LIBERO and LIBERO-PRO, especially for long-horizon tasks, and recovers failures on a real robot.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of RoboDuo and its results. Left: open-loop VLAs fail long-horizon tasks after one unnoticed slip; token/latent dual systems cannot switch executor, and code-as-policy skips the full-task attempt. Center: RoboDuo uses a coding agent to Write a program, a frozen full-task VLA to Act, is_task_complete to Judge, and a frozen atomic VLA to Recover with at most three retries per step; control does not return. Right: matched gains on LIBERO, LIBERO-PRO (S/T), and a real robot. Bottom: one rollout from full-task attempt through failure detection to atomic recovery.

Figure 2. RoboDuo architecture: a generated program dispatches two VLA policies. Given the instruction and the current observation, the coding agent writes a two-layer program. Layer 1 makes one full-task attempt with πfull; if is_task_complete returns false, Layer 2 executes an atomic plan with πatomic, retrying each step at most three times until its goal is verified. Both policies stay frozen, so the same program wraps X-VLA and π0.5 without retraining. The bottom row shows one LIBERO-Goal-Swap rollout: after the full-task attempt fails, the atomic VLA grasps the bowl and places it in the drawer.

Figure 3. Construction of LIBERO-Atomic. An industry VLM labels each LIBERO demonstration with an ordered list of atomic verbs and time windows. Rule-based post-processing cleans these labels, and each clip is re-cut to end where its effect is complete. Each demonstration yields atomic clips with instructions for the atomic VLA, and a Python program of the same calls, which is wrapped into LIBERO-Code for the coding agent.

papers.abstract: Robot tasks require grounding spatial language in physical scenes, but task success alone cannot establish whether spatial instructions are followed. We present BEHAVIOR-Spatial, a benchmark built on BEHAVIOR-1K that measures spatial question answering, point-based target grounding, and robot action to examine how VLM spatial understanding relates to VLA behavior. It comprises 3,256 spatial questions across 49 activities, 1,240 grounding queries across 14 manipulation tasks, and action evaluations covering those 14 tasks and 10 navigation tasks. Our manipulation protocol evaluates held-out configurations and instruction following when the requested target changes within a fixed training layout. The baseline achieves 41.6% on held-out configurations but only 16.1% under changed instructions. VLM adaptation and robot-data pretraining provide limited improvements, whereas oracle visual target cues raise these rates to 60.3% and 38.0%, respectively. Perception evaluations reveal policy-dependent correlations between VLM question-answering and grounding accuracy and VLA manipulation performance. Together, these findings motivate evaluating spatial instruction following alongside task completion and examining when spatial perception performance translates into robot behavior. papers.abstract: Robots that learn from people often see several valid ways to do the same task: pass an obstacle on the left or on the right, open the microwave or move the kettle first. A policy that re-decides at every step can waver between these ways mid-task. We ask when the action head (the part of a policy that turns the state into actions) matters, and how it should make this choice. On a controlled task, heads that sample one way succeed far more often than a head that averages the ways when the demonstrations contain several ways and the state gives no hint which to take (+0.72 success with two ways); this trend was not reproduced on the other tasks we ran. We then present ElevateHead, a head that decides once at a learned decision point, commits to that choice for the episode, and exposes the choice as an input a user can set. We designed it by diagnosis: each version was frozen and tested on tasks it had not seen, and the next version changed only what a measured failure pointed to; predictions were registered before each run. The first four versions each fell below BeT on at least one held-out task. The fifth completed all four subtasks of the held-out Franka Kitchen task in 45.2% of episodes against 29.3% for BeT, the strongest baseline across our tasks (+0.160, 95% CI [+0.129, +0.188]); when a mode was forced, the first completed subtask matched it in 95% of successful episodes. Diagnosis also located where commitment breaks: varied start positions (repaired on the controlled task: commitment 0.22 to 0.81, success 0.74 to 0.91) and varied object placement (partly repaired: in an exploratory variant, commitment 0.03 to 0.59 on aligning with no detectable change in success). On held-out block stacking, version 4 was comparable to BeT and did not exceed it. A real-robot test with predictions fixed in advance is planned for a follow-up version of this paper.
bullets: Per-step averaging can fail when demonstrations contain multiple valid strategies and observations do not reveal which strategy to choose; sampling performed better on one controlled task, but this trend did not generalize to all tasks.
ElevateHead selects a mode once, commits to it, and lets users set the selected mode explicitly.
Through iterative diagnosis on unseen tasks, the fifth version achieved 45.2% success on all four Franka Kitchen subtasks versus 29.3% for BeT.
Forced modes matched the first completed subtask in 95% of successful episodes, supporting controllable behavior.
Commitment was sensitive to varied starts and object placements; performance was comparable to BeT on held-out block stacking, and real-robot evaluation remains future work.

papers.abstract: As Vision-Language Models (VLMs) increasingly enable robots to follow language instructions, understanding their navigation decisions becomes important for reliable deployment. Existing explainability methods overlook a key challenge in Vision-Language Navigation (VLN): evidence for the current action may be distributed across historical and current observations and associated with different instruction stages. We identify instruction-stage insensitivity, where existing methods produce similar explanations despite changes across different navigation stages. To address this issue, we propose a stage-aware attribution framework for VLN. We first construct action-conditioned temporal instruction--visual attributions across observations. These attributions are projected into instruction space to estimate stage associations, which guide the aggregation of relevant historical evidence for refining the current explanation. An instruction-guided spatial filter further suppresses isolated responses while preserving compact, instruction-relevant regions. Experiments across multiple VLN policies and benchmarks show improved attribution quality over existing methods. We further demonstrate that our method acts as a diagnostic tool for analyzing failure cases, and validate its applicability to real-world navigation on a Unitree G1 robot.
authors: Yiyuan Yao, Xinpeng Ding, Minglei Chen, Fei Gao, Lihuo He, Jie Yuan, Aijun Li, Nannan Wang, Xinbo Gao
bullets: Addresses instruction-stage insensitivity in existing VLN explanations.
Builds action-conditioned temporal instruction–visual attributions across observations.
Projects attributions into instruction space to identify stages and aggregate relevant historical evidence.
Uses an instruction-guided spatial filter to remove isolated responses while preserving compact relevant regions.
Improves attribution quality across multiple policies and benchmarks, supports failure analysis, and transfers to a Unitree G1 robot.

(d) We further use instruction–patch associations to suppress spatial noise while preserving decision-relevant visual evidence.

papers.abstract: People have long dreamed of an assistant that is always there to guide them and remind what they forget, from new dishes to lost keys. Powered by multimodal large language models (MLLMs), egocentric AI assistants on wearable devices are bringing this dream within reach: they see what the user sees and give instructions for user's physical work when necessary. However, testing such assistance is challenging and usually requires real people. The expensive and rare real interaction data leaves a key question unanswered: Can today's MLLMs truly help people in physical world? To answer this question, we propose InteractiveWorld, the first verifiable environment for closed-loop interaction between human and AI assistant. Unlike existing robot-centric simulators, InteractiveWorld lets the assistant guide a human agent who observes the scene, understands instructions, and acts independently. It thus realistically simulates how AI assistant collaborates with human: the assistant instructs, the human acts, and the environment executes actions and updates what they see next. Building on it, we introduce InteractiveBench, the first dynamic benchmark for egocentric AI assistants, with 120 multi-turn tasks across six categories. In each task, the assistant guides the human in real time, and every instruction shapes the outcome, which is scored by verifiable, state-based rewards. Experiments with 12 frontier MLLMs show they are still far from reliable assistants. Even the strongest model, Claude Fable 5.1, achieves at most 20% and 25% on long-horizon Guidance and Planning tasks, respectively. Overall, our work offers a verifiable platform and a rigorous evaluation set, laying a solid foundation for research on interactive MLLM assistants that truly help people in the physical world.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation often depends on object properties that cannot be reliably inferred from appearance alone. Physical interaction can reveal these properties, but it can also change the world in ways that invalidate subsequent actions. We present a task and motion planning (TAMP) framework that integrates task-directed interactive information-gathering with interleaved planning and execution. Building on PDDLStream, our framework plans optimistically with these interactive actions, verifies their outcomes during execution, and adapts the remaining plan by retaining still-applicable actions and replanning only the connections needed to continue execution. We evaluate the framework in simulation and on a real robot across tasks that require determining whether an object is movable, a pen has ink, a drawer can be opened, or a container is empty. These experiments demonstrate how interaction-driven state updates and recovery replanning support continued execution under uncertain outcomes and external disturbances.
bullets: Addresses long-horizon manipulation where object properties cannot be determined reliably from appearance.
Integrates task-directed information-gathering actions with interleaved planning and execution.
Plans optimistically, verifies interactive outcomes, and replans only the remaining necessary connections.
Evaluated in simulation and on a real robot across tasks involving movable objects, ink-filled pens, openable drawers, and empty containers.
Supports continued execution despite uncertain interaction outcomes and external disturbances.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Example execution trace with online monitoring and recovery. Blue blocks show the initial plan and successive updated plans, containing retained actions and newly introduced bridging actions. The initial plan consists of actions a1, . . . , a12, while aki,j denotes the kth action of a bridge plan reconnecting execution after ai to retained action aj . After each interactive information-gathering action, AFTERCHECK updates the symbolic state from the observed outcome (green blocks), recording that the object has been checked and whether the tested property holds. VALIDATOR removes actions that are no longer valid: orange crosses denote collision-infeasible actions, while red crosses denote actions whose symbolic preconditions are infeasible. Before each retained action, PRECHECK verifies executability (red blocks). Detected precondition mismatches trigger RECOVERYREPLAN (yellow blocks), which searches for a bridge to the next retained action or, if unsuccessful, to a later retained action. Each successful repair produces an updated plan combining the recovered bridge with the retained suffix. The system executes the bridge and resumes the retained plan, repeating state updates, validation, and on-demand repair until the goal is reached. Robot snapshots show the corresponding physical execution from the initial scene to the goal state.

Fig. 4. Representative simulation experiments in two domains. Top: Container-Emptiness, where a negative interaction result (non-empty mug) leads from picking to pouring. Bottom: Drawer-Openability, where a positive interaction result (openable drawer) leads from pulling to placing the mug inside.

Fig. 3. Recovery replanning through bridge construction. After executing a1 and a2 (gray), the current planning state s′2 differs from the predicted state s2, and a3 fails its PRECHECK (red). RECOVERYREPLAN searches from s′2 for a bridge that establishes Pre(a3); if unsuccessful, it tries later retained actions in order. The first bridge found is prepended to the retained suffix beginning at its target action. If no bridge is found to any retained action, global replanning searches from s′2 toward the active goal set G (green), producing a new action sequence [a′3, a ′ 4, . . .]. If this search also fails, the algorithm returns failure.

papers.abstract: Bimanual robotic control requires simultaneous management of distinct functional demands under motor noise, energetic costs, and communication delays. We investigate how learning responsibility should be organised across modular controllers and the two arms in a simulated musculoskeletal system with two communicating recurrent controllers. Using a 2 x 2 design, we compare differential versus shared controller objectives and fixed versus balanced hand-task assignments. Task-aligned functional specialisation was strongest when differential objectives were combined with a fixed assignment aligned with contralateral control routing. This condition achieved the highest canonical-task performance and control efficiency, reaching 81.33% bimanual success. Its advantage over shared objectives increased with motor noise but narrowed under stronger energy penalties. Stronger specialisation also reduced hand-role flexibility: reversing the hand roles decreased bimanual success by 80.46 percentage points under Differential-Fixed training, compared with 1.51 percentage points under Shared-Balanced training. These results show that controller objectives and hand-task experience jointly determine functional organisation. Stronger role-specific specialisation favours performance and efficiency when roles remain stable, whereas more distributed training favours interchangeability when roles change.

papers.abstract: World action models have demonstrated promising performance in robot policy learning, yet their high inference latency remains a critical bottleneck for real-world deployment. Recent approaches have sought to improve inference efficiency by reducing test-time future-frame imagination or accelerating action prediction. However, these methods often leverage representations from all video world model layers without explicitly considering their varying relevance to action prediction, leading to redundant computation and suboptimal representation utilization. In this work, we propose TurboWAM, a fast world action model that efficiently aggregates structured world representations conditioned on action predictions. Specifically, TurboWAM introduces a structured world representation aggregation module that adaptively fuses representations from different world model layers according to their relevance to the evolving action denoising state. Furthermore, TurboWAM employs a structured action supervision mechanism that adaptively modulates gradients from action supervision across different world model layers during backward propagation, facilitating world representation learning. During inference, by reducing the number of world model layers executed and caching relevant representations across action denoising steps, TurboWAM substantially reduces computational overhead. Extensive experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that TurboWAM achieves low inference latency while maintaining competitive task success rates compared with state-of-the-art methods.

Experiments on multiple robot manipulation benchmarks show low latency with competitive task success rates.

papers.abstract: Predicting the short-term future trajectory of a person from RGB-D cameras is a key capability for mobile robots navigating in dynamic and human populated environment. The key challenge to deploying learned predictors on real robots is the train-deploy pipeline gap. Training data are often prepared with an idealized, smoothed ground truth, whereas at inference, the model is fed noisy estimates from pose detectors and depth sensors. The model is therefore evaluated on an input distribution it never encountered during training. Most existing models rely on recurrent neural networks (RNNs) or transformers, which either struggle to capture short-term temporal dependencies or suffer from computational cost. We present TrajMamba, a lightweight, bidirectional state space model for short-term human trajectory prediction using an RGB-D camera. The model uses a single shared processing path for both training and deployment, aligning human pose extraction, depth back projection, and smoothing processes. It encodes a short window of persons's hip center velocities with stacked bidirectional Mamba blocks and decodes future velocities with a GRU head. On the ETH/UCY benchmark, TrajMamba reaches an average ADE of 0.29 m FDE of 0.51 m. With 262K parameters, it runs in real time on modest hardware and is deployed on a TIAGo robot with an onboard NVIDIA Jetson Orin.
authors: Basheer Al-Tawil, Magnus Jung, Ayoub Al-Hamadi
bullets: Addresses the train-deploy gap caused by idealized training trajectories versus noisy RGB-D pose and depth estimates at inference.
Uses a shared pipeline for pose extraction, depth back projection, and smoothing during both training and deployment.
Encodes recent hip-center velocities with stacked bidirectional Mamba blocks and predicts future velocities using a GRU head.
Achieves 0.29 m average ADE and 0.51 m FDE on ETH/UCY.
Has 262K parameters and runs in real time on modest hardware, including deployment on a TIAGo robot with a Jetson Orin.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to follow instructions in typed text, limiting broader deployment in natural speech. The traditional solution by prepending a speech recognition before VLA to convert speech into texts would incur additional latency and propagate errors. To address this, we present Speech-$\pi_{0.5}$, which maps raw speech directly to motor commands without explicit textual transcriptions. Specifically, built on $\pi_{0.5}$, we use a cross-modal projection to convert voice frames directly into audio tokens with significant response latency reduction. To further improve the accuracy, we adopt split LoRA adaptation with dedicated audio and task adapters, under a two-stage training. Speech-$\pi_{0.5}$ achieves $3\times$ lower response latency than ASR pipeline while maintaining competitive task success on LIBERO, and generalizes robustly to unseen accents where a single adapter degrades significantly.

bullets: VLA robots typically require typed instructions or an intermediate speech-recognition step.

A cross-modal projection produces audio tokens, while split LoRA adapters separately handle audio and task adaptation.
The system achieves 3× lower response latency than an ASR-based pipeline with competitive LIBERO task success.
It generalizes robustly to unseen accents, unlike a single-adapter approach.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires actions whose validity depends on earlier interactions, yet visual progress can conceal missing task prerequisites. We propose RoboLongR, an offline-to-online framework that learns history-dependent rewards to guide policy adaptation to new tasks. Its central objective is causal consistency: aligning rewarded progress with prerequisites supported by execution history. Stage-shuffle supervision encourages execution-order sensitivity, recurrent memory preserves evidence of earlier interactions, and two-round training refines trajectory segments using predicted progress. The resulting rewards guide stage-conditioned policy refinement from behavior cloning to online reinforcement learning. Sparse terminal feedback connects policy experience to reward learning by triggering correction for repeated high-scoring failures. Pretrained on demonstrations from 88 RLBench tasks and Open-X data, RoboLongR achieves 31.8% average success on 18 long-horizon tasks excluded from reward pretraining, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 9.2 percentage points. Across four real-robot tasks, it achieves 57.5% success, a 32.5-percentage-point improvement over the comparison method. Reward-level controls probe sensitivity to synthetic order perturbations, while ablations examine the contributions of individual components to policy improvement.

Reaches 57.5% success across four real-robot tasks, improving by 32.5 percentage points over the comparison method.

papers.abstract: Language is a natural way to command robots, but converting a single instruction into a long-horizon, contact-rich hand-object interaction remains challenging: synthesized references are noisy, human-to-robot retargeting introduces embodiment bias, and fixed-reference tracking lets small errors snowball. We address this with AdaDexTrack, a modulator-in-the-loop framework for language-conditioned manipulation tracking. A distilled generalist tracker serves as the skill carrier, while a tightly aligned modulator performs three feedback corrections: reference modulation (continual adjustment of what to track), object-latent modulation (online adaptation of the object representation to recruit suitable skills), and positional-target modulation (small state-dependent refinements for execution). The tracker is learned via large-scale specialist to generalist distillation on a corpus of language-conditioned hand-object trajectories; the modulator is trained with RL under the same task objective, ensuring tight coupling. Across large-scale evaluations, AdaDexTrack consistently outperforms prior SOTA on unseen-trajectory and unseen-object sets in both average tracking error and success rate, demonstrating robustness and generalization. We further show zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on real hardware, where adding the modulator yields substantial gains over a tracker-only variant. AdaDexTrack reframes language-conditioned dexterous manipulation as modulated tracking, replacing the open-loop, fixed-reference tracking with in-loop modulation that adjusts the reference, object latent, and positional target, yielding drift-resistant execution from noisy text references.
authors: Jianibieke Adalibieke, Qianwei Han, Xueyi Liu, Yuzhe Qin, Li Yi
bullets: Addresses noisy language-generated references, embodiment bias, and error accumulation in long-horizon contact-rich manipulation.
Combines a distilled generalist tracker with an RL-trained, tightly coupled modulator.
The modulator performs reference, object-latent, and positional-target feedback corrections.
Outperforms prior state of the art on unseen trajectories and objects in tracking error and success rate.
Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer, with modulation substantially improving over tracker-only execution.

papers.abstract: Deploying a language-guided navigation policy in a new building usually means watching it fail. Public-benchmark VLAs degrade scene by scene as layout, appearance, and language drift, and the standard fix of teleoperating fresh trajectories on site does not scale. We replace human demonstration with a single brief iPhone scan. Scan2Instruction compiles that scan into a complete training environment, automatically synthesizing executable navigation episodes with grounded instructions. PRPT-KS then adapts the policy through a closed-form Pareto utility read directly off the reconstructed scene, with no learned critic and no human labels. Across five real environments, the two designs together drive our RealNav to an 85% real-robot success rate, compared with 49% for a RealNav baseline post-trained on human demonstrations, and still achieve 82% in unscanned regions of the same buildings, compared with 41% for the same baseline. Our work turns demonstration-free scene adaptation for language-guided navigation from an aspiration into a working reality.

bullets: Addresses policy degradation under changes in building layout, appearance, and language.

Across five real environments, the approach reaches 85% success in scanned areas and 82% in unscanned regions.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance when integrated into robot manipulation pipelines, but real-world evaluation of VLM capabilities on downstream robotics tasks is both difficult and expensive to scale. We propose that spatial and temporal ordering tasks using images from stereo and wrist cameras attached to real-world robots are particularly well-suited for evaluating visual reasoning capabilities, as they assess skills directly applicable to robots. We evaluate VLM reasoning abilities on three questions: ordering shuffled frames conditioned on a language description of the task, ordering objects depthwise based on distance from the camera, and ordering objects from left-to-right in pixel coordinates. The complexity of these tasks can also be modulated by changing the size of the set to sort. Our experiments show that several state-of-the-art vision-language models struggle on ordering tasks. To fix this, we propose a scalable autonomous training data generation pipeline, and show that both supervised finetuning and reinforcement-learning on the generated data can significantly improve VLM reasoning performance both on spatiotemporal ordering tasks as well as downstream robotics and visual reasoning tasks.
authors: Sagnik Anupam, Utkarsh Lal, Aneesh Edara, Botong Zhang, Yao Tang, Jiatao Gu, Dinesh Jayaraman, Osbert Bastani
bullets: Evaluates VLMs on language-conditioned frame ordering, depthwise object ordering, and left-to-right pixel-coordinate ordering.
Uses stereo and wrist-camera images from real-world robots, with task difficulty controlled by the number of items to sort.
Finds that several state-of-the-art VLMs struggle with these robotics-relevant ordering problems.
Introduces an autonomous pipeline for generating scalable training data.
Shows that supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning on this data improve ordering performance and transfer to downstream robotics and visual reasoning tasks.

papers.abstract: Embodied perception requires positional representations that capture both physical geometry and the spatial and temporal extent of observations. We introduce POD-RoPE (Physical Observation Distribution RoPE), which represents token observation footprints as distributions over camera centers, viewing directions, and sampling times. Under independent sampling, expected rotations encode relative relationships between distributions; when each distribution collapses to a single address, the construction recovers pointwise RoPE. The same rotation statistics support Q/K matching and coherence-dependent V/O transformations, allowing observation geometry to guide both information selection and content aggregation. Per-token pre-aggregation avoids increasing sequence length or processing pairs of observation nodes. We evaluate POD-RoPE across four robot policy architectures, simulation and real-world manipulation, and complementary reconstruction, depth-estimation, and novel-view-synthesis tasks. Integrating POD-RoPE into Fast-WAM improves mean success from 91.83% to 92.88% across all 50 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, and from 32.5% to 52.5% on two real-robot tasks on Sharpa North. Controlled reconstruction ablations support the contributions of distribution encoding and V/O transformations. In H20 model-block benchmarks, POD-RoPE achieves median forward-plus-backward speedups of $1.91\times$ over P-RoPE and $5.34\times$ over RayRoPE, with a median latency overhead of 17.4% over Standard RoPE. These results support physical observation distributions as an effective and computationally efficient basis for geometry-aware attention.
authors: Xiaodi Huang, Zilin Wang, Jinpeng Liu, Pengchuan Xiao, Zhenlei Shao, Zhang Zhang, Shuxiang Lu

papers.abstract: Floor traction influences wheel-slip behavior, dead-reckoning accuracy, and the navigation performance of wheeled mobile robots that rely on wheel odometry. As these robots become increasingly common in GNSS-denied indoor environments, including automated manufacturing and retail facilities, their onboard measurements could also be used to characterize floor conditions and improve localization. In this study, a skid-steer robot was driven over five floor surfaces with distinct traction characteristics using commanded velocity profiles designed to induce wheel slip through repeated acceleration and direction reversal. Differences between the body velocity estimated from inertial sensing and the velocity obtained from wheel odometry were evaluated using the integrated relative-velocity error, phase-derived wheel-to-body response delay, and velocity-reversal response delay. Welch power spectral density analysis was additionally applied to characterize the frequency distribution of the velocity mismatch during positive and negative acceleration. Band-integrated spectral power, spectral centroid, and spectral decay rate were extracted from each recording and evaluated using linear discriminant analysis and multiclass classification. The response-delay measurements produced consistent surface-dependent trends, with the longest delays observed on soap and the shortest delays observed on carpet. The spectral features also provided clear separation among the tested surfaces, achieving a balanced classification accuracy of 97.1% under recording-level cross-validation. These results demonstrate that both the magnitude and frequency domain characteristics of wheel-to-body velocity mismatch contain useful information about tire-surface interactions. Such information could support surface recognition and the development of slip-aware wheel-odometry weighting within robot state-estimation frameworks.

papers.abstract: A robot in a home it has never seen must open doors, drawers, lids and taps whose physics a picture does not show. Instructions such as "open the drawer halfway, gently" depend on that physics: how far a part travels, how it resists, and what locks it. We present Open-World Law-to-Action (L2A). A vision-language model (VLM) proposes, for each movable part, its motions, the terms of its law of motion, and what may lock it. Each proposal becomes a prior with a floor, so that touch can always overturn it. The robot identifies each part's law online by Bayesian linear regression with closed-form evidence, for parts that move in one way or in two, and keeps a hypothesis that an unseen part or motion locks the target. We prove that touch alone cannot rule this hypothesis out, derive when another look is worth its cost, and show that a constant load and friction cannot be told apart while a part moves one way. All experiments are in simulation, developed on some scenes and run once on held-out ones. In new kitchens the robot completes 80% of tasks from the VLM's proposals, against 98% when every part is known. Proposed physics raises success on objects that need new terms from 353 to 378-383 of 400 episodes, and a second look raises success in mixed scenes from 284 to 329 of 366 tasks. A mobile robot that takes nothing from the simulator completes 70 of 100 requests in new scenes, against 62 when the simulator says which part each box is (after one change made between two held-out tests).
bullets: Targets open-world tasks such as opening doors, drawers, lids, and taps according to force- and motion-sensitive instructions.

In simulation, proposed physics and second looks improve held-out task success; a mobile robot completes 70/100 requests in new scenes.],

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are bottlenecked by the scarcity of robot data. Egocentric human manipulation videos offer an abundant, diverse, and semantically-rich alternative that inherently captures manipulation intent. However, the embodiment gap makes it difficult to extract action-relevant representations from these videos. From the perspective of action execution, human hands and robots share analogous manipulation primitives---reaching, grasping, placing---yet exhibit distinct kinematics tied to their embodiments. This might motivate our key approach: egocentric video pretraining can yield shared action representations capturing transferable manipulation skills, while human-specific motion patterns should be disentangled to avoid interfering with robot policy learning. To this end, we propose EXE, an Egocentric Cross(X)-Embodiment pretraining framework that learns a factorized latent action representation from egocentric human videos, separating shared manipulation priors from embodiment-specific signals. By leveraging the shared action space, the robot policy acquires generalizable manipulation semantics from diverse human demonstrations without being biased by human-specific kinematics. This shared knowledge transfers across embodiments with different kinematic structures, enabling the same pretraining to benefit both parallel grippers and dexterous hands. EXE yields consistent gains over baseline without pretraining on RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa GR1, and real-world manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Cooperative transport with heterogeneous legged robots requires coordinating different motion capabilities while supporting an unfixed shared payload. We present HA-DiPO (Heterogeneous-Agent Diffusion Policy Optimization), a hierarchical multi-agent reinforcement learning framework under centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE). The framework decouples team-level coordination from embodiment-specific motion control: at the high level, a centralized critic uses team-value estimates to jointly train independent coordination policies, aligning robot-specific action responses with a shared transport objective; at the low level, embodiment-specific robust motion policies track the coordination commands. The high-level diffusion policies offer more flexible action distributions than single-Gaussian parameterizations, allowing potentially multimodal coordination responses to be represented. The coordination policies learn from scratch through reward-driven simulator interaction without demonstrations. At execution, each robot generates coordination commands using only local robot and payload observations, without partner-state inputs or inter-robot messages. Simulation comparisons show that HA-DiPO achieves higher final mean returns and velocity-tracking success rates, as well as lower velocity errors, than the evaluated baselines. Real-world experiments further demonstrate quadrupedal-wheeled-legged and human-robot cooperative transport.
authors: Xuebin Li, Jinpeng Xiao, Zong Chen, Pierluigi Arpenti, Bruno Siciliano, Jiebao Sun, Yiqun Li

papers.abstract: Recent vision-and-language navigation (VLN) policies act on their visual history, and an incorrect action can take them off the instructed route. Paired interventions on four VLN policies show that clearing the history doubles pooled success at the onset of a deviation but lowers it on route, while later in a deviation, removing only the off-route frames helps much less. After a deviation, the retained history keeps the policy from turning where a turn is needed, which we call behavioral inertia. We propose MOON, a framework that equips a frozen VLN policy with two lightweight modules, adding less than 1% of its parameters. A deviation judge decides when to forget, raising an alarm that clears the history when it predicts that the agent is off route. A recovery policy, trained with GRPO from alarm states, learns how to move on, turning more of the successes found only by sampling into a single greedy rollout. Experiments on R2R-CE and RxR-CE show that MOON reaches the highest R2R-CE success rate among the compared methods and raises the success rate of its frozen base by 5.2 and 6.0 points, and an ablation with a random trigger indicates that this gain depends on when the history is cleared. Without retraining, MOON also improves zero-shot object-goal navigation on HM3D-OVON. Together, these results suggest that deviation recovery depends on knowing when to forget, not only how to act. Code is available at https://github.com/AutoLab-SAI-SJTU/MOON.
authors: Jingmeng Zhou, Seson Sun, Binyao Xu, Lingming Zhang, Hanshi Wang, Fudong Ge, Weiming Hu, Jin Gao, Zhipeng Zhang

On R2R-CE and RxR-CE, MOON improves its frozen base success by 5.2 and 6.0 percentage points, respectively, and achieves the highest R2R-CE success among compared methods.
A random-trigger ablation shows that recovery depends on clearing history at the right time, not merely clearing it.
MOON also improves zero-shot object-goal navigation on HM3D-OVON without retraining.

papers.abstract: Humanoid motion trackers reproduce diverse behaviors, but sharing a policy across bodies requires accounting for differences in structure, morphology and dynamics. We present MimicAll, a reinforcement-learning framework for shared whole-body motion tracking across heterogeneous humanoids. A structured embodiment descriptor is encoded into global and joint-aligned conditions, which are combined with observation history and body-matched motion references to predict joint-target offsets. Physics-consistent embodiment randomization, body-calibrated retargeting and heterogeneous simulation support training across 4,096 variants from 16 humanoid families. We introduce a benchmark of 464 bodies across five distribution strata to evaluate motion generalization, within-family embodiment shifts and unseen-family transfer. Controlled ablations show that embodiment information improves motion completion with simple concatenation, while self-attention yields the lowest global position errors. With equal training transitions, shared training achieves 99.4% 30-second success on randomized G1 bodies in 100STYLE, versus 42.9% for a single-body specialist. With Flat-MLP encoding and concatenation, continued training on a motion subset excluding obstacle categories achieves 98.3% and 93.5% 30-second success on 100STYLE for sampled training bodies and out-of-distribution variants within seen families, respectively. On an eight-motion LAFAN1 subset excluding ground and get-up sequences across 464 bodies, mismatched body conditions reduce self-attention's 30-second success from 61.7% to 47.0%, demonstrating a closed-loop benefit from embodiment information.
authors: Jia Li, Lingyun Xu, Yitang Li, Hao Zhao
bullets: Addresses morphology, structure, and dynamics differences that hinder cross-humanoid policy sharing.
Encodes embodiment globally and per joint, combining it with observation history and body-matched motion references to predict joint-target offsets.
Uses physics-consistent embodiment randomization, calibrated retargeting, and heterogeneous simulation across 4,096 variants from 16 humanoid families.
Evaluates generalization on 464 bodies across five distribution strata, including within-family shifts and unseen-family transfer.

Embodiment conditioning substantially improves closed-loop tracking; shared training reaches 99.4% 30-second success on randomized G1 bodies versus 42.9% for a single-body specialist, while self-attention gives the lowest global position errors.

papers.abstract: Robots can use historical observations to answer spatiotemporal queries in familiar environments, but the presence of relevant evidence does not imply that existing tools support the operations a task requires. We introduce ReSight, a task-driven self-improving memory system for embodied agents that expands the capabilities for processing and accessing historical observations as task demands arise. ReSight retains keyframes and their spatiotemporal associations, separating observation evidence from extensible derived fields so that stored observations can be reprocessed for new needs. An execution agent and a coding agent share this memory through different interfaces: the former calls registered tools within a bounded online budget, while the latter uses a programmable workspace and a larger exploration budget to inspect evidence, write programs, and acquire models as needed. To realize capability expansion in ReSight, we develop Explore-Distill-Mount (EDM), which identifies capability gaps from execution and exploration records without task reference answers and converts exploration-derived solutions into reusable memory builders, query tools, and skills, extending memory representations and access capabilities as needed. Experiments on three public benchmarks demonstrate effective base memory access and capability expansion. With the execution model and online budget held fixed within each benchmark, EDM reduces mean position error on OC-NaVQA from 33.10 m to 24.72 m and improves high-level success on FindingDory from 38.3% to 63.8%. With the tools and skill frozen, success still improves by 28.3 percentage points on FindingDory episodes excluded from exploration and distillation. Experiments on real robot patrol memories further demonstrate reuse of these capabilities for subsequent queries and new memories, with fewer online tool calls on average.
authors: Lirong Che, Yang Chen, Yimeng Su, Daqi Liu, Zhenyu Huang, Jiong Wang, Yuzhe Yang, Xu Cao, Chuang Wang, Jian Su, Xueqian Wang
bullets: Addresses the gap between available historical evidence and tools capable of performing task-specific operations.
Stores keyframes and spatiotemporal links separately from extensible derived fields, allowing observations to be reprocessed.
Uses distinct execution and coding agents for bounded online querying versus broader exploration and program/model development.
Its Explore-Distill-Mount process converts discovered solutions into reusable memory builders, query tools, and skills without task reference answers.
Across benchmarks, it reduces OC-NaVQA mean position error from 33.10 m to 24.72 m and raises FindingDory success from 38.3% to 63.8%; real-robot patrol tests show reuse with fewer online tool calls.

papers.abstract: Autonomous vehicles (AVs) operating in dynamic, challenging conditions such as intersections and roundabouts must guarantee collision avoidance under uncertainty while maintaining real-time feasibility. Most existing planners struggle to simultaneously guarantee both requirements. Chance-constrained formulations embed safety constraints directly in the optimization but become infeasible as uncertainty compounds; deterministic planners provide feasible solutions but fail to address the uncertainty that causes collisions; end-to-end learned policies provide neither guarantee in an interpretable form. We present a modular perception-prediction-planning pipeline that closes this gap by propagating uncertainty as structured, interpretable quantities across module boundaries. Rather than embedding probabilistic risk directly in the optimization, our pipeline resolves collision probabilities upstream and constructs convex safe sets within which the planner provides a guaranteed feasible solution at every cycle -- decoupling the safety guarantee from solver feasibility. Across Monte Carlo trials in a four-way unsignalized intersection, our pipeline achieves 0% collisions and 0% solver infeasibility at 12.7ms per cycle, compared to 36% and 10% collision rates for deterministic and chance-constrained baselines respectively. The ablation study confirms the necessity of each uncertainty source and the hardware deployment on Clearpath Jackal UGVs validates the pipeline's real-time viability on physical platforms.
authors: Doris Xu, Jin Hyun Park, Guadalupe Alvarado Fernandez, Adhyan Prasad, Mark Campbell
bullets: Targets safe, feasible autonomous driving in uncertain dynamic scenarios such as intersections and roundabouts.
Propagates structured uncertainty through modular perception, prediction, and planning components.
Resolves collision probabilities upstream and builds convex safe sets for a guaranteed feasible planner solution each cycle.
In four-way unsignalized-intersection Monte Carlo trials, it reported 0% collisions, 0% solver infeasibility, and 12.7 ms per cycle.
Ablations and Clearpath Jackal UGV deployment support the importance of the uncertainty sources and real-time physical viability.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Pipeline Architecture Overview: The IMM estimates the agent’s intent probabilities and states. The forecaster produces the forecasted trajectories. The collision detector combines these forecasted trajectories with the ego localizer’s state estimates to compute per-intent collision probabilities. The decision maker converts these probabilities into a convex safe set, within which the flat MPC plans and the CBF safety filter enforces forward invariance.

Fig. 3. Pipeline snapshot for a two-vehicle intersection encounter. (a) The IMM produces per-intent mode probabilities µj ; the forecaster propagates each into a trajectory (blue) with compounded covariance ellipses. (b) The collision detector finds the closest OBB approach n∗ (blue markers) along each forecast. (c) Combined covariance Σ is projected onto the separation direction to yield P j col analytically. (d) The decision maker sweeps the agent’s OBB along the most likely forecast to form the unsafe region U and constructs the convex safe set S and determines the intermediate goal pose (shown as a red star) for the downstream planner and safety filter.

Fig. 4. Snapshots of three experiment scenarios at three different times: t0 is the start time, t1 is the time of highest collision probability, and t2 is the time when the unsafe set no longer intersects with the lane. The forecasted trajectories are shown in blue (lines and covariance ellipsoids). The ego’s planned trajectory, goal point, and safe set are shown in yellow (as line, dot, and rectangle, respectively)

Fig. 1. Multiple uncertainty sources in a two-vehicle intersection encounter. The agent’s discrete intent is unknown, its forecasted trajectories accumulate covariance over the prediction horizon, and both vehicles carry localization uncertainty. Each source independently degrades collision avoidance if neglected (Table II), motivating a pipeline that preserves all of them as structured quantities across module boundaries.

papers.abstract: Rapid illumination transitions can disturb Visual SLAM (VSLAM) by saturating images before the Automatic Exposure (AE) policy adapts, removing the visual correspondences needed to maintain tracking. Our proposed methods mitigate this disturbance at two levels: B-Adapt acquires adaptive exposure brackets to cover the scene dynamic range while promoting photometric overlap, and BVSLAM directly uses the multi-exposure sequence as constraints in a factor graph state estimator without relying on High Dynamic Range (HDR) merging. We evaluate both methods against state-of-the-art approaches in nominal environments and during a repeated tunnel-exit transition at an emulated vehicle speed of 32 m s-1. In the tunnel, combining our B-Adapt with BVSLAM reduces the state estimation error by 78 % compared with AE images. These results suggest that bracketing efficiently improves visual pose estimation robustness to rapid illumination disturbances while retaining low error under nominal conditions. Our code is available at https://github.com/norlab-ulaval/bracketing-shows-the-way.
authors: Olivier Gamache, Anthony Lavertu, David-Alexandre Duclos, Jean-Michel Fortin, Fran\c{c}ois Pomerleau, Philippe Gigu\`ere
bullets: Rapid illumination transitions can saturate images and disrupt visual correspondences needed for tracking.
B-Adapt captures adaptive exposure brackets that cover scene brightness while preserving photometric overlap.
BVSLAM incorporates the multi-exposure sequence directly into a factor-graph estimator.
In a repeated tunnel-exit test at 32 m/s, combining B-Adapt and BVSLAM reduced state-estimation error by 78% versus automatic-exposure images.
The approach also maintained low error in nominal environments.

papers.abstract: We present RAIWAY, an in-house wheeled bipedal robot with 20-inch wheels, together with a contact-informed control approach for rolling locomotion across irregular and discontinuous terrain. Such locomotion is fundamentally contact-dominated, governed by local wheel--terrain interaction that is impractical to instrument directly and depends on more than terrain geometry alone. The proposed framework exploits the contact information available in simulation, distilling multi-contact events into a latent representation. At deployment, the controller infers this representation online from proprioception, requiring no contact sensing. In real-world experiments, the proposed system traverses diverse environments including steep slopes, gravel beds, studded surfaces, and rocky terrain, and demonstrates continuous ascent on the tested outdoor staircases with riser heights up to 15~cm. On our platform, the proposed controller further outperforms baselines without the contact-informed mechanism across challenging indoor and outdoor settings. The video can be found at https://youtu.be/Ch0divLg64w.
authors: Kyungmin Nam, Jiseong Lee, Donghyuk Choi, Jeongsoo Park, Woojin Kim, Jemin Hwangbo
bullets: Addresses contact-dominated rolling locomotion where wheel–terrain interactions are difficult to measure directly.
Distills simulated multi-contact events into a latent representation and estimates it online during deployment.
Demonstrates locomotion across slopes, gravel, studded and rocky surfaces, plus stair ascent with risers up to 15 cm.
Outperforms controllers without contact-informed representations in tested indoor and outdoor environments.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of the proposed contact-informed policy learning framework: The large wheels of our platform produce informative multi-contact patterns, yielding a diverse set of spatially distributed contact events during training. These noisy multi-contact events from the simulator are assembled into a structured vector ct. A recurrent encoder maps this vector sequence into a latent representation, which a student module learns to infer from onboard proprioceptive history for deployment. The GRU encoder has a hidden size of 128, the estimator and policy are [256, 128] MLPs, the teacher encoder is an LSTM with a hidden size of 8 producing the 32-dimensional latent lt, and the student is a [256, 128] MLP, all with LeakyReLU activations.

Fig. 1. papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform tasks specified through natural-language instructions, but their large weight footprint challenges deployment on memory-constrained onboard platforms. Ultra-low-bit quantization reduces this footprint, yet preserving task performance and controlling weight recovery costs remain challenging. We propose Action-Guided Quantization, which combines action sensitivity with a measured proxy for weight recovery cost to allocate matrix bitwidths under storage budgets. Per-channel calibration compensates for quantization error, while a uniform bitwidth within each matrix preserves regular layouts. Bit-dependent grouped lossless coding reduces resident weight storage, and block-wise recovery limits temporary buffers. On LIBERO, AGQ achieves 92.7% task success at W3, exceeding AWQ and GPTQ by 1.2 and 3.7 percentage points, respectively, and retains 70.5% success at W2.5. An asymmetric configuration, denoted W1.5$^{*}$, uses W4 vision weights and a parameter-weighted average of 1.5 bits for language weights. With lossless coding, it achieves $6.10\times$ complete-model compression relative to BF16 while retaining 25.5% task success. Code and experimental results are available at https://github.com/Qiuxu00/AGQ
authors: Xuhong Qiu, Zhuoyu Wu, Qiawei Zheng, Wenhui Ou, Wenqi Fang, Rapha\"{e}l C. -W. Phan
bullets: Targets the large memory footprint of vision-language-action models on onboard, memory-constrained robots.
Allocates matrix bitwidths under storage budgets using action sensitivity and a proxy for weight recovery cost.
Uses per-channel calibration, matrix-uniform bitwidths, lossless coding, and block-wise recovery to reduce storage and recovery overhead.
On LIBERO, achieves 92.7% success at W3 and 70.5% at W2.5; W3 exceeds AWQ and GPTQ by 1.2 and 3.7 percentage points.
A W1.5* configuration with lossless coding provides 6.10× compression relative to BF16 while retaining 25.5% task success.

papers.abstract: Embodied vision-language models must answer questions from partial, evolving observations. Their success depends on both the reasoning capability selected and the evidence available to it. Expert routers adapt internal computation, while tool-augmented systems acquire external evidence; choosing these independently can leave a suitable expert without the evidence it needs. We introduce EKT-Router, a bounded framework that jointly selects a capability expert, optional knowledge, and perceptual tools. Outcome-derived signatures represent the overlapping strengths of General, Spatial Reasoning, and Spatiotemporal experts. A joint utility scores complete expert-evidence routes under a call budget. After acquisition, a packet verifier admits valid evidence with positive predicted expert-conditioned gain. The selected expert then answers once, reverting to the unchanged observation if all packets are rejected. Across 6 embodied QA benchmarks, EKT-Router achieves a mean score of 61.4, the highest among the compared systems, and averages 74.7 on 10 general vision-language benchmarks. With all external evidence disabled, question-conditioned expert selection alone improves over the best fixed expert by 1.75 points. Ablations show that learned routing is the dominant component and that knowledge and perception are complementary.
authors: Weilin Ruan, Yingjie Xu, Yangkai Wei, Bohan Zhou, Shuaibo Li, Harold Haodong Chen, Kaiwen Zhou, Yinchuan Li, Ying-Cong Chen, James Cheng
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between selected reasoning capability and available evidence in partial, evolving observations.
Uses outcome-derived expert signatures for General, Spatial Reasoning, and Spatiotemporal experts.
Scores complete expert–knowledge–perception routes under a call budget, then verifies evidence for expert-conditioned usefulness.
Achieves a mean score of 61.4 across 6 embodied QA benchmarks and 74.7 across 10 general vision-language benchmarks.
Expert selection alone improves 1.75 points over the best fixed expert; ablations identify learned routing as dominant and knowledge and perception as complementary.
