papers.abstract: Learning humanoid control from monocular human videos offers a scalable way to acquire diverse whole-body behaviors. Yet, existing reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipelines are limited in system-level scalability by separately optimized intermediate stages and cannot directly optimize reference motion executability using downstream tracking feedback. We present ViT-H, a video-to-humanoid control framework following a generation-and-tracking paradigm. ViT-H directly generates humanoid reference motions from videos with a diffusion model, bypassing human motion reconstruction and retargeting, and uses motion-tracking outcomes to post-train the generator with direct preference optimization. We further introduce an autoregressive variant that enables real-time humanoid video teleoperation with sub-400 ms latency. Extensive experiments on the Unitree G1 demonstrate that ViT-H outperforms state-of-the-art reconstruction-retargeting-tracking pipelines in both motion quality and executability. We further show that ViT-H scales favorably with model size and with both pre-training and post-training data scale, while motion-tracking feedback consistently improves executability across different motion trackers.
bullets: Addresses scalability limits of separately optimized reconstruction–retargeting–tracking pipelines.
Uses a diffusion model to generate humanoid reference motions directly from video, avoiding explicit reconstruction and retargeting.
Applies direct preference optimization based on motion-tracking outcomes to improve executability.
An autoregressive variant supports real-time humanoid video teleoperation with sub-400 ms latency.
Experiments on the Unitree G1 show improved motion quality and executability, with favorable scaling across model and data size.

At deployment (right), the offline generator drives video-to-humanoid control and the autoregressive generator drives real-time teleoperation.

papers.abstract: The pace of a robot demonstration is often determined by the teleoperator rather than by the task itself. As a result, the same motion can appear at widely different speeds across demonstrations, and policies trained on such data may inherit operator-specific timing along with task behavior. We propose to learn a speed prior directly from large-scale demonstration data. Given a task instruction, a motion path and the images along it, it predicts a distribution over execution speed along the path, from which a chosen quantile defines a consistent clock for retiming each demonstration. Existing methods derive the acceleration signal from the very data they accelerate, so each new task costs another fit, annotation, or pair of predefined rates. A single trained speed prior instead covers every task in a corpus. We fit a speed prior on both robot teleoperation data and handheld demonstrations in which a human arm, rather than a robot arm, moves the gripper, and use it to retime robot demonstrations to the handheld pace before fine-tuning a vision-language-action policy. For execution, we pair the policy with a real-time optimal-control layer that tracks predicted action chunks under robot constraints using the predicted pace. On 120 RoboLab tasks, policies fine-tuned on our learned clocks succeed more often and move with up to half the jerk compared with policies fine-tuned on the original demonstration timing and uniformly accelerated to the same speed. On a real robot, our policy stacks cups in 3.50s, 1.72$\times$ faster than the default policy's 6.02s while succeeding as often, in 29 of 30 trials. Videos and further material are available at https://mllab.snu.ac.kr/projects/learned_speed_prior.
authors: Seungyong Moon, Deokjae Lee, Hansang Lee, Munkhtselmeg Battsengel, Youngin Kim, Seonghyeon Yun, Sungjin Jeon, SongEun Kim, Jeongmin Park, Hyun Oh Song
bullets: Teleoperator timing can vary across demonstrations and cause policies to learn operator-specific speeds rather than task-relevant motion.
The method predicts a distribution of execution speeds from the task instruction, motion path, and path images; a selected quantile defines each demonstration’s new clock.
One speed prior trained on robot and handheld demonstrations can retime demonstrations across tasks without fitting a separate acceleration model per task.
A real-time optimal-control layer tracks policy action chunks under robot constraints using the predicted pace.
Across 120 RoboLab tasks, learned retiming improved success and reduced jerk by up to half; a real robot stacked cups in 3.50s with 29/30 successes.

papers.abstract: Decision Transformer (DT) has demonstrated strong performance in various offline reinforcement learning (RL) tasks by conditioning action generation on expected future returns and historical trajectories. However, treating expected future returns as the condition provides an incomplete description of the future, as trajectories with different state transitions and behaviors may share similar returns. Moreover, expected future returns inherently depend on task-specific reward functions, which makes policy learning reliant on reward-labeled datasets and restricts its scalability to tasks with similar but unseen rewards. Recently, Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPA) have emerged as a promising paradigm of self-supervised learning-based world models, which learn predictive representations of future dynamics in latent space rather than reconstructing future states in the original space. Inspired by JEPA, we propose DT-JEPA, an offline pretraining and online fine-tuning framework that learns general knowledge from reward-free offline trajectories and achieves excellent adaptation to unseen tasks. Instead of predicting a single deterministic future embedding, we design a novel probabilistic predictor to model the conditional distribution of future representations in the latent space, thereby capturing both predictive information and uncertainty about future dynamics. Theoretically, we show that 1) the JEPA objective seeks to maximize a variational lower bound on the mutual information between historical representations and future trajectories; and 2) predictive future-conditioned policy learning admits a finite-sample performance bound with an O(N-1/4) estimation term. Experiments on D4RL benchmarks demonstrate that DT-JEPA achieves efficient adaptation across varying offline RL tasks, outperforming traditional DT-based and other offline RL methods.
authors: Changxu Ni, Yiyang Ni, Jun Li, Feiran You, Hongyang Du, Haitao Zhao, Shi Jin
bullets: Decision Transformer return-conditioning can miss distinct future dynamics and depends on task-specific reward labels.
DT-JEPA learns general predictive knowledge from reward-free offline trajectories before online task adaptation.
A probabilistic latent-space predictor models both future dynamics and their uncertainty instead of reconstructing future states.
Theoretical analysis connects the JEPA objective to mutual information and establishes a finite-sample performance bound.
On D4RL benchmarks, DT-JEPA adapts efficiently across tasks and outperforms DT-based and other offline RL methods.

papers.abstract: The growing population of orbital debris has intensified interest in active debris removal and on-orbit servicing, for which dual-arm space manipulators offer improved grasping stability and load distribution relative to single-arm systems. However, coordinating two manipulators under inter-arm collision avoidance, orientation alignment, and sensing uncertainty remains challenging. This paper develops a coordinated reinforcement learning framework for cooperative motion planning of a dual-arm space manipulator in a target-reaching task with inter-arm collision-avoidance constraints. A centralized state representation combines joint-space, end-effector, and target-relative information, while a multi-objective reward function promotes target-reaching accuracy, orientation alignment, motion smoothness, synchronized task completion, and collision avoidance. Within this framework, Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) and Soft Actor-Critic (SAC) are compared as representative on-policy and off-policy algorithms, and the learned policies are further evaluated for generalization to previously unseen target configurations. Across five random seeds, SAC substantially outperforms PPO within the considered fixed-base simulation scenarios: it reaches an 80% success threshold in every seed (median 1.6M environment steps) whereas PPO does not reach it within a 4M-step budget, and it attains a higher mean success rate (78.6% versus 7.4%) with lower position and orientation errors and tighter bimanual synchronization. Both algorithms degrade on unseen boundary targets, but SAC retains most of its performance while PPO's collapses. The results also expose a failure mode of PPO: under the two-phase shaped reward, it tends to converge to a reward-loitering local optimum rather than committing to the precision task. This behavior highlights the sensitivity of on-policy learning to reward shaping.
bullets: Addresses dual-arm space-robot coordination with target reaching, inter-arm collision avoidance, orientation alignment, synchronization, and sensing uncertainty.
Uses centralized joint-, end-effector-, and target-relative state information with a multi-objective reward for accuracy, smoothness, alignment, synchronization, and safety.
Compares PPO and SAC across five random seeds and evaluates generalization to unseen target configurations.
SAC reached the 80% success threshold in every seed and achieved a 78.6% mean success rate; PPO achieved 7.4% within the stated training budget.
Both methods degraded on unseen boundary targets, while PPO often converged to a reward-loitering local optimum.

papers.abstract: Intent recognition in human-robot interaction requires agents to resolve ambiguous natural language instructions by inferring the speaker's underlying goals. Research has increasingly focused on two notable paradigms for addressing this task: structured symbolic reasoning and multimodal input enrichment. However, it remains unclear whether enrichment-based methods provide benefit in settings where the ambiguity concerns unstated human intent rather than missing observable scene information. In this paper, we present a comparative and diagnostic study benchmarking FISER - a framework utilizing structured social and embodied reasoning - against CEMIR (Context-Enriched Multimodal Intent Recognition), a method that performs multimodal enrichment by synthesizing narratives and photorealistic images from textual prompts. By evaluating both approaches across four Large Language Models (LLMs), ranging from Qwen2.5-Omni-3B to GPT-5, on the HandMeThat v2 benchmark, we analyze their capability to resolve pragmatic ambiguities. Our statistical analysis, employing multiple-comparison correction, reveals no statistically significant difference in performance between FISER and CEMIR across any model or difficulty level. This pattern holds across all sixteen model-by-difficulty comparisons, as well as in a targeted ablation isolating CEMIR's narrative and visual components. Instead, performance is primarily associated with backbone capability and the inherent difficulty of the ambiguity. These findings suggest a boundary condition for text-derived multimodal enrichment: when the relevant task constraints are already available in the textual instruction, synthetic multimodal augmentation may not provide measurable benefit over structured reasoning on the same text.

Finds no statistically significant performance difference in any of 16 model-by-difficulty comparisons.
Ablation results likewise show no distinct benefit from CEMIR’s narrative or visual components.
Performance is more closely linked to backbone capability and ambiguity difficulty, defining a boundary condition for text-derived multimodal enrichment.

papers.abstract: The Moon changes gravity, terrain, and soil at once. Learned locomotion has studied reduced gravity on rigid ground and granular terrain mostly at Earth gravity, but not humanoids under both, generalist-controller transfer, or the Earth cost of lunar adaptation. On a simulated Unitree G1, we train 12 policies with one recipe, varying gravity, terrain geometry, and ground contact (rigid or three-dimensional resistive force theory, 3D RFT), and including Earth-to-Moon fine-tuning and gravity randomization. We test them at both gravities on rigid ground and 3D RFT, and at their training gravity on three held-out soil models. We also test the frozen SONIC, a released generalist humanoid controller, at both gravities on rigid ground only. Gravity transfer is asymmetric. Earth-trained policies keep 0.64 to 0.75 survival at the Moon on flat rigid ground, Moon-trained and fine-tuned policies cannot stand at Earth, and SONIC survives at most 0.10 at the Moon. Rough training lifts combined-tile survival from 0.53 to 0.98 at Earth and 0.80 to 0.99 at the Moon. In 3D RFT, soil training helps on Earth sand, on tiles and for rough-trained policies also on flat sand. On the stiffer lunar soil it helps only flat-trained Earth policies at Earth and changes the survival of Moon-trained policies by at most a few hundredths. In the sampled rollouts of the held-out soil models, Moon-trained policies keep most of their rigid-ground progress on lunar regolith at the low G1 foot pressure, with per-seed progress ratios of 0.84 to 1.39 apart from one seed with a short rigid reference. A gravity-randomized policy trained on rough 3D RFT terrain has a seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 at the Moon on every key test cell up to 20 degrees. Lunar results are simulation predictions conditional on the contact model and soil stiffness.
bullets: Earth-trained policies retain 0.64–0.75 survival on flat rigid ground at lunar gravity, but lunar-trained policies fail to stand at Earth gravity.

Gravity-randomized rough-terrain training achieves seed-mean survival of at least 0.84 at Earth and 0.96 on the Moon across key tests up to 20°.

papers.abstract: Humanoid fall recovery requires selecting a motion that suits both the surrounding scene and the task. The same fallen pose can admit several ways to stand, with different routes, support transitions, and final headings. Yet reliable recovery alone does not provide control over which of these alternatives the robot executes. Steering this choice requires anticipating the physical consequences of a requested movement. We present RISE, an approach to perceptive humanoid recovery that lets task objectives steer how the robot returns to standing at inference time. It builds on two insights: diverse recoveries can be composed from shared movements, and anticipating how these movements unfold allows recovery to be steered toward a task objective. We learn a recovery vocabulary that connects intended movements to motor actions through sensory feedback. A visual diffusion planner learns from executions of this vocabulary to predict motion intent as future body states. Task costs guide this prediction toward a desired heading, rise speed, or path. The planner then generates motion latents conditioned on the steered intent, allowing the requested movement to shape its execution. Simulation experiments demonstrate diverse recoveries, terrain adaptation, and test-time steering without retraining, complemented by real-world demonstrations on a Unitree G1. Project page: https://osheraz.github.io/RISE/
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing among multiple valid recovery motions based on scene and task requirements.
Learns a recovery vocabulary linking intended movements to motor actions through sensory feedback.
Uses a visual diffusion planner to predict future body-state intent and steer it with task costs.
Generates motion latents conditioned on the steered intent to shape recovery execution.
Simulation shows diverse, terrain-adaptive, and steerable recoveries; real-world demonstrations are provided on a Unitree G1.

papers.abstract: Humanoid dexterous manipulation needs reference motions that are both semantically rich and kinematically feasible for the target robot. Text-conditioned hand-object interaction (HOI) generators supply diverse, language-specified demonstrations, but they synthesize motion in human (MANO) space. The embodiment gap is therefore deferred to post-hoc retargeting, where trajectories deployed on the robot can fail to maintain contact with objects and also degrade policy learning. Our key idea is that robot reachability should constrain the interaction trajectories while they are being generated. We present EmbodyHOI, which runs a differentiable inverse-kinematics (IK) solver for a specific humanoid embodiment inside the sampling loop of a frozen flow-matching HOI trajectory generator. We feed back gradients from the embodiment-aware IK solver into the HOI sampler and jointly optimize the position of the humanoid with respect to the object. Because guidance acts only at inference, one HOI trajectory generator trained on human hand poses transfers across humanoid embodiments without retraining. On ARCTIC trajectories with two contrasting humanoids (Unitree G1 and H1-2), our proposed guidance-based method cuts the retargeted wrist error from 8.9 cm to 0.6 cm while leaving text-to-HOI generation quality intact, and raises task success from 68% to 79% on 50 random G1 tasks and from 62% to 76% on a four-task H1-2 suite. Critically, cheaper alternatives for bridging the embodiment gap fail to beat EmbodyHOI. Post-hoc wrist refinement and compute-matched best-of-N selection both reach lower IK energy than our guidance yet train worse policies. For simulation results, see our website: https://embodyhoi.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the embodiment gap between human-space HOI generation and humanoid robot execution, which can cause contact failures and poor policy learning.
Integrates a differentiable inverse-kinematics solver into the sampling loop of a frozen flow-matching HOI generator.

Outperforms post-hoc wrist refinement and compute-matched best-of-N selection for policy training, despite those alternatives achieving lower IK energy.

papers.abstract: Road scene understanding in automated driving (AD) aims to build a comprehensive analysis of video sequences taken on the road by embedded or fixed cameras (e.g., mounted on vertical road signals). One goal is to identify the relevant actors in the scene and another goal is to determine the causes that have triggered a specific action of the ego car (i.e., stop, slow down, turn left, etc.). In a complex urban environment, these causes can be multiple, confusing, possibly contradictory to other causes and not easily expressible using simplistic reasoning. Still, providing accurate {\it automatic cause determination} supports a) user acceptance by providing appropriate explanations to the car passengers and road users; b) increased road safety by providing detailed road scene understanding to traffic. In this paper, we propose using spatiotemporal reasoning and Belnap's four-valued logic to formulate complex causes of AD action in a road scene. We compute these causes by analysing a Qualitative eXplainable Graph (QXG), which is an abstract representation of the road scene capturing spatiotemporal relations between road entities. Starting from a QXG, our approach called \tool, is targeted to determine complex causes of a selected AD action occurring in a specific frame of a road scene. The usefulness of \tool is demonstrated on several scenes extracted from the well-known NuScene dataset.
bullets: Targets automatic explanations for actions such as stopping, slowing, or turning in complex urban scenes.

Determines the causes of a selected AD action at a specific video frame.
Demonstrates usefulness on several scenes from the nuScenes dataset.

papers.abstract: Generalization in multi-arm collaboration can be studied as composing familiar atomic skills in new ways across arms. However, existing evaluations offer limited insight into which training and architectural choices support this ability under different coordination requirements. We introduce \textbf{ACG-Bench}, a benchmark for \emph{Arm-wise Compositional Generalization} that provides a common testbed for studying skill recomposition in dual-arm policies. It contains 23 task--condition pairs across 8 task families, with 6 in-domain conditions and 17 unseen compositions covering reordering, synchronization, their combination, and cross-task composition. All methods receive the same per-arm atomic prompts, and success requires achieving the task goal while satisfying physical milestones and specified order or timing constraints. Using $π_{0.5}$ as a common vision-language-action backbone, we compare representative data-augmentation and architectural strategies with shared source data and a common evaluation protocol. Our architectural study examines arm-token grouping, skill-specific LoRA adapters (SkillLoRA), and arm-wise attention (AWA), highlighting the complementarity of skill-conditioned parameters and attention structure. Combining these choices yields \textbf{AE-VLA}, which achieves 21.53\% generalization success in simulation, compared with 2.94\% for Single $π_{0.5}$, 3.06\% for MA-VLA, and 5.53\% for two independently controlled $π_{0.5}$ policies. On physical SO101 robots, AE-VLA reaches 39.00\% mean success across five unseen conditions, compared with 10.00\% for the strongest baseline. These findings provide empirical guidance for designing dual-arm policies that generalize beyond fixed training routines.
bullets: Introduces ACG-Bench: 23 task–condition pairs across 8 task families, including 17 unseen compositions.
Evaluates policies using shared per-arm atomic prompts and requires both task success and physical order/timing constraints.
Studies arm-token grouping, SkillLoRA adapters, and arm-wise attention, finding their design choices complementary.
Combining these components in AE-VLA achieves 21.53% simulation success versus 2.94% for Single π₀.₅ and 39.00% mean success on physical SO101 robots versus 10.00% for the strongest baseline.
Scope: the study focuses on dual-arm compositional generalization under the benchmark’s specified conditions and protocols.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning for embodied control remains constrained by the difficulty of reward specification. Although recent large language model (LLM)-based methods can synthesize reward functions from natural-language descriptions, they often fail to capture subtle behavioral properties that humans care about, such as natural gait, posture, and movement style. This limitation arises because many desired behaviors are easier to recognize visually than to encode in a reward function. We introduce Reward Optimization via Observable Trees (ROOT), a framework for discovering reward functions that align learned policies with user-specified embodied behaviors. Rather than relying solely on scalar training statistics, ROOT casts reward design as an observation-guided search over a persistent experiment tree that stores reward programs, trained policies, and rollout observations, together with behavioral insights distilled by a video-language model, to diagnose behavioral failures and guide subsequent reward refinements. We evaluate ROOT on seven tasks across four embodiments: simulated Hopper, HalfCheetah, Ant, Unitree Go2, and as well as the real-world Unitree Go2. ROOT produces behaviors that better align with user intent than those generated by existing LLM-based reward-generation methods, achieving up to 86.8% locomotion-completeness accuracy and improving Vid-LLM behavioral alignment from 3.56/5 to 4.14/5, a 16.5% improvement over baselines. Human evaluations further support these results, with ROOT preferred in 51-63% of pairwise comparisons.
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of encoding visually recognizable behaviors—such as natural gait, posture, and movement style—into scalar rewards.
Searches over a persistent experiment tree containing reward programs, trained policies, rollout observations, and video-language-model behavioral diagnoses.
Evaluated across seven tasks and four embodiments, including simulated and real-world Unitree Go2 robots.
Achieves up to 86.8% locomotion-completeness accuracy and raises Vid-LLM alignment from 3.56/5 to 4.14/5 over baselines.
Human evaluators preferred ROOT in 51–63% of pairwise comparisons.

papers.abstract: In a decentralized multi-robot team under partial observability, the fact that decides a robot's next action is often visible only to a teammate. Existing decentralized methods communicate kinematic information, such as position or planned trajectory, which cannot convey what the teammate perceives. Learned communication in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) can carry perceptual content, but the resulting messages are task-coupled and opaque. We propose Latent Telepathy. Each robot broadcasts the perceptual latent vector it already computes for its own use, the output of an encoder trained with a self-supervised joint-embedding predictive objective, frozen, and shared across the team. A teammate learns to act on it from task reward alone. Because the encoder already runs for perception, the message costs no additional computation and a single compact vector of bandwidth. Because the encoder is frozen before any policy is trained, the message means the same thing to every robot, and the receiving robot is never told what it means. We evaluate Latent Telepathy with a content-controlled protocol in which bandwidth, latency, topology and receiver are held fixed and only the message content varies. Broadcasting the latent lets a navigator avoid an occluded hazard in 99.7% of episodes, matching a noiseless hand-designed message. Position and trajectory messages remain at chance, and the raw camera image, 186 times wider, is less reliable than the compressed latent. The result holds from a discrete gridworld to rendered pixels under continuous velocity control, and the encoder decodes the hazard from a physical robot's camera in 102 of 102 live decisions. We also identify a requirement for porting MARL communication results to continuous control, that the decision a message informs must remain reachable by exploration, and show how to restore it.
bullets: Addresses partial observability where critical perceptual information is visible only to another robot.
Broadcasts each robot’s existing frozen perceptual latent, avoiding extra computation and using one compact message vector.
The shared encoder gives messages consistent meaning across robots while receivers learn to use them from task reward alone.
Latent messages enabled hazard avoidance in 99.7% of episodes, matched a noiseless hand-designed signal, and outperformed position, trajectory, and raw-image messages.
Results span gridworld, rendered pixels with continuous control, and 102/102 live physical-robot decisions; successful transfer requires the informed action to remain reachable through exploration.

papers.selection_reason: Decentralized multi-robot navigation using self-supervised perceptual latent communication to avoid occluded hazards.
papers.title: Latent Telepathy: Multi-Robot Communication with Self-Supervised Perceptual Latents
papers.tldr: Latent Telepathy enables robots to share actionable visual information through compact, shared self-supervised perceptual latents, allowing teammates to avoid occluded hazards without task-specific message semantics.

papers.abstract: Adapting a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model to a new robot, environment, or task requires demonstrations that are collected locally and often discarded. Federated learning is a promising approach to exploiting such distributed demonstrations by learning a shared policy. However, whether it can adapt large pretrained VLAs remains an open question, and a lack of reproducible benchmarks for pretrained VLAs and reusable training frameworks makes existing results difficult to compare. In this paper, we conduct a systematic study of federated fine-tuning of three modern pretrained VLA policies on the 40 simulated tasks of the LIBERO manipulation benchmark, and on six real-world tasks in two real-robot experiments, with demonstrations collected across two and three sites, respectively. Our study analyzes the key choices in this setting, spanning multiple federated parameter scopes, three aggregation algorithms, and evaluation under distribution shift. Based on the study, we derive a series of lessons, including the dominance of the federated scope over the choice of aggregation algorithm and the difficulty of matching centralized fine-tuning on physical robots, where cross-site heterogeneity is stronger than simulation captures. We also highlight opportunities for federated VLA learning, such as the ability to match centralized fine-tuning on heterogeneous data, to remain at least as robust as centralized fine-tuning under distribution shift, and to personalize, with each client federating part of the policy and keeping the rest local, which helps where the policy's pretraining is weak but leaves no usable global model. We open-source \decentvla{}, the model- and runtime-agnostic testbed behind the study, to facilitate future research and fair comparisons in federated VLA learning.
bullets: Evaluates three pretrained VLA policies on 40 simulated LIBERO tasks and six real-world tasks across multiple sites.
Studies federated parameter scopes, three aggregation algorithms, and robustness under distribution shift.
Finds that the federated parameter scope matters more than the aggregation algorithm.
Federated learning can match centralized fine-tuning on heterogeneous data and remain comparably robust to distribution shift, but matching centralized performance on physical robots is difficult.
Personalized federation can help when pretraining is weak, though it does not produce a usable global model.

papers.title: An Empirical Study and Open Testbed for Federated Fine-Tuning of Vision-Language-Action Models

papers.abstract: We present NeuRIO, a streaming neural estimator for anchor-free 6-DoF relative inertial odometry using only identified inter-robot bearings, ranges, and IMU measurements. NeuRIO canonicalizes measurements into gravity-aligned coordinates, represents robots as nodes and mutual observations as factors, and uses attention for spatial reasoning and GRUs for temporal modeling. As a graph network, NeuRIO applies shared node-wise and factor-wise operators throughout the network, enabling it to handle different team sizes and time-varying observation graphs. NeuRIO is trained on a simulator that couples various motion patterns, device-level sensor characteristics, and diverse, realistic modeled, and temporally persistent sensor corruptions. In this way, NeuRIO achieves zero-shot sim-to-real transfer. Across $24$ real-world sequences, NeuRIO achieves $14.1\,\mathrm{cm}$ position RMSE and $3.9^\circ$ rotation RMSE. More importantly, NeuRIO demonstrates strong computational scalability, maintaining an update cost below $20\,\mathrm{ms}$ with up to $400$ robots in simulation, while optimization-based methods exceed $20\,\mathrm{ms}$ at only $24$ robots. Moreover, even trained on limited team sizes, NeuRIO transfers directly to unseen larger teams without architectural or parameter changes.
bullets: Estimates anchor-free 6-DoF relative pose from mutual bearings, ranges, and IMU measurements.
Canonicalizes inputs in gravity-aligned coordinates and combines attention-based spatial reasoning with GRU temporal modeling.
Shared node- and factor-wise operators support changing team sizes and time-varying observation graphs.
Across 24 real-world sequences, it reports 14.1 cm position RMSE and 3.9° rotation RMSE.
Scales to up to 400 simulated robots with under 20 ms update cost and transfers to larger unseen teams without architectural changes.

papers.abstract: Fine-grained object (FO) manipulation requires robots to distinguish a specified FO from visually similar objects and execute actions reliably despite scene distractors. However, scene-level visual conditioning lacks explicit object selection, while category-level guidance cannot reliably distinguish FOs within the same category. We present a SAM3-guided visuomotor policy framework that addresses these challenges through persistent object memory and focused visual conditioning. First, we introduce FO Memory-driven SAM3 (FOM-SAM3), which learns reusable FO memory tokens from limited multi-view registration images, while keeping SAM3 fully frozen. Through one-vs-rest learning, these tokens encode persistent memories for localizing target FOs and rejecting similar alternatives, which can be stored in a memory bank for reuse. Second, we propose Focused Spatial-Appearance Encoding (FSAE), which combines in-FO appearance features with explicit bounding boxes to condition action policies, including Diffusion Policy (DP) and Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT). The effectiveness of the proposed FOM-SAM3 is validated on the FO-30 dataset comprising 30 physical objects across four coarse categories. Across three real-robot FO manipulation tasks, our FOM-SAM3-guided policies demonstrated robustness against distractors, discriminative ability of similar FOs, and extendibility to new FOs.
bullets: Targets fine-grained manipulation where scene-level or category-level guidance cannot reliably select a particular object.
FOM-SAM3 learns reusable target-object memory tokens from limited multi-view images while keeping SAM3 frozen.
FSAE combines target appearance features with bounding-box information to condition Diffusion Policy and ACT controllers.
Validated on 30 physical objects across four categories and three real-robot manipulation tasks.
The framework showed distractor robustness, discrimination among similar objects, and extension to new objects.

Our framework leverages SAM3 for FO-level visual guidance, which can be extended to different FOs belonging to the same coarse category via persistent memory learning.

papers.abstract: Self-play in high-throughput simulators yields driving policies with robust closed-loop performance, but improvement per unit of simulation diminishes as training scales. Policies learn to handle common situations early, while further rollouts repeatedly encounter unresolved failures. Post-training offers an opportunity to target these failures, but existing methods primarily evaluate alternative actions or continuations at visited states, although successful recovery may require changing driving style earlier. We propose CounterPlay, a counterfactual self-play post-training approach that backtracks from failed tasks and retries them under alternate driving styles. CounterPlay rests on three key components. First, failure-driven backtracking uses the policy's value estimates to select an earlier stored state from which to retry the task. Second, reward conditioning enables a single policy to retry the task from this state using candidate styles ranging from cautious to aggressive. Third, CounterPlay retains task-completing retries only if no other vehicle incurs a new or earlier collision or off-road event relative to the factual branch. Retries that pass verification with fresh randomness are then distilled into the policy under its deployment condition. On BehaviorBench, CounterPlay achieves state-of-the-art scores on both the Interactive and Random splits across all eight traffic regimes using 1B post-training transitions, which is just 1% of the anchor's 100B self-play training budget. Improvements over the anchor hold across all three evaluated driving styles. CounterPlay resolves a substantial fraction of the anchor's timeout cases on BehaviorBench and achieves a balance between task completion and safety that neither continued self-play nor adopting a more aggressive driving style attains.
bullets: Targets diminishing self-play gains by focusing on unresolved failures rather than repeatedly sampling common situations.
Backtracks from failures to an earlier state selected using value estimates, then retries with styles from cautious to aggressive via reward conditioning.
Keeps only verified retries that complete the task without introducing earlier or additional collisions or off-road events.
Distills successful retries into the policy under its normal deployment condition.
On BehaviorBench, reaches state-of-the-art scores across eight traffic regimes using 1B post-training transitions—1% of the anchor’s 100B self-play budget—and resolves many timeout cases.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of CounterPlay. Based on a pretrained self-play anchor policy, Stage 1 uses critic estimates recorded along the failed trajectory to select an earlier root. Stage 2 then restores this state and simulates a factual branch under the original reward condition and retries under the candidate profiles. Stage 3 filters and ranks retries using task completion and other-vehicle outcomes relative to the factual branch. It then reruns the factual and selected branches with fresh shared random draws to verify the recovery. Stage 4 distills the verified retry into the policy under the deployment condition.

Fig. 3. Qualitative results. Each pair compares the anchor (left) and CounterPlay (right) in the same scene and traffic regime. Ego trajectories are colored by elapsed time in seconds. Grey arrows show other road users’ motion. Open boxes mark ego starts and stars mark goals. Red crosses mark collisions. Circles and triangles mark timeouts and off-road events, respectively.

papers.abstract: Fast-WAM shows that video-action co-training improves control without generating future video at inference, making the representation from a single video diffusion Transformer forward central to action generation. However, future-observation prediction does not explicitly prioritize the future dynamics and visual structure needed for control. We present MT-WAM, which retains the original training objectives and adds complementary supervision for future two-dimensional point trajectories and visual features. A lightweight dual-stream branch copied from the video backbone's final blocks provides target-specific processing, while a structured attention mask prevents cross-stream attention. Motion-stream tokens supply additional dynamics conditions to the action expert. Future visual-feature prediction provides supervision in a feature space that captures object and spatial structure. This supervision trains the video backbone to provide more informative visual context for action generation under changing visual conditions, without adding visual-feature-stream tokens to action conditioning. At inference, MT-WAM uses video and motion caches computed once per replan and skips future-video prediction. Without additional embodied policy pretraining, MT-WAM achieves 98.2% success on LIBERO and 73.7% on LIBERO-Plus, exceeding Fast-WAM by 23.8 percentage points on the latter. On RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Rand, Random success increases from 6.30% to 19.40%; across four real-world tasks, average success increases from 67.0% to 77.8%.
bullets: Targets a limitation of future-observation prediction: it does not explicitly emphasize control-relevant dynamics and visual structure.
Adds supervision for future 2D point trajectories and visual features while retaining Fast-WAM’s original objectives.
Uses a lightweight dual-stream branch with masked cross-stream attention; motion tokens condition the action expert, while visual-feature tokens are excluded from action conditioning.
Inference remains efficient: video and motion caches are computed once per replan, and future-video prediction is skipped.
Reports gains across benchmarks, including 98.2% success on LIBERO, 73.7% on LIBERO-Plus, and improved real-world average success from 67.0% to 77.8%.

papers.title: MT-WAM: Reorienting the One-Pass Predictive Representation Toward Action Generation
papers.tldr: MT-WAM improves one-pass video-conditioned action generation by adding motion-trajectory and visual-feature supervision, yielding stronger simulated and real-world manipulation performance without future-video prediction at inference.

papers.abstract: Training generalizable embodied agents requires realistic, varied, and simulation-ready indoor environments. Language-guided methods support semantic planning and object-level reasoning, but precise spatial grounding remains difficult. Visual generative models offer rich priors over plausible arrangements, yet their outputs require geometric reasoning to become physically valid 3D scenes. We introduce SceneBloom, an agentic framework that combines visual layout sampling with contract-guided 3D compilation. A hierarchical sampler uses diffusion priors to generate furniture arrangements within functional zones. A compiler then uses relations extracted from each proposal to guide geometric fitting and local pose correction. Across five room types, SceneBloom attains the highest visual quality and physical stability among the compared methods and is the only method with no detected mesh collisions and out-of-bounds objects. Its layouts are also closer to the distribution of real rooms than those of all compared baselines. Object navigation policies trained in these realistic scenes achieve a higher success rate in held-out real scans than those trained on an equal number of real training scans. Code is available at https://github.com/Tinaliu0123/scenebloom.
authors: Yuhan Liu, Lianhui Qin, Shenji Wan
bullets: Targets the challenge of converting visually plausible layouts into simulation-ready, spatially grounded 3D environments.
Uses hierarchical diffusion sampling to arrange furniture within functional room zones.
Compiles proposals by extracting spatial relations, fitting geometry, and locally correcting object poses.
Across five room types, it achieves the highest reported visual quality and physical stability, with no detected collisions or out-of-bounds objects.
Navigation policies trained in SceneBloom scenes outperform those trained on an equal number of real scans when evaluated on held-out real scans.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Framework overview. SceneBloom decouples visual layout sampling from 3D scene compilation. Given a room description and retrieved exemplars, a vision–language model (VLM) produces a zone plan with a prompt qj for each zone, and a diffusion model conditioned on qj and asset LoRAs Λj samples zone visual proposals Ij . 3D perception models lift the proposals into zone layouts Lj , and a VLM extracts relation contracts Cj from the proposal images. Guided by these relation contracts, the geometric compiler applies hierarchical layout fitting and relational refinement to produce the compiled furniture layout. Wall and surface objects are then added, yielding the simulation-ready scene shown in room and agent views.

Figure 1: Overview of SceneBloom. SceneBloom compiles visual proposals of functional zones into a simulation-ready 3D scene, and resampling the same prompt yields different layouts. Its scenes are more physically plausible than those of prior generators and train a better objectnavigation policy than an equal number of real scans.

papers.abstract: Robust reinforcement learning (RL) is critical for reliable real-world deployment, where policies may fail under diverse shifts and disruptions. Existing robust RL algorithms offer a rich set of mechanisms and principles, yet two major barriers limit their broader potential: limited algorithm reusability and an unclear empirical capability boundary. We introduce RobustRLlib, an algorithm-centric library and benchmark that addresses both challenges. It integrates 17 representative robust online, offline, and safe RL algorithms under a unified interface for substantially improved reusability, together with an enhanced evaluation platform spanning diverse real-world shifts and advanced humanoid and vision-language-action tasks. Systematic evaluation over 273 perturbation configurations provides an up-to-date capability map of current robust RL algorithms, revealing where they remain effective and where substantial robustness gaps persist. As an open-source, user-friendly platform, RobustRLlib offers a reproducible and extensible codebase for applying existing methods to new problems and developing new robust RL algorithms.
authors: Xi Chen, Fengqi Hu, Zeyu Shen, Jiaying Xu, Shangding Gu, Pan Xu, Anqi Liu, Laixi Shi
bullets: Addresses limited reusability and unclear empirical boundaries in robust RL.
Integrates 17 representative online, offline, and safe RL algorithms under one interface.
Provides evaluations across real-world shifts, humanoid tasks, and vision-language-action tasks.

Offers an open-source, reproducible, and extensible platform for research and application.

papers.abstract: Collecting high-quality demonstrations remains a central bottleneck for learning dexterous manipulation. Teleoperation records executable robot actions, but it requires a complete robot setup and places the burden of coordinating many finger joints on the operator. Human demonstrations are easier to collect, but their motions must be estimated and retargeted to the robot, and they do not directly provide robot actions. In this paper, we introduce DexPort, a portable data-collection interface for high-DoF robot hands. It uses the same hand hardware for collection and deployment, avoiding a hand embodiment gap, and records both commanded joint targets and measured joint states. Our key observation is that a small set of skills can support a wide range of dexterous tasks. During collection, the operator moves the hand-held interface to specify the robot wrist motion and selects or adjusts skills that coordinate the finger motion. This removes the need to control each joint independently while retaining behaviors such as precise grasping and in-hand manipulation. We collect demonstrations across several real-world tasks and in unstructured environments without a robot arm. We then use behavior cloning to train visuomotor policies directly on the recorded wrist motions and hand commands, without skill labels. We evaluate across 4 tasks: pick-and-place with diverse objects, screwing with in-hand tool use, drawer stowage which requires simultaneous grasp and pulling, and a bimanual scanning task. We collect over 2,500 demonstrations with our portable device, in both laboratory and in-the-wild settings. Across our tasks, we see an improvement from 11% to 64% when using recorded robot commands instead of states, and an improvement from 36% to 78% for task success when using in-the-wild data.
authors: Amber Xie, Jiawei Fu, Xiaofeng Guo, Carmelo Sferrazza, Guanya Shi, Haozhi Qi
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of collecting high-quality dexterous manipulation data with many finger joints.
Uses the same hand hardware for data collection and deployment, avoiding a hand-embodiment gap.
Operators control wrist motion with a hand-held device and select or adjust skills for coordinated finger movements.
Records commanded joint targets and measured states; behavior cloning trains visuomotor policies without skill labels.
Evaluated on four tasks, with success improving from 11% to 64% using commands rather than states and from 36% to 78% with in-the-wild data.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Task Rollouts. We show successful rollouts annotated with the phases of each task. We use these phases to score partial success. We also annotate grasp types that emerge in the rollouts, such as a pinch grasp for the cherry tomato and a power grasp for the cucumber. These annotations describe observed behavior. The policy predicts raw joint targets without skill labels.

Fig. 3. Data Visualization. We show fisheye camera views recorded during data collection. For our pick-and-place task (PnP), we collect in-domain and in-the-wild data. For drawer stowing, we add a third-person camera because the grasped object occludes much of the scene. We show both camera views at three stages of the trajectory. For bimanual scanning and drawer stowing, the operator is occasionally visible, but we do not post-process the data to remove the operator.

Fig. 2. Transferable Hardware Interface and Control Mapping. (a) Transferable Module: The Wuji hand (A) and fisheye camera (B) form a transferable hand–camera module that mounts to the Quest 2 controller for data collection and to the robot wrist for deployment. Reusing the same module preserves hand embodiment and camera-to-hand extrinsics. (b) Ergonomic Redesign: The final hardware interface places the operator’s grasp near the assembly’s center of mass and adds a support strap, shortening the moment arm and reducing wrist torque. (c) Skill Control Mapping: Quest 2 inputs start and stop demonstration episodes, select hand or screw mode, and modulate thumb, grasp, and screwing skills. The joystick adjusts thumb flexion and abduction in Thumb Mode and incrementally tightens or loosens the grasp in Finger Mode.

Fig. 5. Policy Learning Results. We show imitation learning performance across four tasks. Policies trained on recorded hand commands achieve higher success rates and faster screwdriver rotation than the state-as-action baseline. Partial success for pick-and-place denotes grasping and placing one object. For drawer stowing and bimanual scanning, we report success rates for the task phases shown in Fig. 4. A phase counts as successful only if all preceding phases also succeed. Each policy is evaluated for 15 episodes per task.

Fig. 7. State-as-Action Failure. Policies trained with measured joint states as action labels produce weak grasps and fail to hold onto objects. Top: the baseline drops the package when presenting it to the scanner. Bottom: the baseline cannot retain the laundry once it begins to pull the drawer open.

Fig. 6. In-the-Wild Co-Training. One benefit of DEXPORT’s design is its portability. For our pick-and-place task, we collect 1,000 in-the-wild demonstrations (visualized in Fig. 3) and co-train with the 700 laboratory demonstrations. We find that increasing the number of cotrained trajectories increases the success rate of the policy in every condition. In the distractor setting, full success rises from 40% to 87%.

We evaluate on seen objects, unseen objects, and scenes containing distractors. In-the-wild data improves full success on seen objects and with distractors in both data regimes, but improves success on unseen objects only with 700 laboratory demonstrations.

papers.abstract: We introduce RynnUnify, a 16B unified embodied model that combines strong embodied understanding with long-horizon visual planning through interleaved video--language reasoning. With capabilities spanning spatial reasoning, physical prediction, and grounding, RynnUnify connects an understanding of the physical world with visual anticipation of how it evolves across successive subtasks. Building on these capabilities, we further develop an agentic extension through reinforcement learning to selectively use video predictions for reasoning about unobserved states and interaction outcomes. We also develop a world-action extension of the full RynnUnify model, translating its understanding and prediction capabilities into robot control. To evaluate these capabilities, we introduce Rynn-VP and Rynn-GEU for long-horizon visual planning and anticipatory reasoning. Experiments show that RynnUnify achieves the highest average embodied understanding score among the evaluated unified multimodal models and improves the Rynn-VP overall score by 9.75 points over Cosmos 3 Nano. Its agentic extension improves the Rynn-GEU average by 6.0 points over direct reasoning, while the world-action extension achieves 51.5\% success on 20 selected composite RoboCasa365 tasks and 46.7\% average success across three real-robot tasks. Together, these results establish RynnUnify as a shared foundation for embodied understanding, visual planning, and robot control, taking a step toward a unified embodied brain.
authors: Minghao Zhu, Bohan Hou, Kun Xiang, Zixuan Wang, Yinzhou Tang, Yifei Yang, Zhikai Wang, Tianyi Zhang, Kehan Li, Haoyu Zhao, Siteng Huang, Leigang Qu, Sicong Leng, Dongchi Huang, Mingxiu Chen, Shijian Lu, Yue Wang, Xiaodan Liang, Zhenyu Zeng, Deli Zhao, Chengju Liu, Jianfei Yang, Xin Li

The model achieves the highest average embodied-understanding score among evaluated unified multimodal models and improves Rynn-VP by 9.75 points over Cosmos 3 Nano.
Its extensions improve Rynn-GEU by 6.0 points over direct reasoning and achieve 51.5% success on selected RoboCasa365 tasks and 46.7% average success across three real-robot tasks.

papers.abstract: In medical robotics, data-driven soft-tissue shape control requires deforming tissue toward desired morphologies through sequential physical interactions. This challenge is particularly important in microscale manipulation, where localized deformation is difficult to observe, represent, and control, while physics-based models can be computationally expensive and difficult to adapt to realistic environments. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) provides high-resolution volumetric perception of tissue deformation, but target-conditioned control requires effective representations of both observed and desired tissue states. In this work, we introduce an OCT-guided data-driven framework for tissue shape control, learned from user-guided demonstrations and executed with closed-loop OCT feedback. We study full-volume, tissue-masked sparse-volume, and voxelized point-cloud representations, with or without residual conditioning, using deterministic (Explicit) and generative diffusion (Diffusion) policies. Across 12 configurations and 576 phantom rollouts on 3-DoF depth and 6-DoF directional tasks, OCT-derived 3D representations support both Explicit and Diffusion policies, with performance depending on representation and residual conditioning. Residual conditioning reduces directional Shape RMSE from 0.748 to 0.555 mm for full-volume Diffusion, while voxelized point-cloud Explicit with residuals achieves 0.534 mm for depth and 0.443 mm for directional control, with comparable accuracy at intermediate unseen targets and consistent performance across deployments. We further evaluate the framework in 60 ex vivo porcine rollouts, extending to biological tissue with final geometric errors comparable to human demonstrations. These results establish volumetric OCT as current and goal representations for learned closed-loop tissue shape control across deterministic and generative action models.

bullets: Addresses the difficulty of observing, representing, and controlling localized soft-tissue deformation, especially at microscale.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models perform well on robotic manipulation, yet remain brittle once their own actions carry them into states their training data barely covers. Recovering from such failures usually requires recovery demonstrations, policy retraining, or a separate model at inference time. We introduce Backtrack, a lightweight failure detection and recovery mechanism for frozen VLAs that needs none of these. A small failure prediction head, trained only on outcome-labeled rollouts of the frozen policy, reads the VLA's existing internal representations to estimate whether the current episode will fail. When the predicted failure probability exceeds a threshold, a controller pauses the policy, retraces the arm's recently achieved motion, and hands control back to the unchanged policy so it can retry from an earlier configuration. The head adds only 0.48-0.88% to the policy's parameter count. We evaluate Backtrack on LIBERO with three VLAs spanning two action-generation families: SmolVLA and $\pi$0.5, which use flow-matching action experts, and the autoregressive $\pi$0-FAST. On LIBERO-Long, the suite of long-horizon multi-step tasks and the one on which all three policies fail most often, Backtrack reduces each policy's failure rate by 19-48%, raising success by up to 7.4 percentage points; on the three shorter suites, where control success is already 85-99%, its effect is smaller. On MetaWorld, all twelve controller configurations tested with SmolVLA improve on the unassisted policy.
bullets: Targets brittleness when robot actions enter states poorly covered by training data.
Trains a small failure-prediction head on outcome-labeled rollouts using the frozen VLA’s internal representations.
When failure risk crosses a threshold, it pauses control, backtracks the arm, and returns control to the unchanged policy.
Adds only 0.48–0.88% to model parameter counts.
On LIBERO-Long, reduces failure rates by 19–48% and improves success by up to 7.4 percentage points; gains are smaller on easier suites, while all tested MetaWorld configurations improve.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Backtrack. A small failure prediction head reads features already computed by the frozen VLA and estimates the probability that the current episode will fail. When the predicted failure probability exceeds the threshold t, the Backtrack controller suppresses the policy’s proposed actions and instead retraces recent achieved arm motion stored in a buffer. Otherwise, the policy’s actions are executed normally. The resulting state is observed by the unchanged VLA and the control loop continues. Achieved motion is added to the buffer during normal policy execution; motion executed during backtracking is not. The diagram abstracts over differences in action generation between the evaluated VLAs.

papers.title: If at First You Don't Succeed, Backtrack: Lightweight Recovery for Frozen VLAs

papers.abstract: HoloBoxing presents a simple recipe for learning humanoid boxing by building on a pretrained whole-body controller. The recipe separates reusable motor skills from task decisions: a compact planner requests future body-point targets, while the frozen controller handles joint-level execution. A learned decoder maps 32-dimensional actions to structured target windows, and measured-state imitation initializes the planner before reinforcement learning. Task learning then refines interaction behavior while reusing the decoder and controller, avoiding the need to relearn whole-body control. This combination keeps task optimization focused on a compact upper policy and supplies an initial behavior before reward-driven exploration. Starting from that available controller, the recipe accounts for about seven minutes of additional training, including reused representation fitting and a single-GPU task run. This excludes controller pretraining, data preparation, evaluation, and search. Simulated boxing experiments and component controls evaluate the resulting behavior and the roles of imitation initialization and the target representation.
authors: Xihan Ma, Bo Zhang, Boxiong Li, Yuhan Bao, Ziyue Liu, Yucheng Wang
bullets: Separates reusable motor control from task decisions: a frozen controller executes commands while a planner selects future body-point targets.
Uses a learned decoder to map 32-dimensional actions into structured target windows.
Initializes the planner through measured-state imitation before reinforcement learning to provide useful starting behavior.
Refines boxing interactions with task reinforcement learning while reusing the decoder and controller.

Simulated boxing experiments and component controls assess performance and the roles of imitation and target representation; the reported training time excludes controller pretraining, data preparation, evaluation, and search.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies can adapt to local human intervention, while federated learning can combine distributed robot experience without pooling raw records. We examine their prospective intersection: sharing adaptations derived from diverse human corrections across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments. Corrections differ in modality, safety semantics(urgency, behavioral scope, etc.), and privacy sensitivity. A shared update that improves mean task success may suppress a rare safety intervention or produce an unsafe response on another robot. We argue for three requirements: preserve the context and uncertainty of multimodal corrections when deciding what to share; assess candidate updates in each receiving robot's closed loop before deployment; and evaluate leakage alongside retention of safety-critical evidence. Immediate, legible defensive behavior remains necessary during human interaction. We offer counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda, not experimental results.
authors: Vigneshwaran Subbaraju, Obaidullah Zaland, Monowar Bhuyan
bullets: Human corrections vary in modality, urgency, behavioral scope, and privacy sensitivity across tasks, environments, people, and robot embodiments.
Naively shared updates may improve mean performance while suppressing rare safety interventions or causing unsafe behavior on other robots.
Corrections should retain their context and uncertainty when determining what to share.
Each candidate update should be evaluated in the receiving robot’s closed loop before deployment.
The paper proposes counterexamples and a falsifiable evaluation agenda; it reports no experimental results.

papers.abstract: Regularised reinforcement learning (RL) has provable robustness guarantees that should ease the transfer of policies from simulation to robots, known as sim-to-real. Yet, weakly regularised algorithms like Proximal Policy Optimisation (PPO) remain the de facto choice in sim-to-real pipelines, while the practical benefits of regularisation for transfer remain poorly characterised. In this work, we study the sim-to-real performance of commonly used RL algorithms, with the aim of characterising the effects of regularisation on robotic performance. To that end, we derive Soft MellowMax Actor-Critic (SMM-AC), a novel regularised RL algorithm based on the soft mellowmax value function, which carries strong robustness guarantees. On MuJoCo continuous control benchmarks, SMM-AC is competitive with baselines like Soft Actor-Critic (SAC). On real robots, SMM-AC achieves higher return, while exhibiting greater robustness to perturbations in observations, the environment, and dynamics than baselines. Together, these results demonstrate that regularised RL improves real-world policy deployment through better robustness to the sim-to-real gap, and changing real-world conditions.
authors: Danilo Vucetic, Mohamad H. Danesh, Florence Clerc, Hsiu-Chin Lin, Jonathan Tremblay
bullets: Sim-to-real transfer is difficult because simulation and deployment conditions differ.
The study characterises how regularisation affects robotic policy transfer.
It introduces Soft MellowMax Actor-Critic (SMM-AC), a regularised RL algorithm with robustness guarantees.
SMM-AC is competitive with SAC on MuJoCo continuous-control benchmarks.
On real robots, it achieves higher return and greater robustness to observation, environment, and dynamics perturbations.

papers.abstract: On-policy distillation aligns teacher feedback with a student's current behavior, yet acquiring useful supervision for multi-turn agents requires identifying both where guidance is needed and whether the student can sustain the interaction afterward. We introduce Frontier-OPD, which addresses this problem through the student's learning frontier: decision situations that remain challenging but admit useful autonomous continuation after brief teacher guidance. To operationalize this frontier, Frontier-OPD organizes on-policy experience into a shared-state trajectory graph, where trajectory-balanced aggregation of teacher-student disagreement identifies distinct intervention candidates while preserving the histories needed for replay. Short teacher bridges are then assessed by comparing agreement over the bridge and the ensuing student continuation with an equally long segment of the original trajectory, providing a behavioral proxy for guidance that the current student can build on. Accepted teacher responses augment ordinary distillation data, and fresh rollouts renew the frontier estimate as the policy changes. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld report higher mean autonomous performance than the compared distillation baselines across the evaluated student scales and teacher configurations, with ablations indicating complementary effects of candidate selection and guidance filtering. In one ALFWorld timing setting, the additional collection cost is offset by a shorter time to a target success rate.
authors: Zheng Jiang, Yiming Chen, Houde Qian, Ling Li, Chaoyang Li, Lifeng Sun
bullets: Targets the learning frontier: situations that remain challenging but are likely to benefit from brief teacher guidance.
Builds a shared-state trajectory graph and uses trajectory-balanced teacher–student disagreement to identify intervention candidates while preserving replay histories.
Filters short teacher bridges by comparing bridge and subsequent student behavior against the original trajectory as a proxy for useful, sustainable guidance.
Adds accepted teacher responses to distillation data and continually refreshes frontier estimates through new rollouts.
Outperforms compared distillation baselines in mean autonomous performance across ALFWorld, WebShop, and ScienceWorld; candidate selection and guidance filtering have complementary effects.

papers.abstract: Quantitative and dense task progress feedback is essential for robotic manipulation across data curation, policy evaluation, and reinforcement learning. Existing progress annotations often rely on sparse keyframe markings derived from subjective manual judgments, limiting their scalability and cross-task consistency, particularly in long-horizon manipulation. To overcome these challenges, we propose action-aware quantification, a unified progress specification that decomposes long-horizon trajectories into object-level subtasks via a vision-language model (VLM) and assigns weighted action credits to capture fine-grained execution dynamics. Using VLM auto-labeling and human calibration, we construct an 800+ hour training video dataset and LOOM, a long-horizon progress benchmark containing 19,618 human-calibrated evaluation frames. To model these dense progress dynamics, we introduce NimCritic, a predictive progress critic trained via Joint Video-Progress Learning. We further incorporate Historical Progress Perturbation to mitigate sequential drift, and design a contrastive Video-Progress Alignment objective that bridges asymmetric expert streams by mutually grounding intermediate visual dynamics and denoised progress trajectories. NimCritic matches or outperforms state-of-the-art process reward models (PRMs) on the established Video Progress Benchmark (VPB) and LOOM, surpassing GVL (GPT-6-Sol) on VPB by about 65% in terminal success accuracy (TSA). On the large-scale RoboArena policy evaluation benchmark, it also retrieves human-selected successful rollouts with about 97% overall recall. These results establish action-aware quantification as a scalable foundation for dense progress feedback in robotic manipulation.
authors: Tianchi Xu, Yalin Zheng, Yangxin Zhu, Ruonan Ren, Zheng Fu, Yunlong Wang, Yuanxin Zhong
bullets: Addresses the subjectivity, sparsity, and poor scalability of keyframe-based progress annotations.

Introduces LOOM, with 19,618 human-calibrated evaluation frames, plus an 800+ hour training-video dataset.
NimCritic uses Joint Video-Progress Learning, Historical Progress Perturbation, and contrastive Video-Progress Alignment to predict dense progress.
Matches or exceeds leading process reward models, achieves about 65% higher terminal success accuracy than GVL on VPB, and about 97% recall on RoboArena rollout retrieval.

papers.abstract: Navigating complex, high-dimensional biological search spaces necessitates scalable physical and computational intelligence to explore beyond local optima through iterative self-play across ideation, experimentation, and automation. Translating experimental designs into reliable physical execution remains bottlenecked by static laboratory automation and unmodeled physical variability. To address this, we introduce VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories, or VERID, a foundational infrastructure designed to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of artificial intelligence (AI) agents and complex, error-prone physical realities of wet labs. VERID is a persistent, high-fidelity semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell that provides four core services: queryable introspection for agentic reasoning, time-compressed simulation for protocol validation, comprehensive trace persistence for a complete scientific record, and a framework for safe execution. We present three case studies using aqueous dye and deionized water mixtures to validate the optical and fluidic foundations of VERID. These studies demonstrate how VERID enables pre-emptive detection of critical errors in experimental protocols, stateful mid-run error recovery and post-hoc identification of subtle physical failures. The simulation functions as a discrete accounting engine, allowing agents to safely and inexpensively explore experimental designs in silico and refine experimental strategies through iterative self-play. VERID also captures structured multimodal experimental data for downstream analysis, knowledge mining and agent training. We argue that this semantic layer is an essential prerequisite for deploying autonomous agents in the biochemical and biomedical sciences, ensuring data integrity, operational safety, and paving the way for tackling previously intractable grand challenges in biology.
authors: Yves Delley, John Coller, Zachary Cutts, Alexander Daryin, Mathias Bellaiche, Jun W. Kim, Oscar Donosa, Srinidhi B. Seshadri, Tanner Clary, Sandy Klemm, Avinatan Hassidim, Yossi Matias, Pooja Rao, Petar Sirkovic, Annalisa Pawlosky
bullets: Addresses the gap between high-level AI-generated protocols and variable, error-prone physical laboratory execution.

Uses aqueous dye and deionized-water case studies to validate its optical and fluidic foundations.
Enables early protocol-error detection, mid-run recovery, and post-hoc identification of subtle physical failures.

papers.title: Semantic Representation for Agentic Self-Play in Automated Laboratories
papers.tldr: VERID is a semantic digital twin that helps AI agents safely design, simulate, monitor, recover, and learn from automated wet-lab experiments.

papers.abstract: Aerial vision-language navigation (AVLN) requires a UAV to reach a language-described target from partial egocentric observations while reasoning over large outdoor scenes. Existing approaches typically fuse view-centered RGB observations and globally anchored history maps as generic visual embeddings, leaving cross-modal spatial alignment to be learned from sparse navigation supervision. We present SP-Guide, a transformer- based goal-prediction framework that addresses this weakness of alignment through a Spatial Prior Cross-Modal Encoder, an Instruction Enhanced Decoder, and a Goal Convergence Filter for terminal target refinement. Experiments implemented on the CityNav benchmark show that SP-Guide improves success rate over the representative baselines, with the largest gains on unseen environments. These results indicate that physically grounded spatial priors provide an effective inductive bias for robust AVLN.
authors: Haoxiang Tang, Dong Zhou, Shen Tan, Minxuan Jiang, Xitong Li
bullets: AVLN must guide UAVs to language-described targets from partial egocentric views in large outdoor scenes.
Existing methods often use generic visual embeddings, leaving spatial cross-modal alignment to sparse navigation supervision.
SP-Guide combines a Spatial Prior Cross-Modal Encoder, Instruction Enhanced Decoder, and Goal Convergence Filter.
On the CityNav benchmark, it improves success rate over representative baselines, with the largest gains in unseen environments.
The approach suggests spatial priors can provide a robust inductive bias for AVLN.

papers.tldr: SP-Guide improves aerial vision-language navigation by using physically grounded spatial priors to better align visual observations with language instructions and refine terminal goals.

papers.abstract: Inspired by infants' ability to learn novel tasks by imitating others, in this work we evaluate to what extent Conditional Neural Processes can autonomously learn representations of actions that are informative about their underlying goal. We show that the addition of an attention mechanism in the hidden space fosters the emergence of robust goal representations early on in the observation of an action sequence, making it a promising model for a robotic self-supervised general learner.
authors: Marco Gabriele Fedozzi, Yukie Nagai, Francesco Rea, Alessandra Sciutti
bullets: Evaluates Conditional Neural Processes for discovering task goals from observed actions.
Targets representations that capture an action’s underlying goal rather than only its motion.
Adding hidden-space attention promotes robust goal representations early in action sequences.
Suggests potential for self-supervised, general-purpose learning in robots.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots support material transport in warehouses and industrial facilities, where navigation must adapt to changing operating conditions. Sensor observations reveal physical obstacles, but do not by themselves specify temporary access rules, route preferences, or exceptions known to operators. This paper presents a natural-language policy interface that brings this knowledge into ROS 2 Nav2. A local large language model converts instructions into JSON policies specifying destinations, spatial constraints, and temporal or event conditions. Deterministic checks govern mission acceptance, and three costmap adapters project accepted policies into the existing navigation stack without changing its planner or controller. On 150 researcher-authored English commands, four local models produce 107-142 correct accepted policies, compared with 44 for a rule-based parser, with 3-20 incorrect acceptances per model. Fault injection records rejection of eight endpoint/JSON faults and 29 validator-stage faults. Navigation experiments use correct task policies to evaluate keepouts, zone costs, person-dependent regions, and event-conditioned passage in simulation and on a TurtleBot3. For Tasks 1-3, mean travel times are 18.4-24.5% lower in simulation and 23.1-35.0% lower on the physical testbed than with the baseline lacking those policies. A native KeepoutFilter comparison and two-robot demonstrations examine basic keepout behavior and shared policy projection. The interface connects operator instructions to explicit navigation policies while retaining Nav2's planning and control components.
authors: Jiyeong Chae, Hyunkyo Seo, Heonjae Lee, Kyung-Joon Park
bullets: Addresses the gap between sensor-detected obstacles and operator-defined access rules, route preferences, and exceptions.

papers.abstract: Semantics can provide a proxy for physical traversability. Terrain that looks like loose sand or a rock field is likely to have similar physical properties. Open-vocabulary vision-language models (VLMs) enable this physical reasoning over terrain outside any fixed label set. We present Open-world Language-conditioned Speed Fields (OWLS), which plans directly over the dense feature map of a VLM. Prompted with a description of traversable terrain, the VLM scores every pixel of a single camera image; OWLS projects these scores onto the ground, adapts them to the platform with two morphological operations, and uses the result as the speed field of a minimum-time planner, so terrain appearance and obstacle clearance shape one trajectory. OWLS needs no task-specific training, no terrain annotation, no persistent map, and no exteroceptive sensor beyond the camera. We evaluate it on a physical rover indoors and off-road, on simulated Mars and Moon rovers over 200 procedurally generated terrains, and on real planetary imagery.
authors: Chahyon Ku, Erica Tevere, Georgios Georgakis, Rudra Mukherjee, Bernadette Bucher
bullets: Addresses navigation in unfamiliar terrain by using semantic appearance as a proxy for physical traversability.
Scores each image pixel with a language-conditioned VLM prompt describing traversable terrain.
Projects scores onto the ground, adapts them with morphological operations, and plans a minimum-time trajectory incorporating obstacle clearance.
Requires only a camera, with no terrain annotations, task-specific training, or persistent map.
Evaluated on physical indoor and off-road rovers, simulated Mars and Moon rovers across 200 procedural terrains, and real planetary imagery.

papers.abstract: Supervising a multi-UAV reconnaissance mission usually means plotting waypoints and watching every drone. We present UAV SwarmAgent, a hierarchical multi-agent system in which an operator states the mission in one natural-language sentence and a ground-station agent writes and executes code that turns it into per-UAV routes. The agent grounds inspection targets in an aerial map with a vision-language model, splits them among N UAVs by balancing route length, and dispatches worker agents that verify incidents with a compact onboard decision model. In simulation over 4 incident types and 3 foundation models, the swarm located the incident in 244 of 255 missions (95.7%). A paired scaling study with one to 5 UAVs shows that flight time follows an Amdahl-type law. The second UAV delivers half of the attainable saving and the speedup is bounded at 1.52x. We discuss what this predictability, and the false alarms we observed, imply for an operator who supervises the swarm, and outline the user study needed to test it.
authors: Oleg Sautenkov, Yasheerah Yaqoot, Muhammad Ahsan Mustafa, Grigorii Kalinin, Chih-Yung Wen, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: A ground-station agent converts a one-sentence mission description into per-UAV routes and executable code.
The system grounds targets on aerial maps, balances route lengths across UAVs, and assigns onboard agents to verify incidents.
In simulation, it detected incidents in 244 of 255 missions (95.7%) across four incident types and three foundation models.
Scaling from one to five UAVs followed an Amdahl-type pattern, with speedup capped at 1.52× and the second UAV providing half of the attainable saving.
False alarms remain a concern, and a user study is still needed to evaluate operator supervision.
