papers.abstract: Zero-shot object navigation requires an embodied agent to choose where to search while retaining evidence from previous observations. HGWM couples an LLM-generated room-anchor prior with persistent spatial-semantic memory. A coarse stage assigns visual-semantic scores to candidate headings on a 0-10 scale; a fine stage measures symbolic compatibility between observed objects, room context, and the goal prior. Phase-dependent fusion combines these scores with an LLM direction recommendation before local action selection. On HM3D v0.1, the reported HGWM configuration achieves 62.6% success rate (SR) and 31.5% success weighted by path length (SPL), compared with 58.1% and 31.2% for WMNav. On MP3D, the corresponding values are 46.8% and 17.9%, compared with 45.4% and 17.2%. The results indicate higher success point estimates and modest path-efficiency gains. On HM3D v0.2, the full model obtains 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL. Additional component ablations reduce SR by 0.9-2.3 percentage points and SPL by 0.6-1.5 points. These are author-reported aggregate measurements. The accompanying implementation repairs pass offline tests; episode-level rerun records are not available. Evaluation is confined to simulation.
bullets: Uses a coarse-to-fine process: heading scoring followed by symbolic matching of observed objects, room context, and the goal prior.
Fuses phase-dependent graph scores with an LLM direction recommendation for local action selection.

On HM3D v0.2, the full model achieves 74.4% SR and 31.9% SPL; component ablations lower both metrics.
Evaluation is limited to simulation, and episode-level rerun records are unavailable.

papers.abstract: These lecture notes provide an introduction to optimization, optimal control, and reinforcement learning for robotics, emphasizing their mathematical connections and practical relevance. This first version is a preliminary collection of notes, not yet a fully developed textbook, and currently contains no figures or graphs. The notes may be revised, corrected, and expanded in future versions.

papers.abstract: Ultrasound imaging is highly operator-dependent, motivating robotic systems that reproduce expert scanning skills consistently. These skills involve coordinated interpretation of anatomical landmarks, ultrasound images, and probe-tissue interactions that are difficult to encode in hand-designed control strategies. Imitation learning offers an alternative, but its observation and action representations should reflect the anatomically structured nature of scanning. We propose an anatomy-anchored imitation-learning framework that combines anatomy-guided probe placement with learned ultrasound navigation. The placement module identifies a task-specific anatomical starting point from external visual observations and establishes the initial probe pose as the reference frame for scanning. A flow-based policy then generates scanning motions from anchor-relative probe poses, ultrasound images, probe-mounted camera views, and contact forces, while a termination head predicts task completion. This avoids continuous reliance on third-person vision and reduces dependence on the robot-patient configuration. A handheld acquisition platform enables multimodal demonstrations to be collected during natural freehand scanning without a robot. On 16 unseen participants, task success reaches 96%, 94%, 88%, and 94% for kidney, gallbladder, and liver standard-plane acquisition and radial artery sweeping, respectively. Compared with a fine-tuned pi_0 model, success on the abdominal tasks improves by 10-42 percentage points, with lower time-to-target, peak contact force, and trajectory jerk. Ablations support the complementary roles of anatomical anchoring, egocentric vision, and force feedback. End-to-end trials with automatic placement achieve 90-100% success, and the policies transfer without retraining to a second robot with 83-100% success.
authors: Yuan Bi, Fangxu Han, Ye Su, Yiping Zhou, Zhongliang Jiang, Nassir Navab
bullets: Addresses the operator dependence of ultrasound by structuring learning around anatomical landmarks and probe-tissue interaction.
Uses anatomy-guided initial probe placement, anchor-relative probe poses, ultrasound images, egocentric camera views, and contact forces.
A flow-based policy generates scanning motions, while a termination head predicts task completion; demonstrations are collected through natural freehand scanning.
On 16 unseen participants, success rates were 96%, 94%, 88%, and 94% across kidney, gallbladder, liver, and radial-artery tasks.
End-to-end automatic placement achieved 90–100% success, and transfer to a second robot without retraining achieved 83–100% success.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed anatomy-anchored imitation-learning framework. A handheld acquisition platform records synchronized probe poses, contact forces, ultrasound images, and wrist-camera views during freehand demonstrations. These multimodal observations, together with an anchor-relative pose representation, enable learning scanning policies for autonomous robotic ultrasound.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large-scale human motion data, motion retargeting, and motion imitation have enabled increasingly capable whole-body control for individual humanoids. Cooperative carrying is more challenging because successful coordination requires not only plausible individual motions, but also consistent cross-agent and agent-object relations, including shared grasp, relative configuration, and whole-body support. We introduce CoCarry, a cooperative-carrying dataset containing 220 synchronized two-person sequences across 21 task schemes, five shared-object geometries, four terrain types, and approximately 61 minutes of motion. We further propose Contact-Support-Structured Retargeting, which starts from nominal individual motions and jointly refines both humanoids around the same prescribed object trajectory. Cooperation-aware object-local hand anchors preserve compatible four-hand grasp relations, while complementary upper object-interaction and lower support structures retain object-relative geometry and coordinated support. Across all 220 CoCarry sequences retargeted to two A3 humanoids, our method achieves 0.9995 contact preservation, reduces penetration duration by 67.0% and 71.0% relative to GMR and OmniRetarget, respectively, and maintains a 100% retargeting success rate. On CORE4D with Unitree G1 humanoids, it achieves 0.9906 contact preservation with zero measured sliding. We further validate the generated references through physics simulation and multiple real-world cooperative carrying experiments on two physical A3 humanoids, demonstrating their usability for downstream dual-humanoid control.

papers.abstract: Designing effective reward functions is a critical challenge in Reinforcement Learning (RL), which traditionally requires costly manual trial-and-error. While Large Language Model (LLM)-based methods have shown promise in reward design, undifferentiated sampling and limited use of historical feedback often lead to insufficient exploration of the reward space and optimization instability. To address these challenges, we propose $R^2E$, a Role-driven Reward Evolutionary framework for automated reward function design that structures the process through explicit role specialization. $R^2E$ employs multiple LLM roles with complementary objectives: an Explorer that promotes novelty to expand the search space, a Guardian that performs conservative refinements to improve training stability, and an Evolver that recombines high-performing rewards via crossover and mutation to integrate effective structures. A dynamic scheduling strategy coordinates these roles, progressively shifting the search from broad exploration to focused exploitation. To mitigate optimization instability and provide a medium for cross-role collaboration, $R^2E$ incorporates a Global Elite Pool that retains the best-performing rewards to guide subsequent generations, thereby enabling coordinated interaction among roles and ensuring a reliable and consistent refinement process. Extensive experiments on multiple robotic tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our method.
authors: Shouhao Chang, Xuan Liu, Hongye Zhu, Xinning Chen, Shigeng Zhang
bullets: Targets the costly manual trial-and-error required to design effective RL reward functions.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of R2E. (Stage 2 Dynamic Role-driven Iterations): In each iteration, a total of N = 16 candidates are generated through dynamic scheduling by the Explorer, Guardian, and Evolver roles. After RL training and evaluation, the pool is dynamically updated by replacing the worst-performing reward. (Stage 3 End of Iterations): After the search concludes, the Top 1 reward is selected and re-evaluated across five random seeds to produce the final output. (Global Elite Pool): A fixed-capacity memory (K = 5) that stores and ranks the best-performing reward functions across iterations.

papers.abstract: A failed vision-language-action (VLA) rollout does not imply that every action contributed to failure. Yet in group-relative policy optimization (GRPO), a single trajectory-level advantage is assigned to all actions in a rollout. Potentially useful recovery attempts can thus be penalized alongside the errors they aim to correct. Ideal stopping conditions for failure feedback are characterized using success-probability and policy-score martingales. At these stops, the removed gradient contribution has zero conditional expectation given the retained information. Truncation therefore preserves the expectation of a reference GRPO group-gradient estimator and can reduce its covariance. One such stop occurs when the conditional probability of success is zero, motivating error and recovery cues for selecting candidate feedback boundaries. Martingale GRPO (MART-GRPO) is introduced with a vision-language model (VLM) for event-guided truncation. The VLM is fine-tuned on our annotated training set using low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The last visible error without observed recovery is localized by the frozen VLM in complete rollout videos. Failure feedback is retained through the selected error interval and removed afterward, while successful-rollout loss terms and original loss normalization are preserved. For retrospective boundaries, changes in expectation and variance are analyzed to assess departures from ideal stopping. Experiments with OpenVLA-OFT on RoboTwin 2.0 show that MART-GRPO improves success rates over full-trajectory GRPO across multiple tasks.
authors: Zongyao Zhao, Cheng-Jie Zhao, Ruihang Jiang, Bing Zheng, Zhaolin Wang, Yuanwei Liu

papers.abstract: Controlling scientific instruments requires parameters to be adjusted progressively in response to feedback from successive operations. When unobserved operating conditions evolve with operational history, responses become nonstationary, and a static mapping from actions to responses becomes inadequate for decisions across shots. Shot-to-shot tuning of neutral beam injection (NBI) ion sources in magnetic confinement fusion devices is representative of this class of problems: the conditions of electrode surfaces and vacuum are difficult to observe directly, discharge outcomes vary between shots, and experiments are costly and carry operational risks. We propose a physically grounded multimodal agent with three independently auditable components. Deterministic algorithms extract symbolic physical quantities and visual evidence from multichannel waveforms; a memory with two layers organizes trajectories from the current task, experience from earlier tasks, and procedural knowledge, from which a multimodal large language model (MLLM) generates candidate actions; and an independent action feasibility check enforces action constraints before execution. In a strictly chronological replay of 455 shots from four EXL-50U platforms, physical symbols alone outperformed waveform images alone by 0.21-0.32 in macro-F1 for quality classification across all four evaluated models. Retrieved context increased the mean agreement with historical action directions by 22.4-42.7 percentage points, whereas the contribution of visual evidence varied across models. Under supervised operation on five ion sources, the system achieved a beam-extraction rate of 86.80% across 409 executed shots. These results demonstrate the engineering feasibility of the framework for supervised sequential tuning on a physical scientific instrument.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks require a robot to remember what it has done and what it has seen. Frontier vision-language models can plan such tasks without task-specific training, but how such a planner should remember an episode is an open question. We argue that its memory must keep track of what the planner has done and learned, and must let the planner choose what to look at, since every frame costs tokens; a note rewritten at every step meets both poorly. We propose LogLook, whose execution-grounded memory lets the system keep the record, an execution log and the model's earlier notes, while the model decides where to look: frames are returned only where it expects a change, and demonstrations are skimmed before it inspects the parts it chooses. Measured with the benchmark's motion planner, LogLook matches the success of a note-only memory with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, and fails far fewer episodes through what it remembered or saw. With direct control, LogLook solves 93.5% of the RoboMME test set.
authors: Tianyi Jiang, Tianyao Tong, Zhenshan Bing
bullets: Addresses how frontier vision-language robot planners should remember actions and observations during manipulation tasks.
Maintains an execution log alongside the model’s notes instead of rewriting a note at every step.
Uses model-directed visual access: it requests frames where changes are expected and selectively inspects demonstrations.
Matches note-only memory success with 43% fewer tokens and less than half the images, while causing fewer memory- or perception-related failures.
Achieves 93.5% success on the RoboMME test set with direct control.

The model chooses what to see: after an action only the recorded frames that changed near the watched points are returned, and a demonstration is skimmed before the model inspects the ranges it asks for. papers.selection_reason: Execution-grounded memory for VLM-based robot planners that selectively retrieves frames, relevant to embodied memory, VLA, and token efficiency.
papers.title: LogLook: Execution-Grounded Memory for Frontier-Model Robot Planners
papers.tldr: LogLook improves robot-planning memory by grounding it in execution logs and letting the model selectively inspect frames and demonstrations, reducing visual context while maintaining or improving task success.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation involves localized changes: picking up a cup moves the cup while leaving the surrounding scene largely unchanged. Yet existing 3D visual pretraining methods, including recent dynamics-aware variants, model state transitions at the scene level, compressing the motion of everything in a scene into a single global latent action. This conflates semantically distinct transitions in scenes with multiple moving parts, obscures dependencies between changing regions, and leaves the learned representation vulnerable to task-irrelevant scene content. We introduce DynaSlots, an action-free, label-free pretraining framework that decomposes each point cloud frame into a small set of temporally consistent slots and models dynamics at this per-slot level rather than the scene level. A temporal slot propagation module promotes consistent slot assignments across frames; an inverse dynamics model then extracts one latent action per slot from feature differences, and a diffusion-based forward dynamics model, paired with a self-supervised interaction head, predicts each slot's future state while learning pairwise proximity-and-motion relations. Experiments on Meta-World, Adroit, and a RealMan RM65-B robot demonstrate that DynaSlots outperforms prior scene-level baselines. It achieves superior success rates in simulation and exhibits strong robustness to scene clutter and unseen objects in real-world manipulation. Code is available at \href{https://zhucezhanghao12345-source.github.io/DynaSlots-Anonymous/}{https://zhucezhanghao12345-source.github.io/DynaSlots-Anonymous/}.
authors: Meng Li, Lijiang Chen, Qi Zhao, Jun Jiang, Longhao Zou, Shuchang Lyu, Guangliang Cheng
bullets: Addresses scene-level dynamics modeling, which conflates multiple moving parts and incorporates task-irrelevant content.
Decomposes point-cloud frames into a small set of temporally consistent slots without actions or labels.
Learns per-slot latent actions through inverse dynamics and predicts future slot states with diffusion-based forward dynamics.
Uses a self-supervised interaction head to capture pairwise proximity-and-motion relationships.
Outperforms scene-level baselines in Meta-World and Adroit, with robust performance amid clutter and unseen objects on a RealMan RM65-B robot.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. DynaSlots framework. (a) Three point-cloud frames are encoded by a shared Point Transformer and propagated by a temporal slot binder into K=6 aligned soft slots. An EMA target branch supplies noised future slot features, while an auxiliary interaction head predicts pairwise proximity-and-motion relations. The displayed losses are noise prediction, slot VICReg, relation BCE, and assignment entropy. (b) Previous slots query current point tokens through competitive assignment, weighted aggregation, and residual refinement, repeated three times per frame. papers.selection_reason: Slot-centric 3D dynamics pretraining with per-slot latent actions and forward dynamics for manipulation, fitting both world models and robot learning.
papers.title: DynaSlots: Slot-Centric 3D Dynamics Pretraining for Robot Manipulation
papers.tldr: DynaSlots pretrains robot-manipulation representations by modeling localized 3D dynamics per temporally consistent object slot instead of using a single scene-level action.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot manipulation requires a single vision-language-action (VLA) policy to execute diverse skills across scenes and instructions. However, current multi-skill VLA policies often leave two aspects of an instruction insufficiently modeled: which primitive skill to execute and where/how to contact and move objects. We propose MAST-VLA (Multi-skill Adaptation with Skill-conditioned experts and Trajectory-affordance priors), a dual-conditioning framework for robot manipulation. MAST-VLA introduces skill-conditioned LoRA Mixture-of-Experts (LoRA-MoE) adapters in the LLM backbone, where skill-query tokens and routing biases guide low-rank expert specialization, and converts a predicted affordance heatmap into a patch-level trajectory-affordance spatial prior for the action head. On the CALVIN ABC$\rightarrow$D long-horizon multi-skill cross-scene generalization setting, MAST-VLA achieves state-of-the-art performance, reaching an Avg. Len of 4.65 over five-subtask evaluation sequences. Real-robot multi-skill sequence experiments further validate its deployability under real perception and control noise.
authors: Jiachi Yang, Zhiyi Xu, Hongquan Zhang, Xin Tan, Zhizhong Zhang, Jingyu Gong, Yuan Xie
bullets: Addresses insufficient modeling of primitive skill choice and object contact/movement in vision-language-action policies.
Uses skill-conditioned LoRA Mixture-of-Experts adapters with skill-query tokens and routing biases in the language-model backbone.
Converts affordance heatmaps into patch-level trajectory-affordance spatial priors for the action head.
Achieves an Avg. Len of 4.65 on CALVIN ABC→D long-horizon cross-scene evaluation and is validated in real-robot sequence experiments.
Scope includes robustness to real perception and control noise; broader limitations are not specified in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Learned humanoid controllers are usually trained in one simulator and then checked in a second one before they go near hardware. We ask what that check says about command delay. We train motion-tracking policies for a 24-joint humanoid on five motions taken from monocular video and test them in an independent CPU MuJoCo harness, which we first verify against the training model. Every policy completes its motion in at least 26 of 30 episodes under the training randomization. With 40 ms of constant command delay, however, survival drops to 15% on average (0% - 45%), and the delay margin is only 20 - 30 ms. Randomizing the delay during training (0 - 50 ms) lifts survival at 40 ms to 95% on average (75% - 100%) and moves the margin to 50 - 70 ms. A control arm trained for the same number of extra iterations without delay does not improve, so the gain comes from the randomization itself. This holds for all five motions with three training seeds each, and a policy trained in PhysX behaves the same way. The price is slightly looser tracking (0.02 - 0.06 rad on four motions) and, for the most dynamic motion, less robustness to other perturbations. We also show that the first sim-to-sim gap we saw came from the harness, a missing floor and a wrong timestep, and not from the physics engines. The 0 - 20 ms delay ranges common in locomotion training lie inside the margin an unrandomized tracker already has. The benefit comes from randomizing beyond it, so the range should be set from the robot's measured latency, and delay margin belongs next to other sim-to-sim metrics.
bullets: Without delay randomization, 40 ms of constant command delay reduced average survival to 15%, with a 20–30 ms delay margin.
Randomizing delays from 0–50 ms raised 40 ms-delay survival to 95% on average and extended the margin to 50–70 ms.
The improvement was consistent across five video-derived motions, three seeds, and a policy trained in a different simulator.
Extra training alone did not produce the gain, indicating that delay randomization was responsible.
The approach slightly worsened tracking and reduced robustness to some other perturbations in the most dynamic motion; simulator discrepancies were traced to harness errors.

papers.selection_reason: Studies delay randomization for learned humanoid motion tracking policies, relevant to robust robot learning and control.
papers.title: Delay Randomization Widens the Delay Margin of Learned Humanoid Motion Trackers
papers.tldr: Training humanoid motion trackers with delays randomized up to 50 ms substantially improves robustness to command latency, extending the delay margin while slightly loosening tracking.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are typically pretrained on broad, diverse datasets and subsequently fine-tuned on a comparatively small dataset tailored to a specific target robot. Such adaptation recipe is now widely established, achieving its most mature results on fixed-base arms due to their static base dynamics and consistent reference frame. Mounting the same arm on a quadruped extends the workspace to the entire floor, but fundamentally changes the embodiment: rather than controlling the arm in isolation, the policy must jointly coordinate base navigation, body posture, and end-effector motion. In this work, we study the practical demands of this embodiment change across data collection, model adaptation, and inference design to achieve closed-loop loco-manipulation on a Unitree Go2 with an AgileX Piper arm. We report the choices that made this real-robot deployment feasible, namely model variant, action horizon, and demonstration conventions, together with a study tailored to a pick-and-place task, separating data coverage from model capacity. We show that expanding demonstration coverage reduces held-out end-effector error by 30%, and incorporating secondary skills (such as pushing rather than grasping) introduces new behavioral modes without degrading baseline performance. Finally, closed-loop real-world experiments show how dataset composition shapes success and failure, validating the pipeline for more complex loco-manipulation.
authors: Giovanni Minelli, Antonio Langella, Giovanni B. Dessy, Lorenzo Amatucci, Giulio Turrisi, Victor Barasuol, Claudio Semini
bullets: Studies the embodiment shift from fixed-base manipulation to coordinated navigation, posture, and end-effector control on a Unitree Go2 with an AgileX Piper arm.
Examines practical deployment choices across data collection, model adaptation, and inference, including model variant, action horizon, and demonstration conventions.
Finds that broader demonstration coverage reduces held-out end-effector error by 30%.
Shows that adding secondary behaviors such as pushing introduces new modes without degrading baseline grasping performance.
Validates the pipeline in closed-loop real-world pick-and-place experiments and analyzes how dataset composition affects success and failure.

papers.selection_reason: Deploys a VLA policy on a legged manipulator for loco-manipulation, directly matching vision-language-action and robot manipulation interests.
papers.title: From Tabletop to Walking Bot: Deploying a VLA Model on a Legged Manipulator Robot
papers.tldr: The paper develops and evaluates a practical pipeline for deploying VLA models on a quadruped-mounted arm, showing that demonstration coverage and multimodal skills are key to effective closed-loop loco-manipulation.

papers.abstract: Recent robot manipulation policies commonly predict continuous action chunks directly from observations, without explicitly modeling reusable structure in the action space. However, manipulation demonstrations often contain recurring short-horizon motion patterns that are shared across tasks. We introduce \textsc{RoboCode}, which learns these patterns through a shared soft-gated primitive action interface. Rather than assigning each action chunk to a single discrete code, \textsc{RoboCode} represents it as a soft composition of multiple learned primitives, providing a flexible intermediate representation of short-horizon actions. The primitive interface is learned from action chunks pooled across multiple tasks and then frozen while task-specific state encoders are trained to map current state inputs into the shared latent space. Experiments on five ManiSkill manipulation tasks address three questions. First, the learned primitive interface reconstructs action chunks with an average reconstruction MSE of 0.0187. Second, analysis of code activations reveals structured code reuse across tasks. Third, \textsc{RoboCode} achieves the highest or tied closed-loop success rate on all evaluated tasks, with an average success rate of 75.6%, compared with 68.8% for ACT and 41.6% for the larger Diffusion Policy baseline. These results suggest that soft-gated primitive codebooks provide an effective and interpretable intermediate action representation for robot manipulation.
authors: Xianyue Peng, Devi Amarsaikhan, Iman Soltani
bullets: Addresses the lack of reusable action structure in policies that directly predict continuous action chunks.
Learns a shared soft-gated primitive interface, representing each action chunk as a composition of multiple primitives rather than one discrete code.
The primitive interface is learned from action chunks across tasks and frozen while task-specific encoders map states into the shared latent space.
On five ManiSkill tasks, it reconstructs action chunks with 0.0187 average MSE and reveals structured cross-task code reuse.
Achieves the highest or tied closed-loop success on every task, averaging 75.6% success versus 68.8% for ACT and 41.6% for Diffusion Policy.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have emerged as powerful general-purpose robot policies, but their successes and failures remain difficult to diagnose and understand. In this work, we show that sparse autoencoder (SAE) representations of OpenVLA activations contain outcome-predictive information and can be used to predict task failure before the robot reaches an unrecoverable state. Moreover, to provide insights into what common behaviors may contribute to these outcomes, we identify individual SAE features whose strong activations are associated with specific stages of success or failure, and uncover recurring behavioral patterns by localizing temporal intervals where these features exhibit significant activation changes. We further develop a VLM-based interpretation pipeline to generate behavioral descriptions of these patterns and validate their correspondence to feature activations on held-out intervals.
authors: Christian A. Rogers, Qian Lin, Daniel S. Brown
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of diagnosing why vision-language-action robot policies succeed or fail.
Uses sparse autoencoder representations of OpenVLA activations to identify outcome-predictive information.
Links individual SAE features to specific stages and recurring behavioral patterns in task outcomes.
Localizes temporal intervals with significant feature-activation changes to identify relevant behaviors.
Uses a VLM-based pipeline to describe these patterns and validates the descriptions on held-out intervals.

papers.abstract: Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) remains a popular on-policy reinforcement learning algorithm owing to its stability and ease of implementation. Its clipping threshold, however, is fixed, so every training sample receives the same trust-region width regardless of how reliable the corresponding policy update is. This work examines adaptive-clipping variants of PPO in which the constant clipping parameter is replaced by sample-dependent thresholds computed from policy and return statistics. The central method, Dual-Adaptive Z-Score PPO (PPO-DAZ3), sets the clipping interval for each sample from two signals: action confidence, given by the probability of the selected action under the current policy, and update confidence, given by the normalized advantage magnitude. The rest of the standard PPO training pipeline is left unchanged. Evaluation on three classic control benchmarks (LunarLander-v3, CartPole-v1, and Acrobot-v1) indicates that adaptive clipping improves learning in some settings but not all. PPO-DAZ3 performs best on LunarLander-v3, the smooth advantage-based variant PPO-AZ3S leads on Acrobot-v1, and standard PPO stays competitive on CartPole-v1, suggesting that adaptive clipping is most beneficial on harder control tasks.
bullets: Standard PPO uses the same trust-region width for every sample, regardless of update reliability.
PPO-DAZ3 adapts each clipping interval using selected-action probability and normalized advantage magnitude.
The standard PPO training pipeline remains otherwise unchanged.
Across LunarLander-v3, CartPole-v1, and Acrobot-v1, adaptive clipping helps in some environments but not all.
PPO-DAZ3 performs best on LunarLander-v3, PPO-AZ3S on Acrobot-v1, while standard PPO remains competitive on CartPole-v1.

papers.selection_reason: Adaptive-clipping PPO for control tasks; algorithm is transferable to robot policy learning.
papers.title: Dual-Adaptive Z-Score PPO: Dynamic Clipping Using Action Confidence and Normalized Advantage Magnitude
papers.tldr: PPO-DAZ3 replaces PPO’s fixed clipping threshold with sample-specific thresholds based on action confidence and normalized advantage magnitude, improving performance selectively on harder control tasks.

papers.abstract: Robot-assisted dressing is particularly challenging due to narrow openings and articulated body parts. Even small errors in the relative pose between the body part and garment opening can cause snagging, missed insertion, or incomplete dressing. To address these challenges, we formulate dressing as a geometry-aware insertion problem that represents task-relevant spatial relationships between the body part and object opening, rather than relying on the full deformable-object state. Based on this formulation, we propose a Reinforcement Learning (RL) framework combining a staged curriculum, which progressively guides the policy from coarse alignment to insertion and final placement, with a finger-wise insertion soft gate that provides continuous feedback on individual finger insertion progress and helps suppress premature insertion. We evaluate the framework on rigid and deformable bracelet dressing tasks through component ablations, systematic variations in the initial hand pose, and closed-loop execution of the learned policies on a real robotic system. On the post-training deformable evaluation, the full method reaches 84.7 +- 1.2% success. The insertion gate accounts for the largest gain, and adding the curriculum on top of that gate reaches the top score. On a mannequin hand the same full policy succeeds on 15/20 real-robot trials.
authors: Takuma Tsukakoshi, Elle Miller, Tamon Miyake, Namiko Saito, Yushi Wang, Shigeki Sugano, Tetsuya Ogata, Sethu Vijayakumar
bullets: Models dressing through spatial relationships between the body part and garment opening instead of the full deformable-object state.
Uses a staged curriculum from coarse alignment to insertion and final placement.
Introduces a finger-wise soft insertion gate that gives continuous progress feedback and reduces premature insertion.
Evaluated on rigid and deformable bracelet tasks with ablations, varied initial poses, and real-robot closed-loop trials.
Achieves 84.7 ± 1.2% success on post-training deformable evaluation and 15/20 successes on a mannequin hand.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Method overview. The policy uses robot proprioception, user hand keypoints, and wearable-object keypoints to encode relative hand-object geometry and generate dressing actions. papers.abstract: Traversability analysis in off-road settings remains a fundamental challenge for mobile robots. Key difficulties include constructing an accurate and expressive local map from multimodal sensor data, and using the map to design traversability rules that yield desirable navigation behavior. Importantly, this system must be resilient to the limited sensing regime brought about by complex environments and high speeds. In this paper, we present TravSUITE, a traversability system suitable for high-speed navigation in off-road environments. TravSUITE consists of two major components: 1) an efficient voxel mapper that leverages visual foundation models (VFMs) to build a rich geometric-semantic local map from streams of on-board sensor data, and 2) a unified neural network that jointly predicts traversability-relevant quantities in bird's eye view (BEV), including geometry, semantics, speed and cost. Our training strategy is entirely annotation-free and self-supervised, leveraging tasks such as map inpainting and inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to learn both map representations and traversability. We perform a thorough ablation study and comparison to state-of-the-art approaches, and the results indicate that cost learning and auxiliary inpainting each contribute significantly to planning quality, and their combination is critical for achieving state-of-the-art performance in off-road path planning. We also design a simple risk adaptation mechanism to leverage our method's uncertainty estimates at deploy-time, and demonstrate that a combination of inpainting and risk estimation can result in 80% fewer navigation errors and 5% faster autonomous traversal speeds in real-world hardware experiments.
authors: Samuel Triest, Amirreza Shaban, David D. Fan, Wenshan Wang, Sebastian Scherer
bullets: Addresses robust traversability estimation under limited sensing, complex terrain, and high-speed motion.
Builds a geometric-semantic voxel map from onboard multimodal sensors using visual foundation models.
Jointly predicts BEV geometry, semantics, speed, and cost with annotation-free self-supervised learning, including map inpainting and inverse reinforcement learning.
Ablations show that cost learning and auxiliary inpainting improve planning quality, with their combination needed for state-of-the-art off-road planning.
Real-world experiments report 80% fewer navigation errors and 5% faster autonomous traversal when combining inpainting with uncertainty-based risk estimation.

papers.abstract: Offline maximum entropy reinforcement learning seeks to estimate the optimal soft action-value function \(Q^*\) from a fixed dataset without further interaction with the environment. Although \(Q^*\) is characterized by the soft optimal Bellman equation, the corresponding Bellman operator cannot be evaluated directly because both the reward distribution and the transition kernel are unknown. Consequently, estimating \(Q^*\) requires the joint treatment of environment modeling and value function learning. We propose a framework that addresses these tasks separately. Conditional diffusion models based on probability flow ODEs estimate the conditional reward distribution and transition kernel. The resulting distributional estimators define a data driven approximation of the soft optimal Bellman operator, whose empirical Bellman residual is minimized over a class of deep neural networks to estimate \(Q^*\). We establish nonasymptotic guarantees for the proposed method. For operator learning, we derive total variation error bounds for the conditional flow estimators that account explicitly for score estimation, numerical discretization, and terminal smoothing. For soft value learning, we first use the soft Bellman equation to show that $Q^*$ inherits H\"older regularity from the conditional reward and transition densities. For any H\"older index $\beta$, the value learning stage achieves an excess Bellman residual risk bound of order $\widetilde{\mathcal O}\big(n^{-\frac{2\beta}{d+2\beta}}\big),$ where $d$ is the total dimension of the state and action spaces. In contrast to many existing theoretical analyses of deep reinforcement learning, our results do not require Bellman completeness. Numerical experiments support the theoretical findings and demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.
authors: Hao Cheng, Yuling Jiao, Lican Kang, Jerry Zhijian Yang, Chen Zhong
bullets: Addresses offline soft Q-learning when reward distributions and dynamics are unknown.
Uses conditional diffusion models based on probability-flow ODEs to estimate reward and transition distributions.
Learns Q* with deep neural networks through a data-driven soft Bellman operator.
Provides nonasymptotic total-variation and excess Bellman-residual guarantees, without requiring Bellman completeness.
Experiments support the theory and show the method is effective; the stated rate depends on Hölder regularity and state-action dimension.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate expressive continuous trajectories for robotic manipulation, yet balancing real-time responsiveness with execution stability remains a persistent challenge. Standard deployment workflows typically treat numerical solver depth and execution horizon as decoupled choices. The horizon amortizes inference latency, while solver depth is kept high to preserve integration fidelity. In this paper, we reveal a fundamental compute-execution coupling in flow-matching VLAs governed by a systematic sign reversal. While coarse numerical integration degrades precision under rapid replanning, it markedly improves task performance under extended open-loop commitment. Geometrically, numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, serving as an implicit regularizer that suppresses compounding open-loop drift. Across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world Franka manipulation on representative VLA backbones including $\pi_0$, $\pi_{0.5}$, and GR00T, exploiting this joint coupling consistently achieves superior task success while drastically lowering inference latency, entirely training-free and without architectural modifications. These findings establish numerical sampling depth as an operational variance regulator, shifting its role from a static precision budget to an active deployment knob in robot learning. Project page: https://jiabingyang01.github.io/Horizon-Depth-VLA/
authors: Jiabing Yang, Yuan Xu, Yixiang Chen, Qisen Ma, Peiyan Li, Kai Wang, Chenhang Cui, Tao Yu, Zichen Wen, Wen Ye, Bowen Fang, Ziheng He, Xiangnan Wu, Yingda Li, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: Problem: Solver depth and open-loop execution horizon are usually tuned independently, creating a responsiveness–stability trade-off.
Method: Jointly adjust numerical sampling depth and execution horizon, using coarse integration as an implicit regularizer during extended open-loop execution.
Key insight: Numerical truncation contracts lateral action dispersion around an invariant trajectory centroid, reducing compounding drift.
Results: The approach consistently improves task success and substantially lowers inference latency across simulated and real-world manipulation settings and multiple VLA backbones.
Scope: Coarse integration can hurt precision during rapid replanning, so its benefit depends on the execution horizon.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of computational-execution co-design in flow-matching Vision-Language-Action policies. Top: The policy conditions on multimodal observation ot and integrates linear probability flow with N forward Euler steps from prior noise x(0) ∼ N (0, I) to generate action chunk ât, committing to an open-loop prefix of length s on the robot before replanning at t+ s. Bottom: The coupling mechanism. Early solver truncation (N=2) contracts sample dispersion around the conditional centroid (R(2) < R(10)). Under rapid replanning (s=5), high-frequency closed-loop feedback exploits sample diversity; under extended commitment (s=20), coarse integration suppresses compounding lateral drift, reversing solver degradation and delivering up to 5.6× inference speedups.

Fig. 5. Physical Franka platform (left), five evaluated manipulation tasks (top right), and real-world factorial results across three VLA backbones (bottom right). Over 40 matched rollouts per cell across four configurations ((s=10, N0), (s=10, 2), (s=H,N0), and (s=H, 2)), all four quasi-static tasks consistently replicate the sign reversal; shallow sampling degrades success under rapid replanning (s=10) but systematically outperforms deep sampling under full-horizon commitment (s=H). On the dynamic turntable task, tracking moving targets requires high feedback rates, rendering open-loop execution horizon the dominant failure mode.

Fig. 1. Sign-reversing coupling between execution horizon s and sampling depth N . Shallow sampling (N=2) degrades performance under rapid replanning but yields systematic gains under extended open-loop execution. Curves show paired marginal contrasts Ys,2 − Ys,N0 on LIBERO-Long across matched seeds (mean ± sample SD), where solid markers indicate horizons with unanimous sign agreement across all three seeds.

Fig. 4. Geometric mechanism of horizon–depth coupling. (a) Cloud radius vs. sampling depth on π0 (Proposition 1 curve fitted on N ≥ 2). Single-step Euler deviates by retaining a non-zero approximation residual. (b) Openloop trajectory spread accumulated over horizon s. Deep sampling (N=10) generates 2.1× wider lateral dispersion than N=2 while preserving nominal path direction.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robot tasks require retaining and using past information. We integrate Test-Time Training (TTT), which stores context in fast weights, into InternVLA-A1 and Pi0.5 to study action generation conditioned on human demonstrations through training on paired demonstrations and robot trajectories. We implement memory transfer between the two phases and truncated backpropagation, and examine training objectives, gradient coverage, and contrastive regularization across video, short-video, and single-frame cue tasks. In our experiments, adding TTT and training on paired data at the current scale did not lead to consistent target selection based on demonstrations. Under the tested settings, shorter sequences, full trajectory gradient connectivity, and contrastive regularization did not clearly improve responsiveness to demonstrations. When demonstrations were reduced to single-frame cues, real-robot execution still showed a preference for cups at fixed positions. We document the implementation, training configurations, and observations to support further inspection and replication.
authors: Qiangong Zhou, Jiafeng Liang, Yimin Dong, Yang He, Hongxiang Li
bullets: Targets long-horizon robot tasks that require retaining information from human demonstrations.
Adds TTT with fast-weight context memory to InternVLA-A1 and Pi0.5, using paired demonstrations and robot trajectories.
Studies memory transfer, truncated backpropagation, training objectives, gradient connectivity, and contrastive regularization across video and image cues.
At the tested scale, shorter sequences, full trajectory gradient connectivity, and contrastive regularization did not clearly improve responsiveness to demonstrations.
In real-robot tests with single-frame cues, behavior still favored cups at fixed positions, suggesting limited cue use.

The left path queries the updated model with Q, then applies an output projection and a gated residual connection. The two MLPs depict two calls to the same inner model, before and after the update. The batch dimension, head splitting, and inner normalization and residual details are omitted for clarity.

Figure 4: Misalignment under two state-input conditions. In the upper GT-state case, earlier memory carries forward, but subsequent states still come from demonstrations rather than the execution of the model’s decisions. Figure 2: TBPTT and gradient accumulation in our implementation. Yellow boxes at the top are sampled decision anchors, each predicting an action chunk and computing its loss. Vertical dashed lines separate segments; yellow arrows indicate gradient contributions within segments and accumulation across segments. Inner fast-weight updates and state transfer across segments are not drawn separately.

Figure 3: Memory operations in human demonstrations and robot trajectories. Blue denotes the human phase, and green denotes the robot phase. papers.abstract: Behavior cloning for robotic manipulation is highly sensitive to the coverage of its training data, yet collecting diverse successful demonstrations remains costly. We study reinforcement learning (RL) not as a deployable controller, but as a data generator for downstream visuomotor imitation learning. Our key premise is that multiple successful solution modes cover a broader range of successful trajectories than repeatedly collecting a single narrow solution. We introduce DiscoDemo, which trains a privileged latent-conditioned RL generator with a parallel reverse curriculum and a success-gated diversity objective to discover diverse solutions while preserving task success. The trained generator produces multiple successful closed-loop behaviors, which are safety-filtered and exported as a static dataset for downstream imitation learning. Across four manipulation tasks, DiscoDemo produces broader successful-state coverage and improves downstream visuomotor policies in both simulation and the real world. Averaged across tasks, downstream success increases to 62% from 40% for the strongest baseline in simulation, and to 78% from 39% on the real robot, respectively. These results suggest that successful solution diversity improves imitation learning for a pretrained flow-matching VLA and remains complementary to corrective data collection. Project page: https://davian-robotics.github.io/DiscoDemo
authors: Minho Park, Kinam Kim, Donghu Kim, Byungkun Lee, Dongyoon Hwang, Yongjae Shin, Junha Hyung, Hojoon Lee, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Behavior cloning is limited by costly, narrow demonstration data and insufficient coverage of successful states.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can perceive a traffic scene, reason about it, and propose a driving action within a single model. However, existing MLLM-based drivers reason from scratch at each frame and commit to a single explanation, discarding earlier hypotheses about the scene. When the scene is ambiguous, the agent locks in on the wrong interpretation and acts on it before evidence accumulates. In this paper, we propose DriveMind, an MLLM-based driving framework that keeps several hypotheses about the scene alive at the same time and updates their weights as new frames arrive. Inspired by particle filtering, DriveMind propagates each hypothesis through a VLM, scores it against the current observation, and resamples to maintain diversity. On Bench2Drive, adding belief tracking to the same driving pipeline improves the Driving Score (DS) from 68.50 to 81.37 and the Success Rate (SR) from 41.36% to 54.09%. The largest gains occur on ambiguous scenarios such as unsignalized intersections (+20.0 DS) and oncoming-traffic interactions (+20.5 DS). Beyond the overall metrics, DriveMind also improves fine-grained interactive driving abilities such as merging, emergency braking, and give-way.
authors: Yan Shi, Kehua Chen, Jiarui Qi, Yihong Tang, Haichen Liao, Yinhai Wang
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in MLLM-based driving, where committing to one interpretation can cause premature errors.
Uses particle-filter-inspired belief tracking: a VLM propagates, scores, and resamples diverse scene hypotheses as observations arrive.
On Bench2Drive, improves Driving Score from 68.50 to 81.37 and Success Rate from 41.36% to 54.09%.
Shows the largest gains in ambiguous situations, including unsignalized intersections and oncoming-traffic interactions.
Also improves interactive behaviors such as merging, emergency braking, and giving way.

figures.caption: Figure 2: DriveMind overview. (a) An asynchronous fast–slow architecture: a slow vision-language model (VLM) maintains a multi-hypothesis belief state, while a fast diffusion planner generates trajectories. (b) Belief tracking through hypothesis propagation and reweighting. (c) The belief state evolves as new observations arrive.

Figure 1: From single-chain reasoning to mind-evolving belief. (a) Instance-Based Framework: one rationale per timestep. (“CoT” stands for “Chain of Thought”) (b) Mind-Evolving Framework: multiple hypotheses {hk t } propagated over time; darker color indicates higher hypothesis weight.

Figure 4: Belief evolution and weighted action selection. The ego vehicle approaches an intersection with a left-turn command and a cyclist near the crosswalk. DriveMind starts with four equally weighted hypotheses and concentrates belief on cautious behavior as the cyclist’s relevance becomes clear: deceleration receives the highest final weight (0.78), with stopping retained as a fallback (0.22).

Figure 5: Effect of hypothesis count K on behavioral diversity. (a) Weighted action disagreement. (b) Maneuver categories with total weight at least 0.05. (c) ESS after reweighting; dashed lines mark K. Curves show means across four scenarios, each averaged over eight reasoning steps; shaded bands and error bars show one standard deviation across scenario means.

Figure 6: Diversity maintenance through resampling and regeneration. When the effective sample size ESSt falls below the threshold αK, DriveMind resamples high-weight hypotheses and regenerates near-duplicated hypotheses to maintain semantic diversity while preserving consistency with the current observation.

Figure 7: Intersection uncertainty. DriveMind initially maintains multiple plausible actions under ambiguity. As the pedestrian remains near the crosswalk and wet-road conditions persist, the belief concentrates on cautious behavior, assigning final weights of 0.55 to deceleration and 0.45 to stopping, while go-straight and lane-change actions are down-weighted to nearly zero.

Figure 3: Belief dynamics across four scenarios. Foggy Road (red), Urban Intersection (orange), Night Accident (blue), Parking Exit (green). (a) Entropy Ut starts near logK and decays as the scene becomes less ambiguous. (b) The dominant weight maxk w k t climbs toward certainty in most scenarios; Night Accident plateaus at ∼0.6, reflecting persistent ambiguity. (c) ESSt drops below the resampling threshold αK once belief concentrates, except in Night Accident where diversity is maintained throughout. Per-step visualizations appear in Appendix E.

Figure 8: Foggy weather with pedestrian uncertainty. DriveMind handles a foggy and wet-road scenario where a pedestrian appears near the roadside. Early hypotheses include stopping for a potential hazard, decelerating due to low visibility, continuing straight, and lane changing. As the scene evolves, the belief concentrates on the deceleration hypothesis, reaching weight 0.99 at the final timestep. This illustrates how belief tracking supports cautious control under degraded visibility and pedestrian uncertainty.

papers.abstract: In traditional Gaussian process (GP) regression, the inputs are typically assumed to be known, and uncertainty enters only through the measurements. When scalar fields are mapped using GP regression with measurements obtained from a mobile sensor, the inputs correspond to the estimated pose of the mobile sensor. The goal in this letter is to understand how a recorded GP, trained on erroneous inputs (e.g., pose estimates from dead-reckoning), can be corrected in a numerically efficient way when better estimates of the inputs become available. In the developed bias-aware GP (Ba-GP) framework, the recorded GP posterior-mean gradient is used to propagate estimated input bias and noise into mean and covariance corrections. The resulting additive covariance structure is then exploited to develop numerically efficient first-order correction algorithms. A simulation study and an indoor light-intensity mapping experiment show that Ba-GP improves predictive accuracy and uncertainty calibration relative to noisy-input GP baselines, with an order-of-magnitude reduction in computational cost relative to full GP retraining.
authors: Muzaffar Qureshi, Tochukwu E. Ogri, Trivikram Satharasi, Kyle Volle, Rushikesh Kamalapurkar
bullets: Addresses GP regression with input errors caused by uncertain mobile-sensor poses.
Uses the recorded GP posterior-mean gradient to propagate input bias and noise into mean and covariance corrections.
Exploits the resulting additive covariance structure for numerically efficient first-order correction algorithms.
Simulation and indoor light-mapping experiments show improved predictive accuracy and uncertainty calibration over noisy-input GP baselines.
Achieves an order-of-magnitude lower computational cost than full GP retraining.

papers.abstract: Distilling interactive LLM agents requires choosing between teacher-generated demonstrations and student-generated experience, corresponding broadly to off-policy and on-policy distillation. While both have proven effective, we argue that this distinction is inherently hierarchical: the policy that induces an interaction history need not be the same as the policy that generates the token prefix of the current action. We introduce a hierarchical agent distillation framework that formalizes these two levels of on-policiness and enables explicit control over their pairing, mixture proportions, and training schedule. We study this problem through self-distillation, where a frozen teacher has access to task guidance unavailable to the student, and conduct a three-stage controlled study across three models and four interactive environments. We find that student-induced histories paired with teacher-generated action prefixes generally provide the strongest standalone training signal, whereas following the student at both levels generally performs worst. Nevertheless, fully on-policy data becomes beneficial when incorporated into a mixture with other configurations. Moreover, mixtures with identical teacher/student proportions at each level can yield substantially different performance, showing that how the two levels are paired matters beyond the overall amount of on-policy data. Finally, front-loading fully teacher-generated contexts and delaying fully on-policy contexts improves over a static mixture. These findings provide practical principles for deciding where, how much, and when agent distillation should follow the student.
authors: Ya Gao, Zhengtao Zou, Pekka Marttinen
bullets: The study reframes on-policy versus off-policy distillation as two hierarchical choices: history generation and action-prefix generation.
Student-generated histories paired with teacher-generated action prefixes generally provide the strongest standalone signal.
Following the student at both levels usually performs worst, but fully on-policy data helps when mixed with other configurations.
Mixtures with the same teacher/student proportions can perform differently depending on how the two levels are paired.
A schedule that starts with fully teacher-generated contexts and gradually introduces fully on-policy contexts outperforms a static mixture in the studied settings.

papers.abstract: Swarm morphogenesis requires robots to assemble desired shapes through local interactions. We present a modular framework integrating neural cellular automata (NCA) with existing site selection and collision-aware control. Within this framework, we introduce a decentralized attachment-site discovery mechanism. Robots already in the formation update and share local NCA states to identify new attachment sites, enabling progressive growth without a predefined list of sites during deployment. To bridge the mismatch between conventional NCA growth and gradual physical assembly, we additionally propose offline sparse-retention fine-tuning that simulates partial attachment, together with a false-positive loss that penalizes invalid site activations. Simulations demonstrate formation of diverse lattice morphologies, scaling to several hundred robots, and substantial improvements in morphology accuracy from the proposed fine-tuning. Experiments with Crazyflie quadrotors validate the integrated execution pipeline using robot-relative observations reconstructed from external tracking.
authors: Ray Verma, Eliseo Ferrante, Anthony Tzes
bullets: Addresses swarm assembly without requiring a predefined list of attachment sites during deployment.
Combines neural cellular automata with site selection and collision-aware control.
Introduces decentralized discovery by sharing local NCA states among robots already in the formation.
Uses sparse-retention fine-tuning and false-positive loss to adapt NCA growth to gradual physical assembly.
Simulations scale to several hundred robots, while Crazyflie experiments validate the integrated pipeline using externally tracked, robot-relative observations.

papers.abstract: Data-driven robots must learn to avoid collisions with as few demonstrations as possible to avoid collecting large datasets of destructive collision examples. We explore whole-body proximity sensors as inductive biases for learning reflexive collision-dodging behavior and find that lossy sensors with low resolution were stronger biases than high-resolution coverage. We also found that, perhaps unintuitively, anticipating when and where contact happens on the body of a robot reduced its learning sample efficiency. We investigated eight candidate representations in a reinforcement learning environment, which included latent compression, future contact anticipation, lossy corruption, and privileged state estimation. The candidate representations were tested by training over 200 humanoid robots to play a simplified version of dodgeball end-to-end under an intentionally constrained sample and compute budget.
authors: Carson Kohlbrenner, Niraj Pudasaini, William Xie, Naren Sivagnanadasan, Nikolaus Correll, Alessandro Roncone
bullets: Whole-body proximity sensors provide useful inductive biases for reflexive collision avoidance.
Lossy, low-resolution sensing outperformed high-resolution coverage as a learning bias.
Anticipating future contact location and timing unexpectedly reduced sample efficiency.
Eight sensor representations were evaluated in reinforcement-learning simulations with over 200 humanoid robots.
The study focuses on end-to-end dodgeball behavior under intentionally constrained resources.

papers.abstract: Swarms of small robots are an attractive way to survey lunar caves and lava tubes. Missions such as NASA's CADRE will fly cooperating rovers for distributed mapping, but only in daylight. The 354 h lunar night drops the surface towards 95 K, and the radioisotope heaters that let single rovers survive it cannot be supplied at swarm scale. In this study we investigate whether a swarm can instead use its own members as thermal shielding. We train one policy, shared by all twenty robots, by reinforcement learning with an evolution-strategies estimator. The policy receives a single reward, once, at the end of the night: the mean temperature of the five coldest robots. Nothing in that reward refers to position, spacing, exposure or motion. Two behaviors nonetheless emerge. The swarm aggregates, and robots circulate between the sheltered core and the exposed rim, the same pair of behaviors with which emperor penguins survive the Antarctic winter. We measure the survival threshold, the smallest stored energy per robot at which every robot is still alive at sunrise. Across ten runs it is 155.6 +/- 1.3 pcm-h, where one pcm-h is 7.2 kJ of stored heat. That is 37% below a motionless huddle and within 13% of a physics-based lower bound, and at a budget where the motionless huddle loses six robots, every robot survives. The behavior needs no shared spatial reference and no robot-robot contact, and transfers from twenty robots to forty without retraining.
authors: Anais Jeger, Harry Holt, Lennart Puck
bullets: Motivation: Swarm-scale radioisotope heating is impractical for surviving the lunar night, which can cool the surface to 95 K.
Method: Train one policy for 20 robots using evolution-strategy reinforcement learning and a single end-of-night reward based on the five coldest robots’ mean temperature.
Emergent behavior: Robots aggregate into a sheltered core and circulate between the core and exposed rim, despite no explicit spacing, position, exposure, or motion objectives.
Result: The swarm’s survival threshold is 155.6 ± 1.3 pcm-h—37% below a motionless huddle and within 13% of a physics-based lower bound.
Scope: The behavior requires neither shared spatial references nor robot-to-robot contact and transfers from 20 to 40 robots without retraining.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Twenty simulated robots during the 354h lunar night, from one rollout of the learned policy. Ring color is each robot’s sky exposure χ on the scale of Fig. 3. Top: the scattered start at hour 0. Every robot is red: with no neighbor close enough to block it, each one radiates to the full sky. Bottom: hour 73, after the swarm has gathered. The interior is blue, shielded by the bodies around it, and only the rim stays warm-colored; all twenty are alive.

Fig. 4. Transfer to larger swarms. Change in survival requirement relative to N = 20, the size at which all five policies were trained; they were evaluated at N = 30 and N = 40 without retraining. Squares are the mean across policies with bars spanning best and worst; faint points are the individual policies. The grey region is the change available from the equalization bound.

Fig. 2 shows the full system. The optimization term consists of the terminal temperature of the coldest quintile of robots. For N = 20, this corresponds to K = 5. We use the coldest quintile rather than the swarm average so that the objective is dominated by the robots closest to failure, while remaining less sensitive to a single outlier. We use a sparse reward which is returned only once, at the end of the lunar night, and no reward shaping takes place during the episode. We leave out any terms which could influence our emergence claim, such as position, spacing, sky exposure, circulation, huddling, or motion. The only motivating factor is therefore to improve survival.

papers.abstract: When a vision-language-action (VLA) model is fine-tuned with its trainable weights in bfloat16 (bf16) and no fp32 master copy, AdamW writes each update straight into bf16, silently rounding away any update smaller than 1/512 of a weight. In 9 of 12 open VLA codebases a default or documented recipe trains this way, 4 on full weight matrices, including LeRobot's SmolVLA default and its $\pi_0$/$\pi_{0.5}$ guides. In our LIBERO runs without the copy, a probe every 100 steps finds at least 79% of updates to bf16 weights erased. On the Hugging Face Hub, 99% of sampled full-weight SmolVLA fine-tunes store the action expert in bf16, and 84% of recent $\pi_{0.5}$ fine-tunes with a training configuration set the bf16 flag. On LIBERO-Object, with rules fixed in advance, an fp32 copy raises success over LeRobot's storage from 4.3% to 49.3% for SmolVLA and from 5.1% to 80.9% for $\pi_{0.5}$ at a ten-times lower learning rate, where both models are undertrained, and from 89.0% to 97.7% for $\pi_{0.5}$ at its default rate. For SmolVLA at its default rate it adds 10.2 points with open-loop 50-action chunks but only 4.2 when re-planning every 10 actions. In these five comparisons and two more against SmolVLA with every trainable weight in bf16, every run with the copy beats every run without it (p < 0.05); all gaps but the 8.7- and 4.2-point ones clear our 10-point threshold. The fix is to keep the trainable weights in fp32 during training, a one-line change for SmolVLA in LeRobot.
bullets: bf16 rounding removes updates smaller than 1/512 of a weight when no fp32 master copy is used.
This issue appears in documented or default recipes across 9 of 12 surveyed open VLA codebases.
A probe found at least 79% of updates erased in LIBERO runs without an fp32 copy.
Using fp32 training weights improved reported LIBERO-Object success across SmolVLA and π₀.₅ comparisons, including gains up to 76.6 percentage points.
The proposed fix is to keep trainable weights in fp32 during training; for SmolVLA in LeRobot, this requires one line.

papers.title: Full-Weight VLA Fine-Tuning Without an fp32 Master Copy Silently Erases Most Updates
papers.tldr: Training full-weight VLAs directly in bf16 can silently erase most optimizer updates, while keeping an fp32 copy substantially improves LIBERO success.

papers.abstract: Dynamic manipulation of deformable linear objects (DLOs) remains challenging due to underactuated, high-dimensional dynamics, delayed deformation responses, and the presence of multiple feasible motions under obstacle constraints. This paper presents BM2PC, a Bayesian Multimodal MPC framework for agile manipulation of DLOs. Building on the control-as-inference posterior, BM2PC formulates multimodal planning as a set optimization problem that balances control quality and behavioral diversity. An efficient incremental update maintains multiple promising control modes with low additional computational overhead. For real-world deployment, BM2PC incorporates an execution dynamics model that predicts actual end-effector motion and compensates for execution mismatch during fast manipulation. We evaluate BM2PC on rope tracking and obstacle avoidance in simulation and hardware, and on simulated disturbance rejection. In trajectory tracking, BM2PC generalizes better to unseen trajectories than a learning-based baseline without task-specific policy training or fine-tuning. Real-world experiments demonstrate accurate long-horizon tracking, reducing RMSE by 44.0% on the longest task. In obstacle avoidance, BM2PC achieves comparable performance to existing multimodal MPC methods while reducing planning time by 29% to 66%. These results demonstrate accurate dynamic control and efficient multimodal planning within a unified MPC framework. The core implementation of BM2PC and supplementary videos are available at https://github.com/Longyouyuan/BM2PC.
authors: Youyuan Long, Gokhan Solak, Arash Ajoudani
bullets: Addresses underactuated, delayed, high-dimensional DLO dynamics and multiple feasible motions under obstacles.
Formulates multimodal planning as Bayesian set optimization balancing control quality with behavioral diversity.
Uses incremental updates to maintain promising control modes efficiently, plus an execution dynamics model for fast-motion mismatch compensation.
Evaluated on rope tracking, obstacle avoidance, and disturbance rejection in simulation and hardware.
Generalizes to unseen trajectories without task-specific policy training or fine-tuning; reduces longest-task tracking RMSE by 44.0% and planning time by 29–66% versus relevant baselines.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the proposed BM2PC framework. Candidate control sequences are sampled around the multimodal warm-start set and evaluated through parallel rollouts using the execution dynamics model, DLO dynamics model, and collision detection. Based on rollout costs and trajectory features, BM2PC performs an incremental multimodal update to maintain a diverse set of high-quality control modes. One mode is selected for execution, while the updated multimodal set is propagated to the next MPC iteration.

Fig. 4: Trajectory tracking results (Sim). Comparison of trajectory tracking performance of the proposed BM2PC method and the SPiD baseline on both smooth parametric trajectories (Sinusoid, Egg, and Lemniscate) and complex hand-drawn trajectories (SpongeBob, PatrickStar, and Flower) under different execution durations. The proposed method achieves accurate tracking across most trajectories, while SPiD fails to reproduce fine geometric details, particularly on complex trajectories with sharp turns and rapid local variations. Thus, SPiD is not shown in the longer cases (T>12s) to avoid clutter.
Fig. 9: A test-time example of the execution dynamics model.

Fig. 5: Obstacle Avoidance (Sim). Comparison of BM2PC, C-MPPI, and SVMPC on the obstacle avoidance task. The top row presents the rope-tip trajectories together with the tracking RMSE and average inference time. The bottom row shows key snapshots of BM2PC, illustrating mode collapse in unimodal regions (A,C) and multimodal emergence near the obstacle (B,D). The rope tip may pass above the obstacle without touching it, as seen in snapshots B and D.

Fig. 3: Execution dynamics model. A GRU-based history encoder processes recent measured and desired end-effector states to initialize a latent representation of the current execution dynamics. Conditioned on this latent state and the desired future trajectory, the rollout cell recursively predicts future EE motion. At each rollout step, an MLP predicts the executed acceleration, which is integrated by a physicsinformed (PI) head to obtain the next velocity and position.

Fig. 2: The DLO model. The rope is represented by N+1 mass points m j connected by linear spring–damper elements (ks j,c s j) and bending spring–damper elements (kb j ,c b j ). Gravity g and air damping cair are also included.

Fig. 11: Real-world obstacle avoidance results. The rope tracks a Lemniscate (×3) trajectory while a movable obstacle is randomly repositioned along the path to evaluate dynamic obstacle avoidance performance. The blue curve denotes the target trajectory, the orange curve represents the executed trajectory, and the red segments indicate perception failures caused by occlusions, environmental noise, or network instability. Time-lapse snapshots (a)–(h) illustrate the avoidance process under different obstacle configurations. Despite severe perception degradation, including frozen measurements and abrupt trajectory spikes, the controller successfully avoids the obstacle and rapidly returns the rope endpoint to the desired trajectory.

Fig. 7: Multimodal adaptation under sudden blocking. Comparison of representative trajectories from experiments with τ = 0.70 s. (a) Predicted control modes before blocking. (b) The second obstacle appears and blocks the executed plan. (c) Replanning after 25 ms. (d) Predicted modes after 225 ms. (e) Executed rope-tip trajectories. BM2PC switches to an alternative mode on the unblocked side, whereas the ablated variants fail to recover a feasible passage in this example.

Fig. 6: Disturbance Rejection (Sim). The rope tip is subjected to external disturbances at the blue points to evaluate the robustness of the controller. The corresponding rope-tip trajectories and key snapshots of the experiment are presented. BM2PC rapidly suppresses the induced oscillations and drives the rope tip back to the desired trajectory.

papers.title: Multimodal MPC via Bayesian Set Optimization for Dynamic Manipulation of Deformable Linear Objects

papers.abstract: Scaling policy learning requires broad experience and reliable supervision. Robot demonstrations provide high-quality trajectory supervision but are costly to collect. Egocentric videos broaden task and environment coverage, yet motion reconstruction and retargeting introduce noisy action labels. To address this challenge, we introduce EgoForesight, a vision-language-action framework that learns jointly from both sources by reducing the influence of unreliable action labels and exploiting demonstrated outcomes as complementary supervision. A joint vision-action flow couples future visual representation prediction with action generation, unifying reliability-aware action learning with outcome-informed representation transfer. Specifically, reliability-conditioned corruption allocates action supervision across noise levels according to source reliability, while reliability-weighted regression regulates each source's contribution. Complementing this treatment of noisy labels, privileged-future representation distillation draws supervision from demonstrated outcomes. An exponential-moving-average teacher observes the current scene and clean future to encode action-relevant structure from the resulting scene change. Its deeper representations supervise an earlier student layer receiving a corrupted future, providing outcome-informed structure beyond noisy action annotations. Together, these mechanisms support effective scaling with noisy egocentric actions. Over the tested range, EgoForesight exhibits steeper scaling slopes than the baseline, reducing real-world open-loop action MSE by 20.5% and improving RoboCasa few-shot success by 8.1 percentage points at 30,000 hours of pretraining data. After post-training, it also achieves strong absolute performance in both simulated and real-world dexterous manipulation.
authors: Chubin Zhang, Changyuan Wang, Yirui Wang, Ao Li, Shilin Ma, Yue Su, Cai Zhou, Xiuwei Xu, Tianle Zhang, Yansong Tang
bullets: Addresses the high cost of robot demonstrations and noisy action labels from egocentric videos.
Jointly learns visual future prediction and action generation in a vision-language-action framework.
Uses reliability-conditioned corruption and weighted regression to reduce the impact of unreliable action supervision.
Distills action-relevant structure from clean future observations into representations trained with corrupted futures.
Shows steeper scaling than a baseline, with 20.5% lower real-world open-loop action MSE and an 8.1-point RoboCasa few-shot success improvement at 30,000 pretraining hours.

papers.selection_reason: Vision-language-action framework that scales policy learning with noisy egocentric human videos, combining reliability-aware action learning and future-representation distillation.
papers.title: EgoForesight: Effectively Scaling Policy Learning with Noisy Egocentric Actions
papers.tldr: EgoForesight scales robot policy learning with noisy egocentric video actions by weighting supervision by reliability and learning from demonstrated future outcomes.

papers.abstract: How do children learn the meanings of the simple, concrete words that form a majority of their early vocabulary? Statistical information about many word meanings can be recovered from the gradual accumulation of information about the co-occurrence of words with their referents, a proposal known as ``cross-situational learning''. Contrastive vision--language models allow this learning strategy to be tested on egocentric video data capturing children's early real-life experiences with visual and linguistic inputs. Initial successes of this method on small datasets provide a proof-of-concept, but vision models struggle to learn robust visual representations when trained on these same egocentric videos. How dependent is cross-situational word learning performance on the quality of the model's visual representations? And can cross-situational models scale to larger and more diverse datasets? To address these questions, we trained models on the BabyView corpus, including 2,441 hours of longitudinal egocentric video from 48 children. Models trained on this dataset learned object--label mappings, but performance was far higher when they used internet-pretrained visual representations as opposed to when visual representations were learned solely from the developmental video data. Further, the majority of the learning signal was carried by a small proportion of utterances that described a visible referent. Models learned lexical representations that showed recognizable human-like semantic structure, but model performance showed substantially different trajectories over training experiences than those observed in children. Cross-situational learning is a viable word learning strategy for early noun vocabulary, but constructing developmentally plausible models will require understanding how to learn high-quality visual representations from naturalistic data.
authors: Michael C. Frank, Alvin W. M. Tan, Khai Loong Aw, Robert Z. Sparks, Victor Moreno, Grace Keene-Lee, Meesha R. Ryan, Tarun Sepuri, Jane Yang, Virginia A. Marchman, Daniel L. K. Yamins, Bria Long
bullets: Models trained on 2,441 hours of egocentric video from 48 children learned object–label mappings.
Internet-pretrained visual representations substantially outperformed representations learned only from the developmental videos.
Most learning came from utterances describing a currently visible referent.
The learned lexical representations developed recognizable human-like semantic structure.
Model learning trajectories differed substantially from those observed in children.
