papers.selection_reason: Scales cross-situational word learning from egocentric child video, fitting embodied knowledge acquisition from human egocentric experience.
papers.title: Scaling cross-situational word learning on children's naturalistic experiences
papers.tldr: Cross-situational learning can recover early word meanings from large-scale child-centered video, but it depends strongly on high-quality visual representations and does not yet match children’s learning trajectories.

papers.abstract: Coding agents can translate language instructions into robot programs. For contact-rich manipulation, a key challenge is to generate and refine control logic that responds to physical interaction. We present FORCA, a coding agent that takes visual observations and wrist force/torque (F/T) measurements as input to write Python programs for contact probing and force-responsive motion. Between executions, the agent inspects force records alongside visual outcomes to diagnose failures and revise both motion and force-feedback control logic. FORCA requires no demonstrations, task-specific training, or simulation. Across five real-robot tasks, we demonstrate its effectiveness in three forms of contact-rich manipulation: improving manipulation accuracy, adapting to changes in object or surface properties, and regulating contact under surface variation and object motion. Compared with a vision-only variant of the same agent, FORCA improves grasp accuracy and task success and reduces contact loss in wiping and peeling.
authors: Xiao Tan, Yixuan Wang, Zhexi Wang, Wenzhen Yuan
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting control logic to physical contact during manipulation.
Writes Python programs for contact probing and force-responsive motion using visual and F/T observations.
Analyzes force records and visual outcomes after execution to diagnose failures and revise control logic.
Requires no demonstrations, task-specific training, or simulation.
Across five real-robot tasks, improves grasp accuracy and task success while reducing contact loss versus a vision-only agent.

papers.abstract: Temporary traffic control redirects vehicles through work zones, requiring automated vehicles to connect an interpretation of the visible devices to a continuous passing path. Geometric predictors can provide several plausible paths, yet selecting the one consistent with the temporary control remains difficult. We propose SAGE (Semantic-to-Action Grounded Execution), a read-decide-execute-check framework that separates path construction, path preference, and control compliance within a shared candidate space. The central idea is to use a vision-language model's (VLM's) trajectory as a preference over intact geometric candidates. A role-decoupled generator constructs the candidates, and rank fusion combines each candidate's geometric score with its agreement with the VLM trajectory. Supervision structured around the Manual on Uniform Traffic Control Devices (MUTCD) trains SAGE-VLM to state the lane status and hazard side before its passage decision and trajectory. The predicted hazard side enters image-space predicates derived from MUTCD provisions, which support a final intervention bounded in score and displacement. On 2,306 real-world ROADWork validation episodes, the candidates include a path within 10 px of the human demonstration in 87% of episodes, yet selection regret accounts for 53% of the geometric ranker's error. SAGE reduces average and final displacement errors by 8.3% and 12.0% relative to the ranker, mostly in the far field, and hard-constraint violations by 37%. The trajectory opinion improves all four tested generator-selector combinations. SAGE is comparable to state-of-the-art VLM modules in accuracy, with a faster-responding VLM, and outperforms four other adapted driving VLMs in displacement error and safety measures. Project page: https://hhjj233.github.io/SAGE-page/.
authors: Jiaxi Liu, Keshu Wu, Weizhe Tang, Bofeng Cao, Sikai Chen, Xiaopeng Li, Steven T. Parker, Bin Ran
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing the correct path among multiple geometrically plausible work-zone routes.
Generates candidate paths geometrically, then fuses geometric scores with agreement to a VLM-predicted trajectory.
Trains the VLM to identify lane status and hazard side before making a passage decision, with rule-based intervention for control compliance.
On 2,306 ROADWork episodes, SAGE reduces average displacement error by 8.3%, final displacement error by 12.0%, and hard-constraint violations by 37% versus the geometric ranker.
The approach improves all tested generator-selector combinations and is competitive with or better than adapted driving VLMs on reported accuracy and safety measures.

papers.abstract: Real-world reinforcement learning has enabled contact-rich manipulation tasks to be trained directly on physical robots, but unsafe interactions during online learning remain a key barrier to practical deployment. We propose Safe Evidential Real-World Reinforcement Learning (SEVI), a framework for reliability-aware safety intervention during real-world policy learning. SEVI introduces an Evidential Safety Critic that estimates both future constraint-violation risk and epistemic uncertainty in a single forward pass. During online learning, SEVI evaluates each task-policy action before execution; if the action is predicted to be unsafe or the prediction is insufficiently supported by evidence, SEVI overrides it with an offline-trained recovery policy that guides the robot toward a lower-risk region. We evaluate SEVI on two simulated manipulation tasks and a real-world USB insertion task under in-distribution and distribution-shifted conditions. Across task-learning and safety-critic baselines, SEVI achieves the strongest trajectory-level safety prediction, the highest final task success, and the lowest unsafe-event counts. SEVI also reduces unsafe events by 13.4 to 57.1 percent relative to recovery-based safe RL while preserving low-latency execution-time filtering. The project page is available at: https://sevi-safe.github.io/
bullets: Targets unsafe online interactions that hinder deployment of real-world reinforcement learning.
Uses an Evidential Safety Critic to estimate future constraint-violation risk and epistemic uncertainty in one forward pass.
Overrides actions predicted unsafe or insufficiently supported with an offline-trained recovery policy.
Evaluated on two simulated manipulation tasks and a real-world USB insertion task under in-distribution and shifted conditions.
Reports the strongest trajectory-level safety prediction, highest final task success, and 13.4–57.1% fewer unsafe events than recovery-based safe RL, with low-latency filtering.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the SEVI framework. In offline training, failure and recovery demonstrations are used to train the Evidential Safety Critic and recovery policy. During the runtime pipeline, the ESC evaluates task-policy actions using predicted risk and epistemic uncertainty and switches to the recovery policy when needed. In online RL, RLPD updates the task policy using executed transitions from the RL buffer together with prior demonstrations from the demo buffer.

Fig. 1: Illustration of SEVI on the real-world USB insertion task. When the task policy attempts an unsafe insertion, SEVI detects elevated safety risk or epistemic uncertainty and triggers the recovery policy. The recovery policy steers the robot toward a safer region before returning control to the task policy for continued online RL training.

Fig. 5: Effect of recovery-gating criteria on closed-loop execution. Combining risk and uncertainty gives the best safety–performance trade-off across tasks.

papers.abstract: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for learning robot behaviors aligned with human intent. However, its scalability is fundamentally limited by the need to collect expensive human preference labels for every new task. In this work, we present PrefO2O, an offline-to-online latent preference transfer framework that enables zero-shot PbRL on unseen target tasks without requiring any human feedback. The core idea is to learn a task-invariant latent preference space from a small amount of offline preference data on source tasks, where transferable preference structures are disentangled from task-specific variations. This learned manifold allows PrefO2O to transfer preference structures and reward priors to new tasks under distribution shift, while confidence-weighted optimal transport alignment generates reliable pseudo-preference supervision for online reward adaptation. Extensive experiments on robotic manipulation and locomotion benchmarks demonstrate that PrefO2O substantially outperforms existing preference-transfer baselines and matches or exceeds PbRL methods trained with real human feedback, while generalizing across multi-to-one and one-to-one transfer settings as well as across different robot embodiments.
authors: Ruiqi Wang, Dezhong Zhao, Xuesu Xiao, Erdem Biyik, Byung-Cheol Min, Guohua Chen
bullets: Addresses the cost and scalability problem of collecting human preference labels for every new task.
Learns a task-invariant latent preference space that separates transferable preferences from task-specific variations.
Uses confidence-weighted optimal transport to align new tasks and generate pseudo-preference supervision for online reward adaptation.
Evaluated on robotic manipulation and locomotion benchmarks across multi-to-one, one-to-one, and cross-embodiment transfer settings.
Reportedly outperforms preference-transfer baselines and matches or exceeds methods trained with real human feedback.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of PrefO2O. The offline phase jointly learns a trajectory encoder, a preference VAE, and a meta reward model from source-task preference data. In the online phase, the pretrained encoder and reward model warm-start target-task PbRL, and the frozen preference VAE serves as a stable reference for OT-based alignment. Source labels are propagated to target trajectory pairs through the transport matrix, producing pseudo-preference labels with OOD-aware confidence weights for online reward learning and policy optimization.

Fig. 3. Learning curves of all methods on six tasks under two transfer protocols. The left panel shows intra-embodiment transfer, while the right panel shows cross-embodiment transfer. Learning curves for Sweep Into and Walker Walk are provided in Appendix B.

Fig. 7. t-SNE visualization of preference representations with Window Close as the target task, comparing the raw space against the learned latent preference space under intra-embodiment (left) and cross-embodiment (right) transfer. Each point denotes either a raw trajectory-pair difference or its corresponding latent preference vector epref. The upper row colors points by task domain and the lower row by preference label Υ. The learned latent space exhibits strong cross-task mixing and clear separation across preference labels, indicating a task-invariant yet preference-discriminative structure that the raw space lacks.

Fig. 1. Conceptual illustration of PrefO2O. Offline preference data from multiple source tasks are used to learn a task-invariant latent preference space that captures shared preference structures while absorbing task-specific variations. When deployed on an unseen target task, this learned space enables both transferable reward priors and OOD-aware pseudo-preference supervision for zero-shot online PbRL without target-task human feedback.

Fig. 8. Attribute alignment along the learned preference axis with Window Close as the target task, evaluated under intra-embodiment (top) and crossembodiment (bottom) transfer. Each point denotes a latent preference vector epref, colored by preference label Υ. The horizontal axis is the preference-axis projection score, obtained by projecting epref onto the direction between the centroids of samples with Υ = 0 and Υ = 1. The vertical axis reports the attribute value difference for three task-relevant behavioral attributes: approach progress, path directness, and motion smoothness. The dark curve shows the attribute trend along the preference axis, computed as the binned mean attribute value. The Spearman correlation coefficient ρ in each panel quantifies the monotonic association between the preference-axis projection score and the corresponding attribute value difference. The attributes increase consistently along the learned preference axis, indicating that the latent preference space captures a structured behavioral manifold aligned with preference-relevant properties.

Fig. 9. Case study of OT-based preference alignment in the learned latent space, with Sweep Into as the target task. Left: a chord diagram where outer bars denote individual preference pairs grouped by source task, colored by preference label Υ; each chord connects a target pair to a source pair, with width proportional to the transport mass T ∗ ij . Every target pair draws correspondences from all source tasks, but with markedly different mass, showing that alignment is driven by preference structure rather than task identity. Right: for two representative target pairs (Sweep Into #4 and #53), the source pair receiving the highest transport mass, visualized as trajectory rollouts. Despite belonging to entirely different tasks with distinct object interactions, the matched source and target pairs share the same underlying behavioral quality contrast, confirming that the learned latent space aligns preferences along transferable behavioral features rather than task-specific motions.

papers.abstract: Segmenting robot demonstration data into disjoint temporal and semantic subsegments is valuable for learning, cleaning, retrieval, and analysis. Segmentation is often performed manually in a tedious and error prone process. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have the potential for automating this process, but directly ingesting raw multi camera video streams into MLLMs can be costly and can quickly exhaust context windows. In this paper, we introduce KiRoSe (Kinematics for Robot Segmentation), a novel framework that focuses on the companion stream of robot kinematic data. Inspired by the principle of classical entropy coding, such as Huffman coding, where frequently occurring symbols are represented more compactly, we propose Sparse Motion Tokens (SMTs), a discrete kinematic vocabulary designed to compactly represent recurring, temporally localized motion patterns, which we refer to as kinematic events. SMTs are learned by encoding kinematic trajectories with temporal segment supervision and quantizing the resulting features. We use increasingly available robot demonstration subtask annotations to supervise an open language model to interpret the resulting token sequences. Evaluation against human labeled segmentation shows that KiRoSe can substantially outperform baseline segmentation methods in F1 quality and transfers zero shot to unseen robot embodiments and egocentric human motion, while preserving the language models open vocabulary knowledge. Beyond segmentation, KiRoSe tracks task progress on an unseen robot and detects when an action is being reversed.(website: https://berkeleyautomation.github.io/kirose/)
authors: Shuangyu Xie, Kaiyuan Chen, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Richard Cheng, Sergey Zakharov, Ken Goldberg
bullets: Targets costly, error-prone manual segmentation of robot demonstrations and avoids feeding raw multiview video into language models.
Learns Sparse Motion Tokens (SMTs) to compactly encode recurring, temporally localized kinematic patterns.
Uses subtask annotations to supervise an open language model over SMT sequences.
Outperforms baseline segmentation methods in F1 against human labels and transfers zero-shot to unseen robot embodiments and egocentric human motion.
Also supports task-progress tracking on an unseen robot and detection of action reversal.

figures.caption: Figure 2: KiRoSe Pipeline. Given a robot kinematic stream and the task instruction “fold the paper box,” KiRoSe encodes motion using a transition-supervised encoder, then temporally pools and quantizes its features into Sparse Motion Tokens with a learned codebook. The language model reads these tokens, time markers, and the instruction to output action descriptions with start and end times, such as “pick up the object,” “place in the box,” and “adjust.” Transition annotations provide training supervision, while the motion tokenizer remains frozen during language-model adaptation.

Figure 5: Qualitative reversal probe on AgiBot (zero-shot). One subtask per episode is played backwards in place (red frames; stamps give original recording time). Curves show the signed progress rate (green: rising, red: falling); dashed: same model on the original video. ReWiND keeps counting up while the task is undone; KiRoSe’s progress falls; Table 4 reports statistic result.

Figure 7: Segmentation examples on held-out YAM tasks (ABC-130K). The zero-shot video model tends to emit a few coarse segments that restate the instruction (“fold and stack blue towel”, “attempt insert plug”), whereas KiRoSe recovers the repeated grasp–place, flatten–fold, and insert cycles of the reference from kinematics alone. KiRoSe’s Boundary F1 at ±1 s exceeds the video baseline on all five episodes (0.44–0.72 versus 0.07–0.38).

Figure 3: Evaluation Dataset. Top: example tasks and annotated action timelines, with colors indicating action categories. Bottom: representative 40-second traces of linear speed, angular speed, and opening rate for the left (black) and right (orange) arms or hands. The datasets differ in task semantics, temporal structure, and motion characteristics.

Overlays show the hand joints that the conversion of Appendix D uses, projected from the 3D annotations into the image with an approximate equidistant fisheye model: the wrist (dot), which supplies linear velocity; the wrist-toknuckle fan, which defines the palm frame and angular velocity; and the dotted thumb–index line, whose length supplies the aperture. Frames without an overlay for a hand have no valid 3D track at that instant. Although KiRoSe never sees human data and hands have no gripper, it matches or exceeds the video baseline on all five episodes; over all 114 trajectories with video, KiRoSe reaches 0.375 Boundary F1 at ±1 s versus 0.255, and the gain depends on the motion tokens (Appendix D).

Figure 6: Training annotations (YAM, ABC-130K). Keyframes and the human subtask annotation of three training episodes, colored by leading verb as in Figures 7–9. Annotations are dense and follow the arms’ kinematic events: alternating grasp and place cycles when organizing bottles, open, scoop, and close phases when filling the litter box, and explicit mistake intervals (hatched) when a grasp fails.

Figure 1: Encoding Kinematic Events into Sparse Motion Tokens. Across diverse manipulation tasks and objects, continuous robot motion decomposes into recurring, temporally localized patterns termed kinematic events (e.g., bimanual lift, handover, pick, place). Despite visual and spatial variations, end-effector trajectories within the same motion primitive share structural kinematic signatures. KiRoSe compresses kinematic events into a short, ordered sequence of N discrete Sparse Motion Tokens (colored blocks; shaded chronologically).

Figure 13: Human hands as a robot end effector, on real data. (a) Four tasks, one single-frame pose each: the palm frame of each hand (red along the palm, green across, blue normal) and the thumb–index pinch (purple) that serves as the gripper, projected from 3D into the Aria image with an approximate equidistant fisheye model. Frames are shown only where all 14 joints the conversion uses agree with a manual 3D label within 2 cm. (b) The resulting channels for a COVID-test run next to a YAM episode of the same length; dotted lines are annotated boundaries. Wrist speed and aperture rate rise at keystep boundaries much as robot speed and gripper rate do at subtask boundaries. (c) Annotation projection: keystep starts that fall inside a tracked run become that run’s boundaries, in run time.
Figure 4: Boundary F1 (±0.5 s) per embodiment. KiRoSe is trained on YAM only; AgiBot and human hands are zero-shot.

Figure 8: Segmentation examples on AgiBot World (zero-shot embodiment transfer). Neither the motion tokenizer nor the reader sees AgiBot data, yet KiRoSe places boundaries at the grasp and release events and reaches Boundary F1 of 0.73–0.78 on all five episodes, above the video baseline on each (0.00–0.57). Its descriptions transfer at the level of actions (“pick up”, “place”), while object names often follow YAM phrasing.

Figure 12: How each robot channel is built for a robot and for a human hand. Rows are the channels of the shared representation (middle column). Dashed boxes: what each dataset provides; filled boxes: the conversion applied. Robots (left) need only forward kinematics, differentiation, and gripper normalization; human hands (right) require choosing a body frame, fitting a palm frame to the hand keypoints, using the thumb–index distance as a gripper, and projecting keystep annotations onto tracked intervals. The gap thresholds illustrated here describe the short-run conversion; the segmentation evaluation uses the longer-run protocol below.

Figure 10: Dilated temporal convolutions in the kinematic encoder. (a) Each residual block applies a kernel-5 convolution whose dilation doubles from block to block; tracing one output of the fourth block back to the input shows that the same five taps per layer cover 61 input samples. Padding is symmetric, so every feature sees both past and future motion. (b) With seven blocks (dilations 1, . . . , 64), the receptive field grows to 1 + 4 ∑6 i=0 2 i = 509 samples, or 17 s at 30 Hz. This spans several average-length YAM segments, so each feature can encode where the current motion sits relative to neighboring subtasks, while the parameter count grows only linearly with depth.

(b) The focal weight (1− pt)2 against the model’s confidence in the target direction, pt. papers.abstract: The life-cycle of robotics foundation models crucially depends on data labels. Outcome reward labels are needed for monitoring real-world deployments. Process reward labels are needed during RL post-training. Timestamped captions are needed for filtering and balancing pretraining data. We present Flora, an industrial-quality data engine used for training GR00T models, that simultaneously covers these capabilities. Flora achieves SOTA scores on the captioning benchmark WGO-Bench and reward benchmarks RoboReward and Robometer. On internal benchmarks it is competitive with GPT-6 Astra while beating other frontier models. The model is substantially cheaper than API-based alternatives, roughly 125 times cheaper than GPT-6 Astra. Florais battle tested at scale, labeling 200,000 hours of data per day across 512 GB300s. By open-sourcing our data engine, we enable researchers to scale custom robotics datasets and explore emerging applications such as physical auto-research and human-to-robot transfer.
authors: Sicong Leng, Yunze Man, Zhiqi Li, Jing Wang, Yuhe Zhang, Ryan Punamiya, Siddharth Patki, Kaiyuan Zheng, Zi-ang Cao, Zhiding Yu, Sifei Liu, Danfei Xu, Ben Levin, Jan Kautz, Yuke Zhu, Johan Bjorck, Linxi "Jim" Fan
bullets: Supports outcome rewards for deployment monitoring, process rewards for RL post-training, and timestamped captions for pretraining data curation.
Achieves state-of-the-art results on WGO-Bench, RoboReward, and Robometer.
Competes with GPT-6 Astra on internal benchmarks while costing roughly 125× less than API-based alternatives.
Processes 200,000 hours of robotics data daily across 512 GB300 GPUs.
Open-sourcing enables custom robotics datasets and applications such as physical auto-research and human-to-robot transfer.

papers.abstract: What visual representation should a navigation policy act on? Navigation policies built on vision foundation models largely leave representation design to the encoders' pretraining objectives. We present RepresentNav, a navigation foundation model built on a self-constructed representation space: a visual representation constructed by the policy's own objectives from vision foundation models. RepresentNav builds this space with Representation Residuals, a compact three-layer transformer that attends over features spanning the full depth of multiple complementary vision foundation models, so that the policy learns to see what it needs for navigation. In the same space it dreams what it wants: before every action a latent chain-of-thought predicts the representation of the scene a moment ahead. The dream is trained end-to-end with the policy as a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA), with a next-representation prediction loss and a regularizer on its targets. RepresentNav sets a new state of the art on VLNVerse, VLN-CE R2R, EVT-Bench, and two point-goal benchmarks, and its gains carry over to a physical robot amid clutter and moving people. On VLNVerse fine-grained, RepresentNav achieves 83.80% success, outperforming the previous state of the art by 20.05 percentage points, and on EVT-Bench distracted tracking it reaches 85.5% with a single camera (+10.1). With the same encoders, the self-constructed space clearly outperforms concatenating their outputs and learns to weight their layers unevenly, and a dream in it cuts collisions by a quarter. A single dreamed latent decodes into the depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy of the scene a moment ahead, more accurately than pretrained encoders applied to the real future frame, although occupancy is never supervised, and the rollout tracks the robot's own motion over the next second: the dream emerges as a compact latent world model.
authors: Jiawei Chen, Yinxi Wang, Zihan Yang, Meijun Gao, Yaowei Liu, Shuming Zhang, Zecheng Li, Xiangju Mi, Yuxuan Liu, Runzhong Huang, Tianlin Li, Xun Zhang, Zhengyang Wang, Xu Miao, Tong Yang

Reports new state-of-the-art results across VLNVerse, VLN-CE R2R, EVT-Bench, and point-goal benchmarks, with gains transferring to a physical robot.
The learned latent predicts future depth, semantics, and 3D occupancy without direct occupancy supervision; its scope is navigation-focused and evaluated on the stated benchmarks and robot setting.

papers.abstract: Movement primitives commonly represent robot mo- tions through basis functions indexed by time or phase. Inspired by spacetime representations employed in physics, we propose a spline-based formulation in which spatial geometry and temporal progression are represented within a common set of continuous variables. The proposed method jointly estimates a shared Bezier curve, while allowing spatial and temporal model complexity to be adapted independently (e.g., demonstration-specific phase modulation). As use case, we consider an alternating optimization process that simultaneously estimates path intervals observed in partial demonstrations. Simulation experiments demonstrate accurate joint recovery, refinement through modifications in model complexity and continuity, and improved robustness to variance in the demonstration set. Finally, we demonstrate online retiming and synchronization capabilities in a patient-turning task assisted by a robot, evaluated with a physical manikin.
bullets: Represents spatial paths and temporal progression using shared continuous Bezier-curve variables.
Adapts spatial and temporal model complexity independently, including demonstration-specific phase modulation.
Uses alternating optimization to recover path intervals from partial demonstrations.
Simulations show accurate joint recovery and improved robustness to demonstration variance.
A physical-manikin patient-turning task demonstrates online retiming and synchronization.

papers.title: Spacetime Splines for Adaptive Robot Motions
papers.tldr: Spacetime Splines jointly model robot motion geometry and timing with adaptable complexity, enabling robust learning, online retiming, and synchronization.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation, requiring robots to regulate not only motion but also how they yield to external forces, has emerged as the next frontier for Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing VLAs output purely kinematic commands, degrading performance on real-world contact-rich tasks. In this paper, we introduce CompVLA, a unified VLA framework that jointly predicts motion and stiffness matrix from RGB and language inputs. Our approach augments the conventional architecture with a dedicated Compliance Expert, which outputs time-varying stiffness and virtual displacement profiles executed via geometric impedance control. We demonstrate that CompVLA achieves the highest average success rate across diverse contact-rich tasks, outperforming both vanilla and compliance-aware VLA baselines, with ablations confirming each component is essential.
bullets: Addresses the limitation of VLAs that produce only kinematic commands and cannot regulate responses to external forces.
Adds a dedicated Compliance Expert to predict time-varying stiffness and virtual displacement profiles.
Executes predictions through geometric impedance control for contact-aware behavior.
Achieves the highest average success rate across diverse contact-rich tasks against vanilla and compliance-aware VLA baselines.
Ablations indicate that each component is essential to the framework.

papers.abstract: Despite rapid progress, generalist robot policies remain brittle on complex, long-horizon tasks that comprise multiple stages or require repeated attempts and deliberation on the same underlying stage before success. Q-value functions can improve these policies by ranking candidate actions or guiding policy improvement, but learning from sparse task-level rewards entails long credit-assignment horizons, difficult Bellman backups, and broad data-coverage requirements. We introduce SeeQ (Subtask-elicited Q-functions), which instead learns Q-values for the currently active subtask. This shortens the value-prediction horizon and enables effective learning with temporal-difference (TD) objectives. During training, subtask-level annotations present in offline robot data provide the decomposition and enable learning from broad, potentially suboptimal robot datasets. To eliminate the need for human annotations or modular subtask prediction systems at test time, our Q-function architecture is trained to autoregressively predict the active subtask in natural language before estimating its value. We instantiate SeeQ using a base vision-language backbone, pretrain it on diverse open-source robot manipulation data, and finetune it on downstream tasks. Across four real-world manipulation tasks on two bimanual robot platforms, the SeeQ value function substantially improves best-of-N policy steering.
bullets: Long-horizon tasks challenge generalist robot policies because sparse rewards create difficult credit assignment and Bellman backups.
SeeQ learns Q-values for the currently active subtask rather than the entire task, shortening the prediction horizon.
Offline robot-data annotations provide subtask decompositions and support learning from broad, potentially suboptimal datasets.
The model autoregressively predicts the active subtask in natural language, avoiding human annotations or modular subtask predictors at test time.
Across four real-world tasks and two bimanual robot platforms, SeeQ substantially improves best-of-N policy steering.

papers.abstract: Safe whole-body control requires coordinating collision avoidance and balance under high-dimensional, nonlinear dynamics--making safety certificates difficult to design and reuse across behaviors. We present LIMBO, a framework for synthesizing a state-action control barrier function and distilling its safety structure into a task policy. LIMBO learns the safety certificate from black-box transitions and a state-based failure specification over residual actions around a frozen base controller, making Q-CBF synthesis tractable in the full control dimension while placing the certificate in the task policy's control space. During synthesis, the learned safety value drives risk-guided sampling near the estimated boundary of recoverability; during task learning, it serves as a teacher that provides action-level safety feedback, yielding a robust task policy and alleviating the need for an online safety filter at deployment. We demonstrate LIMBO on a 29-degree-of-freedom humanoid performing dodgeball avoidance and locomotion beneath low obstacles. Beyond scaling learned Q-CBFs to whole-body control, we show that risk-guided boundary sampling provides a theoretically grounded way to explore the edge of recoverability. Under the same safety specification, ceteris paribus, varying the sampling concentration produces strategies ranging from crouching to a novel backward-leaning limbo maneuver. In both settings, the learned policies transfer to hardware without online safety filtering, showing that learned safety synthesis scales to agile whole-body control.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coordinating collision avoidance and balance under high-dimensional, nonlinear humanoid dynamics.
Learns a state-action control barrier function from black-box transitions and failure specifications around a frozen base controller.
Uses risk-guided sampling near the boundary of recoverability and safety feedback to train the task policy.
Demonstrated on a 29-DoF humanoid for dodgeball avoidance and locomotion under low obstacles.
Sampling concentration changes the resulting strategy, including crouching and a novel backward-leaning limbo maneuver; policies transfer to hardware without online filtering.

figures.caption: Figure 2: LIMBO Overview. Stage I : Q-CBF synthesis via black-box transitions using the residual formulation and risk-guided boundary replay. Stage II : learned Q-CBF is a safety teacher, shaping task-policy rewards via constraint violations and corrections. Hardware demonstrations operate without online filtering, relying on the safety behavior internalized during Stage II.

papers.abstract: Automatic dense packing is widely desired in warehouse operations but remains a fundamental challenge in robotic manipulation. Existing work on irregular-object packing largely targets simulation with idealized contact, treating the object as an isolated rigid body. The gripper often enters as a discrete, post-hoc feasibility check, if considered at all, and the perception and contact drift accumulated during execution are not addressed. We present a closed-loop pipeline that integrates perception, gripper-aware placement optimization, and force-guided execution on a real manipulator. The optimizer represents the object together with the gripper as a single composite body of hierarchical sphere trees. It searches over five degrees of freedom on a GPU within a CMA-ES framework, with the vertical coordinate grounded analytically against the current heightmap. During execution, a force-monitored vertical descent stops on first contact. A post-release consolidation push then closes the residual lateral clearance that gripper-aware planning leaves behind. The container is re-perceived between placements so that drift does not accumulate. We validate the system on a Franka Emika Panda robot packing a 3D-printed set of flat, curved, and concave objects, and a YCB object subset. An ablation study isolates the contribution of gripper-aware optimization, the consolidation push, and mesh-derived geometry to end-to-end success, achieved density, and computational cost. We further benchmark against the heightmap-minimization method as a baseline representative of prior irregular-object packing work.
bullets: Addresses the limitations of simulation-focused packing methods that ignore gripper geometry and execution-time perception/contact drift.
Optimizes the object–gripper composite shape using hierarchical sphere trees, GPU-accelerated CMA-ES, and analytical grounding from a heightmap.
Uses force-monitored descent for first-contact placement, followed by a consolidation push to reduce residual lateral gaps.
Re-perceives the container between placements to prevent drift accumulation.
Validated on a Franka Panda with 3D-printed and YCB objects, including ablations and comparison with heightmap minimization.

papers.abstract: Effective exploration in high-dimensional continuous control remains a central challenge in reinforcement learning. Planning-based methods address this by combining online planning with learned policies and value functions, but their components can become misaligned during training: learned sampling policies may diverge from planner behavior, while planning distributions stored in replay become stale as the model and value function evolve. Reanalysis can refresh these targets, but at substantial computational cost. We propose GEM-MPC, an MPPI-based reinforcement learning method that improves the interaction between planning and learning. GEM-MPC uses MPPI to combine a policy trained to clone the planner with a KL-regularized policy that explores around it, providing complementary exploitation and guided exploration within planning. We further introduce Gated Prior Distillation, which selectively learns from stored planning distributions only when they provide a better target than the current prior, reducing the impact of stale planning data without requiring full reanalysis. Across continuous-control benchmarks, GEM-MPC consistently outperforms existing planning-based baselines under lower computational budgets.
bullets: Addresses misalignment between learned policies, planners, and stale planning distributions in replay.
Uses MPPI to combine a planner-cloning policy for exploitation with a KL-regularized policy for guided exploration.
Introduces Gated Prior Distillation, which adopts stored planning targets only when they improve on the current prior.
Outperforms existing planning-based baselines across continuous-control benchmarks under lower computational budgets.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of GEM-MPC. Two independent MPPI instances compute distinct planning distributions, from which the higher-scoring plan is selected according to its estimated return. Both instances share the learned environment model and are biased by the sampling policies πs and πbc together with their corresponding bootstrap action-value functions. The selected planning distribution is then used to update the learned sampling policies. The regularized sampling policy πs is trained with KL-regularized RL, using a regularization policy learned with a support-covering objective over stored planning distributions, while the cloned policy πbc is trained with a mode-seeking behavior-cloning objective that concentrates on highdensity planner behavior.

papers.abstract: Humanoid locomotion over complex terrain requires anticipating footholds that may no longer be visible at touchdown. Limited camera coverage and self-occlusion make it necessary to retrieve relevant terrain information from earlier observations. We present FootQuery, a perceptive locomotion framework that queries depth history using each foot's predicted next touchdown. The policy predicts touchdown locations and uncertainty from proprioception and uses these distributions, together with per-foot features, to query sparsely sampled historical depth frames. During training, realized contacts are projected into historical images to supervise retrieval at the regions where those contacts were visible. The retrieved per-foot features are fused with global visual memory to generate control actions. A progressive force-assistance curriculum supports early exploration, while event-consistent tread-midline shaping encourages coordinated stair contacts. Deployment requires only proprioception and onboard depth images. In simulation, the complete framework outperforms its component ablations on the most challenging tested stairs, gaps, and platforms. Real-world experiments on a Unitree G1 demonstrate continuous traversal with a single policy across outdoor stairs and indoor routes combining stair ascent and descent, platforms, and gaps. These results support organizing visual history around anticipated contacts for perceptive humanoid locomotion.
bullets: Addresses limited camera coverage and self-occlusion that can hide footholds before touchdown.
Predicts per-foot touchdown locations and uncertainty from proprioception, then queries relevant regions in sparsely sampled historical depth frames.
Supervises retrieval using projected realized contacts and fuses retrieved per-foot features with global visual memory for control.
Uses force-assistance curriculum training and tread-midline shaping to support exploration and coordinated stair contacts.
Outperforms component ablations in challenging simulated terrain and enables real-world traversal of stairs, platforms, and gaps with one policy.

papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in policy learning, long-horizon manipulation remains difficult because learned policies must avoid compounding errors while preserving future feasibility. While search-based planning can explicitly reason over such future consequences, it quickly becomes expensive in high-dimensional continuous action spaces. This raises a central question: how can long-horizon reasoning from search be transferred into policies in continuous action spaces? To this end, we propose DISCO: Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions. DISCO uses progressive-widening MCTS in physics simulation to generate long-horizon plans. During search, a learned policy proposes continuous actions, while a learned value function scores actions by their expected progress toward task completion. Using GPU-parallelized simulation, DISCO periodically distills MCTS-generated plans into the policy-value model, improving the action proposals and value estimates used in subsequent searches. Finally, the learned policy-value model can be directly deployed without the need for simulator-based search at test time. Across simulated and real-world rearrangement tasks, DISCO outperforms behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, and search-based baselines.
bullets: Addresses compounding errors and costly search in long-horizon manipulation.
Uses progressive-widening MCTS in physics simulation with learned policy proposals and value estimates.
Distills searched plans into the policy-value model through GPU-parallelized simulation.
The resulting model can act without simulator-based search at test time.
Outperforms behavior cloning, reinforcement learning, and search-based baselines in simulated and real-world tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: DISCO: Distilled Tree Search over Continuous Actions. DISCO addresses long-horizon multiobject rearrangement by using progressive-widening Monte Carlo Tree Search over continuous actions. Using an initial behavior-cloned policy to propose short-horizon actions, DISCO expands search trees in parallel GPU simulation to discover long-horizon plans. The search trees are then distilled into a policy and a value function, enabling direct rollout on held-out tasks, such as real-world shelf packing. MCTS and simulation are used only during training. At test time, the distilled model acts directly from point clouds.

Figure 2: MCTS with DISCO. We embed a policy πθ and a value function Qϕ into the MCTS loop. The policy proposes continuous actions for tree expansion, while the value function guides rollout action selection toward terminal states. Periodically, both models are updated from newly generated search trees, enabling direct policy-value deployment at test time.

Figure 9: Policy and Value Function Architectures. Top: the policy πθ encodes the target-object point cloud with EdgeConv layers and denoises a pose token with a flow-matching transformer to predict a grasp or place pose. Bottom: the value function Qϕ embeds the full-scene point cloud with a per-point MLP, and an action-conditioned query attends to the scene tokens to predict the success probability Qϕ(o,a) ∈ [0, 1].
Figure 5: Constrained Packing Metrics. We rollout DISCO zero-shot against test-time abstraction-based planning methods.

Figure 4: Simulation Results. DISCO improves reward and success with increasing simulation budget on shelf packing and object stacking, and remains more robust as task complexity increases. The simulation budget counts simulator calls made by search during offline training, not at test time.

Figure 6: Real World Rollout of DISCO on the table bussing task. In the point cloud, we see that DISCO’s value function gives high scores for cup placements that leave space for the plates to be placed in the future.

Figure 7: Iterative Distillation. Held-out shelf packing success of the policy Pk after the k-th distillation round, executed alone (solid) or with test-time value guidance from Qk (hatched). Both the policy and the value function improve across rounds.

Figure 8: Long-Horizon Dependency. An object stacking search tree in which only placing the pink mug first leads to success, since it supports the blue object placed later. MCTS assigns this action a higher value (Q = 0.99) than its alternatives (Q = 0.75).

papers.abstract: Reliable obstacle perception is challenging for small autonomous surface vessels (ASVs): reflections and glare confound visible-light cameras, vessel motion shifts the apparent waterline, and darkness removes the dominant sensing modality altogether. Rather than treating multimodal fusion as a static accuracy gain, we propose a context-aware architecture that combines RGB and long-wave infrared (LWIR) imagery, frequency-modulated continuous-wave (FMCW) mmWave radar, and inertial context. A bearing-sector interface provides the navigation controller with calibrated obstacle probabilities, radar ranges, and sensor status. It also distinguishes sensor dropout from a valid observation with no detected obstacle. Using new multimodal lake recordings, we deployed the pipeline in a 24-leg closed-loop pilot under uncontrolled lake conditions (16 day, 4 dusk, and 4 night; 351 m), including night legs in which RGB was unusable and the vessel drove on LWIR and radar evidence alone. On eight held-out low-light recordings, the calibrated fusion model achieved average precision (AP) 0.869 and expected calibration error 0.108, compared with AP 0.673 for rule-based fusion, 0.620 for gated fusion, and 0.903 for RGB alone. Our results expose a central tradeoff: RGB ranks best when usable, whereas fusion preserves a navigation input when RGB fails. This work is a step toward perception that remains usable and degrades predictably across multi-day ASV missions.
bullets: Targets reflections, glare, motion-induced waterline shifts, and darkness that undermine RGB-based obstacle detection.
Fuses RGB, LWIR, FMCW mmWave radar, and inertial context, exposing calibrated bearing-sector obstacle probabilities, radar ranges, and sensor status to navigation.
Distinguishes sensor dropout from valid obstacle-free observations, supporting predictable degradation during multimodal failures.
In eight held-out low-light recordings, calibrated fusion reached AP 0.869 and ECE 0.108; RGB alone had higher AP (0.903) when usable, while fusion preserved sensing when RGB failed.
A 24-leg, 351 m lake pilot included night operation using LWIR and radar without usable RGB; scope is limited to the reported lake recordings and pilot conditions.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown strong generalization in robotic manipulation by leveraging rich representations from pretrained vision-language models. However, their deployment in real-world environments remains limited by recurring unreliable behaviors. In this work, we study state hallucination, a recurring failure pattern in which a VLA continues acting as if an unrealized robot-object state had been achieved. Our analyses find that state hallucination coincides with weakened attention to task-relevant visual regions, and a mechanistic interpretation via sparse autoencoders reveals that hallucination-associated sparse features are activated when these failures occur. Based on this analysis, we propose SOUL (Sparse feature pOlicy UnLearning), which selectively unlearns policy knowledge associated with state hallucination behaviors, where sparse features identified from hallucination failures and successful behaviors serve as explicit forgetting and retention targets, respectively. Experiments across VLA architectures in simulated and real-world environments show that our method substantially reduces hallucinated failures and improves task success without substantially compromising the existing manipulation capabilities. These results suggest that interpretable feature analysis provides a practical basis for selectively modifying undesirable knowledge in robot policies.
bullets: State hallucination occurs when a VLA acts as though an unrealized robot-object state has been achieved.
The failure is associated with reduced attention to task-relevant visual regions and activation of specific sparse autoencoder features.
SOUL unlearns hallucination-related policy knowledge while retaining features associated with successful behaviors.
Experiments across simulated and real-world settings and multiple VLA architectures reduce hallucinated failures and improve task success.
The approach is evaluated specifically for state hallucination and aims to preserve existing manipulation capabilities.

figures.caption: Fig. 4: Overall framework. The proposed method provides a framework for improving robot policies by identifying and selectively modifying internal representations associated with undesirable behaviors. It first extracts visual-region-specific sparse features from policy activations and analyzes their activation patterns across execution outcomes, including clean success (CS), hallucination failure (HF), and non-hallucination failure (NF), characterized by task performance and hallucination occurrence. Based on these associations, region-feature pairs are selected as forget or retain targets. The policy is then updated to suppress hallucination-associated features while preserving reliable behavior. In this way, the policy is improved.

papers.abstract: Physical control tasks in the natural world, such as driving or object manipulation, frequently exhibit dramatic variations in sensory and compute complexity over time. Correspondingly, a natural resource-efficient choice for robot control is to dynamically switch between control modes with varying resource allocations. However, such "mode-switching controllers" (MSCs) have historically required laborious, expert-driven design and synthesis for each new task. Driven by these design difficulties, modern robotic control architectures often fall back to a wasteful "monolithic" one-size-fits-all structure, where resource allocation is permanently anchored to the hardest, most resource-intensive task phases. To facilitate the design of performant yet efficient MSCs, we propose LLM-Guided synthesis of Efficient Mode-Switching Control Architectures (LEMCA). LEMCA represents MSC designs as interpretable programs to be iteratively refined in an evolutionary loop. To evaluate design fitness, we propose MSC-compatible extensions of automated controller synthesis approaches, such as reinforcement learning in simulation. LEMCA then leverages the semantic priors, reasoning, and coding capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) to iteratively edit controller modes, their corresponding sensory-compute resource allocations, and mode transitions. Our experiments across diverse control benchmarks show that LEMCA consistently discovers strategies that surpass the Pareto frontier of monolithic designs by reclaiming wasted resources during "easy" task phases. LEMCA thus presents an automated, low-effort path to synthesize resource-efficient MSC designs.
bullets: Addresses the expert effort required to design mode-switching controllers (MSCs) for tasks with varying sensory and compute demands.
Represents MSCs as interpretable programs and iteratively refines their modes, resource allocations, and transitions.
Evaluates candidate designs with MSC-compatible controller synthesis, including reinforcement learning in simulation.
Experiments across diverse control benchmarks show LEMCA surpasses monolithic designs’ Pareto frontier by reclaiming resources during easier phases.
Provides an automated, low-effort approach for synthesizing efficient MSC architectures.

papers.abstract: Human-readable maps provide an intuitive interface for specifying robot destinations, but connecting their schematic geometry to egocentric observations remains challenging. We present NaViRRator, a framework that translates user-specified start and goal locations on such maps into navigation instructions for a pretrained vision-and-language navigation (VLN) policy. Its core method, RouteScribe, separates route inference from verbalization by first generating an explicit route scaffold in map-image coordinates, which a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) converts into a navigation instruction. We construct the scaffold with start--goal line conditional flow matching (SGL-CFM), which deforms a straight start--goal waypoint sequence into a map-conditioned route. During execution, the VLN policy receives only the instruction and egocentric observations, while the map and scaffold remain upstream, allowing executor replacement without retraining the map-to-language modules. Real-world experiments show higher success rates and success weighted by path length (SPL) than direct map-to-instruction generation, A*-based scaffolding, and Gaussian-source conditional flow matching. Qualitative results further show clearer salient turns and better preservation of the intended maneuver sequence, supporting route-grounded language as a modular interface between human-readable maps and pretrained navigation policies.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of connecting schematic map geometry with a robot’s first-person visual navigation.
RouteScribe separates route inference from verbalization by generating an explicit map-coordinate route scaffold before producing instructions.
Uses start–goal line conditional flow matching to deform a straight waypoint sequence into a map-conditioned route.
Real-world experiments report higher success rate and SPL than direct generation, A*-based scaffolding, and Gaussian-source flow matching.
The modular design keeps maps and scaffolds upstream, enabling executor replacement without retraining map-to-language modules.

papers.abstract: Although conventional controllers and disturbance observers (DOBs) are the standard for precision tracking in manipulators, they suffer from parameter uncertainty, nonlinear friction, and compound disturbances. This study proposes a residual reinforcement learning DOB framework that pairs an analytical observer with an RL policy. The deterministic baseline operates within a reliable region, whereas the RL policy explicitly targets the residuals that the model cannot capture. To make this compensation disturbance-aware, an estimator network aligns the observation history with a privileged disturbance context, organizing the latent space by disturbance regime and enabling rapid adaptation across disturbance transitions. To guarantee stability, we derived and enforced a state-dependent action bound on the RL policy from an input-to-state stability (ISS) analysis such that the closed loop provably confines the tracking error to a certified envelope for arbitrary policy outputs. Experiments on a 6-DOF manipulator demonstrated consistent improvements in disturbance estimation and tracking, including a 27.8% tracking-error reduction on real hardware under zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and a 38.0% reduction under a base-vibration disturbance that was not observed during training.
bullets: Combines an analytical disturbance observer with RL that learns only unmodeled residual dynamics.
Uses a disturbance-aware estimator to organize latent representations by disturbance regime and adapt across transitions.
Derives an ISS-based, state-dependent action bound that guarantees the closed-loop tracking error remains within a certified envelope.
On a 6-DOF manipulator, reduced tracking error by 27.8% in zero-shot sim-to-real transfer and 38.0% under unseen base vibration.

papers.abstract: Quadrotors are increasingly deployed in applications such as agriculture, infrastructure inspection, and maintenance. In each of these applications, the robot must navigate complex scene geometry while remaining strictly collision-free. Unlike in ground domains, even minor collisions for aerial vehicles can result in the loss of the robot. This safety requirement induces a pair of technical challenges. First, the environment must be represented with sufficient fidelity to encode complex structure, even when no ground-truth obstacle data is available. Second, a motion planner must leverage this representation to determine a collision-free path to the goal. This paper proposes a system that addresses these complementary challenges. The proposed method, AirSplan, adopts a normalized variant of 3D Gaussian Splatting that encodes high-fidelity scene geometry. It then applies a novel reachability-based motion planner that leverages the differential flatness of quadrotors to compute continuous-time collision constraints that tightly overapproximate the robot's occupancy. Experiments demonstrate that AirSplan successfully finds a path in 81.2% of challenging test cases, a significant improvement over the nearest baseline method's 51.2%.
bullets: Addresses safe aerial navigation when accurate ground-truth obstacle data is unavailable.
Uses a normalized 3D Gaussian Splatting representation to encode detailed scene geometry.
Introduces a reachability-based planner exploiting quadrotor differential flatness.
Computes continuous-time collision constraints that tightly overapproximate vehicle occupancy.
Finds paths in 81.2% of challenging test cases, compared with 51.2% for the nearest baseline.

papers.abstract: Generative robot policies can represent diverse, multimodal behaviors, but adapting pretrained policies to deployment-time constraints such as collision avoidance and orientation maintenance remains challenging. Existing inference-time steering methods typically apply gradient guidance through iterative diffusion or flow processes, which can be computationally expensive for real-time control. We propose INSPO, which formulates inference-time steering of one-step generative policies as trajectory optimization in the policy's input noise space. By optimizing the input noise while evaluating constraints on the induced state trajectory, INSPO searches the policy-induced behavior space without directly modifying generated actions. The optimization includes a regularization term that encourages solutions to remain consistent with the policy's input distribution and is solved online using population-based particle optimization. We evaluate INSPO on state- and image-based task-specific policies and generalist vision-language-action policies across Push-T, Can pick-and-place, and LIBERO-Spatial. INSPO improves task success and constraint satisfaction over best-of-N sampling and action projection, while comparing favorably with gradient-guided generation at lower runtime.
bullets: Addresses deployment-time constraints such as collision avoidance and orientation maintenance in diverse generative robot policies.
Optimizes policy input noise while evaluating constraints on the resulting state trajectory, preserving the policy’s behavior space.
Uses distribution-consistency regularization and online population-based particle optimization.
Evaluated on state-, image-, and vision-language-action policies across Push-T, Can pick-and-place, and LIBERO-Spatial.
Improves task success and constraint satisfaction over best-of-N sampling and action projection, while achieving lower runtime than gradient-guided generation.

papers.abstract: Collision-free motion planning requires reliable collision models from sensed environments and validation of states along a continuous trajectory. To make this tractable, most planners check for collision at discrete states along continuous trajectories against a single determinized model of the environment, introducing a trade-off between safety and computational efficiency. While continuous collision checking approaches that approximate the swept volume of the robot exist, they are computationally expensive or overly conservative. Data-driven approaches can learn the swept volume; however, these neural models are susceptible to approximation errors and are therefore often limited to serving as coarse filters for downstream collision checkers. In this work, we propose to learn a signed distance function of the swept volume as a probabilistic field, enabling quantification of epistemic uncertainty, incorporation of perception noise, and eventual integration into a chance-constrained trajectory optimization framework. We demonstrate our approach on challenging high-dimensional manipulation problems with significant sensor noise, both in simulation and on real hardware.
bullets: Addresses the safety–efficiency trade-off of discrete collision checks and costly or conservative continuous swept-volume approximations.
Learns the swept volume as a probabilistic signed distance field rather than a deterministic neural approximation.
Models epistemic uncertainty and incorporates perception noise for more reliable collision reasoning.
Targets integration with chance-constrained trajectory optimization.
Demonstrated on high-dimensional manipulation tasks in simulation and on real hardware with significant sensor noise.

papers.abstract: Multi-party human-robot collaboration poses a dual challenge: robot decisions should remain interpretable and auditable, while executed actions must satisfy safety constraints during physical interaction. Combining explainable decision-tree policies with control-barrier-function (CBF) filtering provides a promising architecture but creates two learning mismatches in multi-agent reinforcement learning. Safety projection changes the action applied to the environment, while the coupled proposal graph can misalign independently optimized actor updates with a team-level update. We present safety-aligned gradient enforcement (SAGE) to address both mismatches. Its shield-annealed internalization layer (SAIL) uses a differentiable finite-penalty proposal map while retaining the exact CBF quadratic program for execution, preserving constraint-normal sensitivity to internalize repeatedly active safety constraints. Team-averaged Lyapunov policy optimization (TALO) constructs a team-aware update reference and applies a Lyapunov half-space correction to regulate independent actor updates. Physical experiments with two humanoid robots and a human partner demonstrate deployment feasibility. Across nine simulation scenarios, SAGE achieves a 71.0% success rate with 0.5 collision steps per thousand environment steps. Ablations show that direct CBF filtering reduces collision frequency by 98.5% but decreases success from 67.3% to 59.3%. SAIL reduces proposal violation by 48.8% and proposal-execution correction by 85.2%, while TALO reduces the update-consistency gap by 50.8%.
bullets: Addresses two mismatches: CBF safety projection changes executed actions, and independently learned actors can diverge from team-level updates.
SAIL uses a differentiable finite-penalty proposal map for learning while retaining the exact CBF quadratic program during execution.
TALO provides a team-aware reference and Lyapunov correction to regulate independent actor updates.
In nine simulation scenarios, SAGE achieved 71.0% success with 0.5 collision steps per thousand environment steps.
Physical experiments with two humanoid robots and a human partner demonstrated deployment feasibility; ablations reduced proposal violations and update inconsistency.

papers.abstract: Referring scene understanding for embodied robots requires grounding object- and relation-centric language queries from a designated viewpoint. While a local semantic Gaussian map can support such grounding within one agent's observations, cooperative settings require this ability to remain effective after independently reconstructed maps are aligned and fused. In this setting, the referred target or its contextual landmark may come from another agent's observations, while spatial relations must still be interpreted from the querying robot's viewpoint. We formulate this problem as cooperative referring Gaussian grounding over fused maps, which requires geometric alignability, instance-level semantic comparability, and view-conditioned relation reasoning. Existing language-aware Gaussian methods mainly focus on single-map querying, whereas Gaussian registration methods optimize geometric or photometric alignment without preserving language-grounding-oriented semantic compatibility. We propose CoRef-GS, a cooperative referring Gaussian splatting framework. CoRef-GS constructs local open-vocabulary instance-aware Gaussian maps, then aligns partially overlapping maps with a cross-agent alignment module by geometric and semantic consistency, and grounds queries using a view-conditioned mask relation graph. We further introduce CoQuad-Ref, a dual-quadruped benchmark spanning both real-world and simulated indoor scenes. Experiments show that, on simulated scenes, CoRef-GS reduces the rotation error from 2.58° after coarse initialization to 0.15° after refinement, and improves real-world referring mIoU over ReferSplat from 52.6% to 68.8%. The established benchmark and source code will be publicly released at https://github.com/ruojiruoli17/CoRef-GS.git.
bullets: Addresses cooperative referring scene understanding when targets or landmarks originate from another agent’s observations.
Builds local open-vocabulary, instance-aware Gaussian maps and aligns them using geometric and semantic consistency.
Uses a view-conditioned mask relation graph to reason about spatial relationships from the querying robot’s viewpoint.
Introduces CoQuad-Ref, a real-world and simulated indoor benchmark.
Refinement reduces simulated rotation error from 2.58° to 0.15°, while real-world referring mIoU improves from 52.6% to 68.8% over ReferSplat.

papers.abstract: Tactile signals provide direct contact and force measurements that are essential for understanding physical interactions and enabling dexterous robotic manipulation. However, tactile sensing requires direct measurement at contact interfaces, making large-scale data collection reliant on intrusive, costly, and restrictive instrumentation. We present TouchSight, a monocular egocentric vision framework for dense full-hand contact force prediction that leverages 500 hours of pressure-glove recordings and extensive hand-object interaction (HOI) data. To address the appearance gap between gloved training data and bare-hand real-world scenarios, we construct TwinTouch-20H: 20 hours of paired visual data in which generative video models re-render gloved recordings as bare-hand observations against new backgrounds while preserving the original measured tactile labels. TouchSight predicts dense force from both gloved and generated bare-hand videos, outperforms prior contact prediction methods on OakInk2, qualitatively generalizes to natural bare-hand egocentric videos from unseen datasets, and improves consistently as glove supervision scales. These results demonstrate that dense tactile signals can be recovered from egocentric vision alone, without tactile instrumentation at capture time.
bullets: Uses 500 hours of pressure-glove recordings and hand-object interaction data for supervision.
Introduces TwinTouch-20H, 20 hours of generated paired data that converts gloved views into bare-hand appearances while preserving tactile labels.
Predicts dense force from both gloved and generated bare-hand videos.
Outperforms prior contact-prediction methods on OakInk2 and qualitatively generalizes to unseen natural bare-hand videos.
Performance improves with more glove supervision, eliminating the need for tactile instrumentation during video capture.

papers.abstract: When does experience memory help a closed-loop LLM driving agent? Published gains cannot say, because the two factors we find to matter most, which warmup experiences the pool contains and what any injected tokens do to the prompt, are controlled in none of them. We answer with a controlled evaluation on one audited HighwayEnv testbed (1Hz, gpt-4o-mini for the decisive contrasts). We treat the warmup pool as a resampled random factor (ten disjoint pools) and add token-matched irrelevant-filler controls, oracle-certified diagnostics, caution-pricing metrics, and quantified audits of the baseline ports. The probe suite spans flat-text retrieval (a DiLu port), a single-frame grid port (RESPOND-inspired), our episodic temporal-graph memory, a retrieval-free consolidated rulebook, and a flat K-step observation-history baseline. Four findings follow, each a property of this testbed. (1) Headline memory gains belong to the warmup draw. The reported pool is the best of ten for both retrieval memories, which beat No-Memory in only one pool of ten (sign test p=0.011), and even the rulebook's apparent pool-immunity collapsed on five fresh draws. (2) No retrieval design tested exceeds token-matched filler. The collision-only merge ceiling is reached by a single 15-token caution instruction, and metrics that price caution erase the rulebook's lead. (3) Representational sophistication is nowhere robustly operative. (4) Baseline port quality silently inverts conclusions. On this testbed, a single-pool comparison without filler controls would have reported memory gains that these controls reverse. We release the testbed, audited ports, seeds, and caches.
bullets: Memory gains were highly sensitive to which warmup experiences were sampled: retrieval systems beat No-Memory in only 1 of 10 pools.
A single 15-token caution instruction matched the collision-only benefit of retrieval, and caution-aware metrics removed the rulebook’s apparent lead.
More sophisticated memory representations showed no robust advantage in this evaluation.
Baseline implementation quality and uncontrolled prompts could reverse the reported conclusion about whether memory helps.
The study releases the testbed, audited ports, random seeds, and caches; findings are scoped to this testbed and decisive model setting.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon embodied agents must maintain task-relevant information, coordinate heterogeneous robots, and adapt their decisions as execution unfolds. Existing benchmarks investigate dynamic task execution and embodied multi-agent coordination, but provide limited evaluation of their intersection. We introduce MAGMA-Bench, an architecture-agnostic benchmark for persistent task reasoning in dynamic multi-robot environments. MAGMA-Bench evaluates agents across increasing task horizons and controlled online perturbations, including execution failures, task interruptions, and mission updates, with scenarios requiring coordination across robots with heterogeneous capabilities. It uses a structured skill-level interface to separate task-level reasoning from perception and low-level control. We evaluate locally deployable open-weight planners, multi-agent state-tracking strategies, and frontier models. Even the strongest evaluated models fail on a substantial fraction of clean episodes, and their success rates decrease further under online perturbations. Supervised adaptation greatly improves a small model, but performance remains substantially lower on longer and multi-robot missions. We release the benchmark, 261,646 task-level training examples, and an architecture-agnostic expert-trace generation pipeline.
bullets: Tests increasing task horizons with execution failures, interruptions, and mission updates.
Uses a structured skill-level interface to isolate task reasoning from perception and low-level control.
Evaluates open-weight planners, state-tracking strategies, and frontier models across multi-robot scenarios.
Even strong models fail often on clean tasks, with performance declining further under perturbations and longer missions.
Releases the benchmark, 261,646 task-level training examples, and an expert-trace generation pipeline.

papers.abstract: Training a visuomotor policy calls for abundant demonstrations that closely match the target environment, yet collecting them anew remains expensive. Existing demonstration synthesis methods reduce this cost but remain constrained by high manual effort, limited visual fidelity, or heavy reliance on physics simulators. This paper introduces GaussianFactory, a high-fidelity data engine that mass-produces demonstrations with a single video scan as its only human input and no physics engine in the generation loop. Specifically, GaussianFactory reconstructs the scene as an editable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) replica and samples from the object-combination tasks the scene affords. For each task, it plans grasps and trajectories purely kinematically on the geometric reconstruction, rendering photorealistic demonstrations that visually match the target environment. Physical dynamics enter the pipeline only where contact force interactions dictate the outcome---during grasp formation, via a learned contact model pretrained once on an interaction dataset. To evaluate the downstream utility of the synthesized demonstrations, we implement an end-to-end scan-to-deployment workflow in two setups: a simulated scene that stands in for the real world to enable reproducibility, and a real-world workspace with a physical UR10e robot. In each setup, a standard diffusion policy trained solely on the synthesized demonstrations achieves 95.1% and 84.2% success rates, respectively.
bullets: Addresses the cost and effort of collecting environment-specific robot demonstrations.
Reconstructs the scene as an editable 3D Gaussian Splatting replica and samples feasible object-combination tasks.
Plans grasps and trajectories kinematically, using a learned contact model only for grasp formation where contact forces matter.
Demonstrations train a standard diffusion policy in an end-to-end scan-to-deployment workflow.
The policy reaches 95.1% success in simulation and 84.2% in a real UR10e workspace.

papers.abstract: Learning in robotic games is constrained not only by strategic information but also by what the body can still execute. We study this coupling in a hierarchical humanoid-quadruped penalty system in which game-level self-play policies command fixed soccer whole-body controllers (S-WBCs). The humanoid shooting skill is initialized from self-collected motion-capture data, whereas the quadruped saving skill is learned by reinforcement learning. We introduce dynamics-induced commitment mapping (DIC-Map), a body-grounded analysis that estimates continuation capability, identifies the first persistent loss of a terminal alternative, and tests whether the remaining interaction admits a reduced zero-sum game. For symmetric terminal alternatives, the reduced game yields a closed-form bound on optimal strategy concentration determined by the responder's value of deferring. We further show that, when the responder acts through an estimator, equal response values eliminate the direct terminal-allocation gradient and leave an estimator-mediated first-order learning channel. Experiments locate commitment about 0.29 s before contact, and changing only ball speed shifts deferral coverage. Across four responder policies, replacing the estimator raises save rate from 0.240 to 0.472, whereas a comparable gain in read accuracy obtained by waiting raises it only to 0.246. Posterior analysis is used for the equilibrium comparison because the available coverage terms are observational proxies. Project website: https://chris-ruizegeng.github.io/penaltykick/
bullets: Studies hierarchical humanoid–quadruped penalty kicks with fixed whole-body controllers and learned game-level policies.
Introduces DIC-Map to identify when a robot loses the persistent ability to execute alternative terminal actions and to analyze the resulting reduced game.
Derives a strategy-concentration bound based on the responder’s value of deferring, and characterizes an estimator-mediated learning signal when direct terminal-allocation gradients vanish.
Locates commitment roughly 0.29 s before contact; changing ball speed shifts the coverage available through deferral.
Replacing the estimator increases save rate from 0.240 to 0.472, while waiting for similarly improved read accuracy increases it only to 0.246; coverage is treated as an observational proxy.

papers.title: Dynamics-Induced Commitment in Learning-Based Robotic Penalty Kicks
papers.tldr: The paper shows that robotic penalty-kick strategies become committed by body dynamics before contact, and that responder-side estimation—not merely perceptual accuracy—strongly shapes learning and defensive success.

papers.abstract: Temporary obstacles that may block a robot's planned route create a sequential navigation problem: a robot must decide whether to wait for a blockage to clear, reroute, or acquire more information about the obstacle before acting. We formulate graph navigation among temporary obstacles as a partially observable semi-Markov decision process and introduce SPARROW, a belief-space planner built on Partially Observable Monte Carlo Planning (POMCP). SPARROW searches over traversal, observation, and finite-duration waiting actions while maintaining a particle belief over latent obstacle classes and clearance times. Class-conditioned survival models are learned online from both clearance observations and right-censored encounters where the robot reroutes before clearance is observed. A generative model simulates obstacle arrivals and clearances as each action unfolds, so the planner can account for blockages that may occur along alternative routes. We further introduce a value-of-learning criterion that trades the immediate cost of collecting labelled survival data against its expected reduction in future navigation regret. Across two simulation graphs and multiple obstacle-class settings, SPARROW reduces mean time-to-goal by 12-26% relative to OSCAR, a recent survival-based method for the same problem. On a physical mobile robot, SPARROW reduces mean time-to-goal by 20.5% relative to OSCAR while selectively observing, waiting, and rerouting as environment conditions change.
bullets: Models navigation with temporary obstacles as a partially observable semi-Markov decision process.
Uses POMCP to search over traversal, observation, and finite-duration waiting actions.
Learns obstacle survival and clearance behavior online, including from right-censored rerouting encounters.
Selects information-gathering actions using a value-of-learning criterion.
Reduces mean time-to-goal by 12–26% in simulation and 20.5% on a physical robot versus OSCAR.
