papers.abstract: World models are increasingly used to reduce environment interaction when post-training vision-language-action (VLA) policies with reinforcement learning. Yet they are typically trained to predict pixels one step ahead, even though their role here is not merely to render visually faithful videos but to produce learning signals from imagined rollouts that improve the policy. We show that this mismatch is substantial: lower pixel MSE can produce worse policy gradients, and a world model trained for policy utility can yield better downstream policies despite 17% higher pixel MSE on the next frame. We propose the Downstream-Return Imagination Learning Loop (DRILL), a bilevel framework that updates the world model to maximize the policy's return after an inner GRPO update on imagined rollouts. DRILL has two instantiations. DRILL-VWI is a closed-form surrogate, requiring no additional simulator rollouts, that reweights prediction errors by policy visitation, the group-relative GRPO advantage, and model confidence. DRILL-IMG is a full meta-gradient method that differentiates through the inner update using truncated Hessian-vector products. We show that DRILL-VWI recovers the local one-step component of the DRILL-IMG meta-gradient under score-compatibility and small-residual assumptions. Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG raises mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World, and complements RLVR pretraining rather than competing with it. More broadly, we believe video world models for VLA reinforcement learning can be productively trained by the policy gradients they produce, not only by pixel-level prediction.
authors: Zhaolu Kang, Tailong Luo, Lei Wei, Guangyuan Dong, Sihan Liu, Yingjie He, Siheng Wang, Shuaibo Li, Rongchao Zhang, Zhen Tian, Richeng Xuan, Zhichao Hu

DRILL-IMG differentiates through the inner update with truncated Hessian-vector products; DRILL-VWI approximates its local one-step gradient under stated assumptions.
Across five manipulation simulators and two VLA backbones, DRILL-IMG improves mean success rate by 13.1 points over WMPO and 7.9 points over RLVR-World.

papers.abstract: Loco-manipulation extends the workspace of conventional manipulation by combining mobility with physical interaction, while aerial loco-manipulation further expands this capability into three-dimensional space, enabling robots to reach environments inaccessible to ground-based systems. Moving to an aerial platform, however, gives rise to a demanding control problem, since the vehicle must track trajectories accurately in three dimensions while the motion of the arm and its interaction with the environment continuously shift the center of mass, alter the inertia, and impose force and moment disturbances on the body. Conventional controllers address these effects through explicit models and estimation, whereas learning-based controllers infer dynamics from experience, yet control rewards provide no direct target for the response information retained from history, and fixed task sampling can leave persistent tracking difficulties insufficiently explored. We present ALMA, an aerial loco-manipulation framework for adaptive flight control under external arm commands. ALMA employs a contextual flight policy that adapts from recent measurements and actions, using action-conditioned prediction of future measurement representations to train its context to retain response information relevant to flight control. To expand the experience available for this adaptation, an evolutionary process uses a large language model (LLM) to analyze observed control difficulties and propose new structures of arm motion for subsequent training. In simulation, ALMA reduces position root-mean-square error (RMSE) by up to 24.7% relative to the strongest baseline, while the same policy transfers zero-shot to the aerial manipulator and reduces hover position RMSE by 79.6% during periodic arm motion relative to the real-world baseline.

papers.abstract: Flexible endoscopes exploit structural compliance to traverse narrow lumens, pipes, and cavities, where navigation involves distributed environmental contact. This compliance makes tip motion depend on the evolving support configuration. We present external bird's-eye-view contact-aided navigation (EBV-CAN), a vision-language policy that combines one initial global static bird's-eye image with evolving endoscopic observations and motor state. Three supervised semantic queries locate the tip, next waypoint, and instructed target on the cached global image; their residual representations predict bending and insertion commands. We introduce the Vision-Language Contact-Aided (VLCA) dataset, linking 517 demonstrations and 75k action samples to 958k spatial entries and 93k remaining-route records. On 50 held-out episodes, tip-coordinate and waypoint localization reach 97.5% and 94.8%. Swapping the target instruction under identical observations changes target attention and motor output across 17 dual-target episodes. Across 1,920 physical trials of eight policies trained under a shared protocol, EBV-CAN achieves 183/240 successes (76.25%) under automatic blue-area scoring. Gated recurrent unit behavior cloning (GRU-BC) achieves the lowest matched-task offline mean absolute error (MAE), 0.056, and 1/240 physical successes, establishing distinct rankings for action imitation and task completion. Successful multi-guide executions and representative failures connect spatial progress, steering transitions, and visibility to physical navigation.

Offline action imitation and physical task completion produce different rankings: GRU-BC has lower MAE but only 1/240 physical successes.

papers.abstract: Before acting on an object, a robot needs to anticipate how its hand motion will change the physical world and what the resulting scene will look like. Existing approaches typically entangle action-conditioned dynamics, camera motion, and visual synthesis within a video generation model, or represent dynamics as point trajectories without explicit object structure. We introduce DeXplicit, a dexterous manipulation world model that instead predicts how the world evolves explicitly in metric 3D before rendering its visual consequences. Given an initial scene and a future hand trajectory, a lightweight 3D dynamics network predicts object-centric motion and deformation, providing structured and geometrically grounded future world states. These predictions then serve as a strong scaffold for video generation: appearance is transported through the predicted 3D motion and projected into future views, allowing the renderer to focus on completing uncertain and newly visible content rather than implicitly learning world dynamics from pixels. This explicit-3D-first decomposition also enables efficient causal generation, requiring only two denoising steps per block while conditioning on generated history. Across HOT3D, OakInk2, and PhysTwin, DeXplicit reduces moved-point error by 27-40% relative to PointWorld and improves object fidelity IoU+ by 47% on HOT3D under a shared renderer. Our design with two-step causal generation achieves a 57x speedup from our 14B bi-directional configuration in video synthesis.
authors: Adam Lee, Mutian Xu, Yukang Cao, Shulin Tian, Ziwei Liu

papers.abstract: Lunar rovers will primarily rely on cameras for localization until navigation satellite services are deployed, and will continue to need them afterwards for relative navigation, hazard detection, and surface operations. Visual odometry (VO) and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) mostly estimate motion by matching features between frames. However, feature matchers are developed on urban, indoor and driving scenes, planetary studies compare them on orbital registration or within complete SLAM systems, and real lunar imagery with reference poses is scarce, so matching between rover frames on low-texture, harshly lit terrain, and its effect on VO, has not been compared. We benchmark eleven classical and learned detector-matcher combinations on nine synthetic, lunar-testbed, and terrestrial-analogue datasets, and a feature tracker, scoring pairwise pose accuracy against baseline and the trajectory error of the resulting VO. Under a common rotation-only metric, the SuperPoint pairings outperform SIFT with ratio-tested FLANN matching on both lunar testbeds and one analogue site, with smaller or unresolved differences on synthetic data. When rotation and translation direction are scored jointly, this SIFT pairing exceeds both SuperPoint pairings on four synthetic datasets, so synthetic results alone do not establish relative performance on real rover imagery. In stereo VO, the SuperPoint pairings are not consistently more accurate than SIFT, but only they keep tracking on all eight sequential datasets. Pairings with classical detectors depend on lighting while SuperPoint changes little: a low spotlight makes them more accurate than diffuse light on the same testbed views, consistent with more contrast and detected keypoints. SuperPoint with LightGlue is the fastest learned combination (16 ms per frame), and DINOv2 retrieval proposals still need geometric verification.

papers.abstract: Flow matching is now the dominant approach for vision-language action (VLA) robot policies, thanks to its expressiveness and simple training objective. However, inference for standard flow matching requires iteratively solving an ODE, limiting the control frequency at deployment. While several works have proposed novel methods to allow for single-shot action generation, we ask whether such additional objectives are actually necessary. We find that across six flow matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale: multi-step integration confers little to no consistent advantage at inference. We empirically find that this holds as long as models are sufficiently trained and have enough capacity. Practically, the implication is that for large VLAs, the single-step policy comes essentially for free from the multi-step model, enabling low-latency deployment without retraining, distillation, or auxiliary objectives.
authors: Shivakanth Sujit, Luca Nunziante, Rousslan Fernand Julien Dossa, Kai Arulkumaran
bullets: Flow-matching VLA policies typically require iterative ODE integration, which limits deployment control frequency.
Across six flow-matching VLAs, one-step action generation largely matches multi-step sampling at scale.
Multi-step integration provides little or no consistent inference advantage in the studied setting.
The finding depends on models having sufficient training and capacity.
Large VLAs can use single-step inference directly, without distillation, retraining, or auxiliary objectives.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have shown promising results in multi-task robotic manipulation by leveraging visual and language understanding for action generation. However, existing lightweight VLA models employ a single dense action expert to handle all tasks, which limits their multi-task capability under constrained computational budgets. To address this issue, we propose SmolVLA-MoE, a novel framework that introduces sparse Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) into the FFN layers of the action expert in VLA models. SmolVLA-MoE replaces dense FFN layers with multiple parallel expert FFNs and a token-level router, enabling each token to adaptively select the most suitable expert for action generation. We further introduce a shared expert with a tunable weight parameter to balance the inheritance of pre-trained capabilities and task-specific expert specialization. Through sparse activation, SmolVLA-MoE activates only a single expert FFN during inference, with a total activated parameter count of approximately 500M including the frozen VLM backbone, while benefiting from approximately 800M total stored parameters. We evaluate our method on four task suites of the LIBERO benchmark. SmolVLA-MoE achieves an average success rate of 84.25%, outperforming SmolVLA (82.75%) and OpenVLA-7B (76.5%), while maintaining comparable inference efficiency. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/dudu435/smolvla-moe.
authors: Shiyang Zhang, Miao Yang, Zhengda Li, Yang Shao, Ruifang Zhai, Hui Peng, Peng Song
bullets: Addresses the limited multi-task capacity of lightweight VLAs that rely on one dense action expert.
Replaces action-expert FFNs with parallel experts and a token-level router, activating only one expert per token at inference.
Adds a tunable shared expert to balance pretrained capability retention with task-specific specialization.
On four LIBERO task suites, achieves an 84.25% average success rate versus 82.75% for SmolVLA and 76.5% for OpenVLA-7B.
Maintains comparable inference efficiency with approximately 500M activated parameters and 800M stored parameters.

papers.abstract: Agents tasked with intercepting a moving target must learn how to reach it, ideally as efficiently as possible. As observers of animal pursuit behavior have noticed, different strategies are possible: on one extreme, the agent reactively moves toward the target's current location; on the other, the agent predicts the target's future location and moves directly there. Motivated by the desire to understand how such strategies might be learned, we introduce a continuous-time linear-quadratic model of open-loop target pursuit whose optimal control strategies interpolate between these possibilities. Usefully, a small number of interpretable parameters control which type of strategy is optimal, and it is possible to derive closed-form solutions for optimal strategies, policy learning dynamics, and value learning dynamics. Exploiting our model's linear structure, we find that the time scales of learning precisely correspond to the eigenvalues of certain matrices, and that relevant eigenvalue spectra generically have a gap. We show that this gap indicates that agents tend to learn how to reach their target before optimizing their movement. Our results provide a detailed mathematical characterization of pursuit behavior and its learning dynamics, which can both serve as a benchmark for empirical work, and as a foundation for more elaborate theoretical treatments of pursuit.
bullets: Models continuous-time, open-loop pursuit with interpretable parameters controlling reactive versus predictive behavior.
Derives closed-form optimal strategies, policy-learning dynamics, and value-learning dynamics.
Shows learning time scales are determined by matrix eigenvalues, whose generic spectral gap separates learning stages.
Finds agents tend to first learn how to reach the target, then optimize how efficiently they move.
Provides a mathematical benchmark for empirical pursuit studies and a foundation for more complex theories.

papers.abstract: Autonomous robotic surgery has drawn increased attention in recent years due to its potential to relieve surgeons of time-consuming, mentally straining, and tedious tasks, particularly during prolonged operations. One suitable task for automation is suturing, which involves tracking the thread as it deforms during needle retrieval, de-tangling, knot tightening, and other tasks. Unlike rigid-object manipulation, deformable thread manipulation has no fixed pose to track and effectively infinite degrees of freedom, making its configuration difficult to predict and requiring the thread's state to be re-estimated rather than assumed. At the same time, thread manipulations involve sequential motions that depend on past and current thread contact points, which must be accurately and continuously tracked. This paper presents an image-to-manipulation pipeline that concurrently generates live thread reconstruction while conducting safe and optimized sequential manipulations to achieve long-horizon tasks.
authors: Emma Huang, Omar Hernandez, Zih-Yun Chiu, Michael Yip
bullets: Targets autonomous suturing tasks such as needle retrieval, de-tangling, and knot tightening.
Addresses the thread’s deformability, infinite degrees of freedom, and changing configuration.
Continuously tracks current and past thread contact points during sequential manipulation.
Combines live visual thread reconstruction with safe, optimized manipulation planning.
The abstract does not report specific experimental results or limitations.

papers.abstract: Visual Language Action (VLA) models are designed to be generalist robot models that can be implemented across embodiments, tasks and environments. However, their ability to collaborate with other robots and humans remains underexplored. In this work, we propose a framework to automate the generation of multi-robot collaborative data for decentralized VLA training without requiring human teleoperation. Our framework first utilizes a decentralized collaborative planning approach to generate multi-robot collaborative robot plans in the form of an executable function. We then utilize the collaborative plan to produce collaborative demonstration data to finetune VLA models in a decentralized manner. We show that our approach produces demonstration data that when used to finetune VLA models on decentralized collaboration tasks matches the task performance of VLA models finetuned on human-teleoperated collaborative data.
authors: Yi Loo, Siddhant Shrivastava, Minh Long Pham, Malika Meghjani
bullets: Addresses the limited study of VLA-based collaboration among robots and humans.
Uses decentralized collaborative planning to generate executable multi-robot task plans.
Converts these plans into collaborative demonstrations for decentralized VLA fine-tuning.
The resulting models match the task performance of models trained on human-teleoperated collaborative data.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to follow instructions and navigate to target locations. However, current VLN agents often suffer severe performance degradation in unseen environments due to distribution shifts. Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) offers a promising paradigm to bridge this gap, yet existing methods that rely on unsupervised entropy minimization can propagate errors through the trajectory, causing cascading failures in navigation. Recent methods mitigate this by incorporating human feedback, but they apply trajectory-level supervision uniformly across all steps without localizing the actions is truly informative, leading to inefficient feedback utilization and mismatched optimization granularity. To address these limitations, we propose FETA, a Feedback-Efficient Test-Time Adaptation method that improves both feedback efficiency and optimization reliability. To reduce unnecessary human interventions, we introduce a hierarchical sample selection strategy to localize informative samples. Specifically, we first filter trajectories whose normalized policy entropy exhibits large fluctuations. Within each selected trajectory, we further select the critical action via an entropy-gradient saliency criterion and query a single binary feedback on its correctness. A discrepancy-aware entropy optimization objective then updates the policy only at the queried step, with adaptive scaling that assigns larger relative weights to samples with greater prediction-feedback discrepancy. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that FETA achieves state-of-the-art performance with fewer human interventions, while remaining robust under noisy feedback and continual adaptation settings.
authors: Zixu Wang, Huaquan Zhang, Shoukai Xu, Jinwu Hu, Zhiquan Wen, Mingkui Tan
bullets: Unseen environments can cause severe VLN degradation, while entropy minimization may amplify navigation errors.
FETA hierarchically selects high-value feedback: unstable trajectories first, then critical actions using entropy-gradient saliency.
It queries one binary correctness signal per selected action and updates the policy only at that step.
Discrepancy-aware entropy optimization adaptively emphasizes actions where predictions and feedback disagree.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks report state-of-the-art performance with fewer interventions, including robustness to noisy feedback and continual adaptation.

papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) have recently emerged as important remote sensing platforms, and UAV navigation has shown great potential in remote sensing applications. However, existing methods do not explicitly incorporate kinodynamic modeling or safety distances into trajectory generation, resulting in high absolute yaw rates, frequent collisions, and low navigation success rates, which limit safety and motion stability. To address this challenge, we introduce KinoUAV, a kinodynamic benchmark comprising a dataset and KinoUAV-Agent. First, we develop a hierarchical kinodynamic trajectory generation pipeline that drives UAV through acceleration actions. It uses waypoint chains from global planning and generates trajectories segment by segment under velocity, acceleration, and jerk constraints, reducing oscillations and improving trajectory stability. Furthermore, we introduce directional free-space distance (DFD) labels into the constructed dataset to describe the available clearance for safe motion decisions. The proposed KinoUAV-Agent predicts DFDs and uses them to generate safe actions, decoupling perception from action decision-making. This design enables autonomous obstacle avoidance and improves navigation safety. The benchmark incorporates the proposed Cruise-Seek task, in which the UAV first enters the target region and then searches for the target, reducing the difficulty of target search and improving navigation success. Experiments on KinoUAV show that KinoUAV-Agent outperforms existing methods, achieving the highest success rate while maintaining lower absolute yaw rates and collision rates. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of kinodynamic modeling for safe and stable UAV navigation.
authors: Chenyao Yang, Peijin Wang, Yingchao Feng, Wenhui Diao
bullets: Targets unstable and unsafe UAV navigation caused by missing kinodynamic constraints and safety-distance modeling.
Generates trajectories segment by segment from waypoint chains under velocity, acceleration, and jerk constraints.
Adds directional free-space distance (DFD) labels, which the agent predicts to guide safe action selection and obstacle avoidance.
Introduces the Cruise-Seek task, where UAVs first enter a target region before searching for the target.
Experiments report the highest success rate among compared methods, with lower absolute yaw rates and collision rates.

papers.abstract: Motion planning is central to robotics, and it is increasingly used to correct the motions proposed by learned planners and policies. In both uses, constraints must hold at every instant of the motion, not only at sampled times. To our knowledge, no algorithm provably converges to a globally optimal motion once a smoothness cost is combined with such constraints. We cast planning and steering as a single continuous-time program: robots avoid one another and static or moving obstacles, and a learned proposal is steered by keeping the motion close to it. The program is elementary to state, yet nonconvex. We propose GlobMP (Global Motion Planning), a gradient projection method over piecewise-polynomial curves, on which each constraint is one polynomial per piece that must stay nonnegative over the whole motion; it alternates cost reduction with feasibility restoration. Under mild assumptions, we show that, from a fine grid start, its cost approaches the global optimum as the number of polynomial pieces grows, with every constraint met to any chosen tolerance, or exactly on stable instances. We demonstrate its superior performance over strong baselines in real and synthetic experiments, including teams of up to $200$ robots, multi-robot planning on the Robotarium testbed and an extended benchmark, maze navigation, and steering tactile-reactive policies on a bimanual humanoid.
authors: Mohsen Amiri, Sima Didari, Davoud Ataee Tarzanagh, Hankyu Moon, Yeongdae Kwon
bullets: Addresses motion planning and steering with continuous-time collision and obstacle constraints, rather than checking only sampled states.

Demonstrates strong performance across synthetic and real settings, including teams of up to 200 robots, Robotarium planning, maze navigation, and humanoid tactile-reactive policy steering.

papers.abstract: Dynamic interactive object search in large-scale human environments presents substantial challenges for existing methods. Current scene representations like 3D Scene Graphs (3DSG) only provide coarse-grained spatial segmentation and cannot identify functional areas such as storage or leisure areas. Without functional area understanding, existing methods are constrained to exhaustive sequential exploration at large scales, resulting in inefficient search behaviors -- particularly in open-layout environments with numerous interactive objects such as drawers and cabinets. Moreover, these methods lack adaptability to environmental dynamics such as object relocations. To address these limitations, this paper proposes CMAR-search, a novel framework built upon Commonsense and Memory Augmented Reasoning (CMAR). Our approach leverages commonsense about area functionalities and aggregates environmental memory to construct a Functional 3D Scene Graph (F3DSG), which organizes the environment into functional areas with their associated containers. Through this structured representation, CMAR enables hierarchical action planning at both macro-area and micro-container levels, empowering the system to efficiently identify and inspect semantically relevant areas for effective object search. Notably, CMAR continuously integrates real-time perception, accumulated memory, and commonsense to dynamically relocalize objects in changing environments. Extensive experiments in simulation and real-world settings demonstrate that CMAR-search significantly surpasses state-of-the-art baselines in both success rate and search efficiency for object search in dynamic interactive environments.
authors: Kaiyao Liao, Qingfeng Li, Xinlei Zhang, Chen Chen, Qing Sun, Jianwei Niu
bullets: Addresses coarse 3D scene representations, exhaustive exploration, and difficulty handling relocated objects.

Continuously integrates perception, memory, and commonsense to relocalize objects as environments change.
Experiments in simulation and real-world settings show higher search success and efficiency than existing baselines.

papers.abstract: Traversability estimation is critical for ground vehicle teleoperation, yet existing methods often neglect the human operator's preferences for speed and risk tolerance. To address this gap, we propose PATH-Net, a Preference-Aware Traversability estimation Hierarchical Network that adaptively generates preference-conditioned traversability cost maps and speed profiles for off-road teleoperation. Our framework integrates visual and geometric bird's-eye-view features with short-term historical vehicle states through a multi-head shared-backbone architecture. Our PATH-Net infers traversability cost maps while optimizing speed recommendations by using maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning and sparse speed supervision. Our method incorporates operator preference via an asymmetric feature aggregation mechanism, splitting inference into a cost branch that prioritizes high-risk traversability regions and a speed branch that outputs preference-adjusted recommended speeds. Experiments with 15 operators across 225 teleoperated trajectories show alignment with user-specific navigation strategies, achieving modified Hausdorff distance of 0.17 m (aggressive) and 0.15 m (conservative). In the questionnaire assessment, participants reported lower NASA-TLX workload scores with PATH-Net recommendations than without recommendations, decreasing from 34.7 to 22.2. These results support preference-conditioned trajectory and speed recommendation for off-road teleoperation.
authors: Xianghao Meng, Wenshuo Wang, Cheng Shao, Lewei Feng, Qingxiao Liu, Canyu Wang, Junqiang Xi
bullets: Addresses the limited consideration of human preferences in existing traversability estimation methods.

Separates cost and speed branches, emphasizing high-risk regions while adapting speeds to operator preferences.
In studies with 15 operators and 225 trajectories, recommendations aligned with aggressive and conservative strategies and reduced reported NASA-TLX workload from 34.7 to 22.2.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic mapping in dynamic real-world environments is essential for embodied intelligence and long-term autonomy. However, existing methods often involve a trade-off: lightweight online mapping is efficient but captures limited semantic context, while dense mapping provides richer semantics at higher computational cost and is more vulnerable to distractors. They also struggle to relocalize objects after scene changes. To address these challenges, we propose the Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System (OASIS), a unified system for online mapping, complex open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments. Motivated by the observation that indoor scenes are organized around stable semantic anchors, OASIS represents the environment using a sparse set of anchor nodes, each maintaining a unified multimodal representation that integrates semantic descriptions, visual features, and geometric states for reasoning, verification, and navigation. Its compact anchor-centric memory supports on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval, reducing redundant storage while improving retrieval reliability. To handle scene dynamics, OASIS further reuses transient observations collected during navigation to relocalize moved objects. Experiments in both simulation and real-world environments, including standard retrieval benchmarks and navigation tasks under both static and dynamic settings, demonstrate that our system can perform complex open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation, while also enabling relocation of displaced objects after scene changes.
authors: Kaiyao Liao, Qingfeng Li, Chen Chen, Xiaoze Wu, Qing Sun, Jianwei Niu
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–semantic richness trade-off in online mapping and the difficulty of relocalizing objects after scene changes.
Represents scenes with sparse anchor nodes that combine semantic, visual, and geometric information for reasoning, verification, and navigation.
Uses on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval to reduce redundant storage while supporting complex queries.
Reuses transient navigation observations to relocalize objects that have moved.
Validated in simulation and real-world settings across retrieval benchmarks and static/dynamic navigation tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: System architecture of OASIS. Given an RGB-D stream, the system concurrently performs episodic memory curation (top left) and online semantic mapping (bottom left) to extract 3D instances. To build the episodic memory, it utilizes scaleaware scoring and spatial-visual cluster assignment to continuously update and retain high-quality representative frames. By assigning these selected frames to their corresponding stable anchor instances, the system constructs the unified multimodal OASIS Graph, structured as shown on the right. Leveraging this graph alongside multimodal foundation models (LLM/VLM), the agent effectively executes hierarchical retrieval and robust view-driven navigation in dynamic environments.

Figure 3: Visual relocalization via Transient Visual Buffer (TVB). If the retrieved target is absent from the current view, OASIS uses CLIP to match transient crops to the query and a VLM to verify candidate frames and confirm the target’s new location.

Figure 1: Comparison of retrieval paradigms for complex open-vocabulary queries. Unlike traditional dense mapping (left) which struggles with redundant context and visual distractors, our OASIS (right) constructs a lightweight anchor-centric memory. By leveraging an LLM to filter irrelevant regions and performing on-demand VLM verification, OASIS efficiently isolates the target based on fine-grained attributes and spatial relationships, significantly improving retrieval reliability.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in foundation-model agents have enabled increasingly capable embodied systems for long-horizon planning and interaction. However, embodied agents require fast, closed-loop decisions as they continuously perceive and act on a changing environment. Deploying strong cloud agents leaves the platform idle for seconds between consecutive actions, while lightweight local models respond quickly but are more vulnerable to errors. Existing hierarchical architectures typically assign models fixed roles, whereas conventional model routers make stateless per-request decisions. We present CARE, a critic-guided adaptive execution framework that dynamically determines when to escalate control from a local executor to a stronger cloud model. A lightweight critic model monitors execution reliability and triggers escalation when local execution becomes unreliable; once escalated, control persists until the agent recovers, avoiding step-wise switching. To support such control transfer, a shared handoff memory maintains execution context and task-level progress across executors, enabling the model to intervene without restarting from scratch. Across diverse embodied benchmarks, CARE improves task success by 6.3-18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline. CARE further approaches or exceeds Cloud-only success while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8-82.6%.
authors: Wei Zhang, Lirong Xiang, Charles Fleming
bullets: Targets the latency of cloud-only agents and the error vulnerability of lightweight local agents in long-horizon embodied tasks.
Uses a lightweight critic to monitor local execution and trigger persistent escalation rather than making stateless per-step routing decisions.
Maintains shared handoff memory so cloud control preserves execution context and task progress without restarting.
Across diverse embodied benchmarks, improves task success by 6.3–18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline.
Approaches or exceeds Cloud-only success while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8–82.6%.

papers.abstract: Human motion retargeting bridges the embodiment gap between humans and humanoid robots by converting human demonstrations into reference trajectories for whole-body control and loco-manipulation. For object-interaction tasks, successful execution depends on accurately preserving body--object relations at critical stages. However, uniform per-frame iteration budgets do not account for these localized accuracy requirements, limiting the computational efficiency of retargeting. To address this limitation, we present Spatiotemporal Retargeting (STR), which uses keyframes and key body parts to allocate optimization effort. Specifically, a vision-language model selects relevant motion signals and body parts, and keyframes are identified from changes in the selected signals. Based on these selections, STR assigns additional solver iterations to keyframes and higher interaction weights to the selected parts. To further improve contact fidelity, we introduce Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring (MCA) to refine object-surface contact positions using an approximate object-wrench model while retaining the selected surface directions. Building on the resulting references, we develop Spatiotemporal Reinforcement Learning (STRL), which combines adaptive key-stage sampling with a contact reward based on target proximity and object contact forces for downstream control. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 and real-world experiments on a Unitree R1 demonstrate that STR improves geometric contact coverage and continuity at lower computational cost, while the resulting references improve downstream task completion across diverse object-interaction motions.
authors: Xiongbo Shi, Shihang Du, Zongyou Yu, Ao Zhou, Xudong Zhang, Ziyu Lin, Haodong Zhang, Junqiao Zhao, Guang Chen
bullets: Targets the inefficiency of uniform per-frame optimization, especially when accurate body–object relations matter only at critical stages.
Uses a vision-language model to select relevant motion signals and body parts, then detects keyframes from signal changes.
Assigns extra solver iterations to keyframes and higher interaction weights to selected body parts.
Adds Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring to refine object-surface contacts, and STRL uses adaptive key-stage sampling with contact-aware rewards.
Simulation and real-world experiments show improved contact coverage and continuity at lower computational cost, with better downstream task completion across diverse interactions.

Both enter the constrained optimization to produce dense robot references. papers.abstract: Predicting surrounding vehicles' lane-change intentions enables autonomous vehicles to anticipate potential hazards and respond proactively rather than relying solely on reactive maneuvers. This study investigates the benefits of integrating lane-change prediction, based on knowledge graph embeddings and Bayesian inference, into autonomous vehicle decision-making. Three driving strategies are evaluated in risky merging scenarios simulated in CARLA: reactive driving, prediction-based longitudinal action, and prediction-based lateral action. The proposed prediction model anticipates the surrounding vehicle's lane change approximately 3-4 seconds before its occurrence, allowing the ego vehicle to adjust its behavior accordingly. In the representative simulation records, reactive driving results in a collision accompanied by aggressive deceleration. In contrast, prediction-based longitudinal action initiates early braking to establish a safe gap, while prediction-based lateral action performs a lane change when a safe adjacent lane is available. Both predictive strategies avoid collisions in the evaluated records. Compared with reactive driving, peak deceleration before impact is reduced by 31.5% with longitudinal action and 91.0% with lateral action. Additionally, an ISO 2631-1-based horizontal vibration estimate is used to provide a ride comfort assessment. Overall, the results highlight the potential of lane-change prediction to support safer and smoother driving through proactive decision-making, with additional insights into ride comfort provided by vibration-based estimates.
authors: Mohamed Manzour, Aditya Kumar, Rub\'en Izquierdo, Miguel \'Angel Sotelo
bullets: The study addresses the limits of reactive driving when surrounding vehicles make hazardous lane changes.

An ISO 2631-1-based horizontal vibration estimate was used to assess ride comfort alongside safety.

papers.abstract: Motion Diffusion Models (MDMs) can generate diverse and visually appealing human motion; yet, the resulting trajectories frequently violate physical constraints, limiting their downstream use in simulation and control. We present PhysibleMDM, a framework that promotes physical feasibility of MDM output by optimizing at inference time the diffusion noise without retraining the generative model. We introduce a set of surrogate feasibility constraints that can be evaluated without full trajectory simulation. These constraints combine kinematic checks (e.g., ground penetration, slip, and self-collision) with dynamic feasibility tests computed via an inverse-dynamics inner loop formulated as a cone program. We solve the resulting black-box noise optimization problem using the Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (Sep-CMA-ES), thereby avoiding reliance on computationally expensive and discontinuous gradients. An autoregressive scheme then chains optimized segments to synthesize long motion sequences. Across 100 motion styles on an SMPL humanoid, PhysibleMDM reduces mean ground penetration, self-collision penetration, and ground slip by 75%, 92%, and 74%, respectively, relative to unoptimized diffusion output. Across 11 sequences for a custom bipedal robot, it achieves median reductions of 89.5% in per-sequence mean acceleration-reconstruction error and 79.5% in the mean inverse-dynamics residual.
authors: Maximilian St\"olzle, David M\"uller, Agon Serifi, Ruben Grandia, Espen Knoop, Moritz B\"acher
bullets: Addresses physically implausible motion trajectories that limit diffusion models’ use in simulation and control.
Combines surrogate kinematic constraints with dynamic feasibility checks from an inverse-dynamics cone program.
Uses gradient-free Sep-CMA-ES to optimize diffusion noise and an autoregressive scheme to generate long sequences.
On an SMPL humanoid across 100 motion styles, it reduces ground penetration, self-collision penetration, and slip by 75%, 92%, and 74%.
On 11 custom-biped sequences, it reduces acceleration-reconstruction error by 89.5% and inverse-dynamics residual by 79.5% in the median.

papers.abstract: Should an embodied agent's experience be baked into its policy weights, or kept external and retrieved at inference? A memory-augmented teacher (a VLM that retrieves lessons, with their episode images, from its own past attempts) produces trajectories on a vision-conditioned reach task; from the same trajectories we distil LoRA student policies and evaluate them under matched protocols, including one that re-attaches the teacher's frozen retrieval buffer to a fixed set of student weights. We pre-registered the hypotheses, arms, tests, and analysis rules before training and before any p-value. Distilling the memory-augmented behaviour into weights beat an action-only control by +1 pp (n.s.); the registered test proves underpowered for its own minimum effect, so we withdraw - rather than refute - the memory-in-weights claim. Attaching retrieval to a fixed set of student weights added +34 pp (z=5.15), reaching the pooled memory-augmented teacher reference (49.3%); the pre-registered protocol contrast agrees (+23 pp, z=3.36); under a pre-registered auto-reset sensitivity count the two are +36 and +29 pp. An exploratory behavioural probe with pre-registered per-arm predictions is consistent with behavioural distillation transferring the marginal correction but not the conditional, situation-specific correction that retrieval supplies. The recipe that follows is to externalise the memory: in follow-up controls registered before they ran, the same frozen buffer lifts the base model with no adapter to 48% (sensitivity 48%) and the other three adapters from 19-26% to 53-55% (sensitivity 17-21% to 50-55%), and the adapter adds nothing detectable once the buffer is attached. On a second, harder task, the retrieval advantage points the same direction but falls short of significance (+6 pp, 95% CI [-4.5, +16.4]); exploratory diagnostics tie the attenuation to memory coverage.
bullets: A pre-registered study compares memory-augmented retrieval, weight-distilled policies, and fixed student policies with the teacher’s retrieval buffer attached.

Distilling memory-augmented behavior into weights improved performance by only 1 percentage point over an action-only control; the test was underpowered, so the claim was withdrawn rather than refuted.
Attaching the frozen retrieval buffer to student weights produced a large gain (+34 percentage points), matching the memory-augmented teacher’s 49.3% reference performance.
Follow-up controls found the buffer substantially improved the base model and other adapters, while adapters added no detectable benefit once retrieval was attached.
On a harder second task, the retrieval advantage was smaller and not significant, with exploratory evidence linking the reduction to limited memory coverage.

papers.abstract: Learning useful representations from continually changing value targets remains a challenge in deep reinforcement learning. We study the temporal horizon of this supervision: smaller discounts make these targets less sensitive to distant bootstrap changes, but using them for behavior changes the control objective. We introduce Short-to-Long (S2L), which supplies a long-horizon behavior learner with features trained by smaller-discount source networks. Detached connections prevent the behavior value loss from updating the sources, allowing each source to follow its own value objective while the behavior discount remains unchanged. Across Atari, online continuous control, and offline continuous control, the approach yields aggregate performance gains, improving the paired terminal median on 40 of 57 Atari games. Matched Atari ablations support the roles of feature transfer, smaller source discounts, and gradient isolation. Fixed-trajectory measurements further show reduced drift in source value targets with mixed discounts.
authors: Tong Che, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone
bullets: Addresses representation instability from continually changing long-horizon value targets in deep reinforcement learning.
Uses smaller-discount source networks to learn more stable features, while the behavior learner retains its original long-horizon discount.
Detached connections isolate source networks from the behavior value loss, letting each network optimize its own value objective.
Across Atari, online continuous control, and offline continuous control, S2L improves aggregate performance; it improves paired terminal median on 40 of 57 Atari games.
Ablations support feature transfer, smaller source discounts, and gradient isolation; fixed-trajectory measurements show reduced source-target drift with mixed discounts.

papers.abstract: Multi-task generalization is an important yet underexplored problem in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). Many real-world applications require multi-agent systems to generalize across complex, temporally extended tasks with diverse inter-agent coordination requirements. We introduce a specification language that combines temporal-logic task specifications with operators for expressing such requirements. We propose SpecMAGIC, a hierarchical framework that leverages the automaton structure of task specifications for subtask decomposition. A centralized high-level planner identifies and allocates compatible subtask sequences across agents, while decentralized low-level policies execute individual subtasks. This enables zero-shot generalization to new tasks by composing reusable subtask policies according to new specifications, without retraining. We establish soundness and probabilistic completeness of the high-level planner. Experiments on multi-agent navigation tasks show that SpecMAGIC substantially outperforms existing approaches on unseen task specifications and maintains strong performance as the number of agents increases.
authors: Zijian Guo, \.Ilker I\c{s}{\i}k, H. M. Sabbir Ahmad, Wenchao Li
bullets: Targets multi-task generalization in MARL with complex coordination requirements.
Introduces a specification language combining temporal logic with multi-agent requirement operators.
Uses a hierarchical design: centralized planning allocates subtask sequences, while decentralized policies execute them.
Provides soundness and probabilistic completeness guarantees for the high-level planner.
Experiments on multi-agent navigation show strong performance on unseen specifications and as team size grows.

papers.title: SpecMAGIC: Specification-Guided Multi-Task Generalization in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: SpecMAGIC enables multi-agent teams to solve unseen, temporally extended tasks zero-shot by composing reusable subtask policies from formal specifications.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct access to physical interactions at the contact interface, making it a critical modality for robust and dexterous manipulation. Over the past several decades, tactile-based manipulation research has evolved from mechanics-driven approaches, which explicitly interpret tactile signals through contact mechanics and task-specific reasoning, to data-driven approaches that learn tactile representations and manipulation policies directly from data. This paper reviews the development of tactile-based manipulation from these two complementary perspectives. We first introduce the fundamentals of tactile sensing, and then review, from a mechanics-driven perspective, how those signals form manipulation-relevant state representations and subsequently influence the robot action. We then examine the recent advances in data-driven tactile manipulation, covering imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future opportunities toward scalable, generalizable, and robust tactile-enabled robotic systems.
authors: Jingyi Xiang, Yixuan Wang, Wenzhen Yuan
bullets: Tactile sensing exposes physical contact information important for robust and dexterous manipulation.
Mechanics-driven methods interpret tactile signals using contact mechanics and task-specific reasoning to form state representations and guide actions.
Data-driven methods learn tactile representations and manipulation policies from data, including imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models.
The paper surveys tactile sensing fundamentals and developments across both perspectives.
It identifies open challenges and future opportunities for broader, more robust tactile-enabled robotics.
papers.selection_reason: Review of tactile-based manipulation covering mechanics-driven and data-driven approaches, including imitation learning, RL, VLA models, and predictive models.
papers.title: Tactile-Based Robotic Manipulation: From Mechanics-Driven to Data-Driven Perspectives
papers.tldr: This review traces tactile robotic manipulation from mechanics-based reasoning to data-driven learning and outlines challenges for scalable, generalizable, and robust systems.

papers.abstract: We address the problem of real-time multi-agent path planning under prescribed initial and final configurations, formulated as a high-dimensional optimal control problem subject to inter-agent collision avoidance and obstacle constraints. Classical solvers based on the Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman equation or Pontryagin's maximum principle (PMP) become computationally intractable as the number of agents grows, due to the curse of dimensionality and the non-convexity introduced by interaction constraints. We propose OCFormer, a transformer-based neural network that parameterizes the inverse of a coordinate transformation mapping a simple, analytically tractable latent space, in which agents evolve independently under a decoupled Hamiltonian, to the physical space of the coupled, interacting system. The model is trained by minimizing a physics-informed loss comprising the Hamiltonian ODE residual from the PMP and a boundary matching term, without requiring pre-computed trajectory data. The self-attention mechanism endows OCFormer with permutation equivariance over agents, a structural symmetry that prior symplectic network approaches do not natively enforce. When trained on a distribution of boundary conditions, the amortized OCFormer produces near-optimal trajectories for unseen initial and final configurations in a single forward pass ($\sim$220ms), enabling real-time inference without retraining. We further introduce a lightweight transfer learning framework that adapts a pretrained OCFormer to out-of-distribution perturbations in seconds via L-BFGS fine-tuning. Numerical experiments on two- and three-dimensional multi-agent navigation with up to 128 agents demonstrate the scalability and efficiency of the proposed approach.
authors: Qian Zhang, Shanqing Liu, Jerome Darbon, George Karniadakis
bullets: Targets the computational difficulty of high-dimensional optimal control with agent interactions, collision avoidance, and obstacles.
Learns an inverse coordinate transformation from a decoupled latent system to the coupled physical system.
Trains without precomputed trajectories using PMP Hamiltonian ODE residuals and boundary-matching losses.
Self-attention provides permutation equivariance across agents, while amortized inference handles unseen boundary conditions in a single forward pass (~220 ms).
A lightweight L-BFGS transfer-learning procedure adapts pretrained models to out-of-distribution perturbations in seconds; experiments scale to 128 agents in 2D and 3D navigation.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Flowchart of the OCFormer framework. For a pair of prescribed initial and terminal configurations, boundary data are first encoded into latent variables (y, q), which serve as the input to the transformer-based inverse coordinate map ϕ−1. The network predicts the physical position and momentum trajectories (x,p) over the time grid without solving an ODE at inference time. During training, the predicted trajectories are differentiated with respect to time and evaluated in the Hamiltonian system so that the model satisfies the physics-informed residual loss associated with Pontryagin’s maximum principle, while a boundary matching term enforces the initial and final constraints. The total loss is minimized over the network parameters, yielding a model that directly maps varying boundary conditions to feasible multi-agent trajectories in real time.

Figure 3. Architecture of OCFormer. y, q are first reshaped into RN×d. Ey, Eq : Rd → RD are tokenwise embedding layers, which are applied on the last axis of reshaped input. zi, ri ∈ RN×D. Partial transformer blocks Tup and Tlow are depicted by the dashed rounded rectangle. ID is identity mapping in RD. Ti (i = 1, · · · , n) are the transformer blocks. Dx,Dp : RD → Rd are tokenwise deembedding MLPs, whose output are flattened back into RNd. INd is the identity mapping in RNd, serving as residual connection.

Figure 2. Coordinate-transformation view of the proposed trajectory representation. The forward map ϕ sends the physical trajectory pair (x,p) to a simpler latent trajectory pair (y, q) associated with a decoupled Hamiltonian system, while the inverse map ϕ−1 reconstructs the interacting multi-agent trajectories in physical space.

Figure 5. Predicted multi-agent trajectories for the random-perturbation experiment with n = 32 drones at times t = 0, 1 3 , 2 3 , 1 from left to right. Starting from the perturbed initial condition, the transferred model generates collision-free paths that progressively reorganize the swarm toward the prescribed terminal arrangement. The intermediate snapshots show that the learned corrections adapt the reference solution while preserving the overall interaction structure encoded by the original OCFormer.

Figure 6. Predicted trajectories for the 3D room experiment with n = 100 drones at times t = 0, 1 3 , 2 3 , 1 from left to right. The snapshots illustrate how the learned model coordinates a large collection of agents in a confined threedimensional domain, moving them from their initial configuration to the terminal one while maintaining collision-free motion throughout the room. The intermediate frames highlight the scalability of OCFormer to high-dimensional multi-agent path-planning problems.

Figure 7. Predicted trajectories for the 3D ball-obstacle experiment at times t = 0, 1 3 , 2 3 , 1 from left to right. The figure shows the agents moving from their initial to terminal positions while simultaneously avoiding pairwise collisions and steering around the spherical obstacle. The intermediate configurations make clear that the learned dynamics capture both inter-agent avoidance and obstacle-avoidance behavior in a genuinely three-dimensional setting.
Figure 4. Predicted trajectories at t = 0, T/3, 2T/3, T for M = 128 drones, the largest and most demanding configuration in Table 1. Drones shown as colored circles with paths as gray curves.

papers.selection_reason: Learned multi-agent path planning with a transformer and physics-informed training directly fits robot navigation.
papers.title: A Transformer-based Approach for Real-time Multi-agent Path Planning with Varying Initial/Final Conditions
papers.tldr: OCFormer uses a physics-informed transformer to generate near-optimal, collision-free multi-agent paths in real time for varying start and goal configurations.

papers.abstract: We introduce Foundation4D, a unified feed-forward model for geometry estimation, 3D detection, semantic occupancy, and Gaussian reconstruction from multi-camera driving video. A shared backbone uses factorized spatiotemporal attention to efficiently combine observations across cameras and time. Our video inference pipeline uses pose graph optimization to refine camera trajectories and assembles object tracks across input windows. We also develop a data annotation pipeline and release PAI-Foundation4D, a benchmark with dense depth and semantic occupancy labels for 1,253 driving clips. With benchmark-specific fine-tuning, Foundation4D achieves the lowest depth AbsRel on Waymo and nuScenes, the highest detection mAP on nuScenes, and the highest occupancy mIoU on OpenOccupancy among the compared methods. Our task-combination study shows benefits for both detection and geometry: co-training detection with geometry and occupancy improves top-class mAP by 1.2 points over detection-only training, while co-training geometry with detection reduces camera-to-rig translation error by $13.4\%$ relative to geometry-only training. We further use the predicted geometry and trajectories as priors for lidarless NuRec, supporting reconstruction of driving scenes for simulation.
authors: NVIDIA, :, S\'ergio Agostinho, Maximilian Apodaca, Emmanuel Attia, Guillem Braso, George Dong, Ilya Fedorov, Michele Fenzi, Gang Huang, Jiahui Huang, Shengyu Huang, Bingxin Ke, Laura Leal-Taix\'e, Kuan-Ting Lee, Mingxuan Liu, Tian Liu, Tim Meinhardt, Aljo\v{s}a O\v{s}ep, Naveen Kumar Rai, Kefei Ren, Cristiano Saltori, Keqiang Wu, Ning Xu, Fei Xue, Jin-Bey Yu, Lei Zhang, Qunjie Zhou
bullets: Addresses geometry estimation, 3D detection, semantic occupancy, and Gaussian reconstruction in one feed-forward model.
Uses a shared backbone with factorized spatiotemporal attention to fuse camera and temporal observations efficiently.
Refines camera trajectories with pose-graph optimization and assembles object tracks across video windows.
Introduces PAI-Foundation4D, a benchmark with dense depth and semantic occupancy labels for 1,253 driving clips.
Reports leading compared performance on Waymo depth, nuScenes detection, and OpenOccupancy occupancy; supports lidarless scene reconstruction for simulation.

papers.abstract: Designing and tuning reward functions remains one of the main challenges in building effective reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines for humanoid locomotion. While shaping rewards can accelerate learning, naively formulated terms often conflict with the desired behavior, overfit to a specific robot, or become unstable under small weight changes. Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) offers an alternative solution: shaping the reward via differences of a potential function to guide exploration without changing the optimal policy. In this paper, we study Multi-PBRS for humanoid locomotion and propose a unified reward configuration. We then evaluate the same reward structure and weights across nine humanoid robots, requiring only robot-specific metadata (joint/link mappings and default poses) rather than per-robot reward redesign. Our experiments show that, compared to standard shaping, MPBRS provides more consistent scaling behavior and reduced tuning sensitivity across robots, making it easier to tune without altering the optimal policy.
authors: Van Chung Nguyen, Hung Manh La
bullets: Addresses conflicting, robot-specific, and unstable reward shaping in humanoid RL.
Applies Multi-Potential-Based Reward Shaping (Multi-PBRS) to unify reward configuration.

Reports more consistent scaling and reduced tuning sensitivity than standard shaping.
Preserves the optimal policy while guiding exploration through potential differences.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models. A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation. This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations. In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step. Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets. We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better. Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs. It achieves particularly large gains on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks under zero-shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human-to-robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 19.4% for the best competing WAM.
authors: Huiwon Jang, Suhyeok Jang, Hyeonmo Kang, Seungku Kim, Jinwoo Shin, Sihyun Yu
bullets: WAMs use future video representations to guide action prediction without costly iterative video denoising.

For skills shown only in human videos, FRED reaches 50.0% task success versus 19.4% for the best competing WAM.

papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks and real-world deployments. Its standard training recipe, however, is expensive across all existing paradigms: imitation learning requires fleet-scale driving logs whose behavior distribution only thinly covers the safety-critical tail; closed-loop reinforcement learning in a photorealistic simulator, while offering diverse behaviors, is bottlenecked by sample-efficiency, per-step cost of rendering, and a forward pass through a large vision backbone. Self-play in vectorized simulators changes the economics: at millions of rollout steps per second, one can obtain a state distribution with natural diversity in collisions, near-misses, and recoveries that no driving log contains, and a highly reactive policy emerges from a basic driving-quality reward. Our approach exploits this asymmetry. We pretrain a single policy by self-play, distill its rollouts into a flow-matching trajectory teacher that also plans, and train lightweight adapters on a frozen pretrained vision backbone to reproduce the latent space of either teacher through the action KL divergence, a batch-relational low-rank structural loss, and, for the planner, a trajectory-matching loss. Every target traces back to the self-play policy, so alignment never supervises against a logged trajectory: a paired dataset of (image, scene-state) frames suffices, with no need for the curated expert demonstrations that imitation pretraining is built on. From this one self-play teacher we obtain two end-to-end students: a closed-loop policy that outperforms every published imitation-based end-to-end method on the photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting closed-loop benchmark HUGSim, and a planner that reaches 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard, above every published method including DriveZero-Scale (57.1), and 95.5 PDMS on navtest, without human demonstrations.
authors: Zikang Xiong, Weixin Li, Zhouchonghao Wu, Akshay Rangesh, Saarth Bonde, Grantland Hall, Chen Tang, Yihan Hu, Wei Zhan
bullets: Addresses the cost, limited safety-tail coverage, and inefficiency of imitation learning and photorealistic closed-loop reinforcement learning.
Pretrains a policy through self-play in fast vectorized simulators, then distills it into a flow-matching trajectory teacher and end-to-end students.
Trains adapters on a frozen vision backbone using action KL, relational low-rank structural, and trajectory-matching losses from paired image–scene-state data.
Produces both a closed-loop policy and a planner without human or curated expert demonstrations.
Reports 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard and 95.5 PDMS on navtest; the policy also outperforms published imitation-based methods on HUGSim.

figures.caption: Fig. 1.Conventional training pipeline vs. our reinforcement-learning pretraining pipeline. Conventional recipes imitate fleet logs and fine-tune on curated demonstrations, logged trajectories, or rendered simulation. They therefore need human data or rendering at every stage. Phase 1 (top right) trains a self-play policy 𝜋𝜃 with proximal policy optimization (PPO) in a multi-agent vectorized simulator. Phase 2 (middle right) freezes the policy as the self-play teacher and distills its rollouts into a trajectory teacher that also outputs a planned trajectory; both teachers read vector state. Phase 3 (bottom right) aligns an image-conditioned student to either frozen teacher: the self-play teacher yields the closed-loop student, and the trajectory teacher yields the planning student. The student keeps the teacher’s ego encoder unchanged and is not aligned on it; only the teacher’s scene features (road and partner, plus traffic for the trajectory teacher) enter the structural loss. An action loss matches the teacher’s action distribution, while a structural loss matches its pairwise relationships among scenes; for the planning student, an L2 loss also matches the plan the trajectory teacher selects among 16 samples. Alignment uses paired (image, scene-state) frames; it needs neither demonstrations nor online rendering during training. Blue modules are trainable; outlined modules are frozen. In the blue DINOv3 + Adapter block, only the adapter trains; the backbone stays frozen. The trajectory head and the L2 loss apply to the planning student only.

papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into embodied robotic planning, yet standard benchmarks primarily evaluate end-to-end task completion in nominal environments, obscuring failure origins across the execution stack. We present Alpha, a systematic fault-injection and robustness-evaluation framework for LLM-driven manipulation in simulation. Alpha injects calibrated faults across perception (sensor lag), actuation (grip slip), kinematics (unreachable targets), and planning (planner-output corruption), alongside concurrent conditions. To separate physical vulnerabilities from planner sensitivities, we introduce a matched methodology pairing an LLM agent (Llama-3 via Ollama) against a deterministic Scripted Oracle planner across a balanced 150-episode matrix under identical seeds, geometries, and safety criteria. Across the matrix, the Oracle achieves 64.0% (48/75) success while the LLM achieves 44.0% (33/75) (paired McNemar p = 3.01 x 10^-4). Crucially, excluding planner-output corruption, performance across all physical and kinematic conditions is identical: 55.0% (33/60) for both planners with zero discordant pairs (McNemar p = 1.00). This demonstrates that physical actuator slip, kinematic reach boundaries, and perceptual staleness affect deterministic controllers and LLM planners equivalently. The performance gap is driven entirely by planner-output corruption (100% Oracle vs. 0% LLM), isolating the prompt-to-JSON serialization and validation interface rather than a cognitive reasoning deficit. We also audit 169 historical pilot attempts for transparency.
bullets: Evaluates robustness under sensor lag, grip slip, unreachable targets, planner-output corruption, and concurrent faults.
Matches an LLM agent with a deterministic Scripted Oracle across 150 simulated episodes using identical conditions.
The Oracle succeeds in 64.0% of episodes versus 44.0% for the LLM.
Excluding planner-output corruption, both planners achieve 55.0% success with no discordant outcomes.
The performance gap is isolated to the prompt-to-JSON serialization and validation interface, not physical robustness or reasoning deficits.

papers.abstract: Real-time whole-body humanoid teleoperation remains challenging due to the computational latency introduced by optimization-based retargeting pipelines and future-frame conditioning. Existing motion tracking policies typically require dense reference targets including full joint positions, body-part transformations, and even future frames, which tightly couples the controller to expensive upstream modules. In this work, we present HuMiT, a whole-body teleoperation system built on a unified tracking policy that requires only a compact reference target, consisting of root height, root velocity, and the SE(3) poses of four sparse keypoints at the current frame, yet achieves competitive tracking fidelity compared to methods relying on more diverse reference states including complete joint positions, dense body-part transformations, and even future frames. Experiments show that our policy achieves a communication-to-inference latency of $\sim$20 ms measured between headset streaming and policy output and a video-based optical flow latency of 65 ms (median) across different motion types. We validate the system on a Unitree G1 humanoid, showcasing split-second reactive responses such as catching a tossed ball, as well as coordinated loco-manipulation capabilities. Project page: https://xiaohu-art.github.io/Track/.
bullets: Addresses latency and upstream-module dependence in optimization-based whole-body teleoperation.
Uses a unified tracking policy conditioned on root height, root velocity, and SE(3) poses of four sparse keypoints.
Avoids requiring full joint states, dense body transformations, or future frames.
Reports ~20 ms communication-to-inference latency and 65 ms median video-based optical-flow latency.
Validated on a Unitree G1 with reactive ball catching and coordinated loco-manipulation.

papers.tldr: HuMiT enables low-latency whole-body humanoid teleoperation using only compact, current-frame motion references while maintaining competitive tracking fidelity.

papers.abstract: Learning loco-manipulation policies requires demonstrations that capture coordinated base and arm motion on the target embodiment. Robot-free interfaces allow demonstrations to be collected independently of the target robot, increasing flexibility but without directly capturing platform-specific commands, proprioception, and body-mounted observations. On-robot teleoperation allows to capture these signals directly, but requires an interface capable of commanding the complete system concurrently. This paper presents LocoPilot, a single-operator bilateral teleoperation and data-collection framework implemented on a 12-DoF Unitree Go2 quadruped equipped with a 6-DoF AgileX Piper L manipulator, an Intel RealSense D435 wrist camera, and an Intel RealSense D405 head camera. A second 6-DoF Piper L arm, used as the leader and two handheld controllers provide simultaneous control of the base, body posture, manipulator, and gripper. The follower arm interaction forces are estimated without a dedicated force/torque sensor and rendered to the operator through a passivity-constrained haptic channel. A ROS~2 pipeline records synchronized multimodal observations together with a unified 11D action shared by teleoperation and policy deployment. Compared to prior work, LocoPilot uniquely unifies robot-in-the-loop legged data collection, force feedback without motion-capture instrumentation, and the same action interface at deployment. We evaluate the interface across multiple loco-manipulation tasks and validate the complete collection-to-deployment pipeline by fine-tuning MolmoAct2 \cite{MOLMO} on pick-and-place demonstrations and deploying on the physical robot without action retargeting or additional inverse kinematics. Code available at: https://github.com/iit-DLSLab/LocoPilot
bullets: Addresses the challenge of collecting demonstrations that coordinate legged-base and manipulator motion while preserving robot-specific observations and commands.
Uses a leader arm and two handheld controllers to teleoperate a 12-DoF Unitree Go2 with a 6-DoF Piper L arm and onboard cameras.
Estimates interaction forces without a dedicated force/torque sensor and provides passivity-constrained haptic feedback.
Records synchronized multimodal data with a unified 11D action interface shared between teleoperation and deployment.
Demonstrates the full pipeline on multiple tasks, including physical pick-and-place deployment after fine-tuning MolmoAct2 without action retargeting or additional inverse kinematics.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning increasingly relies on novice operators, whose demonstrations fall short of experts' in number and inter-trial consistency. Operators act on what they are shown, yet how the rendering of the robot affects their demonstrations, and the policies trained on them, has not been examined. We study this question with PointHand, a teleoperation interface that renders a multi-fingered robot hand as sparse keypoints at its fingertips and joints, the same keypoints a policy can observe. In a simulated mug-in-box task, 18 novices and 4 experts collected 2,200 trials under three renderings: the real shape of the hand, all keypoints emphasized, or the thumb and index finger alone emphasized. The novices shown the thumb and index finger emphasized collected 441 successful demonstrations from 600 trials, against 320 for those shown the real shape. We then trained diffusion policies on these demonstrations, replacing the scene point cloud and proprioceptive state they observe with the hand keypoints and two object keypoints. Within 400 steps these demonstrations went from the weakest of the three novice conditions under the point-cloud policy (46.3%) to the strongest under the keypoint policy (57.3%), a gain of +11.0 percentage points in all five seeds. Those collected with all keypoints emphasized changed by at most +0.7 percentage points, and in no more than three seeds. The value of a demonstration therefore depends on the rendering shown during collection and on what the policy observes together. A shared representation can pay off on both sides, in the number of successful demonstrations and in the success rate of the policy trained on them. Project page: https://omron-sinicx.github.io/point-hand/
bullets: The study examines how robot-hand rendering affects novice demonstrations and downstream imitation learning.
PointHand renders a multi-fingered hand as fingertip and joint keypoints, matching the policy’s hand observations.
In a simulated mug-in-box task, novices shown thumb-and-index emphasis produced more successful demonstrations than those shown the real hand shape.
Diffusion policies using keypoint observations benefited most from demonstrations collected with the matching thumb-and-index rendering, improving from 46.3% to 57.3% success within 400 steps.
The findings are limited to a simulated task, a specific teleoperation interface, and the tested renderings and keypoint-based policy observations.

Both condition a diffusion head of the same architecture and share the training procedure.

papers.selection_reason: Studies how teleoperation rendering affects demonstrations and downstream diffusion-policy learning, directly relevant to imitation learning and robot manipulation.
papers.title: What Novice Operators See Changes What the Policy Learns: A User Study of Keypoint Hand Visual Representation for Teleoperated Demonstration
papers.tldr: A shared keypoint representation can improve both novice teleoperation demonstrations and the policies trained from them.

papers.abstract: Embodied VLMs can execute increasingly complex manipulation tasks, yet execution errors can leave the environment in states that require replanning for recovery. Existing recovery methods either rely on inference-time mechanisms with fixed policies or learn from failure examples and reference corrections rather than verified action outcomes. To enable recovery learning through verifiable interaction, we introduce the Embodied Replanning for Recovery Environment (ERR-Env), which provides feedback on task progress and execution errors. We further construct ERR-Bench, a benchmark with held-out tasks spanning nominal, intermediate, and error states for evaluating recovery capability and execution reliability. We then propose Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO (AGT-GSPO), an online reinforcement learning method combining turn-level rewards for task progress and error states with action-grouped advantage estimation, and use it to train ERR-VLM, a compact 2B embodied VLM. Evaluation on ERR-Bench reveals a mismatch between task progress and execution reliability across diverse VLMs. AGT-GSPO improves ERR-VLM by 10.25 percentage points in Strict Success Rate for error-free completion and 22.95 percentage points in Recovery Rate, while ablations and zero-shot transfer further validate the effectiveness of our method.
bullets: Introduces ERR-Env, which provides feedback on task progress and execution errors for recovery learning.
Introduces ERR-Bench with held-out nominal, intermediate, and error-state tasks to evaluate recovery and execution reliability.
Proposes Action-Grouped Turn-GSPO, combining turn-level progress/error rewards with action-grouped advantage estimation.
Trains a compact 2B ERR-VLM; on ERR-Bench, it improves Strict Success Rate by 10.25 points and Recovery Rate by 22.95 points.
Finds that task progress and execution reliability can diverge across VLMs; ablations and zero-shot transfer support the method’s effectiveness.

papers.selection_reason: Trains an embodied VLM for manipulation error recovery via online RL, directly fitting robot learning and vision-language-action.
