papers.abstract: As a prototypical latent world model, Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) provide strong semantic representations. However, dense patch representations expose a redundant interface to downstream predictors, which must implicitly infer spatial organization and temporal correspondence, presenting three challenges. First, object information is distributed across patches, forcing each downstream predictor to redundantly recover object structure that could otherwise be reused across tasks before modeling interactions. Second, the lack of explicit entity correspondence across time makes historical transitions expensive, restricting the predictor's flexibility in utilizing context. Third, without explicit transport structure, existing JEPA models typically use pointwise l1/l2 distances, which are insensitive to spatial displacement when predicted and goal supports are largely disjoint. We propose the Slot-based Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (Slot-JEPA), which decomposes dense representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks. Pretrained once and frozen downstream, this decomposition exposes a reusable object-structured interface. Building on it, our Transition Memory Predictor (TMP) stores visual transitions as compact masks and retrieves useful context using statistics of corresponding slots. Its two branches separate slot-specific dynamics from shared cross-slot dynamics. We further use Unbalanced Optimal Transport (UOT) to supervise mask prediction and evaluate candidate plans by transporting mass between aligned predicted and goal masks, providing a signal better aligned with spatial progress. Across seven visual-understanding benchmarks, the slot-reconstructed features remain transferable. Slot-JEPA also improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar environments and four robotic arm planning tasks on the REALM-JEPA benchmark.
authors: Peisong Wen, Qianqian Xu, Minye Lei, Siran Dai, Yang Liu, Qingming Huang
bullets: Addresses redundant object-structure recovery, missing temporal correspondence, and displacement-insensitive pointwise losses in dense JEPA interfaces.
Decomposes representations into stable semantic slots and time-varying spatial masks, then freezes this pretrained interface for downstream use.
Introduces a Transition Memory Predictor with slot-specific and shared cross-slot dynamics, retrieving transitions through corresponding-slot statistics.
Uses Unbalanced Optimal Transport to supervise mask prediction and compare predicted and goal masks based on spatial progress.
Features transfer across seven visual-understanding benchmarks and improves goal-conditioned planning across six planar and four robotic-arm tasks on REALM-JEPA.

papers.abstract: Tactile representation learning for dexterous manipulation often requires substantial robot-side data collection, limiting its scalability across different hands and sensors. We explore whether large-scale human hand-object interaction (HOI) data can provide a useful prior for robotic tactile learning. To this end, we propose HuTact, a framework that pretrains tactile-aware hand representations from human HOI data without requiring real tactile signals during pretraining. HuTact transfers the interaction structure learned from human hand motions to robotic tactile observations and can be further adapted with a small amount of unlabeled robot interaction data. We evaluate HuTact on tactile perception and manipulation tasks, including grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and tactile-conditioned policy learning. Across these tasks, human HOI pretraining improves data efficiency and provides a strong initialization for downstream learning. Notably, with HOI pretraining followed by midtraining on unlabeled robot play data, HuTact achieves 88.26% Macro-F1 on grasp prediction using only 25\% of the labeled downstream data, comparable to training from scratch on the full labeled dataset (88.23%). These results suggest that human interaction data can serve as a scalable complementary source for robotic tactile representation learning.
authors: Yeonguk Yu, Jaehong Kim, Byungok Han
bullets: Addresses the need for costly, robot-specific tactile data collection across diverse hands and sensors.
Pretrains from human hand motions without real tactile signals, then transfers interaction structure to robotic tactile observations.
Can be adapted using a small amount of unlabeled robot interaction data.
Improves data efficiency across grasp prediction, slip detection, object classification, and tactile-conditioned policy learning.
With HOI pretraining and unlabeled robot play-data midtraining, reaches 88.26% Macro-F1 on grasp prediction using 25% of labeled data, comparable to 88.23% from full-data training.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in large (vision) language models have enabled computer-use agents that automate digital workflows via fine-grained keyboard and mouse operations. However, such agents remain fragile in long-horizon settings, where errors accumulate and executed actions leave unintended side effects, making the ability to recover from failures critical. Yet, existing remedies remain inadequate: environment resets are infeasible in proprietary settings, action replay is prohibitively expensive over long horizons, and API-based rollback is limited to web environments, leaving model-based recovery largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present ReTrace, a scalable evaluation framework for systematically studying recovery behavior in computer-use agents. We formalize Transition-Consistent Recovery: identical downstream actions from the recovered and target states must yield identical outcomes. We operationalize this criterion through goal-oriented action replay following controlled error injection. Using ReTrace, we present the first systematic study of autonomous, model-based recovery, revealing that (i) ideal recovery can unlock model's latent task completion capabilities, (ii) current computer-use agents fail to exploit their latent recovery capabilities, and (iii) accurate model-based recovery yields measurable end-to-end gains. Together, these findings establish recovery as a fundamental capability for building reliable computer-use agents. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/BangProx/ReTRACE.
authors: Byeonghun Bang, Sangwoo Park, Jinheon Baek, Kangsan Kim, Youngwan Lee, Sung Ju Hwang
bullets: Long-horizon computer-use agents are fragile because errors accumulate and actions can create unintended side effects.
Existing recovery approaches are limited by infeasible environment resets, costly long-horizon replay, or web-only rollback APIs.
ReTrace introduces Transition-Consistent Recovery, requiring identical downstream actions from recovered and target states to produce identical outcomes.
Its goal-oriented action replay framework systematically evaluates autonomous, model-based recovery after controlled error injection.
The study finds that agents possess latent recovery capabilities but fail to use them effectively; accurate recovery improves end-to-end performance.

papers.abstract: Egocentric action transfer aims to decouple the semantic action from egocentric observations and reproduce them in new visual contexts, enabling scalable world simulation, embodied policy learning, and robotic data generation. Existing approaches to transferring actions rely on condition-guided video generation, which converts the observation video into explicit geometric controls (e.g., hand poses or meshes) to drive synthesis. However, these methods introduce geometric estimation errors, making it difficult to preserve physically plausible interactions when transferred to new scenes. Alternatively, motion transfer methods directly extract motion patterns from the observation video, yet motion-level features alone cannot encode rich contact dynamics, frequently leading to severe hand structural collapse and implausible contact layout. To address both limitations, we present EgoACT, a test-time framework for egocentric action transfer that operates directly on the denoising process of video diffusion models without requiring additional geometric estimators. EgoACT uses Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring to stabilize reference-consistent hand-object structure in the early denoising stage, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration to refine reliable local correspondences in the mid-to-late denoising stages. Together, these two components preserve transferable action semantics while improving temporal coherence and interaction realism. We further establish EgoActionBench, a benchmark for evaluating action preservation, visual quality, and hand-object plausibility across diverse egocentric manipulation scenarios. Experiments show that EgoACT generates more coherent and physically plausible interaction videos than strong baselines.
authors: Yue Ma, Pengjie Song, Xinyu Wang, Yi He, Zeqian Long, Fangneng Zhan, Kaichen Zhou, Hongyu Liu, Hongfa Wang, Peihao Li, Haoyang Huang, Nan Duan, Qifeng Chen
bullets: Existing condition-guided methods suffer from geometric estimation errors, while motion-only transfer often loses contact dynamics and causes hand collapse.
EgoACT is a test-time framework that operates directly during video-diffusion denoising.
Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring stabilizes hand–object structure early in denoising.
Sparse Correspondence Calibration refines reliable local correspondences in later denoising stages.
EgoActionBench evaluates action preservation, visual quality, and hand–object plausibility; experiments report more coherent and physically plausible videos than strong baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Overview of the proposed framework. Given an egocentric manipulation video, our framework uses a reference branch and an optimized generation branch for test-time action transfer. We apply Velocity-guided Structure Anchoring (VSA) in the early denoising steps to preserve hand-object structure, and Sparse Correspondence Calibration (SCC) in the mid-to-late steps to refine local correspondences and improve interaction realism.

Figure 6. The overview of EgoActionBench. EgoActionBench contains 350 reference manipulation videos and 1,400 target prompts, covering indoor/outdoor scenes, single-/two-hand interactions, and diverse manipulation categories. The benchmark evaluates whether generated videos preserve the reference action semantics while adapting to new visual contexts.

Figure 5. Gallery of proposed method. EgoACT can transfer a wide range of egocentric manipulation videos, covering diverse interaction categories, object types, and motion patterns. The generated videos preserve plausible hand-object structure, contact dynamics, and temporal coherence while adapting the reference action to new visual contexts.

Figure 16. More Comparison with Baseline. Our method consistently produces more coherent action transfer and more plausible handobject interactions than baselines, which often suffer from structural collapse, temporal inconsistency, or physically unrealistic interactions.

Figure 14. Failure case. Our method may struggle with actions involving very fast hand or object motion, which can lead to motion blur, temporal aliasing, or loss of hand-object correspondence. This limitation is primarily due to the base video diffusion model, which was not specifically trained to handle rapid egocentric dynamics and tends to produce temporally smoothed outputs when the inter-frame displacement is large.
Figure 8. Qualitative comparison. Compare with previous methods, our method preserves stable hand-object layout and object response.
Figure 10. More visual results.

Figure 4. Illustration of the proposed SCC. (a) Direct transfer injects the reference action without correction, which may lead to errors in weak hand-object interactions. (b) Applying correction throughout the whole denoising process over-constrains early generation, making it difficult to decouple transferable action from source observation. (c) Our SCC performs sparse correspondence calibration only in the mid-to-late denoising stages, where the action layout has been established and local interaction details can be refined, improving temporal consistency and hand-object realism.
Figure 11. More visual results.
Figure 12. More visual results.

Figure 2. Motivation. Motion transfer suffers from hand structural collapse and lacks physical interaction. Condition-guided generation preserves hand shape but produces physically implausible contact. Our method maintains both hand structure and realistic interaction.
Figure 9. Visual ablation. VSA suppresses structural collapse, while SCC improves local correspondence.

Figure 15. Attention Visualization. We visualize the crossframe attention maps before and after enabling VSA during the early denoising stage. Without VSA, attention is dispersed across irrelevant regions, failing to capture coherent hand-object structure. With VSA enabled, the attention concentrates on interactionrelevant areas such as hand, object, and contact regions, indicating that the generation trajectory is better aligned with the reference structural layout. This confirms that VSA effectively anchors the hand-object skeleton through velocity-guided alignment, resulting in more structurally consistent attention patterns.

papers.abstract: Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) enable fast, flexible last-mile and emergency delivery, but their routing remains challenging as the number of clients varies. Classical approaches based on mixed-integer programming and heuristics can scale poorly or require problem-specific design, motivating learning-based alternatives. Reinforcement learning is particularly promising, provided a single policy can generalize across problem sizes without retraining. Although attention-based Pointer Networks are inherently size-agnostic, their solution quality degrades under both upscaling and downscaling. Using the Capacitated Vehicle Routing Problem (CVRP) as a controlled proxy, with fixed capacity reflecting drone payload constraints, we investigate this degradation and identify three contributing factors: shifts in node density, attention dispersion, and dilution of the mean-pooled graph context. We systematically compare architecture-wide, encoder-side, and decoder-side modifications to address these limitations and propose a learned, permutation-invariant graph-context aggregation mechanism, implemented as a weighted average and as Set2Set. Results reveal distinct requirements for transfer in each direction: entropy-based attention scaling reduces the CVRP20-to-CVRP100 performance gap by 1.41 percentage points, while the proposed aggregation methods achieve the largest improvement on the more challenging CVRP100-to-CVRP20 transfer, approximately 0.9 percentage points. Exploiting this complementarity, we introduce an approach selector that chooses the best model for each training-target size pair. The selector reduces cost relative to the reference model across all nine seen train-test pairs and eight of nine pairs involving unseen sizes (CVRP35, CVRP75, and CVRP200), achieving improvements of up to 3.2 percent.
authors: Sofiene Lassoued, Devara Tertia, Stefan Lier, Andreas Schwung
bullets: Pointer Networks are size-agnostic but lose solution quality when routing problems are scaled up or down.
The study attributes cross-scale degradation to node-density shifts, dispersed attention, and diluted mean-pooled graph context.
It compares architecture-, encoder-, and decoder-level changes, including entropy-based attention scaling and learned permutation-invariant graph-context aggregation.
Attention scaling improves CVRP20-to-CVRP100 transfer by 1.41 percentage points; aggregation methods improve CVRP100-to-CVRP20 transfer by about 0.9 points.
An approach selector lowers routing cost across all nine seen size pairs and eight of nine unseen-size pairs, with improvements up to 3.2%.

papers.abstract: Anticipating how users will interact with their surroundings is essential for proactive systems that provide timely assistance in AR, VR, and embodied applications. Prior work typically forecasts hand-object interactions directly from historical observations, leaving intention and contact geometry implicit. However, similar observation histories can precede semantically or geometrically distinct futures. Inspired by behavioral evidence that gaze can provide early cues for underlying intention, we propose Gaze2HOI, a gaze-aware framework that formulates hand-object interaction forecasting as a hierarchical problem comprising intention inference, contact grounding, and coupled hand-object motion generation. Specifically, Gaze2HOI first weights gaze cues by fixation strength and recency, and uses them to modulate the visual representations of a vision-language model (VLM) through Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation (TGSM), thereby reducing semantic ambiguity in intention inference. Subsequently, an Anticipatory Contact Grounding (ACG) module maps these structured intentions into explicit contact, support, and placement fields, effectively mitigating geometric ambiguity. Driven by these explicit conditions, a diffusion-based model jointly generates the 6-DoF object trajectories and future articulated motion of both hands. To evaluate Gaze2HOI, we further introduce EgoAIM, a phase-aware benchmark that organizes egocentric hand-object interactions into four phases defined by evolving hand-object relations and provides fine-grained intention annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Gaze2HOI achieves state-of-the-art performance in both intention inference and motion forecasting, even approaching oracle-level end-to-end performance in specific interaction phases. Project page: https://gaze2hoi.github.io/.
authors: Chuanyang Ma, Chenye Wang, Yixuan Wang, Huiling Zhou, Xingqun Qi, Muyi Sun, Man Zhang, Caifeng Shan, Zhenan Sun
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in predicting semantically and geometrically distinct futures from similar egocentric observation histories.
Uses fixation strength and recency to modulate a vision-language model via Temporal Gaze Saliency Modulation for intention inference.
Maps intentions to contact, support, and placement fields with Anticipatory Contact Grounding.
Generates 6-DoF object trajectories and articulated motion for both hands using a diffusion-based model.
Introduces the phase-aware EgoAIM benchmark with fine-grained intention annotations; reports state-of-the-art intention and motion forecasting, with near-oracle performance in some phases.

(b) ACG grounds inferred intentions into explicit 3D contact, support, and placement fields. papers.abstract: This paper shows that JEPA-style latent world models (LWMs) can learn across diverse domains and data sources by adopting the language-conditioned interface of video generation models. We establish this approach as an effective and efficient basis for planning with imagination and downstream policy fine-tuning. To this end, we introduce LaLa-World, a Language-conditioned Latent World model that learns from simulation and robot trajectories together with broader image and video data. Two designs make this work. First, we describe both numerical actions and visual changes in language, enabling joint training of a single future predictor across heterogeneous datasets. Second, we build the predictor on a language model, allowing it to interpret language conditions while predicting future latent states. The resulting predictor achieves higher average MPC planning performance than existing LWMs trained separately for each domain or task. Adding image and video data further improves average planning performance and robustness to action phrasing. In a matched comparison with an RAEv2-based video generation model baseline, LaLa-World reaches comparable planning performance with $6\times$ less training cost and $13.9\times$ faster planning. Beyond planning, the pretrained LaLa-World serves as an initialization for LaLa-Policy, which jointly predicts actions and future visual representations. LaLa-Policy performs competitively with Cosmos Policy on LIBERO and RoboCasa, with up to $5.5\times$ faster inference.

Uses language to unify numerical actions and visual changes across heterogeneous data.
Achieves higher average MPC planning performance than domain- or task-specific latent world models.
With additional image/video data, planning robustness to action phrasing improves.
Matches an RAEv2 video-generation baseline with 6× lower training cost and 13.9× faster planning; its policy initialization enables competitive performance with up to 5.5× faster inference.

(b) A single predictor built on a language model uses encoded observations and language conditions to predict future visual representations. Fine-tuning the pretrained LaLa-World yields LaLa-Policy, which predicts actions as well as future visual representations. (c) The jointly trained predictor achieves higher average MPC planning performance than both separately trained LWM baselines and the generative world model baseline, RAEv2. (d) LaLa-Policy performs competitively with our adapted Cosmos Policy baseline on RoboCasa, while reducing average inference time per trajectory by a factor of 5.5×.

Each example shows the initial and goal observations, the predicted rollout under the selected language actions, and planning time. Decoded images from LaLa-World may have lower visual quality because it is not trained for pixel reconstruction. Both models predict plausible future states, while LaLa-World requires less planning time.

Figure 2: MPC planning with language actions. LaLa-World imagines future representations under candidate actions with MPC and selects the most promising action toward the goal. Because all actions share one language interface, a single LaLa-World predictor can plan across multiple domains, despite differences in action dimensionality and physical meaning. The predictor also supports language-based actions without numerical values (bottom two rows), as detailed in Section D.4.3. The visualized observations result from executing the selected actions in the simulator.

Figure 3: Examples of language-conditioned transition data. Each example consists of past observations, a language condition, and the next observation. Language conditions describe either numerical control actions from simulation and robotics or visual changes in images and videos. This shared interface enables training a single LWM across different action spaces and data sources.

papers.abstract: Action-free videos are an appealing substitute for costly teleoperated data. Latent action models (LAMs) turn videos into a supervision signal by inferring abstract actions between frames. Existing LAMs observe a single camera view, which resolves 6D robot actions only ambiguously missing out-of-plane movements and potential occlusions. We propose a LAM that ingests synchronized multi-camera views using cross-attention to resolve depth and occlusions before compressing them into latent actions. The latent actions are fed into a policy in which a latent expert and an action expert are coupled by sequential flow matching around a frozen VLM backbone. We further evaluate in strict cross-embodiment settings where task-specific demonstrations come from other embodiments. We show that dual-view LAM pretraining improves the decodability of ground-truth 6D actions by 17% compared to single-view, while scaling single-view data by two orders of magnitude is not sufficient to fully recover out-of-plane motions. The downstream policy improves success rate by +13.5% compared to +6.2% for single-view LAM. A single cross-embodiment is sufficient for skill transfer, and adding a second viewpoint outperforms adding up to four further embodiments. The results transfer to hardware where demonstrations come from a human hand improving success rate by +20% over action-only policies in 850 rollouts. We show that video and robot data are complementary, and that benefits of learning from video are task-dependent. Website: https://learnsyslab.github.io/multiview_latent_action_pretraining/
authors: Oliver Hausd\"orfer, Felix Minzenmay, Mani Majd, Maximilian P. Christof, Shiyuan Zhang, Angela P. Schoellig
bullets: Single-view latent action models ambiguously infer 6D movements, especially out-of-plane actions and occluded interactions.
The proposed model combines cross-attention over multiple views with sequential flow matching between latent and action experts around a frozen VLM.
Dual-view pretraining improves 6D-action decodability by 17% over single-view and yields a +13.5% downstream success-rate gain versus +6.2% for single-view.
One cross-embodiment source is sufficient for skill transfer; adding a second viewpoint is more beneficial than adding up to four additional embodiments.
Hardware experiments using human-hand demonstrations improve success by 20% over action-only policies across 850 rollouts, with benefits varying by task.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Method: We combine latent action pretraining from in-domain cross-embodiment videos with a downstream flow-matching policy. First, latent actions are inferred from a large cross-embodiment video dataset. Second, a sequential policy is learned on the latent actions and a small set of demonstrations on the target embodiment. The LAM uses a spatio-temporal transformer to merge multiple viewpoints before computing the latents. The spatial block attends to patches of other viewpoints, yielding latent actions grounded in 3D space. Latent action labels and real robot actions are jointly used to train a hierarchical downstream policy. The policy uses sequential flow matching experts and outputs actions applied to the robot.
Fig. 8. Failure modes. Models struggle with object grasping (44% of failure cases). The push task requires precision to align the gripper with the milk.

Fig. 4. Real World Tasks: We evaluate the policies and skill-transfer on six tasks consisting of novel movements, novel background, novel objects, and novel placements. For each eval task, we collect 50 human demonstrations and evaluate under settings with 0–50 robot demonstrations per task. We additionally collect an off-task play dataset across 32 tasks, totaling 1000 human demonstrations and 600 robot demonstrations.

Fig. 3. Left: Latent Action Probing. An MLP probe reconstructs ground-truth robot actions from the latents. Adding the second view improves decodability in the directions that are only ambiguously observed by single-view. Right: Cross-embodiment Learning. t-SNE showing 2D correspondence of latent actions to embodiments. Separation by color indicates separate latent per embodiment before training, while mixed colors show a latent space shared between embodiments. Shared latents already occur for a single cross-embodiment present in pretraining.

Fig. 2. Scaling with Data. Policy success rate (SR) when scaling (left) the number of action-annotated demonstrations per task on the deployed embodiment Franka Panda, (middle) the fraction of LIBERO-90 used as off-task play data for latent video pretraining increasing task diversity. Top row shows mean success rate over all 40 tasks; bottom row split by in-distribution and heldout tasks (see Sec. IV). Successes on heldout tasks prove transfer from crossembodiment video demonstrations. (Right): The number of cross-embodiments contained in the video dataset (1 = iiwa, 2 = +kinova3, 3 = +sawyer, 4 = +ur5e) for single- and dual-view pretraining. Dual-view pretraining outperforms adding up to four cross-embodiments.

Fig. 6. Human to Robot Transfer. Left: We apply the latent action computed on a human frame to a robot frame from an eval rollout not seen during training: both yield the same movement to the right. Right: Motion decoded from the predicted latents for a human and a robot video. Both motions decode into similar motions in robot end-effector space. The multi-view LAM shows significantly better reconstruction of the ground-truth robot motion in y-direction. See more qualitative results in the supplementary video.

Fig. 5. Evaluation: Each datapoint represents 25 rollouts. Left: We observe successes without using any robot data for new tasks. On average, using human demonstrations without any robot demonstrations increases SR by +20%, and with 5 robot demonstrations by +19%. Tasks with novel placement locations ([place]) are easiest to solve, followed by novel objects ([obj]). Middle: Multi-view video pretraining scores 46% against 21% for single-view significantly increasing SR. Right: Scaling of SR with increasing robot demonstrations for one task: video and robot demonstrations are complementary.

papers.abstract: Video generation models are promising foundations for embodied world models, but only if their generated rollouts are physically valid and faithful to task instructions. Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) are increasingly used to judge these properties, yet their agreement with human judgments on embodied videos has not been systematically evaluated. To address this gap, we introduce RoboJudge-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating MLLMs as judges of embodied video generation. The benchmark measures two fundamental dimensions, Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment, across 800 human-annotated videos from 8 source corpora and 10 video generators, spanning grippers, human hands, and dexterous hands. Experiments reveal uneven alignment between existing judges and human ratings: general-purpose MLLMs show lower agreement on physical adherence, while specialized video judges designed for general-domain physical reasoning do not consistently transfer to embodied scenarios. Motivated by these findings, we construct RoboJudge-Train, comprising 12K videos annotated with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales for Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment. We fine-tune a 9B MLLM on this dataset with supervised learning followed by reinforcement learning, yielding RoboJudge-9B. Among the model judges evaluated on RoboJudge-Bench, RoboJudge-9B achieves the highest overall agreement, reaching a Pearson correlation of 0.719 with a statistically significant 0.089 gain over Gemini-3.7-Flash, the best-performing proprietary baseline in our evaluation. Training on RoboJudge-Train also yields gains on external benchmarks, including VideoPhy2 and Physion-Eval. We further use RoboJudge-9B as a downstream evaluator to benchmark video generation models according to Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment.
authors: Siyuan Ma, Yu Qi, Cheng Ye, Ruotian Peng, Xinyi Xu, Zitiantao Lin, Zedong Cai, Yijian Huang, Weiyang Liu, Siyuan Wang, Yandong Wen
bullets: RoboJudge-Bench evaluates MLLM judges on Physical Adherence and Instruction Alignment using 800 human-annotated videos from 8 corpora, 10 generators, and varied hand embodiments.
Existing general-purpose and general-domain video judges show limited or inconsistent agreement with human judgments in embodied scenarios, especially for physical adherence.
RoboJudge-Train contains 12K videos with 25K human-verified scores and model-assisted rationales.
RoboJudge-9B is fine-tuned with supervised learning and reinforcement learning, achieving the highest reported agreement on the benchmark with a Pearson correlation of 0.719.
The trained judge also improves performance on external benchmarks and is used to evaluate video generation models.

papers.abstract: 3D Human Pose Estimation (3D HPE) is used in indoor environments, such as smart homes, to analyze human movement and monitor human states. Millimeter-wave (mmWave) radar is suitable for this task because it is robust to lighting variations and does not capture images of human appearance. However, radar observations often provide insufficient information about certain body parts or contain overlapping reflections from multiple body parts, limiting accurate 3D joint localization. To address these limitations, we propose the Initialization-to-Refinement Pose Framework (I2R-Pose), comprising two stages: Motion-Aware Pose Initialization and Observation-Guided Refinement. In the first stage, joint-wise features are learned by incorporating temporal relationships across consecutive radar observations and human skeletal structure to compensate for insufficient joint information and estimate an initial 3D pose sequence. In the second stage, separately extracted radar observation features predict joint-wise positional corrections that refine the initial pose and generate the final pose sequence. The framework supports individual and fused inputs of time-Doppler/time-range (TD/TR) maps and radar point clouds (PCs). To evaluate performance across indoor activities, we construct the Radar Motion and Spatial Information for 3D Human Pose Estimation (RaMoS-Pose) dataset, providing synchronized TD/TR maps, radar PCs, and 3D joint ground truth (GT). Evaluations on RaMoS-Pose and the publicly available MVDoppler-Pose dataset show that I2R-Pose reduces mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) by 39.50% on MVDoppler-Pose and by 15.13% on RaMoS-Pose with fused inputs, compared with the best-performing existing methods evaluated on each dataset.
authors: Woo-Jin Jung, Chan-Bin Lim, Seung-Hyun Kong
bullets: Addresses missing or overlapping mmWave radar reflections that hinder accurate 3D joint localization.
Uses a two-stage pipeline: motion-aware pose initialization followed by observation-guided joint correction.
Supports TD/TR maps, radar point clouds, and their fusion.
Introduces the RaMoS-Pose dataset with synchronized radar data and 3D joint ground truth.
With fused inputs, reduces MPJPE by 39.50% on MVDoppler-Pose and 15.13% on RaMoS-Pose versus the best evaluated existing methods.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the I2R-Pose framework. The TD/TR-only configuration with two observation views is illustrated as an example. The Motion Branch learns joint-wise features from radar observations, while the Pose Branch sequentially performs initial pose estimation using these features and pose refinement using separately extracted observation features. The GT-based Keypoint Motion Encoder and Keypoint HPE Head are used only during training, and Cross-Modal Motion Feature Alignment guides the learning of joint-wise radar features. For visual clarity, the feature tensors are illustrated with the temporal dimension (T ) along the X-axis, the joint or token dimension (J or NO) along the Y-axis, and the channel dimension (C) along the Z-axis.

Fig. 5. Qualitative comparison of 3D human pose estimation results on (a) MVDoppler-Pose and (b) RaMoS-Pose. The numbers below each estimated pose indicate the MPJPE (mm) for the corresponding frame, with bold values indicating the lowest MPJPE in each row. RGB images in (b) are provided solely for visual reference.

Fig. 1. Conceptual overview of I2R-Pose. In the Motion-Aware Pose Initialization stage, joint-wise features are learned by incorporating temporal relationships across consecutive radar observations (TD/TR maps, PCs, or both) and human skeletal structure to estimate an initial 3D pose sequence. In the subsequent Observation-Guided Refinement stage, radar observation features extracted separately from the same radar input are combined with the joint-wise features used for initial pose estimation to predict joint-wise positional corrections. These corrections are applied to the initial pose to generate the final pose sequence. The refinement process and changes in MPJPE are illustrated using a representative frame, while RGB images are provided solely for visual reference.

Fig. 3. Main feature extraction and representation processes in I2R-Pose. (a) Generation of joint-wise radar motion features through TD/TR feature extraction and Time–Joint Cross-Attention. The illustrated motion features are generated in the Radar Motion Encoder, while the same tokenization structure is independently used in the Radar Observation Encoder with separate weights. papers.abstract: Human-collected real-world robotic manipulation demonstrations often contain mixed-quality trajectories, including hesitant, indirect, or inefficient action segments. While diffusion- and flow-based policies can model such multimodal data, standard behavior cloning (BC) assigns equal likelihood to all demonstrated actions and may therefore reproduce suboptimal modes. Offline RL value estimates offer a natural signal for biasing policies toward higher-value behavioral modes, but directly fine-tuning the generative policy or using critic gradients for policy steering can amplify critic errors and induce prior drift. We propose Advantage-Weighted Latent Steering (AWLS), an offline post-training method for improving frozen one-step generative manipulation policies without updating their decoders. AWLS learns a residual noise shaper, an observation-conditioned residual correction to the policy's latent noise, and trains it with an advantage-weighted action reconstruction objective. The advantages are detached, scale-normalized, and used only as supervised weights on demonstrated actions, avoiding critic-gradient policy updates while preserving fast single-step inference. We further introduce a rollout-free decoder-sensitivity criterion for selecting pretrained checkpoints that remain responsive to latent-noise perturbations. Experiments on simulated and real-world robotic manipulation tasks with clean and mixed-quality demonstrations show that AWLS improves over the frozen base policy while limiting drift from the pretrained behavior prior. Project page: https://awls-corl2026.github.io/
authors: Jiahong Tang, Jiaju He, Zhiyuan Yang, Ruyang Han, Haiyue Zhu
bullets: Addresses mixed-quality demonstrations where standard behavior cloning treats inefficient and high-quality actions equally.
Learns an observation-conditioned residual noise shaper using advantage-weighted action reconstruction.
Detaches and normalizes advantages, using them only as supervised weights to reduce critic-error amplification and prior drift.
Introduces a rollout-free decoder-sensitivity criterion for selecting checkpoints responsive to latent perturbations.
Experiments in simulated and real manipulation tasks with clean and mixed-quality data show improvement over the frozen base policy while preserving fast single-step inference.

Figure 1: Trajectory segments from human-collected robomimic can demonstrations [5], with policy rollouts. Thin dashed lines are demonstration segments from a shared start to the goal, and thick curves are illustrative policy rollouts. Behavior cloning treats every demonstration the same, so its rollouts reproduce the hesitant detours as faithfully as the efficient paths. Q-maximization steering pushes actions toward high-Q estimates (arrows), so its rollouts leave the demonstrated region. AWLS weights demonstrations by advantage (green high, blue low) and reshapes the latent noise of the frozen decoder toward the high-advantage demonstrated mode, so its rollouts follow the efficient paths.

Across every task and at every contamination level, the AWLS variants (green) degrade most gracefully, with MF-AWLS (thickest, dark green) retaining the highest success rate even at 100% low-quality data, whereas the behavior-cloning backbones (gray/blue) fall off fastest. papers.abstract: Connected and Autonomous Vehicles (CAVs) face significant challenges in roundabout navigation due to dense traffic interactions and unpredictable agent behaviors, necessitating high levels of adaptability and safety. While the combination of Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Model Predictive Control (MPC) offers a promising approach, existing frameworks suffer from a structural mismatch where pointwise RL decisions fail to align with MPC's trajectory level optimization, and often lack rigorous safety guarantees. This work proposes RLTrajGen-PPMPC-CBF, a hierarchical framework for safe, smooth and comfort roundabout navigation, which regulates the coupling between RL-based planning and MPC-based control. We employ Prescribed Performance Constraints (PPC) to enforce a gradual, stable convergence between reference trajectories and control outputs, ensuring MPC tracking performance remains consistent with intended behavior from RL. Additionally, a Control Barrier Function (CBF) layer provides real-time safety corrections that are fed back into the RL process. Simulation results in the MetaDrive environment demonstrate that our method achieves a 6.25\% increase in average success rate and a 65.87\% reduction in Motion Sickness Dose Value (MSDV) compared to the optimal baseline, meanwhile accelerating training convergence.

papers.abstract: Learned barrier certificates provide a principled mechanism for establishing safety of stochastic systems, but their validity may deteriorate during deployment when the underlying dynamics differ from those used for training. We propose an anytime-valid runtime monitor that audits a learned barrier certificate using observed closed-loop trajectories. The monitor is intended to detect loss of statistical support for the deployed barrier condition; it does not by itself guarantee detection before unsafe entry or safety of a subsequent intervention. Specifically, the conditional barrier-drift condition is formulated as an episode-wise sequential hypothesis test, and observed barrier increments are transformed into a nonnegative test supermartingale, yielding finite-sample false-alarm control under arbitrary stopping times. Inspired by finite-horizon safety verification, we further introduce a deterministic temporal shaping of the monitoring boundary, making the monitor more conservative early in a prescribed deployment horizon while preserving anytime-validity. The monitor is designed to detect statistical evidence that the safety certificate is no longer consistent with the observed dynamics, rather than to predict unsafe entry. To assess the monitor empirically, we evaluate empirical alarm behavior under valid and invalid certificates. Code and data are available at https://github.com/FormalCert-AI/runtime-barrier-monitor.
authors: Zhipeng Cao, Taoran Wu, Weiru Cui, Luke Ong, Bai Xue

papers.abstract: Long-horizon human-object-scene interaction (HOSI) is central to embodied AI, animation, and game development. Existing human-object interaction (HOI) and human-scene interaction (HSI) models excel in their respective domains, but none alone covers tasks requiring multiple interaction skills. Training unified HOSI models is hindered by scarce and costly data. We introduce World2HOSI, a multi-expert orchestration harness that generates continuous HOSI data from 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes and natural language instructions. Our key insight is that long-horizon HOSI hinges not on a stronger single model but on orchestration. Given a shared, structured scene state and an orchestration harness grounded in it, existing experts can jointly accomplish tasks beyond the reach of any of them alone. World2HOSI realizes this insight as a closed loop around a persistent scene state built from decoupled background and object assets. A harness plans action stages over this state, invokes experts via their native conditioning interfaces, and writes each action's effects back, so that every invocation is grounded in the evolving world. To reduce physical artifacts, bounded residual optimization and contact-driven physics simulation further ensure the physical plausibility of human motion and object manipulation, respectively, while preserving interaction intent. Experiments and a perceptual user study show that World2HOSI achieves the best task completion and interaction quality on the evaluated HOSI tasks, while generating more diverse data.

papers.abstract: Semantic occupancy mapping supports embodied perception during exploration and detailed scene understanding afterward, giving rise to two complementary requirements: online incremental mapping for maintaining an up-to-date global map under causal constraints, and offline global map refinement for improving the completed scene representation with additional computation. We present VEOcc++, a unified voxel-centric framework that connects both stages through a persistent sparse voxel feature map. During exploration, the map expands with newly observed regions and integrates aligned local features through reliability-guided updates, while context-aware decoding produces the current semantic occupancy map. After exploration, cached local features are consolidated as complementary evidence and combined with the completed online representation for multi-scale spatial refinement. On EmbodiedOcc-ScanNet, VEOcc++ achieves 67.12\% IoU and 58.40\% mIoU, establishing new state-of-the-art performance for online incremental mapping. With the local predictor fixed, our online mapping pipeline outperforms VEOcc fusion by 3.70 IoU and 3.74 mIoU points, demonstrating substantial gains from the proposed global mapping design. Offline global map refinement further improves the completed map to 67.79% IoU and 59.37% mIoU using only the observations acquired during exploration. Zero-shot deployment on a mobile robot further demonstrates transferability to unseen environments, onboard feasibility, and scalability to large-scale indoor mapping. Project page: https://wryzju.github.io/VEOccpp/.
authors: Ruoyu Wang, Jiahan Li, Yong Liu, Kexin Zhang

Demonstrates transfer to unseen environments, onboard feasibility, and scalable indoor mapping on a mobile robot.

papers.abstract: 3D scene graphs support language-guided navigation by organizing physical entities and their containment and spatial relations into hierarchical maps. Building such structured maps requires a scene representation that consistently distinguishes semantic regions and object instances across viewpoints. To this end, we present PanoGraphGS, a unified framework that integrates panoptic 3D Gaussian representation learning with hierarchical 3D scene graph construction. The framework learns semantic and instance features on shared Gaussian geometry. Prototype-based semantic learning and association-based instance learning produce consistent panoptic predictions across viewpoints. The learned representation supports novel-view panoptic segmentation and direct Gaussian-level panoptic decoding. A semantic-aware scene graph module further recovers a floor-room-stuff-object hierarchy with containment and spatial relations. We further release NaviGS, a real-world dataset for panoramic scene understanding. The dataset provides 3DGS, mesh, RGB, semantic, and depth data. For 3D scene graph identification, PanoGraphGS outperforms the strongest evaluated baseline in object-node accuracy by more than 50\% points on average across Replica and NaviGS. PanoGraphGS also achieves state-of-the-art performance among the evaluated methods in 2D panoptic segmentation. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of PanoGraphGS in both hierarchical 3D scene understanding and 2D panoptic segmentation. The project website is available at: https://github.com/gaojh0333/PanoGraphGS.

papers.abstract: Simulation-ready world reconstruction demands physical interactivity beyond visual realism, which existing black-box 3D generation fails to deliver. We present NeoWorld-3, a coding-agent framework that reconstructs interactive 3D worlds from visual observations via tunable, executable programs. At its core, NeoSDK provides the underlying computational engine for low-level geometries, part composition, differentiable parameter refinement, and physics validation. At the same time, NeoMCP exposes these capabilities as structured, tool-callable APIs for vision-language agents to visually inspect, edit code, and iteratively refine programs. Through a hierarchical coordinator-worker architecture, the framework scales seamlessly from standalone articulated objects to complex compositional scenes. Evaluations across object-level and scene-level reconstruction benchmarks demonstrate that NeoWorld-3 achieves state-of-the-art geometric fidelity and physical readiness. Crucially, manipulation trajectories planned within our reconstructed twins achieve successful zero-shot execution on a physical dual-arm robot, completing the Real-Sim-Real loop.
authors: Eachen Soong, Zijian Niu, Haoran Xu, Yihong Dong, Yunbo Wang, Xiaokang Yang

A hierarchical coordinator-worker design scales from articulated objects to complex scenes.

Object- and scene-level feedback loops guide reconstruction and revision, producing simulation-ready scenes for sim-based policy optimization and sim-to-real deployment.

papers.abstract: Bipedal humanoids can change their effective footprint by adjusting body yaw, enabling both narrow-passage traversal and socially aware yielding. This paper presents a posture-aware navigation framework centered on \emph{Adaptive Traversal Tubes} (ATT), \emph{Interval Velocity--Heading} (IVH) control, and a sidestep-enhanced AMP locomotion prior. ATT represents a behavior-feasible corridor width field along a reference path, unifying geometric clearance and social comfort into a continuous signal. IVH maps this width to a continuous frontal-to-sidestep posture schedule and omnidirectional velocity commands. A velocity-conditioned AMP policy, trained with GVHMR-retargeted frontal/sidestep motions and coupled \((v_x,v_y)\) tracking rewards, is designed to improve transition stability over a generic locomotion controller while remaining interchangeable with the default onboard policy. This preprint presents the full method; a planned evaluation protocol on a Unitree G1 is outlined, with quantitative results to follow. Demo videos of MuJoCo simulation and real-robot deployment are available at: github.com/lborogzj997/Humanoid-Navigation-in-Crowds-and-Narrow-Spaces.
bullets: Adaptive Traversal Tubes represent behavior-feasible corridor width, combining geometric clearance with social comfort.
Interval Velocity–Heading control converts corridor width into continuous posture transitions and omnidirectional velocity commands.
A sidestep-enhanced, velocity-conditioned AMP locomotion prior uses retargeted motions and coupled planar-velocity tracking.
The method is presented with MuJoCo and real-robot demonstrations, while quantitative evaluation on a Unitree G1 is planned.
Quantitative results are not yet reported in the abstract.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. System overview. Mid-360 LiDAR localization supports global A* and local Hybrid A* planning. ATT builds a behavior-feasible width field w(s) along the reference path from geometric clearance and social comfort; IVH maps w(s) to a frontal–sidestep heading schedule and body-frame (vx, vy , ωz) for a sidestep-enhanced AMP locomotion policy. Offline, GVHMR+GMR provide frontal/sidestep reference motions for AMP training; a generic onboard controller remains a compatible fallback.

Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed idea. Top: ATT width field (green→ red as the tube narrows) for a geometric squeeze-through (left) and social comfort compression (right). Bottom: corresponding real-robot behaviors on a Unitree G1, where IVH schedules a frontal-to-sidestep posture response.

Fig. 3. Qualitative illustration of the intended behaviors on a Unitree G1 (not a quantitative benchmark). (a) Socially aware pedestrian encounter: comfortspace compression narrows the tube and IVH schedules a frontal-to-sidestep yield. (b) Narrow-corridor traversal: geometric clearance shrinks w(s) at the gap, triggering a sidestep squeeze-through and recovery to frontal gait. Controlled comparisons against a frontal-only baseline are left to the evaluation protocol in Section IV.

papers.selection_reason: Posture-aware navigation for bipedal humanoids with adaptive traversal tubes and learned locomotion prior; fits embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: Adaptive Traversal Tubes for Posture-Aware Navigation of Bipedal Humanoids
papers.tldr: A posture-aware navigation framework enables bipedal humanoids to adapt body orientation and locomotion between frontal walking and sidestepping for narrow passages and socially comfortable navigation.

papers.abstract: In object goal navigation (ObjectNav), an embodied agent must find a target object (e.g., "find a bed") in a previously unseen environment, relying on spatial commonsense such as object co-occurrence. Large Language Models (LLMs) encode this commonsense, but deploying them on robots exposes a trade-off between reasoning quality and efficiency: cloud-based models incur latency and privacy risks, whereas small on-device LLMs are fast but prone to hallucinated spatial judgments. Hybrid reasoning LLMs offer both a fast non-thinking mode and a slow thinking mode, which raises a key question for embodied agents: when is slow thinking worth its cost? We propose CovNav, a training-free framework that answers this question with Conformal Prediction (CP), turning dual-process (System 1 / System 2) inference into an uncertainty-aware decision. Much like recent decision models such as Jev, CovNav casts each spatial query as a structured binary decision rather than free-form generation: a local LLM in fast mode judges whether the target is likely near an observed object, CP converts its token probabilities into a prediction set, and only ambiguous queries are escalated to slow chain-of-thought reasoning. The object-pair formulation keeps calibration tractable and supports open-set objects through off-the-shelf detectors. Experiments on Gibson and HM3D show that CovNav surpasses the strongest zero-shot baseline by 0.8 and 1.7 percentage points in success rate on HM3D v1 and v2, while invoking slow reasoning for only 12.4% of queries and retaining most of the gain of always-on thinking at a fraction of its latency. Real-robot experiments on a TurtleBot 4 further validate the approach. CovNav shows how calibrated uncertainty can decide when an embodied agent should think slowly, offering a principled form of adaptive test-time reasoning for LLM-based robots.
authors: Pengying Wu, Zhejia Wen, Kang Ding, Kangjie Zhou, Chunxuan Jiao, Wei Pan, Xiangli Nie, Chang Liu
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–reliability trade-off between fast, error-prone on-device reasoning and slower, more capable thinking.
A fast local LLM makes binary object-pair proximity judgments; conformal prediction identifies ambiguous cases for escalation to chain-of-thought reasoning.
The training-free design supports open-set objects detected by off-the-shelf detectors and keeps calibration tractable.
On Gibson and HM3D, CovNav improves HM3D success by 0.8 and 1.7 percentage points over the strongest zero-shot baseline while using slow reasoning for 12.4% of queries.
TurtleBot 4 experiments further validate the approach in real-robot navigation.

figures.caption: Fig. 6. Visualization of Real World Experiments. The figure depicts the navigation trajectory of the TurtleBot 4 platform (setup shown in top-left) searching for a toy. The system dynamically switches between Fast and Slow modes based on uncertainty. During the initial approach (Steps 11-27), the agent operates in Fast Mode for efficient exploration. At Step 42, high uncertainty at a semantic transition triggers the Slow Mode, enabling the agent to infer the correct path into the bedroom. The agent then reverts to Fast Mode (Step 60) and successfully localizes the target (Step 73). This demonstrates the efficacy of the adaptive fast-slow inference mechanism in handling real-world ambiguities.

Fig. 1. We propose a Conformal Prediction (CP)-guided fast-slow inference paradigm for object goal navigation using Qwen3-8B as the local LLM. CP monitors the local LLM’s output confidence to adaptively switch Qwen between its fast direct inference mode and slow deliberative reasoning mode. Clear Case: When observing a bathtub, Qwen confidently predicts a toilet will be nearby (logits: 0.9 vs 0.1), so CP accepts the fast direct inference. Ambiguous Case: When observing a sofa and querying about a bed, Qwen shows low confidence (logits: 0.6 vs 0.4), so CP triggers its slow deliberative reasoning mode for more reliable spatial analysis.

Fig. 5. Comparison of Logit Distributions. (a) Uncalibrated logits from the Fast Mode showing high uncertainty. (b) Calibrated logits after adaptive slowmode deliberation, showing a clean separation and higher confidence in the correct association.

papers.title: CovNav: Conformal Prediction-Guided Adaptive Inference for Object Goal Navigation

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models generate robot actions from visual observations and language instructions, but effective manipulation also requires anticipating how the environment will change. Existing world-action models explore future image prediction and latent dynamics modeling. However, generating complete future images can be computationally expensive, while highly compressed latent representations may obscure local changes. To address these challenges, we propose PLaCA, a world-to-action framework built around future latent change. PLaCA directly predicts spatially structured patch-level future latent change from the current multimodal input, preserving local information about expected environmental changes. We introduce patch-level change-aware supervision to emphasize regions undergoing larger changes and a future-to-action interface that explicitly incorporates predicted future latent change into action generation. Experiments on LIBERO-Long show that PLaCA achieves a 79.0% success rate, improving upon the Action-only baseline by 5.0 percentage points. On CALVIN, PLaCA improves the average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564. These improvements are achieved while updating only 2.95% of the model parameters during the second training stage, demonstrating the effectiveness of future latent change modeling for downstream robotic manipulation.
authors: Zhan Yi, Yuchen Wang, Chao Li, Lei Hong, Boyuan Yang
bullets: Addresses the cost of full future-image prediction and the loss of local detail in heavily compressed latent dynamics.
Predicts spatially structured future latent changes from visual and language inputs.
Uses change-aware supervision to emphasize regions expected to change most.
Feeds predicted future changes into action generation through a future-to-action interface.
Achieves 79.0% success on LIBERO-Long and raises CALVIN average sequence length from 2.784 to 3.564, while updating 2.95% of parameters in the second training stage.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of our world-to-action framework. The shared multimodal backbone produces action-query representations, from which a future-change decoder predicts patch-level future latent change. During training, a frozen visual encoder provides change-aware supervision using current and future observations. The predicted future latent change is then incorporated into the action representation through a gated future-to-action interface to generate the full action chunk. Future observations are not required during inference.

Figure 3. Patch-level future latent change and change-aware supervision. (a) A frozen visual encoder extracts patch-level features from current and future observations. Their differences at corresponding patch locations define the ground-truth future latent change ∆Z∗ t , preserving the spatial structure across camera views. (b) The magnitude of each ground-truth change vector is used to compute patch-wise supervision weights, assigning larger relative weights to patches with greater changes. (c) The predicted future latent change ∆̂Zt is supervised against ∆Z∗ t using weighted regression and directional losses. All patches contribute to the training objective with different weights.

Figure 1. Motivation for spatially structured future latent change. (a) In robotic manipulation, future changes are often concentrated around the robot arm and manipulated objects, while much of the background remains unchanged. (b) Highly compressed state representations do not explicitly preserve the spatial locations of these changes, whereas patch-level future latent change retains their spatial structure and provides future information for action generation.
Figure 4. Per-task success rates on LIBERO-Long. Comparison between the Action-only baseline and PLaCA across all 10 tasks, with 20 closed-loop rollouts per task.

Table 1. Comparison on LIBERO-Long. Params denotes the reported model size. Results from prior methods are taken from their respective papers. † PDF uses a 7B OpenVLA backbone with an additional 9M trainable parameters.

Table 3. Ablation studies of PLaCA on LIBERO-Long. Patch Grid denotes the spatial resolution of the future latent representation. Uniform and Change-aware indicate the patch-wise supervision weighting scheme. F2A denotes the future-to-action interface.
Table 2. Results on CALVIN ABC→D. ASL denotes the average number of consecutively completed subtasks per five-task sequence.

papers.tldr: PLaCA improves robot manipulation by predicting patch-level future latent changes and using them to generate actions.

papers.abstract: Handheld demonstration devices decouple data collection from the robot, but conventional designs burden the hand with a wrist camera, cables and a pose tracker (SLAM, an IMU, a VR controller, or a fixed external camera that the collector's body occludes), and burden the pipeline with as many data streams to timestamp, synchronise and cross-calibrate. We show that a single egocentric camera (USD 122) worn on the collector's head replaces the wrist camera, the pose tracker and their separate streams with one. It reads printed fiducials on an electronics-free glove (USD 22) against paper tiles taped around the workspace, giving the 6-DoF gripper pose and the jaw width from the same frames the policy will see; at deployment the same camera rides a low-cost (USD 120) arm beside the robot that mimics the collector's head from the robot's joint state. Against the robot's encoders the labels are accurate to 6.5 mm and 1.6 degrees median with 93-100% frame coverage, and a policy trained on them instead of encoders pays 3% in validation loss. Adding 194 glove demonstrations to 48 teleoperated episodes lifts rollout success from 10/25 to 17/25, level with 172 teleoperated episodes alone (18/25), and the full co-trained head-camera policy succeeds in 20/25 against 15/25 for the wrist-camera recipe, whose policies drop the object when the goal leaves their view, and 12/25 for a fixed camera.
authors: Yosub Shin, Yuan Liu, Igor Molybog
bullets: Replaces wrist cameras, pose trackers, cables, and separate synchronization streams with one egocentric head camera.
Printed glove markers and workspace tiles recover 6-DoF gripper pose and jaw width from deployment-relevant images.
Labels achieve 6.5 mm median position error, 1.6° orientation error, and 93–100% frame coverage against robot encoders.
Adding 194 glove demonstrations improves rollout success from 10/25 to 17/25, while co-training reaches 20/25.
The approach depends on visible fiducials and a robot-mounted camera that mimics the collector’s head motion.

figures.caption: Figure 1: One camera, two mounts. (a) The collector wears the camera and holds the electronicsfree glove over the tiled workspace. (b) The camera’s own frame: tiles (green), ball (red) and jaw tags (blue, yellow) give the pose and the jaw width. (c) The same camera on a six-joint positioner beside the robot during a rollout. The wrist fisheye on the glove and the fixed camera on the post serve the ablations only.

Table 1: The eight policies. Teleop labels are encoders except arm 6. Val = ACT loss on 6 held-out teleoperated episodes with encoder targets. Rollouts: 25 placements, one trial each, 60 s budget; n = no grasp, d = dropped before the bin, b = dropped at the bin, t = timeout.

papers.title: A Head Camera Is (Almost) All You Need: An Electronics-Free UMI Glove Labelled and Observed by One Moving Camera
papers.tldr: A head-mounted camera and electronics-free fiducial glove provide accurate, low-cost robot demonstrations using a single synchronized visual stream.

papers.abstract: Visual manuals communicate procedural knowledge through stepwise diagrams, but translating these instructions into reliable long-horizon robotic execution remains challenging. We introduce JARVIS, a method-agnostic benchmark for autonomous visual-manual-guided execution without additional language instructions. JARVIS comprises 236,679 LEGO assembly tasks across 8,987 scenes, with a carefully curated JARVIS-v1 suite of 50 tasks for interactive robotic evaluation. Tasks span varying initial structural complexities and assembly horizons, requiring agents to interpret manuals, ground actions in an evolving workspace, and execute the intended procedure. A structure-aware evaluation protocol captures geometric accuracy, structural relations, construction order, partial progress, and completion. We further introduce JARVIS-agentic, a tool-grounded embodied agent that composes robot primitives into executable programs and uses execution feedback for verification and recovery, without task-specific action trajectories or model parameter updates. Across nine multimodal and reasoning models, task-oriented primitives increase the average assembly score. Performance nevertheless declines sharply with assembly horizon, and execution errors remain difficult to correct. Prior-task experience improves initial performance, while repeated reflection provides inconsistent benefits, highlighting persistent limitations in connecting visual procedural reasoning with reliable physical execution.
authors: Fan Ding, Fucai Ke, Kevin Yuchen Ma, Xuewen Luo, Wenyu Liang, Vishnu Monn Baskaran, Hamid Rezatofighi, Yan Wu
bullets: Introduces a method-agnostic benchmark for autonomous assembly from visual manuals without extra language instructions.
Includes 236,679 tasks across 8,987 scenes and a 50-task interactive evaluation suite, JARVIS-v1.
Evaluates geometric accuracy, structural relations, construction order, partial progress, and completion.
JARVIS-agentic composes robot primitives into programs and uses execution feedback for verification and recovery without parameter updates.
Across nine multimodal and reasoning models, task-oriented primitives improve average assembly scores, but performance drops with longer horizons and repeated reflection is inconsistent.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of the benchmark construction and evaluation pipeline. Visual LEGO instructions are first aligned with their corresponding 3D structural models. Long construction procedures are then decomposed into consecutive, self-contained episodes, each defined by an initial state, a set of required bricks, and a target state. These episodes are instantiated as physically interactive robotic assembly environments in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. During evaluation, a method observes the current scene, produces robot actions, and receives updated observations through closed-loop interaction. Performance is measured from the resulting construction state using the proposed Soft Score.
Figure 2: Overview of JARVIS-V1. The framework integrates multimodal task context, agentic code generation, simulation execution, evaluation, and self-reflection in a closed-loop assembly process.
Figure 1: Overview of the visual planning, execution, and reflection workflow in JARVIS.

Figure 9: No-reflection execution comparison on Task 000003. The numbered frames show representative stages from the initial scene through grasping and transfer to the final state. Although both models generate executable manipulation sequences, unintended collisions with surrounding LEGO bricks disturb the existing structure and cause bricks to shift or scatter. Without visual feedback and corrective replanning, the resulting scene deviation persists until termination, yielding soft scores of 0.43 for Claude Opus-4.5 and 0.00 for GPT-5.1.

papers.abstract: Visual navigation in cluttered environments requires robots to recover previously observed structure and infer obstacles and free space that remain occluded. We present a framework that combines temporal aggregation and occupancy completion in an evidential bird's-eye-view (BEV) representation predicted from short RGB sequences. A decoder adapts frozen VGGT-Omega features and combines historical residual proposals using cellwise weights and a learned no-update option. The BEV predictor produces a local map in the latest ego frame without depth or camera-pose inputs or explicit geometric warping. The evidential model treats observed free space separately and predicts occupancy with associated confidence across the remaining supported region. We train the predictor on simulated RGB sequences paired with complete and visibility-masked occupancy annotations. Our experiments evaluate navigation in simulation and on a wheeled robot, with additional demonstrations on quadruped and humanoid robots. In simulated sequential two-goal navigation, our system achieves 89.6% success, outperforming the strongest evaluated baseline by 32.5 percentage points. Across 60 wheeled-robot trials in 20 scenes, it achieves 73.3% success, compared with 33.3% for the strongest evaluated baseline.
authors: Diwen Liu, Yiyang Shao, Borui Wang, Chi Zhang, Yunhui Liu
bullets: Addresses navigation failures caused by occlusions and previously observed but currently hidden structure.
Aggregates temporal RGB observations with frozen VGGT-Omega features, historical residual proposals, cellwise weighting, and a learned no-update option.
Predicts a local ego-frame BEV occupancy map without depth, camera poses, or explicit geometric warping.
Separately models observed free space and predicts occupancy with confidence over the supported region.
Achieves 89.6% simulated sequential two-goal success and 73.3% success across 60 wheeled-robot trials in 20 scenes.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed framework. Frozen VGGT-Omega features from an RGB window are adapted into feature pyramids and frame memories. Historical residual proposals refine a latest-frame BEV anchor through cellwise selective fusion with a learned no-update option. Observation-aware evidential heads produce occupancy, spatial support, and confidence. Right: predicted occupancy with paths to example goals, planned path projections into the latest RGB view, and uncertainty 1− cj .

Fig. 3. Qualitative BEV comparison on a common 10× 10 m grid. Rows (a)–(c) show Gibson, HM3D, and HSSD examples, respectively. We compare our method with VGGT-Omega, DiScene, SplatSSC, OccAnt-RGB, and OccAnt-RGBD. All methods use RGB observations; OccAnt-RGBD additionally receives depth. In the predicted maps, dark blue, blue-gray, and off-white denote occupied, free, and unknown cells, respectively.

papers.selection_reason: Visual navigation via evidential BEV occupancy completion from RGB history; strongly relevant to embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: EchoNav: Evidential BEV Completion from Historical Observations for Visual Navigation
papers.tldr: EchoNav reconstructs occluded obstacles and free space from short RGB histories using evidential BEV completion, improving visual navigation in simulation and on a wheeled robot.

papers.abstract: Can embodied task agents use tactile experience to perform fine manipulation without task-specific model training? We investigate this capability through Tactile-ETA, a system that incorporates tactile experience into an embodied task agent through in-context learning. Successful expert demonstrations show how contact changes during manipulation. We pair each recorded robot movement with its camera views and bilateral tactile observations. We keep tactile observations at the start and end of each movement and add two neighboring time points when the tactile images change markedly in between. The agent combines these demonstrations with current vision, tactile observations, and proprioception to select actions through general-purpose robot tools, without updating model parameters. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, adding tactile observations to the same two expert demonstrations increases average success from 15.75% to 24.00%, with current sensing and execution interfaces held fixed. Further experiments show that performance depends on the sensory content and representation of demonstrations, while comparing agent models on Lift Bottle reveals substantial differences under the same system configuration. On the real-robot tasks, demonstrations with aligned visual and tactile observations increase the task success rate from 0% to 60%. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of using tactile experience in context for fine manipulation and suggest a path toward extending embodied task agents to additional sensory inputs.
authors: Yubang Wang, Zezheng Huai, Yifei Zhang, Jinhao Wu, Yitong Chen, Haozhe Zhang, Sixian Li, Jingjing Gong, Zhenyang Lin, Ziyang Chen, Xipeng Qiu
bullets: Tactile-ETA pairs robot movements with visual, bilateral tactile, and proprioceptive observations from expert demonstrations.
The agent selects actions using these demonstrations and current sensory inputs without updating model parameters.
Across four simulated tasks, adding tactile observations raised average success from 15.75% to 24.00%.
On real-robot tasks, aligned visual-tactile demonstrations increased success from 0% to 60%.
Performance depends on demonstration content and representation, and varies substantially across agent models.​​​​

figures.caption: Figure 4 Intermediate tactile information missed by endpoint-only sampling. Columns show the start, a selected intermediate frame, and the end of an Insert Tube demonstration segment, with synchronized RGB observations above and right-fingertip tactile images below. Although the endpoint tactile patterns look similar, the intermediate frame exhibits a wider blue band in the highlighted region. Endpoint-only sampling omits this intermediate pattern, whereas Selected retains it in the demonstration context. Green boxes and arrows identify the same image region for comparison. papers.abstract: Omnidirectional cameras provide surround-view information, significantly overcoming the field-of-view constraints for traditional visual localization systems. However, existing localization systems fail to fully exploit the characteristics of omnidirectional cameras, struggling to deliver accurate and robust localization performance amidst scene content variations and illumination-induced appearance changes. In this work, we propose OmniVLoc, a surround-view localization system based on a topo-metric framework. By integrating state-of-the-art global place recognition and monocular depth estimation methods, we introduce a multi-constrained visual localization paradigm. By solving a scale-aware pose graph and performing precise spherical bundle adjustment, we accurately recover the metric-level pose for each query frame.Furthermore, a hierarchical verification mechanism is designed to filter out erroneous outputs across different stages, effectively bolstering the overall system robustness. Extensive experiments on both public and our custom datasets validate the superior accuracy and reliability of OmniVLoc. To benefit the community, our source code and dataset will be made publicly available upon publication.

papers.abstract: A failed gaming trajectory reveals that an agent needs intervention, but not necessarily how its execution harness should change. Effective harness adaptation therefore requires gathering diagnostic evidence, rather than merely proposing alternative recovery rules. We present KPHarness, a framework that adapts the external execution harness of a frozen vision-language-action model through knowledge-probing co-evolution. Recovery knowledge supplies context-specific intervention hypotheses that guide active probing; probe outcomes reveal when these hypotheses apply and provide evidence for refining both recovery knowledge and later probe selection. This reciprocal process allows the harness to improve not only which interventions it applies, but also how it investigates failures. KPHarness separates fast policy execution from a slow research loop that translates accumulated knowledge and probing evidence into bounded harness revisions. Each revision is compared with the incumbent under matched sandbox conditions and accepted only when the paired evaluation shows improvement. Recoveries supported by further validation are retained for cross-task reuse, while immediate interaction feedback and delayed episode-success credit update action- and knowledge-probing policies during adaptation. Experiments on Minecraft tasks spanning mining, combat, and crafting show improved task coverage over bare policy execution, a manually specified fixed harness, and knowledge-only harness evolution with non-adaptive probing. Evaluation on previously unseen tasks further shows improved task completion with the evolved harness, knowledge bank, and probing policies held fixed,

papers.abstract: In real-time autonomous field applications, GNSS is often unreliable and inaccurate. A possible solution is localizing against a prebuilt map like a satellite image, as it is georeferenced and already surveyed. In this work, we localize a spinning radar measurement against overhead RGB imagery with a learned observation model. We use a radar representation pretrained by masked reconstruction and align it to features from a satellite image. A particle filter propagated by radar odometry proposes candidate poses, and our observation model provides a likelihood over these poses. We evaluate our method over 31 distinct routes, over 8 datasets spanning both urban and offroad conditions using only ground radar and a coarse local prior. We also examine the robustness over changing weather using repeated traversals over the same route over 13 months, in both urban and offroad conditions.

papers.abstract: The development of embodied models of animal behavior is a major goal of the neuro-AI community. Embodied models will enhance our ability to make direct comparisons between biological and artificial agents. To make such comparisons effective, though, we need embodied models that actually move like animals. Previous work has developed virtual animal bodies and techniques for training realistic motion through imitation. However, to date, there is no system for embodied animal modeling that produces natural movements both during trained goal-directed behavior, and during exploration driven by random generation. Here, we introduce Simulated Control via Augmented Motor Priors for Embodied Reinforcement learning (SCAMPER), a system for training an embodied virtual rat model, enabling natural movements during both goal-directed behavior and random exploration. SCAMPER uses a variational architecture with two distinct priors, a motion prior for control and a behavior prior for exploration. We show that combining both of these priors allows SCAMPER to generate realistic behavior during exploration and exploit the task structure effectively. SCAMPER can also learn from sparse rewards as a result of the diverse movements induced by the behavior prior, allowing the system to model realistic sparse-reward tasks from experimental neuroscience. Altogether, SCAMPER provides the neuro-AI community with an effective new system for training embodied models of rodents on realistic tasks.
