papers.abstract: Underwater robots support a growing range of work, from inspecting offshore structures and pipelines to surveying reefs and accompanying divers. Most of these tasks, however, are still flown by hand by a pilot, which raises the question of whether they can be carried out autonomously instead. On land, vision-language-action (VLA) models already let robots carry out tasks autonomously from language instructions, which makes them a natural candidate for taking the pilot's place. Underwater, however, there is little data to train such models. We take inspiration from how these tasks are flown today: the pilot watches the camera image and steers with a joystick, whose commands the flight controller turns into motion. We therefore record the pilots and introduce AQUAACT, to our knowledge the first publicly available language-annotated underwater dataset pairing camera images with human joystick commands. It comprises 1.9 hours of real-world and 17.9 hours of simulated demonstrations, both flown by human pilots, together with the vehicle's inertial measurements. Experiments with AQUAACT show that its simulated demonstrations transfer to real data and greatly reduce the real demonstrations a policy needs. A closed-loop benchmark of seven policies in simulation, from imitation-learning baselines to VLA models, each trained with its default recipe, shows that these tasks remain far from solved: no policy completes more than a fifth of the episodes. Pretraining on land data gives large VLA models no advantage over small policies trained from scratch, a gap that land-trained models have yet to close underwater.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has enabled sample-efficient learning of continuous control policies from high-dimensional observations through learned latent dynamics models. These models are typically trained with observation reconstruction objectives, which provide strong supervision but can bias representations toward visual fidelity leading to an undertrained prior and unreliable long-horizon predictions. We propose a stochastic gating mechanism that induces controlled partial observability during training by sampling a spatial binary mask from a Beta--Bernoulli random field and applying it to the raw observation. The gate probability is resampled at each time step, exposing the encoder to conditions ranging from near-total occlusion to near-full visibility. Integration of our method requires minimal architectural changes from existing dynamics models: the gated observation and the binary mask are channel-wise concatenated and passed to the encoder as a single augmented input, with no modifications to the broader training pipeline. We evaluate the proposed approach on a set of pixel-based continuous control tasks selected from the DeepMind Control Suite. Using model predictive control for evaluation, which relies solely on open-loop model rollouts, we show that stochastic gating improves planning performance and data efficiency across tasks. Further analysis demonstrates that performance is robust to the spatial scale of the mask, and a balanced observability during training outperforms configurations biased toward either sparser or denser observations.
bullets: Observation reconstruction can overemphasize visual fidelity, weakening latent priors and long-horizon predictions.
A Beta–Bernoulli spatial mask stochastically occludes observations with varying visibility at each timestep.
The masked observation and binary mask are concatenated as encoder input, requiring minimal architectural changes.
Across pixel-based DeepMind Control Suite tasks, model-predictive control with open-loop rollouts shows improved planning performance and data efficiency.
Balanced observability performs better than training focused mainly on sparse or dense observations; results are robust to mask scale.

papers.abstract: Bimanual manipulation with dexterous hands has attracted growing attention in research on robotic action models. However, few studies have developed benchmarks specifically tailored for dexterous manipulation, leaving the dexterous manipulation capabilities of existing models insufficiently characterized. In this paper, we present BiDex-100, a simulation benchmark for bimanual dexterous manipulation that combines broad task coverage, multi-dimensional evaluation, and high-DoF hand embodiments. Concretely, the benchmark comprises 106 tasks organized along five capability axes: generalization, instruction following, limited demonstrations, long horizon, and memory. Each task is paired with an out-of-domain variant featuring controlled visual and spatial changes, allowing systematic assessment of robustness. In addition, the benchmark supports two embodiments and provides 8,080 success-validated teleoperated demonstrations, totaling 6.25 million frames. We evaluate seven recent Vision-Language-Action models under a unified protocol, establishing baselines for capability-specific performance, robustness, and data efficiency. The website is available at https://BiDex-100.github.io/BiDex-100/.

papers.abstract: Classical robot control, Finite State Machines and Behavior Trees (BTs), is deterministic and inspectable but fixed at design time: it fails on situations its designers did not anticipate. Foundation models can synthesize new control logic at runtime, at a cost in latency and non-determinism hard to accept in safety-critical aerial systems. Existing LLM-driven approaches keep the model in the loop permanently and discard what it produces. We propose Self-Crystallizing Behavior Trees (SCBT), in which the foundation model is a compiler rather than a runtime. When a BT node fails, an LLM proposes a minimal, mission-agnostic subtree patch; CMA-ES tunes its parameters in simulation; a contextual bandit decides whether a stored patch or a new LLM call is worth its cost; and a three-stage admission pipeline (static check, invariant-monitored replays, an empirical margin over the unpatched tree) admits only patches that demonstrably recover. Admitted patches are stored in a fleet library and, once the LLM call rate decays, crystallized into a deterministic BT that no human wrote. We implement SCBT on Microsoft Project AirSim with a schema-constrained LLM pipeline (Gemini 3.1 Pro) and a lockstep simulator. Over three seeds of a 20-episode learning phase with wind-gust and battery failures, SCBT used $11\pm1.4$ LLM calls against 26 for whole-tree regeneration and 22 without a library, with 0.33 calls per episode in the second half. The crystallized trees, 28 and 33 nodes with two patches each, reached $97\pm2\%$ mission success with no learning running, against 12\% for the unpatched tree and 98\% for a hand-coded expert tree, and reproduce decision traces exactly when re-ticked offline. Two negative results: replay admission rejected useful wind recoveries by attributing wind-induced geofence excursions to the patch, and a static-only ablation generalized better to held-out failures.
bullets: Addresses the tension between fixed, safe robot controllers and costly, non-deterministic runtime foundation-model reasoning.
Uses an LLM to propose minimal subtree patches only after node failures; CMA-ES tunes parameters and a contextual bandit selects stored patches versus new LLM calls.
Admits patches through static checks, invariant-monitored replays, and empirical recovery margins, then stores them in a reusable fleet library and crystallizes them into deterministic BTs.
In Project AirSim experiments, crystallized trees achieved 97±2% mission success with no online learning, versus 12% for the unpatched tree and 98% for a hand-coded expert tree.
Replay admission rejected some useful wind-recovery patches, while a static-only variant generalized better to held-out failures.

papers.abstract: Onboard inference latency creates a mismatch between the trajectories predicted by vision-language-action (VLA) policies and the ongoing motion of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). We present AeroDASH, an asynchronous VLA framework for continuous language-conditioned flight. A B-spline policy is initialized through supervised fine-tuning on expert demonstrations, providing continuous trajectory references in position and yaw. During execution, trajectory fusion removes the expired prediction prefix and connects the remaining segment to the active reference with derivative continuity while limiting trajectory deformation. To account for deviations induced by asynchronous execution, execution-aware group relative policy optimization (GRPO) further adapts the policy using trajectory-level rewards. On the UAV-Flow test set, AeroDASH achieves a success rate of 76.56%, exceeding OpenVLA-UAV and AeroDASH w/o GRPO by 38.1 and 20.1 percentage points, respectively. Execution experiments show that AeroDASH sustains motion during inference and reduces acceleration, jerk, and speed fluctuations relative to asynchronous tracking of waypoint sequences. We further demonstrate language-conditioned flight with onboard inference and asynchronous trajectory execution. The code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Zhe Liu, Yuxuan Zheng, Jinzhe Qin, Ziqi Gao, Boyu Zhou
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between onboard inference latency and UAV motion during VLA control.
Uses B-spline trajectories initialized from expert demonstrations for continuous position and yaw references.
Fuses new predictions with active trajectories while preserving derivative continuity and limiting deformation.
Applies execution-aware GRPO to adapt the policy to deviations caused by asynchronous execution.
Achieves a 76.56% success rate on UAV-Flow and reduces acceleration, jerk, and speed fluctuations versus waypoint tracking.

papers.abstract: Visual localization is critical for embodied agents, but deploying state-of-the-art deep feature matchers on edge devices is fundamentally limited by their massive computational cost. Standard deep matchers tightly interleave intra-image context building and inter-image matching at every layer, creating a severe interaction bottleneck. Localizing a single query against K database images forces the system to execute the full network K independent times with no capacity for caching. To break this bottleneck, we advocate for a paradigm shift toward cacheable image matching. We realize this paradigm with LateMatch, a versatile approach that restructures existing matchers by deferring inter-image interaction to their final layers. By isolating intra-image processing into offline-cacheable Context Blocks, only a small set of Interaction Blocks must be executed online. To further optimize LateMatch, we introduce E-SToRE (Entropy-guided Spatial Token Reduction and Expansion). E-SToRE leverages the decreasing Shannon entropy of the late Interaction Blocks to dynamically reduce token counts just prior to cross-image interaction. Evaluated across HPatches, ScanNet, MegaDepth, ETH-3D, and Aachen, LateMatch reduces effective computational cost by over 2x compared to standard deep matchers, while E-SToRE yields an additional 10% to 14% savings with negligible degradation in accuracy.
authors: Mohammad Omama, Aeyan Ashraf, Sandeep Chinchali
bullets: Addresses the interaction bottleneck of deep feature matchers on edge devices, where each query must otherwise process every database image independently.
Defers inter-image interaction to the final layers, separating reusable intra-image Context Blocks from lightweight online Interaction Blocks.
Introduces E-SToRE, which reduces spatial tokens before cross-image interaction using entropy-guided token reduction and expansion.
Evaluated on HPatches, ScanNet, MegaDepth, ETH-3D, and Aachen.
LateMatch achieves over 2× lower effective computation; E-SToRE adds 10–14% savings with negligible accuracy degradation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Rethinking visual localization with cacheable image matching via LateMatch. (A) Standard visual localization pipelines require matching a single query image against Top-K (e.g., K = 100) retrieved database images. (B) Traditional matching architectures interleave intra-image context building and interimage cross-attention across all layers, preventing any caching and causing a severe computational bottleneck. (C) Our proposed LateMatch architecture breaks this bottleneck by deferring cross-image interaction to the final layers, decoupling the network into offline-cacheable Context Blocks (CBs) and online Interaction Blocks (IBs), reducing the effective compute cost by over 2× without sacrificing much on performance.
Figure 6: MambaGlue-late consistently and significantly outperforms computationally equivalent MambaGlue-lite baselines. We show the trends on three datasets: A) MegaDepth, B) ScanNet, C) HPatches.

Figure 7: LateMatch outperforms token and model pruning. Performance-compute trade-off on the HPatches dataset. We apply confidence-based token pruning, with different confidence thresholds (ct), to our LightGlue-late4 model (blue) to progressively reduce its E-GFLOPs. We compare it against structurally smaller variants shown in green (LightGlue-late2 and LightGlue-late3). We also compare against attention head pruning (black crosses). LateMatch outperforms both these approaches by a significant margin.

Figure 5: LateMatch consistently dominates the compute-accuracy Pareto frontier. Performance versus online computational cost (E-GFLOPs) evaluated on the ScanNet (A, B) and MegaDepth (C, D) datasets. Across all capacity levels, the -late models (green) achieve strictly higher matching accuracy than the equivalent -lite baselines (red) at the same computational budget.

Figure 2: Strategic positioning of LateMatch in the feature matching landscape. While direct nearest-neighbor matching (A) is extremely fast but highly inaccurate, and lightweight matchers (B) are fast but nowhere close to the accuracy of heavy, computationally prohibitive deep matchers (D), our proposed LateMatch paradigm (C) achieves the high performance of full-capacity models with the online computational footprint of lightweight matchers.

Figure 4: Cross-attention entropy naturally decays across Interaction Blocks, guiding the progressive token reduction in E-SToRE. (A) The cross-attention entropy across the four IBs of LightGlue-late4. Attention smoothly shifts from diffuse global consensus (high entropy) in early IBs to highly peaked, localized matching (low entropy) in later IBs. (B) Progressively decaying r has significantly better performance (homography estimation accuracy) compared to other r selection approaches.

Table 2: LateMatch consistently and significantly outperforms computationally equivalent -lite baselines. We evaluate the -late paradigm applied to LightGlue (top, yellow) and MambaGlue (bottom, blue) against equivalent reduced-capacity (-lite) models. At identical online compute budgets (E-GFLOPs), structurally retaining deep intra-image context yields substantial improvements in matching accuracy over simply scaling down the network, with the most dramatic gains occurring under extreme computational constraints.
Table 4: LateMatch preserves end-to-end accuracy at half the latency. Aachen Day-Night recall at (0.5m, 5◦), K=50, desktop GPU. GF and latency are for the full pipeline.

Table 3: E-SToRE further reduces computational cost with negligible impact on performance. E-SToRE is applied to LightGlue-late4, against ToMe [48] augmented with our merge→ compute → unmerge mechanism for an apples-to-apples comparison. Both preserve accuracy, but E-SToRE yields up to 2× the reduction in Effective GFLOPs (E-GF). All percentages are relative to the LG-late4 column: red is accuracy lost, green is compute saved.

papers.title: LateMatch: Breaking the Interaction Bottleneck via Cacheable Matching for Efficient Visual Localization
papers.tldr: LateMatch makes visual localization more efficient by caching image-specific processing and limiting online cross-image matching, cutting computation by over 2× with minimal accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Human memories are organized in a way that connects events with their corresponding spatial contexts. An AI assistant should also be able to memorize and recall the nexus of events and spaces. Thus we introduce SENRI, a task that studies this space--event connection in long, continuous real-life egocentric video. It contains six task types in two directions: Event$\rightarrow$Space, which recovers spatial knowledge from event cues, and Space$\rightarrow$Event, which retrieves events from regions and trajectories. To evaluate this, we build SENRI-Bench, containing 500 manually annotated multiple-choice questions over 10 uninterrupted self-recorded videos with around 25.3 hours of content. Also, we evaluate three typical long video understanding paradigms: direct perception, evidence seeking, and persistent memory. The task remains challenging across all three paradigms, highlighting substantial room for improvement. Then we show two representative failure modes of existing memory methods and address these evidence gaps with SENRI-Agent, a controller that uses Target-Guided Visual Check (TGVC) to propose local visual check tasks for parallel verifiers and integrate the reports into a working memory to help with reasoning. Built upon existing memory systems, SENRI-Agent improves the performance of existing baselines without modifying their stored memories. We hope SENRI will provide valuable insights into how real-life egocentric understanding should be evaluated, reveal the gaps in existing approaches, and offer a possible direction for improvement.
authors: Kehan Lan, Kaining Ying, Henghui Ding, Kaipeng Zhang
bullets: Covers six tasks in two directions: inferring spaces from events and retrieving events from spaces or trajectories.
SENRI-Bench contains 500 manually annotated multiple-choice questions from about 25.3 hours of uninterrupted self-recorded video.
Evaluates direct perception, evidence seeking, and persistent memory; all remain challenging.
SENRI-Agent uses Target-Guided Visual Check with parallel verifiers and working memory to address evidence gaps.
Improves existing memory-system baselines without changing their stored memories.

papers.abstract: Estimating a humanoid robot's internal state from video has a wide range of real-world applications but remains unexplored. During interactions with a robot, its onboard state information may be unavailable due to privacy, ownership, or communication constraints. Meanwhile, online and AI-generated robot videos provide rich sources of data but typically lack corresponding joint configurations, limiting their direct use in robot learning. To address these issues, we present HumanoidPose, a new framework that treats vision as proprioception to recover full-body joint configurations in world space from video alone. Specifically, we combine pretrained human-pose features with robot kinematics in a unified model that predicts each embodiment's joint configurations. We retarget human motions to sixteen different humanoid embodiments, enabling scalable learning entirely from synthetic data. To improve real-world generalization, we further leverage unlabeled online videos through self-training to develop a 2D robot-pose detector. In our evaluation, HumanoidPose improves joint-angle and joint-position accuracy over the evaluated baselines and reduces joint-angle error by 18-32% relative to the best-performing baseline on each of the three real humanoid platforms. We further show improved global localization and generalization to unseen embodiments. HumanoidPose enables visual understanding of other robots during interaction and extraction of robot motion from online and generated videos.
authors: Jiaxi Jiang, Matthias Heyrman, Ren\'e Zurbr\"ugg, Marco Hutter, Christian Holz
bullets: Addresses missing robot proprioceptive data caused by privacy, ownership, or communication constraints.
Combines pretrained human-pose features with robot kinematics to predict embodiment-specific joint configurations.
Uses synthetic human-to-robot motion retargeting across 16 humanoid embodiments and self-training on unlabeled online videos.
Improves joint-angle and joint-position accuracy over evaluated baselines, reducing joint-angle error by 18–32% across three real humanoid platforms.
Demonstrates improved global localization and generalization to unseen embodiments.

papers.abstract: General purpose multimodal language models (LMs) are increasingly capable of directly controlling robotic arms (e.g., by commanding end effector poses) to manipulate their environment. Tracking the development of these capabilities is important for understanding their potential benefits, such as improving industrial automation, and risks, such as enabling malicious users to produce dangerous chemical or biological agents. To this end, we investigate the ability of frontier multimodal LMs to directly control physical robotic arms. We evaluate seven models at multiple reasoning-effort settings on six manipulation tasks taken from the RoboDojo benchmark. To our knowledge, this is the first systematic comparison of a broad range of frontier LMs across a common suite of manipulation tasks on physical hardware. We find that current frontier models can directly control real robotic arms to perform a variety of manipulation tasks but are not yet precise or efficient enough to complete them within a practical action budget. However, these capabilities are improving rapidly: performance increases on our benchmark between July and September 2026 (inclusive) correspond to a performance doubling time of 44.5 days, while the best recorded execution rate increased by a factor of 4.4 and the lowest recorded execution cost fell by a factor of 6.2. These trends raise the possibility that the Bitter Lesson is coming to robotics; the capabilities of embodied general purpose LMs may one day be comparable to those of more specialized models.
authors: Christopher Leet, Achyutha Menon, Sravanthi Machcha, Sven Koenig, Tzu Kit Chan, Jay Chooi
bullets: Evaluates seven models across six RoboDojo manipulation tasks on physical robotic hardware.
Tests multiple reasoning-effort settings to systematically compare frontier models.
Current systems complete varied tasks but generally exceed practical action budgets.
Performance improved rapidly from July to September 2026, including a 44.5-day performance doubling time.
The findings suggest general-purpose embodied models could eventually approach specialized robotics systems, with associated safety risks.

papers.abstract: Vision-language navigation is moving into photorealistic, physically simulated scenes, where the leading zero-shot agents put a vision-language model in the control loop to choose every move and stop. Robots favour small models, whose abilities are uneven: Qwen3-VL-4B can judge whether a single view looks like the goal, but its route reasoning is at chance, its distance estimates nearly constant, its stop votes unreliable. Our agent therefore asks it two perceptual questions per step, which direction looks like the goal and whether the view justifies stopping, plus one gated frontier query on route-bearing instructions, and treats the answers as evidence, not actions: a route-blind semantic field over a bird's-eye map accumulates the directional scores through a tempered update, a skeleton graph supplies frontiers and geodesic distances, and a two-stage terminator turns stop votes into termini through a trail-consistency gate and a budget-forced return. With every baseline re-run in one installation at one budget, the agent exceeds all four zero-shot baselines of the VLNVerse subset in mean success on both granularities, though the paired interval against the strongest coarse-grained baseline includes zero. Termination is the dominant lever in ablation, thirteen attempts to give the model more of the navigation establish no reliable gain, and the agent runs on a Unitree Go2 quadruped with off-board inference. Code, per-episode logs and a robot video will be released at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/structure-over-reasoning-PAGE.
authors: Zeqi Li, Xunyi Zhao, Zerui Li, Sihao Lin, Qi Wu, ShiJie Li
bullets: Small models show useful visual goal judgment but unreliable route reasoning, distance estimation, and stopping decisions.
The agent asks directional and stopping questions, plus a gated route query, and treats responses as evidence rather than actions.
A bird’s-eye semantic field, skeleton graph, geodesic frontiers, and a two-stage terminator convert these signals into navigation behavior.
It outperforms four zero-shot baselines on both VLNVerse evaluation granularities, although the interval against the strongest coarse-grained baseline includes zero.
Termination is the main ablation lever; additional navigation queries provide no reliable gain, and the system runs on a Unitree Go2 with off-board inference.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. One navigation step in four lanes. Inputs (grey): the instruction, twelve RGB views, the matching depth views and the pose. The model (orange): a five-point sector score per view, a stop vote on the best-scoring view and, on route-bearing instructions, a gated chain-of-thought query over the frontier list. Structure (blue): depth becomes a range scan and an occupancy map, the map a skeleton graph with frontier nodes, and the sector scores a route-blind belief field; the proposal enters the field through a gate closed on coarse-grained instructions, and a utility over the waypoint candidates picks the move. The terminator (green): a vote is accepted only within a tolerance δ of the best trail score; otherwise the agent walks back to that position when the budget runs short. The model, structure and terminator panels and the strip below them are real data from one fine-grained episode.

papers.abstract: Embodied AI lacks the data-rich pretraining that gave language models their agents and skills, so new manipulation capability costs demonstrations per task or a frontier model in every episode. We study a third route: a strong general model acts only as an offline author that writes, runs, diagnoses and repairs a manipulation skill in simulation until it passes an exam on layouts drawn after freezing; the frozen skill then runs as code alone or under a cheap caller that reads only its description. We call this skill-level recursive self-improvement Skill-RSI and specify a compile protocol (isolated, audited author; hidden validation layouts; no-feedback and inherit-only controls; tamper-evident ledger) and a reuse protocol that runs the identical files with executors from another model family. On 7 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks with cluttered tables, Claude Code compiled 4 tasks into 7 frozen skills, 5 from a first draft needing only qualification, at USD 4.29-8.22 of author cost each (USD 55 per skill counting the 13 failed campaigns). The other three tasks did not compile in 18 campaigns, including five with GPT-6 and a pre-registered 150-layout run: on the hardest task every campaign scored 78-95 of 100 but had 3-16 safety aborts, failing the gate of 95% success with zero aborts; a 100-episode exam bounds an abort rate only to 3.6%. On hidden layouts, repair that inherits the previous version beat from-scratch rewriting in 8 of 8 controlled campaigns (sign test p = 0.004); an inherit-only lineage attributes most of the gap to inheritance, with development feedback adding a little (3 of 3, p = 0.125). Write-once campaigns found no detectable first-draft effect of practice (minimum detectable effect 14 points). The frozen skills kept 148/150 successes on new layouts with no model and 147/150 with a DeepSeek-flash caller at USD 0.00028-0.00054 per episode; no direct-control baseline was run.
authors: Jingwen Bai, Guochao Bai, Canbo Zhang, Shuangqi Li, Minchao Hu, Weichun Huang, Shuang Liu
bullets: A strong model writes, tests, diagnoses, and repairs skills in simulation; frozen skills then run as code or with a low-cost caller.
Across 7 RoboTwin 2.0 tasks, 4 tasks produced 7 frozen skills, while 3 failed to meet the safety gate despite extensive campaigns.
Inheritance-based repair beat from-scratch rewriting in all 8 controlled campaigns; development feedback added only a small, uncertain benefit.
Compiled skills achieved 148/150 successes without a model and 147/150 with a DeepSeek-flash caller on hidden layouts.
Authoring cost was low per successful campaign, but repeated failures substantially increased cost; no direct-control baseline was run.

papers.abstract: Resource-constrained robots and autonomous vehicles need scene memories that localize a camera and render nearby views without a desktop GPU. Scene-coordinate regression (SCR) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS) fit because they avoid an SfM stage, but ACEsplat-style pipelines are GPU-centered, and moving them to an edge FPGA is hard because SCR is pose-sensitive and 3DGS rendering is irregular and capacity-sensitive. We present LENS, an edge scene-memory acceleration system on the AMD KR260 that brings an ACEsplat-style workload to a low-power FPGA/ARM platform. Rather than proposing a new scene model, LENS co-designs the two dominant kernels with the board data path: an INT16 SCR accelerator that preserves pose accuracy, and a bit-exact fixed-point ordered 3DGS renderer that rewrites alpha transmittance as a log-sum-exp recurrence and removes provably useless streamed Gaussians. All LENS latency, power, and quality results are board-measured. The SCR engine preserves DSAC* localization accuracy at 25.42 ms, the on-board renderer reaches 34.11 dB on Cambridge against ACEsplat's 33.20, novel-view synthesis on RealEstate10K reaches 27.84 dB against 26.11, and all ten Wayspots scenes reach the ACEsplat rendering target. LENS wins performance per watt over a Jetson Orin NX on every deployment task, by 1.9x to 5.7x at about a quarter of the power, and is faster in absolute latency on localization and Wayspots rendering. On-device training reaches ACEsplat-level quality but not the GPU's time or energy, marking the remaining boundary for a future training accelerator.
authors: Que Haohua, Mingkai Liu, Handong Yao
bullets: Targets GPU-dependent scene memories for resource-constrained robots and autonomous vehicles.
Co-designs an INT16 scene-coordinate regression accelerator and a fixed-point, bit-exact ordered 3DGS renderer for the AMD KR260.
Preserves DSAC* localization accuracy with 25.42 ms latency and achieves 34.11 dB on Cambridge and 27.84 dB on RealEstate10K.
Outperforms the Jetson Orin NX by 1.9×–5.7× in performance per watt at roughly one-quarter the power.
On-device training matches ACEsplat quality but remains slower and less energy-efficient than GPU training.

papers.abstract: Flow-matching vision-language-action (VLA) models generate an action chunk by iteratively denoising Gaussian noise, but typically execute only a short prefix before replanning with updated observations. Under this receding-horizon paradigm, the unexecuted remainder---the action tail---is discarded, and the next chunk is regenerated from fresh noise. We show that this discarded tail retains transferable denoising progress: action-tail initialization can match or outperform a native 10-step Gaussian baseline using fewer denoising steps. However, the optimal denoising budget varies substantially across samples, indicating that tail reuse should be adapted to the updated environment. Based on this observation, we introduce VLA-Rolling, a lightweight inference framework that reuses action tails through three stages: action-tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided refinement through renoising and denoising budget allocation, while the underlying VLA remains frozen. Across $\pi_{0.5}$, SmolVLA, X-VLA, and MolmoAct2 on LIBERO, MetaWorld, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0, VLA-Rolling reduces action-chunk inference cost in all 16 model--benchmark pairs, achieving up to a $1.48\times$ speedup, while improving success rate in 14 pairs by up to $15.08$ percentage points. These results show that action tails are not merely discarded predictions, but reusable intermediate states that enable more efficient and accurate VLA inference. These results demonstrate that the action tail can support the generation of better actions with fewer denoising steps. Our project is available at https://chenbao123ww.github.io/VLA-Rolling/.
authors: Sicheng He, Yi Pan, Qiuting Yu, Jiaming Huang, Qi Lu, Shuyan Wu, Hongyan Feng, Xuanyu Liu, Jun Zhang, Jie Zhang, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang, Jianwei Yin

The framework combines tail inheritance, per-action confidence estimation, and confidence-guided renoising/refinement.

Success rate improves in 14 pairs, by up to 15.08 percentage points.

papers.abstract: Multi-quadrotor passage planning requires coordinated spatial routes and passage times under vehicle dynamics and actuation constraints. Optimizing these decisions jointly couples temporal allocation, nonlinear motion, and inter-vehicle interactions, creating a computational challenge for local trajectory generation. We propose a learning-optimization framework that predicts spatial waypoints and ordered passage events for independently solved quadrotor planners. A common physical time grid aligns the vehicles, with intermediate events fixed by the networks and terminal progress optimized locally to permit different completion metrics. Differentiable sequential convex programming incorporates rigid-body dynamics and rotor-thrust bounds, allowing collision and completion gradients to train both networks through the generated trajectories. In a two-quadrotor evaluation across 24 layouts, the adapted policy passes physical feasibility and sampled separation checks in all five held-out layouts. Their mean completion metric decreases by 1.52% relative to the inherited policy. The median forward time is 21.01 ms on the held-out exchange layout with matching numerical trajectory references. These results demonstrate that learned spatial and event parameters can coordinate independent rigid-body planners while preserving local vehicle constraints in the evaluated scenarios.
authors: Yunhan Shi, Jia Deng, Zehao Jia, Lin Cheng, Shengping Gong
bullets: Addresses the coupled problem of spatial routing, passage timing, nonlinear dynamics, and inter-vehicle interactions.

In a two-quadrotor evaluation across 24 layouts, all five held-out layouts met physical-feasibility and sampled-separation checks.

papers.abstract: Nowadays, robotic telemanipulation enables humans to control robots so as to execute tasks in a manner similar to how they perform them, and serves as an essential approach for collecting on-robot data for robot learning by human demonstrations. The quality of collected demonstrations directly impacts the performance of the learned policy. However, existing telemanipulation systems rely heavily on human operation, particularly for large-scale data collection. Collecting dozens or hundreds of demonstrations is a demanding process, as operators tend to fatigue quickly, especially during the execution of dexterous tasks that require sustained concentration. Recently, semi-autonomous robotic telemanipulation has emerged as a promising direction that reduces operator workload while preserving human-in-the-loop control for task execution. We therefore introduce a scalable, intuitive, semi-autonomous robotic telemanipulation system that leverages a mixed reality (MR) headset for on-robot data collection. The system autonomously executes the majority of the task trajectories and only requires the operator to make fine adjustments at key stages. We validate the effectiveness of our system by collecting data and training imitation learning policies on the execution of a high-precision, fine-grained bimanual peg-in-hole task. With lower data collection effort, our system obtains high-quality demonstrations that can be used to train fully autonomous task execution policies.

papers.abstract: Video models provide rich priors for generalizable robotic manipulation, but plausible visual futures are not always executable. We introduce DreamCan, a hierarchical policy that grounds video models through sparse visual planning: a high-level planner adapted from a pre-trained video model and a low-level visuomotor policy. Rather than predicting dense trajectories, the high-level planner generates sparse visual subgoals that balance reachability and task utility. From offline, action-free robot videos, we estimate these quantities and use dynamic programming to select subgoal sequences without manual annotations. The resulting subgoals are more reliably attained than uniformly spaced alternatives, and the full system outperforms language, dense-video, and uniform-subgoal planners, reaching high planning success rates on Language-Table tasks and 91.2% success on LIBERO-Long with a 0.1B-parameter low-level policy. Additional suboptimal videos and test-time compute further improve success. The system also performs challenging real-world bimanual tasks, including box folding and packing with unseen object combinations. More results are available at https://dreamcan.github.io/.
authors: Chongkai Gao, Wenlong Huang, Haonan Chen, Lin Shao, Yilun Du, Jiajun Wu, Ruohan Zhang, Li Fei-Fei

Sparse subgoals are more reliably achieved than uniformly spaced ones, and the system outperforms language, dense-video, and uniform-subgoal planners.
Achieves 91.2% success on LIBERO-Long and handles challenging real-world bimanual tasks such as box folding and packing with unseen object combinations.

papers.abstract: We present Stable Signer V3, an interactive high-resolution sign language avatar system built on 4D Deformable Primitive Splatting. It addresses three limitations of existing avatars: restricted facial expression, inaccurate identity-specific body deformation, and loss of fine appearance details. Shared Face Primitive Splatting adds transferable superquadric primitives for richer expression control; Test-Time Body Primitive Splatting learns an identity-specific virtual muscle layer for more faithful motion; and Test-Time Tunneling Super-Resolution uses TunnelingNet to recover identity-specific high-resolution details. Both test-time modules are optimized once per signer identity; inference then runs entirely from the stored identity parameters. Together, they reduce facial geometry error by 71.4%, body-boundary error by 35.1% across ten identities, and high-resolution RGB reconstruction error by 24.2% on held-out evaluations, while retaining interactive streaming.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agent training, including software engineering, is advancing rapidly, but the recipe and infrastructure needed for a strong reinforcement-learning baseline remain difficult to reproduce. This makes gains from new algorithms or data hard to distinguish from improvements to an under-tuned baseline. We present Arctic-SWE, a fully asynchronous RL framework that establishes such a baseline through model-system co-design, using overfitting on a small task pool as the testbed. This testbed exposes failures that early reward gains conceal and guides the integration of established components: gated reward, importance-weight control, aligned training and inference engines, and consistent state across policy updates. No single component is new, yet together they form the missing foundation. On raw R2E-Gym data, without new algorithms or data work, Arctic-SWE trains Qwen3.5-4B to 62.0% pass@1 on SWE-bench Verified. This is comparable to concurrent FrogNano (61.5%), which relies on online task synthesis, after about one-sixth as many training rollouts. Building on this foundation, we further filter and refine R2E-Gym, SWE-rebench V2, and Scale-SWE. With this curated subset, the 4B model improves from 47.4%/25.0%/37.9% to 65.0%/38.3%/59.7% on SWE-bench Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2, and the recipe also improves Qwen3.5-9B from 56.2%/31.9%/48.8% to 65.7%/39.6%/70.2% on Verified/Pro-v1/Pro-v2. Controlled comparisons show that both curation and test strengthening improve held-out performance, although stronger tests reduce apparent training-task mastery. Arctic-SWE provides a documented starting point for studying better algorithms, data and environments for asynchronous agent RL.

papers.abstract: Quadruped robots often switch gaits to traverse mixed terrain safely. Many practical supervisors enforce hardware constraints (e.g., dwell or guard intervals) using a transition handler. However, the switch decision itself is often driven by near-field thresholds, which can delay commitment when rough terrain is only detected shortly before contact in the local height map. We propose a lightweight height-map-only gait supervisor that unifies look-ahead and locomotion constraints in a single decision policy. A robot-centered height map is partitioned into near-, mid-, and far-field bands, each discretized into a terrain class, and band evolution is modeled as a Markov process. Gait selection is cast as a look-ahead Markov Decision Process whose transition model and cost explicitly encode platform-specific switching constraints. Indoor and outdoor experiments on a Unitree Go2 platform show reduced late switching, lower time spent using ineffective gaits on rough terrain, and improved roll stability compared to tuned reactive baselines. Overall, the MDP formulation yields anticipative constraint-aware gait switching that improves robustness without course-specific retuning.
authors: Kelvin Aladum, Justin Peel, Nisar Ahmed
bullets: Addresses delayed gait changes when rough terrain appears only shortly before contact.
Partitions robot-centered height maps into near-, mid-, and far-field terrain bands modeled as a Markov process.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation is particularly challenging because it requires coordinating locomotion, balance, and object interaction, making it difficult to learn from limited demonstrations or from scratch through Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce DiPLO (self-distilled Diffusion Planning for Loco-manipulation), a framework that combines a self-distilled diffusion planner with a low-level whole-body tracking policy. Our planner is pretrained via supervised learning on motions derived from human-to-humanoid retargeting, while the tracker is trained via RL to execute them. DiPLO centers around two complementary post-training stages. First, we introduce Self-Distillation Diffusion Policy Optimisation (SD:DPO) to remove the planner's dependence on strong task conditioning, which we identify as a crucial ingredient for effective pretraining, as downstream fine-tuning does not recover comparable performance when it is omitted.. We then fine-tune this distilled model with Diffusion-Augmented Proximal Policy Optimization (DA:PPO), a maximum-entropy RL method for diffusion models, to improve task success and align generated plans with the frozen tracker's execution capabilities. Together, these stages enable motion generation through state-history and goal conditioning alone, enabling 99% task success in pick-carry-place tasks, compared to just 45% for the pretrained model. The resulting planner also generates motions for unseen object goals, with further evaluations on kicking and pushing/pulling tasks. Finally, we deploy our pipeline on the hardware, using our DA:PPO planner-tracker on a Unitree G1, achieving repeated successful executions without any real-world fine-tuning.
authors: Shafeef Omar, Sebastian Sanokowski, Elham Daneshmand, Dian Yu, Daniel Cremers, Cordelia Schmid, Majid Khadiv
bullets: Addresses the challenge of coordinating locomotion, balance, and object interaction in humanoid loco-manipulation.
Pretrains a diffusion planner on human-to-humanoid retargeted motions and trains a low-level tracker with RL.
Uses SD:DPO to remove dependence on strong task conditioning, then DA:PPO to improve success and match plans to tracker capabilities.
Generates plans using only state history and goal conditioning, including for unseen object goals.
Evaluates kicking and pushing/pulling tasks and deploys successfully on a Unitree G1 without real-world fine-tuning.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of the pipeline. (a) SBTO turns each IK-retargeted demonstration sIK into a set of dynamically feasible motions sD, and symmetries further enlarge the data corpus. (b) The diffusion motion generator Gϕ is pretrained to generate an n-step feasible motion conditioned on the IK-retargeted motion prior, the state history and the goal, while the tracking policy πθ is trained separately with RL to track sD. (c) Self-distillation with SD:DPO removes the need for the task prior: the student Gϕ, with the prior token nulled, rolls out with the frozen tracker πθ; each plan it produces is noised to a random denoising step k and denoised twice by the same network, with and without sIK , and the student’s reverse kernel pϕ is matched to the self-teacher’s stop-gradient kernel sg(pϕ). (d) The distilled Gϕ is then post-trained with DA:PPO, conditioned on the state history and the goal alone. papers.abstract: Wheeled planetary rovers immobilised in loose regolith have no principled recovery controller: scripted maneuvers are terrain-specific, and naive driving deepens entrapment. We introduce a recurrent policy that learns to escape without a predefined maneuver. The framework rests on a verified trap: in a continuum material point method (MPM) simulator we identify a configuration at sinkage-to-radius ratio z/r = 2.0 where the strongest of ten scripted controllers succeeds in only 7/32 trials, yet the regolith retains traction and continues to shear, confirming granular entrapment rather than a numerical artifact. A frozen entrapment detector, trained on 81,771 windows spanning three materials and six sinkage levels, supplies a three-state belief to the policy observation. A separate simulator mobility latch gates training rewards. Across five training seeds, mean action evaluation achieves 62.5% escape (range 28.1-81.3%; 32 trials per seed) versus 7/32 for the strongest scripted controller and 0/32 for action noise. A numerical audit identifies a coupling-buffer fault that silently discarded 9.7% of contact nodes at 16 parallel environments. Results establish recovery in the tested simulation regime; physical transfer remains unverified.
authors: Meraj Hossain Promit, Chandak Chakma, Md Jubair Ahmed Sourov, Sejuti Rahman
bullets: Addresses terrain-specific scripted recovery and the risk that naive driving worsens entrapment.
Uses a recurrent policy informed by a frozen three-state entrapment detector and a simulator mobility latch for reward gating.
At the verified trap condition, the learned policy averaged 62.5% escape across five seeds, versus 7/32 for the strongest scripted controller and 0/32 for action noise.
A numerical audit found a coupling-buffer fault that discarded 9.7% of contact nodes in parallel simulation.
Physical transfer is unverified, and results are limited to the tested simulation regime.

papers.abstract: Lifelong robot learning requires acquiring new tasks sequentially without forgetting earlier ones. With large pre-trained vision-language-action (VLA) backbones, adapter-based methods effectively mitigate this challenge. However, their task-specific adapters and selection modules accumulate with the task stream, creating a scalability challenge in on-disk storage and deployment cost under fixed onboard resource budgets. We propose SARAM, a lifelong learning framework that limits storage growth while keeping GPU memory and per-step inference cost independent of the task stream length. For each new task, SARAM reuses frozen adapters from previous tasks and introduces new adapters only at sparsely selected layers, with a duplication penalty encouraging them to capture information not already represented by the adapter library. At deployment, a compact signature derived from backbone activation statistics identifies the task once per episode, and the corresponding task update is merged into the backbone, leaving only the backbone in the control loop. Across four LIBERO suites, SARAM matches or exceeds adapter-based baselines while adding up to 4.5x less on-disk state per task. GPU memory usage and control frequency remain comparable to those of the backbone as the task stream grows. Experiments on a real UR5 arm with a different backbone further demonstrate retention throughout a sequential task stream.
authors: SeongJun Jeong, Chungwoo Lee, Gi-Cheon Kang, Byoung-Tak Zhang
bullets: Addresses adapter and task-selection module growth under fixed onboard storage and compute budgets.
Reuses frozen adapters and adds new adapters only at selected layers, with a penalty discouraging redundant information.
Uses activation-statistic signatures for one-time task identification, then merges the task update into the backbone for control.
Across four LIBERO suites, matches or exceeds adapter baselines while using up to 4.5× less on-disk state per task.
GPU memory and control frequency remain comparable to the backbone as tasks accumulate; retention is also shown on a real UR5 arm.

papers.abstract: Can a better robot policy become harder to monitor? We study a fixed vision-language model (VLM) that judges success while a policy improves. In a controlled 20-seed tray-placement experiment, training selects only simulator-verified successes. Success rises from 66.8% to 97.0%, and accepted hover failures fall from 5.0% to 0.9% of executions. Yet the judge accepts 50.0% of remaining hovers, versus 31.1% under untrained sampling. These residual failures more often lie below the tray rim, which can conceal the gap beneath a grasped cube. A separate boundary probe accepts 148/160 below-rim hovers and 0/160 above-rim hovers. We call this change in conditional monitoring sensitivity coverage shift: learning changes which failures reach a fixed judge. A broader diagnosis covers nine judges and 1,392 stimuli. Judge-filtered experiments across eight settings further show heterogeneous effects of state-dependent acceptance. The results distinguish task improvement from failure detectability and motivate reporting absolute misses, conditional misses, and audit coverage together.
authors: Isabel Guan, Dingyuan Zhang, Shipeng Lyu, I-Ming Chen
bullets: In a 20-seed tray-placement experiment, success increased from 66.8% to 97.0%, while accepted hover failures fell from 5.0% to 0.9% of executions.

Residual failures more often occurred below the tray rim, where the grasped cube can conceal the gap.
A boundary probe found 148/160 below-rim hovers accepted versus 0/160 above-rim hovers.
Across nine judges, 1,392 stimuli, and eight settings, effects of state-dependent acceptance were heterogeneous.

papers.abstract: General-sum games are more challenging than fully cooperative or adversarial settings because agents may deceive or exploit one another. Achieving high social welfare requires sustained cooperation, while a single defection can drive agents toward a welfare suboptimal Nash equilibrium. Moreover, assuming access to other agents' rewards or internal states is often unrealistic and implicitly introduces additional cooperation into the setting. To address this issue, we introduce \textit{Reciprocal Q-Augmentation} (RQA), a method that uses a latent-variable opponent model to augment the Q-function with estimates of how one's actions affects other agents. RQA allows agents to learn both cooperative and defective policies using only their own Q-function. We show that, in social dilemmas, agents that all follow the cooperative policy of RQA learn to cooperate faster and reach higher levels of cooperation than fully cooperative algorithms. Moreover, a single RQA agent that switches appropriately between its cooperative and defecting policies can induce cooperation in agents trained with standard RL algorithms, which would otherwise end up defecting. We evaluate our approach on the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma, Iterated Traveler's Dilemma, Iterated Stag Hunt, and \texttt{CleanUp-Lite}. Our experiments show that the algorithms implementing RQA outperforms fully cooperative methods with shared rewards and enables cooperation with algorithms that otherwise fail to reach high social welfare.
authors: Francesco Morri, Adel Abusitta, Quentin Cappart, Margarida Carvalho
bullets: Targets general-sum settings where defection can trap agents in low-welfare equilibria.

papers.abstract: Quadruped locomotion requires coordinating body motion,contact forces, foothold placement, and gait timing. We present a hierarchical controller in which reinforcement learning adapts these structured locomotion references while a gait scheduler, reactive footstep planner, and whole-body impulse controller retain responsibility for high-frequency execution. The model-based backbone can sustain a nominal trot independently, allowing the policy to focus on when and how to modify an already functional locomotion controller. We train the complete hierarchy in a vectorized controller-in-the-loop environment using a six-direction disturbance curriculum. Under a common simulator and evaluation protocol, the proposed controller achieves 77.29% mean survival across the tested disturbance grid, compared with 50.35% for the model-based reference controller. Training-time channel ablations identify adaptive foothold placement as the largest marginal contributor to grid survival and reveal direction-dependent effects of gait-rate adaptation. Together, these results demonstrate the viability of the proposed hierarchical controller architecture for integrating learned adaptation with optimization-based whole-body control through structured locomotion references.

papers.abstract: The scan-then-revisit workflow of upper gastrointestinal endoscopy requires bringing a previously observed suspicious region back into view for closer inspection. Acquiring such targets requires translating anatomical and appearance descriptions into camera motions from partial observations of a confined, deformable environment. We present EndoVLA-OOV, a language-conditioned vision-language-action policy for out-of-view target acquisition in robotic endoscopy. The policy adapts a pretrained backbone to continuous two-degree-of-freedom distal bending commands and combines initial, intermediate, and current images to guide search. To support policy learning, we provide an open-source VLA dataset containing 1,050 episodes across six tasks and approximately 262k observation-action pairs. Physical evaluation spans wet-lens and low-light conditions, two unseen stomach phantoms, and cross-embodiment transfer to an unseen ex-vivo environment. In the cross-embodiment evaluation, the full-data policy achieves 93.3% target acquisition success (28/30). In a controlled training-data comparison, expanding the corpus from 312 to 1,050 episodes increases acquisition success from 40.0% to 90.0% under the same model, training, and test configuration. Instruction and observation interventions further support the use of language and temporal context in the evaluated acquisition tasks. These results support language-guided endoscopic revisitation across the evaluated environments and robot embodiments and demonstrate the benefit of expanded task-specific demonstrations.
authors: Chi Kit Ng, Yidong Zhang, Tianchun Wu, Zhiqing Tang, Hanlin Zhao, Siu Hing Lui, Tao Yang, Jingsong Lin, Huxin Gao, Yeung Trevor, Raymond Tang, Hongliang Ren

papers.abstract: Spatial understanding is essential for robots to perceive their surrounding environments and execute actions. Existing approaches typically encode 3D awareness into vision-language-action (VLA) models by directly aligning their representations with pre-trained 3D foundation models. However, we observe that such direct geometric feature alignment essentially exploits 3D foundation priors as a form of low-rank regularization in the feature space, resulting in severe rank collapse of the pre-trained VLA representations. In contrast, we shift the focus from enforcing point-wise equality to aligning pair-wise relationships. We propose a representation-alignment method that enables the injection of 3D spatial awareness without compromising the model's original expressivity. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks, our new spatial reasoning benchmark, and real-world manipulation scenarios demonstrate that our approach effectively incorporates 3D spatial representations into VLA reasoning, achieving robust performance and enhanced spatial awareness across diverse manipulation tasks.
authors: Chaoran Zhu, Hengyi Wang, Chenglin Cui, Yazhe Wan, Taein Kwon, Changjae Oh
bullets: Directly matching VLA and 3D foundation-model features can cause severe rank collapse.
The proposed method aligns pair-wise relationships rather than enforcing point-wise feature equality.
It integrates 3D spatial representations into VLA reasoning without compromising original expressivity.
Experiments across public benchmarks, a new spatial reasoning benchmark, and real-world manipulation show robust spatial understanding across diverse tasks.

Figure 1: Spectral and rank analysis of different alignment methods. (a) Traditional 3D knowledge distillation aligns the point-wise magnitudes (i.e, vector norm) or angles (i.e, cos-similarity) across feature spaces, which often leads to rank collapse (b). In contrast, we align pair-wise relationships to achieve a rotation-invariant alignment that effectively prevents feature collapse. See Sec. 3.1 for details. VGGT [16] is used as the 3D teacher model.

papers.abstract: Learning a single perceptive policy for diverse humanoid loco-manipulation requires unifying high-level task decisions without losing the state-dependent physical responses that make each interaction succeed. This makes the representation between high-level planning and whole-body control critical: kinematic or contact targets provide compact abstractions but do not directly encode interaction-specific control responses, while directly predicting low-level actions requires the planner to model high-frequency closed-loop feedback. We propose FIBER, a framework that uses the executable latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM) as a shared planning representation for heterogeneous interaction skills. Our latent policy projection (LPP) maps independently acquired task-specific policies into this representation by identifying latent commands whose induced actions match their local control responses, enabling lower-rate planning while retaining the BFM's high-frequency state feedback. After projection, we aggregate closed-loop latent rollouts from all skills and train a single perceptive flow planner entirely offline. We further introduce AH-BFM, an adaptive-horizon BFM trained with multi-gamma forward-backward (FB) learning to support both precise control and temporally extended whole-body behavior. We evaluate FIBER on box pickup, door opening, and object grasping in simulation and on a real Unitree G1 humanoid. Across 128 diverse variations per task in simulation, FIBER achieves 42.0% mean success, more than tripling projected latent replay (11.6%) and substantially outperforming kinematic planning (3.5%). Real-world experiments further demonstrate sim-to-real transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering through the same unified planner.
authors: Yutang Lin, Guanya Shi, C. Karen Liu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of unifying task-level planning with interaction-specific, state-dependent whole-body control.
Projects independently learned skill policies into the latent space of a frozen behavioral foundation model (BFM).
Trains a single offline perceptive flow planner on aggregated closed-loop latent rollouts from multiple skills.
Introduces AH-BFM with adaptive horizons for both precise control and extended whole-body behavior.
Across three simulated tasks, achieves 42.0% mean success versus 11.6% for latent replay and 3.5% for kinematic planning; real-robot tests show transfer, skill chaining, and conditional steering.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of FIBER. (a) Heterogeneous interaction experts are acquired through motion imitation, reward shaping, or successorfeature-guided behavior reuse. (b) Action-aligned latent policy projection maps their short-horizon control responses into a frozen adaptivehorizon BFM; closed-loop rollouts produce executable latent trajectories. (c) These trajectories train a unified perceptive planner entirely offline. Language commands or waypoint conditions are encoded as steering tokens, and a DiT planner predicts future latent trajectories. During deployment, the planner replans from onboard observations while the frozen BFM provides high-frequency feedback.

Fig. 4: Qualitative real-world behaviors of FIBER. (a) During box carrying, the robot reacts to an unstable grasp by briefly lifting the box and repositioning its hands underneath for more secure support, illustrating high-frequency closed-loop adjustment. (b) After picking up the box, the same policy follows waypoint commands while carrying it; after stumbling, the robot stabilizes on its knees and recovers before continuing, demonstrating interaction-preserving skill chaining, steering, and recovery. (c) For a heavy door, the robot leans its whole body into the interaction to generate sufficient pushing force, showing adaptive whole-body realization of contact-rich tasks.

Fig. 3: Skill chaining with FIBER. In a single rollout, the policy sequentially opens the door in (i), picks up the box in (ii), and carries it back through the doorway in (iii), demonstrating closed-loop chaining of multiple interaction skills under changing high-level commands.

papers.abstract: 3D manipulation policies derive actions from explicit scene geometry rather than color images alone, enabling them to reason over metric distances, object relations, and robot-scene reachability. This geometric interface is also a vulnerability: commodity RGB-D sensors return missing measurements, boundary artifacts, and plausible but wrong surfaces around transparent, reflective, thin, or textureless objects. We study this failure under realistic depth corruption and observe a sharp depth-noise cliff across modern 3D policies, even when they are trained with matched noisy depth. This residual gap motivates a spatial-encoding approach: corrupted depth becomes entangled with the token coordinates and geometry features consumed by the action expert. We propose Noise-Invariant Spatial Encoding (NISE), a 3D policy architecture that learns trustworthy geometry features even facing imperfect depth. NISE uses Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision to shape shared policy features with calibrated multi-view depth, and Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention to carry position uncertainty into deployed attention rather than treating every lifted token as exact. Across simulated benchmarks with sensor-realistic corruption and real-robot tasks involving transparent and reflective materials, NISE improves depth-noise robustness while preserving clean-depth performance, supporting 3D policies designed for commodity RGB-D deployment rather than clean-depth benchmarks alone.
authors: Zhiyuan Yang, Jiaju He, Ruiteng Zhao, Anqi Cheng, Haiyue Zhu, Kezhi Mao
bullets: Commodity RGB-D sensors produce missing, distorted, or incorrect geometry, causing a sharp performance drop in modern 3D policies.
NISE learns trustworthy spatial features using Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision with calibrated multi-view depth.
Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention propagates position uncertainty instead of treating corrupted 3D tokens as exact.
Simulated sensor-corruption benchmarks and real-robot tasks with transparent and reflective objects show improved noise robustness.
The approach targets deployment with imperfect commodity RGB-D sensors, beyond clean-depth evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: NISE framework. Per-camera RGB-D is encoded by a frozen visual backbone ViT and a trainable DPT-style head [21] into a shared spatial feature map. NISE acts on this shared map: during training, Geometric Cross-View Self-Supervision attaches a cross-view geometry head to encourage view-consistent geometry in the same features consumed by the policy; at deployment, this head is removed. Gaussian Marginalized 3D Attention remains in the deployed policy and carries per-token coordinate uncertainty into 3D attention, so lifted tokens influence action features according to their spatial reliability.
Figure 4: Real-robot Success Rate. Each task group compares DP3, 3DDA, RVT-2, and NISE, with N = 30 trials per task and method.

Figure 1: Realistic depth corruption breaks what 3D policies can trust. (a) In a transparent test-tube manipulation scene, raw depth contains missing and geometrically wrong measurements; a standard 3D policy consumes this corrupted geometry as exact and fails, while NISE succeeds. (b) Depth-noise robustness on RLBench PerAct-18 [1, 2] and MetaWorld [3]. NISE maintains higher success rates as depth corruption increases, with a smaller clean-to-saturated decline than the compared baselines.

Each cell reports the success rate and successful trials out of 30. The base model uses the same policy stack as NISE with GCVSS and GM3A disabled.

Figure 7: Cross-view depth becomes a geometry target only after calibrated warping. The source camera is forward-warped into the target camera frame and filtered by a visibility/validity mask before it supervises the shared feature map. This is the practical difference between a raw cross-camera noisy target and GCVSS: the auxiliary signal is still noisy, but it is expressed in the same camera frame as the target feature map.
Figure 3: Real-robot setup: single-arm UR5e (left) and bimanual UR3e (right). Camera labels identify Azure Kinect and RealSense D455/D405.

papers.abstract: Pedipulating a freestanding articulated object requires controlling its pose and internal configuration while maintaining balance. We demonstrate this capability by autonomously solving a giant Rubik's Cube with a quadruped using only its feet. The task demands repeated precise interactions, since unintended layer motion can invalidate subsequent operations. We develop an onboard RGB-D perception pipeline that estimates the cube's metric pose and its full color state from partial views acquired through locomotion and flipping. A planner converts the computed solve into robot-executable skill sequences. Learned whole-body skills reorient the cube while preserving its layer configuration and turn its layers with one foot pinning the cube as the other pushes. We train these skills using reinforcement learning with privileged observations and distill them into policies that map onboard depth and proprioception to joint targets. The deployed policies tolerate variations in relative robot-cube placement and recover from external disturbances. The system completes three autonomous hardware solves, each about 30 steps over 8-9 minutes. These results show that combining onboard perception with coordinated pedipulation enables a quadruped to complete extended multi-step physical tasks. Additional material can be found at: https://leggedrobotics.github.io/rubik-skills/
authors: Lukas Amiet, Gabriel S\'anchez-Blanco Repgen, Mayank Mittal, Victor Klemm, Andrei Cramariuc, Marco Hutter, Cesar Cadena
bullets: The task requires precise control of the cube’s pose and layer configuration while maintaining robot balance.
An onboard RGB-D pipeline reconstructs the cube’s metric pose and full color state from partial views gathered during locomotion and flipping.
A planner translates the cube solution into executable skills, including reorientation and one-foot-pinning layer turns.
Reinforcement-learned whole-body skills are distilled into policies using onboard depth and proprioception, with recovery from placement variation and external disturbances.
The system completed three autonomous hardware solves of roughly 30 steps each in 8–9 minutes.

papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used in embodied AI for robotic manipulation and planning, but their deployment in physical systems exposes vulnerabilities such as jailbreak attacks that induce unsafe behavior. Existing inference-time defenses are mainly evaluated on short instructions containing a single hazard, whereas realistic tasks may interleave safe and unsafe sub-tasks, conceal hazardous steps, or combine individually safe actions into unsafe outcomes. Such compound instructions make it harder for a single safety decision to distinguish hazardous sub-tasks from legitimate ones, risking either overlooking the hazard or rejecting the whole instruction. We introduce safe task completion, a task that requires an LLM-enabled robot to refuse the harmful part of an instruction while completing its legitimate part. To address this problem, we propose RuleGraph, a multi-agent Graph-of-Rules planning framework that distributes safety enforcement across multiple reasoning and verification stages. Five cooperating agents are used to ground general safety principles into world-specific rules, assess the instruction's sub-tasks in context, and derive a safe goal from the legitimate ones. Planning toward this goal is then organized as a graph of rule-specific nodes, where higher-level nodes inherit the union of their parents' rules, and candidate plans are progressively verified and aggregated until a single plan satisfies every relevant rule. In this way, RuleGraph reduces reliance on a single centralized safety decision. We evaluate RuleGraph on pure-attack and compound instructions across two benchmarks in two environments using Attack Success Rate (ASR) and Task Success Rate (TSR). RuleGraph reduces ASR to 0% on both benchmarks while achieving the highest TSR among all methods, reaching 98.57% on the RoboGuard benchmark and 84.54% on our long-horizon compound instructions.
authors: Ali Taheri, Alireza Taban, Qizhou Wang, Wanhua Li
bullets: Addresses compound instructions that mix safe and unsafe actions or hide hazards in longer task sequences.
Uses five cooperating agents to ground safety principles, assess sub-tasks contextually, and derive a safe goal.
Plans with a graph of rule-specific nodes, progressively verifying candidate plans against inherited safety rules.
Evaluated on pure attacks and compound instructions across two benchmarks and two environments.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising paradigm for autonomous driving. However, the massive parameter scale of VLAs strains onboard computational resources during real-time inference. This directly increases energy consumption and limits vehicle battery range, making it critical to minimize computational overhead without compromising driving capability and explainability. Current research on efficient VLA-based driving focuses on sequential adaptation (\textit{e.g.}, Chain-of-Thought and token adjustment), leaving structural adaptation underexplored despite parameter redundancy across dynamic driving scenes. To address this gap, we propose Scene-Adaptive VLA, an efficient framework leveraging dynamic layer routing to adjust active parameters based on real-time scenes. Inspired by the temporal continuity of scenes and model predictive uncertainty, our approach characterizes model-perceived scene complexity via frame-level temporal scene variations and decision deviations. To uncover latent scene-to-parameter correspondences, we encode this characterization into scene-aware tokens, alongside two specialized queries. A budget-conditioned layer routing mechanism evaluates these refined queries to allocate a budget that determines the active parameter ratio and subsequently selects appropriate layer combinations. The entire framework is optimized end-to-end. Extensive evaluations on the Bench2Drive benchmark show that when adapted to a state-of-the-art VLA model, our approach significantly reduces inference-time computational overhead by 53.5\% with negligible degradation in driving and language capabilities. Code is available at https:github.com/yang-luvu/Scene-Adaptive-VLA.
authors: Yujia Yang, Quan Yuan, Jiawei Fan, Yang Li, Tiange Fu, Xiaoyuan Fu, Guiyang Luo, Jinglin Li
bullets: Addresses the high computational and energy costs of large VLA models for real-time autonomous driving.
Uses temporal scene variations and decision deviations to estimate scene complexity and model uncertainty.
Encodes this information into scene-aware tokens and specialized queries for budget-conditioned layer routing.
Dynamically selects layer combinations and active parameter ratios through end-to-end optimization.
On Bench2Drive, reduces inference-time computational overhead by 53.5% with negligible capability degradation.

papers.abstract: LIBERO has emerged as a widely adopted benchmark for evaluating robotic manipulation policies. However, strong performance on LIBERO does not necessarily indicate robust embodied capabilities, as models may exploit benchmark-specific regularities rather than generalize to diverse operating conditions. In this work, we introduce LIBERO-Pro2.0, a comprehensive benchmark for systematically evaluating the robustness of embodied foundation models under distribution shifts. LIBERO-Pro2.0 encompasses 22 static perturbations and 20 runtime interventions across six dimensions: Condition, Environment, Observation, Execution, Robot State Configuration, and Language, yielding 1,648 validated shifted task instances. To support robustness-oriented learning, we further collect 39,390 training trajectories through model-generated and human demonstrations. All shifted task instances undergo six rounds of iterative human review and correction to ensure physical plausibility and task validity. We evaluate 17 representative robot policies spanning vision-language-action models, world-action models, and robustness-oriented policies. Our results reveal substantial robustness gaps across all evaluated paradigms: under runtime distribution shifts, the evaluated models exhibit an average performance drop of 26.5 percentage points, with individual drops reaching 32.5 points. These findings highlight the gap between nominal benchmark performance and robustness under distribution shifts, underscoring the need for systematic robustness evaluation of embodied foundation models.

papers.abstract: Most simulation benchmarks for robotic manipulation keep target objects static and treat policy inference as instantaneous. These assumptions simplify evaluation but hide how a moving target evolves during computation and how stale an observation is when an action is executed. We introduce LIBERO-Dynamic, a dynamic extension of all 40 LIBERO tasks. It drives objects through contact friction along three trajectory families and speed tiers, while advancing the physical world according to calibrated, model-specific inference latency. The same mechanism supports training by replaying verified static demonstrations and compensating robot actions online for target displacement, producing 9,000 quality-filtered dynamic trajectories. We evaluate six pretrained policies on 1,800 dynamic conditions per configuration, compare execution strategies and action horizons with fixed checkpoints, and fine-tune three architectures using dynamic and mixed data. Faster motion degrades every policy but not uniformly; execution timing and horizon can change the behavior of the same policy; and asynchronous replanning benefits from frequent feedback only when the action queue avoids underflow. Dynamic demonstrations improve each architecture under at least one recipe, with gains varying by temporal conditioning, data composition, and training budget. A small-scale physical study shows task-dependent execution-strategy differences consistent with simulation. LIBERO-Dynamic makes object motion, inference latency, and action execution explicit and controllable for evaluating and improving robot policies in moving-target manipulation.

papers.abstract: Frozen Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies cannot incorporate previously encountered failures without updating the underlying model. We present retrieval-triggered projection correction (RTPC), an auditable external-memory wrapper for frozen OpenVLA policies that retrieves stress-collected local-depth records and applies translation-only projection correction while keeping rotation and gripper commands unchanged. RTPC is evaluated on CALVIN single-task manipulation using primary and independent replication cohorts. In the primary evaluation, RTPC reduced a depth-based near-collision or stall proxy event rate without changing task-success count. However, this reduction was not reproduced in the independent replication, and retrieved correction directions were not distinguishable from random same-family directions. Analysis identifies endpoint coupling, batch sensitivity, and the lack of a trigger-matched memory-free baseline as limitations for attributing effects to retrieval-based correction. These findings do not establish physical safety improvement or memory-specific benefits, but provide an empirical evaluation and failure analysis of retrieval-conditioned intervention for frozen VLA policies.

papers.abstract: Enabling humanoid robots to participate effectively in social interactions is important for their integration into human-centered environments. Existing methods, however, typically map pre-generated speech directly to continuous motion trajectories but have limited awareness of complex social environments and lack explicit high-level semantic action planning. We introduce SocialCoAct, a unified agent-centered framework for VLM-based egocentric social co-action. We formulate egocentric social co-action as an end-to-end agent task and develop SocialCoAct-Agent, which transforms egocentric observations and dialogue history into verbal responses and atomic action sequences, aligns each action with its corresponding utterance span, and executes the resulting behaviors in MuJoCo and on a physical humanoid robot. To evaluate the VLM capabilities required by this task, we construct SocialCoAct-Bench from continuous egocentric recordings of natural multi-party interactions. The benchmark comprises 423 human-verified multiple-choice questions across three subtasks: Long Episode Understanding (LEU), Speaker Intention Understanding (SIU), and Coordinated Action Planning (CAP). Across a diverse set of closed-source and open-weight VLMs, including general and egocentric models, the highest overall accuracy is 77.54%, while accuracy on the hard subset reaches only 46.51%. Extended reasoning improves Qwen3-VL-2B and Qwen3-VL-4B by 19.62 and 17.02 percentage points, respectively, but reduces inference throughput by 53.6$\times$ and 20.2$\times$. Visual-input ablations further show that the benefits of visual context vary across models. SocialCoAct provides a foundation for developing and evaluating VLM-based humanoid agents that coordinate context-aware speech and action in complex social interactions. The codebase and benchmark will be made publicly available upon publication.
