papers.abstract: While data collection for model training is relatively easy, curating high-quality datasets from large collections is inherently challenging. Coreset estimation methods address this problem by identifying the best data subsets to train models on. However, existing approaches often require proxy model training, extensive annotations, or task-specific tailoring. Unsupervised alternatives typically exploit geometric properties in foundation model feature spaces, but are limited to pairwise image-to-image comparisons or comparisons against a fixed subset. We introduce CoreDNA, an unsupervised, task-agnostic coreset estimation approach that pools neuron activations from vision foundation models into per-image and per-dataset distributions. By comparing each image's distribution to the dataset-level distribution, CoreDNA can capture both low-level visual structure and high-level semantic information across layers. We find that high-quality samples concentrate in the tails of the last layer's activation statistics, which we validate by relating them to training-based coreset methods. Building on these findings, we develop a computationally efficient selection mechanism to construct task-agnostic, high-quality coresets for selective annotation and model training. Across image classification, semantic segmentation, depth estimation, and imitation learning for end-to-end driving and mobile manipulation, CoreDNA matches or outperforms the state of the art, demonstrating unprecedented generalization across perception and action tasks. These results highlight the effectiveness of compact activation-based representations for data selection.
authors: Julia Hindel, Benjamin Ramtoula, Kyuhwan Yeon, Nick Heppert, Paul Newman, Daniele De Martini, Abhinav Valada
bullets: Addresses the challenge of curating large datasets without extensive annotations, proxy training, or task-specific design.

Provides an efficient coreset selection method for annotation and model-training subset construction.
Performs competitively with or better than prior methods across classification, segmentation, depth estimation, imitation learning, driving, and mobile manipulation.

papers.abstract: Obstacle avoidance for autonomous quadrotors in cluttered environments remains challenging, especially when both dense static obstacles and moving obstacles are present. Existing methods are often tailored to either static or dynamic settings, which always limit their adaptability across diverse environments. This paper presents TransNav, a transformer-based end-to-end navigation method for quadrotor obstacle avoidance in both static and dynamic environments. TransNav employs a patch-based point-cloud encoding scheme that combines local feature extraction with global contextual modeling, enabling compact yet informative environment representation. The method integrates perception and navigation in a single architecture and directly predicts a finite-horizon action sequence, from which the first action is executed. Moreover, we develop an unsupervised learning strategy by incorporating a lightweight point-mass dynamics model, which directly optimizes trajectory-level costs over the predicted sequence through numerical gradient propagation. Thus, the policy can be efficiently trained without expert demonstrations. Simulation and real-world experiments show that the proposed method achieves strong performance in dense static environments and competitive obstacle-avoidance capability in dynamic scenarios, while maintaining low inference cost for onboard deployment.

Simulation and real-world tests show strong static-environment performance, competitive dynamic avoidance, and low onboard inference cost.

papers.abstract: Geometric and Semantic Foundation models are becoming increasingly popular tools for generating spatial maps for robots. Recent work (e.g., FOUND-IT) has leveraged these tools to construct real-time, task-driven, and open-set 3D scene graphs from a single uncalibrated camera. However, while classical robot mapping techniques have undergone extensive system demonstrations, limited work has been done to develop both the fundamental and the systems wide advancements needed to integrate these new types of robot spatial memory into a full, useable autonomy pipeline. In this paper, we bridge this gap, and in doing so we also evaluate the effectiveness and limitations of this type of 3D memory. Towards this end, we integrate FOUND-IT into a mobile manipulator platform and demonstrate it is well-suited to support multiple objectives such as object change detection, support for multiple mapping sessions, determination of navigable paths, and directly support object grasping for the task of scene re-arrangement. Furthermore, we provide nuanced insights into the effectiveness and limitations of a monocular, foundation-model-driven 3D scene graph construction system using observations from rigorous on-robot experiments. Code is available at https://github. com/MIT-SPARK/FOUND-IT.
authors: Dominic Maggio, Lorenzo Shaikewitz, Aryan Naveen, Kris Hauser, Luca Carlone

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable language-guided robot manipulation, but remain vulnerable to visual attacks that undermine user control over robot behavior. Prior studies optimize visual perturbations using fixed target supervision. However, the perturbation can change earlier actions and, in turn, the physical states reached later. As the attacked trajectory evolves, this supervision may no longer match the behavior needed at the states actually reached. Accurately matching these targets can therefore fail to advance the attacker-specified task. Even with suitable supervision, reducing average matching error does not ensure sustained task progress. The robot may still fail at a critical stage, and further updates can disrupt previously successful behavior. To address these limitations, we propose TRACO, a framework that enhances existing targeted visual attacks through closed-loop optimization. Its Execution-Driven Supervision rebuilds supervision for the states reached under attack to guide subsequent updates. Within this framework, Progress-Guided Selection focuses updates where progress stalls while maintaining supervision on the earlier behavior needed to reach that point. Experiments across VLA models and simulation environments show improved task-redirection success with TRACO, highlighting the security implications of closed-loop attack optimization.
authors: Chunjin Ye, Guanying Chen, Jianjie Huang, Jianhao Chen, Quanlin Chen, Hanjie Zhao, Haozhe Liang, Tieyun Qian, Xiaochun Cao
bullets: Problem: Fixed target supervision can become mismatched as visual perturbations alter earlier actions and later physical states.
Method: Execution-Driven Supervision rebuilds targets from attacked states, while Progress-Guided Selection concentrates updates where task progress stalls.
Contribution: A closed-loop framework that enhances existing targeted visual attacks without relying solely on average matching-error reduction.
Result: Experiments across VLA models and simulation environments report improved task-redirection success.
Scope: The work highlights security risks for language-guided robot manipulation; the abstract does not specify real-world evaluation.

papers.abstract: Many manipulation tasks that are effortless for dexterous human hands remain challenging for robotic systems equipped with simple, task-specialized grippers. Industrial platforms commonly rely on end-effectors such as suction cups or parallel-jaw grippers, yet no single mode can reliably satisfy the diverse constraints encountered across different phases of complex manipulation tasks, including pickup, reorientation, insertion, and constrained placement. In this work, we investigate whether complementary simple grippers within a heterogeneous bimanual setup can collectively realize tasks that exceed the capability of any individual gripper alone. Given a single human demonstration specifying the desired object motion, we formulate embodiment-aware execution as a finite-horizon optimization over arm-trajectory assignments. At each segment, the planner determines whether single-arm manipulation or a coordinated dual arm handover is required, jointly reasoning over heterogeneous grasp feasibility, motion constraints, manipulability, and cross-gripper compatibility. Exploiting this formulation, we compute globally consistent assignments with explicit switching regularization. Experiments on a dual Franka FR3 platform equipped with suction and parallel-jaw grippers demonstrate improved feasibility and reliability in tasks that are infeasible under single-gripper execution.

papers.abstract: Legged robots equipped with manipulators offer promising capabilities for loco-manipulation tasks in unstructured environments. However, achieving task-consistent end-effector behavior during locomotion remains challenging due to terrain-induced disturbances and the strong coupling between locomotion and manipulation, particularly for small-scale quadruped platforms. A reinforcement-learning based whole-body control framework is proposed for quadruped loco-manipulation on complex terrain. The proposed framework combines a hybrid task representation with task-prioritized whole-body learning to coordinate locomotion and manipulation while preserving task-consistent end-effector behavior. A lightweight quadruped manipulator platform is further developed to validate the proposed framework on a small-scale quadruped system. Real-world experiments demonstrate successful deployment on complex terrains such as slopes up to 30 degrees, stairs, and deformable terrain. These results demonstrate the feasibility of deploying learned whole-body control policy for quadruped loco-manipulation in real-world environments and highlight the importance of task-consistent whole-body coordination for terrain-adaptive loco-manipulation.

papers.abstract: Agents built on vision language models (VLMs) now compete with learned policies on robot manipulation leaderboards. We ask how far a coding agent can go when it controls a robot instead of a computer, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, keeps the harness thin: it only turns the agent's commands into robot motion. The agent drives a robot with two arms through one command line. It sees three RGB cameras and knows their calibration. After each failed attempt, the agent reads the log, finds the cause, and writes or fixes small programs called tools. In this way it keeps what it learns as code, as a coding agent does when it fixes a failing test. The tools may use only what the robot observes. They use triangulation to find where objects are, relative to each other and to the gripper. If two cameras see the same point, the point lies where the two camera rays meet. If a point lies on a known plane, such as the table or the top of a block, it lies where its ray meets that plane. When the head camera is not enough, the robot moves a wrist camera to get a second view. We build the tools on only ten layouts of one seed per task, then freeze them and test them on ten new layouts of the same seed. We use Codex with GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort. On all 42 RoboDojo tasks, HexaShell reaches a success rate of 39.7% and a progress score of 48.0, averaged in the same way as the leaderboard. This is a new state of the art on RoboDojo. The limit is contact, not reasoning: pushing reaches 92.5% and memory tasks 65.0%, but tight insertion only 8.3%. When the agent fails, it usually sees the failure but cannot make the motion work. We open source the tools evolved so far at https://github.com/HexaFuture/HexaShell.

papers.abstract: Humans manipulate objects within their hands through touch alone with remarkable ease, but for robots, achieving sustained real-world manipulation without vision remains an open challenge. Although reinforcement learning (RL) can generate sophisticated blind manipulation policies in simulation, transferring them to a real dexterous hand remains hindered by continuously changing contacts, motion-induced tactile information drift, and the gap between simulated and physical dynamics. We study this problem through Baoding ball rotation on the Shadow Dexterous Hand Lite, using only proprioception and binary tactile feedback as observations. We achieve successful zero-shot transfer through a combination of a sensor-aligned, coupling-aware embodiment in simulation, tactile calibration, and two novel episodic domain randomisations: slew-rate action limits and STuck-AT Taxels. On the physical hand, the policy achieves sustained blind Baoding rotation, completing 225 consecutive $\mathbf{180^\circ}$ rotations (112.5 full rotations) at $\sim0.36 \;\text{rot/s}$ in a single continuous trial without any vision or object-state information. Furthermore, we evaluate the contribution of tactile sensing relative to proprioception alone and identify the hand regions where tactile information is most important. This is the strongest reported hardware result for Baoding ball manipulation in both rotation count and speed, irrespective of the sensing modality used. By effectively bridging the sim-to-real gap, our framework sets a new benchmark for sustained tactile-driven dexterous manipulation on physical hardware.

papers.abstract: Rapid progress in embodied intelligence has enabled increasingly capable robots to follow language instructions and manipulate diverse objects. However, strong results in structured environments do not automatically transfer to open-world conditions, where clutter, occlusion, and changing viewpoints can obscure the spatial relationships required for action. To address this perceptual gap, a virtual active-perception paradigm is introduced. AWAM, an Active World-Action Model actively plans where to observe and imagines what will be seen along the planned trajectory before acting. Task-related virtual camera motion is predicted and used as a structured query into a geometry-conditioned world model, producing a reusable spatial prior for manipulation, which is later compressed into a fixed memory and fused with live observations through cross-attention for diffusion-based action prediction. AWAM achieves competitive success rates with 75.9% on LIBERO-Occ, 62.4% on LIBERO-Plus, 76.5% on RLBench-OG Occlusion1, and 94.4% in real-robot trials. These results support improved robustness to the evaluated occlusions and distribution shifts, addressing part of the gap between structured manipulation and less controlled environments.

papers.abstract: Robots manipulating objects in clutter must decide not only how to act, but also where to look. Although active camera motion can expose an occluded target, it may move the robot into an initial observation-state distribution that differs from the manipulation policy's training distribution. We identify this problem as first-frame distribution sensitivity: under perturbed starts in LIBERO, naively prepending camera repositioning to pi_0.5 reduces success from 46.3% to 11.5%. We introduce ActiveAlign, a data-adaptation framework that trains a Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policy from the states at which active perception terminates. A learned viewpoint module first generates a camera trajectory. Offline, ActiveAlign uses closed-loop alignment to connect the trajectory endpoint to an existing demonstration, replays the remaining manipulation trajectory, and retains successful continuations for fine-tuning. At deployment, the same viewpoint module precedes the adapted VLA without modifying its architecture. Across 40 LIBERO tasks, ActiveAlign achieves 70.7% success with pi_0 and 72.7% with pi_0.5, outperforming their standard-training baselines by 40.0% and 26.4% respectively. Matched-state and data-matched controls support gains beyond prefix shortening and generic viewpoint augmentation; OpenVLA and GR00T N1 also show the same trend. Success rate under physical occlusion in real world increases from 35/90 to 83/90. These results show that active perception benefits manipulation when policy training is aligned with the observation and robot-state distribution induced by viewpoint selection.
authors: Jiawei Geng, Zhenyang Liu, Yuzheng Wu, Yongchong Gu, Yanwei Fu
bullets: Problem: Camera repositioning can create first-frame observation and robot-state distributions unlike those seen during policy training, sharply reducing performance.
Method: A viewpoint module selects a camera trajectory; offline closed-loop alignment connects its endpoint to demonstrations and retains successful manipulation continuations for VLA fine-tuning.
Contribution: The adapted policy uses active perception without changing the VLA architecture and aligns training data with viewpoint-induced states.
Results: On 40 LIBERO tasks, success reaches 70.7% with π₀ and 72.7% with π₀.₅; real-world occlusion success rises from 35/90 to 83/90.
Scope: Gains are supported across controls and also observed with OpenVLA and GR00T N1, indicating the approach is not limited to one VLA.

papers.abstract: When we say that a robot uses memory, does that memory actually play a role? Success-rate ablations alone cannot establish the use of task-relevant facts: they change information and computation together, while aggregate rates can hide offsetting gains and losses. We propose an Interventional Memory Evaluation Protocol (IMEP) for vision-language-action (VLA) systems to address four questions: (1) Does memory provide a net benefit? (2) Under what conditions does memory help? (3) Do changes to memory alter task outcomes? (4) Are these effects specific to task-relevant facts? At the retrieval interface, we compare target-fact substitutions with fact-preserving replacements, minimal numerical perturbations, and exact replicas, while assessing decision correctness separately from motor execution success. We evaluate within-episode, cross-episode, and agentic memory. In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-unit-in-the-last-place (ULP) intervention, including its installation procedure, changes 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while changing key facts produces no clear additional effect over fact-preserving replacements. To examine when memory helps, we introduce ChainBench, where correct decisions require historical information unavailable in current observations. The full memory configuration raises task success from 39.1% to 74.3%, matching the oracle-decision condition under shared recorded executions. These results show that correct history can support robot decisions, but establishing whether a memory system realizes this benefit requires fact-specific evidence beyond aggregate success rates.
authors: Keyuan Luo, Yi Xie, Wanyun Ling, Yuanzhe Li, Ziyue Li, Zhuoqi Zeng

In cross-episode learned-bank experiments, a one-ULP intervention changed 11.9% of seed-paired outcomes, while key-fact changes showed no clear extra effect over fact-preserving replacements.
ChainBench tests tasks requiring historical information absent from current observations.

papers.abstract: World-action models jointly predict actions and future world states, but long-horizon manipulation further requires language reasoning to plan subtask objectives, assess execution progress, and guide action selection. We present LAW, a closed-loop VLM--WAM framework that unifies language reasoning, action generation, and world modeling through semantic subtask progress. Within the LAW agent, a hybrid-expert vision-language model plans the remaining subtasks, estimates the values of and fuses actions proposed by a world-action model, and asynchronously assesses execution status to support continued execution and subtask transitions. Within the world-action model, Mixture-of-Transformer Experts integrates modality-specific and shared computation for joint video--action modeling. Dual-stream hierarchical visual memory maintains temporal context for both models, while subtask-local value learning aligns action evaluation with semantic objectives and preserves supervision from successful prefixes of failed trajectories. LAW achieves 94.21% average success across 50 RoboTwin tasks. Replacing the WAM backbone with OpenWAM-$alpha$ further raises the average success rate to 95.56%, establishing a new open-source state of the art on RoboTwin. Despite having only 2B parameters, our VLM also outperforms variants using Embodied-R1.5 and GPT-5.5 High. On three long-horizon real-robot tasks, LAW achieves 65% average success, compared with 28.33% for $pi_{0.5}$ and 25% for Fast-WAM.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robotic tasks expose a fundamental limitation of current Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models because their restricted temporal context pre-vents effective accumulation and reuse of past experiences. As a result, memory has become a fundamental component for enabling embodied agents to perform long-horizon reasoning and adaptive decision-making. This survey presents a systematic taxonomy of VLA memory mechanisms based on memory scope and persistence, categorizing existing approaches into five representative paradigms and one emerging frontier. Based on this taxonomy, we compare representative VLA memory systems in terms of memory characteristics, architectural com-plexity, and open-source maturity, revealing a clear trade-off in which increasing architectural complexity is generally accompanied by decreasing open-source ma-turity. Finally, we discuss the key challenges in building full-lifecycle memory systems, including efficient memory management and lifelong knowledge evolu-tion. Overall, this survey provides a unified perspective on memory architectures for VLA agents and offers insights into the development of lifelong embodied in-telligence.

papers.abstract: Continuous aerial search builds target hypotheses from sparse, viewpoint-dependent observations. When later evidence contradicts a stored hypothesis, however, the candidate can remain available to the planner and continue triggering approach or verification actions. We call this trajectory-level failure false candidate persistence (FCP). We equip SkyAgent with Revisable Target Memory (RTM), which associates evidence with persistent candidates, discounts correlated views, and revises each candidate through Tentative, Confirmed, and Rejected states. The key interface binds every generated waypoint to its source candidate: rejection therefore invalidates stale goals, while conservative reactivation protects temporarily occluded targets. Across four splits from the CityAVOS, UAV-ON, and OpenUAV benchmarks, our SkyAgent equipped with RTM outperforms all competitors, improving SR by 2.90--6.31 points while substantially reducing Behavior-FCP and post-contradiction travel with a low false-rejection rate. Across 35 matched real-world DJI scenarios per method, RTM consistently improves task success and behavioral reliability, further validating its state-to-action correction under physical deployment conditions.
authors: Kaibo Yang, Xingyu Wu, Enze Zhu, Yajie Chai, Xuyang Li, Jiahui Cui, Xiaoxuan Liu, Lei Wang, Zhan Chen

Across benchmark splits, improves success rate by 2.90–6.31 points while reducing behavioral FCP and post-contradiction travel.
Real-world DJI scenarios show improved task success and behavioral reliability with a low false-rejection rate.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World Action Models (WAMs) have expanded the manipulation and whole body capabilities of individual robots. Yet a single robot remains limited by its embodiment, and many real world tasks require capabilities that can only emerge through cooperation. Existing multi robot frameworks largely emphasize task decomposition, allocation, and replanning, while providing limited support for adapting executable coordination when physical execution deviates from the intended behavior. We present CoEvolve, a framework that represents team coordination as executable code over fixed robot motor skills. CoEvolve introduces Verifier Guided Coordination Evolution, where a multimodal foundation model instantiates coordination strategies through motion primitives, semantic objectives, temporary robot roles, and bounded execution parameters. Physical verification evaluates each executed transition, rejected behaviors trigger structured coordination revision from an accepted checkpoint, and verified experience is retained to guide subsequent decisions. We evaluate CoEvolve with two simulated Unitree G1 humanoids transporting a freely supported rigid payload through constrained corridors. Across 15 base task runs with three multimodal backbone families, CoEvolve completes 8 tasks, with every backbone achieving end to end success. Additional evaluations yield verified placement on two additional corridor layouts and after both same-backbone and cross-backbone experience initialization, while exposing persistent limitations in motion precision and contact stability. These results support executable coordination as a practical interface for adapting long horizon multi robot collaboration under shared physical constraints.

In simulations with two Unitree G1 robots transporting a payload through constrained corridors, all tested multimodal backbones achieved some end-to-end successes, completing 8 of 15 base runs overall.
The approach remains limited by motion precision and contact stability.

papers.abstract: We present LY-GWM-RoboCasa-Human300, a policy that combines a Human300-fine-tuned GR00T-N1.5 action generator, an action-conditioned graph dynamics model, and a learned binary state-reward scorer. At inference, the policy samples four action chunks, predicts the future latent features and robot state for each, and executes the candidate with the highest predicted-state reward logit. Predictions therefore influence the actions sent to the environment. The evaluated system uses a 16-step prediction horizon and keeps all three components frozen during evaluation. In the local evaluation on 50 RoboCasa 1.0.1 tasks in the pretrain kitchen split, with 50 episodes per task, the system records 207/2,500 successes (8.28%), compared with 181/2,500 (7.24%) in the historical self-trained GR00T-N1.5 baseline. The observed difference is 26 successes, or 1.04 percentage points. The atomic group improves from 141/900 to 150/900. Separately, the RoboCasa maintainers re-evaluated the submission and reported 354/1,500 successes (23.6%) across 50 tasks, with leaderboard rates of 48.3%, 16.3%, and 3.1% for Atomic-Seen, Composite-Seen, and Composite-Unseen. The local and official results are reported separately; their difference is not attributed to a model improvement. Recorded local audits identify 212,700 changed environment-input chunks, including 28,223 in atomic tasks. We describe the actual training stages, implemented inference mechanism, evaluation provenance, and public reproduction entrypoints. These results document an active prediction-and-selection system and a positive historical difference.

papers.abstract: Vision--Language--Action (VLA) models promise generalist robotic agents, yet consolidating skills learned across heterogeneous tasks and environments remains difficult: training data is fragmented across platforms, joint multi-task training suffers from interference, and model merging tends to introduce parameter conflicts or require architectural changes. We instead advocate a paradigm in which skills are first learned independently and then consolidated post hoc. To this end, we propose NestedVLA, which replaces parameter aggregation with parameter generation: a nested hypernetwork, conditioned on the target task, synthesizes task-adaptive action-expert parameters that compose with a frozen base VLA. Task-specific compressed VLM residuals are retained separately. This formulation enables flexible task-conditioned skill reuse while mitigating interference. Across three RL benchmarks (MetaWorld, ManiSkill, CALVIN), NestedVLA outperforms the strongest model-merging baseline by 41 pp on average, matches per-task fine-tuning within 1 pp on ManiSkill, and substantially closes the gap on CALVIN, pointing toward a storage-efficient route to skill consolidation. Code is available at https://github.com/WanyuGroup/NeurIPS2026-NestedVLA.
bullets: Addresses fragmented training data, multi-task interference, and conflicts caused by conventional model merging in VLA models.
Uses a nested hypernetwork conditioned on the target task to generate adaptive action-expert parameters alongside a frozen base VLA.
Stores task-specific compressed VLM residuals separately for flexible skill reuse and storage efficiency.
Across MetaWorld, ManiSkill, and CALVIN, it outperforms the strongest merging baseline by 41 percentage points on average.
Matches per-task fine-tuning within 1 percentage point on ManiSkill and substantially narrows the gap on CALVIN.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Architecture of the nested hypernetwork Gϕ. Patches are addressed by (ptype, layer, patch_h, patch_w) and mapped to four per-task patch embeddings (patch path). The task id m is mapped to a task embedding and processed by a lightweight task encoder (2D convolutions plus average pooling) into a single task feature ftask. ftask is broadcast across all patches and concatenated with the patch embeddings, then passed through a shared FC trunk augmented with a per-task low-rank LoRA path (LoRA path). The trunk output is decoded by a multihead output module that allocates one fully-connected projection per task (multi-head path) into a flat patch prediction. The precomputed action-expert mask MA m and global rescale α produce τ̂Am = α · Gϕ(m)⊙MA m; the compressed VLM update is retained separately.

Figure 2: NestedVLA pipeline. (1) Skill acquisition: each task is fine-tuned independently from the same base Θ0 and the resulting task vector τm is compressed into a sparse skill zm = α · τm ⊙Mm via drop-and-rescale. (2) Skill consolidation: a single nested hypernetwork Gϕ is trained against the action-expert portions of {zm} with a multi-task masked MSE loss. (3) Skill generation: at inference, querying Gϕ with task id m generates the action-expert update; the corresponding compressed VLM update is retrieved and both compose with the frozen base.

Figure 1: Motivation and overview of NestedVLA. (a) Model merging combines independently fine-tuned VLA weights into a shared model, where incompatible updates can impair the source tasks. (b) NestedVLA retains a compressed task-specific VLM update and uses an embedded taskconditioned hypernetwork to generate the action-expert update. Both updates are applied to a shared base to materialize the selected VLA.

papers.abstract: Candidate-based end-to-end driving planners reason over a finite set of trajectory hypotheses. However, for sparse planners, a limited candidate set may provide insufficient support for scene-relevant maneuvers, while fixed downstream candidate budgets do not account for prediction uncertainty. To address these challenges, we introduce Expand-and-Prune, a test-time framework that jointly adapts candidate support and capacity without updating learned parameters. The framework expands the native candidate set using semantic driving intent and temporally propagated predictions and then uses uncertainty in intermediate trajectory scores to adaptively prune the resulting candidates. Across four heterogeneous candidate-based planners and four benchmarks, Expand-and-Prune consistently improves planning performance. It achieves state-of-the-art results on LangAuto, increasing the Driving Score from 68.2 to 75.9, while providing further improvement on Bench2Drive, Fail2Drive, and NAVSIMv2, with particularly strong improvements in out-of-distribution scenarios. Moreover, in its full instantiation, 72.5% of selected trajectories originate from the newly introduced intent-guided or temporal candidates, confirming that candidate-space expansion provides useful hypotheses beyond those generated natively by the planner. The code is available at https://github.com/iis-esslingen/Expand-and-Prune.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN) requires embodied agents to ground language in visual observations and make long-horizon decisions. Existing methods often address these demands through task-specific architectures. As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly capable, an important question remains: Have we truly unlocked the potential of native MLLMs for VLN before introducing task-specific architecture? We present SimpleVLN, an architecture-preserving framework developed through studies of navigation formulation, data construction, and optimization. At the formulation level, SimpleVLN combines single-turn decision inputs with fixed-budget global-local memory to efficiently use navigation history without unbounded context growth, while action chunks enable efficient output of multiple primitive actions per model invocation. For data construction, we combine expert demonstrations with policy-dependent DAgger experience and develop a scalable synthesis pipeline that generates large-scale tasks for reinforcement learning. At the optimization level, a progressive IL-DAgger-RL pipeline advances from action imitation to task-level outcome optimization. Comprehensive experiments validate the effectiveness of these three aspects. We instantiate SimpleVLN across multiple MLLM backbones and model sizes, demonstrating its generality. SimpleVLN achieves 76.7% and 80.1% success rates on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE splits, respectively, substantially outperforming existing methods. These results show that the navigation capabilities of native MLLMs can be effectively unlocked without task-specific architectural designs.
authors: Lingyi Hong, Weiren Cai, Jiayu Chen, Xinyu Zhou, Bailin He, Yunfei Guo, Qiao Sun, Boyu Ma, Jianfei Yang, Wenqiang Zhang
bullets: Uses single-turn decisions with fixed-budget global-local memory to retain navigation history efficiently.
Predicts action chunks, reducing the number of model invocations needed for long-horizon navigation.
Combines expert demonstrations, policy-dependent DAgger data, and scalable task synthesis for reinforcement learning.
Trains progressively from imitation learning to DAgger and task-level reinforcement learning.
Achieves 76.7% success on R2R-CE and 80.1% on RxR-CE across multiple MLLM backbones and sizes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of SimpleVLN. At each decision, sampled history frames, current observation, and the instruction are fed to an MLLM, which directly predicts an action chunk for navigation.

For RL, it synthesizes navigation episodes from sampled start–goal paths and generated instructions, then optimizes the policy through environment interaction and outcome feedback.

papers.abstract: World models provide robots with a predictive mechanism for reasoning about how actions change object states in manipulation tasks. However, existing image-based and dense 3D world models do not explicitly impose object-level rigid motion, leaving rigid-object geometry preservation to be learned implicitly and making multi-step rollouts susceptible to shape drift or object-level motion inconsistency. To address this, we propose ORD-WM, a 3D world model that learns object-centric rigid dynamics for robotic manipulation. ORD-WM learns a vector-neuron variational autoencoder supervised by signed distance fields, which encodes each object point cloud as a geometry-aware latent representation composed of 3D vector features, and uses an action-conditioned dynamics model to predict object-wise SE(3) motion increments. Rather than generating unconstrained next latent states, ORD-WM analytically applies predicted object-wise rigid transformations to the current latent states, separating persistent object geometry from pose changes. Experiments show that ORD-WM enables stable, geometry-preserving multi-step prediction and supports efficient real-time replanning for closed-loop model predictive control in simulated and real-world manipulation scenarios.

bullets: Addresses shape drift and inconsistent object motion in existing image-based and dense 3D world models.

Applies rigid transformations analytically, separating persistent geometry from pose changes.

papers.abstract: Embodied heuristic learning must balance strategic adaptation with the preservation of previously successful behavior. Local repairs may leave structural failures unresolved, whereas broader revisions can introduce regressions that are costly to detect through repeated environment interaction. We introduce SCOPE (Selective Certification Of Program Edits), which uses failed and successful executions as complementary evidence for program revision. Frontier-guided program search annotates a shared diagnostic graph with execution evidence to distinguish supported progress from unresolved checks. Selective behavioral certification uses stateful API replay to restore recorded responses and mutations, checking whether edits preserve selected historical successes. Diagnosis and certification feedback, supplemented by sparse environment diagnostics, guide consecutive repairs across configurations. SCOPE outperforms the strongest baseline in both simulation and real-world tasks. On LIBERO-PRO and Robosuite, it achieves mean success rates of 80.66% and 84.48%, with respective gains of 6.51 and 3.48 percentage points. Our code is available at https://github.com/VDIGPKU/SCOPE.
authors: Junyang Shu, Bingqing Wei, Jishuo Li, Zheqi He, Yongtao Wang
bullets: Addresses the tension between adapting failed behavior and preserving previously successful behavior.
Uses frontier-guided program search to combine failed and successful executions in a shared diagnostic graph.
Applies stateful API replay to test whether edits preserve selected historical successes.

Outperforms the strongest baseline, reaching 80.66% mean success on LIBERO-PRO and 84.48% on Robosuite.

papers.abstract: Humanoid control requires coordinating whole-body posture with position and heading in the world frame. Mainstream controllers imitate trajectories in the root frame, but struggle to regain the target world pose after displacement. We introduce BeJEPA, a goal-conditioned Behavior World Model learned through unsupervised reinforcement learning from human motion priors and robot interaction. BeJEPA learns a shared representation of body configuration and world placement through a joint-embedding predictive architecture (JEPA). A Dynamic Predictor predicts the next state embedding under an action, while a Successor Predictor summarizes a goal-conditioned policy's expected discounted future state embeddings in a single vector. During joint training, Dynamic grounds the initial representation in observed physical transitions, while Successor increasingly organizes it around long-term behavior. Their composition guides policy improvement through one physical prediction and one behavioral summary, without long imagined rollouts. In 20-second motion-tracking experiments, BeJEPA with online action refinement using Dynamic outperforms all evaluated baselines in global body-position error, reducing it on AMASS by 61.7% relative to BFM-Zero with world-pose inputs and 58.7% relative to SONIC. Physical deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates joint attainment of posture, world position, and heading goals, recovery from the ground, and closed-loop return after disturbances and goal changes. authors: Liyun Yan, Haoyang Li, Yang Zhang, Jialing Zhu, Zhanxiang Cao, Zihao Zhou, Keqi Zhu, Yizhi Chen, Huang Chuxuan, Shengcheng Fu, Zhong Jiangwei, Qiao Sun, Chen Zhang, Yue Gao

Guides policy improvement without requiring long imagined rollouts.

In 20-second tracking experiments, it reduces global body-position error by 61.7% on AMASS versus BFM-Zero and 58.7% versus SONIC; deployment on a Unitree G1 demonstrates recovery and closed-loop goal changes.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models that directly regress joint-space actions avoid the deployment-time cost of inverse kinematics. However, their training objectives remain misaligned with task success, as joint-space losses ignore the unequal physical consequences of joint errors and visual conditioning lacks explicit focus on hand-object interaction regions. To address these issues, we propose a training-phase prior injection framework for fine-grained bimanual manipulation. First, a physics-grounded flow-matching loss maps the implicit clean-action estimate at every noise level through differentiable forward kinematics (FK) and supervises the resulting Tool Center Point (TCP) pose and inter-arm relative pose, with a bounded noise-level weighting that compensates gradient decay. Second, we introduce a global prediction query group distilled from a frozen DINOv3 teacher through future-frame feature prediction, together with a local interaction query supervised by Grounding DINO at the attention level. Both teachers are removed at inference, and the deployment pipeline is that of a standard joint-space flow policy, adding only the learned query pathway. Simulation and real-robot experiments on long-horizon bimanual tasks show that the two priors are complementary across different deployment settings. The full model excels in in-distribution deployment, while the distilled query branch is preferable under strong visual randomization.

Teachers are removed at inference, preserving a standard joint-space flow-policy deployment with a learned query pathway.

Experiments on simulated and real long-horizon bimanual tasks find complementary benefits: the full model suits in-distribution settings, while the distilled query branch is preferable under strong visual randomization.

papers.abstract: Heterogeneous robot teams enable complex, long-horizon tasks by combining complementary sensing, mobility, and manipulation capabilities across multiple embodiments. Yet existing systems struggle to retain execution-time corrections as reusable experience, maintain task-relevant context memory across space and time for reliable handoffs, and explicitly represent the inter-robot dependencies required for structured collaboration. In order to address these challenges, we present InstAgent, a recursively self-improving (RSI) Agent Operating System for heterogeneous robot collaboration. InstAgent organizes team behaviors as agentic behavior trees (BTs) that explicitly model capability assignment, inter-robot dependencies and handoff checks. The RSI mechanism updates these collaboration programs from execution feedback and preserves successful revisions for reuse in future tasks, while shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory provides context for planning and handoff validation. Experiments on 20 real-world multi-robot tasks with three high-level models show consistent gains in task success, first-attempt completion, and execution efficiency.
authors: Haoyang Luo, Junhao Qin, Jingyan Cao, Yi Huang, Guangjie Yang, Xiaoyu Chen, Haotao Lu, Tianxiang Gui, Ye Shi, Jingya Wang
bullets: Targets reusable execution-time corrections, reliable context-aware handoffs, and explicit inter-robot dependency modeling.
Represents collaboration with agentic behavior trees for capability assignment, dependencies, and handoff checks.
Uses recursive self-improvement to revise collaboration programs from feedback and retain successful revisions.
Provides shared multimodal spatio-temporal memory for planning and validating handoffs.
Experiments across 20 real-world multi-robot tasks and three high-level models report gains in task success, first-attempt completion, and execution efficiency.

papers.abstract: Space robots must interpret tasks and act despite unfamiliar dynamics, difficult sensing conditions, and limited opportunities for human intervention. Foundation models offer reusable perceptual and behavioral knowledge, but their value depends on how that knowledge reaches physical execution. This critical review follows space-specific requirements through perception, prediction, planning, and action to deployment and validation, emphasizing orbital manipulation and proximity operations. Terrestrial comparisons establish benefits of particular pretraining stages and model interfaces; their transfer to space dynamics and constrained onboard operation remains insufficiently tested. Event cameras offer timely motion observations across strong illumination contrasts, while spiking neural networks provide possible routes to sparse local computation. We examine how sensor degradation, state estimation and computing choices affect feedback and recovery. Higher action throughput need not yield fresher feedback; lower processor power can also coexist with higher energy per inference. We organize validation as an iterative sim-to-ground-to-space pathway, connecting physical tests with telemetry-based diagnosis and closed-loop revalidation. A satellite-capture example links observations to approach, contact and recovery, while a corresponding protocol separates generalization from adaptation with limited target-domain interaction. These comparisons identify what models already contribute and the physical evidence needed to support autonomous space operation.
authors: Zizhe Wang, Jia Deng, Xin Lu, Zehao Jia, Yi Huang, Yao Zhu, Jianing Li
bullets: Traces the autonomy pipeline from perception and prediction through planning, action, deployment, and validation, with emphasis on orbital manipulation and proximity operations.
Highlights the gap between strong terrestrial pretraining results and insufficient testing under space dynamics, degraded sensing, and limited onboard computing.
Discusses event cameras and spiking neural networks as possible approaches for timely, sparse local computation under difficult illumination and energy constraints.
Proposes an iterative sim-to-ground-to-space validation pathway using physical tests, telemetry diagnosis, and closed-loop revalidation.
Uses satellite capture to connect observation, approach, contact, and recovery, while distinguishing generalization from target-domain adaptation.

papers.title: Foundation Models for Autonomous Space Robotics: Architectures, Physical Adaptation, and Validation
papers.tldr: A critical review maps how foundation models could support autonomous space robotics, emphasizing physical adaptation, onboard constraints, and evidence-based validation before deployment.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as promising approaches to robot learning and control. These models integrate multimodal perception and action generation, but differ in their architectures, output representations, and learning objectives. In this paper, we present a unified, architecture-agnostic probabilistic formulation for embodied foundation models based on stochastic kernels. Our formulation has two key components: (i) we characterize embodied foundation models through conditional output distributions and action-realization kernels, which together induce task-conditioned robot policies; and (ii) we connect pretraining and post-training to policy deployment, accommodating model-specific pretraining objectives and offline or online post-training strategies. We instantiate the formulation for OpenVLA and DreamZero, covering autoregressive action-token prediction and joint video-action generation.
bullets: Motivates unification of vision-language-action models and world-action models despite differing architectures, outputs, and objectives.
Represents models with conditional output distributions and action-realization kernels.
Connects pretraining and offline or online post-training to policy deployment.
Instantiates the framework for OpenVLA and DreamZero, covering autoregressive action-token prediction and joint video-action generation.
papers.selection_reason: Unified probabilistic formulation for embodied foundation models covering VLA and world-action models; directly relevant to embodied AI and robot learning.
papers.title: Unifying Embodied Foundation Models via a Model-to-Policy Formulation
papers.tldr: A stochastic-kernel formulation unifies diverse embodied foundation models by translating their outputs into task-conditioned robot policies.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are rapidly expanding what individual robots can accomplish, yet many real-world manipulation settings require multiple arms to operate as a coordinated system. Existing approaches organize multi-arm coordination in different ways, including centralized joint policies, high-level task or role assignment, and locally executed policies that react to teammates. However, how complete action-producing VLAs should explicitly interact with one another during action generation remains largely unexplored. We introduce VLA-Fabric, which organizes one complete VLA per arm while preserving local perception and action ownership, and enables coordination through learned interaction across policy boundaries. We first systematically study where such interaction should occur, how peer information should be aggregated, and how the interaction should be learned, revealing complementary coordination functions spanning shared context, peer-specific latent information, and action-stage interaction. We then re-instantiate these functions in a structurally different VLA architecture, showing that the coordination principle is not tied to a particular tensor layout or backbone implementation. Finally, we compose teams of three and four arms and evaluate them in simulation and physical experiments. On all four physical tasks, Full interaction improves success over independently trained local policies by 16--40 percentage points. Together, these results suggest that explicit interaction among complete VLA policies offers a scalable path toward networked embodied intelligence.
authors: Chenglong Zhang, Shuaijun Liu, Feiyang You, Shuyang Hao, Chengyu Wu, Ningxin Su
bullets: Targets coordinated multi-arm manipulation, where each arm retains local perception and action ownership.
Studies where interaction should occur, how peer information should be aggregated, and how coordination should be learned.
Identifies complementary roles for shared context, peer-specific latent information, and action-stage interaction.
Reproduces the coordination design in a structurally different VLA architecture, suggesting backbone-agnostic applicability.

In physical experiments across four tasks, full interaction improves success over independent local policies by 16–40 percentage points; teams of three and four arms are evaluated in simulation and on hardware.

papers.abstract: The physical world has continuous state and action spaces, yet robot planning often benefits from hybrid discrete-continuous formulations that explicitly expose combinatorial structure, such as contact modes or discrete primitive actions. Existing methods typically rely on human-defined symbol sets or symbols derived from language supervision, without asking what makes a symbol computationally useful. In this paper, we take an inference-algorithm--centric view to define usefulness: a good symbol should expose the discrete commitments that simplify solving the original planning problem. We first introduce the concept of solver-sufficient symbolization by studying finite-horizon piecewise-affine systems, for which solver sufficiency can be precisely characterized, and develop a counterexample-guided algorithm for symbol invention. We then extend this principle to invent symbols for optimization objectives parameterized by general neural networks as energy functions, showing that solver-sufficient symbols can nevertheless be induced from their continuous optimization landscapes. Experiments on simulated and real-robot tasks show that the resulting symbols reduce solving cost while preserving solution quality, while also improving interpretability and steerability. Furthermore, our theoretical and algorithmic insights help explain why certain human-defined symbols are computationally useful.
authors: Yiyuan Pan, Changliu Liu, Jiayuan Mao
bullets: Frames symbol usefulness around the inference algorithm rather than human intuition or language supervision.
Introduces solver-sufficient symbolization for finite-horizon piecewise-affine systems and characterizes when it is sufficient.
Develops a counterexample-guided algorithm for inventing symbols, extending the idea to neural-network energy functions.
Simulated and real-robot experiments show reduced solving cost while preserving solution quality, with improved interpretability and steerability.
The framework also helps explain why some human-defined symbols are computationally useful.

papers.abstract: Generative policies can synthesize robot behaviors, yet controlling and editing them through diverse spatiotemporal references remains challenging. In the real world, human intent requires robot behaviors that satisfy constraints on where, when, and how actions are executed. Our key insight is that spatiotemporal control references, such as keypoints, flows, orientations, and keyposes, can be viewed as partial specifications of the same temporal Cartesian action space. We introduce the MAP (Masked Action Space) interface to unify these action references and formulate controllable manipulation as an action inpainting problem. Our Inpainting Policy (IP) reconstructs missing action dimensions of the end-effector, combining progress-guided alignment with multi-mask training to support unseen action-constraint combinations. We further adopt a training-free RePaint variant that iteratively inpaints the action during denoising to reduce control error. On ManiSkill and LIBERO-10, our policy achieves average task success rates of 92.67% and 64.67%, respectively.Real-world experiments demonstrate spatiotemporal control with average positional and rotational errors of 44.3 mm and 7{\deg}, respectively, showing that our policy can use diverse references to guide executable robot behaviors.
authors: Yanbang Li, Bu He, Yi Tian, Yu-Chiao Huang, Chenyu Zhang, Ruoqu Chen, Yuanzhe Liu, Yuxiang Gao, Mengdi Xu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of editing robot behaviors according to where, when, and how actions occur.
Introduces the Masked Action Space (MAP) interface to represent keypoints, flows, orientations, and keyposes within one temporal Cartesian action space.
Uses an Inpainting Policy with progress-guided alignment and multi-mask training to reconstruct unspecified end-effector action dimensions and handle unseen constraint combinations.
Adds a training-free RePaint-style denoising procedure to reduce control error during action inpainting.
Reports task success rates of 92.67% on ManiSkill and 64.67% on LIBERO-10; real-world experiments achieve 44.3 mm positional and 7° rotational average errors.

papers.selection_reason: Controllable robot action generation via masked action inpainting directly targets learned manipulation policies.
papers.title: Robotic Spatiotemporal Editing: A Unified Interface for Controllable Action Generation via Masked Action Reconstruction
papers.tldr: MAP unifies diverse spatiotemporal robot-action references as partial action specifications, enabling controllable behavior generation through masked action reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Achieving precise terminal position and heading alignment remains a significant challenge for learning-based mobile robot control. Recent vision-based learning methods have shown promise for precise target-relative control and generalization to unseen environments with pretrained visual encoders, but general-purpose visual representations are not specifically designed to capture the fine-grained spatial differences between current and goal views required for precise control, and real-world demonstrations combining millimeter-scale terminal accuracy with zero-shot transfer across environments remain limited. To address these challenges, we propose Geometric Representation Conditioning for Precise Visuomotor Policy (GR-VIP), a goal-conditioned visuomotor policy that leverages a visual encoder pretrained for relative camera pose estimation. Rather than using the final relative-pose estimate, GR-VIP conditions action prediction on the dense relational features produced before pose regression, preserving fine-grained cross-view information for learning corrective actions from demonstrations. We evaluate GR-VIP on a real-world docking task and demonstrate high docking success rates and millimeter-scale terminal accuracy in both the training and unseen environments, without additional training for transfer. Furthermore, supplementary experiments illustrate the policy's ability to align with non-docking targets and complete docking under a tested low-light condition.
authors: Chanhwi Lee, Jiwon Seong, Eunje Choi, Hohyung Lee, Jongsoo Lee, Junyeong Bae, Inveom Kwak, Woosang Shin, Soohee Han
bullets: Targets precise terminal position and heading alignment, including millimeter-scale docking accuracy and transfer to unseen environments.
Uses a goal-conditioned visuomotor policy with dense relational features extracted before the encoder’s relative-pose regression head.
Evaluated on a real-world docking task in training and unseen environments without additional transfer training.
Also demonstrates alignment to non-docking targets and docking under a tested low-light condition.

papers.abstract: Low-cost passive leader arms enable scalable data collection for imitation learning, but their lack of restoring forces leaves redundant joints unconstrained, yielding highly inconsistent joint-space trajectories. We address this with a low-cost passive joint module (an adjustable mechanical clutch and a 3D-printed spiral spring) that pulls each joint toward a user-defined neutral posture. This passive restoring force acts as a physical prior equivalent to joint-space $L_2$ regularization (``Hardware-as-Regularization''), improving kinematic consistency with shorter completion time than an unregularized arm and preserved movement smoothness. Experiments show substantial variance reduction over a naive passive arm, trajectory consistency on par with an active virtual spring of the same actuator class, and substantially higher downstream success rates (e.g., 73.3% vs. 36.7% on Block Stacking); a stiffness sweep shows consistency degrading monotonically as stiffness decreases, confirming that mechanical stiffness behaves like a regularization weight.
authors: Hideyuki Ichiwara, Yushi Kaida, Hirokazu Ishida
bullets: Passive leader arms can produce inconsistent joint trajectories because redundant joints lack restoring forces.
A mechanical clutch and 3D-printed spiral spring pull each joint toward a user-defined neutral posture.
The restoring force acts like joint-space L2 regularization, preserving smoothness while reducing trajectory variance and completion time.
Consistency matches that of an active virtual spring, while Block Stacking success improves from 36.7% to 73.3%.
A stiffness sweep confirms that lower stiffness yields worse consistency, analogous to reducing the regularization weight.

This physical prior effectively solves the optimization problem minq 1 2 (q− q0) TK(q− q0) subject to the task-space constraint f(q) = xd, allowing users to collect highly consistent imitation learning data.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise for generalist robotic manipulation, but their inference cost remains a major bottleneck for real-time control. This limitation is especially pronounced in flow-matching VLAs such as $\pi_{0.5}$, where the action expert is evaluated repeatedly during iterative denoising. We introduce MambaAct, an efficient Mamba action expert for flow-matching VLA policies. MambaAct retains the pretrained visual-language prefix encoder of $\pi_{0.5}$, while replacing its transformer-based action expert with a compact Mamba-based action expert. Within this expert, Mamba serves as the action mixer that models dependencies across the noisy continuous-action sequence. To preserve visual-language conditioning without repeated token-level cross-attention, MambaAct uses a lightweight Context Compressor to map Vision-language model (VLM) prefix tokens into a compact conditioning signal that gates and modulates each Mamba action block. MambaAct uses a $10\times$ smaller action expert and reduces flow-matching denoising latency by $64.8\%$ on LIBERO and $58.8\%$ in real-world deployment, while improving mean LIBERO success by $1.08$ percentage points across three independent fine-tuning seeds and maintaining gains on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks. Our code and model weights are publicly available at https://github.com/giakhuyendihoc/MambaAct.
authors: Khuyen Pham, Tran Nguyen Le, Edoardo Fazzari, Cesare Stefanini
bullets: Targets the repeated action-expert evaluations that make flow-matching VLAs costly for real-time robotic control.
Retains π₀.₅’s pretrained vision-language encoder and uses Mamba to model dependencies across noisy continuous-action sequences.
Compresses vision-language prefix tokens into a conditioning signal that gates and modulates Mamba blocks without repeated token-level cross-attention.
Uses a 10× smaller action expert and reduces denoising latency by 64.8% on LIBERO and 58.8% in real-world deployment.
Improves mean LIBERO success by 1.08 percentage points across three seeds, with gains also reported on LIBERO-Plus and real-world benchmarks.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: MambaAct architecture. The noisy action chunk Xt is projected into the initial action-token sequence H(0), while the embedded flow time ct is injected through block-specific projections. The L = 4 gated Mamba-3 blocks transform the full action-token sequence into H(L), and a final RMSNorm-linear head predicts the flow velocity V̂θ. papers.abstract: Contact locations and interaction forces are critical for contact-rich robot manipulation but are often ambiguous from vision alone. Measuring them on robots requires specialized tactile hardware and platform-specific data collection, which keeps robot tactile data scarce. Human egocentric video is far easier to scale but lacks touch. Recent predictors trained on egocentric recordings paired with tactile-glove measurements can predict this missing signal from video alone. These predictors, however, remain confined to human hands, which differ from robot hands in appearance and tactile layout. We present Ego2Contact, which learns a visual-tactile prior from human interactions and transfers it to robot hands. Its predictor fuses temporal scene context with hand-local visual features to infer bimanual tactile fields from the RGB video. Anatomical region correspondences align varying robot tactile layouts with the predictor's canonical grid, turning robot measurements into fine-tuning targets and predictions into policy inputs. Ego2Contact outperforms prior tactile predictors on human data, including unseen objects, and on robot data after adaptation. The adapted predictor provides tactile inputs for both simulated reinforcement learning and real-robot policy post-training. In simulation, policies using predicted touch outperform non-tactile baselines and recover part of the benefit of ground-truth tactile sensing. These results show that human-learned tactile priors can supply touch when direct tactile sensing is limited.
authors: Qianqian Yang, Dayou Li, Bangya Liu, Zihao Zhu, Nuo Chen, Siyuan Xu, Hezhen Hu, Chen Yu, Rebecca Friesen, Minghui Zheng, Cynthia Hipwell, Xiaoning Qian, Kenji Shimada, Zhiwen Fan

Improves tactile prediction on human data, including unseen objects, and on adapted robot data.
Predicted touch improves simulated reinforcement-learning policies over non-tactile baselines and recovers some benefit of ground-truth touch.

papers.abstract: A robot swarm covers a building faster with more robots, but the map is only as complete as the space the robots have physically visited. We target the amount of an unknown building a decentralized swarm knows at each instant, ahead of physical coverage. SenseSwarm serves a lightweight learned map predictor on the swarm's shared occupancy map and folds the predicted structure back into a stigmergic guidance field. Its 709K-parameter predictor is fine-tuned on the swarm's own multi-front observations, which we show is necessary: a single-robot predictor collapses on such views. We build a benchmark of twelve real building floors from HouseExpo, HKUST, and KTH, up to 24,000 square meters, and run 1,620 simulations across nine coordination methods, swarm sizes 32 to 512, and three seeds. On physical coverage the swarm is near parity with a greedy frontier planner, as expected. On map reconstruction, every non-predictive baseline needs 1.3 to 1.9 times longer to reach an 80 percent known map, and SenseSwarm holds an equal-time area lead of about 670 square meters, up to 1,359. Folding the prediction into the shared field matters: the same predictor applied per robot matches our speed but suffers a 6.9 times higher inter-robot contact rate at 512 robots. The prediction is computed once per shared map, so its cost stayed flat from 32 to 512 robots.
authors: Haohua Que, Haojia Gao, Mingkai Liu, Hoiian Au, Qian Zhang, Jiayue Xie, Yule Cai, Bokui Chen, Xueqian Wang, Fei Qiao
bullets: Targets earlier knowledge of unknown building structure, beyond physical exploration coverage.
A lightweight 709K-parameter predictor is fine-tuned on multi-front swarm observations and integrated into a stigmergic guidance field.
Evaluated across 12 real building floors, 1,620 simulations, swarm sizes of 32–512, and nine coordination methods.
Non-predictive baselines took 1.3–1.9× longer to reach 80% map knowledge; SenseSwarm led equal-time mapped area by about 670 m², up to 1,359 m².
Shared-field integration maintained similar speed while reducing inter-robot contact versus per-robot prediction; prediction cost remained flat with swarm size.

papers.abstract: Autonomously navigating off-road terrain at high speed demands accurate control, which often relies on dynamics models that capture complex interactions between the robot and terrain. In off-road regimes, terrain interaction is a major component of the vehicle's dynamics. Prior work attempts to capture this effect by training learned models of the vehicle's dynamics, conditioned on its perception of the local environment. However, said conditioning is often overly simplistic, ignoring the spatial structure of the dynamics problem. Our approach, SpatialBEV, exploits this spatial structure. At each step, we query the bird's-eye-view (BEV) features around the predicted state, conditioning the next prediction on current geometric and semantic cues. We additionally present a benchmarking approach that mines a dataset's most difficult scenarios. On datasets collected across seasons, SpatialBEV reduces prediction error by 17.1%, compared to physics-based and learned baselines. We further evaluate on hardware on high-speed ($\geq$10 m/s) and geometrically challenging courses with a 25.3% reduction in maximum cross-track error. More details can be found at https://theairlab.org/spatial-bev-dynamics .
authors: Micah Nye, Samuel Triest, Matthew Sivaprakasam, Isaiah Adu, Sebastian Scherer, Wenshan Wang
bullets: Off-road terrain interactions create complex dynamics that simplistic perception conditioning may miss.
SpatialBEV queries BEV features around the predicted state at each step to capture local spatial structure.
The paper introduces a benchmark that mines the most difficult scenarios from datasets collected across seasons.
It reduces prediction error by 17.1% versus physics-based and learned baselines.
Hardware tests on high-speed (≥10 m/s), challenging courses show a 25.3% reduction in maximum cross-track error.

papers.abstract: Physical reasoning about humans in videos has largely focused on everyday interactions, where contact, pressure, pose, and motion support embodied perception and contact-aware applications. Still, short and forceful properties like impact events remain relatively underexplored, despite their relevance to broader understanding of how abrupt physical events affect the human body. To fill this gap, we introduce human-centric impact localization, a new task that localizes target physical impacts temporally within a video and spatially on the human body. We further present HAPACT, a HumAn-centric imPACT dataset and benchmark built from movie clips, containing over 2.8K video-query pairs with more than 20K fine-grained human-annotated frames. We built HAPACT around viewer-grounded annotation, text-conditioned localization, and supervision at frame-level temporal and SMPL-X-based spatial granularity. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our benchmark, we conduct extensive evaluations of existing methods, employing video moment retrieval models for temporal localization and human-scene contact models for spatial localization. For the spatial task, we propose a text-conditioned baseline by reformulating localization as query-guided body-region selection. Benchmark results show that physical impact localization remains challenging for existing methods, motivating HAPACT as a dedicated benchmark to support physical impact reasoning in videos.
authors: Youngrae Kim, Yejin Jang, Eunho Kim, Youjin Sung, Kun-Woo Song, Sangpil Kim, Sang Ho Yoon
bullets: Defines human-centric impact localization as joint temporal and spatial localization of abrupt physical impacts.
Provides over 2.8K video-query pairs and more than 20K fine-grained, human-annotated frames from movie clips.
Uses viewer-grounded, text-conditioned annotations with frame-level timing and SMPL-X-based body-region supervision.
Evaluates video moment retrieval and human-scene contact models, and introduces a text-conditioned body-region selection baseline.
Results indicate that existing methods face substantial challenges in physical impact reasoning.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot policies offer strong behavioral priors, but achieving deployment-level reliability and throughput remains difficult. Reinforcement learning (RL) can improve these policies, yet its effectiveness is constrained by the cost of online interaction. Existing methods adapt frozen flow-matching policies by treating noise space as a continuous action space. We show that this behaviorally unstructured space makes exploration inefficient, often preventing these methods from extracting meaningful learning signals on challenging tasks. We introduce AnchorQ, which enables coarse-to-fine policy improvement through a structured, refinable latent action representation. At each decision step, AnchorQ uses flow reversal to map reference behaviors to state-conditioned latent anchors, samples local particles around those anchors, and applies value-guided sampling to explore promising refinements. Our analysis shows that anchors reduce identification complexity at the cost of support bias; particle refinement trades this bias against action-class complexity; and critic accuracy determines the reliability of KL-regularized, value-guided selection. Across simulated and real-world manipulation tasks, AnchorQ outperforms state-of-the-art post-training baselines in sample efficiency, delivering a 37% improvement in real-world success rate and 97% higher simulated task throughput under the same interaction budget. Additional visualizations are available on our website https://anchorq-rl.com/.
authors: Carl Qi, Weijun Dong, Xiaojie Wang, Peiyi Chen, Rahul Sajnani, Mingyuan Zhang, Amy Zhang, Jose Barreiros, Manikatan Nambi, Lillian J. Ratliff, Dylan Randle
bullets: Addresses the high online-interaction cost of reinforcement-learning-based policy improvement for generalist robot policies.
Uses flow reversal to map reference behaviors to state-conditioned latent anchors, then refines local particle samples with value-guided selection.
Provides a coarse-to-fine, KL-regularized exploration strategy whose effectiveness depends on anchor support bias, action-class complexity, and critic accuracy.

Outperforms post-training baselines across simulated and real manipulation tasks, with reported gains of 37% in real-world success rate and 97% in simulated throughput under the same interaction budget.

papers.abstract: Manipulating deformable objects toward desired 3D configurations is a fundamental capability for robots operating in unstructured physical environments. However, as the range of possible initial and target configurations grows, goal-conditioned deformable manipulation requires a robot to infer increasingly diverse manipulation behaviors in addition to precise continuous actions. We introduce DefFlow, a framework for goal-conditioned manipulation of deformable objects toward a broad range of 3D configurations. DefFlow learns from demonstrations by jointly predicting the goal-conditioned 3D point flow of the robot and deformable object. We show that this formulation better captures both the manipulation decisions, such as when and where to grasp, release, or re-grasp, and the precise continuous motions required for goal reaching, rather than predicting only the robot flow. Across rope, granular-media, and cloth manipulation settings with diverse initial and target configurations, DefFlow substantially outperforms goal-conditioned action-prediction and robot-flow-only baselines on success rates and goal-distance metrics. We further demonstrate deployment of our framework on a real robot using real point-cloud observations and unseen goal configurations.
authors: Gaurav Singh, Sergio Orozco, Ryan Duong, Mete Tuluhan Akbulut, George Konidaris, Srinath Sridhar
bullets: Addresses the challenge of choosing varied manipulation behaviors and precise motions for deformable objects.
Learns goal-conditioned 3D point flows for both the robot and deformable object from demonstrations.
Captures decisions such as when and where to grasp, release, or re-grasp alongside continuous motion.
Outperforms action-prediction and robot-flow-only baselines across rope, granular-media, and cloth settings.
Demonstrates real-robot deployment using point-cloud observations and unseen goal configurations.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: DefFlow architecture. Given the scene (including the robot) and a goal point cloud, DefFlow processes all points in a unified 3D space using a PTv3 backbone with learned typeembeddings, which is passed through an MLP to get 3D scene flow. The robot flows are then used to recover executable robot actions.

Fig. 3: Simulation benchmarking environments. This figure shows the distribution of tasks in each environment. As can be seen in (a), each task differs not only in the deformed shape, orientation, and position of both start and goal configurations, but also in the action trajectory required to reach the goal. Some require grasping the middle of the rope, others an end or a point in between. Some require only one grasp, while others require multiple grasps; some may require dragging forward, to the left, or in a zigzag pattern, or swishing. For (b), each task involves a different target shape and requires a different combination of paddle sweeps, varying in number, angle, and extent. Some target shapes require the sweeps to be performed in a specific order. In (c), tasks differ not only in the cloth’s starting position and orientation and its goal configuration, but also significantly in the actions required, as some might require grasping the middle of an edge and simply draping the cloth over the bunny, while others require a corner grasp, a slight swish, and then draping. All three environments share large scene configuration spaces and combinatorial action spaces, much broader than those explored previously [4]–[6], [18].

Fig. 5: Qualitative Results on rope manipulation. In (a) the robot needs to grasp the rope, lift and swish back in a precise manner to reach the exact shape. As can be seen, DefFlow predicts the precise grasp+swishing, while the baselines either get the grasp incorrect and collide with the rope, or do not predict the precise swish resulting in the rope not reaching the exact shape. In (b) we showcase two settings with the same goal but different initial configurations, one from the same demo as the goal and the other from a separate demo, while in (c) we show settings with the same starting state but another goal from a separate demo. As can be seen, DefFlow also generalizes to these unseen settings by predicting different action trajectories as in (c) and taking different decisions in (b) where for one it grasps and lifts while for the second it first grasps and moves the rope to align it and then re-grasps and lifts.

papers.abstract: Blindness and low vision limit many people's ability to complete daily tasks, motivating AI assistants that provide useful guidance. Yet, existing benchmarks do not adequately test whether vision models can provide effective everyday assistance. In particular, i) existing benchmarks primarily rely on visual and textual inputs, with limited support for other modalities that are increasingly available in egocentric wearable devices such as gaze, inertial measurements, spatial trajectories, and others; and ii) existing evaluations emphasize scene understanding and question answering, with limited coverage of goal-conditioned guidance for blind and low-vision users across everyday tasks. To bridge this gap, we introduce VISTA (Visually Impaired Scene and Task Annotations), a multimodal egocentric benchmark for goal-oriented assistance for blind and low-vision users. VISTA contains $\sim$1,000 egocentric recordings captured with Project Aria glasses; each recording provides synchronized sensor streams, six of which serve as model inputs, and three different types of annotation, covering ten task categories (TC), from object localization to hazard detection. We evaluate 14 representative vision-language models zero-shot on VISTA and design a lightweight multimodal model baseline that integrates all six modalities. Experimental results show that, although existing models can often describe egocentric scenes, they remain limited in generating goal-directed assistive guidance. VISTA thus provides a benchmark for evaluating multimodal models that could improve everyday accessibility.
authors: No\'e Mosca, Mohamed Rayan Barhdadi, Muhammad Hamza, Joshua Yeh, Suryodaya Bikram Shahi, Zhiyan Li, Selim-Antoine Lali, Weiyue Li, Hasan Kurban, Erchin Serpedin, Gang Luo, Yue Zhang, Minghan Li, Mengyu Wang
bullets: Addresses gaps in benchmarks that lack wearable sensor modalities and goal-conditioned assistive guidance.
Includes ~1,000 Project Aria egocentric recordings with synchronized streams, six model-input modalities, and three annotation types.
Covers ten task categories, including object localization and hazard detection.
Evaluates 14 vision-language models zero-shot and introduces a lightweight baseline integrating all six modalities.
Finds that existing models can describe scenes but remain limited in producing effective goal-directed guidance.
