papers.abstract: Propulsive drones are a promising new technology for generating high-resolution terrain models of the Moon. In future lunar missions, propulsive drones will complete a series of hops across the lunar surface while capturing images with downward-facing cameras. We present an autonomous motion planning framework that uses a vision-guided optimal control strategy for performing safe, efficient hops between specified waypoints. The drone plans parabolic hops between waypoints generated by a global-level planner; if a nominal waypoint is unsafe or unreachable, the drone then completes a diversion maneuver to safely land. To evaluate the validity of potential landing sites, we develop a custom semantic segmentation model for identifying obstacles from aerial images, and we introduce an approach for rapidly calculating reachable terrain. We then use model predictive control (MPC) to robustly track hop trajectories that guide the drone towards safe landing sites. We test the optimal hop planner in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. Our results demonstrate that our unified motion planning framework yields safe, fuel-efficient hop trajectories which can be tracked rapidly and with low error via MPC.
bullets: Plans parabolic hops and diverts to safe landing sites when nominal waypoints are unsafe or unreachable.
Uses semantic segmentation to detect obstacles and rapidly computes reachable terrain.
Applies model predictive control (MPC) to track hop trajectories toward safe landing sites.
High-fidelity lunar simulations show safe, fuel-efficient trajectories that MPC tracks rapidly with low error.

figures.caption: Figure 1. The drone hops between global waypoints. In-flight, when the drone can see its next waypoint, it identifies unsafe obstacles near the waypoint using semantic segmentation. It also calculates the reachable set of landing sites from a starting point a few seconds in the future along the tracked launch trajectory. The nominal landing site is unsafe, so the drone starts calculating the optimal descent trajectory to the nearest safe and reachable landing site. A few seconds in the future, when the descent trajectory is calculated, the drone diverts to its new landing site. Closer to the ground, it checks for smaller obstacles that the semantic segmentation model may have missed from its high vantage point. It identifies a rock at its new landing site and adjusts the remaining descent trajectory to divert to a safe final landing position.

papers.abstract: In robotic manipulation, the same observation often admits multiple feasible actions. Generative policies such as diffusion and flow matching naturally capture such multimodal behaviors, yet which mode is executed is left to random sampling and cannot be actively controlled. We propose Mode-Oriented Source Shaping (MOSS), which turns mode selection into an explicit choice of where generation starts. We first reveal, both empirically and theoretically, that deterministic flow transport induces mode-dependent structure in the source space. Under ideal deterministic ODE transport, distinct behavioral modes have distinct source-space preimages, while practical approximation errors can blur their boundaries due to imbalanced data, limited model capacity, and few inference steps. Motivated by this source-space structure, MOSS constructs semantically aligned mode-specific Gaussian sources that encode mode identity in the initial noise. A modality-strength estimator predicts the local degree of multimodality, which adaptively controls the geometry of the mode-specific sources. It contracts them toward a shared Gaussian where behaviors are similar and separates them near behavioral branching points. During deployment, the desired behavior is selected at inference simply by sampling from the corresponding component. Across 6 simulated and 3 real-world manipulation tasks, MOSS steers to the target mode up to 100% of the time with high task success, recovers minority modes at over 90% guidance rate under a 10:90 imbalance dataset, and surpasses mode-conditioned flow policy by 43.3 points of guidance rate on real robots.
authors: Zirun Ma, Jindou Jia, Tuo An, Jiaqi Bai, Jiahua Dong, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Deterministic flow transport creates mode-dependent structure in source space, but approximation errors can blur mode boundaries.
MOSS builds semantically aligned, mode-specific Gaussian source distributions to represent behavior choices.
A modality-strength estimator adaptively contracts or separates these sources based on local behavioral multimodality.
At inference, users select a behavior by sampling from its corresponding source component.

Across 6 simulated and 3 real-world tasks, MOSS achieves up to 100% mode guidance, over 90% minority-mode recovery under 10:90 imbalance, and a 43.3-point guidance-rate gain over a mode-conditioned flow policy on real robots.

papers.abstract: Current humanoid dexterous manipulation remains largely confined to end-effectors and simple grasps, falling short of humans' ability to engage the entire body by bracing and sliding bulky objects against the arms and torso. We introduce Whole-Body Dexterity (WBD), a general framework that uses the robot's body and appendages as contact surfaces to grasp and manipulate objects. Our sim-to-real pipeline first generates a dataset of feasible whole-body grasps, then trains reinforcement-learning experts on a general any-to-any repositioning objective by sampling initial and goal grasps from the dataset, and distills these experts into a single policy that uses proprioception and object geometry. We show that the distilled policy transfers zero-shot to a real Unitree G1, where it repositions a basketball and a cardboard box to regions around the torso and completes a long-horizon task that stows a box under one arm, carries it from a shelf to a table, and places it. The controller operates interactively, steered by coarse motion references from a human teleoperator. Across real-world whole-body manipulation tasks, the distilled controller completes 90% of trials, compared with 18% for direct retargeting and 4% for a generalist whole-body controller.
authors: Conor Mc Gartoll, An Dang, Pranay Thangeda, Arjun Gupta, Carolina Higuera, Nima Fazeli, Mustafa Mukadam, Manikantan Nambi
bullets: Addresses the limitation of end-effector-only grasping for bulky-object manipulation.
Builds a feasible whole-body grasp dataset, trains reinforcement-learning experts for grasp-to-grasp repositioning, and distills them into one policy.
The policy uses proprioception and object geometry and transfers zero-shot from simulation to a real Unitree G1.
Demonstrations include repositioning a basketball and box, plus carrying and stowing a box in a long-horizon task.
Across real-world tasks, it completes 90% of trials versus 18% for direct retargeting and 4% for a generalist whole-body controller.

papers.abstract: We introduce REKI, a 2.4B vision-language-action model (VLA) pretrained exclusively on public data that sets a new Pareto frontier between performance and model size: on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand and RoboCasa365, it is outperformed only by models about twice its size. REKI consists of a vision-language model (VLM) followed by a flow-matching action expert, and is pretrained on a curated mixture of public robot, egocentric human and vision-language data. Additionally, we endow it with a memory that gives the policy access to its recent past at negligible cost: a few register tokens in the action expert summarise the output of the VLM at each frame and persist in the expert's cache. This memory improves success in simulation and on real robots, and makes oscillations between poses about four times rarer. REKI uses a simple model design and training paradigm, and is optimised to be efficient at training and inference. We release the full code across data curation, training, inference and evaluation, deployment, and all pretrained and finetuned model weights: https://github.com/kyutai-labs/reki.
authors: Juliette Marrie, Paul Pacaud, Adrien Ramanana Rahary, Shizhe Chen, Moritz B\"ohle
bullets: Pretrained exclusively on curated public robot, egocentric human, and vision-language data.
Combines a vision-language model with a flow-matching action expert.
Uses register tokens to summarize recent VLM outputs in the action expert’s cache at negligible cost.
Improves simulated and real-robot success, while making pose oscillations about four times rarer.
Outperformed only by roughly twice-as-large models on LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin Clean2Rand, and RoboCasa365.

Figure 3: REKI. (a) Camera views and instruction are encoded as context Et, which every expert block reads by cross-attention. The state embedding gt and the flow time modulate the actions through adaptive normalisation. The noisy chunk enters the expert’s stream, and the flow loss compares the predicted velocity with its target. The register keys and values of past frames are kept in a cache and read by self-attention, which is the memory of §4.1. (b) One of the ten blocks, holding nr=32 registers and the action tokens of the current frame. Arrows run from a query to what it reads. Action tokens read the current and past registers and themselves, and registers never read them.

Figure 2: How VLAs carry the past. Each panel shows one training window of three frames, with a loss under each frame that receives one. (a) Past frames enter the VLM with the current one, in full (Yuan et al., 2026), compressed (Torne et al., 2026; Physical Intelligence et al., 2026) or from a cache (Jang et al., 2025). The VLM takes the whole window as input, and only the last frame is supervised. (b) A state is written at each step and read at the next, in the backbone (Cherepanov et al., 2026; Xiao et al., 2026) or as fast weights in the head (Jiang et al., 2026). Each step needs the output of the previous one, so the window is unrolled step by step. (c) Each frame is encoded on its own, and an added module mixes the memory tokens of past frames into the prediction for the current one. HAMLET (Koo et al., 2026) supervises the last frame only, and MemoryVLA (Shi et al., 2026) every frame, with the bank entries stored without gradient. (d) In REKI, the memory tokens are registers in the action expert. Their keys and values are kept across frames and read by the self-attention already present. The window is one batched pass, and every frame receives a loss.

A vision–language model encodes the views and the prompt; its final-layer hidden states are the encoded context and its LM head predicts the subtask. (b) The registers and noisy action tokens of a frame cross-attend the context of that frame and self-attend the registers of the K frames up to it, so the past reaches the current chunk only through the registers, and only these are kept for later frames.

The registers of frame t read its context and the cached registers of frames t−1 and t−2. The action tokens read the context and the registers of the three frames; past frames are not encoded again. (b) In the N−1 other Euler steps, only the action tokens are updated, and they read the context and the register keys and values from the cache. The registers do not read the action tokens and skip adaptive normalisation, so they do not depend on the flow time and are computed once per frame. When the next frame enters, the registers of frame t−2 are dropped.

papers.abstract: Most existing agentic reinforcement learning methods assume single-session trajectories, where interaction proceeds within one continuously accumulated context. However, agentic techniques such as context compaction and subagent forking may produce trajectories spanning multiple sessions, creating a mismatch between the single-session training assumption and inference-time execution. Therefore, we introduce Multi-Session Agentic Reinforcement Learning, a more general setting that supports an arbitrary number of sessions within a trajectory. Under this setting, a widely adopted method is to broadcast trajectory-level advantages to all sessions, but this does not distinguish contributions from various sessions or guide session allocation within trajectories. To address this issue, we propose Mosaic, a multi-session agentic RL method with critic-free hierarchical optimization. At the trajectory level, it incorporates session-usage signals into advantage estimation. At the session level, it shapes each session's advantage according to the estimated marginal contribution. Experiments on BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B show that Mosaic outperforms broadcasting in both context compaction and subagent forking scenarios while using fewer sessions on average. Further analyses show that our method achieves improvements in session utility and allocation, which we suggested is a promising target for future advances in multi-session agentic RL.
authors: Yilong Xu, Minrui Xu, Xinyu Zhou, Xiang Long, Haochen Tan, Zhijiang Guo
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between single-session RL training and inference trajectories spanning multiple sessions.
Introduces a general multi-session RL setting supporting arbitrarily many sessions per trajectory.
Uses critic-free hierarchical optimization: trajectory-level session-usage signals and session-level marginal-contribution advantages.
On BrowseComp with Qwen3.5-4B, outperforms broadcasting in context compaction and subagent forking while using fewer sessions on average.
Analysis indicates gains in session utility and allocation; broader advances in multi-session RL remain future work.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning agents optimize exactly the reward signal they are given, which can diverge sharply from an intended true objective when that signal is only a proxy for it; this failure mode is known as specification gaming. Existing evidence for this failure mode is largely observational, with comparatively few demonstrations pairing a controlled, deliberately constructed proxy/true gap with a mitigation that carries a verifiable guarantee rather than only an empirical improvement. We construct a minimal gridworld in which a cleaning-robot agent can either genuinely remove dirt or conceal it from a cheap sensor, and show that a standard deep Q-network trained only on the sensor's proxy reward converges to a policy that games it completely, reaching near-maximal proxy reward while never achieving the true objective. We then introduce a constrained reinforcement learning fix, penalizing the specific behaviors through which the agent exploits the gap, and show that it eliminates the gaming behavior from the final policy while substantially recovering true-objective performance. We further derive and empirically verify an exact accounting identity relating the proxy reward, true reward, and our cost signal for this environment, showing that the cost signal measures the proxy/true gap exactly rather than merely tracking it, and yields a deterministic guarantee under a hard-constrained variant of the method.
bullets: A cleaning robot can either remove dirt or hide it from a cheap sensor, creating a deliberate proxy–true objective gap.
A standard deep Q-network trained on proxy reward converges to complete specification gaming: near-maximal proxy reward but no true cleaning.
The proposed constrained RL method penalizes the specific exploitative behaviors and eliminates gaming in the final policy.
An exact identity links proxy reward, true reward, and the cost signal, proving that the cost measures the objective gap in this environment.
A hard-constrained variant provides a deterministic guarantee, with substantial recovery of true-objective performance.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models present a promising paradigm for general-purpose robot manipulation, but closed-loop deployment is often limited by inference efficiency: at each timestep, high-resolution, often multi-view images are encoded into hundreds of visual tokens that dominate transformer computation and latency. Token compression via attention is a natural solution but is challenging for VLA control because (1) decision-critical tokens are determined by the task, not generic visual saliency, and (2) the token budget varies substantially across steps, so static metrics and budgets waste computation or discard control-critical tokens. We introduce FastVLA, a training-free, task-aware, and temporally adaptive visual token compression framework. At each step, FastVLA scores token importance via task-to-vision attention and adaptively sets the compression rate from the importance-distribution uniformity, measured by an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration. We evaluate FastVLA on OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT across LIBERO and SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot. In simulation, it reduces LLM-backbone FLOPs by 35-59\% and action latency by 9-32\% (a 1.09$\times$-1.46$\times$ speedup) while maintaining task success, achieving a comparable or better efficiency-performance trade-off than existing plug-and-play token compression/pruning/reuse baselines. On the real robot, it cuts end-to-end latency by 20\% (1.25$\times$ speedup) at comparable success. Code is available at https://github.com/jiuyixu25/FastVLA.
authors: Jiuyi Xu, Chengyuan Qian, Zhengzhong Tu, Yang Sui, Yangming Shi
bullets: Targets VLA inference bottlenecks caused by hundreds of visual tokens from high-resolution, multi-view observations.
Ranks tokens using task-to-vision attention rather than generic visual saliency.
Adapts compression rates from attention-distribution uniformity using an inverse-Simpson metric with online sliding-window calibration.
Evaluated across OpenVLA, OpenVLA-OFT, and CogACT in LIBERO, SIMPLER, and on a physical Franka Research 3 robot.
Reduces simulation backbone FLOPs by 35–59% and action latency by 9–32% while maintaining success; real-robot end-to-end latency drops 20% at comparable success.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of FastVLA, our temporally adaptive, training-free visual token compression framework for Vision-Language-Action models. At each action prediction step, FastVLA estimates task-conditioned patch importance via attention, measures distributional uniformity over selected vision tokens, and dynamically adjusts the compression rate using an online sliding-window calibration. By retaining task-relevant yet information-diverse tokens across timesteps, our approach reduces LLM backbone computation while preserving action performance.

papers.title: FastVLA: Task-Conditioned and Temporally Adaptive Visual Token Compression for Efficient Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: FastVLA accelerates vision-language-action robot control by selecting task-relevant visual tokens and adapting their budget over time without retraining.

papers.abstract: We propose Compliant GMT (C-GMT), a modular framework for full-body compliant responses in general motion tracking. As humanoid robots move into real world deployment, they not only need to perform any motion but also respond safely and robustly to interaction forces. Existing general motion tracking policies can imitate diverse motions but are trained to be stiff, leading to unexpected and unsafe behaviors under disturbance. Prior work in compliant humanoid control trades off compliance and generality. There exist examples of full-body compliant responses, but these are heavily curated to single-reference policies. On the other hand, general motion trackers (GMT) are trained to rigidly imitate massive motion capture datasets. Our key insight is to leverage the generality of pretrained GMTs for motion tracking while introducing compliance from a residual adapter that conditions on a history of proprioception. This enables our approach, C-GMT, to achieve both general motion tracking and whole-body compliant responses. Compared to state-of-the-art general motion trackers and single-motion compliant policies, C-GMT demonstrates competitive performance in both motion tracking accuracy and compliance adherence. We further demonstrate improved safety, robustness, and error tolerance in simulation and real-world G1 experiments.
authors: Venki Parsuram, Michelle Wang, Jin-Hyuk Hong, Pulkit Agrawal
bullets: Addresses the stiffness and unsafe disturbance responses of general motion tracking policies.
Adds a residual adapter conditioned on proprioceptive history to a pretrained general motion tracker.
Combines broad motion-tracking capability with whole-body compliant responses without relying on single-motion policies.
Shows competitive tracking accuracy and compliance adherence, with improved safety, robustness, and error tolerance in simulation and real-world G1 experiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of C-GMT training and deployment. During training, a privileged teacher generates compliant references from external force and stiffness commands, which are distilled into a proprioceptive residual adapter on top of a force-robust GMT. At deployment, the same adapter modifies the motion reference using only proprioceptive observations and the commanded stiffness.

In (a), we plot the contact force of the robot’s hand on the wall over time and observe that C-GMT reduces the interaction force. In (b), we show post-impact snapshots and observe that C-GMT yielded to the contact, remaining in the same position and continuing to track the motion. Both SONIC and TWIST2 push themselves away from the wall.
Fig. 5: C-GMT safely yields to humans and the environment even while performing a highly dynamic dancing motion clip.

Fig. 9: Effect of feasibility-based force sampling on compliance learning for a standing reference motion. Feasibility-based sampling achieves faster convergence and higher adherence to the commanded give-way compared with uniform force sampling.

papers.title: Compliant GMT: Making General Motion Tracking Compliant via Residual Reference Adaptation

papers.abstract: Aerial robots operating near people must treat a pedestrian, a parked car, and a wall differently, yet conventional perception--planning stacks reduce all of them to occupied geometry---a \emph{human-aware safety gap} in which category-specific clearance is unavailable to the planner and temporary occlusions remove pedestrian-specific constraints from its map. We present a modular, fully onboard pipeline that closes this gap by turning visual observations into context-dependent safety constraints for real-time UAV navigation. A shared BLIP encoder drives scene captioning and text-conditioned segmentation, which is fused with depth to localize obstacles in 3D. Obstacle-specific risk is inferred by a lightweight LLM (Qwen-2.5-0.5B) stabilized with retrieval-augmented generation and grammar-constrained decoding that restricts its output to a planner-compatible JSON schema. The LLM reasons once per object category rather than per frame: its verdicts are cached per class, so previously seen categories are resolved without inference and new ones trigger a fresh retrieval-grounded query; detections are additionally given persistent identities and held in the map across occlusions. The perception pipeline runs at 10\,Hz on a Jetson Orin NX, while fallback LLM queries take approximately 0.8\,s and remain off the control-critical path. In Gazebo, low-altitude urban navigation among pedestrians and vehicles shows a roughly $3\times$ reduction in collision events over a geometric planner, and semantics-aware landing among moving actors raises success from 34\% to 96\%. The 224-pixel encoder input limits reliable small-object perception at range; conservative pedestrian margins and short-term persistence mitigate this limitation during navigation.
authors: Siwei Cai, Yuwei Wu, Vijay Kumar, Lifeng Zhou
bullets: Addresses the human-aware safety gap: pedestrians, vehicles, and walls receive different clearance requirements instead of being treated as generic occupied geometry.
Fuses BLIP-based captioning and text-conditioned segmentation with depth to localize obstacles in 3D.
Uses a lightweight Qwen-2.5-0.5B LLM with retrieval grounding and grammar-constrained JSON outputs; category-level verdicts are cached and detections persist through occlusions.
Runs perception at 10 Hz on a Jetson Orin NX, with fallback LLM queries kept off the control-critical path.
In Gazebo, collision events decrease by roughly 3×, while semantic landing success among moving actors increases from 34% to 96%; small-object perception at range remains limited.

papers.tldr: A fully onboard UAV system uses lightweight vision and LLM-based object reasoning to impose category-specific safety constraints, reducing collisions and improving semantic landing success in simulation.

papers.abstract: Streaming vision-language models (VLMs) must continuously integrate information from the past while remaining responsive to current observations and user queries. Existing memory mechanisms typically compress, retrieve, or cache historical observations and reintroduce them into the input context, forcing historical memory and current observations to compete for limited context. We propose MaLoW, a streaming memory framework that instead internalizes historical context into evolving lightweight parameter updates. MaLoW uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to incrementally consolidate incoming video observations into fixed-size LoRA weights, allowing historical information to be carried forward without revisiting the full video stream. In doing so, MaLoW represents history as weights, while keeping the current observation as input. To support training, we further construct MaLoW-Instruct, a large-scale streaming video dataset containing 381K question-answer pairs over 56K videos. We conduct extensive experiments to demonstrate that MaLoW achieves strong performance on OVO-Bench, StreamingBench, and StreamArena. On the backward split of OVO-Bench, MaLoW outperforms prior memory approaches by 3.9% to 11.8% across different video backbones while incurring only modest latency overhead. Beyond streaming video understanding, MaLoW also generalizes to vision-language-action models, improving the action success rate on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%.
authors: Zhuoming Liu, Jinhong Lin, Lin Zhang, Yiwu Zhong, Yin Li
bullets: Addresses the context bottleneck caused by memory methods that retrieve or append historical video observations to current inputs.
Uses a recurrent HyperNetwork to consolidate incoming observations into fixed-size LoRA parameter updates while keeping current observations as input.
Introduces MaLoW-Instruct, a streaming-video instruction dataset with 381K question-answer pairs across 56K videos.
Achieves 3.9%–11.8% higher performance than prior memory approaches on OVO-Bench’s backward split, with modest latency overhead.
Also improves action success on Simpler WidowX by 9.3%, suggesting applicability to vision-language-action models.

papers.abstract: Traditional reinforcement learning (RL) algorithms face significant limitations in handling long-term tasks with sparse rewards. Recent advancements have leveraged large language models (LLMs) to enhance RL by utilizing their world knowledge for task planning and reward generation. However, planning-based approaches often depend on pre-defined skill libraries and fail to optimize low-level control policies, while reward-based methods require extensive human feedback or exhaustive searching due to the complexity of tasks. In this paper, we propose the Progress Reward Model for RL (PRM4RL), a novel framework that integrates task planning and dense reward to enhance RL. For high-level planning, a complex task is decomposed into a series of simple manageable subtasks, with a subtask-oriented, fine-grained progress function designed to monitor task execution progress. For low-level reward generation, inspired by potential-based reward shaping, we use the progress function to construct a Progress Reward Model (PRM), providing theoretically grounded optimality and convergence guarantees, thereby enabling effective policy optimization. Experimental results on robotics control tasks demonstrate that our approach outperforms both LLM-based planning and reward methods, achieving state-of-the-art performance. Code is available at https://github.com/deng-ai-lab/PRM4RL.
authors: Xiuhui Zhang, Ning Gao, Xingyu Jiang, Yihui Chen, Yuheng Pan, Mohan Zhang, Yue Deng
bullets: Addresses sparse rewards and the difficulty of learning long-term tasks with conventional RL.
Decomposes complex tasks into manageable subtasks and monitors fine-grained execution progress.
Uses a progress function to construct dense rewards inspired by potential-based reward shaping.
Provides theoretical optimality and convergence guarantees for policy optimization.
Outperforms existing LLM-based planning and reward methods on robotics control tasks, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: World-model planners evaluate candidate trajectories by predicting their future consequences, implicitly relying on the plan-to-motion relationship learned during training. At deployment, a different downstream controller may execute the same planned trajectory differently, creating a planning-execution gap between the frozen model's imagined future and actual execution. A natural remedy is to replace the planned trajectory with its predicted or observed execution. However, we find that better execution fidelity does not necessarily yield better decisions: directly substituting predicted execution trajectories yields only a 0.048 PDMS improvement across 10 unseen controller configurations, far smaller than the gain from our proposed adaptation. This suggests a semantic mismatch between a planned trajectory, which serves as a reference for downstream control, and an executed trajectory, which already describes the resulting post-controller motion. We introduce ExecutionBridge, which infers controller-specific execution characteristics from planned-executed trajectory pairs and uses them to adapt the native ego latent rollout while keeping the original planned trajectory unchanged. The planner, world model, and reward head remain frozen. On NAVSIM, ExecutionBridge consistently improves planning across unseen controller configurations and multiple frozen world-model planners, with substantially larger gains in challenging driving scenes where execution mismatch more strongly affects candidate evaluation.
authors: Danqi Zhao, Keyu Chen, Wenchao Sun, Minglei Huang, Jianhe Zhang, Yan Zhu, Hao Cheng, Zifan Cao, Sifa Zheng
bullets: Problem: Different downstream controllers can execute the same plan differently, causing a gap between imagined and actual outcomes.
Naively substituting predicted or observed execution trajectories improves fidelity but does not reliably improve planning decisions.
Method: Infer controller-specific execution characteristics from planned–executed trajectory pairs and adapt the planner’s native ego latent rollout.
The world model, planner, and reward head remain frozen; the original planned trajectory is preserved.
On NAVSIM, the method consistently improves planning across unseen controllers and multiple frozen planners, especially in challenging driving scenes.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Architecture of ExecutionBridge. (a) Controller Encoder. Given a support set of planned–executed trajectory pairs Sc, the Controller Encoder summarizes these observations into a compact controller representation ec that captures persistent controller-specific execution characteristics. An auxiliary execution decoder predicts the execution of a held-out query trajectory for training supervision and is discarded at deployment. (b) Controller-Conditioned Latent Bridge. For each candidate, the frozen world model first produces its native rollout from the original planned trajectory. Conditioned on ec, the Latent Bridge predicts a gated correction to the ego latent, which is bounded by a trust-region projection before being injected into the rollout. The resulting controller-conditioned rollout is evaluated by the unchanged reward model for candidate scoring.

Fig. 2. Planning–execution gap and motivation for ExecutionBridge. (a) The same planned trajectory can lead to different executions at deployment from those implicitly assumed by the frozen world model, causing its imagined future to deviate from the future actually encountered. (b) Directly substituting the planned trajectory with its executed counterpart improves execution fidelity, but introduces a plan–execution semantic mismatch: the executed trajectory can still be interpreted through the model’s implicit plan-to-motion mapping, and therefore does not necessarily improve candidate ranking. (c) ExecutionBridge instead retains the original planned trajectory as the conditioning input and uses controller-specific execution evidence to adapt the imagined future used for candidate evaluation.

Fig. 4. Representative planning results under the standard NAVSIM setting. Compared with frozen WoTE, ExecutionBridge yields trajectory selections that are better aligned with controller-dependent execution in representative collision and drivable-area failure cases.

Fig. 1. Evolution of end-to-end planning paradigms. Model-free planners predict or score trajectories directly from the current scene, without explicitly modeling their future consequences. Model-based planners additionally use a learned world model to imagine candidate-conditioned futures for trajectory evaluation. Conventional model-based planning typically assumes that candidate trajectories are executed according to the planto-motion relationship learned during training. Execution-adaptive modelbased planning further incorporates controller-specific information, allowing candidate futures to be evaluated under deployment-specific execution.

Fig. 6. Adaptation under representative controller styles. We show four representative controller configurations, including aggressive, conservative, steering-lag, and steering-gain behaviors. Controller-conditioned candidate evaluation consistently improves both PDM and Time to Collision (TTC) across these diverse controller styles. Examples on the right illustrate safetycritical cases in which accounting for controller-specific execution changes the selected trajectory and avoids failures under frozen evaluation.

Fig. 5. Planning under unseen controller shifts. Performance of the frozen planner and ExecutionBridge across ten unseen deployment controller configurations. (a) ExecutionBridge consistently improves PDMS across controller styles (mean: 87.98 → 88.59, +0.61). (b) It also improves TTC (mean: 94.53 → 94.86, +0.33). (c) The improvement is substantially larger on the low-score subset, where PDMS increases from 32.04 to 46.13 (+14.09). These results indicate that controller-conditioned adaptation is particularly beneficial in challenging driving scenes where candidate evaluation is more sensitive to execution differences.

Fig. 7. Execution fidelity does not imply decision fidelity. (a) Predicted and exact controller execution substantially reduce geometric execution error. (b–c) Nevertheless, candidate-ranking fidelity changes only marginally on the frozen-defined difficult-scene subset. (d) Direct execution substitution improves selected-candidate quality, but ExecutionBridge performs best by preserving the original plan and adapting its imagined future. Pairwise-oracle PDMS in (d) is a candidate-level diagnostic distinct from final navtest PDMS.

papers.title: Plans Are Not Executions: Adapting Frozen World-Model Planners to Controller-Induced Execution Shift

papers.abstract: Learning from demonstration is an effective strategy for endowing robots with manipulation capabilities but requires training on datasets comprised of massive amounts of demonstrations. Existing demonstration collection approaches either require constant human involvement, for example, via teleoperation or are specialized for a single task. Task and Motion Planning (TAMP) systems are able to autonomously solve and therefore generate demonstrations for general-purpose tasks; however, learning from their demonstrations has proven difficult due to multi-modality in their solutions. In this work, we build on recent work leveraging GPU acceleration for TAMP and propose DemoStream, a TAMP system that optimizes demonstration quality in order to improve behavior cloning success rates. First, we introduce batched TAMP sampling operations along with a new TAMP algorithm that correspondingly performs batched constraint satisfaction in order to explore many solutions in parallel. We conduct simulation experiments ablating different action spaces, cost functions, and batch sizes to analyze the effect of these choices on downstream policy success rates. Finally, we show that we can leverage the safety guarantees of TAMP to directly collect real-world demonstrations at an average rate of 66 demos per hour. See our website for policy rollout videos: demostream.github.io.
authors: Caelan Garrett, Neel Jawale, Fabio Ramos
bullets: Addresses the need for scalable, autonomous demonstration collection beyond teleoperation or task-specific systems.
Introduces batched TAMP sampling and batched constraint satisfaction to explore many solutions in parallel.
Optimizes demonstration quality to mitigate multimodal solutions and improve behavior-cloning success rates.
Evaluates action spaces, cost functions, and batch sizes in simulation, and collects real-world demonstrations at an average of 66 per hour.
Scope: Results are presented through simulation ablations and a real-world demonstration-collection demonstration; the abstract does not specify broader task coverage or policy performance details.

papers.abstract: Embodied Visual Tracking (EVT) is an essential capability for intelligent robots in human-robot collaboration, requiring an agent to follow a designated target person in dynamic environments relying solely on egocentric visual perception. However, persistent pedestrian occlusions in dynamic scenes pose critical challenges to existing EVT methods. Lacking proactive visibility preservation, reactive tracking methods frequently experience prolonged target loss under severe occlusions. Therefore, we propose VP-EVT, a framework that treats target visibility as an explicit objective of motion control rather than a by-product of following. Acting on this objective requires understanding both what obstructs the target and how robot motion can change that obstruction. VP-EVT therefore uses language-guided perception to extract separate target and pedestrian observations. When occlusion makes current observations incomplete, VP-EVT combines visual history with ego-motion to maintain estimates of their relative positions and motion. Using these estimates and the current following waypoints, VP-EVT predicts whether continued following will sustain the obstruction. When the predicted risk is low, the original following motion is retained; otherwise, a recurrent controller combines updated estimates with maneuver context from preceding decisions to coordinate viewpoint adjustment and the return to stable following. Moreover, we introduce OccEVT-Bench for closed-loop evaluation of persistent occlusion and collect expert demonstrations for training. On its Risk split, VP-EVT improves success rate by 121.4% relative to a competitive baseline and reduces visibility deficit and longest target-loss duration by 78.8% and 74.4%, respectively.
authors: Yanci Wen, Tianle Zeng, Jianwei Peng, Weixi Situ, Hanjing Ye, Hong Zhang
bullets: Addresses prolonged target loss caused by pedestrian occlusions in dynamic environments.
Uses language-guided perception to separate target and occluder observations, then combines visual history with ego-motion to estimate relative motion during partial visibility.
Predicts whether continued following will maintain occlusion and selectively triggers viewpoint-adjustment maneuvers through a recurrent controller.
Introduces OccEVT-Bench and expert demonstrations for closed-loop evaluation and training.
On the Risk split, improves success rate by 121.4% and reduces visibility deficit and longest target-loss duration by 78.8% and 74.4%.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of VP-EVT. (a) A causal RGB history and a language prompt produce Current Entity Observations: zTt for the designated target (T ) and zPt for a potential occluding pedestrian (P ). (b) Visual observations and robot ego-motion ∆Et update a persistent target belief BT t and a short-term pedestrian belief BP t . Uncertainty increases when visual evidence becomes unavailable. (c) The target and pedestrian beliefs, together with following waypoints Wt, condition persistent-occlusion risk prediction and recurrent visibility-preserving control. The curves schematically illustrate visibility degradation, while the motion example contrasts continued following with a visibility-preserving maneuver. The controller produces linear and angular velocity commands [v, ω], and the resulting ego-motion ∆Et+1 informs the next belief update.

Fig. 3. Overview of OccEVT-Bench. Episodes span indoor and outdoor scenes, diverse target appearances and motions, and dynamic pedestrian interactions. Risk episodes assess persistent-occlusion handling, while complementary Safe episodes assess continued following without unnecessary intervention. Easy, Medium, and Hard levels cover different interaction difficulties.

Fig. 4. Temporal visibility comparison. We compare target visibility and cumulative visibility deficit across methods on selected Risk episodes. The dashed line marks the target-loss threshold τloss = 0.35. Higher visibility and lower cumulative deficit indicate better visibility preservation.

Fig. 1. Standard following and VP-EVT under dynamic pedestrian occlusion. Continuing behind an occluding pedestrian can prolong target loss, whereas visibility-preserving motion changes the robot’s viewpoint to reduce the obstruction while continuing to follow the target. The upper and lower panels provide perspective and bird’s-eye illustrations, respectively.

Fig. 5. Real-world deployment of VP-EVT. The robot adjusts its viewpoint around the pedestrian in the patterned shirt to reduce occlusion and resume following the target in black. Gray dotted paths indicate the following reference, while green dotted paths illustrate visibility-preserving motion. Frames are ordered chronologically from left to right, top to bottom.

papers.abstract: Flow-based Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies are inherently stochastic: different noise seeds can produce action chunks of varying quality from the same observation. At test time, however, the policy typically commits to a single sample without an explicit estimate of its quality. In fine-grained manipulation, executing a suboptimal action can irreversibly disrupt task progress and lead to failure. To exploit policy stochasticity, we introduce a training-free two-axis trigger that uses two initial samples to measure within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance, detecting the critical states. Once triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicting action-conditioned future latent states and the corresponding changes in task progress. By operating in latent space, the verifier avoids pixel reconstruction and enables efficient and more accurate ranking. Across three real-world tasks, $\textit{i.e.,}$ pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement), our method raises the average completion score from 50.8% to 65.5%, while adding 326 ms for sampling and verification per triggered decision on a single RTX 4090. Consistent gains are also observed in simulation, where the average success rate rises from 66.4% to 73.6% in the clean setting of RoboTwin 2.0, from 62.8% to 69.6% in its randomized setting, and from 96.9% to 97.6% on LIBERO.
authors: Xueli Sun, Yuxiang Lu, Yantong Liu, Xianzhe Fan, Xi Chen, Zhe Liu, Hengshuang Zhao
bullets: Addresses failures caused by committing to a poor action sample during fine-grained manipulation.
Uses two initial samples to detect critical states from within-chunk temporal variation and cross-sample variance.
When triggered, a JEPA-based latent world model ranks candidate action chunks by predicted future latent states and task-progress changes.
Improves average real-world completion from 50.8% to 65.5% across pen insertion, pipetting, and apple placement, with 326 ms added per triggered decision.
Also reports consistent simulation gains across RoboTwin 2.0 and LIBERO; verification is applied selectively rather than at every decision.

papers.abstract: Autonomous driving planning requires selecting trajectories that remain safe, rule-compliant, and comfortable under complex multi-agent interactions, yet robust closed-loop decision making in planning-critical scenes remains challenging. Existing diffusion- and RL-based planners often rely on generic rewards and use relational structure mainly for representation, limiting how planning-critical rollouts shape policy improvement. We present GRID-Planner, a graph--reward integrated diffusion planning framework that aligns generative planning with structured relational signals. Specifically, GRID-Planner combines graph-aware importance weighting, a time-indexed relational reward surrogate, and an advantage-weighted diffusion objective with on-policy self-distillation, forming a rollout-return-advantage-update loop without explicit likelihoods. Experiments on nuPlan and interPlan show that, compared with the diffusion-only baseline, GRID-Planner reduces collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk by 35.8\%, 60.8\%, and 27.4\%, respectively, and improves the planning score by 3.4\%. Project website: https://github.com/yangzhaojason/GRID-Planner.
authors: Zhao Yang, Zezhong Qian, Yinan Shi, Longjun Liu, Yawei Jueluo
bullets: Targets safer, rule-compliant, and more comfortable planning in complex multi-agent scenes.
Combines graph-aware importance weighting, time-indexed relational reward surrogates, and advantage-weighted diffusion training.
Uses on-policy self-distillation to form a rollout–return–advantage–update loop without explicit likelihoods.
On nuPlan and interPlan, reduces collision rate, lane deviation, and jerk by 35.8%, 60.8%, and 27.4%, respectively, while improving planning score by 3.4% over a diffusion-only baseline.

papers.abstract: Learning from experience requires recovering reusable knowledge and determining when it applies to a new situation. We introduce OntoAct, a hypothesis-based neuro-symbolic framework built on ontological abstraction. OntoAct turns individual experiences into axioms over entity types, relations, and conditions, making their underlying patterns reusable across situations. A large language model (LLM) uses this world knowledge to propose hypotheses and actions, while a symbolic verifier assesses their supporting conditions against current observations. Verification identifies missing evidence, and new observations and intervention outcomes update hypothesis assessments and guide subsequent actions. We also introduce Tacit-FLE, a benchmark built on the Factorio Learning Environment (FLE) for diagnosing and repairing hidden faults in existing factories using inherited operational records. Its synthetic maintenance corpus distributes evidence across records, and an executed repair may leave the fault unresolved, requiring agents to reassess their diagnoses through interaction. Across Tacit-FLE, Mars, and ALFWorld, OntoAct achieves leading task performance with efficient interaction and inference.
authors: Donghyeok Lee, Bong Gyun Kang, Junyong Ahn, Sungroh Yoon

papers.abstract: Biological visual navigation achieves remarkable robustness at extremely low power, whereas frame-based robotic systems relying on artificial neural networks remain limited in both respects, particularly for energy-constrained micro aerial vehicles (MAVs) operating in complex environments. Inspired by the event-driven, sparse, and asynchronous principles of biological visual systems, neuromorphic sensing and computation provide a promising alternative for robust and energy-efficient navigation. In this paper, we propose the first end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic paradigm for MAV visual navigation in complex environments by integrating neuromorphic vision, spiking neural networks, and neuromorphic processors. The proposed method first extracts the environmental representation from event streams using a spiking perceptual representation module. This representation is fed into a spiking navigation module, where guidance learning and population coding enable efficient policy learning with few time steps. The navigation module then outputs a waypoint converted into executable trajectory points. Experiments show that the proposed neuromorphic method achieves navigation performance comparable to ANN-based methods while markedly reducing power consumption. The spiking perceptual module consumes only 19.57% of the power of its ANN counterpart, while the spiking navigation module deployed on Intel Loihi consumes only 12.37% of that required by its ANN counterpart running on NVIDIA Orin NX. Beyond prior neuromorphic systems focused mainly on relatively simple navigation subtasks, we demonstrate a complete neuromorphic visual navigation system spanning simulation and real-world deployment. Our results establish the feasibility of the neuromorphic paradigm for autonomous navigation and provide a bio-inspired pathway toward robust and low-power MAV navigation.
authors: Junjie Jiang, Ankang Zhou, Zheng Fang
bullets: Targets robust, energy-efficient navigation for micro aerial vehicles in complex environments.
Combines neuromorphic vision, spiking neural networks, and neuromorphic processors.
Uses spiking perceptual representations, guidance learning, and population coding to produce executable waypoints.
Reports power use of 19.57% for the spiking perceptual module and 12.37% for the Loihi-based spiking navigation module relative to ANN counterparts.
Demonstrates a complete system in simulation and real-world deployment, extending beyond simpler neuromorphic navigation subtasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: End-to-end event-driven neuromorphic MAV navigation system. (A) Architecture of the proposed end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic navigation system. The system comprises a spiking perceptual representation module and a spiking navigation policy module. The perceptual module converts event streams into compact, geometry-aware features, while the navigation policy module maps these visual features, together with the robot state and goal direction, to navigation actions. (B) Key hardware components of the neuromorphic system. The platform consists of a neuromorphic vision sensor (Prophesee EVK4), an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, an x86 host computer, a neuromorphic processor (Intel Kapoho Bay), and a micro aerial vehicle. The NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX communicates wirelessly with the x86 host computer. (C) Deployment and communication pipeline of the proposed system. Owing to the limited neuron models supported by Intel Kapoho Bay, the spiking perceptual representation module is deployed on the NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX, whereas the spiking navigation policy module is deployed on Intel Kapoho Bay. The Jetson Orin NX acquires the event stream and transmits control commands to the Pixhawk flight controller. The Jetson Orin NX and the x86 host computer exchange system information wirelessly. The x86 host computer exchanges spike trains with Intel Kapoho Bay through NxSDK.

Figure 3: Training pipeline of the proposed end-to-end event-driven neuromorphic navigation method. Continuous grayscale image sequences are first transformed into asynchronous event streams using an event simulator. Depth estimation is then introduced as an auxiliary task to enable geometry-aware spiking features learning from event streams. The learned event features are fused with the MAV state and goal direction, and then encoded into spike trains via population coding. The resulting spikes are processed by the spiking navigation network and decoded to predict the action. Finally, collision loss, smoothness loss, and goal-reaching loss are defined based on the predicted action, providing physically meaningful supervision for end-to-end optimization of all network modules.

Figure 4: Navigation trajectories of the proposed method in simulation environments. (A) Continuous navigation performance is evaluated by requiring the MAV to sequentially pass through multiple waypoints in a simulated environment. (B) Robustness is evaluated by placing target points in eight directions within each of six testing environments.

Figure 7: Navigation trajectories comparison between the proposed method and the ANNbased method. The navigation trajectories of the two methods are compared across six different simulation environments, with the trajectories of the proposed method shown in red and those of the ANN-based method shown in blue.

Figure 5: Average trajectory distance comparison between our method and the ANN-based method across six environments. (A) Average trajectory distance at a maximum speed of 0.5 m/s. (B) Average trajectory distance at a maximum speed of 1 m/s. (C) Average trajectory distance at a maximum speed of 2 m/s.

Figure 10: Navigation performance of the proposed method in real-world environments. Indoor and outdoor navigation tests were conducted by placing the target point behind a series of obstacles, requiring the MAV to avoid the obstacles and successfully reach the target.

Figure 6: Average navigation time comparison between our method and the ANN-based method across six environments. (A) Average navigation time at a maximum speed of 0.5 m/s. (B) Average navigation time at a maximum speed of 1 m/s. (C) Average navigation time at a maximum speed of 2 m/s.

Figure 1: Visual navigation mechanisms across biological, conventional, and neuromorphic paradigms. (A) The biological visual navigation paradigm relies on the retina and neural circuits. Visual information is sensed asynchronously at the pixel level and processed through sparse, eventdriven neural activity to produce navigation behaviors. (B) Comparison between conventional and neuromorphic visual navigation paradigms for MAVs. The conventional visual navigation paradigm relies on frame-based cameras and artificial neural networks. Visual information is acquired synchronously as image frames and processed through dense, clock-driven computation to generate navigation actions. The neuromorphic visual navigation paradigm employs event-based vision sensors and spiking neural networks. Inspired by biological visual processing, it captures visual information asynchronously at the pixel level and processes it through sparse, event-driven computation to generate navigation actions.

Figure 9: Comparison of navigation trajectories with and without depth supervision. The green and red lines indicate trajectories without and with depth supervision, respectively. Removing depth supervision leads to collisions, ground crashes, and substantial target deviations.

Figure 11: Operations and per-inference energy consumption of ANN-based and SNN-based perceptual representation networks. The ANN-based network is evaluated based on multiply–accumulate operations (MACs), whereas the SNN-based network is evaluated based on spiketriggered accumulate operations (ACs). Per-inference energy consumption is estimated from the corresponding operation counts using energy costs of 4.6 pJ per MAC and 0.9 pJ per AC under a 45-nm CMOS technology assumption.

The inference rate denotes the number of forward inferences performed per second, and the energy per inference is calculated by dividing the dynamic power by the inference rate. The NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX is evaluated in both high-performance mode (25 W) and power-saving mode (10 W).

papers.abstract: Many vision-language-action policies rely on action-labeled robot demonstrations and lack an explicit mechanism for predicting future visual states. These limitations hinder learning from action-free videos and can encourage overfitting to demonstration conditions, weakening generalization and robustness. We present TS-WAM, a lightweight Teacher-Student World-Action Model that addresses these challenges through self-supervised temporal learning and explicit future prediction. Its vlm-jepa framework learns from heterogeneous data, including robot demonstrations and action-free human videos, using an EMA target branch without requiring a separately trained external teacher. By coupling vlm-jepa with delta-lwm, TS-WAM learns to predict latent actions from the current observation and instruction and uses them to predict future visual features that guide action generation at inference. A unified end-to-end training architecture jointly optimizes temporal representation learning, visual dynamics, and robot control without a separate latent-action or world-model pretraining stage. The EMA target branch is removed at inference, keeping the deployed policy lightweight. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and SimplerEnv, together with real-world manipulation experiments on Franka Research 3 and RevoTron, demonstrate that TS-WAM achieves strong manipulation performance, generalization, and robustness.
authors: Menghao Yin, Jiaju Yin, Xiyue Dong, Lixin Xu, Zhenhui Zhang, Ke Zhang, Yating Feng, Renjing Xu
bullets: Addresses reliance on action-labeled demonstrations and limited future-state modeling in vision-language-action policies.
Uses self-supervised temporal learning with an EMA target branch to train on heterogeneous robot and human-video data without an external teacher.
Couples latent-action prediction with future visual-feature prediction to guide action generation at inference.
Jointly trains temporal representations, visual dynamics, and robot control end to end, without separate latent-action or world-model pretraining.
Shows strong manipulation performance, generalization, and robustness in simulated benchmarks and real-world experiments.

papers.selection_reason: Jointly learns temporal latent actions, future visual prediction, and robot control from demonstrations and human videos.
papers.title: TS-WAM: Temporal Latent Actions and World-Action Coupling for Vision-Language Robot Control
papers.tldr: TS-WAM is a lightweight vision-language-action policy that learns from both robot demonstrations and action-free videos by predicting latent actions and future visual states for more robust control.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies are typically trained with action prediction as the primary supervision signal, since robots ultimately execute actions. Auxiliary objectives such as latent-action (LA) and future-vision (FV) prediction are often added to improve policy learning, yet they compete with action prediction for the same training budget. We ask whether, under a fixed budget, allocating a substantial share of training samples to such objectives, rather than to further action prediction, can improve policy learning. We build a unified VLA framework that couples a two-stream multimodal diffusion transformer (MMDiT) with a sample-level router, which assigns each training sample to either action prediction or an auxiliary objective and thus makes supervision allocation explicit. Within this framework, we instantiate three LA targets based on LAPA and its DINO-feature variants, and three FV targets based on DINOv3, V-JEPA 2, and Wan2.2 representations. Across LIBERO, CALVIN, and four real-robot tasks, suitable LA and FV supervision outperforms action-only training under the same budget, even when action prediction receives no more than half of the training samples. FV generally outperforms LA, although the strongest LA target remains competitive on CALVIN. Diagnostic analyses suggest that DINO-based LA targets emphasize relative motion, whereas FV targets emphasize absolute position and task identity. We therefore argue that what robot policies learn to predict, and how training is allocated among these targets, should be treated as explicit design choices rather than defaulting to action-dominant training.
authors: Haitao Shen, Hanyu Liu, Yihan Lin, Huiping Liu, Junbo Cui, Daoheng Li, Yang Li, Jing Zhang, Wenxin Li, Yuan Yao

Suitable auxiliary supervision outperforms action-only training, even when action prediction receives at most half the samples; future-vision generally performs best.
DINO-based latent-action targets emphasize relative motion, while future-vision targets emphasize absolute position and task identity.

papers.selection_reason: Rethinks VLA supervision by trading action prediction against latent-action and future-vision world-model objectives.
papers.title: What Should Robot Policies Learn to Predict? Rethinking Supervision Targets in Vision-Language-Action Learning
papers.tldr: Under a fixed training budget, explicitly allocating samples to auxiliary latent-action or future-vision prediction can improve vision-language-action robot policies over action-only supervision.

papers.abstract: Continuous physical human-robot interaction requires robots to rapidly adapt their control behaviour without interrupting task execution. However, existing ROS 2 control architectures rely on stop-to-switch mechanisms that introduce substantial delays and interrupt execution. We present an open-source, sub-millisecond reflex engine based on an enhanced ROS 2-compatible multimode controller that enables deterministic switching between control modalities and integrates reflex behaviours for mitigating contact hazards and kinematic limit violations. Experiments on a Franka Robotics manipulator demonstrate switching delays below 0.1 ms, more than four orders of magnitude faster than conventional ros2_control, while maintaining continuous operation during safety-critical events. In a multi-stage manipulation task, the proposed framework reduced execution time by 3.5% and peak trajectory jerk by more than threefold. By eliminating runtime middleware overhead, controller transitions are implemented as lock-free pointer operations, enabling reflex-level responsiveness within an open-source robotics framework.
bullets: Addresses delays and task interruptions caused by stop-to-switch mechanisms in existing ROS 2 control architectures.
Uses an enhanced multimode controller with integrated reflexes for contact hazards and kinematic-limit violations.
Implements transitions as lock-free pointer operations to avoid runtime middleware overhead.
On a Franka manipulator, switching delays were below 0.1 ms and continuous operation was maintained during safety-critical events.
A multi-stage manipulation task showed 3.5% lower execution time and more than threefold lower peak trajectory jerk.

papers.abstract: Embodied spatial intelligence requires more than visual recognition: models must localize entities, reason about their relations, and express this knowledge in action-relevant forms. Yet joint training can conflate the knowledge needed at different stages because supervision is fragmented across incompatible geometric and semantic outputs. We introduce Anvil, a unified framework for data generation, training, and benchmarking for embodied spatial intelligence. (1) Anvil-Gen is a heterogeneous data flywheel that combines form-specific generation, cross-stage consistency verification, and failure-driven recollection across 11 Ground--Relation--Act forms. (2) Anvil-Ben provides scene-aligned supervision for learning diverse embodied spatial capabilities and scene-linked assessments that distinguish stage competence from error propagation. (3) Anvil-MOPD is a 9B student that consolidates heterogeneous spatial knowledge through distillation from specialist teachers. Semantic-first-fault routing targets teacher supervision to the student's earliest decisive failure, while stage normalization controls the loss scale across native outputs of different lengths. We construct 5.8M source-grounded records spanning 160K images, reserving 580K spatial records for held-out evaluation and using the remaining 5.22M records for training. On average across seven public benchmarks, Anvil-MOPD outperforms Qwen3.5-9B and RynnBrain-8B by 9.29 and 11.03 percentage points, respectively, while reaching 80.67% on VABench-Point. Controlled studies support targeted coverage, selective transfer, and feedback-guided repair as complementary framework components.
authors: Weilin Ruan, Bohan Zhou, Jinghao Li, Yangkai Wei, Wenqian Li, Peiran Dong, Yingjie Xu, Leyi Wu, Haojian Huang, Binghui Xie, Han Yang, Kaiwen Zhou, Yinchuan Li, Ying-Cong Chen, James Cheng

Anvil-MOPD is a 9B student distilled from specialist teachers using earliest-failure routing and stage-normalized losses.
Across seven public benchmarks, it reports average gains of 9.29 and 11.03 percentage points over Qwen3.5-9B and RynnBrain-8B, respectively; it reaches 80.67% on VABench-Point.

papers.abstract: Solving optimal control problems for high-dimensional mechanical systems subject to constraints remains challenging due to nonlinear dynamics and non-convex feasible sets. This paper introduces MAGMA(Multiplier-Augmented Geometric Motion Algorithm), an Affine Geometric Heat Flow (AGHF)-based trajectory optimizer that incorporates an augmented Lagrangian framework solved via a primal-dual flow. A theoretical characterization of the primal-dual AGHF is provided, establishing that MAGMA is a gradient flow on an appropriately defined energy. MAGMA is validated across a variety of challenging trajectory generation problems with obstacles, state limits, and actuation limits. Comparative evaluations against state-of-the-art solvers demonstrate that MAGMA achieves high quality solutions with significantly reduced tuning effort on the hardest problems.
authors: C\'esar E. Ramos Chuquiure, Vansh Thakur, Challen Enninful Adu, Ram Vasudevan
bullets: Targets optimal control with nonlinear dynamics, non-convex feasible sets, obstacles, state limits, and actuation limits.
Uses an augmented Lagrangian framework solved through a primal-dual flow within the AGHF trajectory optimizer.
Provides a theoretical characterization showing MAGMA is a gradient flow of a suitably defined energy.
Experiments across challenging trajectory-generation problems report high-quality solutions with reduced tuning effort compared with state-of-the-art solvers.

papers.abstract: Retrieval tasks are a form of search task where a robot must explore, find an object, and return with it as quickly as possible. Recent work in ergodic control has demonstrated time-optimal path planning for search tasks where visitation is proportionally matched, within some tolerance, to a given target distribution. However, these planners minimize the duration of a full deterministic search, while retrieval missions end their search at an unknown point in the trajectory and must return to a given base. In this work, we propose a new formulation of the time-optimal ergodic search problem that models detection as a Poisson process and minimizes total mission time by including the return phase in the objective. Experimental results show that time-optimal ergodic retrieval (TOER) achieves up to $19\%$ shorter mission durations relative to ergodic baselines and that this advantage grows as the return phase becomes more costly. Simulation and hardware implementations validate TOER's compatibility with environments of non-convex geometry as well as both 2D and 3D search domains.
authors: Christian Sulana, Christian Hughes, Ian Abraham
bullets: Addresses retrieval missions where detection occurs at an unknown point and the robot must return to a base.
Models object detection as a Poisson process and incorporates the return phase into the optimization objective.
Validated in simulation and hardware for non-convex environments and 2D and 3D search spaces.
Achieves up to 19% shorter mission durations than ergodic baselines, with larger benefits when returning is more costly.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. Belief Fidelity Impact on Mission. Search in the room setting from Fig. 3 as the true target is displaced by δ from the given belief. (Left) InfoMax’s detection collapses once the belief is wrong (0.93 → 0.22) while the ergodic methods degrade slowly, since covering the belief’s support leaves detection mass where the target can still be found. (Right) TOER holds the lowest mission time until the target leaves the belief entirely, where its tradeoff between detection speed and terminal position is no longer beneficial.

Fig. 1. Time-Optimal Ergodic Retrieval. A Franka arm executes a full retrieval mission of a green block in an occluded 3D search domain. From its start pose (t0), the arm sweeps the bin along an ergodic trajectory (t1) until the overhead camera detects the target. Once detected, the arm abandons the remaining plan, grasps the object (t2) and delivers it to the base (t3). We propose time-optimal ergodic retrieval (TOER), which includes the expected return cost explicitly in the objective such that searches prioritize likely detection sites that are closer to the base.

Fig. 6. Computational Scaling of TOER. Log-log wall time for a single solve at fixed iterations (95% CI bands on each slope). TOER and TOES scale identically in trajectory knots N , while the Poisson detection term makes TOER grow linearly in domain samples M while TOES is sublinear.

Fig. 5. Return Bound and Detection Certificate. Validation of the return bound and detection certificate on the non-convex room grid from Fig. 3. (Left) The two return-cost estimates from one detection site. The obstacle-blind bound cuts through walls while the true geodesic routes around them. (Right, Top) Planning against the loose bound costs 0.1% of realized mission time relative to the geodesic bound. (Right, Bottom) With survival ≤ δ imposed, realized survival stays inside the certified region at every δ.

Fig. 2. Expected Mission Time Comparison. Single-target search in an open planar field as the sensor’s detection gain is swept at fixed κ = 6.6. When detection is unreliable, the target is usually not found, thus mission time is dominated by return, and TOES + Return suffers additional return cost at every unsuccessful episode. TOER holds a ≥ 12% advantage over TOES + Return throughout while matching TOES (End @ Base) without imposing a terminal constraint.

Fig. 3. Return Discrepancy Profile. Object search in a planar 12-room lattice. (Left) Search scene with uniform target draws and sensor footprint, occluded by walls. (Right) TOER’s paired mission-time advantage over each baseline vs. return discrepancy κ. Advantage grows logarithmically (R2 = 0.95) toward the ceiling from Prop. 2. The gap to TOER (search-only) isolates the return term, which is null at κ = 1 and 7.9% at κ = 10.

papers.abstract: Scaling robot manipulation models requires large amounts of interaction data, yet collecting diverse real-robot experience remains costly. Human manipulation videos, in contrast, provide abundant and diverse task experience that could potentially benefit robot learning. However, differences in morphology, action spaces, and control mechanisms make human motions unsuitable as direct supervision for robot actions, raising a scientific question: what knowledge in human videos should be transferred across embodiments to robot manipulation? To address this question, we analyze subtask transfer through the lens of causal beams, focusing on which contextual conditions and interaction dependencies should be retained to support local task effects. Based on this perspective, we propose Causal-Beam-Guided Subtask Transfer (CBST). CBST learns manipulation-related representations from human videos and grounds them in task-level semantic variables using robot demonstrations. Within a predefined manipulation model, causal-beam constraints guide contextual information selection by requiring retained assignments to sustain local mechanism outputs while preserving nontrivial responsiveness to retained inputs. The selected semantic information conditions a world-action model, allowing the robot to generate actions from its own observations without requiring human-robot motion correspondence. Experiments on robot manipulation benchmarks show improvements in task success over the corresponding world-action model baselines.
authors: Xingyu Zhang, Yingchao Li, Peizheng Guo, Jie Hu, Changwen Zheng, Wenwen Qiang
bullets: Human videos offer abundant manipulation experience, but morphology and action-space differences prevent direct action supervision.
The method identifies contextual conditions and interaction dependencies that preserve local task effects, termed causal beams.
CBST learns manipulation representations from human videos and grounds them in task-level semantic variables using robot demonstrations.
Causal-beam constraints select useful semantic information to condition a world-action model that generates robot actions from its own observations.
Experiments report higher task success than corresponding world-action-model baselines on robot manipulation benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Imitation learning enables robots to perform complex tasks by leveraging human-collected demonstrations. However, most existing approaches require labor-intensive data collection with additional teleoperation systems, which hinders scalability. Human videos represent a natural source of data that implicitly contain knowledge of manipulation behaviors. However, transferring them to robots remains challenging due to the visual domain gap and the absence of explicit action labels. In this work, we introduce TDV, a trajectory-based framework that leverages data generation to enable generalizable manipulation. TDV focuses on task-relevant objects by leveraging plug-and-play 6D pose estimation techniques to extract object trajectories from human videos, thereby mitigating the impact of irrelevant backgrounds and varying viewpoints. As a modality-agnostic intermediate representation, trajectories are inherently independent of the visual domains and different embodiments, enabling efficient data generation. Our method outperforms previous approaches on RLBench simulation tasks, achieving near 100\% success rates across seven tasks. In real-world experiments, TDV enables cross-embodiment generalization manipulation from one-shot human demonstrations by leveraging efficient trajectory generation techniques.
authors: Guoping Pan, Xinmiao Yu, Wannan Cao, Jincheng Li, Baolin Jiang, Yizhe Li, Yi Cheng, Houde Liu
bullets: Addresses the costly data collection, visual-domain gap, and missing action labels in learning from human videos.
Extracts task-relevant object trajectories using plug-and-play 6D pose estimation.
Uses trajectories as a modality-agnostic intermediate representation for efficient data generation.
Achieves near-100% success across seven RLBench simulation tasks.
Demonstrates cross-embodiment manipulation from one-shot human demonstrations in real-world experiments.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of TDV. Our framework consists of three stages: video parsing, trajectory generation, and closed-loop execution. For hand tasks, we extract 3D hand trajectories and remap them to a two-finger gripper. For object tasks, we apply 6D object pose estimation and perform data augmentation by sampling diverse initial poses. A trajectory-based diffusion policy is trained on the resulting data. During deployment, real-time pose estimation and a switch policy enable closed-loop control and multi-procedure task execution.

papers.abstract: We study how vision-language models (VLMs) can learn to think and actively explore in 3D space. Instead of providing multi-view images, videos, or 3D representations to the model, we preserve the native visual encoding of VLMs, i.e., a single image, one at a time, just like humans, and treat the 3D representation only as an environment with which the model can interact through actions (e.g., move left) and observations (rendered images). Each rollout begins from an initial first-person view and a visual question. The model can then iteratively reason, navigate, and reorient its viewpoint before committing to a final answer. Following an initial trajectory-supervised finetuning, we apply reinforcement learning (RL) with rewards driven primarily by final-answer correctness. Crucially, RL provides no direct supervision over which viewpoints the model should visit or which exploration actions it should take. Instead, the model must learn an effective exploration policy solely from the extent to which its interactions improve performance. Across six 3D benchmarks, our model ACT3D achieves an average accuracy of 53.2% that improves its base Qwen model by 22.0% and surpasses proprietary Gemini 3.6 Flash. ACT3D also outperforms existing open-source 3D methods while using 50-70% fewer input frames, and generalizes to unseen domains with an average improvement of 5.9% over its supervised initialization. Further analysis reveals adaptive, question-conditioned exploration. Performance gains over the base model increase from 0.6% on questions answerable from the initial view to 16.3% on those requiring extensive exploration. ACT3D searches for occluded targets, avoids unnecessary exploration, and acquires complementary viewpoints for spatial comparisons. These findings demonstrate that outcome-based RL enables VLMs not only to reason over visual evidence, but also to learn when and how to acquire it.
authors: Yijiang Li, Bingyang Wang, Nuno Vasconcelos
bullets: Uses one rendered image at a time, with actions such as moving and reorienting, rather than preloaded multi-view or 3D inputs.
Combines trajectory-supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning driven mainly by final-answer correctness, without viewpoint or action labels.
Achieves 53.2% average accuracy across six 3D benchmarks, improving its base Qwen model by 22.0% and using 50–70% fewer input frames than existing open-source methods.
Learns question-conditioned exploration: it searches for occluded targets, avoids unnecessary movement, and gathers complementary views for spatial comparisons.
Generalizes to unseen domains, improving 5.9% over supervised initialization; gains are largest for questions requiring extensive exploration.
