papers.abstract: Closed-loop evaluation is widely regarded as a more faithful way to assess end-to-end (E2E) driving models than open-loop evaluation, and Bench2Drive, built on the CARLA simulator, has become the dominant benchmark for it. We show that its evaluation protocol itself contains pitfalls that can misrepresent the models scored on it. Bench2Drive's comfort metric, adapted from nuPlan, has several implementation errors and a segmentation scheme that rewards standing still, so it mostly measures how long a vehicle stays stationary, correlating with stationary time at r = 0.97 across eight models. We propose a corrected, distance-based metric that cuts that correlation to r = 0.06. Under it, the strong driving-score/comfort tradeoff the original metric reports is no longer detectable once models are compared at matched driving speed, which suggests that comfort trades against how fast a model drives rather than against how well it drives. We also uncover two pitfalls in how the harness supplies navigation signals: the default controller can replace a model's own steering with an angle toward the route target point, and the target point supplied at evaluation time can differ substantially from what a model saw in training. We demonstrate both on UniAD and VAD, where their effects differ sharply, and argue that future closed-loop evaluations should check for them. We will release all fixes as standalone code, so corrected comfort scores can be obtained from logged trajectories without re-running closed-loop simulation.
authors: Thomas Schwarzfischer, Emad Aghajanzadeh, Moritz Thoma, Nael Fasfous, Manoj Rohit Vemparala, Pierpaolo Mori, Daniel Mueller-Gritschneder, Ulf Schlichtmann
bullets: The original comfort metric contains implementation and segmentation flaws, with comfort strongly correlated with stationary time (r = 0.97 across eight models).
A corrected distance-based metric reduces this correlation to r = 0.06 and removes the apparent driving-score/comfort tradeoff when comparing models at matched speeds.
The reported tradeoff likely reflects driving speed rather than driving quality.
The evaluation harness may override a model’s steering with route-target guidance and provide target points that differ from training inputs.
The authors demonstrate differing effects on UniAD and VAD and release fixes that can recalculate comfort from logged trajectories.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Target-point distance supplied to UniAD in training and at evaluation time, on a logarithmic axis, with statistics (m) for both models below. The shaded band is the training p5 to p95 range, 4.06m to 6.60m, shared by both models. The original planner places UniAD’s target at a median of 64.6m, over an order of magnitude beyond the 4.94m training median, and behind the ego in 13.7% of frames. Ours restores the median for both models, to 6.28m and 6.09m. For UniAD it also removes the tail (p95 130.2m to 20.0m) and the behind-ego frames (13.7% to 0.9%); for VAD it does not, and we report that residual in section III-B.

Fig. 1. Illustration of two closed-loop evaluation pitfalls. In both panels blue marks the model’s own output: its predicted waypoints and the steering vector they imply. (a) Steering overruling: the red vector is the steering the controller substitutes, aimed at the navigation target point (red pin). This can mask a model’s failure to compensate its own steering error (left) and can override a maneuver around an obstacle (right). (b) Target-point mismatch: because the evaluation route planner samples the route differently than the planner that collected the training data, the navigation command switches at a different place along the route at test time (faded red pins) than during training (red pins). Here the ego receives turn right early and begins to rotate, then receives straight at the junction: the command calls for the straight continuation (purple) while its heading and the road geometry support completing the right turn (green), a command-context combination absent from training. Interpolating between the two can produce dangerous behavior. SO: steering overruling; TPM: target point mismatch.

Fig. 3. Sample route of SimLingo [3], showing driving speed over time together with the cumulative comfort scores of the different implementations. We re-project our distance-based implementation on the time axis. The traditional metric considers driving comfortable when and only when the ego vehicle is standing still, marked by the red shaded bands. Even the slight movement from seconds 35 to 38 is deemed uncomfortable. When we apply our fixes, the metric correctly scores segments when the vehicle is driving comfortably, but still incentivizes standing still. Further applying our distance-based segmentation fixes both problems, not changing the comfort score when the ego vehicle is stationary.

Table I. Cumulative impact of removing steering overruling (SO) and aligning target-point sampling (TPM) on driving score (DS) and success rate (SR), on Dev10, against a constant-velocity baseline. ✓ marks a fix applied. TPM is applied on top of SO, not independently.

papers.selection_reason: Identifies and corrects evaluation pitfalls in closed-loop benchmarking of end-to-end driving/navigation models.
papers.title: Comfortably Stuck: Evaluation Pitfalls in Bench2Drive's Closed-Loop Protocol
papers.tldr: Bench2Drive’s closed-loop evaluation can misrepresent driving models because its comfort metric rewards stopping and its navigation inputs may alter or mismatch model behavior.

papers.abstract: Object manipulation often requires combining non-prehensile actions with grasping. However, existing approaches typically develop these capabilities separately and integrate them by sequencing distinct primitives through prescribed intermediate objectives, limiting the coordination of contact motions and grasping. Their integration also remains sensitive to object and gripper geometry and depends on particular environmental supports, complicating real-world deployment. We present Uni-PNP, a unified policy that jointly learns prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation for object pose reaching across diverse objects and grippers. To achieve this, we first pretrain a geometry encoder to predict contact-induced object motion using a contact-dynamics dataset constructed from simulated interactions between diverse objects and grippers. We then train the policy in a two-stage reinforcement learning curriculum from graspable objects to ungraspable peers, encouraging the discovery of non-prehensile interactions and their integration with grasping. Experiments show 76.39% success on hundreds of seen objects with grippers, and 57.91% on unseen peers, outperforming the strongest pose-reaching baseline by 20.52 and 17.79 percentage points, respectively. We also analyze emergent behaviors, including nonprehensile and prehensile repositioning, grasp acquisition that requires grasping after tipping, and table-assisted reorientation while grasping, and transfer to the real-world scenario. Project page available at lgswdn.github.io/Uni-PNP.
authors: Wenxuan Zhu, Yuze Wang, Jiangran Lyu, Jiayi Chen, Yixin Zheng, Mi Yan, Li Yi, Zhizheng Zhang, He Wang
bullets: Addresses the limitations of separately designed and sequenced prehensile and non-prehensile manipulation skills.
Pretrains a geometry encoder on simulated contact-dynamics interactions to predict contact-induced object motion.
Uses a two-stage reinforcement-learning curriculum progressing from graspable objects to ungraspable peers.
Achieves 76.39% success on seen objects and 57.91% on unseen peers, outperforming the strongest baseline by 20.52 and 17.79 percentage points.
Demonstrates emergent repositioning, grasp-after-tipping, table-assisted reorientation, and transfer to a real-world scenario.

papers.abstract: Reliable contact-rich manipulation requires detecting execution deviations early enough for corrective action. Yet most monitoring methods are reactive, identifying anomalies only after they become observable. Anticipating such anomalies is challenging because visual observations only partially reveal physical interaction, while planned actions describe intended motion rather than their actual physical consequences. We address this problem with MAIA, a multimodal framework for anomaly anticipation. Its vision-action-force world model learns nominal interaction dynamics and predicts the visual and force responses of planned actions, while a lightweight anomaly head predicts impending interaction anomalies. To enable systematic evaluation, we introduce CRIA, a real-world multimodal dataset of 2,852 trajectories spanning 18 contact-rich manipulation tasks, with frame-level annotations of anomaly onset and evolution. Experiments on both seen and novel tasks show that MAIA achieves more accurate anomaly discrimination than representative baselines while providing earlier warnings, with bACC scores of 0.765 and 0.710 and median anticipation lead times of 28.0 and 25.1 steps, respectively. Moreover, using these predictions for anomaly-aware action selection improves end-to-end task success from 52.6% to 61.5% without retraining the underlying manipulation policy. These results highlight the value of modeling future physical consequences for proactive anomaly anticipation.
authors: Yi Qiao, Maolin Zheng, Haoran Sun, Lujia Dong, Wenzhao Lian
bullets: Reactive monitors detect anomalies too late, while vision alone cannot fully reveal physical interactions.
MAIA uses a vision-action-force world model to predict planned-action outcomes and a lightweight head to anticipate anomalies.
CRIA provides 2,852 real-world trajectories across 18 contact-rich tasks with frame-level anomaly annotations.
On seen and novel tasks, MAIA achieves bACC scores of 0.765 and 0.710 with median warnings 28.0 and 25.1 steps early.
Anomaly-aware action selection raises end-to-end success from 52.6% to 61.5% without policy retraining.

figures.caption: Fig. 4. MAIA Overview. The framework consists of a Vision-Action-Force World Model (VAF-WM) and a predictive anomaly head. VAF-WM extends GE-Base with gated action-force adapters to forecast future visual and force dynamics. The anomaly head fuses these predictions with interaction tokens and uses a temporal transformer to predict anomaly occurrence, temporal prevalence, and localization within the future window.

Fig. 3. CRIA overview. The central ring presents all 18 tasks grouped by interaction category, while the surrounding panels illustrate category-specific interaction characteristics and typical anomaly modes. The hardware setup used for data collection is shown on the right.

Fig. 5. Qualitative comparison of anomaly predictions. Shaded regions indicate correct predictions (green), prediction errors (red), and early warnings (yellow) prior to the true anomaly onset (dashed line). (a) Nominal execution: our method produces fewer false alarms than the baselines. (b) Anomalous execution: our method provides an earlier sustained warning than WCM, while reward-model warnings are intermittent.

Fig. 6. Qualitative modality ablation on representative anomaly cases. The examples illustrate how incorporating physical feedback enables MAIA to distinguish anomalous interactions that remain ambiguous when only visual and action cues are available.

papers.abstract: Small observation or action errors can compound during closed-loop execution and disrupt a trained imitation learning policy. We study whether the original expert demonstrations can improve robustness through test-time hidden-state steering without additional demonstrations or policy retraining. Our analysis of a trained policy finds that expert hidden-state variation is concentrated in relatively few dimensions, while the directions capturing this variation differ across regions. Motivated by this geometry, we propose Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering (DHS), which learns an invertible nonlinear coordinate map from expert hidden states obtained by replaying the demonstrations through the frozen policy. DHS attenuates coordinates with low expert variance more strongly than those with high variance, then maps the modified coordinates back to hidden-state space. This allows steering directions to vary with the current hidden state while retaining every coordinate. Across four simulated manipulation tasks, DHS improves mean success under observation noise over the unmodified Transformer policies. Controlled comparisons yield higher mean success with learned nonlinear coordinates than with linear coordinates under both hard projection and full-rank rescaling. Combining DHS with action smoothing improves mean success rate under observation noise in certain tasks compared with action smoothing alone.
bullets: Expert hidden-state variation is concentrated in a few dimensions, with important directions varying across regions of state space.
DHS learns an invertible nonlinear coordinate map from expert hidden states replayed through the frozen policy.
It suppresses low-variance coordinates more strongly than high-variance ones, then maps states back while retaining all coordinates.
Across four simulated manipulation tasks, DHS improves mean success under observation noise over unmodified Transformer policies.
Nonlinear coordinates outperform linear alternatives in controlled comparisons; combining DHS with action smoothing helps on some tasks.

(a) Expert hidden-states concentrate near a curved structure with locally varying tangent and normal subspaces; blue arrows indicate tangent directions. (b) A learned diffeomorphic chart maps hidden-states to coordinates where DHS attenuates low variance coordinates more strongly than high variance coordinates while retaining every coordinate. (c) Mapping back through the inverse chart produces location dependent hidden-state updates. Gray points denote expert samples; open orange and filled blue markers indicate states before and after steering. Here, ai is the fitted expert variance of chart coordinate i, and β controls steering strength.

papers.title: Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering: Improving Imitation Learning Policy Robustness through Expert Hidden-State Geometry
papers.tldr: Diffeomorphic Hidden-State Steering improves imitation-policy robustness to observation noise by reshaping hidden states according to expert-state geometry at test time, without retraining or new demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language Models (VLMs) enable automated preference labeling for robotic manipulation, yet their deployment remains impractical since each query incurs substantial inference cost, while VLMs frequently abstain on visually challenging comparisons. We propose SPEAR, a framework that transforms VLMs into efficient preference oracles via two synergistic mechanisms. First, we design distinguishability-aware query selection to reduce abstention rates by targeting only informative and distinguishable comparisons. Second, we deploy an adaptive reward transition that bootstraps exploration with VLM-synthesized guidance before preference-based refinement. Experiments on the manipulation benchmarks demonstrate that SPEAR achieves 88.9% average success, outperforming baselines by 23.3 percentage points, while significantly reducing abstention and wall-clock training time on contact-rich tasks. SPEAR learns three Mobile ALOHA manipulation tasks fully online on real hardware, demonstrating end-to-end real-world applicability. By addressing query efficiency and exploration challenges, SPEAR establishes VLMs as practical preference oracles for scalable robot learning without manual reward engineering.
authors: Zewen Wu, Ruizhe Liu, Pei Zhou, Feng Chen, Yanchao Yang
bullets: Addresses high VLM query costs and abstentions on visually difficult comparisons.
Uses distinguishability-aware query selection to target informative, answerable comparisons.
Applies adaptive rewards that bootstrap exploration with VLM-synthesized guidance before preference-based refinement.
Achieves 88.9% average success, 23.3 percentage points above baselines, while reducing abstention and wall-clock training time on contact-rich tasks.
Demonstrates fully online learning for three real-hardware Mobile ALOHA tasks without manual reward engineering.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of SPEAR. (1) Distinguishability-aware query selection (top, blue) predicts VLM response likelihood via multi-scale features and weights information gain accordingly, selecting only answerable and informative trajectory pairs for querying; (2) Adaptive reward transition (bottom, green) bootstraps exploration using VLM-synthesized warm-up rewards before transitioning to refined preference-based learning. Together, these mechanisms enable efficient online learning by ensuring both high-quality query selection and sufficient behavioral diversity for meaningful preference elicitation.

Fig. 2: Learning curves across six Meta-World tasks. Our method (green) consistently outperforms baselines in both mid-range and final performance. Shaded regions indicate standard deviation over 5 seeds.
Fig. 3: Average fit probability of 5 VLM backbone behaviors. As visual distinguishability increases, the abstention rate decreases and the accuracy increases.
Fig. 4: Real-robot experiment task settings. (a) draweropen. (b) window-open. (c) soccer.

papers.title: SPEAR: Selective Preference Elicitation with Adaptive Rewards for VLM-Guided Robotic Manipulation
papers.tldr: SPEAR makes VLM-guided preference learning for robotic manipulation more practical by selecting distinguishable queries and adaptively transitioning from VLM guidance to preference refinement.

papers.abstract: Indoor service robots often enter unmapped buildings whose layouts and task constraints are already familiar to users. We address this human-familiar, robot-unseen setting with AVALON, a topological navigation framework organized around human-seeded layered spatial memory, node-verified topological execution, and task-triggered, evidence-gated human--robot memory co-updating. The robot has no prior on-site traversal or site-specific training. Deployment requires only a floor plan, place clues, and an initial topology-odometry alignment. Visual depth point-goal navigation leverages verified node arrivals to perform translational re-anchoring, without requiring a robot-constructed global SLAM map. Human--robot memory co-updating fuses complementary sources of information. Human operators specify task constraints that are unobservable via vision and report offline environmental modifications, whereas the robot provides physical-state evidence through active in-situ validation. Task relevance governs whether human-reported environmental changes undergo robot validation during the active mission. Field-collected perceptual evidence gates memory updates, maintaining an explicit separation between human-specified permissions and robot-observed traversability. Our experiments on a Unitree Go2 show that AVALON with X-NavDP completes a 12.81 m Intersection-to-Dining mission in 46.4 s (5/5) with no mapping, 40.9% less robot time than DimOS-Go2 (78.5 s, 4/5), while policy-only X-NavDP times out in all of the 5 runs. These demonstrate the superiority of the proposed topological navigation framework.

papers.abstract: Specialized vision-language-action (VLA) policies acquire strong domain-specific skills, yet consolidating these skills into one shared policy remains challenging. On-policy distillation (OPD) transfers teacher knowledge on inputs induced by the student, addressing the distribution mismatch encountered during deployment. For flow-based VLAs, this mismatch arises at two levels: environment observations and intermediate action-generation states. We propose a two-level on-policy distillation framework that couples student-driven environment interaction with teacher velocity supervision along student-generated action flow trajectories. Frozen domain specialists jointly supervise one student. After each update, the student collects new environment experience and generates fresh action-flow trajectories. Starting from a joint supervised fine-tuning (SFT) initialization, Velocity Loss OPD yields absolute success-rate gains of 22.55% on LIBERO-40, 33.4% on CALVIN five-instruction sequences, and 22.6% on Meta-World MT50. Compared with Action Loss OPD and Teacher-rollout SFT, it achieves absolute success-rate gains of 6.4-9.5% on LIBERO-40, 9.7-18.3% on CALVIN, and 3.2-4.2% on Meta-World MT50. Analysis by sequence length further shows larger success-rate gains on longer CALVIN sequences. These results demonstrate effective multi-domain capability consolidation through two-level on-policy supervision, with a single student deployed across domains.
authors: Lichao Ni, Yuhan Liu, Pengfei Li, Guanghuan Fang
bullets: Addresses distribution mismatch at both the environment-observation and intermediate action-flow levels.
Uses frozen domain-specialist teachers to provide velocity supervision along student-generated flow trajectories.
Alternates student updates with fresh environment interaction and action-flow generation, starting from joint supervised fine-tuning.
Improves success rates across LIBERO-40, CALVIN, and Meta-World, with especially larger gains on longer CALVIN sequences.
Produces a single student policy capable of deployment across multiple domains.

papers.abstract: Language-conditioned humanoid motion generation enables users to create and refine robot movements through natural language. The central challenge is to connect an underspecified request to concrete motion structure that can subsequently be revised relative to an accepted reference. We present TRACE, a generation and editing framework for the Unitree G1 humanoid robot built around typed, measurable kinematic quantities. Our insight is to ground generation conditions in paired training motions and editing goals in the current motion. A language model learns to predict support, root, and hand events from motion-derived supervision; their time-aligned encodings complement the original text in a diffusion generator. Gravity-referenced states and trajectory--contact objectives improve kinematic consistency. For editing, typed requests define body--time scopes and source-relative goals. A separate reference-conditioned diffusion editor uses these goals and revised events to realize changes, while sampling-time projection preserves protected state coordinates. Quantitative evaluation and human assessment show improved semantic alignment and motion quality over the compared methods. Controlled ablations support the value of motion-grounded conditioning and kinematic consistency, while multi-turn editing evaluations demonstrate more reliable execution of successive relative requests under shared preservation constraints. Together, these results support typed kinematic structure as a common basis for motion generation and reference-aware revision.
authors: Zejian Kang, Yifu Luo, Boyang Shen, Jingxuan Li, Zekai Chen, Zekun Shi, Yongxue Xu, Zhenyu Hou, Bingqian Wu, Shaolei Zhang, Wentao Yang, Xiangru Huang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of translating underspecified language into concrete, revisable humanoid motion structure.

A reference-conditioned diffusion editor applies typed body–time goals relative to the current motion, with sampling-time projection protecting selected states.
Gravity-referenced states and trajectory–contact objectives improve kinematic consistency.
Quantitative, human, ablation, and multi-turn evaluations report better semantic alignment, motion quality, and successive relative-edit execution than compared methods.

papers.abstract: In endovascular interventions, physicians rely on planar DSA and X-ray fluoroscopy to interpret vessel anatomy and device motion, yet converting these images into feedback for autonomous navigation remains difficult. A perception and control method is formulated for two-dimensional image feedback. Vessel masks are converted into a labeled centerline graph, and device-tip estimates are projected onto a planned path to obtain progress, deviation, and direction. A rule-based controller uses these quantities for delivery, branch selection, probing, rollback, and recovery. The method was evaluated on a physical dual-device robotic platform in 65 closed-loop runs using simulator-rendered planar images across three paths. All runs reached at least 0.95 maximum observed guidewire progress; two runs (3.1%) met the prespecified failure rule of three or more autonomous stop events. The results establish route-level performance on the tested platform; clinical image sequences and broader anatomy remain to be evaluated.

Online, device masks provide frame-wise tip and direction estimates, whereas the averaged vessel output is locked as a labeled centerline graph. Operator-selected start and target points define the topology-constrained route. Operator-marked interaction-risk points form a separate early-trigger channel: proximity invokes priority retreat before the delayed off-path condition, without modifying the graph or replanning the route. This heuristic response is not a formal safety guarantee. Projection of both tips onto the route produces the visual state used by the priority controller. A discrete command drives the robot and changes the physical device configuration. Mentice updates the device–vessel interaction and renders the realized motion in the next simulator-rendered image, which closes the visual feedback loop.

papers.abstract: While generalist vision-language-action (VLA) models have enabled diverse open-world manipulation, real-world robotic assistance requires two critical capabilities they currently lack: personalization and reliable execution. First, executing an instruction like "make me a sandwich" requires grounding subtask decomposition in persistent user preferences rather than relying on a single generic solution. Second, reliable deployment demands explainable safety assurance that proactively prevents hazards and gracefully recovers from occasional physical failures. To address these gaps, we present CarryOn, a dual-loop harness designed to augment a frozen VLA policy. The planning loop maintains persistent user-level and scene-level context that is continually grounded against new observations and revised through interaction, enabling personalized task selection and execution grounding across conversations and changing scenes. The execution loop actively supervises policy rollouts, shielding actions from predicted hazardous contact. When execution fails, the system invokes reusable control-based recovery skills that restore task progress and are refined through reflection on earlier failures. On a real robot and in simulation, CarryOn dispatches preference-consistent subtasks across users and scenes, reduces the violation rate of an already safety-finetuned VLA from 52.6% to 6.1%, and increases recovery success from 13% to 80% when refined skills are reused.

Supervises policy rollouts and shields actions predicted to cause hazardous contact.
Uses reusable control-based recovery skills after failures, refining them through reflection on prior errors.
Demonstrated preference-consistent task execution on a real robot and in simulation.
Reduced safety violations from 52.6% to 6.1% and increased recovery success from 13% to 80% when refined skills were reused.

papers.abstract: Aerial vision-language navigation (VLN) agents built on large vision-language models are expensive to query. Executing a complete predicted action chunk before replanning amortizes this cost, reducing model inference from 195 to 42 ms per executed waypoint for our policy. It also moves the states at which the policy is queried away from expert demonstrations, which supervise neither recovery from these states nor termination at the learner's own arrival. On OpenFly test-seen, no-stop failures account for 47.78% of full-chunk behavior cloning (BC) outcomes. We present X-Fly, a staged training framework for full-chunk aerial VLN. Recovery DAgger labels learner-visited decision states with smooth chunks that reconnect to future expert segments and with STOP at the first in-region state. Flow-GRPO then jointly refines the chunked flow controller and a Bernoulli STOP policy from same-task closed-loop outcomes, supplemented by outcome-verified stopping supervision. With eight controls per decision, X-Fly reaches 74.18% SR on test-seen and 51.73% on test-unseen, compared with 16.45% and 18.43% for full-chunk BC and 32.04% and 29.46% for DreamFly.
authors: Ruibin Ju, Ruifeng Cai, Min Xu, Lin Wang
bullets: Full-chunk execution reduces inference cost from 195 to 42 ms per executed waypoint, but creates recovery and termination challenges.
Recovery DAgger labels learner-visited states with reconnecting action chunks and STOP targets at the first in-region state.
Flow-GRPO jointly refines the chunked controller and Bernoulli STOP policy using closed-loop task outcomes.
On OpenFly, X-Fly achieves 74.18% test-seen and 51.73% test-unseen success rates, versus 16.45%/18.43% for full-chunk BC and 32.04%/29.46% for DreamFly.
No-stop errors comprise 47.78% of full-chunk BC failures on test-seen; results are reported with eight controls per decision.

figures.caption: Figure 3. Policy backbone shared by the three training stages. A slow path runs the frozen Qwen3.5-4B VLM on the instruction and causal keyframes; a fast path runs only its visual tower on the current frame. Fused with ten state/anchor/action tokens (ego state, slow-cache anchor, and the last eight executed actions), the representation drives a rectified-flow controller that emits eight 4-D controls (∆x,∆y,∆z,∆ψ) and a separate Bernoulli STOP head; if CONTINUE is sampled, all eight controls are executed.

Figure 1. Accuracy–inference trade-off of X-FLY stages. SR under single-step (k=1) and full-chunk (k=8) execution; x-labels give amortized model inference per executed waypoint. On testseen, full-chunk BC reaches the goal but often does not stop. Recovery DAgger makes full-chunk execution viable, and Flow-GRPO, trained and evaluated at k=8 only, gives the highest SR among the evaluated operating points at 4.7× less amortized model inference time per executed waypoint than single-step execution. Inference timings apply to the X-FLY backbone; DreamFly [9] is shown as an SR reference at k=1.

Figure 2. The full-chunk support gap and how X-FLY addresses it. (a) Full-chunk BC flies eight controls between decisions and visits learner-induced anchors that expert demonstrations cover poorly, with neither a corrective chunk nor an arrival STOP label; the policy overshoots the goal. (b) Recovery DAgger relabels each learner anchor with a chunk whose offset dt decays by a smoothstep (inset) and rejoins the expert route at the chunk end; the first in-region anchor receives STOP. (c) Flow-GRPO samples six free and two STOP-override attempts per task with low-frequency chunk noise (inset: the four cosine modes) and a Bernoulli STOP policy, and uses their relative outcomes to update both.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies generate action sequences that reduce repeated inference, but deciding how much of each sequence to execute is critical to task success. Existing adaptive methods make this decision using generation stability or prediction agreement, yet these signals do not establish whether executing a candidate prefix preserves the ability to complete the task. We introduce a policy-aligned predictive verifier (PAV) that anticipates the consequences of candidate action prefixes and evaluates their compatibility with successful continuation before execution. Rather than using future prediction to generate actions, our method evaluates existing proposals in the VLA's internal task-conditioned representation space. To learn local judgments from terminal task outcomes, we combine trajectory-level survival supervision with a localization prior that preserves useful behavior within failed rollouts. The resulting validity scores guide execution-horizon selection. Evaluations with pi_0 and pi_0.5 across LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation show improved success-query trade-offs. These findings point toward a different role for future prediction in robotics, using it to assess how far to trust a policy's proposed actions rather than to generate new ones.
authors: Minkyu Kim, Junhoo Lee, Seungyeon Kim, Suhyun Jeon, Baekseung Kim, Donghoon Han, Nojun Kwak
bullets: Existing adaptive execution methods rely on generation stability or prediction agreement, which may not reflect task-completion potential.

Validity scores guide how many actions to execute at each step.
Experiments with pi_0 and pi_0.5 on LIBERO, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation show improved success–query trade-offs.

papers.abstract: Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (STMM) requires robots to respond to sound events by navigating to the associated objects and performing appropriate physical interactions. Existing STMM evaluations primarily vary object layouts within limited architectural structures, leaving challenges to unseen scenes insufficiently explored. We introduce Multi-scene Sound-Triggered Mobile Manipulation (MuSTMM), a dataset that combines spatial audio rendering and physical interaction across 31 scenes with diverse architectures and object layouts. MuSTMM contains 14.36 million precomputed binaural Room Impulse Responses (RIRs) and a scene-disjoint split for evaluating single-event and multi-event settings in unseen scenes. We further augment the Navigation Policy Model with explicit spatial memory that complements acoustic cues with observed geometry. Specifically, we accumulate pose-aligned depth observations in a shared coordinate frame and project this memory into an egocentric Bird's-Eye View (BEV) occupancy map. Fusing map features with sound context produces a goal descriptor that provides both target-location and scene-structure priors, guiding navigation to the target region required for subsequent physical interaction. This policy achieves a 2.60% success rate boost over existing methods, while component ablations further support the effectiveness of spatial memory. MuSTMM and the navigation policy provide a testbed for the new challenge of studying sound-triggered mobile manipulation in unseen scenes. The code and dataset will be released upon acceptance.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly place a multi-billion-parameter model inside the feedback loop, repeatedly recomputing task context whenever they predict a new action chunk. Yet task understanding changes far more slowly than the robot state. We introduce Fast-VLA, which invokes a frozen 4B VLM once per episode to contextualize the instruction and initial views as fixed, multi-layer key-value task memory. During execution, a lightweight online actor fuses learned time- and arm-indexed queries with current visual and proprioceptive feedback to form action queries. These queries retrieve task context from the fixed memory and predict action chunks without re-running the foundation model. Fast-VLA achieves 92.46% and 92.40% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean and Randomized, and 95.95% and 79.11% on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus evaluation. Against three continually conditioned baselines on the same hardware, it reduces RoboTwin amortized policy inference time by 10.9-17.1x and requires 1.22 GiB of post-prefill online resident memory. Task-memory swaps further show that the actor relies on episode-matched task memory. These results show that task context can be established once while closed-loop control remains responsive throughout execution. Project page: https://garfield-kh.github.io/FastVLA
authors: Kehong Gong, Guanli Hou, Xiaoxu Zheng, Qi Wang, Mingxi Xu, Anbang Zhai, Xiaoyu He, Mingyuan Zhang, Michael Bi Mi
bullets: Addresses the high inference cost of repeatedly recomputing task context in VLA policies.
Stores instruction and initial-view context as fixed, multi-layer key-value task memory.

Reports strong success across RoboTwin 2.0, LIBERO, and LIBERO-Plus, with 10.9–17.1× lower amortized RoboTwin inference time than continually conditioned baselines.
Task-memory swaps indicate that performance depends on episode-matched task context.

papers.abstract: Safe autonomous navigation using monocular vision remains challenging because explicit obstacle states are not directly observable. This letter introduces a visual safety-certification paradigm that uses scale-free, depth-normalized relative motion encoded by monocular optical flow as the representation for collision-risk certification, without reconstructing obstacle position, velocity, geometry, or a metric world model. Unlike conventional optical-flow-based navigation approaches that rely on image motion to shape avoidance behavior, the proposed framework directly encodes collision-cone geometry and safety constraints in this relative-motion representation. An online Concurrent Learning observer estimates the normalized relative velocity and provides a computable estimation-error bound. This uncertainty is propagated into the collision cone through angular inflation and a monocular robot-footprint margin, yielding a Robust Vision-Based Collision Cone Control Barrier Function (RV-C$^3$BF). An optimal-decay CBF quadratic program minimally modifies the nominal control input to enforce the resulting robust safety constraint under the stated assumptions. Extensive simulation and real-world experiments on a TurtleBot3 in cluttered environments with static and dynamic obstacles demonstrate collision avoidance using only monocular vision and onboard proprioception, with the estimation-error bound containing the measured error in $98.3\%$ of simulation samples and the robot achieving collision-free navigation in $93$ of $100$ real-world trials.
bullets: Represents collision risk using depth-normalized relative motion inferred from monocular optical flow.
Uses a Concurrent Learning observer to estimate normalized relative velocity and bound estimation error online.
Propagates uncertainty through angular inflation and a robot-footprint margin to construct a robust vision-based collision-cone control barrier function.
An optimal-decay CBF quadratic program minimally adjusts nominal control to enforce safety.
In experiments, the error bound contained measured error in 98.3% of simulation samples, and TurtleBot3 completed 93/100 real-world trials without collisions.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Monocular vision-based perception-to-control pipeline. An optimal-decay CBF-QP enforces the resulting safety constraint. The resulting loop performs safety-critical navigation using monocular vision and onboard proprioception, without explicit reconstruction of obstacle position, velocity, or geometry.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation often requires remembering interactions that are no longer visible. We introduce Latent Transition Memory (LTM), which stores history as compact latent transitions between consecutive observations. Instantiated on $\pi_{0.5}$ as LTM-$\pi$, our method uses a frozen latent action encoder, a lightweight adapter, and causal KV caching for incremental inference without memory-specific semantic annotations or external reasoning-model calls. With DreamDojo transitions, LTM-$\pi$ achieves 58.54% success on RoboMME and 80.5% on LIBERO-Mem, performing best among baselines without external reasoning models or memory-specific annotations. Ablations support the contribution of transition content beyond temporal cues and the efficiency of delayed memory admission. Scaling RoboMME demonstrations tenfold improves success from 57.67% to 87.50%, while a Cup Swap diagnostic highlights the role of process supervision in temporal composition. Under a 200-token memory budget, success remains 84.00%, versus 87.50% without compression. Finally, real-robot counting success improves from 11.25% to 82.50%. Together, these results demonstrate the effectiveness, scalability, and efficiency of latent transition memory, highlighting its capacity for complex temporal information, bounded-context operation, and real-world robotic control.
authors: Qixin Sun, WenLong Gao, Xiansheng Chen, Zhongyuan Wang, Si Liu, Pengwei Wang

Real-robot counting success improves from 11.25% to 82.50%; a Cup Swap diagnostic underscores the importance of process supervision for temporal composition.

papers.abstract: Autonomous delivery in large scale buildings requires coordinated planning across multiple spatial levels, including building, floor, and room, while ensuring scheduling efficiency. Existing methods often focus solely on algorithmic development, neglecting integration with physical robotic platforms, and rarely validate performance in real world scenarios. Many approaches also overlook hierarchical building structures and room level privacy constraints, limiting practical applicability. To address these challenges, this paper presents a hierarchical delivery framework based on a Building-Floor-Room abstraction, which decomposes the problem across multiple levels to significantly reduce optimization complexity. We formulate a building aware extension of the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP) that explicitly models inter building and inter floor connectivity, room level access constraints, and privacy sensitive areas, enabling globally feasible and privacy compliant task assignment and routing. Based on this hierarchical model, the framework can evaluate delivery efficiency across different building layouts and optimize depot placement for specific configurations. At the execution level, we introduce a novel hardware design for non interactive, privacy preserving delivery, supported by reachability aware distances and a closed loop mapping, localization, and navigation system, ensuring consistency between planned routes and physical navigation. The proposed framework is validated on a real multi sensor robotic platform, demonstrating reliable multi floor delivery with improved path rationality and overall efficiency.

papers.abstract: Efficient synthesis of contact-rich manipulation trajectories is essential for downstream robot learning. Gradient-based planning offers a promising approach, but jointly optimizing motion and contact decisions remains challenging. Meanwhile, many existing planners run on CPUs with limited throughput. We present CQDC-Warp, a GPU-accelerated differentiable quasi-dynamic simulator for batched model predictive control (MPC). We use it to study contact-guided trajectory optimization, in which intended robot--object contacts are specified before planning and encouraged through soft costs, while the simulated dynamics determine contact geometry and frictional response without a prescribed contact-mode schedule. Across $17{,}408$ trials on the $17$-object Allegro in-hand rotation benchmark, our framework achieves $79.8\%$ success, compared with $73.7\%$ for CFree and $65.2\%$ for IMPACT, and reduces mean trajectory-generation time by factors of $27.0$ and $50.2$, respectively. On a single NVIDIA RTX 4090 with $2{,}048$ parallel worlds, forward and backward throughput reach $2.06\times10^5$ and $2.25\times10^5$ world-steps per second, respectively. Further experiments cover manipulation with LEAP and Shadow hands, environmental contact exploitation, bimanual manipulation, whole-body control, and real-world trajectory replay on a Sharpa hand.
authors: Yanchen Ding, Jiayi Chen, Jianfeng Xu, Wei Zhao, Li Yi, He Wang
bullets: Targets the joint optimization of robot motion and contact decisions, a challenge for gradient-based manipulation planning.
Uses a GPU-accelerated differentiable quasi-dynamic simulator with batched model predictive control (MPC).
Specifies intended contacts through soft costs while allowing simulated dynamics to determine contact geometry and friction without a fixed contact-mode schedule.
On the 17-object Allegro in-hand rotation benchmark, achieves 79.8% success versus 73.7% for CFree and 65.2% for IMPACT.
Demonstrates broad applicability across multiple hands, environmental and bimanual manipulation, whole-body control, and real-world trajectory replay.

papers.abstract: Predicting cost in a multi-agent world model moves most constrained policy updates into imagination: the stronger model-free baseline needs $10$ to $20$ times CA-MAMBA's interactions on the median SMAC configuration, and CA-MAMBA earns $2.8$ to $12$ times the baselines' MAMuJoCo reward at equal budget. In controlled tests on one task per benchmark, pricing the model's cost advantages at parity more than halves a cost-blind learner's cost and meets a tight continuous-control limit the learned multiplier misses, suggesting the model's cost estimates are not the bottleneck.
bullets: Moves most constrained policy updates into imagination using a multi-agent world model.
Requires 10–20× fewer interactions than a stronger model-free baseline on median SMAC configurations.
Achieves 2.8–12× the baselines’ MAMuJoCo reward at equal interaction budgets.
Cost-aware pricing more than halves a cost-blind learner’s cost in controlled benchmark tests.
On one task per benchmark, learned cost estimates meet a tight continuous-control limit, indicating cost prediction is not the main bottleneck.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models transfer semantic knowledge acquired through vision-language pretraining to robot control, achieving strong performance across various benchmarks. However, most VLAs directly map observations to demonstrated actions without explicit supervision of intermediate physical state changes, making them prone to overfitting observation-action correspondences. Some methods introduce intermediate reasoning or future-state prediction in language, visual, or latent spaces to guide action generation, but do not explicitly supervise the physical state transition itself. We therefore propose VLA-$\Delta$, a general framework that uses physical changes between current and future states as explicit learning targets. To support this objective, we construct a large-scale pretraining dataset and derive physical state-transition annotations covering task-relevant semantics and visual motion changes, providing more direct supervision for continuous action generation. During inference, the model generates actions directly from current observations without additional inference overhead. VLA-$\Delta$ achieves performance competitive with the state of the art on LIBERO and RoboTwin, and outperforms $\pi_{0.5}$ in real-robot experiments. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-OmniAI/VLA-Delta
authors: Qi Lu, Jiarun Li, Ce Zhang, Miao Pan, Yi Pan, Xu Wang, Wenqi Zhang, Xuhong Zhang
bullets: Most VLA models learn observation-to-action mappings without direct supervision of intermediate physical changes, risking overfitting.
The framework uses current-to-future physical state changes as explicit targets, including task-relevant semantics and visual motion.
A large-scale pretraining dataset provides annotations for these state transitions.
At inference, actions are generated directly from current observations without extra inference overhead.
It is competitive on LIBERO and RoboTwin and outperforms π₀.₅ in real-robot experiments.

papers.abstract: Maintaining small path-tracking errors under moving reference frames is essential for robotic manipulation tasks with tight execution tolerances, such as machining and surgical automation. Conventional time-indexed controllers, including tracking Model Predictive Control (MPC), rely on a fixed temporal correspondence with the reference trajectory and may therefore accumulate path-relative error under abrupt reference-frame motion or timing mismatch. This paper presents MR-MPCC, a Model Predictive Contouring Control (MPCC) framework for velocity-controlled robotic manipulators with 6-DoF end-effector pose regulation under Moving-Reference disturbances. A hierarchical control architecture is adopted, in which an upper-level MPCC optimizes path progress while penalizing contouring and orientation errors, and a constrained resolved motion rate control (RMRC) layer maps the commanded Cartesian twist to feasible joint velocities under joint-level and safety constraints. MR-MPCC is implemented in a ROS2--MuJoCo pipeline and validated on a UR5e platform under moving-reference disturbances, where the path frame is perturbed and tracked by electromagnetic sensors. Compared with PI control and time-indexed tracking MPC under matched disturbance, MR-MPCC achieves lower geometric path-following error and smaller deviations in the moving path frame, demonstrating improved path-following performance under reference-frame motion.
authors: Chonghao Cheng, Tiancheng Li, Jonathan Woolfrey, Liang Zhao, Shoudong Huang
bullets: Targets path-tracking errors caused by abrupt reference-frame motion and timing mismatch.
Uses an upper-level MPCC to optimize path progress while penalizing contouring and orientation errors.
Employs constrained resolved motion rate control to convert Cartesian twists into feasible joint velocities under safety constraints.
Validated on a UR5e in a ROS2–MuJoCo setup with electromagnetic sensing of moving path frames.
Achieves lower geometric path-following error and smaller moving-frame deviations than PI control and time-indexed tracking MPC under matched disturbances.

papers.abstract: Spatial augmented reality (SAR) augments physical environments with projected content, but most systems assume that the projector pose, target region, or motion path has been fixed or specified. We instead make projected light an embodied action: given a language instruction and current visual observations, a system must decide how to move and where and at what scale to place the projection. We introduce LICOA to realize this capability. Its differential-drive chassis provides room-scale approach and repositioning, while a steerable mirror with two degrees of freedom (2DoF) and projection scale provide rapid local control of the beam. A shared interface maps synchronized external and onboard RGB cameras with robot control state to physical optical actions across pretrained action models. Because instruction-conditioned optical action lacks dedicated training data and a common evaluation protocol, we construct a matched simulation embodiment and a corpus with 150 tasks and 7,500 rendered episodes, then evaluate models trained only on this corpus in previously unseen real-world environments. Across 480 complete closed-loop real-world execution trials (rollouts) on 12 tasks, the best adapted action model achieves a 57.50% success rate and 40.64% success weighted by path length, compared with 8.33% and 5.15% for the same architecture trained from scratch. A further 150 real-world ablation rollouts support the need for both camera views and coordinated control of the chassis and mirror. These results establish a physical platform, shared perception and optical action interface, corpus, and real-world evaluation protocol for treating projected light as an embodied action.
authors: Yuchen Deng, Shunkai Zhou, Ruixuan Zhu, Haibin Ling, Bingyao Huang
bullets: Addresses SAR settings where projector pose, target region, and motion path are not fixed in advance.
Combines differential-drive chassis movement with 2DoF steerable-mirror and projection-scale control.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are expected to follow instructions like their language backbones, yet prior work has focused on What-level instructions that specify the task rather than How-level instructions that specify how to carry it out. Through our diagnoses, we find that How-level instructions do not help current VLAs and lower task success. We hypothesize that pairing each training episode with a single instruction limits How-level instruction following, and show that training with segment-level enriched instructions makes actions respond to such instructions without consistently raising task success. To measure How-level instruction following beyond standard benchmarks, we introduce SIMPLER-IN, where success requires conditions given only in the instruction. It shows that the gained responsiveness does not extend to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions. How-level instruction following thus remains an open challenge.
authors: Sangwu Park, Wonjoong Kim, Yeonjun In, Chanyoung Park
bullets: Prior VLA research mainly evaluates What-level instructions that specify the task, overlooking How-level instructions that specify execution.
The authors find that How-level instructions can reduce task success in current VLAs.
Training with segment-level enriched instructions improves action responsiveness to How-level guidance, but not consistently overall task success.
SIMPLER-IN evaluates instruction-specific success beyond standard benchmarks and reveals poor generalization to demanding or out-of-distribution How-level instructions.
How-level instruction following remains an open challenge.

papers.selection_reason: Directly investigates instruction following in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, specifically diagnosing the gap between 'What-level' and 'How-level' instructions. This is highly relevant to the development of capable embodied agents.
papers.title: Do VLAs Really Follow Instructions? Diagnosing How-Level Instruction Following in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: Current vision-language-action models struggle to follow instructions about how to perform tasks, and improved responsiveness does not reliably translate to success.

papers.abstract: Sampling-based motion planning such as Model Predictive Path Integral (MPPI) control has become attractive for robotics due to its ability to handle nonlinear dynamics and non-smooth objectives without gradient information, while leveraging parallel rollout computation for real-time performance. However, in real-world robotic systems, the optimized control input is often applied after a non-negligible planning delay, causing a mismatch between the state used in forward simulation and the actual state at control execution, which can significantly degrade planning accuracy and may even lead to unsafe behavior such as collisions. This paper proposes Closed-Loop MPPI with Initial-State Sampling (CLIS-MPPI), which explicitly addresses execution-time state mismatch by modeling planning delay as a distribution over plausible execution-time initial states, performing rollout optimization from sampled initial states, and applying a rollout-based local feedback correction during control execution. The proposed method is validated through real-world experiments on a 6-DoF UR5e manipulator in a narrow-passage task involving obstacle avoidance and end-effector target reaching. Across 5 real-world runs of the same task, standard MPPI collided in 2 runs, whereas CLIS-MPPI remained collision-free in all 5 runs. Averaged over all collision-free runs for each method (3 for MPPI and 5 for CLIS-MPPI), CLIS-MPPI reduced the average task completion time from 25.4s to 24.4s and the average end-effector path length from 0.456 m to 0.425 m. It also reduced the overall joint-position and joint-velocity root mean square errors (RMSEs) from 0.100 rad and 0.108 rad/s to 0.017 rad and 0.011 rad/s, respectively. These results demonstrate improved safety, planning-execution consistency, and motion smoothness.
bullets: Execution delays create a mismatch between the planned and actual robot states, potentially causing collisions.
CLIS-MPPI models delay-induced uncertainty as a distribution over execution-time initial states.
It optimizes rollouts from sampled initial states and adds rollout-based local feedback during execution.
On a UR5e narrow-passage task, CLIS-MPPI had 0 collisions in 5 runs, while standard MPPI collided in 2 of 5.
Collision-free CLIS-MPPI runs also showed shorter completion time and path length, with lower joint-position and velocity RMSEs.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed CLIS-MPPI. CLIS-MPPI converts execution delay into an initial-state uncertainty distribution, samples both perturbed initial states and control sequences, and performs parallel forward simulation to obtain rollout trajectories and costs. The weighted rollout distribution is then used to construct a nominal trajectory and extract local feedback gains. Finally, the applied control is computed as a closed-loop combination of the MPPI feedforward term and a state-feedback correction.

Fig. 1. Illustration of execution-time state mismatch in the i-th planning cycle. At planning time tplan i , MPPI optimizes using the measured state xref i . During the delay window, the robot continues executing the previous control ui−1. Consequently, when the newly planned control ui actually becomes effective at tsend i , the system state has already evolved to xapply

papers.abstract: Artificial microbots capable of precise and autonomous navigation could provide versatile platforms for microscale transport, manipulation, and task execution in complex environments. However, reliable navigation becomes increasingly challenging at the micrometre scale, particularly when the surrounding environment changes dynamically. Here, we develop a vision-guided closed-loop navigation framework for light-driven cube-shaped hematite/TiO2 Janus microbots with a characteristic size of approximately 3 {\mu}m. Real-time visual localization using a custom-trained YOLOv11 object-detection model is integrated with discretized waypoint-based magnetic steering to enable precise navigation along complex prescribed trajectories, with more than 90% of the measured trajectory deviations remaining below 6 {\mu}m across the tested path geometries. The framework further enables arbitrary user-defined free-hand trajectories and autonomous navigation through a physically confined maze. In dynamically changing environments, A* path planning enables real-time path replanning while avoiding multiple independently swimming 5 {\mu}m spherical Janus micromotors. Finally, the microbot selectively captures multiple cargo particles and autonomously transports and delivers them to a predefined location while simultaneously avoiding dynamic obstacles. These results establish an integrated platform combining programmable trajectory control, autonomous path planning, real-time environmental adaptation, and task execution within a single light-driven Janus microbot system.
authors: Kanhu Charan Andia, Harsh Prashant Katole, Parth Nitinkumar Bhosale, Hemant Kumar, Dhruv Pratap Singh
bullets: Real-time YOLOv11-based visual localization is combined with waypoint-based magnetic steering.
Over 90% of measured trajectory deviations were below 6 μm across tested path geometries.
The microbots followed user-defined free-hand paths and navigated a physically confined maze.
A* planning enabled real-time replanning around multiple swimming micromotor obstacles.
The system supported selective cargo capture, transport, and delivery while avoiding dynamic obstacles.

papers.abstract: Proactive robots should anticipate user needs and provide assistance before being explicitly asked. A straightforward approach is to infer human intentions from commonsense knowledge, but the same observed behavior can imply different needs across users, potentially leading to unwanted assistance. We observe that everyday routines in the real world exhibit recurring patterns, so learning these patterns can reduce ambiguity in proactive decisions. Based on this, we propose a memory-based agentic framework in which a VLM task predictor reads a Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) alongside the current observation to decide when to assist and what task to perform, and a VLA executor performs the predicted task. PAM is structured as a finite-state machine over activity phases, per-state assistance rules, and event-driven transitions; a reflection VLM revises PAM from each day's interaction trace without weight updates or retraining. In our 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, memory-free baselines remain conservative, with limited recall on proactive tasks. Our system improves consistently with accumulated experience, achieving the highest precision, recall, and F1 and reducing first-fire delay from approximately 5 seconds on Day 1 to 1 second by Day 5. Our approach also adapts to changes in the user's routine through continued memory reflection, recovering from memory--routine misalignment after a single memory update. The project page is available at https://davian-robotics.github.io/PAM/
authors: Dohyun Lee, Minho Park, Jeonghoon Park, Dongyoon Hwang, Junha Hyung, Sungwon Hwang, Byungkun Lee, Jaegul Choo
bullets: Addresses ambiguity in proactive assistance, where identical behaviors may indicate different user needs.
Uses a VLM task predictor with Procedural Assistance Memory (PAM) to select when and how to assist, and a VLA executor to perform tasks.
Represents routines as a finite-state machine with activity phases, assistance rules, and event-driven transitions.
A reflection VLM updates PAM from daily interaction traces without weight updates or retraining.
In a 5-day desk-assistance evaluation, the system improved with experience, achieved the best reported precision, recall, and F1, and reduced first-fire delay from about 5 seconds to 1 second.

papers.abstract: Geometric light detection and ranging (LiDAR)--inertial simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) provides efficient state estimation but lacks the continuous map representation and global refinement capabilities of neural implicit SLAM, while neural implicit methods remain computationally expensive. We propose Lightweight LiDAR--Inertial Neural SLAM (LIN-SLAM), a hybrid method that couples high-rate geometric LiDAR--inertial estimation with neural implicit tracking, continual mapping, and global refinement for accurate real-time onboard SLAM. Experiments on twelve representative sequences from three datasets spanning 32-, 64-, and 128-channel LiDAR configurations show that LIN-SLAM achieves the lowest overall mean absolute trajectory error (ATE) among the evaluated state-of-the-art geometric and neural implicit methods, while substantially reducing runtime compared with existing neural implicit SLAM methods. On a Unitree Go2 equipped with an NVIDIA Jetson Orin NX and a 16-channel LiDAR, LIN-SLAM sustains real-time localization and neural mapping over a 1.47-km indoor trajectory through challenging repetitive corridor environments, with an endpoint closure error of only 0.141~m. To the best of our knowledge, LIN-SLAM is the first LiDAR--inertial SLAM system with a neural implicit backend to achieve real-time online operation on a mobile robotic platform while maintaining state-of-the-art localization accuracy. The code will be released upon acceptance.
authors: Shiqi Che, Yijie Liu, Shuo Wang, Wenxin Liu
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between efficient geometric SLAM and computationally costly neural implicit SLAM.
Uses high-rate geometric estimation alongside neural implicit tracking, continual mapping, and global refinement.
Evaluated across twelve sequences from three datasets and multiple LiDAR configurations.
Reports the lowest overall mean ATE among evaluated geometric and neural implicit methods, with reduced runtime versus neural implicit baselines.
Runs online on a Unitree Go2 with a Jetson Orin NX over a 1.47-km indoor trajectory, achieving 0.141 m endpoint closure error.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the lightweight LIN-SLAM pipeline. A geometric generalized iterative closest point (GICP)–IESKF frontend processes LiDAR sub-sweeps and IMU measurements to provide local poses and motion-compensated scans. Full-sweep keyframe candidates associate geometry with source intervals, terminal poses, and covariances for asynchronous transfer. The neural implicit backend uses optimized C++/CUDA computation to reduce processing overhead, fixed-capacity replay storage and local neural windows to control stored data, and preallocated workspaces to reduce repeated allocation. Frontend relative motion initializes neural tracking; continual mapping and loop-based global optimization update the neural map. Backend corrections provide globally corrected poses at the frontend rate.

papers.abstract: General-purpose dexterous manipulation requires policies to transfer knowledge from related tasks to new tasks with only a few target demonstrations. Existing benchmarks often provide too many target demonstrations. They also leave the differences between source and target tasks uncontrolled. As a result, they cannot clearly distinguish knowledge transfer from task memorization. Our key insight is the Core-Gen principle. Core tasks are related tasks that share a functional interaction and provide source knowledge, while a Gen task is a novel target within the same functional family that has only a few demonstrations. This setup tests whether a policy can reuse functional interaction knowledge. Based on this principle, we propose Evo-DexBench, which controls both source-task relatedness and target-task exposure. It comprises 30 tasks in six functional families and a VR teleoperation pipeline. The resulting dataset covers three everyday scenes per task. It contains 1,248 multimodal demonstrations collected with simulated Shadow Hands equipped with 123 taxels. Experiments show that even the best-performing method achieves an average success rate of only 38.5%, highlighting the challenges existing methods face in transferring functional interaction knowledge. Further analysis shows that, across the two tasks, joint Core+Gen training improves performance by 12% and 38%, respectively, over training on Core followed by fine-tuning on Gen. This indicates that joint training makes better use of Core knowledge and that functionally matched Core data yields greater gains in success rate than mismatched data. We release the Evo-DexBench dataset and benchmark to support the evaluation of dexterous manipulation policies' generalization across related tasks.
authors: Bing Cheng, Yiran Mao, Zewei Ye, Yifan Jin, Xinyi Chen, Ruifeng Tu, Shuhuai Wang, Tao Lin, Zhimu Zhou, Yuxin Du, Fangwei Zhong, Junchi Yan, Bo Zhao
bullets: Defines the Core-Gen principle: related Core tasks provide source knowledge, while novel Gen tasks test few-shot transfer within the same functional family.
Controls both source-task relatedness and target-task exposure to distinguish knowledge transfer from task memorization.
Includes 30 tasks across six functional families, three everyday scenes per task, and 1,248 multimodal demonstrations from simulated Shadow Hands with 123 taxels.
Existing methods remain challenged, with the best average success rate reaching only 38.5%.
Joint Core+Gen training improves performance over Core pretraining followed by Gen fine-tuning, especially when Core data is functionally matched.

papers.abstract: Dual-system vision-language-action (VLA) models pair a high-frequency fast policy with a slow, expensive module, and published trigger mechanisms for invoking it lack a shared objective, measured costs, and any standard separating schedule quality from module quality. We provide the missing account: invocation is formalized as a calibrated decision problem whose fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated schedules are degenerate cases of one quantity, the Value of Intervention (VoI); a renewal baseline proves the optimal schedule periodic under state-independent collapse, with adaptive gains governed by the cost ratio $\rho$ and the dispersion of collapse. Measured systems span three orders of magnitude in $\rho$ (FiS-VLA $0.95$; RoboICL about $10^3$), and a direct test confirms the low-$\rho$ prediction: calibrated gains vanish under homogeneous collapse and grow with heterogeneity. Fourteen closed-loop arms on LIBERO test the contested middle of the continuum ($\rho=1.53$): the adaptive trigger allocates its queries exactly as the threshold rule predicts, yet the language-rewrite channel cannot convert them into success on either suite, and a revert actuator that undoes a failed rewrite is the only intervention with zero net downside on both LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Goal, where the rewrite deficit deepens from thirteen to forty-two points. A four-measure leak-free protocol cuts apparent early-warning AUC from $0.93$ to $0.62$ on $929$ deployment traces, a detection-limited frontier theorem converts detection quality into a schedulability statement, and a compilation loop turns measured value functions into per-task refresh periods within $2.4\%$ of the closed-loop oracle. Together these results turn slow-module invocation from a design opinion into a measured decision.
authors: Shilin Zhang (North China University of Technology)
bullets: Unifies fixed-ratio, fixed-budget, and history-gated triggers as special cases of Value of Intervention; periodic scheduling is optimal when collapse is state-independent.
Adaptive scheduling benefits depend on intervention cost relative to fast-policy operation and on heterogeneity in policy collapse.
At intermediate cost (ρ=1.53), the adaptive trigger follows its predicted threshold, but language rewrites fail to improve either LIBERO suite; only reverting failed rewrites avoids net downside.
A leak-free evaluation protocol reduces apparent early-warning AUC from 0.93 to 0.62 across 929 deployment traces.
A detection-limited theorem and compilation loop connect measured intervention value to schedulability and produce refresh periods within 2.4% of a closed-loop oracle.

papers.abstract: Training humanoid whole-body vision-language-action (VLA) policies requires costly robot demonstrations with aligned robot-view observations and controller-compatible whole-body state-action labels. Egocentric human demonstrations offer scalable supervision but have misaligned views and sparse motion cues. Existing approaches either pretrain policies that still require robot data for adaptation or generate controller-specific commands that limit reuse. Conversion also requires robot-view observations aligned with the generated whole-body motion. We present KODA (Kinematics-Observation Data Alignment), which converts egocentric RGB demonstrations into whole-body VLA training data using a reusable canonical trajectory to guide robot-view synthesis and generate controller-specific whole-body state-action supervision. KODA first generates a simulator-checked whole-body trajectory using a sparse tracker with sampling-based command optimization. This generated trajectory directly determines the onboard camera poses used to synthesize corresponding robot-view observations. The motion, observations, and task instruction form a canonical record. For each deployment controller, KODA optimizes commands to track the stored motion and records the corresponding action labels and proprioceptive states. When switching controllers, KODA retains this canonical record and regenerates whole-body state-action supervision for co-training with matching robot demonstrations. We evaluate KODA on four Unitree G1 loco-manipulation tasks using two whole-body controllers, SONIC and HEFT. With robot data held fixed, macro-average success on conditions covered by human demonstrations but absent from robot data improves by 45.0 and 46.25 percentage points, respectively. Under both controllers, this metric shows an upward trend across the evaluated human-data budgets, suggesting potential for further scaling.
authors: Zibo Zhou, Yueru Chen, Junsong Wu, Weiji Xie, Qingyao Xu, Sheng Yin, Shiqing Wang, Jiyuan Shi, Siheng Chen, Chenjia Bai, Xuelong Li
bullets: Addresses the costly need for robot demonstrations with aligned observations and whole-body state-action labels.
Generates a simulator-checked canonical whole-body trajectory from sparse human motion using sampling-based command optimization.
Uses the trajectory to synthesize aligned robot-camera observations, then regenerates controller-specific actions and proprioceptive states.
Evaluated on four Unitree G1 loco-manipulation tasks with SONIC and HEFT controllers.
With fixed robot data, success on human-covered but robot-unseen conditions improves by 45.0 and 46.25 percentage points; performance trends upward with more human data.

The resulting data are combined with matching real-robot demonstrations to co-train a controller-specific vision–language–action (VLA) policy for language-guided humanoid loco-manipulation.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich robotic tasks require coordinated motion and impedance under uncertain interaction dynamics and physical constraints. While recent methods on learned policies provide useful interaction strategies, they may fail when contact conditions differ from those encountered during training. Model-based generative methods show promising receding-horizon trajectories optimization results, but often lack structured behavioral guidance and refinement that jointly accounts for constraint geometry and actual contact responses. To this end, we propose Manifold Generative Annealing (MGA), a joint model-free and model-based generative framework for motion--impedance optimization. MGA first organizes pretrained reinforcement learning policies into structured sequence proposals, retaining task-specific interaction strategies without committing to their execution. It then evaluates these proposals alongside exploratory samples through model-based rollouts for refinement or separate execution selection. Crucially, realization-aware manifold refinement aligns updates from the refinement bank with both task constraints and locally achievable physical responses, allowing learned experience to guide online adaptation under changing contact conditions. Experiments cover surface scanning, peg insertion, and humanoid pushing, with improved safety success rate of impedance control under nominal and sensing-shift conditions.
authors: Zhilin He, Guoquan Qi, Changliu Liu
bullets: Targets contact-rich robotic tasks with uncertain dynamics and physical constraints.
Structures pretrained RL policies into sequence proposals that preserve task-specific interaction strategies without directly executing them.
Uses model-based rollouts to refine or select proposals alongside exploratory samples.
Applies realization-aware manifold refinement to respect task constraints and locally achievable contact responses.
Evaluated on surface scanning, peg insertion, and humanoid pushing, with improved impedance-control safety success under nominal and sensing-shift conditions.

papers.abstract: The next AI will not win by knowing more about the world. It will win because it knows you: because it lives on your body, works for you and answers to you. That is what the term OnBodyAI stands for. It describes what happens when large language models are given a body, and what research and industry need to make that happen. This article is based on my talk in the Industrial Panel at UbiComp/ISWC 2026 in Shanghai (October 13, 2026) and follows its ten key statements.
bullets: Defines OnBodyAI as large language models given a body.
Emphasizes AI that lives on the body, works for the user, and answers to the user.
Frames embodiment and personalization as priorities for future AI research and industry.
Presents ten key statements based on an Industrial Panel talk at UbiComp/ISWC 2026.

papers.abstract: World and action modeling are closely related, yet their reciprocal benefits under unified causal training remain unclear. We introduce OneWM, a simple framework for unified causal training that treats actions as both conditions for world prediction and targets for policy learning within a shared video-action architecture. Using this framework, we investigate whether learning forward dynamics conditioned on specified actions improves action learning, and whether learning to generate actions in turn improves action-conditioned world modeling. We use LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboCasa365 as embodied testbeds to evaluate both policy learning and world modeling, complemented by real-world policy experiments. Learning the visual consequences of specified actions improves policy performance and generalization across changing scenes. In turn, action learning improves multi-view world-prediction fidelity under the same architecture. Together, these results answer both questions positively, supporting reciprocal benefits between world modeling and action generation under unified causal training.
authors: Yue Su, Bokai Lin, Xinkai Wang, Chubin Zhang, Xiangnan Wu, Kuan Zhang, Weiyang Jin, Jiwen Yu, Yiming Li, Cewu Lu, Lixin Yang, Xihui Liu
bullets: Unifies world modeling and policy learning in a shared video-action architecture.
Treats actions as conditions for predicting future worlds and as targets for learning policies.

Action-conditioned dynamics improve policy performance and generalization across changing scenes.
Action learning improves multi-view world-prediction fidelity, indicating reciprocal benefits.

papers.abstract: Camera-to-robot pose estimation from a monocular image is significant for vision-based robot navigation and control. However, recovering 3D structural features from 2D observations remains a challenging task. Existing camera-to-robot pose estimation methods either rely on time-consuming iterative rendering or involve sophisticated 2D-3D registration which suffers from projection ambiguity, accumulated errors for distal joints and imbalanced learning for different joints. In this work, we propose RoPE-Flow, an end-to-end flow matching-based framework for camera-to-robot pose estimation. From the predicted 2D heatmaps, we propose a Keypoint-centered Feature Extractor to obtain positional features along with contextual representations from keypoints-centered multi-scale patches. Moreover, we introduce Graph-guided Condition Generator, which embeds a learnable adjacency map to generate condition for flow matching based on correlation among keypoints. Besides, we introduce Bone Length Loss and Ray-Depth Loss for topological consistency and scale stability, with joint-wise weighting to mitigate varied prediction difficulty across joints. The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art methods for pose estimation across different types of robots with mutiple cameras. Besides, we establish a novel cross-scene benchmark to demonstrate the outstanding performance of RoPE-Flow on zero-shot cross-scene robot pose estimation. Meanwhile, animated visualizations are shown on the website: ropeflow.netlify.app
authors: Liangjing Shao, Wanhao Liu, Zhiwei Fang, Rulin Zhou, Quanlu Zhang, Changjing Liu, Beilei Cui, Yiming Huang, Hongliang Ren

Introduces bone-length and ray-depth losses with joint-wise weighting for topological consistency and scale stability.
Reports state-of-the-art performance across robot types and cameras, including zero-shot cross-scene evaluation on a new benchmark.
