papers.abstract: Passive human videos of everyday activity offer robots access to a massive amount of human experience without requiring a demonstration for each task. However, using this experience requires recovering knowledge from unstructured video recordings and adapting it to a different body (i.e., the robot). To overcome these challenges, we present mobile code-as-policy (MoCaP), an agentic framework that turns passive human video recordings into guidance for an end-to-end mobile manipulation policy. MoCaP extracts spatial memory and cues of how people prepare to interact with objects, which inform navigation and the search for a manipulation-ready configuration. Guided by passive human experience and current observations, MoCaP uses a closed-loop code-as-policy to coordinate planning and tool use primitives to solve motions under the robot's geometry and kinematic constraints. On a real mobile manipulator, MoCaP achieves 80% success on each of two mobile manipulation tasks in an indoor environment whereas existing approaches cannot succeed at the task. Video-derived spatial memory improves object-navigation success from 70% to 100%, and human approach prior raises the rate of finding a reachable base pose from 0% to 100% at an unfavorable start location. Videos and code are available on the project website: https://mocap-7.github.io/MoCAP-page/.
authors: Yiyang Cai, Tatsuya Kamijo, Ninghao Lu, Zijin Hu, Sherry Yang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring knowledge from unstructured human videos to robots with different bodies and constraints.
Extracts spatial memory and human approach cues to guide object navigation and selection of manipulation-ready base poses.

On a real mobile manipulator, achieves 80% success on each of two indoor tasks where existing approaches fail.
Video-derived memory improves object-navigation success from 70% to 100%, while human approach priors improve reachable-base-pose discovery from 0% to 100% in an unfavorable start setting.

papers.abstract: Executing heavy-duty physical manipulation in unpredictable environments remains a major challenge for quadrupedal robots lacking dedicated manipulators. This paper presents SOMA, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework for whole-body non-prehensile manipulation of multi-object stacks using a quadruped robot. Unlike traditional methods restricted to two-dimensional planar pushing, SOMA integrates explicit robot base-height control, unlocking full three-dimensional pushing strategies. This capability enables the quadruped to manipulate complex payload stacks as a unified system while preventing relative sliding or tipping of upper layers. The architecture factorizes control into a high-level manipulation policy using a Simplified Structured State Space Sequence (S5) encoder to reason over long-horizon temporal history and predict bounded target tracking commands via Beta distributions, and a low-level locomotion policy that dynamically adapts leg stance configurations. In extensive simulation benchmarks, SOMA achieves a $90.3\%$ success rate for single-object reposing and up to $90.1\%$ for dynamic two-box stacks under stringent error margins ($0.05\text{ m}$ position error, $1^\circ$ orientation error). Finally, we validate zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go1 quadruped robot across diverse payload masses and geometries, demonstrating active base-height adjustments to maintain traction and balance during heavy pushing tasks.
bullets: Addresses heavy-duty manipulation in unpredictable environments for quadrupeds lacking dedicated manipulators.
Uses hierarchical reinforcement learning with a high-level S5-based temporal policy and a low-level locomotion controller that adapts leg stances.
Explicit base-height control enables three-dimensional non-prehensile pushing while reducing upper-layer sliding and tipping.
In simulation, it achieves 90.3% success for single-object reposing and up to 90.1% for dynamic two-box stacks under strict pose-error limits.
Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real transfer on a Unitree Go1 across varied payload masses and geometries.

papers.abstract: Autonomous mobile robots in warehouses and production facilities operate in precisely the environments that defeat point-feature visual odometry: featureless aisles, uniform walls, repetitive racking and specular floors. Such environments are, however, rich in straight-edge structure: rack uprights, door frames, wall junctions and cabinet outlines present high-contrast linear edges stable across wide viewpoint changes. A line-feature extension to cuVSLAM, a CUDA-accelerated visual-SLAM system, is presented that recovers this signal. Lines are parameterised as Pl\"ucker coordinates for geometric transport and as the minimal 4-DOF orthonormal representation of Bartoli and Sturm for optimisation; a Cauchy-robust point-to-line residual with analytic Jacobians is folded directly into cuVSLAM's per-frame Gauss-Newton pose solve, and the same line state is jointly refined in the Schur-complement sliding-window bundle adjustment. An adaptive information weight causes lines to assume more of the estimation burden exactly as point features become scarce, and the extension adds residual blocks to existing solvers rather than introducing a second estimator, reducing exactly to the unmodified point pipeline when disabled. Evaluated in RGB-D mode under SE(3) Umeyama alignment with no scale correction, line features reduce mean absolute trajectory error by 38.5% over the 22 sequences of the TUM RGB-D Freiburg3 collection and by 30.1% over the 8 Replica room and office sequences, where median translation error falls by 38.9% and median rotation error by 66.4%, with zero tracking failures in any configuration tested.
authors: Dara Molloy, Terry Wu, Wonju Lee, Abhilash Nand Kumar, David Adley, Conor Ferguson, Hesam Rabeti
bullets: Targets warehouse and production scenes where point features are sparse but straight structural edges remain reliable.
Represents and optimizes line features geometrically, integrating robust point-to-line residuals and analytic Jacobians into cuVSLAM’s pose solver and sliding-window bundle adjustment.
Adaptively increases line-feature influence as point features become scarce.
In RGB-D evaluations, reduced mean absolute trajectory error by 38.5% on TUM RGB-D Freiburg3 and 30.1% on Replica; no tracking failures occurred.
Scope: evaluated on 22 Freiburg3 and 8 Replica sequences under SE(3) alignment without scale correction.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Line-augmented cuVSLAM pipeline. papers.abstract: Online reinforcement learning (RL) with verifiable rewards has driven rapid progress in mathematics, coding, and tool use, but scaling this success to GUI agents remains challenging due to the high cost of interactive environments and the scarcity of realistic training tasks. We introduce MAI-Gym, an open all-in-one platform that unifies GUI agent evaluation, data collection, and online RL training across mobile, computer, and web environments. Through a shared rollout pipeline, MAI-Gym ensures consistent agent behavior across evaluation and training, supports ten established benchmarks, and scales to 20,000 parallel environment instances. Beyond scalable infrastructure, MAI-Gym enables automated synthesis of diverse GUI applications and challenging tasks, including resettable mocked apps and coherent cross-app worlds with execution-validated task verifiers. Using MAI-Gym, we train MAI-Gym-9B, a unified 9B agent for mobile and computer use, achieving state-of-the-art performance among open GUI agents under 10B parameters: 78.4% on MobileWorld and 76.2% on OSWorld-Verified. Importantly, RL in a mocked train-ticketing app transfers to its real-world counterpart, improving task success on a phys- ical phone from 28.8% to 48.1%. We release the framework, synthesis skills, mocked apps, 2,000 verified tasks, and the model checkpoint to support repro- ducible research and further advances in scalable GUI agent training.
authors: Panrong Tong, Quyu Kong, Pengxiang Li, Tianyu Xia, Hanzhang Zhou, Lei Wang, Chenglin Cai, Long Li, Long Chen, Jianan Zhang, Zhengwen Zeng, Xu Zhang, Gongjie Zhang, Yue Wang, Steven Hoi

papers.abstract: Robust adaptive control is vital for keeping robots safe while actively reducing uncertainty in unfamiliar settings. However, traditional methods are often conservative since they fail to account for guaranteed future parameter learning during planning and struggle to scale to high-dimensional systems. In this work, we present A-SLS, a learning-aware robust adaptive model predictive control (RAMPC) framework based on system-level synthesis. A-SLS forecasts future parameter uncertainty and preserves correlations between process disturbances, parameter error, and estimate updates to construct tight, guaranteed reachable sets that account for future information gain. We also develop a GPU-accelerated A-SLS solver to enable real-time performance. Across nonlinear robotic systems, A-SLS reduces reachable-tube conservativeness, maintains real-time performance, and scales to whole-body control for a quadruped with 61 states, 8 uncertain parameters, and 12 control inputs. We further demonstrate the approach on hardware, where a physical Crazyflie drone learns an uncertain dynamics parameter online to stabilize on the fly.
authors: Anutam Srinivasan, Siddhant Panse, Glen Chou
bullets: Addresses conservative robust adaptive control that ignores guaranteed future parameter learning and struggles with high-dimensional robots.
Uses system-level synthesis to forecast parameter uncertainty and preserve correlations among disturbances, parameter errors, and estimate updates.
Builds tighter guaranteed reachable sets that incorporate expected information gain during planning.
Demonstrates real-time scalability on nonlinear robots, including whole-body control for a 61-state quadruped.
Validates online dynamics learning and stabilization on a physical Crazyflie drone.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human videos offer a scalable alternative to costly robot demonstra- tions, yet transferring their manipulation priors to robot control remains chal- lenging. The commonly adopted retargeting-based approaches convert human wrist and finger poses into embodiment-specific action commands through hand- crafted geometric mappings. However, such mappings require meticulous recal- ibration across different embodiments and risk propagating hand-tracking errors into downstream robot control pipelines. To this end, we propose EgoJEPA, a three-stage framework that learns embodiment-agnostic representations from ego- centric human videos without rule-based human-to-robot retargeting: 1) Human- action pre-training learns effect-aware latent actions through JEPA-style visual prediction conditioned on hand-motion differences; 2) Latent-action-based world modeling jointly predicts future visual dynamics and latent actions, which decou- ples human prior pre-training from robot-specific control parameterizations; 3) Embodiment-specific tuning adapts the pretrained model to diverse robots through lightweight action adapters. Experiments on five real-world manipulation tasks across three robot embodiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of EgoJEPA. It achieves a 74% average success rate under the out-of-domain evalu- ation, compared with 65% for the retargeting baseline, while reducing cumulative cross-embodiment wall-clock cost by 47.2%, from 743.2 to 392.7 hours.
authors: Meng Cao, Can Zhao, Jinjie Wei, Haonan Zhao, Yulong Zhang, Duo Han, Xiaofan Li, Ziwu Song, Rongtao Xu, Ruyi Gan, Hao Wang, Qian Wang, Daolin Ma, Ian Reid, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Addresses the calibration burden and error propagation of human-to-robot retargeting.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the EgoJEPA framework. Stage 1: An effect-aware latent action space is learned from ego-centric human video data without embodiment-specific action re-targeting. Figure 4: Qualitative results on five real-world robotic manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Task-Oriented Grasping (TOG) has emerged as an important skill for purposeful robotic manipulation. Given the task of using a knife to "slice bread," a robot must choose to grasp from the handle, whereas for "hand[ing] the knife over," it is preferable for the handle to remain unobstructed for safe handoff. Current approaches for TOG either focus on 2D planar grasping, remain limited by their reliance on task-agnostic grasp generators, or are constrained by reliance on finite, manually-annotated, task-specific grasp datasets that cannot cover all possible grasp-task pairs. To that end, we present TGrasp6D, a vision-language based approach for generating task-oriented 6DoF grasps in a zero-shot manner. Given a task and a single RGB-D image of an associated object, TGrasp6D reasons about the appropriate semantic affordance for the given task and object geometry to produce an initial task- informed prior. This generated prior is further refined via 6DoF pose optimization for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency. Our approach achieves state-of-the-art success rate of 94% on the TaskGrasp dataset, with the best baseline at 74%. We also deploy our approach on a Franka Research 3 robot to demonstrate zero-shot generalization to real world objects
authors: Manav Kulshrestha, Apoorva Vashisth, Damon Conover, Aniket Bera
bullets: Addresses limitations of 2D, task-agnostic, and manually annotated task-specific grasping methods.
Uses vision-language reasoning to infer semantic affordances from the task and object geometry.
Refines the task-informed grasp prior with 6DoF pose optimization for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency.
Reports a 94% success rate on TaskGrasp, compared with 74% for the best baseline.
Demonstrates zero-shot generalization to real-world objects on a Franka Research 3 robot.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of TGrasp6D. Given a single RGB-D observation and a natural-language task instruction, a vision-language model identifies and localizes the task-relevant affordance and predicts an image-space grasp orientation. These cues are lifted into 3D to form a task-informed grasp prior, from which candidate 6DoF grasps are sampled and refined for collision avoidance while preserving task consistency, yielding the final task-oriented grasp.

Fig. 3: Qualitative comparison of different 6DoF TOG approaches on objects from the TaskGrasp [9] dataset. For each method, we show 5 task-oriented grasps per object. Compared to other approaches, our TGrasp6D produces more successful grasps across diverse object types and tasks. For cases like “scoop[ing]” with the “spoon,” most approaches generate feasible grasps. However, performance drops sharply for more challenging cases like doing a “handover” with the “measuring cup.” Of note, compared to the pure vision-language prior (f), grasp-pose refinement (g) appears to visually diversify grasps by generating feasible stable and task-consistent alternates. In some cases, like the “measuring cup,” it even recovers some failures despite noise and missing points due to occlusion in the object point-cloud.

Fig. 1: Example of TGrasp6D producing distinct 6DoF grasps for different tasks on the same real-world object. “handover” task results in grasps that keep the handle clear whereas tasks like “pound” and “cook” that require holding the hammer and pan from the handle are reflected.

Fig. 4: Analysis of failure modes, including the effect of grasp refinement for GPT-5.5. Note the y-axis breaks between 4%-10% and 12%-19% to accommodate Gemini-3.7 (11.0%) and Qwen3.5-35B (19.7%) without compressing the smaller values.

TABLE I: Comparison with baseline methods. Note that fOE and fPE are reported only for grasps marked as failures. All baseline results use unmodified author-released code and, where available, author-provided pretrained weights; we do not alter any baseline’s inference pipeline.
TABLE II: Real-robot task-oriented grasping success rate comparison.
TABLE III: Pre-pose refinement ablation using other visionlanguage models for affordance reasoning, localization, and grasp-prior generation.

papers.abstract: Vehicles that lose control at the handling limit through icing, hydroplaning, or an abrupt evasive maneuver fall outside the operating envelope of production safety systems such as electronic stability control, which focus on preventing instability rather than recovering from it. Expert drivers regain authority in these conditions by drifting. Existing autonomous recovery approaches are validated on idealized scenarios, define "recovered" states empirically and inconsistently, or rely on offline-planned trajectories rather than acting online. We address these gaps by first training a racing policy with reinforcement learning that learns drifting as a time-optimal maneuver, then adapting it to recovery through continued training with a minimum-time reward. We define recovery relative to a phase-plane-grounded stable equilibrium and introduce Gym-Khana for controller training and evaluation. Across 294 initial loss-of-control states, the transferred policy improves recovery by 186.8% over a Stanley path tracker and outperforms both a nonlinear model predictive controller and a recovery-only policy trained from scratch, while also recovering faster on states the baseline can already handle. An ablation shows that racing pretraining, rather than broader initial-state exposure alone, drives this gain. Deployed on a physical 1:10-scale F1TENTH vehicle using system identification, actuator-lag modelling, and domain randomization, the transferred policy outperforms Stanley on every tested loss-of-control state, including recovering 50% of the time from a hard state the baseline never recovers from.
authors: Teodor Ilie, Kleber Cabral, Sidney Givigi
bullets: Targets failures beyond production electronic stability control, including icing, hydroplaning, and abrupt evasive maneuvers.
Pretrains a policy to drift as a time-optimal racing maneuver, then adapts it for recovery with continued minimum-time training.
Defines recovery using a phase-plane-grounded stable equilibrium and introduces Gym-Khana for training and evaluation.
Across 294 simulated initial states, the transferred policy improves recovery by 186.8% over a Stanley path tracker and outperforms nonlinear MPC and recovery-only training.
On a 1:10-scale F1TENTH vehicle, it outperforms Stanley on every tested state and recovers 50% of the time from a state the baseline never recovers from.

figures.caption: Fig. 3. Overview of the approach. 1. A policy is trained with proximal policy optimization (PPO) to race on the Drift track and its mirror image, where drifting emerges as the time-optimal technique. 2. Its actor πrace is transferred unchanged to the recovery task, and its critic is reinitialized. 3. Training continues under the recovery reward, which drives the vehicle from an unrecovered state in U into the recovered set R; the two tasks share one vehicle model, observation and action space, so only the reward changes between them. 4. The resulting πrace→rec is deployed on the physical F1TENTH vehicle. Before deployment, system identification, actuator-lag modelling and domain randomization adapt the simulator to the vehicle, and the controller is retrained on it from racing onwards (Sections IV-D and VI). Every image is taken from our experiments: the racing and recovery panels are rollouts of the trained policies in simulation, the bottom-left plot is the loss (6) of the identification run across four parallel covariance matrix adaptation evolution strategy (CMA-ES) workers, and the bottom-right photo overlays frames of a recovery run on the physical vehicle. In both recovery panels time runs downwards: the shading marks U (red) and its complement R (green), the dotted line the initial state z0 where the policy takes over, and the solid line the first recovered state zT .

papers.abstract: Realistic traffic simulation and autonomous planning both depend on modeling interactions among heterogeneous road users whose dynamics, constraints, and behaviors differ fundamentally. Existing approaches predominantly learn realistic interaction behavior from large-scale human driving demonstrations. In this work, we ask whether such behavior can instead emerge purely through self-play. We present SHRED, a framework that jointly trains vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists through large-scale heterogeneous self-play from random initialization, without demonstrations or logged-trajectory replay. SHRED combines type-specific dynamics and objectives with procedural scenario generation and per-agent randomization, allowing diverse behaviors to emerge through closed-loop interaction. On the Waymo Open Sim Agents Challenge (WOSAC), SHRED jointly controls all three road-user types and outperforms both the closest demonstration-free self-play baseline and prior self-play methods that use demonstration-trained reference policies. Policies trained only on nuPlan map geometry retain comparable realism under zero-shot evaluation on Waymo. For planning, SHRED outperforms all compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark. Controlled ablations show that heterogeneity in self-play improves both traffic realism and planning performance, with particularly large planning gains in interaction-heavy scenarios. Together, these results establish heterogeneous procedural self-play as a scalable, demonstration-free paradigm for learning realistic and interactive traffic behavior.
authors: Wei-Jer Chang, Zhouchonghao Wu, Akshay Rangesh, Weixin Li, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Wei Zhan

Outperforms demonstration-free and prior demonstration-assisted self-play baselines on WOSAC while controlling all three road-user types.
Policies trained on nuPlan map geometry maintain comparable realism in zero-shot Waymo evaluation and outperform compared planners on the interaction-heavy InterPlan benchmark.
Ablations show that heterogeneous self-play improves both realism and planning, especially in interaction-heavy scenarios.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. SHRED Training Architecture. Simulation produces mixed transitions across all agent types. The model consists of shared encoders followed by per-type LSTM cells, action heads, and value heads. Per-type rewards and value normalization accommodate distinct reward scales across road-user types. Each type uses its own dynamics model: jerk-integrated Ackermann dynamics for vehicles, unicycle dynamics for pedestrians, and kinematic bicycle dynamics for cyclists.

Fig. 1.Qualitative Rollout Distributions. Qualitative trajectory distributions from SHRED across a diverse range of scenarios, from urban intersections to parking lots. Each panel shows 32 closed-loop policy rollouts (blue: vehicle, red: pedestrian, green: cyclist); orange traces show the ground-truth log trajectory. The panels show alternative maneuvers alongside the logged trajectory.

Fig. 3.Group Behavior Metrics. Proximity clustering and directional alignment versus pedestrian population 𝑁ped. Shaded bands: ±1 standard deviation across scenarios. Left axis: in-group fraction 𝑓grp; local alignment 𝜇align; right axis: mean group size ̄𝑔. All three GBMs increase monotonically with crowd density for the policy while remaining near zero / unity for the stationary baseline.

Table 4. Interactive planning on InterPlan. SHRED achieves the highest score among the compared planners on both the official 80-scenario split and the full 335-scenario evaluation. Comparison with a vehicle-only variant, trained with scripted pedestrians and no cyclists, showcases the benefit of heterogeneous self-play for interactive planning. Table 10 in Appendix E.3 gives the full comparison.

Table 3.Realism and diversity on WOSAC 2024. Unlike HR-PPO and SPACeR, which anchor self-play to demonstration-trained policies, SHRED uses no demonstrations, yet achieves the highest interactive score and higher realism than both, with greater rollout diversity. The nuPlan-trained policy retains comparable realism zero-shot on Waymo.

Table 2. Ablation of heterogeneous dynamics and rewards on WOSAC 2024. Overall and per-type realism for vehicles, pedestrians, and cyclists. Removing either component modestly reduces realism, while removing both causes the largest drop, most strongly for vehicles. Removing random initialization and goals also degrades realism.
Table 8. Agreement between the GPU evaluator and the official WOSAC evaluator on 50 scenarios.

Table 10. Full comparison of interactive planners on InterPlan. InterPlan (80) is the official 80-scenario split, and Full Scale (335) evaluates all 335 scenarios. Table 5. Per-type kinematic parameters and domain-randomization ranges. Coefficient ranges (𝐶∗) are sampled uniformly per agent per episode; scalar values are fixed. Clip bounds are hard limits enforced by the dynamics integrator. Bounding-box ranges are sampled uniformly per agent at spawn, calibrated to the Waymo Open Motion Dataset distribution. Vehicles additionally draw a Bernoulli truck/car bodywork class that selects from an extended length range [6.1, 12.2]m for trucks.

Table 6. Per-type reward terms and domain-randomization ranges. Dashes mark terms that are disabled (𝛼 = 0) for that type. Const. values are not randomized; ranges denote uniform sampling per agent per episode. All weights are multiplied by Δ𝑡 = 0.1 s per step except collision and goal, which fire as one-shot events.

papers.abstract: Robotic manipulation is inherently geometric, but what shape does the world take inside the policy that performs it? Prior work on vision-language-action (VLA) policies establishes that task-relevant variables are linearly readable from activations, yet readability certifies only that a variable is present and says nothing about the shape its values trace, which may be curved and multi-dimensional. Using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions, we build a taxonomy of seven task-relevant concepts in VLA models. We find that realized geometry is predominantly multi-dimensional and is shaped by the constraints under which the policy acts. Physical joint limits, for example, leave wrist orientation an open arc rather than a circle, and distance to the target, a single scalar, is realized in two orthogonal subspaces, a coarse ruler for the approach and a fine ruler for the grasp. The same geometries reappear in two further VLA models on real-world robot data, indicating that they are neither model-specific nor artifacts of simulation. We demonstrate how the findings are actionable by steering along the geometry a concept realizes. Overall, this work lays out an initial phenomenology of realized geometry in VLA policies and demonstrates that a concept's shape carries as much importance as its readability.
authors: Mozes Jacobs, Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, Fenil R. Doshi, Usha Bhalla, Thomas Icard, Matt Feiszli, Thomas McGrath, Vasudev Shyam, Demba Ba, Leon Bergen, Nina Miolane, Owen Lewis, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Atticus Geiger, Matthew Kowal, Thomas Fel
bullets: Maps seven task-relevant concepts using controlled sweeps, natural rollouts, linear probes, and activation interventions.
Finds geometries are predominantly multi-dimensional and reflect the constraints under which the robot acts.
Shows joint limits turn wrist orientation into an open arc, while target distance forms separate coarse- and fine-scale subspaces.
Observes similar geometries across two additional VLAs using real-world robot data, suggesting the patterns are not model- or simulation-specific.
Demonstrates that understanding a concept’s geometry enables targeted activation steering.

Top: (a) held-out per-axis error relative to gripper width; (b) held-out R2 vs. readout rank; (c) singular values of the rank-3 readout; (d) residual of a linear map from world to activation displacements across layers (solid: general linear; dashed: orthogonal; reference line: no linear relation); (e) curvature of straight world paths inside each subspace vs. distance to the gripper, compared with a random 3-D projection. Figure 22: After a full turn of the wrist joint the action expert’s activation does not return to its start; the VLM’s returns exactly. From one pose of the roll sweep (App. C.8; a single house), the wrist joint (Franka joint 7) is driven through successive full turns by writing the joint value directly into the simulator, far past the joint’s physical range (shaded band), so the sweep tests the models’ inputs rather than a reachable motion. At every full turn (dashed lines, large markers) the rendered frames and text tokens are identical to the start and only the raw joint value differs, and only the action expert receives that value. Figure 3: MolmoBot’s VLM encodes distance to the target in nearly orthogonal near- and far-range codes (layer 21). (a) Near (<15 cm) and far (15–70 cm) probe R2 after erasing the top-k directions of the other probe, computed against each range’s own variance. Erasing far directions leaves near decoding intact while far decoding collapses, and vice versa. The intact (k = 0) probes have errors of ∼1.3 cm (near) and ∼3.6 cm (far). (b) Near R2 (<c) vs. far R2 (≥c) as the cutoff c is swept. Clipped (‘round to c’) probes match probes fit separately on each range and outperform a single full-range probe. (c) Cosine between the near- and far-probe weight vectors as the cutoff c is swept, for range-split and clipped (‘round to c’) pairs (fold mean ± s.d.). For c ≲ 30 cm, both cosines stay below the cosine between two copies of the same probe fit on different halves of the data (dashed). On synthetic activations that encode distance along a single direction, the same probes are nearly parallel for c ≳ 15 cm (dotted). (d) Activations plotted by their meter- and centimeter-probe readouts, colored by true distance in meters (left) and centimeters (right). Far samples vary along the meter axis while the centimeter readout saturates, and near samples do the opposite, tracing an L.

Figure 9: The action expert (layer 12) also maintains a rank-3 EE position subspace. Panels as in the top and middle rows of Figure 2, for EE position read from the action expert, which receives proprioception; the paths are from a single scene excluded when fitting the subspace. The readout is near-exact and the paths are recovered almost without distortion. The gap between the general-linear and orthogonal residuals shows the subspace is a scaled, not isometric, copy of world coordinates.

Figure 10: The action expert (layer 22) also maintains a rank-3 target object position subspace. Panels as in Figure 9, for the target object’s position; the paths are from a single scene excluded when fitting the subspace. The action expert receives the object only through cross-attention to the VLM, and it carries target position with larger error than the VLM (Figure 2), recovering the paths with more distortion.

Figure 11: Within a scene, target object position is computed on the VLM’s instruction and final tokens between layers 12 and 21 and appears in the action expert from layer 18; EE position is present from the first layer in both. Held-out R2 of the rank-3 ridge readout of end-effector position (left) and target object position (right) at every layer, scored after removing each held-out house’s mean from the true and predicted positions, so only position changes within a scene count; one line per VLM token pool, the action expert dashed, rings on the readouts of Figure 2, values below the axis floor clipped. The target’s height is constant within a scene, so the target panel’s variance is horizontal and any within-scene variation in the predicted height counts as error; scores fall below zero where a readout’s predictions vary within a scene without tracking the object. On the instruction and final tokens the target read stays at or below zero until layer 12 and peaks at layers 18–21, while the image patches carry little of it at any layer. The action expert tracks EE position near-perfectly at every layer and the target only from layer 18 on.

Figure 12: Distance is compressive within the near range and closest to linear beyond 30 cm, and each ruler reads only its own range (VLM, layer 21). (Left) Held-out mean absolute error per bin of true distance for a single full-range ridge probe fit to d, log d, or 1/d and mapped back to metres; the compressive links have the lower error below 15 cm and the linear link in the farthest bins. (Right) Held-out R2 against true distance for the centimeter ruler and the meter ruler of Figure 3, scored separately on states below and above that cutoff; negative (saturated) values are drawn at zero and printed. Each ruler saturates outside its own range, as does a single unclipped metre-scale probe (not shown) on the near-range states.

Figure 29: DROID real world behavioral manifolds. Here we show the behavioral manifolds realized by MolmoAct2 and π0.5. The EE position and wrist orientation point clouds show the activations of all 3,321 queries, sampled from MolmoAct2 AE L16 of 36 and π0.5 VLM L7 of 18, demonstrating the structures appear across multiple streams. We plot a natural episode trajectory in the EE position subplots and the wrist roll sweep of Figure 30 in the Wrist Orientation subplots. In the Gripper plot we project the 379 landmark activations from each model’s final action-expert block onto the principal components of the pullback steering vectors, with binned steering vectors as arrows.

Figure 26: Gripper control for action expert layer 9 (Top left) A linear probe decodes the commanded gripper aperture; one principal component of the pullback steering vectors decodes it nearly as well as the full activation. (Top right) Natural-rollout activations colored by gripper state; notably, the steering vectors from each cluster do not point toward the other, unlike layer 32 in Figure 7. (Bottom left) One component captures ∼55% of steering-vector variance. papers.abstract: Damage-recovery algorithms often rank gaits from short trials, yet a gait that performs well briefly may not remain effective during continued execution. In reset-free recovery, each trial also changes the physical state inherited by the next. We introduce persistent profile-guided reset-free recovery (PGRR), which predicts multiple outcomes over repeated gait execution and uses conservative uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot. Across 108 matched MuJoCo tasks spanning leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock, PGRR improves final quality by 0.106 and slot-averaged recovery quality (SRQ) by 0.044 relative to an IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline, while reducing low-quality failures by 27.8 percentage points. Final-quality gains occur in all three damage classes. Against no adaptation, PGRR also improves final quality and reduces low-quality failures, whereas the aggregate SRQ difference is inconclusive. Development ablations identify conservative uncertainty handling as the clearest supported contributor to the observed gains. These results show that PGRR can identify stronger post-damage gaits under continuous physical state and that final-gait quality and recovery-summary performance provide complementary evidence for evaluating reset-free recovery.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between short-trial gait rankings and long-term gait effectiveness after irreversible leg damage.
Uses persistent outcome profiles and conservative uncertainty-aware estimates to guide short online probes without resetting the robot.
Evaluated across 108 MuJoCo tasks involving leg amputation, distal fracture, and joint lock.
Improved final gait quality and reduced low-quality failures versus an IT&E-inspired Gaussian-process baseline; gains appeared across all damage classes.
Ablations most strongly supported conservative uncertainty handling, while aggregate SRQ improvement versus no adaptation was inconclusive.

papers.abstract: A mesh of interceptors defending a fixed site must spread over the predicted arrival point of an approaching object. This is a recurring task in multi-agent robotics: N agents, each covering a disc of radius r, spread over a probability density so that a point drawn from it falls within some agent's disc. We give closed forms for the quantities that bound performance before any policy is chosen, and validate each by Monte Carlo. The uncertainty of a point predicted by extrapolating a noisy linear track follows from least-squares variance propagation plus a delta-method term for the uncertain arrival time, agreeing with simulation to within 1.8%. The coverage probability of a packed mesh admits a closed form accurate to 0.007 absolute, with a volumetric analogue. A naive area ratio misses a ceiling: while agents stay at least 2r apart, no mesh exceeds 90.69% coverage in the plane or 74.05% in a volume. This ceiling belongs to the separation constraint, not to the problem - permitting overlap substitutes Kershner's thinnest-covering density and removes it, the better regime above a crossover at p=0.80. Hexagonal packing is optimal among five arrangements; the centroidal-Voronoi configuration coverage control supplies reaches only half its coverage at small budgets. The Gaussian assumption is conservative under heavy tails and anisotropy but fragile under bias: a one-sigma aim-point offset costs 14 points of coverage. A repositioning team must also choose a commit time, and the admissible window can be empty. Against the applicable ceiling, analytic placement attains 85% of what the configuration permits while centralised PPO averages 15% over three trainer seeds, with a paired bootstrap against a null policy containing zero at every seed. We argue such ceilings should be computed before any learning experiment and quoted alongside every result.
bullets: Closed-form bounds estimate arrival-point uncertainty, mesh coverage, packing limits, and the admissible repositioning commit window.
With non-overlapping agents, coverage is capped at 90.69% in 2D and 74.05% in 3D; overlap removes this separation-induced ceiling above a crossover of p=0.80.
Analytic placement reaches 85% of the applicable ceiling, whereas centralized PPO averages 15% across three training seeds.
Gaussian uncertainty is conservative under heavy tails and anisotropy but sensitive to bias: a one-standard-deviation aim-point offset reduces coverage by 14 percentage points.
The study validates its formulas by Monte Carlo and argues that feasibility ceilings should accompany learning results.

papers.abstract: Can better feature discovery improve control over robot behavior through internal interventions and training data? Recent work in vision and language models reveals multidimensional features, motivating block-sparse featurizers (BSFs), which represent each feature in a low-dimensional subspace. We investigate whether recovering this structure provides an interpretable interface for steering vision-language-action models and shaping the data from which they learn. We show that BSFs recover several multi-dimensional task-relevant features underlying the model's computation (e.g., perception, language, proprioceptive state, episode phase, and control variables). We causally validate these features through fine-grained steering: targeted changes in visual perception, semantic representation, and spatial localization produce predictable changes in downstream action prediction. Finally, we use feature-based data attribution to isolate where a specific behavior (failure recovery) arises in the training dataset, identifying fewer than $1.4\%$ of training tokens whose masking is sufficient to remove the targeted behavior. Overall, our results show how matching featurizers to representation geometry can provide more effective tools for understanding and changing robot behavior.
authors: Aiden Swann, Mozes Jacobs, Mathilde Papillon, Siddharth Boppana, David Chanin, Dron Hazra, Usha Bhalla, Curt Tigges, Mac Schwager, Owen Lewis, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Atticus Geiger, Thomas Fel, Matthew Kowal
bullets: Recover task-relevant features spanning perception, language, proprioception, episode phase, and control variables.
Causal interventions show that steering visual, semantic, and spatial features predictably changes action predictions.
Feature-based data attribution traces failure-recovery behavior to fewer than 1.4% of training tokens.
Results support matching featurizers to representation geometry for more effective robot behavior analysis and modification.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models are a promising approach to general purpose robot manipulation. While the internal computation of vision-language models, which compose the backbone of VLAs, has been studied extensively, less is known about how their perceptual and semantic representations are transformed into action in VLA models. We study this question mechanistically in three frontier VLA models ($\pi_{0.5}$, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot) by analyzing the causal pathways through which the input image and the instruction shape actions. Across the three models, activation patching shows that causally relevant information influences the action expert (AE) through a narrow band of mid-to-late cross-attention layers, which we term the action-conditioning interface. The content of this information changes with token and layer within the model. Early-to-mid layer representations of the target noun token determine which object is selected, whereas mid-to-late layers carry the spatial information in text tokens that redirects the movement when patched. Where spatial information is stored in prompt tokens various based on the architecture. In MolmoAct2 the model forms task-conditioned representations at the text positions that follow the instruction, whereas $\pi_{0.5}$ additionally stores this information at image token positions. We show that these findings can be translated directly into improving model efficiency. We find that restricting MolmoBot's action expert conditioning to only 3 out of 36 layers reduces inference FLOPs by up to $33\%$ while maintaining comparable task success with the default model across 3,000 evaluation episodes ($46.7\%$ vs. $46.9\%$), and the same principle carries over to real-robot deployment of $\pi_{0.5}$.
authors: Aiden Swann, Mathilde Papillon, Mozes Jacobs, Siddharth Boppana, Tal Haklay, Eric Bigelow, Andrew Lee, Conor Watts, Thomas Icard, Mac Schwager, Owen Lewis, Jack Merullo, Ekdeep Singh Lubana, Atticus Geiger, Thomas Fel, Matthew Kowal
bullets: Studies how perceptual and semantic representations become actions in three frontier VLA models: π₀.₅, MolmoAct2, and MolmoBot.
Activation patching identifies mid-to-late cross-attention layers as the main causal pathway into the action expert.
Early-to-mid representations of target nouns determine object selection, while later text representations encode spatial redirection.
Spatial information is stored differently across architectures, including instruction-following text positions and image-token positions.
Restricting MolmoBot conditioning to 3 of 36 layers cuts inference FLOPs by up to 33% while retaining comparable success; the approach also transfers to real-robot π₀.₅ deployment.

papers.abstract: Verifiable instruction-following benchmarks emphasize output-constraint satisfaction but can overlook whether responses meaningfully answer the underlying request, creating an evaluation blind spot. We show that frontier models can receive full credit for responses with little substantive answer content. Using the same verifier-based criterion as a training reward can induce reward hacking, as publicly released checkpoints exhibit higher constraint satisfaction but lower response quality after reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards. To address this reward hacking, we introduce CALIF, a lightweight method that augments verifier rewards with a calibrated likelihood-based bonus to preserve response quality. CALIF evaluates response likelihood under the request alone using the existing frozen reference policy, requiring no additional judge or learned reward model. Across models ranging from 1.7B to 8B in reasoning and non-reasoning modes, CALIF improves constraint satisfaction on IFBench while maintaining response quality near or above pre-RL levels. It also outperforms corresponding base policies in 40 of 45 model-metric comparisons across three rubric-based instruction-following benchmarks, demonstrating gains beyond training verifiers.
bullets: Verifiable benchmarks may award full credit to responses with little substantive content.
Reinforcement learning with verifier rewards increases constraint satisfaction but can reduce response quality.
CALIF uses the frozen reference policy to reward likelihood under the request alone, without an extra judge or learned reward model.
Across 1.7B–8B models, CALIF improves IFBench constraint satisfaction while preserving response quality near or above pre-RL levels.
It outperforms corresponding base policies in 40 of 45 model-metric comparisons across three rubric-based benchmarks.

papers.selection_reason: Reward-hacking correction via a calibrated likelihood bonus is transferable to RL-based robot policy learning with verifiable rewards.

papers.tldr: Verifier-based rewards can encourage models to satisfy output constraints while neglecting the user’s request; CALIF mitigates this by adding a reference-policy likelihood bonus.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon agents have drawn growing attention for their ability to work autonomously -- from hours to days -- on economically valuable tasks, a capability essential to automated discovery and recursive self-improvement (RSI). Yet open-source models still struggle on long-horizon tasks, largely for lack of both training data and a working recipe, and scaling both is hard: long, complex tasks are difficult to curate and verify, and their rewards are sparse. We address both. First, we introduce Tev-Gym, the first long-horizon agent training dataset with verifiable, dense, progressive rewards -- 1,170 verified task environments across 7 domains. It is built on a latent-world-first approach that first constructs a latent world: a complete and correct hidden specification of the task domain, workflow, and expected state after each step. Each task is then progressively rendered from this specification into an agent-facing environment, enabling controllable complexity and a natural progress metric. Second, we turn this metric into a training recipe: via progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS), we convert progress into a dense per-step reward that improves training efficiency and makes otherwise-intractable tasks trainable. Training with this recipe yields Tev-27B, which achieves substantial gains on the Agents' Last Exam computing and math sciences domains (ALE-CM), matching GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5. Despite training only on ALE-related data, it generalizes to the Terminal-Bench (TB) 3.0 and 4.0 subsets, surpassing GLM 5.2 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks such as TB 2.1.
bullets: Introduces Tev-Gym, a dataset of 1,170 verified task environments spanning 7 domains.
Uses a latent-world-first design to specify task workflows and expected intermediate states before rendering environments.
Applies progress-potential reward shaping (PPRS) to convert task progress into dense per-step rewards.
Trains Tev-27B, which matches GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5 at Pass@5 on ALE-CM.
Despite ALE-focused training, Tev-27B generalizes to Terminal-Bench subsets and reaches Claude Opus 4.8-level performance on middle-horizon tasks.

papers.abstract: Latent Action Models (LAMs) can capture manipulation priors from action-free videos, but discrete latents usually impose a granularity bottleneck, limiting their ability to represent fine-grained action. Recent continuous alternatives mitigate this, but they are typically used as proxies for world modeling and require a further planning step to produce executable actions. We thus introduce UniLAP, a unified continuous latent-action policy that models the latent space via flow matching and bypasses reliance on future frames during inference. By distilling a LAM teacher with a flow-adaptive objective, UniLAP inherits the teacher's action representation while retaining the multimodal distribution of feasible behaviors. To decouple latent representations from task-irrelevant appearance, we extract a label-free motion target to isolate relevant kinematic cues from spurious visual dynamics. With the established embodiment-agnostic latent manifold, UniLAP can be easily adapted to novel platforms. Pretrained on multi-source videos at a compact 1.1B parameter scale, UniLAP outperforms state-of-the-art latent-action and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) baselines across hand pose forecasting, single-arm and humanoid manipulation, and real-world deployment.
bullets: Addresses the granularity limits of discrete latent actions and the extra planning required by continuous world-modeling approaches.
Uses flow matching to model continuous latent actions and distills a latent action model teacher with a flow-adaptive objective.
Extracts label-free motion targets to separate task-relevant kinematics from task-irrelevant appearance.
Builds an embodiment-agnostic latent manifold that adapts to new robotic platforms.
At 1.1B parameters, outperforms latent-action and VLA baselines across pose forecasting, single-arm and humanoid manipulation, and real-world deployment.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots still struggle to plan contact-rich whole-body manipulation from egocentric RGB and proprioception. Workhorse learns such manipulation from robot-free human demonstrations. A visual planner predicts five-link targets: the poses of the torso, both wrists, and both feet. A reinforcement-learning whole-body tracker follows them on the robot. Both policies train separately on the same recorded human poses, without retargeting. We augment the training data of each policy to imitate the errors that the other makes at deployment. On a real Unitree G1, Workhorse transport boxes with its hands and a kick, catches a thrown box, and topples and climbs a suitcase. During box transport, we show recoveries after a person pushes the robot or takes the box away. In a simulated copy of the demonstration room, the system completes box transport in 77% of episodes, and in 64% under 40 N.s pushes. With both policies retrained from the same demonstrations, a simulated second humanoid completes box transport in 83% of episodes without pushes.
bullets: Addresses contact-rich humanoid manipulation from egocentric RGB and proprioception.
Predicts target poses for the torso, both wrists, and both feet, then tracks them with a whole-body RL policy.
Trains both policies separately on the same human pose recordings and augments data with the other policy’s deployment errors.
Demonstrates box transport, catching, kicking, and suitcase climbing on a real Unitree G1, including recovery from pushes and box removal.
Completes simulated box transport in 77% of episodes, 64% under 40 N·s pushes, and 83% on a second humanoid without pushes.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots operating in unstructured environments must combine robust whole-body control with the ability to perceive and physically interact with surrounding objects. While large-scale human motion data provides powerful priors for natural and versatile humanoid control, effectively transferring such priors to perception-driven object interaction remains challenging. To address this bottleneck, we propose a framework that extends the recently proposed Generative Pretrained Controller (GPC) from general human motion to full-body humanoid-environment interaction. First, we adapt GPC into interaction experts conditioned on scene affordance cues and privileged state information. This adaptation begins with interaction and affordance pre-training on human motions paired with support scenes. These experts leverage the pretrained human motion prior while learning task-specific contact behaviors, including reaching toward objects, grasping environmental supports for stabilization, and pushing movable objects. Second, we introduce a perception-driven student that retains the pretrained GPC policy and distills interaction skills from the experts using onboard sensory observations. To bridge the gap between privileged expert observations and sensory inputs, we train the student's perception not only to reconstruct expert observations, but also to preserve the expert's motion decisions and resulting joint targets. Notably, our experiments across multiple whole-body interaction tasks demonstrate that large-scale generative human motion priors provide an effective foundation for learning deployable policies for humanoid interactions in contact-rich real-world environments.
bullets: Targets humanoid interaction in unstructured environments, where control must combine natural motion, perception, and physical contact.
Adapts GPC into interaction experts conditioned on scene affordances and privileged state information.
Pretrains experts to learn behaviors such as reaching, grasping supports for stability, and pushing objects.
Distills these skills into a sensory-driven student that preserves both expert observations and motion decisions.
Experiments across multiple whole-body tasks support the feasibility of deployable interaction policies in real-world environments.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) such as Cosmos 3 jointly generate future video and robot actions from an observation and instruction. Adapting one such model with a lightweight LoRA fine-tune to a previously unseen robot, a Unitree G1 humanoid with five-fingered BrainCo hands, exposes a video-action asymmetry: the video renders plausible task executions, while the co-generated action is systematically mis-targeted. We evaluate closed-loop real-robot trials at three cumulative stages: pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place. The native action succeeds only approximately 17%, 10%, and 7% of the time, respectively, and performs worse on held-out objects. We propose AutodidactWAM, a hand-pose estimator trained without teleoperation, followed by inverse kinematics, that runs on the model's generated video to recover action estimates. Paired with the native prediction, these recovered actions provide preferred targets for fine-tuning only the action-related layers, while the generated video is teacher-forced. We compare supervised relabeling with a rectified-flow adaptation of Diffusion-DPO. After one-time embodiment adaptation, self-distillation requires no additional task-specific teleoperation. The recovered-action gate reaches approximately 75%, 47%, and 42% pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place success, compared with 17%, 10%, and 7% for the native action. A hybrid objective combining preference supervision, supervised target fitting, and Cartesian trajectory anchoring (DPO+SFT+DTW) performs best: on Oreo, the training object, it reaches 90% pre-grasp and 20% full-task success; on a held-out object, it reaches 80% and 30%. Plain Flow-DPO reaches 0% success despite 1.000 validation preference accuracy, indicating that the combination of training objectives, rather than the contrastive objective alone, drives the observed gains.
bullets: A LoRA-adapted WAM generates plausible video but systematically mis-targeted actions on a Unitree G1 humanoid.
The method estimates hand poses from generated video, converts them to actions with inverse kinematics, and uses them as preferred fine-tuning targets.
A hybrid DPO+SFT+DTW objective performs best, outperforming supervised relabeling and plain Flow-DPO.
Recovered-action gating raises pre-grasp, grasp, and pick-and-place success from approximately 17%, 10%, and 7% to 75%, 47%, and 42%.
On the reported objects, the best model achieves 90% pre-grasp/20% full-task success on Oreo and 80%/30% on a held-out object.

papers.abstract: Underwater manipulation couples visual decisions, contact forces and a thruster-controlled floating base. We introduce WasserMan, to our knowledge the first multi-task simulation benchmark for visuomotor learning of floating-base underwater contact manipulation. It provides ten expert-solvable tasks, two vehicle-arm platforms, a bimanual configuration and underwater dynamics. Nine tasks have learned-policy evaluations. We compare ACT, diffusion policies (DP) and behavioral cloning on six tasks, with three training runs and equal sampled-window budgets. Pretrained SmolVLA adds evaluations on three tasks. In the tested settings, removing integral action can prevent completion, while changing action interfaces can reduce learned-policy success despite successful expert replay. Currents produce task-dependent changes in completion and actuation effort. Versioned tasks, demonstrations and per-episode evidence support a protocol separating expert feasibility, learned completion and execution effort.
bullets: Covers ten expert-solvable tasks, two vehicle-arm platforms, a bimanual setup, and underwater dynamics.
Evaluates learned policies on nine tasks, comparing ACT, diffusion policies, behavioral cloning, and pretrained SmolVLA in selected settings.
Finds that removing integral action or changing action interfaces can hinder task completion, even when expert replay succeeds.
Shows that environmental currents affect completion and actuation effort differently across tasks.
Provides versioned tasks, demonstrations, and per-episode evidence to distinguish expert feasibility, learned completion, and execution effort.

papers.abstract: Large datasets and high capacity models have accelerated progress in vision and language. This work introduces a platform aimed at bringing comparable gains to embodied learning, world models, and robotics. We present EnvDreamer, a framework that uses large language and vision language models to generate Unreal Engine 5 environments for embodied AI and robot training. EnvDreamer enables sampling of large, diverse, interactive, customizable, and validator passed virtual environments for training and evaluation across navigation, interaction, and manipulation. We illustrate the platform with a large set of generated scenes and simple baselines. Policies trained on EnvDreamer generated environments, without explicit mapping or human task supervision, achieve competitive results on multiple embodied benchmarks spanning navigation, rearrangement, and manipulation. EnvDreamer also supports image-conditioned reconstruction for real-to-sim studies. Finally, we release EnvDreamer-20k, a dataset of 20,000 validator passed environments with task programs, scene graphs, trajectories, and metadata to support reproducible benchmarking.
bullets: Uses large language and vision-language models to create interactive, customizable, validator-passed virtual environments.
Supports embodied learning without explicit mapping or human task supervision, including navigation, rearrangement, and manipulation.
Policies trained in generated environments achieve competitive results across multiple embodied benchmarks.
Enables image-conditioned reconstruction for real-to-sim studies.
Releases EnvDreamer-20k: 20,000 environments with task programs, scene graphs, trajectories, and metadata.

figures.caption: Figure 1: EnvDreamer system overview. The system builds environments from scratch using vision–language models (vLLMs) to plan and control Unreal Engine 5. User-provided text or image prompts along with system information such as Remote Control API commands and viewport screenshots (left) are passed to a vLLM-based Home Agent which decomposes the request into sub-tasks with Chain of ThoughtWei et al. [2022], generates a structured layout plan and task list in JSON, and compiles them into EnvDreamer API Python code for execution (middle). An Evaluator Agent then performs iterative task-completion checks on scene layout, furniture placement, and rationality, providing feedback until the environment passes validation (right). Finally, users can inspect the completeness of the environment by entering a play session in either an ego-centric or bird’s-eye view.

Figure 5: Task-conditioned dataset generation pipeline for EnvDreamer–20k. A user specifies a scenario by providing a prompt and a high-resolution viewport screenshot plus the current environment JSON description (left). A language model decomposes the request into a sequence of grounded sub-tasks such as “Walk to the kitchen” or “Put pizza on the plate” (middle). The system then checks which preconditions are satisfied by comparing object relations and automatically adding missing objects required to solve each task (e.g., placing a plate on the table). Finally, the validated environment details and the set of available tasks are exported as JSON and rendered through the EnvDreamer API to produce entries in the EnvDreamer–20k dataset (right).

Figure 7: High-level architecture of the EnvDreamer Remote Control API. Python clients issue JSON commands to AJsonSceneBuilder, which resolves assets, spawns actors, and returns structured responses.

Figure 2: Diverse and realistic floor plan generation with EnvDreamer. Unlike traditional procedural methods that rely on fixed generation pipelines with limited variation, EnvDreamer leverages language-driven synthesis to create diverse, realistic home layouts. Each layout shown was generated from natural language prompts (e.g., "Create a modern 2-bedroom apartment," "Design a spacious family home with open kitchen"), producing architectural arrangements that follows realworld constraints. The diversity spans from compact studios (left) to complex multi-room residences (right), with rooms color-coded by type: bedrooms (yellow), bathrooms (green), living areas (red), and other spaces. This prompt-based approach enables researchers to specify exact requirements for embodied AI and robotics experiments while maintaining architectural realism that fixed procedural pipelines struggle to achieve.

Figure 4: Interactive scene in EnvDreamer. Ego-centric view from the embodied agent with annotated object relations (on, under, between, near, inside) and a bird’s-eye view of the procedurally generated multi-room layout. The robot is rendered in-scene, and objects are spawned with realistic and diverse geometry, materials, and placements that afford navigation and manipulation.
Figure 8: Remote web session for EnvDreamer. The live UE5 viewport is streamed to the browser, while a simple builder UI issues layout updates through HTTP endpoints backed by the RC API.

Figure 3: Interactive prompt-driven environment editing with EnvDreamer. A GPT-5–based vLLM-based smart agent receives natural-language chat prompts from the user to constantly edit the environment, translates them into EnvDreamer API calls, and applies edits to a running UE5 scene over the web. Users can inspect the updated environment, accept or refine the changes, and leverage additional web-session tools such as restoring prior states, direct drag-and-drop editing, and image-instructed edits, while the system maintains a synchronized JSON representation of the scene.

papers.abstract: Safe and robust robot navigation across diverse environments requires a high-level understanding of complex scenes and the ability to carry it into stable motion. Recent works tackle this with learning-based models trained at scale and with approaches built on vision-language models (VLMs). However, learning-based models break down outside their training distribution, while VLM-based approaches bring that understanding but rarely ground it in the scene or align the action with it. To address these limitations, we present RECAST, a robot navigation framework that combines the reasoning of a VLM with the spatial grounding of vision foundation models to build an Actionable Cost map. Given the robot's front view and the user's instruction, we first decompose the scene with the VLM, judging which surfaces are traversable, which objects pose a risk, which heading to prefer, and which gaps are passable. Vision foundation models then ground these surfaces and objects in the image, and all four judgments are spatially recast into one compact cost map. This map both conditions the trajectory decoders and scores their proposals to select the one to execute. As the VLM's answers trail the live scene, both steps draw on cost maps from two points in time: the pivot frame the VLM judged, which carries all four judgments, and the current frame, whose terrain and collision costs are rebuilt from the current image. RECAST improves success over the strongest prior method by 13.3 points in simulation and 31.4 points on a real quadruped, and reduces the collision rate relative to it by 9.6 and 14.3 points, reaching the lowest collision rate among all methods. The project page is available at https://recast-nav.github.io/
bullets: Addresses the gap between VLM reasoning and spatially grounded, executable actions in diverse environments.
A VLM evaluates traversability, risks, preferred heading, and passable gaps from the robot view and instruction.
Vision foundation models ground these judgments in the image and recast them into a compact cost map.
The map conditions trajectory decoders and ranks their proposals for execution, using both past VLM judgments and current terrain/collision estimates.
Improves success over the strongest prior method by 13.3 points in simulation and 31.4 points on a real quadruped, while reducing collision rates by 9.6 and 14.3 points.

papers.abstract: Urban uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV) vision-language navigation (VLN) requires agents to follow instructions across extended urban spaces, inherently demanding long-term memory and geospatial grounding. However, scaling existing benchmarks remains difficult because of their reliance on costly reconstructed 3D assets, limiting geographic diversity and episode scale. To address this, we introduce SatNav, a scalable, long-horizon UAV VLN benchmark built from high-resolution satellite imagery. SatNav targets city-level navigation missions and uses satellite crops as approximations of UAV nadir views for visual observations. Through an automated cue-to-episode pipeline, SatNav constructs 118K episodes from 59 scenes across 18 cities, with an average trajectory length of 379 m. To stress-test long-horizon memory and geospatial reasoning, SatNav defines three task families: Boundary, Landmark, and Route, targeting loop progress tracking, landmark-based spatial grounding, and route following with counting cues. Benchmarking classical VLN agents and recent agents based on large vision-language models (LVLMs) on SatNav shows that city-scale navigation remains challenging. We further introduce SwiftVLN, a modular framework with switchable memory components, and conduct systematic memory-design ablations. Finally, satellite-to-UAV transfer experiments show that satellite-trained navigation models can operate on real-flight UAV observations, showing the practical relevance of SatNav. Our project page: https://eku127.github.io/SatNav/
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited geographic diversity of existing UAV VLN benchmarks built from reconstructed 3D assets.
Provides 118K episodes across 59 scenes in 18 cities, with average trajectories of 379 m.
Defines Boundary, Landmark, and Route tasks to evaluate memory, spatial grounding, and route following.
Finds that both classical VLN and large vision-language-model agents struggle with city-scale navigation.
Introduces SwiftVLN for modular memory studies and demonstrates transfer from satellite-trained models to real UAV observations.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models tell a robot where to move, but not how hard to push. Contact-rich tasks depend on that second quantity, compliance, yet no widely used demonstration interface records it. The obstacle is identifiability as realized pose and measured force cannot separate the operator's intended equilibrium from their stiffness, so VR controllers, SpaceMouse and handheld grippers cannot supply compliance supervision even in principle. Prior compliance-output policies work around this with hand-specified task structure, privileged simulation contact state, or dedicated force and tactile hardware. Four-channel bilateral teleoperation removes the ambiguity directly by using the leader arm as a separate measurement of the intended equilibrium, making per-axis stiffness identifiable by regression using only the joint-torque sensing already on the manipulator. This yields per-timestep, direction-dependent compliance labels at zero annotation cost, which we use to fine-tune a VLA to emit stiffness alongside pose. On a Franka Research 3 wiping task, ours is the only policy of five whose contact force changes when the instruction asks for a firm wipe rather than a normal one (6.4N (normal) to 9.1N (firm) RMS, Cohen's d = 0.89, p = 0.023
bullets: Compliance is essential for contact-rich tasks but is not captured by common robot demonstration interfaces.
Four-channel bilateral teleoperation uses the leader arm to measure intended equilibrium separately from realized pose and force.
Per-axis, direction-dependent stiffness is recovered by regression without dedicated force/tactile hardware or manual annotation.
The resulting labels fine-tune a VLA to output stiffness alongside pose.
In a Franka Research 3 wiping task, commanded contact force rose from 6.4 N for normal wiping to 9.1 N for firm wiping; the policy was the only one of five to respond this way.

papers.abstract: Capturing hand motion and interaction forces is critical for interactive computing, VR, and high-fidelity tactile demonstrations for robot learning. We introduce a wrist-worn pressure-sensing wristband that recovers continuous full-hand pose and distributed contact force on a single wearable. The system consists of flexible capacitive sensor arrays around the wrist, which require no electrical skin contact, and a recurrent network that maps the resulting pressure signal to hand state. Our key insight is that muscle contraction and tendon displacement produce pressure patterns, which correlate strongly with hand pose and interaction force. To validate this, we collect synchronized recordings of wrist pressure, optical motion-capture hand pose, and tactile-glove interaction force, covering isolated finger motion, fingertip-force stress tests, and natural hand-object manipulation. On isolated single-user motion the wristband attains $4.6^\circ$ mean finger-joint MAE, and across four users manipulating everyday objects it estimates per-finger contact force at $R^2=0.57$, which an external pose signal brings up to $0.75$. We see the wristband as one node in a constellation of everyday wearables -- e.g. paired with an egocentric camera -- adding the contact force that vision cannot observe and taking over when the hand is occluded.
bullets: Targets hand-motion and interaction-force capture for interactive computing, VR, and robot learning.
Uses flexible capacitive sensors around the wrist, exploiting pressure patterns from muscle contraction and tendon displacement.
Validated with synchronized wrist pressure, optical hand pose, and tactile-glove force recordings across motion, force, and manipulation tasks.
Achieves 4.6° mean finger-joint error for isolated single-user motion and force-estimation R² of 0.57 across four users, rising to 0.75 with an external pose signal.
The system is positioned as a wearable complement to vision, especially when the hand is occluded.

papers.abstract: Enabling human stakeholders to specify reward functions that lead to their desired outcomes is a key challenge in deploying reinforcement learning agents. Preference-based methods such as online RLHF can reduce the burden of manual reward design, but they require repeatedly training policies, sampling trajectories from the real world, and eliciting feedback, making them impractical in settings where environment interaction is computationally expensive or unsafe. We introduce Experience-Free Autonomous Reward Specification (EARS), a method for learning reward functions from preferences without environment interaction. Our approach uses a structured LLM-mediated process to construct a small set of expressive reward features from a task description and the environment observation space, then strategically samples imagined trajectories in this feature space and learns feature weights from preferences over the imagined trajectory pairs. We evaluate on three long-horizon domains: pandemic lockdown regulation design, insulin administration for diabetes patients, and autonomous vehicle control on a highway. We compare EARS to baselines that also enable reward specification without environment interaction--namely, methods that directly prompt an LLM to generate a reward function. When learning from either ground-truth preference labels or preferences labeled by a LLM, EARS designs reward functions that are more aligned with the ground truth reward function that produced the preferences or LLM context than these baselines. These results suggest that preference-based reward specification remains effective without environment sampling, enabling practical reward design in settings where collecting real trajectories is costly or infeasible.
bullets: Addresses the cost and safety barriers of online RLHF, which requires repeated policy training, real-world trajectories, and human feedback.
Uses an LLM to construct expressive reward features from the task description and observation space.
Strategically samples imagined trajectories in the feature space and learns feature weights from preferences over trajectory pairs.
Evaluated on pandemic regulation, insulin administration, and highway autonomous driving tasks.
EARS outperformed direct LLM reward-generation baselines in alignment with ground-truth or LLM-context rewards, using either ground-truth or LLM-labeled preferences.

papers.abstract: Robust point tracking in endoscopic videos is essential for computer-assisted intervention and autonomous robotic surgery, enabling continuous registration between intraoperative video and preoperative imaging despite soft tissue deformation. However, supervised tracking methods depend on large annotated datasets, while surgical conditions make reliable trajectory annotation challenging. We propose a self-supervised Track-Any-Point approach that learns from unlabeled surgical videos by establishing global pixel correspondences and inferring point trajectories through contrastive random walks. Trained without annotations, our method achieves performance comparable to existing semi-supervised approaches while implicitly handling tissue deformation. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of self-supervised point tracking in surgical environments and its potential to reduce reliance on annotated data.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of obtaining reliable trajectory annotations for endoscopic surgical videos.
Uses a self-supervised Track-Any-Point framework trained on unlabeled surgical videos.
Establishes global pixel correspondences and infers trajectories through contrastive random walks.
Implicitly handles soft-tissue deformation during tracking.
Achieves performance comparable to existing semi-supervised methods, according to the abstract.

papers.abstract: Generalizable bimanual robotic manipulation requires a reusable task prior that can persist across increasingly diverse tasks, objects, scenes, embodiments, and execution conditions, thus avoiding the prohibitive cost of large-scale teleoperated demonstrations and policy retraining. In this work, we present VLBiMan++, an extended framework that expands the generalization boundary of vision-language anchored one-shot bimanual manipulation. Starting from a single human demonstration, VLBiMan++ performs task-aware decomposition to identify reusable and adaptable skill components, and employs vision-language grounded geometric adaptation to transfer these skills to novel configurations without retraining. Building on this foundation, we systematically extend generalization along five dimensions: task generalization through diverse and long-horizon skill compositions; object generalization across unseen categories, varying geometries, and more complex articulated or deformable objects; scene generalization under clutter, occlusion, and dynamic interference; embodiment generalization across heterogeneous dual-arm robotic platforms; and deployment generalization through prolonged closed-loop execution under repeated external perturbations. To support this broader scope, we further introduce object-state-aware adaptation and lightweight trajectory optimization mechanisms that accommodate changes beyond simple rigid 6-DoF pose variations while preserving reliable bimanual coordination. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that VLBiMan++ maintains strong task success and adaptation capability across these increasingly challenging settings. Overall, VLBiMan++ advances one-shot bimanual manipulation from demonstrating isolated transferability toward a more systematic and scalable framework for generalization across tasks, objects, scenes, embodiments, and long-term deployment conditions.
bullets: Uses task-aware decomposition to separate reusable and adaptable skill components from a single human demonstration.
Applies vision-language-grounded geometric adaptation to transfer skills to novel configurations.
Extends generalization across long-horizon tasks, unseen and articulated/deformable objects, cluttered or dynamic scenes, heterogeneous dual-arm platforms, and long-term execution.
Adds object-state-aware adaptation and lightweight trajectory optimization beyond simple rigid 6-DoF pose changes.
Real-world experiments show strong task success and adaptation across increasingly challenging settings.
