papers.abstract: Biological swimmers and flyers exploit unsteady vortices for propulsion, whereas engineered vehicles usually suppress them as disturbances. Learning such flow exploitation in machines is difficult because real-fluid interaction data are scarce and unstructured exploration is unstable in high-dimensional, history-dependent flows. Here we present REEF, a co-designed physical-learning framework that integrates SHOAL, an eight-channel high-throughput array for real fluid--structure interaction, with V-STAR, a staged algorithm that converts these interactions into policies through imitation, offline internalization, and online adaptation. Across lift-based, drag-based, and momentum-jet propulsors, REEF expands the attainable force envelope to more than twice that of parameterized search. Particle image velocimetry shows that these gains arise from coordinated vortex formation, growth, and force projection, rather than refinement of a fixed motion-to-force mapping. Force-trained policies transfer zero-shot to free-moving robots whose body motion changes the surrounding flow, suggesting that REEF learns transferable wake-coupling principles for embodied propulsion in unsteady fluids.
bullets: Addresses scarce, unstructured fluid-interaction data and unstable exploration in history-dependent flows.
Integrates SHOAL, an eight-channel fluid–structure interaction platform, with V-STAR’s imitation, offline learning, and online adaptation stages.
Works across lift-based, drag-based, and momentum-jet propulsors, expanding the attainable force envelope to more than twice that of parameterized search.
Flow measurements link performance gains to coordinated vortex formation, growth, and force projection.
Force-trained policies transfer zero-shot to free-moving robots, indicating learned wake-coupling principles.

(B) Three representative propulsors, including a 3-DOF flapper, 2-DOF webbed foot, and 1-DOF caudal fin, span distinct locomotion modes and force-generation regimes. (D) SHOAL enables parallel real-flow learning with an eight-channel towing array, rapid flow reset, synchronized actuation, and real-time six-axis force sensing.

Compared with EMOA4, REEF policies coordinate LEV formation, growth, and force projection with wing orientation, producing expanded thrust–lift performance.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant. Video demonstrations are available on our project page.
authors: Shaoyuan Xie, Zihan Zhang, Jingxuan Wang, Jiashu Qu, Xiaoqing Liang, Lingdong Kong, Junchi Lu, Henrik I. Christensen, Qi Alfred Chen
bullets: Introduces a benchmark jointly evaluating navigation following, conflict awareness, and adversarial robustness.
Predicts three navigation-compliance modes to separate conflict reasoning from action generation.
Uses navigation-conditioned world-model rollouts that simulate strictly following instructions to assess their safety.
Achieves 88.16 Driving Score and 68.64% Success Rate on Bench2Drive.
Improves closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 versus the best SimLingo variant.

At inference, (1) the meta-command implied by the navigation signal selects an anchor; (2) the frozen world model rolls the current latent forward under it; (3) the world tokens (projected dreamed latents), the camera frame, and the navigation signal are fed to the VLA, which emits a mode token, the beginning-of-action token <ACTIONS>, and action tokens sequentially.

papers.abstract: Mobile Manipulation (MoMa) is a cornerstone of autonomous robotic systems, yet real-world fine-tuning remains a formidable challenge because of high-dimensional action spaces and intricate coupling between heterogeneous modules. In this paper, we propose HiRe-MoMa (Hierarchical Residual Mobile Manipulation), a systematic framework for stable and sample-efficient real-world fine-tuning of complex MoMa systems. At its core, HiRe-MoMa adopts a Hierarchical Residual Architecture that fine-tunes a frozen base policy. A Policy-Agnostic Residual learns additive corrections atop the base policy, while Hierarchical Decoupling splits the residual into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads with unidirectional conditioning, mitigating gradient interference and aligning corrections with the platform's physical hierarchy. To improve sample efficiency in data-expensive real-world settings, we propose Expert-Guided Value Alignment, which leverages sparse human interventions with under 20% training coverage to reshape the critic's value landscape, effectively guiding autonomous exploration through expert priors. Extensive real-world experiments on the TIAGo++ platform demonstrate that HiRe-MoMa consistently enhances task performance with only around 30 minutes of online interaction, regardless of the base policy architecture. To our knowledge, this is among the first frameworks to enable efficient on-robot fine-tuning for mobile manipulation in the real world, providing a practical paradigm for deploying complex robotic systems in dynamic, human-centric environments. Further details can be found on our project website: https://hire-moma.github.io/
authors: Zhefei Gong, Hefeifei Jiang, Zehao Wang, Jiachen Li
bullets: Targets the difficulty of fine-tuning high-dimensional, tightly coupled mobile-manipulation systems on real robots.
Fine-tunes a frozen base policy with additive residuals, separated into mobile-base and manipulator-arm heads with unidirectional conditioning.
Uses sparse human interventions covering under 20% of training to reshape value estimates and guide exploration.
Real-world experiments on TIAGo++ report improved task performance with about 30 minutes of online interaction across base-policy architectures.
Scope: demonstrated for dynamic, human-centric real-world mobile manipulation; specific task details and quantitative gains are not provided in the abstract.

figures.caption: Figure 2: HiRe-MoMa Framework enables policy-agnostic real-world fine-tuning of mobile manipulators through an asynchronous residual reinforcement learning paradigm. (Right) Shared-Control Rollout: an onboard rollout worker augments a frozen base policy with learnable residuals; sparse human interventions during critical or hazardous phases are stored in an expert buffer. (Left) Asynchronous Central Learner: the residual policy is optimized along two pillars: a) a Hierarchical Residual Architecture (Sec. 4.1) that decouples the residual into mobile and manipulator heads with unidirectional conditioning, embedding the platform’s physical hierarchy directly into the policy; and b) an Expert-Guided Value Alignment loss (Sec. 4.2) that fuses sparse environment rewards with sparse human corrections to reshape the critic toward expert-preferred behaviors.

Figure 4: Training Dynamics. Comparison across methods over training time, where we construct the figure along the actual training time. (a) Success rate: HiRe-MoMa(full) attains a consistently higher success rate throughout training, validating the effectiveness of our design combining hierarchical residual architecture and alignment. (b) Human intervention steps: HiRe-MoMa requires fewer human interventions and converges faster than the baselines, and the comparison with and without alignment (+Hierarchical Decoupling) demonstrates the effectiveness of the extra alignment loss.

Figure 1: HiRe-MoMa System Overview. (a) Training Paradigm: A real-world dual-unit configuration consisting of an onboard controller for real-time interaction and a computing unit for policy optimization and action prediction. (b) Coordinated Execution: The red dashed lines illustrate the stringent spatiotemporal precision required for base-arm synchronization. In mobile manipulation, marginal tracking deviations are often magnified by kinematic coupling, causing even routine grasping maneuvers to fail.

Figure 7: Training-Step Progression vs. Wall-Clock Time. HG-DAgger advances through training steps faster than the SAC-based residual methods, but its higher step throughput does not translate into higher success rates (Fig. 4(a)). HiRe-MoMa adds only a modest per-step overhead over +Flat Residual (1–2×) while delivering clear gains in success rate and episode length.

Figure 3: Real-World Experimental Tasks. Our evaluation encompasses three tasks, Place Only, Sweep Litter, and Pick Place, that demand varying levels of inter-module coordination. These tasks are particularly challenging for mobile manipulators as they require the simultaneous optimization of base positioning and arm reaching, where minor misalignments in the platform’s pose propagate as significant errors at the end-effector.

Figure 6: Residual Correction Visualization. Base longitudinal velocity and manipulator vertical position throughout the Place Only task. HiRe-MoMa applies coherent corrections at critical trajectory phases, most notably during base acceleration and the manipulator’s lay-down motion.

Figure 5: Disentangling Decomposition and Conditioning. Training-time success-rate curves for +Flat Residual, +DecompositionOnly, and +Hierarchical Decoupling on Place Only and Sweep Litter; see App. A.1.

Table 3: Policy-Agnostic Generalization. Our HiRe-MoMa yields consistent gains when applied to ACT [47], demonstrating architecture-independent efficacy. While the performance ceiling is inherently tied to the base policy’s quality, the results confirm HiRe-MoMa’s capacity to fine-tune diverse base policies.

Table 4: Decomposition vs. Conditioning within Hierarchical Decoupling. Decomposition alone provides the dominant gain by mitigating gradient interference (+30 pt average success rate). Conditioning adds a targeted improvement (+5 pt on average) that manifests on the coupled dual-arm task (Sweep Litter).

papers.abstract: Recent advances in robot learning have driven rapid progress in humanoid control, enabling increasingly agile behaviors in the real world. However, humanoid control networks are typically obtained through conventional training procedures, while comparatively little attention has been given to directly modeling the distribution of their learned weights and generating functional networks in weight space. In this work, we investigate whether high-performing humanoid control networks can be generatively modeled directly through their weights. We adopt a latent diffusion framework that couples a linear autoencoder with a Diffusion Transformer. The autoencoder compresses actor network parameters into a compact latent space, and the Diffusion Transformer models the distribution of these latents. Trained on networks collected from reinforcement learning for the Unitree G1 robot, our approach generates deployable networks that perform various motions in the real world, including walking, dancing, and spin kick. Beyond generation, we further study the learned weight space to better understand the structure captured by these humanoid control networks. We identify a structural principle in the first-layer weights that consistently reflects the robot's kinematic prior. Notably, this kinematic prior emerges under both Reinforcement Learning (RL) and Imitation Learning (IL) training, suggesting that it is not specific to a particular optimization process but may instead reflect common knowledge associated with humanoid embodiment. Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of generative modeling in humanoid network weight space, while providing initial insights into the information encoded by their learned weights. Additional results are available on our project website: https://humanoid-weight-diffusion.github.io/
authors: Huixuan Cheng, Bike Zhang, Shankar Sastry, Koushil Sreenath
bullets: Targets direct generation and analysis of learned humanoid-control network weights, rather than conventional policy training alone.
Uses a linear autoencoder to compress actor parameters and a Diffusion Transformer to model their latent distribution.
Trained on reinforcement-learning policies for the Unitree G1, it generates real-world networks performing walking, dancing, and spin-kick motions.
Finds a consistent kinematic-prior structure in first-layer weights under both reinforcement and imitation learning.
Scope: results focus on Unitree G1 policies and initial understanding of the learned weight space.

(c) A diffusion transformer is trained with x-pred loss to model the latent distribution. During inference, the model generates novel network weights that can be deployed in the real world.

papers.tldr: A latent diffusion model can generate deployable humanoid control policies directly in neural-weight space while revealing weight structures tied to robot kinematics.

papers.abstract: World-action models aim to turn visual anticipation into driving decisions, yet typically train action experts on trajectory representations defined independently of visual dynamics. This motivates deriving action targets directly from visual motion. We first examine a simpler setting in which trajectories are reconstructed from recorded future images. Even without the need for future prediction, reconstruction captures the dominant maneuver but leaves centimeter-scale errors. We therefore introduce VITAL (Vision-Induced Tokens for Action Learning), an action tokenizer that couples a visually derived motion scaffold with a compact residual encoding the trajectory error left by that scaffold. This representation makes visual motion the principal prediction target and gives small metric corrections a separate, normalized learning scale. Using flow matching, the action expert jointly predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command, without generating future images at inference. The same residual coordinates support bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the predicted visual scaffold fixed. With only one action denoising step, VITAL achieves 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 navtest, within 0.13 points of its ten-step score at 3.29x the end-to-end inference speed. Without retraining, it achieves 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 navtest and 38.6 on navhard. Project page: https://worldbench.github.io/vital
authors: Ao Liang, Youquan Liu, Mingxiao Li, Wei Chow, Lingdong Kong, Yue Liao, Dongyue Lu, Yu Yang, Wei Yin, Runnan Chen
bullets: Addresses trajectory errors caused by action representations that are disconnected from visual dynamics.
Uses a visually derived motion scaffold plus a compact residual encoding for centimeter-scale corrections.
A flow-matching action expert predicts both components from the current image, ego state, and navigation command.
Supports bounded reinforcement post-training that refines execution while keeping the visual scaffold fixed.
Reaches 90.8 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 with one denoising step, near its ten-step score at 3.29× higher end-to-end speed; also reports 91.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2 and 38.6 on navhard.

papers.title: VITAL: From Visual Motion to Precise Action
papers.tldr: VITAL derives action representations from visual motion and adds normalized residual corrections, enabling fast, precise driving decisions without predicting future images.

papers.abstract: Unlike singles, humanoid table tennis doubles requires teammates to strike in strict alternation while sharing a confined workspace. Rapid repositioning can compromise striking accuracy, while uncoordinated teammate movements introduce collision risks. We present PingpongDuo, a hierarchical framework for agile humanoid doubles with safe team coordination. At the team level, a planner jointly selects positioning targets and uses learned risk estimates to filter risky proposals, preferentially preserving the current striker's target. At the individual level, separate footwork and striking skills combine agile movement with precise racket control. The skills are guided by human motion references, including footwork collected from human doubles play, and trained from states produced by one another to support rapid transitions. A racket-arm residual further refines strikes after movement using return feedback from a simulator calibrated with real ball-flight and contact measurements. In simulation, PingpongDuo improves the ball-return success rate by 13.2% over the state-of-the-art baseline, while achieving approximately 2 cm positioning error during clearance. In real-world experiments, a robot completes a 2.15 m clearance-and-recovery cycle in 2.4 s with a peak speed of 2.23 m/s, while two robots sustain more than 10 consecutive strikes in strict alternation.
authors: Haoran Jiang, Yichao Zhong, Kai Zhang, Cheng Liu, Yixuan Pan, Zhenjie Yang, Jingbo Wang, Tianyu Li, Li Chen
bullets: Addresses strict strike alternation, confined-space navigation, accuracy loss during repositioning, and collision risk between teammates.
A team-level planner jointly selects positions and filters risky actions, prioritizing the current striker’s target.
Individual footwork and striking skills use human-motion references and mutually generated training states for rapid transitions.
A simulator-calibrated racket-arm residual refines strikes using ball-flight and contact feedback.
Simulation improves ball-return success by 13.2% over the baseline; real robots achieve 2 cm clearance positioning, 2.4 s recovery cycles, and over 10 alternating strikes.

papers.abstract: 3D object composition is pivotal to digital content creation and robot simulation, while also serving as a critical testbed for physical intelligence in foundation models. Previous methods either leverage large language models to directly predict object coordinates, or utilize generative diffusion priors to synthesize composite images for visual alignment, both of which rely on static priors in digital spaces. However, these methods consistently struggle with complex compositions such as precise hanging, gravity-driven settling and hidden containment, as these tasks require interactive construction processes involving global planning, fine-grained alignment, and physical simulation. To address these challenges, we propose PhySGA, a Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for 3D composition via agent exploration and physical simulation, enabling the universal interactive assembly of rigid, articulated, and deformable objects. Directly applying vanilla LLMs or VLMs to this task proves insufficient, as current models inherently lack grounded physical understanding and interactive construction experience. To overcome this limitation, we design a collaborative feedforward-feedback architecture: an Assembly Agent focuses on geometric and kinematic reasoning for global step planning and coarse adjustment, while a Critic Agent reasons over contact dynamics for simulator state diagnosis and fine-grained closed-loop correction. Furthermore, Action Routers map semantic planning and analysis onto executable physical primitives within the simulator, while a task-specific Self-Evolving Skill Library distills historical trial-and-error feedback into reusable experiences, boosting success rates and minimizing exploration attempts. Extensive experiments within Isaac Sim demonstrate that PhySGA significantly surpasses existing methods in relation fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality.
authors: Weichen Lyu, Chong Xia, Mingyu Dong, Long Xu, Shengjun Zhang, Yueqi Duan
bullets: Targets difficult compositions such as hanging, gravity-driven settling, and hidden containment that static coordinate or image-generation approaches often mishandle.
Combines an Assembly Agent for geometric and kinematic planning with a Critic Agent for contact-dynamics diagnosis and closed-loop correction.
Uses Action Routers to convert semantic plans into executable simulator primitives.
Builds a self-evolving skill library from trial-and-error feedback to improve success and reduce exploration.
Experiments in Isaac Sim show improved relation fidelity, physical plausibility, and visual quality over existing methods.

papers.title: PhySGA: A Physics-Space Grounded Agentic Framework for Generalizable and Interactive 3D Composition

papers.abstract: We present KinoGen, a framework that synthesizes customizable humanoid loco-manipulation references through kinematically grounded video generation. KinoGen conditions a pretrained video generator on calibrated renders of the target robot and object in a simulated task instance and recovers the reference by fitting the same models to the generated two-view video, so that the reference lies in the robot configuration space by construction without a human body proxy or retargeting. Body, hand, and object priors initialize the reconstruction, and direct optimization against cross-view evidence refines it. Since an edited keyframe is simply another rendered state, a user can prescribe a goal object pose, regenerate the video around the edited keyframe, and obtain a reference that satisfies the pose exactly. Across eight loco-manipulation tasks, KinoGen yields lower penetration and foot skating than video-based baselines and preserves over 90% of annotated contacts, and its customized references satisfy every prescribed target with substantially less penetration than direct interpolation. Tracking policies trained on the synthesized references are deployed on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands. Project webpage: https://kinogen-humanoid.github.io/.
authors: Qi Wu, Lulu Zhao, Sanghyun Hahn, Rishi Yennu, Emmy Yang, Dingqi Zhang, Tao Pang, Jiuguang Wang, Kuan Fang
bullets: Conditions a pretrained video generator on simulated renders of the target robot, object, and task.
Reconstructs robot and object motion by fitting the same models to generated video, avoiding human-body proxies and retargeting.
Supports exact goal-pose customization by editing a keyframe and regenerating the surrounding video.
Across eight tasks, reduces penetration and foot skating versus video-based baselines while preserving over 90% of annotated contacts.
References satisfy prescribed object poses and support deployment of tracking policies on a Unitree G1 humanoid with dexterous hands.

papers.abstract: Human listeners can often identify the intended object several words before an instruction ends. Robots, however, are typically designed to wait until the speaker has finished before deciding how to act. We present EarlyCommit, an open-source tool that lets a robot commit to the intended object while the instruction is being spoken. After every recognized word, a fine-tuned text encoder scores each object in the scene. The robot acts when the calibrated probability of the best object reaches a threshold tau set by the user, so 1 - tau is the accepted risk of choosing the wrong object. Otherwise, it waits or asks. The tool includes a streaming speech front end, a scene and instruction generator with exact word-by-word ground truth, and scripts to train, calibrate, and evaluate. On instructions containing words never seen in training, EarlyCommit commits correctly 1.6 to 2 times as often as keyword matching, is right at least 92 percent of the time when it commits at tau = 0.9, and needs 31 to 35 ms per word on consumer GPUs.
bullets: Addresses robots’ tendency to wait for complete instructions before acting.
Uses a fine-tuned text encoder to score scene objects word by word and commits when the best calibrated probability reaches a user-set threshold.
Supports waiting or asking when confidence is insufficient, with 1 − τ representing accepted error risk.
On instructions with unseen words, it commits correctly 1.6–2× as often as keyword matching and is at least 92% correct at τ = 0.9.
Runs in 31–35 ms per word on consumer GPUs and includes streaming, data-generation, training, calibration, and evaluation tools.

Three word pools with no shared words supply unseen language: the train pool for augmentation, the calibration pool for fitting the temperature and the test pool for evaluation. Right: the loop that runs after every recognised word. The judge scores each scene object, the probabilities are calibrated, and the robot commits, waits for the next word or asks which object is meant. The evaluation feeds generated words to the judge directly, without speech recognition.

papers.title: EarlyCommit: Calibrated Word-by-Word Commitment for Robots Acting Before You Finish Speaking
papers.tldr: EarlyCommit enables robots to choose the intended object before a spoken instruction ends by making calibrated, risk-controlled decisions after each word.

papers.abstract: Existing robot policy memories typically evolve with observation sequences, implicitly treating each update as the same amount of physical time. Yet identical observation histories can span different durations and require different actions, exposing physical time as a missing dimension of policy memory. We introduce Temporal Flow Policy (TFP), which learns memory dynamics to retain past events and evolve the memory state over measured time intervals. Observations and prior memory determine the content and time scales of each transition; elapsed time determines how far the state advances. TFP conditions diffusion and flow-matching policies through this memory state and is trained with their native imitation objectives. We evaluate TFP with Diffusion Policy and $\pi_{0.5}$ through controlled comparisons of memory designs. These experiments show that successful timing depends on both measured intervals and retained history. TFP achieves higher average success than the recurrent and state-space memories we equip with the same intervals and than a variant that feeds the interval to a learned gate. Memory readouts recover the time since an event and motion information after occlusion. Changing the supplied intervals systematically delays or advances actions, linking time inputs to behavior. Real-robot tasks requiring timing or memory, together with LIBERO evaluations, demonstrate benefits in physical and general manipulation. These results suggest viewing robot memory not as stored observation history, but as a state that retains past events and evolves with physical time.
authors: Yushen Liang, Yue Peng, Baosheng Jin, Tianluo Zhang, Xinyu Zhang, Shuyi Zhou, Zhuoran Chen, Xinqi Liu, Shenji Wan
bullets: Problem: Standard robot memories treat each update as equal time, so identical observations over different durations can produce inappropriate actions.

Method: TFP learns memory dynamics where observations and prior memory determine transitions, while measured elapsed intervals control state evolution; it conditions diffusion and flow-matching policies.
Results: Controlled comparisons with Diffusion Policy and π₀.₅ show higher average success than matched recurrent, state-space, and interval-gated memories.
Evidence: Memory readouts recover event timing and motion after occlusion, while changing supplied intervals systematically delays or advances actions.
Scope: Real-robot timing and memory tasks plus LIBERO evaluations indicate benefits for physical and general manipulation.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces physical time into robot policy memory, directly relevant to embodied memory and policy learning.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon precise manipulation produces mixed-quality data for post-training vision-language-action (VLA) models: even successful demonstrations and intervention-assisted rollouts may contain detours, hesitations, failed attempts, and imperfect recoveries. The key challenge is to identify which action chunks actually advance the task, rather than uniformly cloning or discarding imperfect trajectories. We propose Graph-Reweighted Behavior Cloning (GR-BC), an offline iterative post-training framework that builds a task-conditioned goal-reachability graph over demonstrations and iteratively collected rollouts, including both successful and failed episodes with human interventions. Reverse graph search computes minimal remaining steps to task success within the dataset support, and each action chunk is weighted by how much its execution reduces this potential. This consequence-based weighting reuses recoverable segments from failed trajectories, leverages interventions as recovery paths, and down-weights locally regressive chunks even inside successful trajectories. New rollouts are incorporated by appending them to the graph and rerunning search, without training a reward model, action-conditioned critic, or progress predictor. Across four precise manipulation tasks and three VLA backbones, GR-BC improves single-round supervised fine-tuning and reaches 91% success after a few offline iterations, without trajectory comparisons or progress labels. More details and videos are available at: https://gr-bc.github.io
authors: Xiaoman Li, Zhiqiang Yang, Jiayu Hu, Jipeng Kong, Yang Zhang, Jingwei Zhang, Fangzheng Yan, Chunhua Shen, Chenjia Bai
bullets: Addresses mixed-quality long-horizon demonstrations containing detours, failures, hesitations, and imperfect recoveries.
Builds a task-conditioned goal-reachability graph over successful and failed intervention-assisted rollouts.
Uses reverse graph search to estimate minimal remaining steps and reweight chunks by their reduction in this potential.
Reuses recoverable segments and intervention paths without reward models, critics, progress predictors, trajectory comparisons, or progress labels.
Evaluated on four manipulation tasks and three VLA backbones, reaching 91% success after a few offline iterations.

papers.abstract: In reinforcement learning, an agent must explore an unknown environment to learn how to make good decisions. Unlike methods that can freely sample any state--action pair, an agent learning from a single trajectory must spend additional time navigating between states. It is therefore natural to expect that learning from a single trajectory requires more experience. In this paper, we show that this additional cost is not always necessary. For average-reward reinforcement learning, we develop an algorithm that learns where to collect information while ensuring that the required samples can be obtained efficiently. We establish an upper bound on the number of interactions needed to identify a near-optimal policy. Furthermore, we prove a matching information theoretic lower bound, showing that, for a broad class of environments and at sufficiently high accuracy, learning from a single trajectory is no harder in the worst case than learning with unrestricted access to state action samples. Our results reveal that the additional complexity cost of navigation can be avoided by adapting information gathering requirements to how the environment provides information.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action models (VLAs) often fail midway through unseen long-horizon tasks. Recursive self-improvement (RSI) offers a remedy, but embodied RSI methods either refine the harness around a frozen executor and so cannot add a missing motion, or train the executor on persistent failures without asking whether a failure lies in how the executor is called or in what it can do. We ask when a self-improving embodied system should change the weights of its executor, and propose AdaRSI, an on-demand RSI framework for embodied agents. A coding agent first improves its skills and harness, then attributes persistent failures by retrying failing sub-steps from saved states, and fine-tunes only the sub-steps that remain unreliable, with demonstrations it collects itself and experience carried over from earlier tasks. On all 50 target tasks of RoboCasa365, with GR00T N1.5 as the executor and no human demonstrations, AdaRSI improves the VLA on all three suites and raises its success on unseen composite tasks from 4.6% to 13.8%. Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, it reaches slightly higher success while using only 28% of the GPU time and 22% of the self-collected demonstrations, and fine-tuning without a harness trains more yet gains far less.

Fine-tunes only unreliable executor sub-steps using self-collected demonstrations and experience reused across tasks.
On 50 RoboCasa365 target tasks, success on unseen composite tasks increases from 4.6% to 13.8% without human demonstrations.
Compared with fine-tuning every sub-step, uses 28% of GPU time and 22% of self-collected demonstrations while achieving slightly higher success.

papers.abstract: Value-based Q-learning for continuous control can discretise the action space, but the resolution of the discretisation trades early exploration against final precision. Growing Q-Networks (GQN) grow the resolution uniformly from coarse to fine. We introduce Selective Growing Q-Networks (SGQN), which keeps decoupled Q-learning and replaces uniform growth with an adaptive action grid: bins are added next to bins with high estimated Q-value, bins with low Q-value are pruned, and actions are chosen epsilon-greedily. On eight DeepMind Control Suite (DMControl) tasks with 2 to 12 action dimensions, SGQN has the highest mean final return among the compared methods on four, is within 1.1% of the best method on three more, and is 3.4% below Bang-Bang MPO on Walker Run, using on average 7.5 of 9 available bins per dimension. We then test whether the adaptive grid explains these results, and find that it does not. Growth activates every candidate bin and behaves like uniform growth, and removing pruning changes the return by at most 1.1%. Two other choices matter: starting from a coarse grid, since starting with all 9 bins produces collapsed seeds, and epsilon-greedy selection, since an annealed softmax lowers the return by 23% to 100%. SGQN is insensitive to its growth and pruning hyperparameters. It also differs from the GQN and DecQN baselines in other respects, notably one gradient update per environment step instead of one per eight, which we did not control for, so we do not attribute its advantage to a single component. We present SGQN as a competitive value-based method and as an analysis of which ingredients of a growing action grid matter.
authors: Parham Nooranbakht, Seyed Mahdi Basiri Azad, Joschka B\"odecker
bullets: Uses an adaptive action grid: high-value regions gain bins, while low-value bins are pruned.

Analysis finds growth effectively activates all candidate bins, resembling uniform growth, while pruning has little impact.
Coarse initialization is important; starting with all bins causes collapsed seeds, and annealed softmax selection sharply reduces return.
Results may also reflect an uncontrolled difference in update frequency versus baselines.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are driving a paradigm shift in robotic intelligence, moving beyond low-level action prediction to goal-directed orchestration of data collection, model training, task planning, and real-world execution. We characterize this emerging paradigm as an agentic robots, in which agents reason over human instructions, interact with robotic environments, rectify execution errors autonomously, and dynamically adjust operational strategies. Although this field develops fast, current studies are not well connected. Researchers have no consistent view of how to combine different agentic functions into a complete robot system. This paper provides a unified overview of existing research on agentic robots. We first trace the development from robot policies to agentic systems, covering vision-language-action models, world models, and world-action models. We then clarify the definition and scope of agentic robots and organize existing research into seventeen categories across four functional domains: Model, Data, Environment, and Harness. Across these domains, we examine how agents shape model learning and robot decisions, collect and curate robot data, construct worlds, tasks, and tests for learning and evaluation, and organize capabilities for robot use. Finally, we discuss open challenges and outline directions for future research. Looking forward, we hope this work contributes to a clearer understanding of agentic robots and supports new approaches to making them more capable, reliable, and adaptive.
authors: Chonghan Qin, Dongming Wu, Kaituo Feng, Jiaxu Wang, Xinlei Yu, Peiwen Sun, Yijia Fan, Xilin He, Bingao Chen, Weitong Lian, Ryan Ji, Wenqi Ren, Xiaobin Hu, Dahua Lin, Yu-Gang Jiang, Xiangyu Yue

papers.abstract: Though modern AI models like LLMs predict discrete tokens, today's robotic foundation models represent actions as continuous vectors. In this paper, we challenge this common consensus by asking if continuous action parametrizations are superior to their discrete counterparts. We conduct an extensive comparison of single-step regression and multi-step flow variants of both continuous and discrete policies in both from-scratch single-task and multi-task VLA training, in both simulation and on real hardware. In all regimes, we find that discrete action prediction, even the most naive, uniform-bin quantization, can match or even outperform continuous-action policies in task success rate. Moreover, we find that the challenge to discrete action policies is \emph{not} action precision, but rather factorization error introduced by product-distribution predictions across time and action dimensions. We show that, when paired with the correct interventions---iterative computation through discrete flows, or distribution sharpening through classifier-free guidance---discrete flow policies can turn this weakness into a strength, enabling more responsive action changes during a predicted action chunk. Lastly, we show that attempts to explicitly inject geometric information into discrete policies, e.g. through corruption processes that emulate continuous flow matching, do \emph{not} yield consistent improvements. Taken together, our findings question existing assumptions that robotic action prediction requires distinct design decisions compared to other AI domains, and motivates the possibility of discrete action prediction as a compelling alternative to today's continuous action parametrizations. Link for the webpage \href{https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/}{https://iscoyizj.github.io/discrete-action-website/}
authors: Zeji Yi, Soham Dasgupta, Xinyang Zhang, Koushil Sreenath, Guannan Qu, Xi Chen, Max Simchowitz, Guanya Shi

papers.abstract: We develop a self-supervised reinforcement learning algorithm that learns to build towers of up to eight cubes from scratch, without prior data, rewards, demonstrations, or pretrained models. Our method, Contrastive Planning via Spherical Linear Interpolation (C-Slerp), uses contrastive representations as reusable building blocks and repeatedly composes them to infer a sequence of intermediate waypoints. Under our hyperspherical parameterization, the learned representations allow intermediate waypoints to be inferred in closed form through spherical linear interpolation, without training a separate high-level policy or performing graph search. Importantly, the representation geometry also tells us how to adjust the number of waypoints based on the difficulty of each goal-reaching problem. Experiments show that our method succeeds on long-horizon navigation and robotic manipulation tasks, including settings where strong baselines fail to achieve a single success. Ablations further show that using a fixed number of waypoints substantially degrades performance, highlighting the importance of adapting the plan to task difficulty.

Adapts the number of waypoints to goal difficulty based on representation geometry.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations are today used largely for pretraining vision-language-action models, with little ability to use the same data for target-embodiment or task-oriented training, which scalable deployment of robots in industrial and general environments depends on. A human demonstration recorded on a simple and scalable device such as a mobile phone can serve as post-training data for a robot whose body differs in structure and capability from the human who recorded it. This is made possible not by retargeting the hand's motion but the object's. A capture yields a body-free record: the object's pose over time, its contact intervals, and a reconstructed 3D object with provenance. Any robot, given as a URDF and a short descriptor, is solved against that record and scored in simulation against the demonstrated object motion as ground truth: the human-to-simulation leg of human-to-simulation-to-robot transfer, measured per robot. Each (robot, episode) pair gets one outcome: pass, failure with a named mode, or refusal, with its reason, before any motion. The method runs as a working system over a growing collection; the set analysed here is a sample of it: 42 captures solved on 8 robots, 157 pairs, of which 31.2% pass, 52.2% fail, 14.0% are refused and 2.5% are unauditable (kinematic feasibility, +/-50 mm / +/-15 deg, in simulation). Refusals held up: every pair the checks refuse on stored evidence yet ran anyway failed (13 of 13; 5 on a body whose public model welds its hand). A description file could not be shown to screen a robot: its outcomes were barely more predictable than guessing. No policy has yet been trained on the record. The record decides what a robot may post-train on; whether the policy then works on the real robot is the simulation-to-robot question, answered downstream.
bullets: Phone-recorded demonstrations capture object poses, contact intervals, and reconstructed 3D objects without tying data to a human body.
Each robot, specified by a URDF and brief descriptor, is evaluated in simulation against the demonstrated object motion before any policy execution.
For 157 robot–episode pairs across 42 captures and 8 robots, 31.2% passed, 52.2% failed, 14.0% were refused, and 2.5% were unauditable.
Refusal checks were reliable: all 13 pairs that ran despite being refused failed.
The study assesses data eligibility for robot post-training; it does not yet train policies or establish real-robot performance.

papers.abstract: We study the finite-sample convergence of Q-learning algorithms for the average-reward formulation of Reinforcement Learning (RL) with options. While options allow temporarily extended and hierarchical actions, the average-reward formulation incorporates continual tasks beyond discounted and episodic RL. We establish the first $\tilde{O}(1/\text{iterations})$ convergence guarantees, in the mean-square sense, for average-reward option Q-learning algorithms in both the inter- and intra-option settings. First, we prove that both inter- and intra-option Bellman operators satisfy multi-step span contractions under unichain assumptions. Then, we propose synchronous estimators of these multi-step option Bellman operators leading to two variants of option Q-learning. Finally, we extend the stochastic approximation framework to prove convergence rates of these two algorithms under the minimal assumptions used in the literature.
authors: Kintan Saha, Ahana Deb, Anders Jonsson, Debabrota Basu
bullets: Addresses continual-task RL with average rewards and temporally extended, hierarchical actions.
Shows that both inter- and intra-option Bellman operators satisfy multi-step span contractions under unichain assumptions.
Introduces synchronous estimators of these operators, yielding two option Q-learning variants.
Proves the first \tilde{O}(1/iterations) mean-square convergence rates for these algorithms.
The guarantees rely on minimal assumptions commonly used in prior work.

papers.abstract: Scaling embodied robot learning requires large and diverse manipulation datasets, but collecting real-world demonstrations remains expensive in human effort and robot time. Simulation provides a scalable alternative, yet converting a real workspace into a robot-learning-ready environment still requires substantial manual effort for object extraction, asset processing, coordinate calibration, and trajectory specification. We present AutoRSR, a highly automated real-to-sim-to real framework that converts scanned real-world workspaces into reusable embodied simulation assets and scalable manipulation data. Given multi-view observations, robot states, and open-vocabulary semantic queries, AutoRSR reconstructs the workspace, extracts individual object assets, and automatically registers the reconstructed scene to the robot base frame at metric scale. Starting from a small number of reference motions, AutoRSR then generates executable manipulation trajectories and scales them through trajectory interpolation and domain randomization. After workspace scanning and semantic queries, the remaining pipeline requires no manual object annotation, scene-to-robot calibration, or robot teleoperation. Across three real-world manipulation tasks, policies trained on 1K automatically generated episodes per task achieve 73.3--86.7% real-world success rates, comparable to pi 0.5 trained from 150 human teleoperated demonstrations, while reducing the human time required for data generation by an order of magnitude. These results demonstrate that real-world observations can be converted into metrically aligned, executable, and scalable simulation data with substantially reduced human effort.
authors: Jiawei Zhang, Chang Liu, Litao Deng, Tao Zhang, Qin Jin
bullets: Addresses the cost and labor of collecting real-world manipulation demonstrations and manually building simulation environments.
Reconstructs workspaces, extracts object assets, aligns scenes to the robot base at metric scale, and uses semantic queries to automate setup.
Generates and scales manipulation trajectories through interpolation and domain randomization from a small number of reference motions.
Across three tasks, 1K automatically generated episodes achieved 73.3–86.7% real-world success rates, comparable to a policy trained from 150 teleoperated demonstrations.
The reported scope covers three real-world manipulation tasks and depends on workspace scans, semantic queries, and reference motions.

papers.abstract: Controlling an agent in an environment solely perceived through onboard vision is challenging: perception yields noisy, variable-length, and partially occluded context, while onboard compute is shared between perception and control, limiting the planning horizon executable in real time. We propose VIGOR-MPC, a modular student-teacher framework, agnostic to the perception pipeline, which addresses reference tracking across navigation tasks by distilling a privileged, field-of-view-aware long-horizon MPC into a computationally lightweight short-horizon MPC whose cost parameters are determined online from vision. The teacher operates in simulation with full state knowledge and a multi-trajectory formulation that guarantees the agent can stay within its field of view. The student observes only the noisy, occluded context produced by a perception module and learns, via a multi-level recurrent mapping, to infer cost parameters that aim to recover the teacher's behavior despite missing information. We evaluate VIGOR-MPC on vision-based autonomous racing in simulation and on hardware. Using only onboard perception of the track, VIGOR-MPC generalizes to tracks unseen during training and approaches the lap times of the privileged long-horizon teacher while reducing per-step computation by over 90%.

papers.abstract: Large-scale robot learning increasingly relies on diverse human demonstrations, yet tactile manipulation data remain difficult to scale, and existing multimodal datasets often lack consistent quality control and structured supervision. We present TacClaw-Infinity, a large-scale structured Vision-Tactile-Language-Action (VTLA) dataset for contact-rich manipulation, collected with TacClaw, a tactile-enabled UMI-style handheld interface that records synchronized visual observations, fingertip tactile signals, and end-effector trajectories without requiring a target robot during data collection. TacClaw-Infinity is built through a distributed worldwide collection across homes, laboratories, industrial workplaces, retail stores, and outdoor environments including tasks contributed by academic and industrial collaborators. Together, these efforts yield over 10,000 hours, 1 million episodes, and 1 billion frames spanning more than 1,000 task types. We develop a scalable pipeline for trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and structured annotation, covering contact-centric segmentation, subtask description, and spatial grounding. We validate TacClaw-Infinity at both the data and model levels: At the data level, we assess the collection interface, the action-space compatibility of the curated demonstrations, and the structured annotations, while for the model level, we demonstrate cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.

Uses TacClaw, a tactile-enabled handheld interface that synchronously records vision, fingertip touch, and end-effector trajectories without a target robot.

Provides trajectory reconstruction, multimodal quality control, embodiment-aware filtering, and annotations for contact segmentation, subtasks, and spatial grounding.
Demonstrates cross-embodiment transfer across three heterogeneous robots without robot-specific demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement-learning policies for robot locomotion can fail at deployment when operating conditions shift (e.g., rough or slippery terrain, payload changes, sensing degradation), and retraining or manual recalibration is often infeasible under on-device latency and memory constraints. We study test-time adaptation (TTA) for robotic control: adapting a pretrained policy online and in a self-supervised manner during execution, without access to rewards. Our starting point is a lightweight baseline that updates only the actor using a frozen pretrained critic as a deployment-time performance surrogate. Building on this, we introduce TEMPO, a test-time entropy-regularized, memory-guided policy optimization method that stabilizes critic-driven updates under severe shift. TEMPO combines (i) an entropy-promoting regularizer on the critic's predictive distribution to mitigate overconfident extrapolation, and (ii) a score-based memory, inspired by prioritized replay, that prioritizes low-value ("hard") observations and applies importance sampling to focus limited computation on the most informative deployment conditions. Across Go1, Go2, and G1 in MuJoCo Playground under four representative shifts and multiple architectures, TEMPO yields consistent gains, reaching up to 80% improvement in a single-device setting. We further validate on a physical Unitree Go2 with an added calf payload, where fully on-device adaptation improves performance over the non-adapted baseline across real-world episodes.
authors: Motasem Alfarra, Pietro Mazzaglia, Markus Peschl, Daniel Dijkman, Christos Louizos
bullets: Addresses failures from terrain, payload, and sensing shifts when retraining or manual recalibration is impractical.
Adapts only the actor online using a frozen critic as a deployment-time performance surrogate.
TEMPO regularizes the critic’s predictive distribution to reduce overconfident extrapolation.
A score-based memory prioritizes hard, low-value observations and uses importance sampling under limited compute.
Improves performance across simulated robots and shifts, with gains up to 80%, and transfers to a physical Go2 with added payload.

papers.abstract: Despite the Markov assumption, safety failures in robot reinforcement learning rarely occur instantaneously; they typically emerge over several steps as the policy enters unfamiliar states under disturbances and domain shift. We address this limitation by learning a receding-horizon safety critic that predicts whether a state will remain non-terminating over the next receding horizon, enabling anticipatory detection of impending locomotion failures. The critic is trained from rollout-derived horizon labels with a composite objective that combines horizon classification, control-barrier-function-inspired temporal consistency, and smoothness regularization, and we aggregate an ensemble of critics with a conservative Conditional Value at Risk estimate to account for uncertainty. Building on the learned critic, we derive a closed-form, differentiable CBF-style safety filter that minimally modifies the policy action to improve predicted safety, and integrate it into PPO with an anticipation loss to reduce policy-filter mismatch during training. In simulated quadruped locomotion, our method improves robustness under action noise, external perturbations, and terrain shifts, reducing catastrophic failures while maintaining competitive returns.
authors: Siwei Ju, Jan Peters, Oleg Arenz
bullets: Targets safety failures that develop over multiple steps rather than occurring instantaneously.
Learns an ensemble safety critic using horizon labels, temporal-consistency constraints, and smoothness regularization.
Uses conservative uncertainty aggregation and a closed-form differentiable CBF-style filter to minimally adjust actions.
Integrates the shield with PPO through an anticipation loss to reduce policy–filter mismatch.
In simulated quadruped locomotion, improves robustness and reduces catastrophic failures while maintaining competitive returns.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Overview of the training pipeline. Rollouts are collected in simulation under domain randomization and disturbances, and states are labeled by horizon-H safety to populate separate safe/unsafe buffers (with discounted weighting for delayed violations). A predictive safety critic is trained with a composite objective (labeling, temporal consistency, and smoothness), and an ensemble is aggregated via CVaR to obtain a conservative safety estimate and uncertainty σt. At each step, a differentiable closed-form safety layer projects the raw policy action to a minimally modified safe action, which is used both during PPO training (with an anticipation loss to reduce interventions) and at deployment for safety-shielded control.

Fig. 2: Top row: success rate; bottom row: average return. Columns correspond to four evaluation suites (action-noise and external-perturbation, each on flat terrain and heightfield terrain). Curves show mean performance over independent runs for PPO-RL, PPO-RL-NCBF, and our method, with shaded bands indicating standard error across different seeds. The x-axis denotes the perturbation/noise sampling probability.

Fig. 8: Comparison of SafeFall and our method in Safe RL training using each as a safety critic. The plot compares success rate (top row) and average return (bottom row) across different levels of action noise and external perturbations. Both methods show similar robustness under action noise, but our method outperforms SafeFall when faced with perturbations, demonstrating its superior generalizability.

Fig. 5: Comparison of state-only and state-action safety critics. The state-action safety critic demonstrates better generalizability and robustness, particularly under perturbations and domain shifts. The results are shown for success rate (top) and average return (bottom) across different perturbation settings. The result is aggregated over 5 seeds, and the shaded area shows the standard error. The state-action model outperforms the state-only model under external perturbation and domain shift.

Fig. 7: Safety predictions from the SafeFall predictor across several random episodes. The trajectory length is set to 250 timesteps. SafeFall’s predictions tend to be more binary, predicting failure only shortly before the event. This contrasts with our receding-horizon method, which provides earlier and more gradual safety estimates.

Fig. 6: Prediction of the state-based safety critic under domain shift. Top: ensemble safety predictions (gray), CVaR-aggregated safety prediction (black), and ensemble standard deviation σt (red dashed, right axis). Middle: action norms before and after shielding, ∥u0 t∥ (orange dashed), ∥ũt∥ (blue), and correction magnitude ∥ũt − u0 t∥ (green). Bottom: nominal-model-based one-step safety estimate hϕ(f̂nom(xt, ut)) (orange) versus the corresponding value evaluated on the realized next state h(xt+1) (black dashed). Under heightfield terrain with enlarged perturbations, the nominal estimate can diverge substantially from the next-state reference (e.g., around t ≈ 175–190), leading to spurious risk alarms and unnecessary interventions.

Fig. 9: Complete ablation on prediction horizon H . Success rate (top row) and average return (bottom row) under action noise and external perturbations on flat and heightfield terrain. The x-axis represents the action noise or disturbance sampling probability. Curves show mean performance over 5 seeds; shaded bands indicate standard error.

Fig. 3: Example rollout diagnostics of the predictive safety shield. Top: ensemble safety predictions (gray, “single prediction”), their CVaR-aggregated safety estimate p̂CVaR(xt) (black), and the ensemble standard deviation σt (red, right axis). Peaks in σt indicate increased epistemic uncertainty and coincide with sharp drops in the predicted safety. Bottom: action magnitudes before and after shielding, showing the raw action norm ∥u0 t∥ (orange), the shielded action norm ∥ũt∥ (blue), and the correction magnitude ∥ũt − u0 t∥ (green). Non-zero corrections occur primarily during high-uncertainty and low-safety intervals, illustrating successful interventions.

Fig. 4: Ablation on prediction horizon H for selecting the safetycritic/shield horizon under sim-to-sim domain shift. Experiment settings are similar to Fig. 2. Curves show mean performance, with shaded bands indicating standard error across different seeds

papers.abstract: Offline navigation demonstrations are multimodal, because one observation often allows several valid actions, such as passing an obstacle on either side. Behavior cloning averages these actions, potentially leading to unsafe routes. Multimodal policies must discover the alternatives from the data, but similar states can lead to different routes whose current actions overlap. In navigation, the alternatives have a geometric cause and can be computed from one observation. We propose a hierarchical neural-network policy that computes candidate modes from local geometry and learns from demonstrations which mode to follow and how. A high-level policy selects a mode using the goal and its previous choice among a set of candidate modes, and a low-level policy turns it into an action. In simulation, the policy succeeds in over 95\% of seen and unseen test cases, compared with at most 43\% and 20\% for four offline learning baselines and 79\% and 67\% for a heuristic that uses the same modes without learning. The simulation-trained policy also transfers to a LimX Tron 1 bipedal robot.
authors: Chengyang Peng, Zhihao Zhang, Upama Pant, Yiming Wang, Keith A. Redmill, Ayonga Hereid
bullets: Addresses behavior cloning’s tendency to average distinct valid routes into unsafe actions.
Computes alternative navigation modes from local geometry rather than discovering them solely from data.
A high-level policy selects a mode using the goal and prior mode; a low-level policy generates the action.
Achieves over 95% success on seen and unseen simulated cases, outperforming the reported baselines and heuristic.
The simulation-trained policy transfers to a LimX Tron 1 bipedal robot.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have emerged as a powerful paradigm for robotic manipulation, enabling robots to generate actions from visual observations and language instructions. However, most existing VLA models still operate on image-level visual representations inherited from pretrained vision-language backbones, while lacking fine-grained object understanding for manipulation. As a result, their robustness can degrade under out-of-distribution object layouts, clutter, and background variations. To address these limitations, we introduce ObjDream, an object-centric VLA framework centered on object-level understanding and future object state prediction. ObjDream uses a spatio-temporal object encoder to organize visual observations into temporal object slots, where persistent object identity and dynamic object state are represented through separate channels. These structured object representations are inserted into the token sequence of the vision-language model (VLM), where identity-guided routing modulates VLM attention to the corresponding object tokens. In addition, an action-conditioned object dynamics module predicts compact future object states relevant to manipulation during training, explicitly supervising object state evolution under robot actions without requiring future prediction at inference. Experiments on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and RoboTwin 2.0 show that ObjDream improves generalization under diverse distribution shifts and scene perturbations. Real-world robot experiments further demonstrate that ObjDream transfers to physical manipulation settings with novel object arrangements and background changes.
authors: Huailiang Ma, Yuxuan Li, Ziyi Zhao, Xinkai Wang, Mingyu Li, Xinyu Guo, Lifeng Zhu, Aiguo Song, Cewu Lu, Jianhua Sun
bullets: Targets weak fine-grained object understanding in existing image-level VLA models, especially under layout, clutter, and background shifts.
Encodes observations into temporal object slots with separate representations for persistent identity and changing object state.
Routes VLM attention toward relevant object tokens using identity-guided modulation.
Trains an action-conditioned dynamics module to predict future object states, while avoiding future prediction at inference.
Improves generalization across LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, RoboTwin 2.0, and real-world manipulation with novel arrangements and backgrounds.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of ObjDream. We introduce ObjDream, an object-centric VLA framework for robust manipulation. Unlike prior VLA models (a), which primarily rely on image-level understanding and entangled object representations, ObjDream (b) introduces explicit object-level representations and future object state prediction. This object-centric formulation improves manipulation robustness, leading to stronger performance than baseline methods (c).

Figure 2: Overview of the ObjDream architecture. The model integrates three main components: (1) a spatio-temporal object encoder that constructs factorized object slots by separately representing persistent object identity and time-varying object state; (2) an object-level dynamics module that decodes current object states and predicts action-conditioned future object states; and (3) a flow-matching action expert that predicts robot action chunks. ObjDream enhances object-level understanding through factorized object representations and future object state modeling, enabling more generalizable language-conditioned manipulation under object and scene variations.

Figure 3: Experimental overview. We evaluate ObjDream on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, a fixed 8-task subset of RoboTwin 2.0, and four real-world manipulation tasks, covering standard and perturbed evaluation settings.

Figure 5: Automatic offline annotation pipeline for object encoder pretraining. Qwen3-VL8B extracts task-relevant object phrases from demonstration instructions and initial observations, while a separate robot gripper label is used for robot annotation. Grounding DINO initializes the corresponding object regions, SAM2 propagates segmentation masks across frames, and DINOv2 extracts object-specific features from the initial grounded regions. Masks, geometry, visibility, and phrase–region correspondences are automatically constructed from this pipeline without manual frame-wise object annotation. The resulting annotations supervise encoder pretraining, while the DINOv2 features provide visual identity references.

Figure 6: Qualitative future object mask predictions on LIBERO. Rows show three representative manipulation tasks. The decoder predicts all future steps h = 1, . . . , Hf for non-robot objects; for clarity, we visualize only h = 1, 4, 8. The predicted masks are overlaid on the corresponding future RGB frames, which are used only for visualization and are not provided to the decoder.

The decoder predicts all future steps for non-robot objects; for clarity, we visualize masks and bounding boxes only at h = 1, 4, 8. The predictions are overlaid on the corresponding future RGB frames, which are used only for visualization and are not provided to the decoder.

Figure 8: Qualitative future object state predictions on real-world tasks. Rows show button pressing, two-fruit placement, block pick-and-place, and tabletop sweeping. The decoder predicts all future steps for non-robot objects; for clarity, we visualize masks and bounding boxes only at h = 1, 4, 8. Table 2: Ablation study of object-centric components. Success rates (%) on LIBERO-Long and LIBERO-Plus. Overall is the trial-weighted LIBERO-Plus average. Best results are shown in bold, and second-best results are underlined.

Table 3: Real-robot manipulation results. Success rates (%) on four real-world tasks under ID and OOD evaluation. Best and second-best results within each setting are bold and underlined.
Table 4: Future object state prediction accuracy on LIBERO. Current state persistence repeats the current object state at each future target. Bold indicates the better value within each comparison.

papers.abstract: This paper investigates the use of Behavior Cloning (BC) for autonomous driving from a bird's-eye view (BEV) perspective in simulated urban environments. BC uses supervised learning to mimic expert driving behaviors. Previous works have applied BC in the CARLA simulator but did not fully address the challenges of traffic light compliance. Our approach enhances BC by integrating a kernel density estimator to adjust training sample weights based on action density, thereby improving the learning of rare but critical actions such as stopping at red lights and accelerating at green lights, specially in scenarios of scarce number of expert demonstrations. Using BEV inputs, which provide an abstract top-down view of the driving environment, our method simplifies the policy learning process. The trained convolutional neural network (CNN) outputs steering and acceleration actions based on these BEV inputs and additional state variables. Experimental results in the CARLA simulator demonstrate that our weighted BC method significantly improves driving performance, achieving higher route completion compared to standard BC. This weighted approach proved to be crucial in learning correct driving behaviors, particularly in test environments not encountered during training, highlighting its potential for enhancing autonomous vehicle navigation.
authors: Eric Aislan Antonelo, Gustavo Claudio Karl Couto, Christian M\"oller, Pedro Henrique Fernandes
bullets: Targets behavior cloning for autonomous driving in simulated urban environments with scarce expert demonstrations.
Uses bird’s-eye-view inputs plus state variables to simplify policy learning.
Applies a kernel density estimator to upweight rare actions, including stopping at red lights and accelerating at green lights.
A CNN predicts steering and acceleration actions.
In CARLA, weighted behavior cloning achieves higher route completion than standard BC, including in unseen test environments.

Fig. 2. Network architecture. The BEV (state) input is processed by a CNN (MLP) to create an image (state) encoding. Both image and state encodings are concatenated and fed into a final MLP that outputs the actions.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) typically adapt video foundation models to robotic control through joint video and action prediction. However, task-level instructions may leave the next physical interaction underspecified, requiring semantic grounding and state-dependent motion selection. To this end, we introduce Atomic-WAM, an understand-then-execute framework that connects task reasoning to action generation through atomic-motion descriptions. Specifically, a vision-language reasoner describes the next local motion from the task instruction and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict future video and an action chunk. Furthermore, an automatic annotation pipeline curates temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations. To make atomic-motion predictions executable by the WAM, we post-train the reasoner with Execution-Grounded GRPO (EG-GRPO). With the WAM fixed, EG-GRPO adapts the reasoner through rewards for motion appropriateness and execution success. Finally, Atomic-WAM achieves 39.6% task success under default instructions and 31.6% under vague instructions in a real-to-sim evaluation on RoboLab. Project page: https://ssj9596.github.io/Atomic-WAM-project
authors: Shijun Shi, Zhe Liu, Zhi Hou, Yinan Chen, Tao Zhang, Kai Hu, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
bullets: Addresses underspecified task instructions that do not clearly specify the next physical interaction.
Uses a vision-language reasoner to infer the next local motion from instructions and visual context, guiding a WAM to predict video and action chunks.
Builds temporally aligned, contact-enriched supervision from multi-view DROID demonstrations.
Introduces Execution-Grounded GRPO to train motion descriptions for appropriateness and execution success while keeping the WAM fixed.
Achieves 39.6% task success with default instructions and 31.6% with vague instructions in RoboLab real-to-sim evaluation.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Atomic-WAM overview. At decision step t, the reasoner predicts an atomic-motion description d̂t from the task instruction l and visual context ot−h:t, where each multi-view observation is formed by concatenating the wrist, left, and right camera views. The WAM conditions on d̂t, ot, and st to generate video latents x̂v and actions x̂a. The lower frames show selected decision steps from a full-task rollout, beginning at Start (t = 0).

Fig. 4: Closed-loop execution-grounded reasoner training. The reasoner samples four candidate atomic motions from a shared observation, while the frozen WAM executes them independently. An evaluator scores motion appropriateness and execution success, and the resulting group-normalized advantages update the reasoner. After each sampling round, one of the highest-reward endpoints is randomly selected as the starting state for the next round.

Fig. 2: Atomic-motion data curation. Displacement and gripper events first divide a demonstration into physical clips. We then annotate each clip from three views, then use temporal context to merge adjacent clips and refine their descriptions. Visible grasp details further enrich grasp-related captions. Finally, we check caption correctness and execution success; mismatched captions are revised and checked again.
Fig. 5: RoboLab success rate across training checkpoints. Results are averaged over three runs on RoboLab-120 with default instructions.

Fig. 1: Language specificity shapes predicted futures. Given the same initial observation and video backbone, we compare video predictions conditioned on (a) an abstract task instruction and (b) a concrete multi-step description. By explicitly specifying the target objects and action sequence, the latter produces a more coherent predicted manipulation sequence in this example.

TABLE I: RoboLab-120 results under vague and default instructions, evaluated over ten runs per task. SR denotes task success rate (%), and Score denotes subtask progress ×100. The episode counts shown in parentheses; the best and secondbest results are shown in bold and underline, respectively; ties share the same marking. Baseline results follow the official RoboLab leaderboard (accessed September 10, 2026). ⋄ denotes entries with closed-source weights. We denote Atomic-WAM as VLM + WAM to highlight its explicit use of vision–language reasoning, while the model retains a unified architecture.
TABLE III: Ablation of reasoner adaptation. Results are averaged over three runs on RoboLab-120 with default instructions.
TABLE II: Ablation of atomic-motion supervision. Results are averaged over three runs on RoboLab-120 with default instructions.

papers.abstract: Tactile sensing is becoming central to robust, adaptive, and dexterous robotic manipulation. Beyond its traditional role in contact detection and reactive control, touch is increasingly used to learn transferable representations, condition manipulation policies, and support embodied physical reasoning. Yet existing surveys largely emphasize tactile hardware and perception, leaving the rapid shift toward learning-based tactile manipulation insufficiently synthesized. This paper reviews tactile-guided skill learning from a learning-centric perspective, organized by the functional role of touch across the learning and control pipeline. We examine tactile representation and policy learning, tactile foundation models, predictive and adaptive control, and generalization across objects, tasks, sensors, embodiments, and simulation-to-real transfer. Across these directions, we identify common design principles and remaining challenges in learning transferable physical representations, integrating semantic reasoning with contact-level control, and scaling tactile learning across heterogeneous data and hardware. Finally, we outline emerging directions toward tactile foundation and world models that can predict, reason about, and adapt physical interactions. Together, this review characterizes the transition of touch from a task-specific feedback signal toward a core modality for general-purpose embodied intelligence. An accompanying database of the reviewed literature and associated resources is available at https://sites.google.com/view/touch-in-robot-learning-review.
authors: Kiyanoush Nazari, Luchen Li, Haoshu Fang, Nima Fazeli, Zhibin Li, Fumiya Iida, Thomas George Thuruthel
bullets: Reviews tactile representation learning, policy learning, foundation models, predictive and adaptive control, and cross-domain generalization.

papers.abstract: Rapid progress in AI agents and robotics makes it a matter of the near future that humans are served by a team of robots. Such a team will receive several goals at once, each specified in whatever form is convenient for the human, such as a category name, a photo, or a spoken description. Existing benchmarks study multi-agent, multi-modal, and multi-object goal navigation in isolation, and a benchmark that places all three in one episode is missing. To fill this gap, we introduce HM3D-M3. A team of K agents starts at distributed locations in a photorealistic indoor scene and searches for an unordered set of M object goals, each given as an open-vocabulary category, an instance image, or an instance description. HM3D-M3 provides 1,000 validation episodes over 3,926 goals from 379 open-vocabulary categories, 100K observation-assignment training samples, and two team-level metrics, goal-level SR and makespan-normalized SPL. We further contribute two baselines. HiGA is a trained hierarchical goal assigner on top of a frozen open-vocabulary navigation policy, and LaViRA-M3 is a training-free team of VLM agents with shared mapping and progress analysis. Adapted multi-robot and zero-shot methods reach 16--27% SR, while our baselines reach 38--41% with complementary strengths and distinct failure modes. Furthermore, we deploy LaViRA-M3 on a heterogeneous three-robot team. Project page: https://robo-lavira.github.io/hm3d-m3/
authors: Hongyu Ding, Kanyu Xu, Mingjia Chen, Zixuan Chen, Jieqi Shi, Jing Huo, Yifan Zhang, Yang Gao
bullets: Targets the previously uncombined setting of multi-agent, multi-modal, multi-object goal navigation in photorealistic indoor scenes.

Provides 1,000 validation episodes, 3,926 goals across 379 categories, 100K training samples, and team-level SR and makespan-normalized SPL metrics.
Introduces HiGA, a trained hierarchical goal assigner, and LaViRA-M3, a training-free VLM-agent team with shared mapping and progress analysis.
Adapted and zero-shot methods achieve 16–27% SR, while the proposed baselines reach 38–41%; LaViRA-M3 is also deployed on three heterogeneous robots.

papers.abstract: Web agents built on vision language models decide every action by generating text such as click(12), although most of that text encodes a choice among a few action types and a few dozen marked elements. We read these choices directly from the hidden states that the generator computes while it reads the goal and the screenshot. Plug-in decision heads on a frozen generator predict the action type, pool the visual tokens inside each numbered box to pick the target, and point at a listed text option or at a WRITE slot that leaves the writing of new text to the generator. A confidence cascade executes the heads' action when they are sure and otherwise lets the generator decode from the KV cache of the same forward pass. With Qwen3-VL 4B and 8B generators trained on 213k web steps, a strict threshold keeps the cascade between 0.3 points below and 1.4 points above the generator on seven offline test sets while the heads decide 12 to 64% of the steps. A looser threshold raises step success on unseen Mind2Web websites by 3.1 and 1.8 points, costs up to 2 points on GUIAct and MiniWoB++, and lifts WebArena task success from 12.5 to 13.8% (4B) and from 13.6 to 14.6% (8B) with less than half of the generated tokens. Training the heads jointly with the generator lowers the generator's own step success by up to 4.9 points; heads on a frozen generator avoid this cost.
authors: Chengguang Gan, Yunhao Liang, Hanjun Wei, Qinghao Zhang, Zhixi Cai, Shiwen Ni
bullets: The method reads action choices from hidden states of a frozen vision-language generator processing the goal and screenshot.

A confidence cascade uses head decisions when confident and otherwise falls back to generator decoding from the same forward pass.
Across seven offline test sets, heads controlled 12–64% of steps with performance within 1.4 points above or 0.3 points below the generator under a strict threshold.
A looser threshold improved WebArena success and used less than half the generated tokens, but results varied across benchmarks.
