A high-level decision policy produces provisional navigation intents, while the deterministic validation and execution layer Γ resolves grounded references and retains authority over physical execution and terminal acceptance.

Fig. 4. Representative closed-loop navigation trace with online map construction for the relational instruction “Find a chair next to a plant.” Starting without a pre-existing map, S3-Nav incrementally expands the occupancy representation while accumulating spatial-semantic evidence during exploration. The robot subsequently identifies goal-compatible relational evidence, approaches the selected target, and terminates after execution-layer validation. The final map shows the occupancy representation and trajectory accumulated during the episode.

papers.abstract: Simulated environments enable scalable training data generation for embodied agents, but more data does not necessarily provide what a particular agent needs to learn. Existing environment-generation pipelines largely optimize generic properties such as realism, diversity, or task coverage, while different pretrained policies can fail for different environmental reasons. We therefore introduce WEDGE, a framework for weakness-guided navigation learning in which the failure modes of a pretrained agent guide the generation of training environments at each adaptation round. Given a pretrained policy, WEDGE uses an LLM to propose executable weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, automatically validates them on the diagnostic set, and selects the strongest validated weakness based on its success-rate gap. The validated weaknesses are then mapped to the environmental factors that control them. WEDGE varies these factors to construct environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles, producing targeted training experience for adaptation. Across three navigation agents with different adaptation mechanisms, we find that policies exhibit distinct weakness profiles and benefit from different training environments. Weakness-conditioned adaptation consistently outperforms matched random and hard-example alternatives on ProcTHOR, while the resulting gains for Uni-NaVid and Gemini also extend to HM3D after ProcTHOR adaptation. Iterative re-diagnosis further shows that dominant weaknesses can persist or shift as the policy improves, providing updated guidance for subsequent environment construction. Together, these results show that policy failures are not only diagnostic signals, but actionable guidance for constructing training environments that target a policy's current weaknesses.
authors: Yue Zhang, Han Lin, Zun Wang, Yidong Huang, Zaid Khan, Mohit Bansal
bullets: Generic realism, diversity, and task coverage may not target the distinct failure modes of different pretrained navigation policies.
An LLM extracts and validates weakness features from contrasting successful and failed rollouts, then selects the strongest weakness by success-rate gap.
The framework maps validated weaknesses to controllable environmental factors and generates environments in the difficulty regimes where the policy struggles.
Across three navigation agents, weakness-conditioned adaptation outperforms matched random and hard-example alternatives on ProcTHOR; gains for Uni-NaVid and Gemini transfer to HM3D.
Iterative re-diagnosis tracks weaknesses that persist or shift as policies improve, enabling updated environment generation.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of WEDGE. Unlike existing environment generators, which are largely policyagnostic, WEDGE uses agent failures to guide generation. (a) We mine policy-specific weaknesses from successful and failed rollouts. (b) The mined weaknesses determine which environmental factors to control and which learnable regimes to target. Training on the resulting environments improves the agent and can yield cross-domain transfer beyond the generation simulator.

Figure 3: Weakness-conditioned environment construction and rollout verification. (a) Each policy is associated with its top mined weakness. (b) Candidate episodes are constructed by modifying the factors relevant to that weakness, such as target placement for target visibility or start state and layout for blind path ratio. Candidates are retained only when their feature values fall within the weakness range, with new layouts generated when existing ones are insufficient. (c) The policy is rolled out five times in each retained candidate, and episodes with two or three successful rollouts are selected for training.

Figure 2: LLM-guided discovery and validation of executable policy weaknesses. (a) We construct a diagnostic set by contrasting successful and failed episodes represented with a shared vocabulary of measurable primitives. (b) An LLM uses these structured examples to propose candidate weakness features and their executable definitions. (c) Each candidate is evaluated on the full diagnostic set, and (d) retained only if it satisfies the validation criteria for coverage, non-redundancy, predictiveness, and incremental value. Candidates that fail any criterion trigger a new round of episode sampling and feature proposal. This proposal–validation process repeats until the stopping criterion is met, with validated weaknesses retained for subsequent environment generation.

Figure 4: Analysis of weakness-conditioned adaptation. (a) We re-diagnose each agent after every adaptation round and track the SR gap associated with its dominant weakness. papers.abstract: Whole-body control plays a crucial role in enabling humanoid robots to execute expressive motions. Faithful execution requires preserving both the intended action and its expressive characteristics. Existing whole-body trackers typically balance joint and keypoint tracking with physical stability across diverse motions, but these objectives do not necessarily prioritize the expressive characteristics of each action. Our analysis shows that lower average positional tracking error does not guarantee better preservation of dynamic and postural motion characteristics. To address this gap, we propose a residual learning framework with compensation objectives targeting amplitude, energy, body expansion, body lean, and pelvis height. To concentrate compensation while limiting interference with the underlying tracking behavior, motion-aware gating allocates correction capacity according to body-part activity, preserving larger correction ranges in more active parts and restricting them elsewhere. For each frozen tracker, we train motion-specific residual policies and distill them into a unified policy shared across motion categories. Simulation and physical experiments on the Unitree G1 across eight motion categories demonstrate superior preservation of dynamic and postural motion characteristics compared with the corresponding baselines.

papers.abstract: Embodied visual tracking requires a robot to identify a designated target from visual observations and control its own motion to follow that target through an environment. Following an isolated person is a comparatively simple demonstration of embodied visual tracking, but following the intended person among distractors remains challenging. Existing methods exhibit a substantial drop in success from single-target to distractor tracking, motivating a focus on the shared spaces that person-following robots must navigate. We present \method{}, a vision--language waypoint policy built around the hypothesis that visual and language representations should be aligned before tracking-specific motion is learned. The policy combines complementary frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer backbone, and a lightweight head for robot-centric waypoint prediction. Its training progresses through vision--language alignment, multimodal reasoning mid-training, and tracking specialization on 19,532 oracle episodes. Compared with 41.54\% distractor-tracking success for our earlier OmTrackVLA model, the complete multi-stage recipe achieves 55.80\%. We then explore on-policy refinement using filtered oracle labels for states visited by the policy. This preliminary study adds 2.42 percentage points of distractor-tracking success, reaching 58.22\%, while reducing collision rate by 1.99 pts. The final policy records the highest distractor- and ambiguous-tracking success rates among the compared methods. These results support staged multimodal learning as a promising direction for tracking among distractors and motivate further study of on-policy refinement for person following in shared spaces.
authors: Kyusong Lee, Heting Ying, Tiancheng Zhao
bullets: Targets the challenge of following the intended person in shared spaces with visual distractors.
Uses frozen visual encoders, multiscale temporal context, a transformer, and waypoint prediction.

On-policy refinement raises distractor-tracking success from 55.80% to 58.22% and reduces collision rate by 1.99 percentage points.
The study is preliminary and motivates further work on on-policy refinement for person following.

papers.abstract: Reliable recognition of accessibility-critical objects (e.g., audible pedestrian signals, door-activation buttons, and handrails) is essential for assistive navigation technologies that support safe, independent mobility for blind and low-vision (BLV) users. Yet these categories are underrepresented in existing large-scale vision datasets, and the few datasets that include them suffer from limited class coverage, inconsistent annotations, and poor diversity. We introduce NavAble, a large-scale dataset spanning 11 accessibility-critical object classes, combining 41K curated open-source images with 8K newly collected, densely annotated real-world images. To extend scale and diversity, we develop a synthetic data generation pipeline that renders high-fidelity 3D assets across 37 environments under diverse styles and viewpoints, yielding 452K frames with rich ground-truth annotations from 565 assets. The pipeline minimizes manual effort by combining automated web image crawling, VLM-based filtering, SAM 3D-based asset generation, and convenient camera trajectory configuration, enabling large-scale data generation at a diversity unattainable through manual collection. Experiments show that fine-tuning existing segmentation models on the NavAble Dataset achieves reliable accessibility-object segmentation (>80% mIoU on our held-out test set). We also demonstrate the effectiveness of synthetic data augmentation, which yields up to +3.5 mIoU over real-world-only fine-tuning. Beyond benchmark evaluation, validation on egocentric data from two mobility-assistive robots demonstrates improved perception reliability in real-world navigation scenarios. Together, NavAble establishes a scalable foundation for BLV navigation perception, directly addressing the data scarcity and embodiment gaps. The dataset and pipeline are publicly available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/NavAble/NeurIPS_2026_BLV.
authors: Hochul Hwang, Jahir Sadik Monon, Soowan Yang, Shiven Umeshbhai Patel, Anh Nhat Hong Nguyen, Kien Nguyen, Keshav Garg, Dylan Gage, Duretti Hordofaa, Anshu Anjna, Eshed Ohn-Bar, Donghyun Kim

Robot egocentric validation shows improved perception reliability in real-world mobility-assistive navigation scenarios.

papers.abstract: We present Keypoint Constraint Learning (KCL), a framework for learning task-relevant motion constraints from visual demonstrations and for planning safely with the extracted constraints. To make constraint learning tractable from RGB-D observations, we represent demonstrations using sparse 3D object-centric keypoints and semantic mask centroids extracted through segmentation, visual feature clustering, and point tracking. In this reduced geometric space, we learn keypoint dynamics and infer distance- and orientation-based constraints that make the expert trajectories feasible and approximately locally optimal by enforcing KKT optimality conditions in the reduced state space. We then plan with the learned constraints under uncertainty, using robustness margins derived from accumulated prediction error, and provide a theoretical analysis of how keypoint perception error and learned dynamics error affect the recovered constraints. We evaluate KCL on visual demonstrations from navigation to rigid/deformable manipulation, showing that it recovers multi-stage geometric constraints and outperforms baselines in downstream safe planning.

Analyzes how perception and learned-dynamics errors affect the recovered constraints.
Evaluations across navigation and rigid/deformable manipulation show recovery of multi-stage constraints and improved downstream safe planning over baselines.

papers.abstract: Robots following persistent language instructions must decide which cached room judgments remain valid as their environment changes. We present MIND (Maintenance via INstruction-conditioned Dependencies), a framework for maintaining target-room decisions without re-evaluating every room after each event. A language model compiles each instruction into dependencies for semantic qualification and target selection. The controller intersects semantic dependencies with event footprints, refreshes affected judgments, and updates reachability and selection separately. For fixed deterministic evaluation, planning, and selection, conservative dependency and footprint coverage preserves the decisions of full recomputation. On 240 five-event ProcTHOR sequences with an exact benchmark predicate, MIND reduces mean semantic evaluations from 30.6 to 11.2 while preserving all 1,200 post-event decisions. Frozen-evaluator experiments with Phi-4 and Qwen3-14B also preserve all 1,200 decisions, without improving the evaluators' underlying task accuracy. In 32 closed-loop AI2-THOR episodes using exact-predicate qualification and metadata-derived footprints, MIND matches the final target decision of full recomputation in every episode. Unitree G1 experiments demonstrate target reuse and reselection across room transitions without additional semantic evaluations under MIND, and abstention after a barrier and an object removal at 4 evaluations against 15 to 18. Additional materials are available at https://mind-icra27.github.io/.
authors: Mohamed Abouagour, Junhyun Nam, Wonse Jo, Byung-Cheol Min

Preserves all benchmark decisions with frozen Phi-4 and Qwen3-14B evaluators, and matches full recomputation in all 32 closed-loop AI2-THOR episodes.
Scope: guarantees depend on fixed deterministic evaluation, planning, and selection, plus conservative dependency and footprint coverage; it does not improve evaluator accuracy.

papers.abstract: Robotic disassembly of end-of-life (EoL) products requires robots to accommodate product variation, follow prerequisite sequences, and approach components precisely for contact-rich manipulation. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) provides a practical path for adaptation, but limited and costly disassembly data cannot capture the distribution shifts arising from changing environments and product uncertainties. The policy's own rollouts record its approach attempts, and human corrections demonstrate recovery from its errors, but turning these experiences into better policy performance remains challenging. We introduce PACER, a Process-Aware Correction and Evidence Reweighting framework that learns from these experiences through SFT, using progress toward the target and each trace's source and outcome to weight valid action chunks in the native supervised action loss. PACER trains one policy per weighting setting and selects one of the resulting policies through held-out validation. We evaluate PACER on UR5e motherboard disassembly across five component classes, where it achieves 87/100 successful approach-and-handoff trials on the held-out benchmark, compared with 54/100 for vanilla post-SFT.

papers.abstract: Surface navigation on the Moon is subject to extreme illumination contrast and deployment-time perceptual disturbances. While modular navigation pipelines have long supported planetary rover navigation, robustness is compromised by measurement errors that propagate through hand-engineered components. End-to-end learned policies are an alternative approach to navigation, which maps observations directly to control actions without intermediate components. Vision-language-action models, in particular, have driven significant breakthroughs in robotics and autonomous vehicle research. By leveraging internet-scale vision-language pretraining, these models can be exploited for their commonsense reasoning and visual understanding to provide robust generalization with limited task-specific data. However, their applicability and performance have yet to be characterized for lunar surface operations. In this study, we design a vision-language-action policy for autonomous lunar rover docking and characterize its performance relative to a modular navigation pipeline. We develop a scalable training framework that generates safety-aware expert demonstrations in a high-fidelity lunar simulation environment. In closed-loop evaluations, our policy performs competitively relative to the modular baseline under perceptual disturbances unseen during training. To address the tradeoff between compute consumption and closed-loop safety, the policy adapts its execution horizon by determining how far the rover may safely travel in open loop. Adaptive-horizon execution reduces inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates relative to fixed horizons in the evaluated scenarios.
bullets: Addresses robustness challenges from extreme lunar illumination and deployment-time perceptual disturbances.
Uses an end-to-end vision-language-action policy mapping observations directly to rover control actions.
Trains with safety-aware expert demonstrations generated in a high-fidelity lunar simulation.
Performs competitively with a modular navigation baseline in closed-loop evaluation under unseen disturbances.
Adaptive execution horizons reduce inference frequency while limiting hazard-contact rates versus fixed horizons in evaluated scenarios.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative to costly robot data collection for dexterous manipulation, but most human datasets lack force measurements. Dexterous manipulation requires not only visual and proprioceptive understanding but also the ability to anticipate and regulate interaction forces. To scale force-aware human-robot co-training, we introduce EgoForce, a large-scale human tactile dataset capturing force-rich manipulation experience, and combine it with robot demonstrations for pretraining. We present FACT, a robot foundation model that cascades from prospective visual planning to force-aware refinement for dexterous manipulation. FACT comprises two jointly trained components. A Track-Guided Coarse Planner jointly predicts actions, future video, and visual tracks. Future video and visual tracks also provide a shared task representation that facilitates cross-embodiment knowledge transfer and coarse action generation. Building on this coarse plan, a Force-Action Joint Refiner jointly predicts future force and refines the coarse action, allowing anticipated force and action to shape each other during refinement. We evaluate the model on ten tasks requiring fine-grained coordination and force feedback, including tool use, musical instruments, and precision laboratory procedures. Using as few as 10 robot trajectories with 90 human trajectories for fine-tuning, FACT outperforms both baselines, with success-rate gains of up to 60 percentage points over T-Rex. Ablations show that force supervision in human pretraining data is crucial for downstream robot performance after fine-tuning, while visual track prediction and training with future-force prediction improve dexterous execution. Experiments varying the human-robot data ratio during fine-tuning further suggest that FACT learns from human demonstrations nearly as effectively as from robot demonstrations.
authors: Zhi Cao, Yining Hong, Jiaolong Yang, Yejin Choi, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu, Huang Huang
bullets: Problem: Most human manipulation datasets lack force measurements, limiting force-aware human-to-robot transfer.
Method: FACT cascades a track-guided coarse planner with a force-action joint refiner that predicts future video, visual tracks, actions, and interaction forces.
Data: The model is pretrained on the EgoForce human tactile dataset together with robot demonstrations.
Results: Across ten fine-grained manipulation tasks, FACT improves success rates by up to 60 percentage points over T-Rex using as few as 10 robot and 90 human trajectories for fine-tuning.
Scope: Force supervision, visual-track prediction, and future-force prediction each support improved dexterous execution; the study focuses on tasks requiring fine coordination and force feedback.

papers.abstract: While Vision-Language-Action models have enabled impressive cross-task transfer in zero-shot settings, \emph{adaptation} methods are often necessary to achieve consistent performance on novel tasks. However, even though a wealth of methods for adaptation have been proposed, it is unclear how to choose the best method based on available trajectories. We close this gap by studying the impact of the adaptation method under a variety of common data scenarios: on- and off-policy data, offline vs online adaptation, and whether the data contains optimal or suboptimal trajectories. Our evaluation spans simulated tasks in the LIBERO suite and real tasks on a Franka platform. In the offline data regime, critic-based steering approaches outperform supervised finetuning when failure data is available. However, offline RL techniques for training critic functions fail to outperform simpler Monte-Carlo-based approaches. Finally, in the online setting, critic-based steering is significantly more sample efficient compared to policy-gradient-based finetuning methods, but has a lower performance ceiling than full finetuning.
authors: Maria Attarian, Yifan Ruan, Claas Voelcker, Chenyang Cao, Amy Zhang, Peter Stone, Nicholas Rhinehart, Igor Gilitschenski
bullets: Compares supervised finetuning, critic-based steering, and offline RL across on/off-policy, offline/online, and optimal/suboptimal data scenarios.
Evaluates simulated LIBERO tasks and real Franka-robot tasks.
With offline failure data, critic-based steering outperforms supervised finetuning.
Offline RL-trained critics do not outperform simpler Monte Carlo-based critics.
Online critic-based steering is more sample-efficient than policy-gradient finetuning but reaches a lower performance ceiling.

papers.abstract: Learning a collective policy for state-based Cartesian manipulation across diverse robotic embodiments presents a fundamental challenge due to embodiment-dependent transition dynamics. Collective learning aggregates multi-robot experience to discover shared task structure, yet naive aggregation can average incompatible action modes when different embodiments realize the same Cartesian command through different transition behavior. This leads to strategy ambiguity and performance collapse on dynamically outlying embodiments. To address this, we propose PACE, a two-stage collective learning framework that separates shared task-space intent from embodiment-dependent transition dynamics. The first stage employs a representation layer pre-trained on offline trajectories to extract task-level context from collective data. The second stage introduces a decision layer equipped with a predictive dynamics adapter. By forcing the latent state to predict future transitions, this adapter acts as a latent regularizer that grounds the policy in the transition behavior of the executing robot while preserving real-time inference without online planning. Evaluations across simulated embodiments demonstrate that our method prevents performance collapse on distinct robots. It achieves over 93\% overall success and 89\% on dynamically out-of-distribution zero-shot simulated robots, outperforming the Transformer behavior cloning (82\%) and diffusion policy baselines (66\%). Physical KUKA deployment further validates the feasibility of the full state-based pipeline under zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
authors: Shaocheng Liu, Yuan Meng, Zhenshan Bing, Alois Knoll
bullets: Addresses performance collapse caused by aggregating incompatible action-transition behaviors across embodiments.
Uses a two-stage framework: offline trajectory representation learning followed by decision-making with a predictive dynamics adapter.
The adapter predicts future transitions to ground actions in the executing robot’s dynamics without online planning.
Achieves over 93% overall success and 89% success on dynamically out-of-distribution simulated robots.
Demonstrates zero-shot sim-to-real feasibility on a physical KUKA platform.

papers.abstract: Training from offline data has allowed for substantial progress in domains such as robotics, leading to general-purpose policies that can be easily applied zero-shot or efficiently finetuned for downstream tasks. However, these policies can still have poor generalization, both due to the choice of modeling objective and from learning from a static dataset. In this work, we focus on the challenging task of zero-shot goal generalization, where a policy is evaluated on unseen tasks that require combining its existing knowledge (compositional generalization). An avenue for improving a policy's generalization is by generating new experience with world models; however, such generation has proven difficult for longer horizons. Thus, to alleviate this issue, we propose TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model and allows for directly imagining novel outcomes that can be achieved by composing existing knowledge. We demonstrate that training on these future outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned BC policies significantly improves generalization in stitching-based OGBench tasks.
authors: Daniel Lawson, Dhruv Sreenivas, Adriana Hugessen, Khimya Khetarpal, Glen Berseth
bullets: Addresses poor generalization from static offline datasets, especially on unseen tasks requiring composition of known skills.
Proposes TD-Aug, which samples from a geometric horizon model to generate achievable future outcomes.
Uses imagined outcomes as goals for goal-conditioned behavioral cloning policies.
Demonstrates significant generalization gains on stitching-based OGBench tasks.
Scope: focuses on zero-shot goal generalization and avoids the difficulty of long-horizon world-model generation.

papers.abstract: Deep space missions increasingly require spacecraft capable of autonomously operating in environments with communication delays and bandwidth limitations. A key enabler of such autonomy is the ability to run learning-based algorithms directly onboard. In this work, we present a flight deployment on a 6U CubeSat that demonstrates (1) onboard training and inference of a thermal segmentation model on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 NX GPU in space and (2) closed-loop attitude control using the segmentation model on a real-time, thermal image feed to track the Moon. In addition to this demonstration, we implement ROS 2 Foxy as a data transport middleware and integrate an open-source file system that provides strong data integrity guarantees and self-healing features. Over the course of approximately one year, we performed 12 experiments on the spacecraft, advancing the state of the art in autonomous spacecraft systems by showing how modern learning-based pipelines, commercially available hardware, and open-source software can operate reliably under the compute and environmental constraints of Low Earth Orbit (LEO).
authors: Elena Sorina Lupu, Hannah Grauer, Phaedrus Leeds, Nikhil Ranganathan, Connor Lee, Sulekha Kishore, Cailyn Smith, Shon Cortes, Brian Hardy, Benjamen Bycroft, Darren W. Rowen, Soon-Jo Chung
bullets: Addresses spacecraft autonomy under communication delays and limited bandwidth by moving learning pipelines onboard.
Deploys a thermal segmentation model on an NVIDIA Jetson TX2 NX GPU for real-time image-based control.
Integrates ROS 2 Foxy for data transport and an open-source, integrity-focused self-healing file system.
Conducted 12 spacecraft experiments over approximately one year in Low Earth Orbit.
Demonstrates that learning-based software, commercial hardware, and open-source tools can operate under LEO constraints.

papers.abstract: Achieving human-like dexterous manipulation remains a central challenge in robotics. Learning from human hand-object interaction (HOI) datasets offers a promising pathway to diverse dexterous skills, yet existing physics-based approaches train specialist policies for individual trajectories, thereby limiting skill reuse at scale. We introduce DexMimic, a generalist dexterous hand-object tracking policy jointly trained across diverse HOI trajectories. Efficient joint training requires allocating each rollout to both an undertrained phase and a starting state that supports continued tracking. DexMimic realizes this insight through Value-Guided Reset Allocation, which adapts the initialization distribution online to prioritize difficult phases and select reset states with higher expected tracking returns. We further introduce a benchmark spanning training, fine-tuning, and generalization. Experiments show improved tracking success and training efficiency, faster fine-tuning, and the potential for zero-shot generalization to unseen trajectories and objects; larger training sets further improve efficiency and generalization. papers.abstract: Robotic systems that must acquire information about a specific target often face severe occlusion from sur- rounding structures or from the target itself, such that a single camera viewpoint provides only partial information. Active perception must therefore select viewpoints that progressively reveal unobserved regions. However, conventional local next- best-view (NBV) methods typically select viewpoints according to their immediate utility, which can overlook views that provide limited information initially but enable more informative obser- vations from subsequent viewpoints. We formulated local target perception as a short-horizon sequential view-planning problem and proposed a Receding-Horizon Next-Best-View (RH-NBV) planner that evaluates candidate sequences of future viewpoints rather than isolated views. RH-NBV is evaluated on a UR5e manipulator with an eye-in-hand RGB-D camera in simulation as well as on physical robot against a gradient-based NBV planner, and random search, using a coffee mug and Stanford bunny under controlled occlusion and a tomato plant with natural self-occlusion. Under heavy occlusion, RH-NBV achieves substantially higher target information recovery, reaching 63.8% ROI coverage versus 34.2% and 85.5% occluded-surface recall versus 7.4% for the single-step NBV baselines on the most occluded mug configuration. A controlled horizon ablation shows that this improvement arises from multi-step reasoning rather than additional computation. RH-NBV provides the greatest benefit for strongly occluded targets, while myopic NBV remains competitive and substantially cheaper when visibility is less constrained.
bullets: Severe occlusion makes single-view target perception incomplete and can cause local NBV methods to miss strategically useful viewpoints.
The planner evaluates candidate multi-step viewpoint sequences in a receding-horizon framework, then executes the next view.
On a UR5e with an eye-in-hand RGB-D camera, it was tested in simulation and on a physical robot across synthetic and natural occlusion scenarios.
Under the most occluded mug configuration, RH-NBV achieved 63.8% ROI coverage and 85.5% occluded-surface recall, versus 34.2% and 7.4% for single-step NBV baselines.
Its advantage is greatest under strong occlusion; myopic NBV remains cheaper and competitive when visibility is less constrained.

papers.abstract: Humanoid policies trained in simulation can transfer qualitatively to hardware while failing to transfer the force interactions learned during training, compromising torque efficiency, load regulation, and robustness to impacts. This failure can arise from actuator sim-to-real gaps because forces depend on actuator torques. We introduce Contact-UAN, a residual world model that preserves a simulator's physics priors while correcting actuator dynamics to align simulated rollouts with recorded hardware rollouts. For humanoid motion with contact, this requires contact-consistent replay: if hardware playback in simulation begins with misaligned contact wrenches, the residual model learns to correct reset artifacts rather than actuator discrepancies. Using only onboard proprioception, Contact-UAN infers the simulator-side stance-foot pose needed to initialize replay with consistent contact forces. We show that a UAN trained on 6.5 minutes of real-world walking data generalizes to tasks that benefit from accurate force and impulse regulation and produces policies that transfer seamlessly to the real world, yielding 20% lower running torque, 43% lower force-tracking error, extreme compliance, accurate impedance control, and dynamic, robust jumps.
authors: Nolan Fey, Khai Nguyen, Yash Prabhu, Gabriel B. Margolis, Pulkit Agrawal

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated whole-body interaction with the physical world, yet collecting robot demonstrations at scale remains costly. Human demonstrations offer a scalable alternative, but existing egocentric human supervision often omits locomotion and posture, while embodiment differences and controller dynamics hinder accurate end-effector execution. We introduce HumanVerse, a 500-hour dataset of open-world human loco-manipulation pairing egocentric video with synchronized body and hand motion. Our human-to-humanoid pipeline aligns camera viewpoints and arm appearance, and refines motion references and controller inputs offline to reduce end-effector errors while preserving whole-body coordination. We validate the pipeline through zero-shot transfer to Unitree G1 on representative whole-body manipulation and long-range loco-manipulation tasks, without target-task robot demonstrations. Building on this pipeline, we develop $\lambda_0$, a humanoid foundation model for whole-body loco-manipulation, with robot-aligned human demonstrations providing supervision for mid-training. Increasing whole-body human data consistently improves downstream task progress. $\lambda_0$ achieves 90.0% success on SIMPLE and 62.5% across real-world loco-manipulation tasks. We expect this study to guide scalable whole-body human data collection toward humanoid foundation models for richer interaction with the physical world. Homepage: https://lambdahumanoid.github.io/

papers.abstract: Finite safety assessments cannot exclude an adversary that preserves unattacked behavior until certification and activates afterward. We characterize this limitation for embodied and tool-use AI. An adversary that matches the complete observation law until observable, irrevocable certification and retains intervention access afterward attains $v\mathbb{E}[(n-S_0)_+]$ expected post-certification events over $n$ trials, where $v$ is the active event probability and $S_0$ the unattacked certification time. The result covers adaptive and privately randomized evaluators. Switching at certification is exactly optimal for a fixed likelihood-ratio test under memoryless, event-increasing interventions without a binding intervention budget. A positive clean-certification requirement forces linear worst-case expected excess when intervention raises event rates over an authorized deployment horizon, even if certification is deferred to the deadline. In simulated RoCo collaboration, switching yields commanded-separation violations in 34 of 36 post-certification episodes. Preregistered randomized AgentDojo trials estimate 1.98 additional security violations per four-task continuation (95% interval [1.67, 2.29]). An adversarial language-model controller infers hidden certification from noisy evaluation receipts and times intervention accordingly. With permanent revocation, a mixture likelihood-ratio monitor bounds cumulative excess above a prespecified reference rate at square-root order, up to logarithmic factors, on every sample path. A single fixed alternative can permit linear expected excess under stationary attacks. Against a controller observing the monitor's rule and statistic, live mixture monitoring reduces violations from 12.00 to 3.81 per 24 assigned task opportunities. Revocation also reduces tasks executed.
bullets: An adversary can mimic safe behavior until observable, irreversible certification, then activate interventions; expected harm scales with remaining deployment opportunities.
Switching precisely at certification is optimal under fixed likelihood-ratio testing, memoryless event-increasing interventions, and no binding intervention budget.
Simulations and randomized tool-use trials show substantial post-certification violations, including 1.98 additional security violations per four-task continuation in AgentDojo.
Permanent revocation with mixture monitoring bounds cumulative excess at roughly square-root order up to logarithmic factors, but reduces tasks executed.
A controller aware of the monitoring rule still caused fewer violations under live monitoring: 3.81 versus 12.00 per 24 task opportunities.

papers.abstract: How should demonstration quality be used during vision-language-action (VLA) pretraining to improve performance after target-task fine-tuning? We compare weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 naturally suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks. Within each VLA, we match demonstrations and training budgets. Additional comparisons examine pretraining data size and the roles of quality tags during fine-tuning and inference. Across three VLAs, we find that approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning; conditioning and filtering favor episode and chunk labels, respectively, on average, with model-dependent reversals; and constant-tag fine-tuning improves mean success after conditioned pretraining with either tagged or untagged inference. We introduce AXIS-Bench to support these controlled comparisons. Built on crowdsourced simulation demonstrations, it provides recorded object and contact states for recomputing quality labels on shared trajectories. Replayable trajectories support workspace-aligned rendering and user-defined real-world target tasks. In our real-world experiment, simulation pretraining raises success from 9.6\% to 31.7\%. Project page: https://axis-bench.github.io/.
authors: Mingxuan Yan, Litian Gong, Dihong Huang, Zhixu Li, Tianyu Zhang, Wenqian Zhang, Hefeifei Jiang, Peihao Li, Jian Zhang, Mengfei Zhao, Yikai Tang, Hai Zhai, Zehao Wang, Ruijian Liang, Yanjia Huang, Lin Shao, Changliu Liu, Kaiyu Hang, Zhiwen Fan, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Jianfei Yang, Jiachen Li
bullets: Benchmarks weighting, filtering, and conditioning across reward definitions and label granularities using 5,000 suboptimal human demonstrations and 24 target tasks.
Across three VLAs, approach-aware episode conditioning improves mean success over plain behavioral cloning, while the best label granularity depends on the approach and model.
Constant-tag fine-tuning further improves mean success after conditioned pretraining, regardless of tagged or untagged inference.
AXIS-Bench provides replayable simulation trajectories with object and contact states for controlled, user-defined quality-label comparisons.
In a real-world experiment, simulation pretraining increased success from 9.6% to 31.7%.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. AXIS-Bench workflow for quality-aware VLA pretraining. Human demonstrations provide policy observations and action targets, while recorded object and contact states enable offline computation of state-derived quality. Quality is represented at the chunk or episode level and incorporated into pretraining through weighting, filtering, or conditioning across three VLA backbones. The simulation benchmark evaluates performance after fine-tuning on 24 target tasks, with matched pretraining data, training budgets, and target-task demonstrations within each VLA comparison. The real-world workflow supports user-defined workspaces and tasks by aligning the simulation workspace, re-rendering demonstrations under the target workspace and camera configuration, fine-tuning on real-world target-task demonstrations, and evaluating task success. Photos illustrate our reference real-world setup.

papers.abstract: Online decision-making faces a tension between efficient inference and long-horizon reasoning. Value-based methods rely on short-horizon bootstrapping that limits the propagation of long-term information, while trajectory optimization methods plan explicitly but must solve a high-dimensional optimization problem at every decision step. We propose Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP), a model-based framework that addresses this tension by learning a generative model as a proposal distribution over action sequences. Instead of optimizing sequences from scratch, GTP samples candidate sequences from a diffusion prior and refines them using learned dynamics, reward, and value models, enabling efficient trajectory-level reasoning. Across continuous control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, GTP matches or exceeds state-of-the-art model-free, diffusion-policy, and model-based baselines, and remains stable in regimes where strong baselines degrade. Our results suggest that generative models are best understood not as policies, but as structured proposal distributions for planning, offering a new perspective on how to integrate generative modeling with model-based decision-making.
authors: Haldun Balim, Yilun Du, Na Li
bullets: Addresses the trade-off between short-horizon value bootstrapping and costly trajectory optimization.
Samples candidate action sequences from a learned diffusion prior rather than optimizing from scratch.
Refines proposals using learned dynamics, reward, and value models for trajectory-level reasoning.
Matches or exceeds reported baselines across continuous-control and long-horizon manipulation tasks, with improved stability in difficult regimes.
Reframes generative models as structured planning proposals rather than direct policies.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Generative Trajectory Planning (GTP). Planning proceeds via iterative beam search. Starting from an initial beam, GTP repeatedly (1) branches candidate trajectory prefixes by duplicating, (2) refines action suffixes through partial forward diffusion and denoising under the diffusion prior, and (3) prunes candidates using rollouts through learned dynamics, reward, and value models. The top-scoring trajectories are retained and expanded at the next depth, progressively constructing long-horizon plans toward high-return regions.

Figure 1: Generative Trajectory Planning. GTP combines the data-driven nature of RL with the long-horizon reasoning of trajectory optimization. A learned diffusion prior proposes candidate action sequences, which are evaluated and iteratively refined through learned models. By using a generative prior, GTP avoids computational cost of optimization while preserving long-horizon reasoning.
Figure 7: Effect of planning horizon. Evaluation returns under varying horizon.
Figure 6: Exploration on PushT-Vision. End-effector visitation heatmaps over training in an object-centric frame.
Figure 10: Trajectory reuse reduces training overhead while preserving performance. Reusing elite trajectories maintains comparable learning curves (top) and final success rates (bottom).

Figure 4: GTP improves sample efficiency in long-horizon settings. Evaluation return curves on Fetch and PushT environments. Solid lines show the mean and shaded regions the standard error over 5 random seeds.

Figure 8: Effect of ensemble aggregation on Ant-v4. Pessimistic aggregation (min/median for update/rollout) substantially outperforms optimistic aggregation (median/max) on this termination-sensitive environment.
Figure 3: GTP consistently outperforms baselines. Evaluation return curves on OpenAI Gym MuJoCo environments. Solid lines show the mean and shaded regions the standard error over 5 random seeds.
Figure 5: Ablations of key components. Best mean returns and standard errors over 5 random seeds.

papers.abstract: LLMs are used as high-level controllers for embodied agents, but it remains unclear whether they support collaborative reasoning, such as anticipating a collaborator's actions in real-time teamwork without dialogue. We ask if observing the partner's state, exchanging object knowledge, and predicting the partner's next action, shape task outcomes and coordination when agents can share percepts but never intentions, plans, or task-level messages, and whether the two agents occupy symmetric roles. Using the Habitat-based PARTNR benchmark, we introduce a Decoupled Partial Observability regime that enforces strictly individual perception, and we augment decentralized zero-shot ReAct planners with Other Agent's State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE) between co-located agents, and Other Agent's Next Action (OANA) prediction, evaluated on the full 2 x 2 x 2 grid with four planners on 1,000 validation tasks. OAS observation improves task quality, reducing extraneous effort for every planner, whereas KE primarily improves execution efficiency, cutting simulation steps by up to 25% with little change in success. The two are largely redundant for strong planners but complementary for the weakest, for which KE without the OAS is the worst configuration. OANA prediction lowers the success rate in 15 of 16 model x context pairs while raising explicit partner mentions to 55-100%, and its accuracy gains lie mainly in the coarse action type, partly because agents recognize the action the partner is already performing. The robot retrieves objects sooner and completes its tasks earlier than the simulated human. Shared context reduces total task time by shortening the remaining duration that the human works alone. Also, coordination benefits arise from responding to shared context, especially the OAS, rather than explicit anticipation, yielding shallow, planner-dependent partner modeling.
authors: Adri\'an Szlatincs\'an, Filippo Ziliotto, Bruno Lepri, Luciano Serafini, Massimiliano Luca, Tommaso Campari
bullets: The study tests partner-state observation, object knowledge exchange, and next-action prediction under strict partial observability without intentions or task-level messages.
Other Agent’s State (OAS) improves task quality and reduces unnecessary effort across all planners.
Knowledge Exchange (KE) mainly improves efficiency, reducing simulation steps by up to 25%, with limited effect on success.
Next-action prediction decreases success in most model–context settings, despite increasing explicit partner mentions.
Coordination primarily comes from reacting to shared context—especially OAS—rather than explicit anticipation, with planner-dependent partner modeling.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Decoupled architecture with Other Agent’s State (OAS) observation, object Knowledge Exchange (KE), and Other Agent’s Next Action (OANA) prediction. Both agents build a world graph using their own environmental object observations and their actions. The graph’s nodes represent the house, rooms, furniture, receptacles, objects, and agents. The edges represent the type of relation between them. If allowed, the agents also observe the OAS and exchange their knowledge about the objects when they are in the same room. Their high-level LLM planners call a High-Level Action (at replanning) and the corresponding low-level skills (action execution in the simulator), and predict the OANA. The predicted OANA is then compared with the other agent’s current and next actions (union target, Section 3.3), retrieved from its list of all called high-level actions.

Figure 3: Success Rate against episode length (Simulation Steps) for every configuration in Table 1. Marker shape and color give the shared context (none, KE, OAS, OAS + KE); filled markers are runs without OANA prediction, and each arrow points to the same context with prediction enabled. For Gemini and DeepSeek, KE and OAS both shorten episodes, and OAS also raises Success Rate; all arrows but one point down, since prediction lowers Success Rate in fifteen of sixteen model×context pairs (the exception is the Llama 8B with KE only). The y-axis ranges differ per panel.

Figure 1: Observation settings and OANA prediction. In the object-only baseline (KE and OAS both off) of Decoupled Partial Observability, agents observe only objects and their positions (including whether an agent holds them). With object KE, co-located agents synchronize their accumulated object knowledge. With OAS observation, agents also observe the partner’s state, but only when co-located. With OANA prediction, each replanning step predicts the partner’s next action before the agent selects its own. Text in the figure is simplified relative to the prompts; the background image is AI-generated.

Figure 5: Partner-prediction accuracy by shared context, for the robot predicting the human (top) and the human predicting the robot (bottom): Action Type accuracy (blue) and all-parameter accuracy given a correct action type (orange), under the union target (solid, filled markers; Table 2) and the strict next-action target (dashed, hollow markers; Table 7). Each point is a table entry; markers are offset horizontally so that close values remain visible. From None to OAS + KE, Action Type accuracy rises more than the conditional term for every planner and agent (+14.7/+14.6 against +4.8/+1.8 points for robot/human, averaged over planners, union target). The strict target lowers Action Type accuracy by 36.5% on average (27–48% across cells), while the conditional term is unchanged on average (52.2% vs. 52.4%) but planner-dependent: lower in every cell for the Llama 8B and higher in most cells for the Llama 70B and DeepSeek.

Figure 4: Completion lag between the agents: human minus robot Extra Planning Ratio (percentage points) for each shared context, without (blue) and with (orange) OANA prediction. Positive values mean the human keeps replanning after the robot has finished. Without prediction, the human trails in every configuration, and the full shared context (OAS + KE) shrinks the lag in every model; prediction widens it for the Llama 8B and reverses it for DeepSeek, for Gemini in two contexts, and marginally for the Llama 70B with KE only (−0.5 points).

Table 2: Other Agent’s Next Action (OANA) prediction accuracy (%) across action abstraction levels for robot (R) and human (H) agents. papers.abstract: Industrial manipulation in flexible manufacturing, e.g., high-mix, low-volume (HMLV) electronics assembly, requires robot policies to adapt to changing products and production conditions. Such settings impose industrial process constraints, including product variants, moving material flows, finite execution windows, and tight geometric tolerances. However, existing evaluation frameworks do not systematically capture these constraints when assessing generalist robot policies. To address this gap, we introduce LIBERO-Industry, a novel benchmark built on the widely used robot learning benchmark LIBERO, that translates the aforementioned industrial constraints into controllable task conditions and measurable success criteria. Specifically, LIBERO-Industry comprises three classic task scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic (S2D) loading, Dynamic-to-Static (D2S) unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic (D2D) transfer. The suites contain 216 tasks in total that systematically vary object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance region size. Extensive experiments across five generalist robot policies (including vision-language-action models and world-action models) show that performance progressively degrades as industrial constraints are introduced and combined. Under a shared fine-tuning and evaluation protocol, the LIBERO-Industry co-training condition achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than the original-LIBERO condition.
authors: Ming Shin Cindy Sung, Duan Leijiahao, Haoxiang Wang, Boning Tan, Liangna Fu, Chao Tan, Yafu Li, Yulong Chen, Chaoqun Wan, Zhen Huang, Shuxian Liang, Xian-Sheng Hua
bullets: Introduces three scenarios: Static-to-Dynamic loading, Dynamic-to-Static unloading, and Dynamic-to-Dynamic transfer.
Provides 216 tasks varying object geometry, conveyor speed, interaction-window duration, and geometric acceptance-region size.
Experiments with five generalist policies show performance degrades as industrial constraints are added and combined.
Under a shared protocol, LIBERO-Industry co-training achieved higher observed target-transfer completion than training on original LIBERO alone.

figures.caption: Figure 1: LIBERO-Industry overview. Motivated by industrial process constraints, the benchmark evaluates generalist robot policies across three classic industrial scenarios.

Figure 2: Task generation and scripted demonstration collection in LIBERO-Industry. BDDL specifies objects, process states, and goals; sampled layouts pass a feasibility gate or are resampled (top). A task-specific scripted expert attempts a rollout from a fixed initial state and seed (bottom). The diagram shows completion, kinematic-safety, and replay checks before accepted trajectories are stored as HDF5 demonstrations with provenance. Figure 3: Cumulative diagnostic stress progression for π0.5. Each bar denotes complete-task success of the stress settings for n trials (D0–D1: n = 200; D2–D6: n = 240), and PCRT denotes mean targetobject transfer completion. papers.abstract: Expressive flow policies can represent multiple high-value actions, but sampling them with few integration steps while retaining tractable action densities remains challenging. We introduce DEFlow, a deep equilibrium flow policy that replaces explicit Euler sampling with implicit Euler integration and solves all intermediate actions jointly as an equilibrium system. We combine implicit differentiation with a discrete change-of-variables formula for the final-action density, enabling off-policy training within soft actor-critic without backpropagating through solver iterations. DEFlow achieves an average relative improvement of approximately 10% in mean successful coverage over the strongest baseline across four Multi-Goal docking variants. It also achieves the highest mean time-averaged return on four of five manipulation tasks, while remaining broadly competitive across five MuJoCo tasks. These results support implicit flow policies for tasks requiring both diversity and precision, at the cost of additional nonlinear and linear solves. Primary
bullets: Addresses the challenge of sampling expressive flow policies with few integration steps while preserving tractable action densities.
Replaces explicit Euler sampling with implicit Euler integration, jointly solving intermediate actions as an equilibrium system.
Uses implicit differentiation and a discrete change-of-variables formula to support off-policy soft actor-critic training without differentiating through solver iterations.
Improves mean successful coverage by approximately 10% over the strongest baseline on four Multi-Goal docking variants.
Achieves the highest mean time-averaged return on four of five manipulation tasks and remains broadly competitive on five MuJoCo tasks, with added nonlinear and linear solve costs.

papers.abstract: Flow matching is a common generative recipe for robot foundation models. Vision-language-action models (VLAs) generate action chunks, while world-action models (WAMs) additionally generate future visual states. Both start generation from a fixed Gaussian prior, despite temporal continuity between past and future states and actions. This requires costly training and iterative sampling, especially for WAMs with an additional visual branch. We introduce $Δ$-flow, which constructs the source from recent history with mild noise rather than from a fixed Gaussian prior. This moves the source closer to the target, reducing transport to a small residual $Δ$ that can be learned efficiently and enables single-step inference. We integrate $Δ$-flow into the VLA policy $π_{0.5}$ and the WAM policies ImageWAM and Fast-WAM. On LIBERO, ImageWAM reaches 90% success in one epoch rather than six, and Fast-WAM reaches 95% in two epochs rather than eight. With LoRA fine-tuning, $π_{0.5}$ exceeds its baseline's five-epoch performance after one epoch. Single-step inference gives $1.54\times$, $2.49\times$, and $4.45\times$ speedups on $π_{0.5}$, ImageWAM, and Fast-WAM, respectively. It preserves action smoothness, achieving a $4.5\times$ reduction in action jerk compared with one-step Gaussian sampling. $Δ$-flow reaches state-of-the-art generalization performance on LIBERO-Plus. Action-history sources can be applied to pretrained WAM policies without retraining. Replacing the Gaussian action source at inference largely preserves task success with a single sampling step and can slightly improve it. We further study how action representation and visual information in action learning affect history-to-future prediction in $Δ$-flow. These results show that $Δ$-flow is simple yet effective, improving the efficiency and generalization of robot foundation models.
bullets: Targets costly iterative sampling and training in vision-language-action and world-action robot models.
Builds the flow source from recent action and visual history, learning only the residual transition to future actions and states.
Integrated into π₀.₅, ImageWAM, and Fast-WAM, it achieves faster training and 1.54×–4.45× inference speedups on LIBERO.
Maintains smooth actions, reducing action jerk 4.5× versus one-step Gaussian sampling, and reaches state-of-the-art generalization on LIBERO-Plus.
History-based action sources can be applied to pretrained world-action models without retraining, though visual and action representations affect prediction quality.

Figure 1 ∆-flow matching learns past-to-future changes for efficient robot foundation models. Unlike Gaussian-source flow matching, which reconstructs future visual states and actions from noise through iterative sampling, ∆-flow constructs each source from its corresponding recent history with mild Gaussian perturbation and learns only the residual change ∆. This shorter transport substantially improves training efficiency, enables fast single-step inference, strengthens generalization under distribution shift, and preserves smooth action generation across chunk boundaries.

papers.abstract: Recent multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and vision--language--action models have provided robots with new capabilities for long-horizon task understanding and planning. In surgical robotics, however, end-to-end prediction of low-level actions remains limited by insufficient precision, opaque decisions, and scarce data. This paper presents SurgiCLAW, a hierarchical skill-based framework for precision surgical manipulation. SurgiCLAW confines an MLLM to intraoperative visual understanding, structured explanation, and atomic surgical-skill selection, while delegating physical execution to verifiable deterministic control programs. For brain--machine-interface implantation, a representative high-precision surgical task, we construct a state-to-skill invocation dataset and expand it through visual and state perturbations. The model first learns structured skill invocation through supervised fine-tuning and is then optimized using three rewards for action correctness, operation prerequisites, and format validity, improving action selection, operational safety, and output parseability. We evaluate subtask success, offline model comparison, real-robot performance, and ablations. On a fixed test set, SurgiCLAW achieves 94.6% skill-selection accuracy and 93.0% macro-averaged F1 (Macro-F1). Across 50 closed-loop real-robot implantation trials, it achieves an 88.0% task success rate.
authors: Angen Ye, junjie xie, Yujia Song, Junkai Huang, Dapeng Zhang
bullets: Targets the precision, opacity, and data-scarcity challenges of end-to-end low-level action prediction in surgical robotics.
Uses an MLLM for visual understanding, structured explanations, and skill selection, while verified control programs execute actions.
Trains on a state-to-skill dataset augmented with visual and state perturbations, then optimizes correctness, prerequisites, and output validity.
For brain–machine-interface implantation, reaches 94.6% skill-selection accuracy and 93.0% Macro-F1 on a fixed test set.
Achieves 88.0% task success across 50 closed-loop real-robot trials.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. SFT and GDPO training pipeline. The MLLM first learns structured reasoning, answers, and function calls through SFT. GDPO then optimizes action correctness, operation prerequisites, and output format under a reference-model constraint.

Fig. 1. Multi-MLLM collaborative data-generation pipeline. Starting from raw image, robot-state, instruction, and skill-label samples, the pipeline expands the data through image/text augmentation and constructs structured rationales using three MLLMs. Candidate outputs are filtered by rule-based checks, leaveone-generator-out cross-validation, and human spot inspection before being retained in the final structured dataset.

Fig. 3. Closed-loop decision example for flexible-electrode implantation. At each step, SurgiCLAW receives the current microscopic image, robot state, and operation query, then outputs a structured rationale, an operator-facing answer, and a single atomic-skill call. The example illustrates a typical decision sequence from spatial registration and image-quality correction to needle alignment and final insertion. surgical data: a multi-MLLM data-generation pipeline expands 5,000 state–skill samples into 30,000 structured ones, and a three-reward group reward-decoupled normalization policy optimization objective improves skill selection, prerequisite safety, and output parseability. On the fixed test set SurgiCLAW reaches 94.6% accuracy and 93.0% Macro-F1, and it completes 88.0% of 50 closed-loop implantation trials. We interpret these results as a feasibility demonstration rather than evidence of clinical efficacy: the evaluation covers a single high-precision task using phantom and ex-vivo material, and the closed-loop comparisons are constrained by the modest number of paired trials. Whether the safety and interpretability benefits generalize to other tasks, to more stringent clinical conditions, or to long-horizon unattended operation remains to be established.

papers.abstract: Visual world models predict the consequences of actions from images, but planning with them is typically done by optimizers such as CEM and MPPI. However, these optimizers stall on long-horizon tasks where progress requires motion the objective does not reward, such as moving around a block before pushing it. This paper revisits kinodynamic sampling-based motion planning for world models, using the learned model as the propagator of a tree search in latent space. Our key insight is that the sampling strategies devised for high-dimensional search in configuration space apply directly to the latent space of a world model, where they rapidly expand through intermediate states that myopic optimizers never sample. We present two exploration strategies for the high-dimensional latent space, nearest-neighbor-guided RRT and projection-based KPIECE, with GPU-native batched expansion for efficient device utilization. We evaluate with an off-the-shelf DINO-WM on four simulated domains and a real-world block-pushing task. Our approaches match or exceed the success rate of CEM and MPPI at up to 13.8x lower planning time in simulation, and improve the success rate by 20% on the real robot.
bullets: Addresses optimizer failures when successful actions require temporarily unrewarded intermediate motion.
Uses the world model as a latent-space propagator for kinodynamic tree search.
Introduces nearest-neighbor-guided RRT and projection-based KPIECE with GPU-batched expansion.
Evaluated in four simulated domains and a real-world block-pushing task.
Matches or exceeds CEM/MPPI success rates with up to 13.8× lower simulation planning time and 20% higher real-robot success.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Planning paradigms and receding-horizon execution in latent space. (a) Shooting methods (CEM) iteratively collapse trajectories toward a mean, risking entrapment in local minima around non-convex obstacles. (b) Tree search (RRT) finds a valid path through the latent space, committing only its first 𝑛exec actions. (c) System execution introduces minor drift from the planned path, requiring re-grounding and replanning from the new observation. (d) KPIECE projects states onto a grid and prioritizes under-explored frontier cells (shaded) for subsequent expansions.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards improves reasoning, while the allocation of learning signal shapes which solutions remain accessible under repeated sampling. Group-relative objectives assign equal advantages to equally rewarded responses, making aggregate credit proportional to sampled mode frequency. We introduce Exploration-Preserving Policy Optimization (ExPPO), a lightweight advantage-shaping rule that redistributes credit using prompt-relative, length-normalized response surprisal and prompt pass rate. ExPPO combines bounded shaping with shared normalization to preserve verifier polarity and approximately maintain each prompt group's total absolute sequence-advantage mass. Our analysis characterizes response-level credit allocation alongside sampled mode updates, deriving local conditions for gains in entropy and correct-mode discovery. Experiments show improved in-domain and out-of-domain reasoning coverage, higher aggregate response accuracy, and strong coverage at large sampling budgets. A controlled multi-answer evaluation further demonstrates increased correct-mode yield and gains in diversity among verified-correct responses. Code is available at https://github.com/jinhangzhan/ExPPO
bullets: Addresses group-relative objectives that can concentrate learning on frequently sampled solution modes.

Experiments report improved in- and out-of-domain coverage, aggregate accuracy, large-budget coverage, and diversity among verified-correct responses.

papers.abstract: Legged robots can learn expressive whole-body skills from the motions of humans and animals. Due to the morphology gap between the source and the robot, however, the motion must be tailored to the dynamic properties of the robot. In particular, dynamic motions such as a jump require careful adjustment, since their timing and control are interdependent. We propose dense temporal motion retargeting (DTMR), which jointly optimizes timing and control within a single optimization, where dense means that the timing is adjusted for every control step. This dense formulation enables DTMR to deform only the parts of the motion that need a change in timing. The problem is solved with sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) in parallel on a GPU. We evaluate DTMR against baselines on two hours of human motion with four humanoid robots, where the results show that DTMR outperforms baseline methods, particularly on dynamic motions. We also show that allowing more temporal deformation yields more precise retargeting. We further compare DTMR with a baseline that optimizes the temporal dimension, where the result shows that DTMR retargets more precisely under the same deformation budget while being ~19x faster. Lastly, policies trained on our references transfer to a real humanoid robot.
bullets: Addresses the morphology gap when transferring expressive human or animal motions to legged robots, especially timing-sensitive dynamics such as jumps.
Uses a single optimization combining dense per-control-step temporal deformation with control, solved via GPU-parallel sampling-based model predictive control.
Evaluated on two hours of human motion across four humanoid robots; outperforms baseline methods, particularly for dynamic motions.
Allows localized timing changes and achieves more precise retargeting than a temporal-optimization baseline under the same deformation budget, while being approximately 19× faster.
Policies trained from the retargeted references transfer to a real humanoid robot.

papers.abstract: Cross-structural motion retargeting aims to transfer motion between different skeletal topologies. Despite recent progress, existing state-of-the-art models struggle with reliability in zero-shot settings, i.e. skeletons with different topologies which were unseen during training, and recent Transformer-based attempts have failed to outperform specialized geometric methods. We bridge this gap with a Transformer Autoencoder that learns a topology- and translation-invariant latent space. Our core contribution is a learnable flattening of skeletal graphs that captures both local dependencies and global structure. Unlike the standard transformer architecture, which adds positional information to token content, we integrate graph-based positional encodings multiplicatively, a design choice that follows directly from our flattening formulation. The resulting model handles diverse skeletal topologies within a single unified architecture and trains in a fully unsupervised manner, requiring no paired retargeting data. Ablation studies show, that the graph encodings, multiplicative formulation, and Transformer backbone is critical for the performance. In zero-shot evaluations, our method reduces global joint position error by $43-47\%$ over current benchmarks. A user study ($n = 37$), including expert animators, further ranks our approach highest in motion alignment and physical plausibility ($p < 0.05$). These results demonstrate that our model design is key to making transformer architectures effective for motion retargeting, outperforming existing approaches.
bullets: Addresses poor zero-shot retargeting when test skeleton topologies differ from those seen during training.
Learns to flatten skeletal graphs while preserving local dependencies and global structure.
Uses multiplicative graph-based positional encodings in a Transformer Autoencoder.
Trains fully unsupervised and supports diverse skeleton topologies in one architecture.
Reduces global joint position error by 43–47% in zero-shot evaluations and ranks highest in a 37-person user study.

papers.abstract: Class 8 trucks differ from passenger cars in geometry, dynamics, and maneuvering requirements. As a result, vision-language-action (VLA) models trained for passenger vehicles do not readily transfer to Class 8 trucks, particularly in unstructured scenarios such as accident scenes and construction zones. Rather than training a truck-driving VLA from scratch, we propose an adapt-then-steer strategy that adapts an off-the-shelf VLA to generate trajectories for Class-8 trucks in these challenging scenarios. In the adapt stage, we use NVIDIA's Alpamayo 1.5 as the base model, fine-tuning only its action-generation stack on a few hundred real-world construction and accident-related highway scenarios. In the steer stage, we introduce Flow Velocity Steering (FVS) to further refine the model's predictions while holding the adapted VLA fixed. FVS is a compact, flow-time-conditioned residual module that adds learned corrections to the action-space flow velocity used to update the action sequence at each generation step. In open-loop evaluation on a scenario-disjoint held-out set, targeted fine-tuning more than halves single-candidate average displacement error (ADE) and final displacement error (FDE) over the entire 6.4 s horizon compared to the base model. Using the same targeted demonstrations, FVS further reduces the fine-tuned model's full-horizon ADE and FDE by 13.9% and 16.5%, respectively. At matched data budgets, targeted supervision yields 19-26% lower full-horizon ADE than general truck-driving supervision, while the targeted model remains competitive with a model fine-tuned on approximately 65 times as many general truck-driving scenarios. These results support adapt-then-steer for data-efficient vehicle-domain transfer to Class 8 trucks. Our project website is available at https://truckvla.github.io.
bullets: Class 8 trucks differ substantially from passenger cars, limiting direct transfer of existing VLAs in unstructured scenes such as accidents and construction zones.
The method fine-tunes only the action-generation stack of NVIDIA’s Alpamayo 1.5, then applies Flow Velocity Steering (FVS), a residual correction module for action-sequence generation.
On a scenario-disjoint open-loop test set, targeted fine-tuning more than halves full-horizon ADE and FDE versus the base model.
FVS further lowers ADE by 13.9% and FDE by 16.5% relative to the fine-tuned model.
Targeted supervision outperforms equally sized general truck-driving supervision and remains competitive with training on roughly 65× more general scenarios.

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based large language models (dLLMs) promise to break the sequential latency bottleneck of autoregressive agents through parallel decoding, but recent evaluations show this efficiency does not transfer to embodied agentic competence: dLLM-backed agents repeatedly fall into retry loops, re-issuing an action long after it has failed. We give a mechanistic account of this failure and a training-free remedy. We trace the retry loop to the adaptivity of masked decoding: the sampler commits the positions it is most confident about and defers the uncertain ones, and at a failure state the context already offers a confident fill for the deferred decision, i.e. the failed action itself, so the retry is committed without the failure feedback ever being confronted. We model the resulting distortion of the action distribution as a task-blind corruption: contextually salient actions (e.g., the action just taken) receive inflated probability by a factor that depends on the state and the action but not on the task. Under this model, we analyse an invariance proposition: the task-blind factor cancels exactly from the reverse conditional, i.e. the likelihood of the task given the state and a candidate action, which coincides with the task posterior of an idealized uncorrupted model. Masked dLLMs evaluate the reverse conditional natively, unlike autoregressive models, by masking the task tokens and denoising, at the cost of a few parallel passes per candidate. We instantiate the rule as Reflect Reverse and evaluate it on four multi-turn embodied benchmarks, where it improves task success and progression rates over forward-scoring baselines.
bullets: dLLM agents can enter retry loops because masked decoding re-commits contextually salient failed actions before incorporating failure feedback.
The failure is modeled as task-blind corruption that overweights salient actions without depending on the task.
Reverse conditioning—scoring the likelihood of the task given the state and candidate action—cancels this corruption under the proposed invariance.
Reflect Reverse masks task tokens and denoises for each candidate action, requiring a few parallel passes and no additional training.
Across four multi-turn embodied benchmarks, it improves task success and progression rates over forward-scoring baselines.

papers.abstract: Indirect manipulation of deep-seated deformable anatomy inaccessible to the robot is challenging in robot-assisted minimally invasive surgery (RAMIS) because intervening tissues spatially filter deformation transmission. Passive observations can be ambiguous because the Decoupled and Blocked modes may produce similar motion responses. We propose CADeT, a causal-aware deformation transmission framework that integrates structural causal model (SCM) with active sensing to infer a latent transmission mode and estimate a state-dependent adhesion Jacobian online. During normal manipulation, control actions update the mode belief; when ambiguity persists, an additional probing action is selected to improve mode distinguishability. The mode belief and learned Jacobian are incorporated into a belief-aware model predictive controller for indirect target-shape control. Validation in simulation and on the da Vinci research kit (dVRK), using phantom and ex vivo porcine tissues, shows higher mode-identification accuracy and faster shape-error convergence than the evaluated model-free and model-based baselines. These results show that active sensing improves mode identification and indirect deformation control under the evaluated conditions.
bullets: Addresses ambiguous deformation responses caused by intervening tissues in indirect manipulation.
Combines a structural causal model with active probing to infer latent transmission modes.
Learns a state-dependent adhesion Jacobian online and integrates it into a belief-aware model predictive controller.
Validated in simulation and on the dVRK with phantom and ex vivo porcine tissues.
Achieved higher mode-identification accuracy and faster shape-error convergence than evaluated baselines under the tested conditions.

papers.abstract: Behavior cloning provides an offline route to autonomous-driving policy learning, but mean-squared-error regression is poorly matched to demonstrations in which one observation admits several valid actions. Diffusion policies can represent conditional multimodal action distributions, yet their closed-loop performance may be unstable when visual features and control are learned from limited data. This paper presents Diffusion-2BC, which combines a diffusion denoising objective with an auxiliary deterministic behavior-cloning loss over a shared visual encoder. The auxiliary branch is used only during training; inference remains diffusion-based. The proposed method is evaluated in the controlled Claw environment and in bird's-eye-view CARLA navigation, including route-conditioned driving, route-free navigation through multiple intersections, and cross-map evaluation from Town01 to Town02. In the Claw task, Diffusion-2BC reduced the mean mask-distance error by approximately 10% relative to a diffusion-based behavior-cloning baseline and by 85% relative to standard deterministic behavior cloning. In route-free CARLA, Diffusion-2BC traveled substantially farther before termination under the evaluation protocol than both baselines in Town01 and Town02. Additional qualitative rollouts revealed distinct route choices, showing the multimodal behavior of the proposed diffusion-based agent. The results indicate that an auxiliary regression signal can improve the closed-loop reliability of diffusion behavior cloning while preserving multimodal prediction in the controlled benchmark.
