papers.abstract: Occupancy world models provide a structured, metric representation of future driving scenes, making them a promising basis for end-to-end autonomous driving. However, existing occupancy-aware planners typically couple occupancy prediction and action generation through either hierarchical coupling or parallel multi-task learning. Hierarchical methods use occupancy either as a fully predicted future preceding action generation or as an action-conditioned rollout for trajectory evaluation, whereas parallel multi-task methods predict occupancy alongside planning through a separate branch or auxiliary objective. These interfaces retain either an explicit generation order or a role asymmetry, limiting reciprocal interaction between world prediction and action generation during trajectory formation. We propose OccWAM, an occupancy-native world-action model that jointly generates dense future occupancy and continuous ego trajectories via flow matching conditioned on scene representations. Building on this joint formulation, we introduce scene-to-ego world-action flow matching, a two-stage formulation. The first stage predicts scene-centric occupancy together with an absolute ego trajectory, providing a stable representation of future scene evolution. The same predicted world is then re-indexed into the future ego frames induced by the initial trajectory, where ego motion is represented through adjacent pose increments and a second joint flow refines ego-centric occupancy and motion for action-aligned planning. Unlike video-based world-action models, OccWAM preserves explicit semantic geometry for direct planning reasoning without pixel synthesis. Extensive experiments on Bench2Drive and nuScenes demonstrate state-of-the-art performance in closed-loop driving, open-loop planning, and future occupancy prediction.
authors: Qihang Huang, Wenhui Huang, Collister Chua, Shiyu Fang, Zhan Chen, Songyan Zhang, Zhidong Wang, Daiying Tian, Chen Lv
bullets: Addresses limited reciprocal interaction in hierarchical and parallel occupancy-aware planning methods.
Generates dense scene occupancy and continuous ego trajectories jointly from scene representations.
First predicts scene-centric occupancy and an absolute ego trajectory, then refines ego-centric occupancy and motion in future ego frames.
Uses explicit semantic geometry rather than pixel synthesis for direct planning reasoning.
Reports state-of-the-art results in closed-loop driving, open-loop planning, and future occupancy prediction on Bench2Drive and nuScenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overall architecture of OccWAM. A frozen Understanding Expert provides semantic driving context, while the World and Action Experts interact through layer-wise joint attention to parameterize a coupled occupancy–action vector field. Stage I jointly generates scenecentric occupancy and an absolute ego trajectory from Gaussian sources. The predicted trajectory then defines future ego frames for warping the occupancy and is converted into ego-motion increments; together, they form the source of Stage II. Using the same three-expert backbone, Stage II applies a second joint flow in ego-centric coordinates to produce the final occupancy and trajectory.

Figure 1: Comparison of occupancy–action interfaces. Hierarchical methods impose an action-first or world-first order, while parallel methods retain separate prediction pathways. papers.abstract: Diffusion models and Flow Matching can represent flexible distributions over robot actions, but many reinforcement learning algorithms also require the probability of each action. We introduce PrT-Flow (Probability-Tractable Flow Matching), which computes probability density while retaining multimodal, multi-step action generation. Its Jacobian-Tractable Transformer (JTT) makes each sampling step invertible and enables efficient computation of its Jacobian determinant. We train these finite steps with Conditional Euler-step Training (CET), which supervises their displacement over one step during sampling rather than their instantaneous velocity. We prove that, under certain assumptions, CET has the same minimizers as fitting the Euler-solver updates of Flow Matching. PrT-Flow achieves 96% success on Robomimic Lift after 300 epochs of imitation learning, matching the diffusion policy reference, and 96% success on OGBench Cube-Triple after 600k online steps. These results demonstrate that invertible networks with tractable probability densities can learn effective robot policies and support SAC-style actor-critic training. Our code is available at https://github.com/Sunlight-zero/PrT-Flow .
bullets: Addresses the need for action likelihoods in RL while preserving the flexibility of diffusion and Flow Matching policies.
Uses Jacobian-Tractable Transformers to make each sampling step invertible and efficiently compute its density.
Trains finite sampling steps with Conditional Euler-step Training, which theoretically aligns with fitting Flow Matching Euler updates under stated assumptions.
Reaches 96% success on Robomimic Lift and OGBench Cube-Triple, and supports SAC-style actor-critic training.
Scope: the theoretical equivalence relies on specific assumptions, and reported evaluation is limited to the stated robotic tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The architecture of Jacobian-Tractable Transformer (JTT). (A) A complete update applies M map heads in sequence and returns the next noisy sample xk+1 and the absolute Jacobian determinant D. (B) A causal Transformer with L decoder blocks uses shifted scalar tokens to predict monotone spline parameters. Cross-attention provides time and observation information. The projected outputs are converted to bounded parameter rates and multiplied by h to obtain offsets from the identity settings. These offsets determine the spline parameters. Between the two orthogonal rotations, the splines transform the unshifted scalar values. (C) For a fixed coordinate prefix, time, and observation, yi determines where its spline is evaluated, but not the spline’s shape. The positive analytic derivatives form the diagonal of the lower-triangular spline Jacobian, and their product gives the head determinant without evaluating off-diagonal entries. The orthogonal rotations preserve its magnitude. At step k, summing the head log-determinants at their respective inputs gives ℓk = logD.

Figure 1: The overview of PrT-Flow. (a) Conditioned on an observation, the Jacobian-Tractable Transformer (JTT) transforms standard Gaussian noise through K invertible steps of size h = 1/K. Each step returns both the updated sample and the Jacobian determinant D, without constructing a dense Jacobian matrix. (b) The deformed grid illustrates how the probability density of a sample evolves under these steps. At each step, JTT computes the absolute Jacobian determinant D. The local volume is scaled by D and the corresponding density is divided by D, allowing us to track the probability density of a sample. (c) A final tanh transformation maps the generated sample to a bounded action chunk a with its probability density p(a). SAC-style actor–critic training then uses sampled actions, their log-densities, and learned Q-values to update the FM policy.

Figure 3: Learning curves on Cube-Triple for PrT-Flow and Flow-G (σ = 0.01 and 0.05). Panels A and B show success rate and mean return on the shared set of 50 development episodes. papers.abstract: Spatial understanding is essential for embodied agents navigating and interacting with the physical world. As observations arrive incrementally, agents must reason in a streaming manner. Yet streaming understanding must also be closed-loop: task-relevant evidence may require both recalling past observations and actively acquiring new views. Existing streaming approaches largely emphasize processing incoming observations, leaving task-driven active exploration underexplored. We introduce MemAct, a framework for streaming spatial understanding with memory and action. A shared vision--language model incrementally writes structured historical memory, retrieves records and past frames on demand, and acquires additional evidence through movement and turning. Retrieved evidence and action observations inform subsequent decisions, enabling the agent to continue exploring or answer within a unified reasoning loop. We develop the MemAct suite, a data generation pipeline and collection across real and simulated environments, with approximately 1M training examples for spatial reasoning, memory writing, retrieval, and exploration. Its MemAct-bench comprises 20,000 main QA pairs evaluating current-observation understanding, historical evidence use, and active exploration, plus 2,000 separate Timing questions. MemAct combines supervised fine-tuning for memory and interaction with counterfactual action optimization using cumulative evidence gains, action costs, and terminal answer quality to improve exploration and stopping decisions. Experiments show that MemAct outperforms existing spatial understanding and streaming baselines and approaches frontier multimodal models on MemAct-bench while retaining streaming inference efficiency.
authors: Yuxi Wei, Wei Huang, Qirui Chen, Lu Hou, Xiaojuan Qi
bullets: Addresses the gap between passive streaming observation and task-driven exploration that acquires missing evidence.

Introduces MemAct data and benchmarks spanning current observations, historical evidence, active exploration, and timing.
Trains memory and interaction with supervised fine-tuning plus counterfactual action optimization for evidence gain, action cost, and answer quality.
Outperforms existing spatial and streaming baselines, approaches frontier multimodal models, and maintains streaming inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) use generative visual representations to condition robot actions, yet how these representations organize action-relevant information remains poorly understood. We identify persistent high-norm spatial outliers in WAM representations and find that their action relevance persists even after normalization and K/V projection attenuate their extreme magnitude. Motivated by this observation, we introduce RegisterWAM, which adds learnable non-spatial registers to the world model and uses them directly for action conditioning. Registers alone do not fully eliminate spatial outliers; pairing them with observation flow-matching (FM) loss supervision suppresses spatial outliers while concentrating high-norm responses in registers. Beyond this reorganization, observation FM loss supervision also improves action learning without registers, motivating an additional noised-observation FM objective that learns current-scene recovery from corrupted inputs. The resulting model achieves 81.64\% success on LIBERO-Plus without additional embodied pretraining data or foundation models, reaches 93.0\% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, and improves real-world manipulation performance.
authors: Yiwei Zhang, Yantai Yang, Jin Gao, Jin Lou, Andong Chen, Yufei Liu, Boyang Xing, Yuchen Zhu, Weiming Hu, Zhipeng Zhang
bullets: WAMs contain persistent high-norm spatial outliers that remain action-relevant even after normalization and K/V projection.
RegisterWAM adds non-spatial learnable registers for action conditioning, while observation flow-matching supervision suppresses spatial outliers and concentrates responses in registers.
Flow-matching supervision improves action learning even without registers, motivating a noised-observation objective for recovering current scenes from corrupted inputs.
The resulting model reports 81.64% success on LIBERO-Plus and 93.0% average success on RoboTwin 2.0, with improved real-world manipulation performance.

papers.abstract: Language provides a natural interface for humans to specify and reason about goals, but training language-conditioned robotic policies and reasoning typically requires expensive manual annotations. We propose Action Self-Distillation (ASD), a method for learning language-conditioned reasoning for robotic navigation without human-annotated language or reasoning labels. ASD uses an open-source VLM, which contains broad world knowledge and reasoning capabilities, as both a teacher network and a student policy. During training, the self-teacher receives privileged trajectory feedback and infers the underlying navigation goal together with goal-oriented reasoning. The student is then trained to condition on the inferred navigation goal, predict future ego-frame trajectory, and provide a description of the scene semantics, plan, and reasoning, from onboard observations alone. Across 13 challenging indoor and outdoor real-world navigation tasks, our method improves success rate over the strongest baseline by $30\%$ in indoor settings, $30\%$ on multi-stage tasks, and achieves $95\%$ success rate on outdoor tasks, validating that privileged trajectory feedback can enable self-distillation for scalable generalist navigation policies without human annotations.

papers.abstract: Estimating simulation-ready material parameters from visual observations is crucial for deformable-object manipulation but challenging because material properties are only indirectly revealed through physical responses. We introduce physical-field-bridged material inference, a single-pass framework that uses dense physical responses to connect multi-view RGB deformation videos with constitutive-type classification and continuous parameter regression. Unlike inverse-physics methods requiring per-scene reconstruction, online tuning, or simulation-in-the-loop optimization, our model predicts force/contact masks, projected motion-flow fields, and projected stress-response maps, then conditions material inference on these fields to reduce reliance on appearance or category shortcuts. We construct DeformFieldBench, a 3DGS MPM learning environment comprising 5,000 simulations across 100 object shapes and five mechanically informative loading modes, with dense pixel-aligned physical supervision. Our method achieves the best median errors on all four continuous parameters, improves stress-hotspot recall from 0.0762 to 0.5121, and attains 0.8676 SSIM/36.82 dB PSNR in same-simulator replay on unseen objects. Under a protocol-matched GSO evaluation, inference and future-state prediction take approximately 30 seconds, compared with 15-120 minutes for per-scene optimization. The method also yields measurable replay agreement on five real-world sequences. These results support dense physical fields as an effective bridge for fast material inference, while cross-simulator and real-world tests reveal remaining domain and identifiability gaps.
authors: Linrui Shou, Jie Li, Yu Liu, Tao Huang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of recovering simulation-ready material properties from visual deformation, where properties are only indirectly observable.

Reports best median errors across four continuous parameters, improved stress-hotspot recall, and strong same-simulator replay quality on unseen objects.
Inference and future-state prediction take about 30 seconds versus 15–120 minutes for per-scene optimization; cross-simulator and real-world tests expose remaining gaps.

papers.abstract: Tracking object motion within a gripper provides essential feedback for robotic manipulation. However, limited contact coverage and uneven deformation make tactile estimation challenging. In this study, we present TacSpin, a method that tracks in-gripper object rotation on SO(3) using only two vision-based tactile sensors. The key idea is to estimate the axis and magnitude of the rotation response separately, rather than fitting a rigid-body model by least squares. Each finger's response is further refined with contact-boundary cues. The two fingers are then fused according to their agreement. On standard objects, TacSpin achieves lower mean checkpoint errors. Qualitative demonstrations on real-world objects, using calibration transferred from a standard sphere, illustrate tracking under different contact geometries.

papers.abstract: While expert demonstrations on real robots are difficult to collect, human ego-centric videos are easy to collect and abundant on the internet. However, learning dexterous manipulation policies from human videos remains challenging---one of the most important challenges being the difficulty of reconstructing physically grounded robot trajectories due to the large embodiment gap. In this paper, we propose EgoCPT, a novel paradigm for learning high-quality retargeted dexterous hand trajectories directly from an ego-centric video, which can then be deployed directly on real robots. The only inputs to our method are an ego-centric RGB video and a reference hand pose trajectory, which can be easily obtained through off-the-shelf software or specialized cameras during recording. Our method is particularly robust to noisy hand poses attributed to our novel contact-aware optimization framework, which iteratively optimizes the contact points between the robot hands and objects. Across five manipulation tasks, our method achieves overall success rates of 67.3% on noisy EgoDex hand-pose reconstructions and 92.0% on high-quality TACO reconstructions collected using motion-capture hardware, outperforming multiple baselines on both benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot exploration under communication and mobility constraints requires balancing information gain with reachability. We present a distributed semantic exploration framework that combines Dirichlet mapping, budget-constrained trajectory selection, and Resource-Aware distributed Greedy (RAG) coordination. Each robot clusters frontiers, computes terrain- and heading-aware least-cost paths with a single budget-limited Dijkstra search, and selects feasible paths by marginal information gain, represented by the expected reduction in Dirichlet entropy. Each robot's per-round selection is exact, the team's joint per-round information gain is at least half the centralized optimum, and the bound degrades gracefully under limited communication. Ten-run gridworld ablations show improved coverage, semantic mIoU, and map certainty with lower entropy and traversal cost per unit distance than shortest-distance frontier selection. Budget-sensitivity experiments show that an intermediate budget best balances path reach and receding-horizon execution. In photorealistic full-system simulation against five coordination rules run in their native published forms, the proposed method attains the highest mean coverage and semantic accuracy while being the only one that respects the per-trajectory mobility budget.

papers.abstract: We propose ATOM (Abstract Transition and Option Modeling), a hierarchical navigation framework that combines higher-level graph planning with reusable lower-level option policies for efficient repeated navigation in large-scale 3D environments represented by hierarchical structures such as 3D scene graphs (3DSGs). ATOM operates on a hierarchical graph representation, implemented using, for instance, the Rooms and Places layers of a 3DSG, where each directed abstract transition is associated with a navigation option. For each transition, ATOM computes and stores a reusable option policy along with its state-dependent cost-to-go. Across repeated navigation tasks, ATOM maintains a smoothed empirical distribution over option initiation states and uses it to progressively refine the corresponding abstract transition cost. Ablation studies show that ATOM reduces cumulative repeated-planning time by 97.5% relative to a monolithic MDP baseline while maintaining trajectories within approximately 7% of a Global Places A* shortest-path reference. Experience-informed refinement further reduces abstract transition-cost estimation error by 10.3%. Physical experiments validate ATOM on an F1Tenth vehicle, successfully completing all five navigation queries with 43% of inter-region option executions reusing previously generated solutions.
bullets: Uses hierarchical scene-graph transitions for high-level planning and option policies for low-level navigation.
Stores each option’s policy and state-dependent cost-to-go for reuse across tasks.

Reduces cumulative repeated-planning time by 97.5% versus a monolithic MDP baseline while keeping trajectories within approximately 7% of a shortest-path reference.

papers.abstract: Textual reasoning before acting has improved vision-language-action (VLA) models, but at the cost of latency: every action conditioned on the reasoning text must wait for autoregressive decoding. We show that actions do not need to wait for or condition on the generated reasoning to benefit from it, because the reasoning supervision already improves the backbone representation. We introduce TacitVLA, a reasoning VLA whose action expert never attends to the reasoning it generates for the current call. On long-horizon tasks where the reasoning text also serves as episodic memory, it can generate each entry during action execution rather than before acting. We evaluate it in a controlled study on four benchmarks spanning manipulation and autonomous driving, memory and non-memory tasks: RoboMME, RMBench, LIBERO, and PhysicalAI-AV. On all four, TacitVLA matches the performance of its explicit-reasoning counterpart at up to 3.4x lower latency, and matches the latency of the same architecture trained without reasoning at up to +17.1% success. In absolute terms, it surpasses the best previously published results on the RoboMME Counting suite (82.7% vs. 66.8%) and RMBench (77.5% vs. 56.5%), and reaches 72.9% on LIBERO-Plus and a 52.5% scene score on the public split of the PhysicalAI-AV closed-loop driving challenge. Project page: https://tacitvla.github.io.
authors: Jack Lu, Yurong You, Boyi Li, Yulong Cao, Thomas Tian, Chaowei Xiao, Xiangyu Chen, Wenjie Luo, Boris Ivanovic, Marco Pavone, Yan Wang
bullets: Reasoning text improves the VLA backbone, even when the action expert does not attend to the reasoning generated during the current call.
For long-horizon tasks, reasoning can be generated during execution and used as episodic memory rather than delaying action.
Across four manipulation and driving benchmarks, TacitVLA matches explicit-reasoning performance with up to 3.4× lower latency.
It matches the latency of non-reasoning training while achieving up to 17.1% higher success.
It reports strong results on RoboMME Counting, RMBench, LIBERO-Plus, and PhysicalAI-AV.

figures.caption: Figure 1: TacitVLA retains the benefit of reasoning supervision without conditioning its actions on the generated text. Left: how the policies act in one call. Given the context 𝑐𝑡, on memory tasks including the ledger 𝑀𝑡 of past subtasks, the backbone generates the reasoning 𝑟𝑡 and conditions the action expert that outputs the action chunk 𝑎𝑡. In Explicit Reasoning, the action expert attends to 𝑟𝑡, so every action chunk waits for it. TacitVLA trains on the same sequence with 𝑟𝑡 masked from the action expert, bypassing the need to generate 𝑟𝑡 on non-memory tasks. On memory tasks, 𝑟𝑡 still becomes the next ledger entry (dashed loop), but is generated asynchronously during execution instead of making the action expert wait. No Reasoning is the same architecture trained without reasoning supervision. Right: TacitVLA matches Explicit Reasoning’s success at 1.7× and 3.4× lower latency, andmatches No Reasoning’s latency at +3.5% and+5.3% success (Tables 3, 5, 15).

Figure 3: TacitVLA matches the latency of No Reasoning on every benchmark, and Explicit Reasoning’s latency is 1.4× to 3.4× higher. Each bar is one policy’s latency per call: 𝑇action for No Reasoning and TacitVLA, and 𝑇action + 𝑇reason for Explicit Reasoning, whose actions wait for text generation. The ratio above each group is Explicit Reasoning’s latency over TacitVLA’s. On the memory tasks, TacitVLA generates the ledger entry during execution, taking at most 23% of the execution window, so the next call never waits for generation. All values are means over model calls on one H100, with the per-stage breakdown in Table 15 (Appendix C).

papers.abstract: World action models (WAMs) are a category of policy models that ex- plicitly predict both actions and future world states. They have been shown to outperform action-only models across various robotic manipulation tasks. How- ever, representing the future with full-frame video prediction can be computation- ally expensive during both training and inference. This raises a central question: what compact state representation preserves the planning and supervision bene- fits of future prediction? In this paper, we propose BoxWAM, which replaces dense future frames with oriented bounding box trajectories of task-relevant ob- jects. By explicitly imagining object-centric future motion, our method provides a lightweight prediction target that captures the key physical changes induced by robot actions. We show that box trajectory prediction substantially reduces com- putational cost while improving action prediction performance, suggesting that object-centric compact states can serve as an efficient alternative to video-based world action modeling for robotic manipulation. Result videos can be found on https://box-wam.github.io
authors: Qinxi Yu, Wenzhou Ding, Gloria X. Wang, Albert J. Zhai, Shenlong Wang
bullets: Addresses the high training and inference cost of dense future-frame prediction in world action models.
Represents task-relevant object motion with object-centric oriented bounding-box trajectories.
Uses predicted future object motion as a compact planning and supervision signal.
Reports substantially lower computational cost and improved action prediction performance.
Focuses on robotic manipulation; the abstract does not specify datasets or numeric results.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of BoxWAM. Observation images are encoded into visual context tokens, which condition a rectified-flow transformer that jointly denoises future state tokens and action tokens. An enforced causal attention allows action tokens to condition on imagined object motion while preventing future state tokens from depending on future action tokens. The decoded future state forms a compact box trajectory, and the decoded action tokens form the robot action chunk.

The first two columns show early and late coffee-making stages; the remaining columns show watering and toy placement. Each row shows a different frame, illustrating how BoxWAM predicts compact object-motion plans for action generation under real-world perception noise, actuation error, and object pose variation.

papers.abstract: Evaluating VLA policies on real robots is costly, time-consuming, and difficult to reproduce, making real-to-sim simulation essential for scalable evaluation. While 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables rapid real-to-sim scene generation, the reconstruction quality required for reliable policy evaluation remains unquantified. In particular, policies relying on wrist-mounted fisheye cameras (e.g., YUBI handheld gripper data) are heavily exposed to visual artifacts (holes, floaters) in wide-angle views, directly degrading task performance. To address this, we present YUBI-Real2Sim, a unified framework for 3DGS-based scene reconstruction and real-to-sim policy evaluation under dual fisheye wrist views. We develop an integrated pipeline combining 200-degree fisheye camera capture, 3DGS training, 3D foundation models for object modeling, and MuJoCo-based physical simulation, reproducing the observed real-world policy ordering in eight of nine scene-task comparisons. Using this framework, we construct a benchmark across two bimanual robot platforms, three scenes, three tasks, and dual pi0.5-based policies. This systematically measures real-to-sim rank agreement and evaluates policy sensitivity against counterfactual 3DGS artifacts (ceiling holes, floaters, warping) and capture disturbances. We further analyze whether novel-view quality scores can indicate policy-ranking reliability under a scene-held-out evaluation protocol. The results show task-dependent performance and limitations of quality-based reliability prediction, highlighting the need to assess reconstruction quality when using Real2Sim for policy evaluation. These results do not yet establish a generally reliable scene-acceptance rule. Project Page: https://yubi-real2sim.airoa.io.
authors: Hiroki Nishizawa, Takehiko Ohkawa, Nicola Scianca, Tatsuya Matsushima, Shigeo Morishima, Kei Ota
bullets: Addresses costly, difficult-to-reproduce real-robot policy evaluation through real-to-sim simulation.

Benchmarks two bimanual platforms, three scenes, three tasks, and two pi0.5-based policies, reproducing real-world policy ordering in 8 of 9 scene-task comparisons.
Tests policy sensitivity to ceiling holes, floaters, warping, and capture disturbances, and examines whether novel-view quality predicts ranking reliability.
Finds task-dependent effects and limitations of quality-based reliability prediction; no general scene-acceptance rule is established.

figures.caption: Figure 2 | YUBI-Real2Sim pipeline. We capture the background with a single 200◦ FOV camera, estimate camera poses with COLMAP, and densify the point cloud with OpenMVS to initialize Gaussian Wrapping for high-fidelity reconstruction. We generate object geometry and textures with TRELLIS 2.0 and approximate collision meshes with CoACD. The reconstructed scene and objects are integrated into MuJoCo simulation. For wrist-view rendering, we independently render the background Gaussians and the MuJoCo visual meshes, then composite their pixels using depth maps.

We evaluated two task-specific VLA checkpoints for each of three tasks (Cup, Tape, and Pen) in all three scenes (FR3 Flat, FR3 Duo, and TX-G2).

Policy labels are fixed within each task across scenes and domains. Error bars are marginal 95% Wilson confidence intervals from 20 real and 80 simulated trials per policy. The observed ranking agrees in 8/9 scene–task pairs (88.9%); Flat Cup is reversed.

Figure 1 | YUBI-Real2Sim analyzes and verifies 3DGS scenes for reliable policy-ranking evaluation. The quality of 3DGS can easily degrade depending on the camera views. We analyze how variations in 3DGS quality affect policy rankings and examine whether scene-quality scores can indicate policy-ranking reliability.

papers.abstract: As the complexity of space missions increases, autonomous spacecraft guidance must accommodate transitions between mission phases with distinct dynamics, objectives, and constraints. Rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) are particularly challenging because they span multiple operating regimes, from orbital-scale matching and far-range approach to close-range maneuvering and terminal docking. Existing reinforcement-learning approaches generally address only a subset of this sequence or rely on manually defined switching conditions between controllers. This study presents a hierarchical reinforcement-learning framework for autonomous, three-degree-of-freedom RPO that spans the complete trajectory from orbit matching to docking. Five specialized policies are trained for orbit matching, far-range approach, mid-range approach, close-range approach, and docking. A learned high-level manager policy then selects among these phase-specific controllers based on the evolving spacecraft state. The hierarchical approach is evaluated over the full end-to-end rendezvous sequence and compared with a fixed sequential-invocation heuristic to assess trajectory performance and transition behavior. Training and inference metrics are also analyzed for the individual phase policies and the complete hierarchical system.

papers.abstract: Precise control of movement across various robotic embodiments is a longstanding challenge. Modeling complex robotic structures requires significant time, dedicated sensors, and manual labeling. Recent advancements in 4D representation learning offer an interesting alternative: can we leverage 4D features lifted from 2D observations to densely map a robot's spatial movement based on the action signal? To this end, we propose Act4R, a framework that builds on 3D foundation model to predict a robot's 3D scene flow with any given action. Act4R introduces a Spatial-Action Encoder, which encodes the current 2D robot state and its action signals into embeddings that represent future robot state in 3D. Then, both the current and future spatial embeddings are decoded into point maps to estimate action-conditioned scene flow. To effectively learn the mapping between action and future state, Act4R introduces spatial-action fusion in its transformer-based encoder, and a spatial alignment loss that guides the encoder for future flow prediction. After training on some samples of a given embodiment, Act4R can perform inverse control by optimizing the signal to achieve the desired scene flow. We evaluate Act4R on a public real-world dataset and synthetic data collected in simulator. Experiments on various robotic platforms show that Act4R outperforms the previous SoTA in scene flow prediction. Our method also performs better in inverse control, both on the action accuracy metric and in closed-loop control in simulation.
authors: Zhaoliang Zhang, Chenhao Yu, Zhimin Shao, Xijun Liu, Cheng Peng
bullets: Addresses the costly modeling, sensing, and labeling required for precise control across robot embodiments.
Uses a 3D foundation model with a Spatial-Action Encoder to combine 2D robot observations and actions into future 3D spatial embeddings.
Decodes current and future embeddings into point maps and estimates action-conditioned 3D scene flow.
Introduces spatial-action fusion and a spatial alignment loss to improve future-flow prediction.
Outperforms prior state of the art in scene-flow prediction and improves inverse control on real-world and simulated data.

At inference time, It+1 is not used.

papers.abstract: Trajectory smoothness has been proposed as a cheap, training-free signal for curating imitation-learning demonstrations, most recently by rinse, which introduces Spectral Arc Length (SAL) and a contact-aware Trajectory-Envelope Distance (TED). We test whether these published metrics survive episode-length controls on real robomimic data. On can/mh, SAL separates better from worse operators with AUROC 0.952, but episode length alone achieves 0.957, and inside a duration-matched band SAL falls to 0.628 while raw mean jerk, the baseline rinse argues against, rises to 0.896. The confound replicates on square/mh. On can/mg, where every episode is exactly 150 steps, SAL is at chance (0.454) and TED is inverted (0.376) against task success, while jerk reaches 0.706. Training GMM behavior-cloning policies on each metric's curated subset (10 seeds), curating by TED costs roughly a third of downstream success relative to random selection of the same size (0.240 vs. 0.360, p=0.0001, surviving Bonferroni correction), while SAL and jerk are indistinguishable from not curating. Under a diffusion policy TED still ranks worst, though its deficit is not resolvable at five seeds, and jerk becomes significantly better than both baselines, so the curation decision does not transfer unchanged across the two policy configurations we tested. Inspecting trajectories shows why TED inverts: successful manipulation requires sustained high-deviation motion through contact, while failure is low-amplitude hovering that a smoothed envelope follows closely.
bullets: On can/mh, episode length alone slightly outperformed SAL; duration matching reduced SAL’s AUROC from 0.952 to 0.628, while mean jerk reached 0.896.
The confound replicated on square/mh; on fixed-length can/mg, SAL was near chance and TED was inversely associated with success, whereas jerk reached 0.706.
TED-curated data produced substantially worse GMM behavior-cloning performance than random selection, while SAL and jerk were not different from random curation.
Under diffusion policies, TED still ranked worst, but jerk became significantly better than both baselines, indicating policy-dependent curation effects.
Trajectory inspection suggests TED fails because successful contact requires sustained high-deviation motion, whereas unsuccessful hovering remains close to a smoothed envelope.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Failure stays inside the envelope; success does not. A successful (left) and failed (right) can/mg demonstration, with end-effector position, TED’s gripper-contact segment boundaries (red), the per-segment Bézier envelope (dashed), and the per-timestep envelope residual (bottom, orange bars are persegment means). Both trajectories contain one high-deviation segment, but in the success it spans timesteps 12–96 and coincides with the descend-and-grasp, while in the failure it is confined to the initial free-space approach (0–24) and the remaining 126 steps are a flat tail of repeated gripper cycles that never completes a placement. TED averages over the alignment path and so rates the failure as the cleaner trajectory. Illustrative of the mechanism only; the quantitative claim is Figure 2b.

Figure 1: What the four metrics reward, on illustrative synthetic data. Left: end-effector speed profiles of three synthetic pick-and-place demonstrations built from minimum-jerk segments between identical waypoints, with the same small band-limited jitter added to each (shaded: gripper closed). (a) is short and smooth. (b) is the same motion executed twice as slowly, so the episode is twice as long and every segment is just as smooth. (c) is (a) with a committed correction inserted before the grasp: lift, shift sideways, descend again. Right: how each metric ranks the three, computed with the implementations used throughout the paper, with every score given relative to the best of the three under that metric. SAL rates the slow copy (b) worst, by a wider margin than it charges the correction in (c). TED rates the correction (c) worst and the slow copy (b) best. Jerk also rates (c) worst and barely separates (a) from (b). Path length cannot separate (a) from (b), which travel the same route. Every ordering shown is stable across 30 noise seeds except the (a)/(b) near-tie under jerk, which swaps in about a third of them, and the (a)/(c) order under SAL, which swapped once (scripts/fig metric primer.py). Synthetic and illustrative only: no number in this figure is measured on robomimic.

Figure 2: Smoothness metrics rank duration, not quality. (a) Better-vs-worse operator AUROC on can/mh across duration bands of increasing tightness (shaded: 95% bootstrap CI). SAL (red) tracks the episode-length baseline (gray, dashed) almost exactly and falls from 0.952 to 0.628 as the band tightens; raw jerk (blue) moves the opposite way, 0.584 to 0.896; TED (green) never clears chance and inverts in the tightest band. In that band episode length itself is at chance (0.485), confirming the control. (b) On can/mg every episode is exactly 150 steps, so length carries no information by construction; against the task-success label, jerk retains signal (0.706), SAL is at chance (0.454), and TED is inverted (0.376).

papers.selection_reason: Audits trajectory-smoothness curation metrics for imitation-learning demonstrations and evaluates downstream behavior-cloning performance, fitting robot learning.
papers.title: Smoothness Ranks Skill, Not Success: An Audit of Published Trajectory-Smoothness Curation Metrics Under Episode-Length Controls
papers.tldr: Episode length can make trajectory-smoothness metrics appear skill-sensitive, while contact-aware TED may favor unsuccessful hovering over successful manipulation.

papers.abstract: Symmetry-aware robot policy learning requires coupled observation-action transformations. For pixel observations, even simple physical symmetries can induce complex, viewpoint-dependent image transformations that are difficult to specify by hand. Existing symmetry-aware methods often rely on representations with predefined transformations, requiring preprocessing tailored to the sensing setup and task. We introduce MIRROR, a framework that learns how a known symmetry group operates jointly on observations and actions in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) from offline interaction data. MIRROR couples these transformations through adversarial tuple matching over one-step transition tuples, while explicit group-consistency regularization penalizes violations of the group-operation axioms. On four Robosuite tabletop manipulation tasks, MIRROR achieves the lowest aggregate error on three of four symmetry-quality metrics, including a 61% reduction in compatibility error (which measures consistency under transformation composition) relative to an adapted LaLiGAN baseline. Using the learned transformations in frame-averaged behavior cloning (BC) yields higher mean success rates than vanilla BC on all four tasks, increasing average success from 80.48% to 85.12%, with per-task gains up to 9.66 percentage points. We also repeat symmetry discovery and policy training in simulation with heightmap and segmentation-mask observations, then deploy the resulting policy zero-shot on a real Kinova GEN3 arm. papers.abstract: Autonomous quadrotor flight in cluttered environment is an key capability for tasks like inspection and search. Navigation policies trained in simulation and transferred to hardware can fly at high speed in open space, but they can still collide as obstacle clearance shrinks. We attribute most of these collisions to a single mechanism, namely motion in directions the onboard camera does not observe. Heading that is not aligned with the direction of travel and lateral excursion during obstacle avoidance both carry the vehicle toward obstacles outside its field of view. We introduce ClearNav, a navigation policy trained with two reward terms that constrain motion to the observed direction, a forward-looking heading target and a penalty on lateral velocity. A third term penalizes speed near obstacles so that an obstacle entering the field of view remains avoidable. In simulation, across 18 held-out scenarios with 2304 paired flights per policy unseen in training, ClearNav improves success by 6.8 points, cuts the collision rate by 65% relative to the state of the arts, and flies at maximum 5m/s. For the proximity term alone under matched commanded speeds, the collision reduction still holds at 70%. The effect is significant on static scenes and consistent in direction on moving obstacles, though not significant there at the suite level, showing that safer flight in clutter is possible even on the limited sensors and compute of small drones. We also validate our navigation policy in a real-world cluttered environment, showing that it enables the quadrotor to navigate through the cluttered environment successfully and safely.

bullets: Targets a key failure mode in simulation-to-hardware flight: moving toward obstacles outside the onboard camera’s field of view.

Validated in a real-world cluttered environment, with consistent benefits on static scenes but no suite-level significance on moving obstacles.

papers.abstract: We use a frozen frontier vision-language model, GPT-6-Astra, directly as the robot policy on RoboMME, a benchmark of 16 memory-dependent manipulation tasks spanning temporal, spatial, object, and procedural memory. The model keeps the whole episode in context and outputs every end-effector waypoint and gripper command, with no RoboMME-specific training. On the 800 test episodes it succeeds in 92.1%, above the previously reported human score of 90.5%, which was obtained with an oracle skill interface, and far ahead of the best leaderboard entry (60.8%) and of a hierarchical system that pairs the same model with a RoboMME-trained policy (79.1%). It matches or exceeds the human score on 13 of the 16 tasks. Its 63 failures concentrate in two tasks and are mostly premature completions and mistimed or unintended button presses. These results blur the usual division between long-horizon planning, memory and end-effector control, and raise the question of how much of this stack a single general-purpose model can take over in embodied systems. papers.abstract: Household robots must successfully navigate im-perfect circumstances, both in their internal models and the external world. We introduce a benchmark of seven long-horizon household tasks in Habitat that vary initial robot memory and environment configurations. We evaluate adaptations of ReAct, VLM-TAMP, and Tru-POMDP within a shared execution framework across 90 tasks-environment-memory combinations, totaling 1,350 episodes. Our evaluation measures task success, partial completion, and action efficiency, along with rule-based analysis of execution traces. ReAct achieves the highest overall task success (45.3%) and completion (71.7%), while having accurate initial memory does not consistently yield the highest performance for every planner. We identify recurring placement errors, precondition errors, and redundant actions through trace analysis. These findings highlight differences in how the evaluated planners use initial knowledge and respond to uncertainty.

papers.abstract: In this work, we explore the idea of expert intervention delays in human-supervised robotic systems for imitation learning system. Previous works in imitation learning have primarily examined the impact of suboptimal experts, where the expert policy makes mistakes, but assumed expert interventions occur immediately after errors are made. Although delayed expert intervention can be viewed as a form of noise that might improve policy robustness, our results show that learning from delayed expert interventions is overall less effective than learning from non-delayed expert interventions; delayed expert interventions are less effective at demonstrating error avoidance behaviors. To address this, we propose Learning from Delayed Intervention (LfDI), which learns a cost function based on where and when the expert intervenes, combined with limited information about the extent of intervention delays provided by the expert. This cost function is then used to infer additional supervision for states without expert data, guiding the policy to avoid states that would likely trigger interventions. We evaluate our method, Learning from Delayed Intervention (LfDI), on simulated environments and show that it outperforms other methods that do not account for intervention delays.
authors: Xiru Zhu, David Meger, Gregory Dudek
bullets: Delayed interventions are less effective than immediate interventions at teaching error-avoidance behavior.

papers.abstract: SE(3)-equivariance provides a useful geometric inductive bias for visuomotor policies, encoding that actions covary with rigid transformations of the observation. However, existing SE(3)-equivariant visuomotor policies build this bias on a global equivariance assumption that treats the entire observation as governed by a single rigid transformation, which breaks down in real-world manipulation tasks where the task-relevant region changes across different objects. We address this by learning a phase-conditioned affordance field (PAF) over the observed point cloud, a per-point score that the SE(3)-equivariant policy uses in two complementary ways. Its score-weighted centroid serves as a learned, phase-conditioned anchor that canonicalizes the observation and the action around the active region, replacing the fixed gripper-frame reference, and the score itself is appended as a per-point feature. This introduces a local geometric inductive bias, while preserving the policy's global SE(3) equivariance. We validate on multiple MimicGen tasks under varying spatial randomization, and PAF consistently improves the success rate of the underlying policy. On multi-object real-robot tasks, PAF outperforms baselines and keeps its lead under lighting variations.

papers.tldr: Phase-conditioned affordance fields add a learned, local geometric reference to SE(3)-equivariant visuomotor policies, improving manipulation robustness across changing active regions and visual conditions.

papers.abstract: Robots sharing walkways need to know where people will be, yet semantic occupancy maps show only where they are. We present ReForesight, an open-source ROS 2 toolkit that adds instance-level future occupancy and re-identification after occlusion to a particle-based semantic mapping pipeline. A 36.6k-parameter MLP predicts each tracked person or vehicle up to 3 s ahead, guarded by a Kalman fallback and a stationary gate, and the object's own points are moved to the forecast pose, forming a "ghost" point cloud in the map frame without an occupancy decoder. An optional tracker re-associates objects after occlusion using keypoint descriptors the pipeline already computes and a metric 3D gate. On four held-out CODa sequences, the MLP lowers the mean 3 s final displacement error from 0.728 m (Kalman) to 0.662 m and beats a similar-size GRU (0.692 m) on every sequence, at 0.04 ms per instance on one CPU core. Code, all models, and a ROS-free demo are released; field demonstrations use an outdoor cleaning robot.
authors: Didar Seyidov, Faith Ogunwoye, Hajira Amjad, Danil Tolkachev, Yuri Sarkisov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: Extends particle-based semantic mapping with instance-level future occupancy and post-occlusion re-identification.
Uses a 36.6k-parameter MLP, with Kalman fallback and a stationary-object gate, to forecast motion up to 3 seconds.
Moves tracked objects’ point clouds to predicted poses to create map-frame “ghost” occupancy without an occupancy decoder.
Optional re-association combines existing keypoint descriptors with a metric 3D gate.

On four held-out CODa sequences, the MLP achieves 0.662 m mean 3-second final displacement error versus 0.728 m for Kalman and 0.692 m for a similar-size GRU; runtime is 0.04 ms per instance on one CPU core.

papers.abstract: Learning symmetries through data augmentation offers an alternative to architectural equivariance, but does not guarantee that a network respects those symmetries. Measuring learned equivariance is especially difficult for intermediate representations, whose group actions are not specified. In a finite discrete setting, we show that equivariance requires representations of original and transformed inputs to determine one another exactly, yielding a test based on normalized mutual information (NMI). For high-dimensional activations, we use centered kernel alignment (CKA) as a scalable test, with an exact guarantee for orthogonal feature transformations. Across architectures and tasks, augmentation usually increases transformation consistency, showing that learned equivariance can be probed directly from representations without recovering the hidden transformation rules that relate them.
authors: Claire Schlesinger, Wolfgang Gatterbauer, Robin Walters
bullets: Data augmentation can encourage, but does not guarantee, equivariant behavior.
For finite discrete representations, equivariance requires original and transformed representations to determine each other exactly.
Normalized mutual information (NMI) provides a test for this exact recoverability.
Centered kernel alignment (CKA) offers a scalable test for high-dimensional activations, with guarantees for orthogonal feature transformations.
Across architectures and tasks, augmentation generally increases transformation consistency.

Table 5: Changing the granularity of what mutual information sees from 4 bits to the full 16 bits shows that the null reading rises with it due to the larger alphabet, making mutual information a much worse measure the more unique outputs there are. In a continuous space with infinite outputs, mutual information is not only intractable to compute, but also loses its ability to distinguish real equivariance from scrambles.

Table 8: Comparison on SEIS equivariance measure between spatial and channel re-encoding. SEIS is able to detect spatial re-encodings but not channel re-encodings and is therefore unable to detect equivariance of steerable models.

Table 7: LieGG makes an assumption that the input space has to be equivariant and the output space has to be invariant to rotation. Purposely building a model that has an equivariant output space shows that LieGG is unable to detect it.

The ∥∇∥ column is the mechanism: LEE = ∥LXf∥/∥f∥ is invariant to uniformly rescaling the features but not to their being nearly constant, where the numerator vanishes and the denominator does not. The untrained network’s input gradient is over 700× smaller than the others’. LieGG normalizes by its polarization matrix’s largest singular value, where rescaling cancels, and is unaffected.

Table 3: Measuring equivariance after a Laplace operation is applied to the discretized images. The transformation is applied so we have a more interesting probability distribution under transformations. Under certain operations applied to the output we see how CKA, MI, and SVCCA either fails or succeeds to detect equivariance. SVCCA is able to detect one more group than CKA, but lacks an unbiased estimator, so we chose to utilize CKA.

Table 2: CKA versus MI on a discrete set of data points. We apply the Laplacian to the input image, then either keep the output unchanged, scramble the alphabet (relabel outputs while keeping points with the same label together), or merge the alphabet (map multiple distinct outputs to the same value). CKA reads the lossless relabeling as non-equivariant, while MI correctly detects equivariance. A high null indicates the metric may be less informative due to a large alphabet.

Equivariance error is ∥f(gx) − ρ(g)f(x)∥/∥ρ(g)f(x)∥ with ρ(g) read off escnn’s declared FieldType, so it is ground truth rather than a competing estimate. The null is the shuffled control: the pairing between the clean and rotated branches is destroyed while marginals, dimensionality and sample count are held fixed. θ = 2.0 rad (114.6◦), 256 MNIST images.

Table 1: NMI between filtered original and rotated images for the Sobel-X filter (not C4-equivariant) and the Laplacian (C4-equivariant) on a restricted, discretized image set. The Laplacian stays at 1. Sobel-X is C2-equivariant and anti-commutes, so it reads 1 at 180◦; a metric assuming the output action matches the input action would report a large error here, but NMI detects the equivariance without being told the action is a sign flip.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes a general method to measure learned equivariance in representations, transferable to evaluating equivariant visuomotor and robot policies.
papers.title: Measuring Learned Equivariance: An Information Theoretic Approach
papers.tldr: The paper introduces information-theoretic tests for measuring whether learned representations respect symmetries without explicitly recovering their hidden transformation rules.

papers.abstract: Search-based policy learning, such as Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS), offers the flexibility to trade runtime computation for data efficiency and adaptation to novel environments. For robot learning, however, applying search requires discretizing the continuous action space and associated dynamics, typically through action quantization. While reconstruction-based quantization is sufficient for representing the continuous action space alone, policy learning additionally requires the quantized actions to preserve their effects on future states and values. We show that such requirement is not necessarily captured by action reconstruction error. Instead, we prove that the error in the value function resulting from action quantization is tightly bounded by the reconstruction error of state reachability under the quantized actions. Based on these results, we propose value-preserving action quantization (VAQ), which quantizes actions by preserving state reachability. We further combine VAQ with MCTS (VAQ-MCTS) as a value-preserving, search-based policy learning framework for behavioral cloning. Using a wide range of object pushing tasks as a controlled benchmark, we evaluate VAQ-MCTS against state-of-the-art behavioral cloning methods. VAQ-MCTS matches or exceeds their performance under standard settings, while substantially improving data efficiency and robustness to heterogeneous demonstrations, while enabling zero-shot adaptation to novel environments. Hardware experiments further demonstrate the effectiveness of VAQ-MCTS, completing all 30 real-world object pushing trials with only 10 minutes of demonstration data.
authors: Max Muchen Sun, Jueun Kwon, Benjamin Riviere, Todd Murphey
bullets: Action reconstruction error alone may not preserve the values relevant to policy learning.
Theoretical analysis bounds value-function error by state-reachability reconstruction error under quantized actions.
VAQ quantizes actions to preserve state reachability and is integrated with MCTS in VAQ-MCTS.
On object-pushing benchmarks, VAQ-MCTS matches or exceeds behavioral cloning baselines while improving data efficiency, robustness to heterogeneous demonstrations, and zero-shot adaptation.
Hardware trials completed all 30 real-world object-pushing tasks using 10 minutes of demonstration data.

papers.selection_reason: Value-preserving action quantization for search-based robot policy learning and manipulation.
papers.title: Value-Preserving Action Quantization
papers.tldr: Value-Preserving Action Quantization discretizes robot actions by preserving their effects on future states, enabling more data-efficient and adaptable search-based policy learning.

papers.abstract: Navigating humanoid robots through dynamic, non-convex environments requires tightly coupling onboard perception with footstep planning and dynamic locomotion control. Existing methods frequently discard complex free space through simplified convex obstacle bounds and fail to account for real-time dynamic occupancy predictions. This paper presents a real-time framework for humanoid navigation that directly constructs spatio-temporal safe corridors from LiDAR-based particle representations and couples them with Linear Inverted Pendulum (LIP)-based planning and Whole Body Control (WBC) to enable navigation around and within moving non-convex structures without restrictive geometric assumptions. Simulations on the Digit humanoid yield a 96% success rate in navigating around and inside moving non-convex obstacles in a 24 by 24 m^2 arena. Ablation studies confirm that the proposed iterative polytope generation significantly outperforms single-iteration baselines in narrow corridors, while evaluations demonstrate robustness to clutter, sensor noise, control delays, and force perturbations.
bullets: Addresses the loss of usable free space and poor handling of dynamic occupancy in existing navigation methods.
Builds spatio-temporal safe corridors directly from LiDAR-based particle representations without restrictive convex obstacle assumptions.
Couples corridor generation with Linear Inverted Pendulum planning and Whole Body Control for dynamic locomotion.
In Digit simulations, achieves a 96% success rate around and inside moving non-convex obstacles in a 24 × 24 m² arena.
Shows improved narrow-corridor performance with iterative polytope generation and robustness to clutter, sensor noise, delays, and force perturbations.

(b) Corresponding safe corridors generated by the proposed algorithm and the future occupancy maps for the regions highlighted by the black boxes in (a). Five prediction windows are illustrated, with the first shown in green and the color gradually transitioning to red for the fifth prediction window. The green circle represents the goal position inside the gray-colored U-shaped moving object. (c) Success rates for three arena scales, force perturbations, measurement noise, and delays. (d) Success rates for varying narrow-corridor widths for both iterative and non-iterative cases. (e) Computation time of each module for a successful experiment in each of the three arena scales. The center of each bar represents the mean computation time, while the upper and lower extents indicate one standard deviation.

papers.selection_reason: Presents real-time humanoid navigation with spatio-temporal safe corridors in dynamic non-convex environments, directly relevant to embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: LiDAR-based Humanoid Navigation in Dynamic, Non-Convex Environments via Spatio-Temporal Safe Corridors
papers.tldr: A real-time LiDAR-driven framework enables Digit humanoid navigation through moving, non-convex environments using spatio-temporal safe corridors coupled with footstep and whole-body control.

papers.abstract: What information does a reinforcement learning policy omit? At each state, a standard policy stores one probability per action. It has no place to record how actions relate to each other, such as which pairs go together and which conflict. We ask when this missing structure matters, and we give exact answers. We store the policy at each state as a density matrix, a positive semidefinite, unit-trace matrix borrowed from quantum information theory. We use it here as a purely classical data structure, computed on ordinary classical hardware. The diagonal holds the usual action probabilities. The off-diagonal entries, called coherences, are new parameters. This gives density-matrix reinforcement learning (DMRL). Coherences change outcomes in two settings. First, suppose a policy is regularized toward a coherent reference policy using matrix relative entropy. The optimum then has coherences that no diagonal reference policy produces, and its action probabilities can depend on the reference policy's coherences. This is relevant to fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs) with a Kullback--Leibler penalty. Second, suppose the agent chooses a unit-vector action and the reward is a quadratic function of that vector. This could arise when an LLM judge scores a weighted consolidation of reasoning paths, or when coupled robotic sensors each respond to a mix of actions. Then some coherent policies earn strictly more expected reward than every classical policy with the same action probabilities, and we give the margin in closed form. In a two-action example, both policies assign probability $0.5$ to each action, yet the classical one earns expected reward $0$ while the coherent one earns $1$, the maximum. Outside these two settings, DMRL matches or transfers the classical results. This is a theory paper. All results are proved, and we report no empirical evaluation.
bullets: Standard policies record action probabilities but not relationships such as action compatibility or conflict.
DMRL represents each state policy as a positive semidefinite, unit-trace density matrix; its diagonal gives probabilities and off-diagonal terms encode coherences.
With matrix-relative-entropy regularization, coherent reference policies can induce optimal coherences and alter action probabilities, including in LLM fine-tuning with a KL penalty.
For unit-vector actions with quadratic rewards, coherent policies can outperform every classical policy sharing the same action probabilities; a two-action example reaches reward 1 versus 0.
The paper is theoretical: it proves the results and reports no empirical evaluation.

figures.caption: Table 1: Operator concepts and their classical analogues. Setting the off-diagonal entries of ρ (and of ρ′ and O, where relevant) to zero recovers the right-hand column. The diagonal is unchanged by this operation. The coherences have no classical counterpart because they vanish.

Table 2: Two action models. The standard basis vectors ei are unit vectors, and choosing x = ±ei earns x⊤Ox = Oii, the reward of action ai. So an agent that chooses only ±e1, . . . ,±ek is exactly the left column. This restriction is the classical baseline used throughout this subsection.

papers.selection_reason: Novel RL policy representation with coherent action structure; transferable to robot learning and LLM fine-tuning settings.
papers.title: Density-Matrix Reinforcement Learning
papers.tldr: Density-Matrix Reinforcement Learning augments action probabilities with coherence terms, enabling provable benefits in regularized policies and quadratic-reward settings while recovering classical RL otherwise.

papers.abstract: Cutting a piece of food looks effortless in human hands. For a robot, however, every cut is a high-contact interaction with a deformable, elasto-plastic object whose behavior changes with pose, contact mode, and cutting stage. Collecting real-world data is expensive and wasteful: each trial typically contaminates or damages the food, so obtaining scalable real world data for dexterous cutting is expensive and difficult. Simulation is an appealing alternative, but a large sim-to-real gap exists in both physics and perception. This gap is especially severe for topology-changing interactions like cutting, where small errors in contact, friction, or material and elasticity responses quickly compound. We propose \textsc{DexNinja}, a real2sim2real framework that turns a handful of real demonstrations into a dense and realistic training distribution. \textsc{DexNinja} (i) reconstructs object instances from real captures, (ii) randomizes physically meaningful parameters under category-level constraints, and (iii) produces augmented dexterous manipulation episodes using a custom differentiable simulator that couples robot dynamics, tactile contact, and deformable cutting. We evaluate \textsc{DexNinja} on a dexterous food-slicing task and show that (1) with tens of real demonstrations and hundreds of augmented simulator data, the success rate could reach more than 60\%. (2) the augmented data consistently improves success rates when only using real data with more than 20\% via sim-to-real, and (3) the resulting policies generalize to out-of-distribution objects with varying shapes and sizes.
authors: Haozhe Lou, Runyi Yang, Wanqi Zhong, Caiyun Liu, Yicheng Liu, Wenhao Liu, Wenlong Ma, Jiawei Xia, Kanzhi Wu, Danda Pani Paudel, Luc Van Gool, Hang Zhao, Yiming Li
bullets: Dexterous cutting is difficult because it involves high-contact interactions with deformable objects and changing contact dynamics.

The framework reconstructs objects from real captures, randomizes physically meaningful parameters, and generates episodes in a differentiable simulator coupling robot, tactile, and deformable-cutting dynamics.
Using tens of real demonstrations plus hundreds of simulated episodes, the evaluated policy achieved over 60% success on food slicing.
Simulation augmentation improved success by more than 20% compared with using real data alone.
Policies generalized to unseen objects with different shapes and sizes.

papers.abstract: Achieving complex, long-horizon robot behavior remains challenging because successful execution depends on skills grounded in a robot's physical affordances. Existing training-task distributions are often handcrafted or sampled from large language models (LLMs), relying on semantic plausibility rather than embodiment-specific feasibility. This mismatch can produce curricula that are too difficult, redundant, or blind to non-obvious but learnable behaviors. We propose Generative Flow on Symbolic Abstractions (FOSA), a framework for discovering embodiment-specific capabilities by learning a grounded task generator. FOSA parameterizes an abstract policy as a Generative Flow Network that constructs symbolic task skeletons. Each skeleton is compiled into a simulation environment, where low-level policy-learning performance provides the reward signal for the abstract policy. Across heterogeneous robot platforms, FOSA discovers diverse and executable tasks near the robot's empirical capability frontier. After distilling the discovered task policies into a single language-conditioned policy, FOSA improves performance on unseen complex and long-horizon tasks. The code and demonstration videos are available at https://www.youwei-yu.com/fosa.
bullets: Addresses the mismatch between semantically plausible task curricula and tasks that are feasible for a robot’s physical embodiment.
Builds symbolic task skeletons with a Generative Flow Network and compiles them into simulation environments.
Uses low-level policy-learning performance as the reward for discovering tasks near each robot’s empirical capability frontier.
Works across heterogeneous robot platforms and finds diverse, executable behaviors.
Distilling the discovered policies into one language-conditioned policy improves performance on unseen complex, long-horizon tasks.

papers.abstract: Teleoperation is widely used to collect high-quality demonstrations for robot learning. Dexterous manipulation, however, requires coordinated control of motion and contact forces. Operators can specify motion, but struggle to reproduce the subtle force adjustments of human manipulation without feeling the robot's contacts. We introduce Force-Modulated Dexterity (FOMO-Dex), a unified compliance formulation for contact-rich manipulation. FOMO-Dex expresses nominal actions in coordinates defined by task geometry and contact structure. It applies force-driven motion corrections along selected directions while leaving the remaining command components unchanged. Across card picking, paper cutting, screwdriving, and nut-and-bolt assembly, FOMO-Dex reduces excessive contact forces compared with stiff control. A user study shows that operators collect more successful demonstration data per hour after brief practice. For policy learning, imitating the corrected actions improves card-picking success over imitating raw operator commands. Policies trained on FOMO-Dex demonstrations also achieve more rotation in nut-and-bolt manipulation and screwdriving than those trained on demonstrations collected with the stiff controller. Videos are shown on https://yingyuan0414.github.io/fomo-dex/ .

Represents actions using task geometry and contact structure, then applies force-driven corrections only along selected directions.
Reduces excessive contact forces across card picking, paper cutting, screwdriving, and nut-and-bolt assembly compared with stiff control.
Helps operators collect more successful demonstrations per hour after brief practice.
Learning from corrected demonstrations improves card-picking success and rotational performance in nut-and-bolt manipulation and screwdriving.

papers.abstract: Frontier large language models (LLMs) now reason about space well enough to program robots, yet the world models behind robot policies are implicit, held in network weights or predicted video, and cannot be inspected or corrected directly. We present D-World, an explicit world-language-action model built on the Sense, Plan and Act decomposition. A perception agent writes the scene as an executable digital twin using generated vision and geometry code. A planning agent searches for actions in simulation and, after each executed action chunk, revises the twin's object states and named physical parameters against what the robot measured. A parameter revision is accepted only if replaying the latest chunk does not increase any measured residual beyond its tolerance, and every chunk is checked in the updated twin before it runs. Structural mismatches return to perception for reconstruction. We call this measurement-grounded cycle of correction and revision recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which the LLM stays frozen while the world it acts in improves. We model the choice of actions that both advance the task and expose model error as a dual control problem and show that the cost of incorporating evidence into the twin sets the threshold at which probing pays, so cheap local revision counteracts the turn-off of cautious controllers. Each episode runs a real-to-sim-to-real loop, and its recorded twins can be refitted and re-rendered offline into higher-fidelity environments for post-training. Because perception and planning communicate only through the twin and language, either can be replaced by a learned model, and since inference dominates the loop, the loop speeds up with faster models. On a dual-arm robot, towel and toaster tasks show local revisions, such as one reducing the bread's rendered-depth residual from 22.4 to 1.5 mm, that let execution continue without reconstruction.
bullets: Addresses the opacity and lack of direct correction in implicit robot world models.
Uses a Sense–Plan–Act architecture where perception builds an executable scene twin and planning searches for actions in simulation.
Revises object states and physical parameters after each action chunk, accepting updates only when replayed measurements remain within residual tolerances.
Frames information-seeking actions as dual control, balancing task progress with exposing and correcting model errors.
Demonstrates real-to-sim-to-real operation on dual-arm towel and toaster tasks, including local corrections that avoid full scene reconstruction.

figures.caption: Figure 1: D-World, an explicit world-language-action model. Implicit models (left) keep the world in network weights or predicted video. D-World (right) writes it as an executable twin. SENSE constructs the twin, PLAN proposes trajectories and twin revisions, and a gate checks each action chunk before execution. Measurements of the real robot drive state correction and replay-checked parameter revision (RSI), and the dashed path requests reconstruction. In a bread-grasp episode, the twin shows both grippers open, ACTION shows the robot holding a lifted bread slice, and the measurement pair compares this post-lift observation with the reconstructed twin. In the language channel, PLAN asks and SENSE answers.

Figure 2: Replay-checked revision after a failed lift. In a failed bread grasp, the real bread remains in its rack while the twin lifts it with the gripper. Reducing the modeled thickness reproduces the slip during replay and reduces both the depth and the closure residual. Friction, to which this chunk is insensitive, is left unchanged. The revision passes the non-regression check and is accepted, and the next chunk attempts another grasp without reconstruction. Here j is the latest executed round and t the revision round. An earlier thickness proposal had increased the residual on the preceding chunk and was rejected.

Figure 3: Towel handling. (a) The top row shows camera images and the initial twin rendered from the same cameras, and the bottom row selected interaction and reconstruction stages, numbered by chunk. Dashed outlines mark the grasp mismatch between the twin and the robot, after which reconstruction changes the towel representation to match its observed configuration. (b) Where the time goes in the same episode. SENSE is blue, lighter while it answers a question, PLAN is orange, and the robot’s chunks are green with the numbers of (a). The bottom lanes magnify the three chunks between the two reconstructions. Model inference fills almost the entire hour, whereas the robot moves for seconds per chunk.

Figure 4: From episodes to high-fidelity worlds. (a) Each episode records observations, twins, controls and revisions. (b) Versioned libraries collect agent-written skills, such as perception and motion primitives, and scene bodies from completed episodes, whose parameters RSI has validated against the robot’s measurements. (c) Offline, recorded chunks are replayed jointly to refit parameters, and the refitted twin is rendered again with the same geometry, here in MuJoCo and in Blender. Skills and assets can be reused in later episodes, and refitted twins can serve post-training.

papers.abstract: Existing embodied navigation tasks commonly assume that traversability and object states remain fixed during an episode. Yet reaching a goal may require opening a door to access a room and then opening a container to reveal a hidden target. We formulate interactive navigation beyond reachability, unifying channel-induced changes in spatial connectivity, container-induced changes in target visibility, and their sequential dependencies. We introduce MultINav-Bench, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark in MolmoSpaces spanning channel, container, and mixed tasks, with interaction-necessity annotations covering required and unnecessary episodes. Its data generation pipeline automates task construction across multiple task types. The evaluation protocol separately measures navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and cost. We further propose MultINav-Agent, a three-stage agentic framework built on a persistent, state-conditioned interaction graph. Semantic interactive perception grounds entities and interaction states; a vision-language model selects task-relevant actions based on expected changes in connectivity and target observability; and post-interaction verification updates the graph to guide subsequent navigation, exploration, or interaction. Experiments on MultINav-Bench show that MultINav-Agent consistently outperforms adapted baselines across channel, container, and mixed tasks.
authors: Delun Li, Xueyao Wei, Rui Chen, Yifei Wang, Junzhi Yu, Wenjie Song, Xingyu Chen
bullets: Models navigation where interactions change spatial connectivity, target visibility, or both sequentially.
Introduces MultINav-Bench, a 3K-episode ObjectGoal benchmark covering channel, container, and mixed tasks with interaction-necessity annotations.
Evaluates navigation success, interaction effectiveness, and interaction cost separately.

Reports consistent improvements over adapted baselines across all task types.
