papers.abstract: Generative policies such as diffusion models provide expressive data-driven priors for robot behavior, yet the situations a robot faces at execution time rarely match its training data and impose constraints and objectives the policy never learned. Existing inference-time guidance methods either rely on gradients that can push samples away from the learned prior, or on sampling procedures that can be inefficient, collapse modes, or average them into out-of-distribution predictions. We introduce MOSAIC, a mode- and support-aware framework for gradient-free inference-time control of robotic diffusion models. MOSAIC treats the initial noise and all stochastic reverse-step perturbations as a joint input to the pretrained denoising process and adapts a distribution over this input using importance weights computed from fully denoised outputs. Physical feasibility and consistency with the learned support are balanced using adaptive penalties, while mode-wise importance-weighted updates preserve modes and avoid destructive averaging. The same formulation can jointly steer multiple independently trained diffusion models through shared coupling costs, enabling coordinated behavior without requiring a joint model. We evaluate MOSAIC on navigation, dexterous grasping, motion planning with unseen geometry, and collaborative box manipulation with independently trained robot priors. Across these settings, MOSAIC adapts and composes frozen diffusion priors under new deployment constraints without retraining.
authors: Sabrina Bodmer, Rahel Rickenbach, Ren\'e Zurbr\"ugg, Melanie N. Zeilinger, Colin Jones
bullets: Addresses deployment constraints and objectives not represented during diffusion-policy training.
Adapts the joint distribution of initial noise and reverse-process perturbations using importance weights on fully denoised outputs.
Balances physical feasibility with support consistency through adaptive penalties and preserves modes with mode-wise updates.
Can coordinate independently trained diffusion models using shared coupling costs, without a joint model or retraining.
Evaluated across navigation, dexterous grasping, unseen-geometry planning, and collaborative manipulation tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 3: Overview of the evaluated tasks. From left to right: (I) Robot Navigation, where a mobile robot must find feasible paths through a 2D environment; (II) Grasping, where a robotic manipulator must generate collision-free grasps in clutter; (III) Path Planning, where a robot arm must find a collision-free trajectory from a start to a goal configuration; and (IV) Collaborative Box Manipulation, where two arms must jointly move a box to a target pose without dropping or crushing it.

Fig. 2: MOSAIC evaluates complete denoising rollouts and updates each solution mode separately. A reverse-process input consists of the initial diffusion noise xT and all reverse-step perturbations δT , . . . , δ1. The frozen model maps this input to a clean prediction x0, on which arbitrary task, physical, support, and coupling costs can be evaluated. The clean predictions are grouped into modes, and a separate importance-weighted update is performed for each mode.

Fig. 5: Real-world collaborative manipulation. Each row shows one MOSAIC rollout from grasp establishment (left) through transport to the target pose (right). The two arms use independently trained frozen diffusion priors coupled only at inference time through Eq. (28).
Fig. 1: Inference-time composition. MOSAIC couples independent diffusion priors through a shared objective, enabling coordinated behavior without joint training.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models show strong potential for end-to-end autonomous driving by leveraging world knowledge and understanding to excel in long-tail scenarios. However, current VLAs have two limitations: 1) Degeneration into vision-action (VA) models. For low latency, regression/flow-based methods directly generate actions but underuse VLM understanding, causing unsafe, unexplainable actions. 2) Autoregressive high latency. Autoregressive methods sequentially generate chain-of-thought (CoT) and action tokens, fully leveraging VLM understanding, but high latency hinders deployment. To enable low-latency deployment while using CoT to assist action generation, we propose AUGUstus, an Autonomous-driving VLA model with Unified Generation and Understanding. We unify diffusion-based action generation and autoregressive CoT understanding in one model, where understanding only serves generation. Joint CoT supervision preserves VLM spatial understanding in shared representation for safer, more accurate trajectories. AUGUstus-mode orders action generation before CoT, so CoT supervises reliable actions during training while inference needs only action output, enabling low latency. AUGUstus-GRPO, a unified GRPO algorithm, jointly optimizes action and CoT, improving action performance. Experiments show AUGUstus achieves 94.6 PDMS on NAVSIMv1 and 90.7 EPDMS on NAVSIMv2, SOTA planning without scorer module. On nuScenes, it achieves average L2 error 0.27 m and average collision rate 0.05%, best among compared methods. To validate AUGUstus practicality, we train on in-house data with 512 NVIDIA H800 GPUs for ~2 days, evaluate on an internal 1,000 km dataset, and preliminarily deploy on a real vehicle, achieving 12 Hz operation. Project page: https://augustus-ad.github.io
authors: Yuqi Ye, Caigao Jiang, Zhuonan Wang, Congyuan Pei, Chao Qu, Changhao Peng, Junhong Lin, Qize Yu, Zetian Song, Guangzhao Fu, Chongruo Wu, Shiyu Huang, Shuchang Zhou, Honggou Yang, Wei Gao

papers.abstract: Offline reinforcement learning aims to learn effective policies from fixed datasets without environment interaction. Although generative models such as diffusion and flow matching enhance policy expressiveness, they typically start from uninformative Gaussian noise and generate actions through multi-step iteration, leading to high computational costs and failing to effectively leverage suboptimal trajectories in datasets. We propose MeanFlow2Better (MF2B), which reformulates offline RL as generative decision chunk optimization from current performance status to better performance status in a high-level latent decision space. MF2B maps trajectory chunks to high-level latent decision representations through an encoder, placing generation starting points within a structured decision space sculpted by behavioral data. The model learns a shared conditional mean velocity field in this space, constructing two flow mappings: from Gaussian-Induced Decision Sources toward positive behavioral decision regions, and from suboptimal decisions toward high-value decision regions. Both flow mappings complete decision refinement through one-step ODE integration over the unit time interval $\Delta t=1$, requiring neither multi-step iterative sampling nor backpropagation through time. Furthermore, we propose hierarchical chunk-level advantage to guide the flow direction toward high-return regions, where the high-level decisions cover multiple low-level actions, leading to sequence length compression from $T$ to $K \approx T/H$ and significantly lower computational overhead. On the D4RL Gym-MuJoCo benchmark, MF2B achieves an average score of 90.91, matching or surpassing strong baselines.
authors: Shenghua Lu, Zixuan Yang, Rongxu Zhao, Bohao Qu, Jifeng Hu, Hechang Chen

Uses hierarchical chunk-level advantages to guide refinement while compressing sequences from T to approximately T/H.
Achieves an average score of 90.91 on D4RL Gym-MuJoCo, matching or surpassing strong baselines.

papers.abstract: Physical AI is commonly formulated around an explicitly specified task: given a goal or instruction, a system perceives, reasons, and acts. In many real-world settings, however, important tasks emerge from continuously changing world states before a person explicitly formulates them. We study this complementary problem as Proactive Physical AI, where an AI system continuously observes the physical world, identifies situations that warrant intervention, and initiates appropriate actions at the right time. We develop ProAgent, an end-to-end system built around two components: a Jev-style proactive timing model (dubbed StreamingJev) that determines whether and when intervention is needed, and a Response Model that generates responses for people or invokes available device capabilities for physical execution. To support learning at scale, we develop an automated data pipeline that converts videos into supervision for proactive timing. Experiments demonstrate strong proactive performance under both explicit objectives and standing roles, combining more accurate intervention timing with fewer false triggers than the source-backbone baseline. Real-robot evaluations further demonstrate ProAgent's ability to identify emerging needs and translate them into appropriate physical actions.
authors: Zhenhua Yang, Jiafeng Liang, Xingyu Zhou, Yi Jiang, Xiayu Cao, Zui Chen, Luqi Wang, Haiyang Sun, Yufei Xiang, Chang Li, Rongchuan Mu, Bowen Chi, Zihe Tong, Mingyu Li, Huijie Ma, Yiqiao Yang, Baoqi Ren, Zhiming Ma, Zhihao Zhu, Jiahao Ji, Zhuoyao Wang, Qianyu Wang, Xiangyu Liu, Wang Zixiang, Shunliang Zhang, Ming Liu, Xiaocheng Feng, Duyu Tang, Bing Qin
bullets: Addresses proactive intervention in changing physical environments, where tasks arise before users specify them.
Combines StreamingJev for deciding whether and when to intervene with a Response Model for generating human or device actions.
Uses an automated video-to-supervision pipeline to support scalable learning of proactive timing.
Experiments show more accurate timing and fewer false triggers than the source-backbone baseline across explicit objectives and standing roles.
Real-robot evaluations demonstrate detection of emerging needs followed by appropriate physical actions.

figures.caption: Figure 1. ProAgent architecture. Both models consume the causal world stream asynchronously; the Response Model can accumulate context while the Timing Model (StreamingJev) remains silent. A response decision enables output generation, not the ingestion of observations. Human-facing text is passed to external TTS. Physical outputs use typed function calls, while runtime validation and dispatch connect them to device providers. Feedback returns to the continuing observation loop.

Figure 2. Event-driven supervision with causal model inputs. Offline annotators use full videos to identify event context and intervention windows, while model inputs at time t contain only observations up to t. Event descriptions ground the construction of explicit-condition and role- or anomaly-conditioned timing supervision; the Timing Model learns causal decision sequences, with unknown intervals excluded from supervision.

Figure 4. Recorded embodied interaction trajectories. Four frames per row show changes in the scene, robot interaction, and subsequent observations. (a) A person sits down holding their lower leg; the robot approaches and stays nearby. (b) A person slumps back onto a sofa; the robot approaches and remains nearby. (c) A visitor encounters the robot, moves with it toward a doorway, and enters. (d) A person preparing to leave returns to retrieve a phone before resuming departure. External-camera recordings document visible behavior; frame labels describe the observed actions and states. Timestamps are video positions, not model-trigger times. Quantitative performance is measured in the separate 60-case evaluation (Table 3).

papers.selection_reason: Proposes an embodied system that continuously observes the physical world, identifies intervention needs, and executes physical actions; includes real-robot evaluation.
papers.title: Proactive Physical AI through Continuous Observation and Timely Intervention
papers.tldr: ProAgent enables Physical AI to continuously detect emerging needs and intervene at the appropriate time without waiting for explicit instructions.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving requires rich spatiotemporal representations to support scene understanding and trajectory planning under strict latency constraints. However, most systems initialize their visual encoders from generic image pretraining and densely process all patch tokens for each camera view and input frame, limiting both representation quality and inference efficiency. To address these challenges, we present ConDenseDrive, a knowledge-dense and token-sparse visual encoder for end-to-end autonomous driving. Our three-stage framework first makes the encoder knowledge-dense by distilling complementary visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from three vision foundation models. It then adapts the distilled encoder to multi-frame end-to-end driving and integrates spatiotemporal context into register tokens for planning. Finally, it makes the encoder token-sparse by applying register-guided token compression, reducing redundant patch computation and yielding a 2.0$\times$ speedup while improving planning performance. ConDenseDrive achieves 94.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1 and 90.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and reaches 37.4 HD-Score in zero-shot evaluation on HUGSIM. Extensive experiments and qualitative analyses demonstrate that visual encoder design provides an effective route to reliable and efficient end-to-end driving.
authors: Shengzhen Li, Yongkang Li, Hao Gao, Chenxi Wu, Yajing Sun, Lu Hou, Wenyu Liu, Xinggang Wang
bullets: Addresses the limited representation quality and high latency caused by generic visual pretraining and dense patch processing.
Distills complementary visual, semantic, and geometric knowledge from three vision foundation models.
Adapts the encoder to multi-frame driving and stores spatiotemporal context in register tokens for planning.
Uses register-guided token compression to reduce redundant patch computation while improving planning performance.
Reports 94.5 PDMS on NAVSIM v1, 90.8 EPDMS on NAVSIM v2, and 37.4 HD-Score in zero-shot HUGSIM evaluation.

papers.title: ConDenseDrive: Knowledge-Dense, Token-Sparse Visual Encoder for End-to-End Autonomous Driving

papers.abstract: Multi-modal fusion for 3D object detection assumes that cameras and LiDAR are broadly complementary. In practice, how much each modality is trusted at a given location is decided by learned weights that are neither characterized nor auditable. We label every ground-truth object by which modalities detected it, then mine the resulting 0.4M-object database across nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo. Because the patterns shift with distance from the ego vehicle, we read the mined model through Spatially Stratified Feature Attribution (SSFA), which conditions Shapley attribution on distance zones and exposes structure that global attribution averages away. Three assumptions built into the current fusion design do not hold. The modality-preference boundary tracks the object itself: a traffic cone is nearly six times as likely as a truck to be seen by the camera alone (16.8% vs. 2.9%), regardless of range. Camera-only detections peak at 10-30 m, inside the band usually ceded to LiDAR, and fall away on either side. The drivers of failure are not additive either: the distance - density interaction alone outweighs the entire main effect of viewing direction. We further find that modality dominance is directionally non-stationary, with objects behind the vehicle being markedly more LiDAR-dominant than those in front. We compile the mined structure into a Modality Reliability Map and inject it into four pretrained fusion detectors through a lightweight attention layer. This improves performance by up to 1.3 mean Average Precision (mAP) while fine-tuning under 4% of their parameters in 2-3 GPU-hours. Our work lifts reliability out of the weights and treats it as a quantity that can be examined before deployment. That is what a safety measure for multi-modal perception must rest on.
authors: Hongsen Cao, Mona Jaber, Shanxin Yuan, Ahmed Sayed
bullets: Mines modality detections for 0.4M objects across nuScenes, KITTI, and Waymo to characterize when cameras and LiDAR disagree.
Introduces Spatially Stratified Feature Attribution to reveal distance-dependent structure hidden by global attribution.
Finds that modality preference depends on object type and location: cameras favor some objects and peak at 10–30 m, while rear-facing objects are more LiDAR-dominant.
Shows failure drivers are interactive rather than purely additive, with distance–density effects outweighing viewing-direction main effects.
Injecting a Modality Reliability Map into four pretrained fusion detectors improves performance by up to 1.3 mAP while fine-tuning under 4% of parameters.

papers.selection_reason: Analyzes and corrects camera-LiDAR perception reliability for autonomous driving 3D detection; relevant to embodied perception and 3D scene understanding.
papers.title: Mining Cross-Modal Perception Gaps in Autonomous Driving: When Camera and LiDAR Disagree
papers.tldr: A large-scale analysis shows that camera–LiDAR reliability varies by object type, distance, interaction effects, and direction, enabling a lightweight reliability map that improves fusion detection with minimal fine-tuning.

papers.abstract: Interacting with unfamiliar objects requires understanding how their parts connect and move. We introduce ViewStruct, a framework for jointly predicting connectivity and articulation in objects and scenes. Given an RGB image with aligned part segmentation and depth, optionally supplemented by images or video, ViewStruct predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters. Its view-grounded representation links predictions to observed regions and expresses joint geometry in a gravity-aligned, view-relative frame, without requiring category-specific canonical orientations. A pretrained vision--language model is adapted to predict structure in seconds, without requiring observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation. Experiments demonstrate improved structural prediction over evaluated baselines and transfer to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos, despite task-specific training exclusively on synthetic data. Simulated manipulation experiments further demonstrate the utility of predicted joints for generating robot motion trajectories.
authors: Wenjing Bian, Ranran Huang, Andreas Geiger
bullets: Predicts rigid-body groupings, attachments, and joint parameters from RGB, aligned segmentation, and depth, with optional additional images or video.
Represents joint geometry in gravity-aligned, view-relative coordinates without requiring category-specific canonical orientations.
Adapts a pretrained vision–language model for inference in seconds, without observed articulation motion or per-instance optimisation.
Outperforms evaluated baselines and transfers to unseen categories, asset sources, and real-world human-interaction videos.
Predicted joints support simulated robot manipulation trajectory generation; training is task-specific and exclusively synthetic.

papers.abstract: Video-to-robot pipelines for quadrupedal imitation insert a learned lifting stage, either a monocular depth model or a per-clip 3D reconstruction, to recover the one axis a side-view camera cannot see. We present CopyQuad, which omits that stage and pins the missing axis to the robot's own stance width instead. The setting is side-view footage of sagittally dominated motion, where limb motion is almost entirely in the image plane. A frozen 2D keypoint detector and a fixed analytic retargeting then turn a single uncalibrated clip into a robot reference whose foot targets are reachable by construction, so no per-clip trajectory optimization is needed. One phase-indexed reward structure, whose only per-behavior freedom is three scalars from a shared sweep, learns a dog walk, a horse walk, a horse trot and two non-periodic gestures, all deployed zero-shot on hardware. We then measure what omitting the axis costs. In a training-free rigidity test, a video depth model varies the distance between the animal's hips by $40$ to $107\%$ of its own mean and a single-image metric model by $22$ to $58\%$, though that distance cannot move. Motion capture puts the true lateral paw travel of a dog walk at $4.5$ cm peak to peak, a mean deviation near $1.4$ cm against the $3.5$ cm of lateral foot error our policies already leave, so the discarded axis sits below the pipeline's resolution. Depth repaired to feasibility never beats the constant, and the unrepaired estimates put the robot on the ground.
authors: Mohamad H. Danesh, Raina Hu, Mengxue Xu, Hsiu-Chin Lin
bullets: Targets sagittally dominated motion, where limb movement is mostly visible in the image plane.
Uses frozen 2D keypoints and fixed analytic retargeting to produce reachable foot targets without per-clip optimization.
A shared phase-indexed reward structure learns four gaits and two non-periodic gestures, all deployed zero-shot on hardware.
Measurements show true lateral paw motion is smaller than existing policy foot error, while depth-based alternatives are unstable or infeasible.
Scope is limited to motions where the discarded lateral axis is small relative to the pipeline’s resolution.

papers.abstract: Accurate modelling of soft tactile sensors remains difficult because finite element methods (FEM) are computa- tionally expensive, while real-time simulators often lack fidelity for hyperelastic deformation. Large physical datasets are also impractical to collect because repeated testing can damage fragile sensors. We present a data-efficient framework that combines limited real-world validation, high-fidelity FEM, and graph neural networks (GNNs) for accurate real-time prediction of two-dimensional tactile deformation in a planar soft tactile structure. The key idea is to decouple validation from training: 82 camera-tracked contact configurations are used only to tune and validate an ANSYS FEM model, which then generates 768 synthetic contact scenarios for GNN training. We evaluate both forward prediction from marker deformation to contact localisation and inverse inference from contact configuration to marker deformation. The validated FEM achieves sub-0.5 mm error in more than 90% of validation cases, while the learned GNN surrogate reaches a mean absolute error of 0.32 mm with millisecond-scale inference, compared with minute-scale FEM simulation. Models trained entirely on synthetic FEM data retain sub-millimetre accuracy on real measurements from the 2D tactile structure, demonstrating strong sim-to-real transfer within the tested planar setting. We further integrate the learned model into a real-time visualisation pipeline, enabling rapid deformation prediction for virtual prototyping and simulator-based design exploration without extensive physical testing.
authors: Silvia Terrile, Kaichen Shi, Taejun Kwon, Jiseok Lee, Nathan Lepora, Yeejin Lee, Saekwang Nam, Efi Psomopoulou
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost of FEM and the difficulty of collecting large physical datasets for fragile tactile sensors.
Uses 82 camera-tracked real contact configurations to validate FEM, then generates 768 synthetic scenarios for GNN training.
Supports both forward contact localisation from marker deformation and inverse deformation prediction from contact configuration.
Validated FEM has sub-0.5 mm error in over 90% of cases; the GNN achieves 0.32 mm mean absolute error with millisecond-scale inference versus minute-scale FEM simulation.
Demonstrates sub-millimetre sim-to-real performance and integration into a real-time visualisation pipeline for planar tactile structures.

papers.abstract: Recent Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models increasingly use natural-language instructions to condition autonomous driving behavior. Yet existing closed-loop benchmarks primarily measure route completion, safety, and rule compliance, leaving a fundamental question unresolved: does language actually determine which feasible behavior the vehicle executes? A trajectory may be safe and successful while still violating or even ignoring the passenger's instruction. To address this, we introduce \ltd, a benchmark designed to directly test this capability. Its key evaluation unit, the paired counterfactual unit (PCU), holds the initial driving scene fixed while changing only the instruction. This design enables us to distinguish isolated instruction success from counterfactual paired success across four instruction-following scopes. To test whether this distinction persists across evaluation regimes, we instantiate Language2Drive in complementary closed-loop CARLA simulation, reconstructed real-world scenes, and open-loop driving benchmarks, including our released CARLA-Language2Drive simulator with purpose-built maps. Evaluating representative driving VLAs across these settings reveals a striking mismatch between strong driving competence and weak language control: 93.2% of successful rollouts do not have a successful counterpart under the alternative feasible instruction. This failure is dominated by one-sided completion, where a model repeatedly executes one preferred behavior but fails when the same scene requires the counterfactual alternative. These results expose two fundamental limitations of current evaluation: isolated success and driving scores, which are widely used by conventional driving benchmarks, can substantially overstate language-following capability, while current driving VLAs themselves lack reliable instruction following under matched counterfactual tests.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) have achieved high success rates on familiar manipulation tasks, yet it remains unclear whether such scores reflect genuine zero-shot generalization and perturbation robustness. Existing evaluation frameworks provide limited capability-level diagnosis and combinatorial perturbation coverage, often without connecting diagnosis to targeted model refinement. We introduce VLA-GAUGE, a diagnostic framework that unifies both evaluations under a shared executable task representation. It combines (1) paired in-distribution and out-of-distribution tasks across six capability suites, (2) single-factor sensitivity analysis with combinatorial perturbation screening and evaluation, and (3) diagnosis-driven refinement through targeted data augmentation and model fine-tuning. We evaluate 12 VLAs spanning different model sizes and action-modeling paradigms under a unified protocol. We find that (1) The mean Zero-Shot Score on VLA-GAUGE is only 22.3%, with SimpleVLA-RL scoring 8.0% and ranking second to last among the evaluated models. (2) Under three representative combinatorial perturbation configurations, the mean R-Score is 9.3. (3) Diagnosis-driven fine-tuning improves $\pi_{0.5}$'s zero-shot generalization and robustness under a selected perturbation combination on held-out scenarios by 72.4 and 31.8 scoring points, respectively; the latter exceeds the 10.9-point gain from LIBERO-Plus single-factor fine-tuning despite fewer successful training trajectories. These results show that high reported success rates on familiar manipulation tasks do not guarantee strong zero-shot generalization to unseen tasks or robustness to combinatorial perturbations, while diagnostic evaluation provides actionable signals for targeted model improvement.

papers.abstract: World models capture environment dynamics and support counterfactual reasoning for planning. In image-goal navigation, where the target often lies beyond the current field of view, the agent must not only model environmental dynamics but also maintain a persistent spatial memory of the scene. Existing approaches either introduce spatial context by fine-tuning pretrained models on the target task, which underexploits their spatial priors, or rely on external 3D reconstruction, which is computationally expensive for real-world deployment. In this paper, we propose the Geometry Grounded World Action Model (G$^2$WAM) for image-goal navigation. G$^2$WAM encodes spatial cues through a learned scene-coordinate localization module that anchors the current, goal, and history frames in a common reference frame, yielding a stable and consistent spatial context that enables efficient navigation without explicit 3D reconstruction. Following the world-action-model paradigm, G$^2$WAM jointly predicts future states and actions, eliminating the need for costly cross-entropy method (CEM) style planning. In addition, G$^2$WAM operates entirely in latent space, avoiding the computational burden of pixel-level reconstruction and substantially reducing inference cost. Across four trajectory prediction benchmarks, G$^2$WAM reduces average ATE and RPE by 40.1% and 35.2%, respectively. In closed-loop navigation experiments, it improves the success rate from 54.0% to 63.0% and the success weighted by path length (SPL) from 36.4% to 59.2%, while maintaining high efficiency.

papers.abstract: Safe robot navigation in unknown, dynamic environments requires more than geometric collision checking: a robot still far from an obstacle may be unable to avoid it because of its speed, orientation, or the obstacle's motion. Hamilton--Jacobi (HJ) reachability analysis captures this in a value function whose sign separates states that admit a safe continuation from those where collision is unavoidable, but computing it online for every newly observed environment is too expensive. This dissertation trains neural implicit representations offline on reachability solutions to give optimization-based controllers this information in real time. Since the value function never exceeds the constraint, it equals a directly computed constraint, such as a signed distance, minus a nonnegative dynamics correction. Learning only this correction keeps represented obstacles outside the predicted safe set despite approximation errors. The first two of five methods use the learned function as a terminal constraint in model predictive control, for static local environments and predicted obstacle motion. The next two use it as a barrier candidate in control barrier function safety filters, for static environments and, through pairwise barriers in relative coordinates, for a varying number of moving obstacles. Simulations and hardware experiments on ground and aerial robots show better collision avoidance than geometric and hand-designed baselines, especially for short horizons and moving obstacles. The fifth method replaces the grid-based offline solver, which limits the first four to low-dimensional models. For control-affine dynamics with polytopic inputs, the HJ Hamiltonian is maximized at a vertex, so a parallelizable tree search over vertex inputs can generate training labels. With a loss from the HJ variational inequality, these labels yield barrier candidates for systems with up to 13 states.
bullets: HJ reachability identifies states where collision is unavoidable, but online computation is too expensive for newly observed environments.
Neural implicit models learn the nonnegative dynamics correction to signed-distance constraints, preserving conservative safety under approximation error.
The learned representations support model predictive control and control-barrier-function filters for static environments and moving obstacles.
Simulations and hardware experiments on ground and aerial robots show improved collision avoidance, particularly with short planning horizons and moving obstacles.
A tree-search labeling method avoids grid-based solvers and extends barrier-candidate generation to control-affine systems with up to 13 states.

figures.caption: Figure 2.3: Offline–online pipeline shared by the methods of this dissertation. Offline, a solver computes HJ value functions Vw for a set of training conditioning inputs, and these solutions supervise the learned safety model. Chapters 3 to 6 obtain them from a grid-based solver, while Chapter 7 replaces this block by vertex-restricted search combined with a physics-informed loss. Online, the current conditioning input w selects the scalar field V̂ ( · | w) whose value and gradient the optimization-based controller evaluates. The compact main network takes the robot state x as input and is conditioned on w, either through parameters generated by the optional hypernetwork (dashed) once per update, as in Chapters 3 to 5, or directly when the hypernetwork is omitted. The main network is evaluated and differentiated at every query.

Figure 1.3: Typical mobile robot navigation architecture. Perception converts sensor data into maps, state estimates, and obstacle information. A global planner provides a route toward the task goal, a local planner converts this route and the latest observations into executable local motion, and a feedback controller tracks the resulting reference. An optional safety filter (dashed) supervises the nominal command and modifies it when it violates the specified safety condition.

Figure 3.7: Success rates in the Monte Carlo simulation study for the two robot models (columns) and the two environments (rows), with 100 runs per configuration. The models are trained on warehouse data only and evaluated in both environments. The performance of the distance-based baselines degrades considerably as the prediction horizon becomes shorter, while the NTC-MPC method maintains higher success rates across all horizon lengths. The RWMSE-trained model also consistently matches or outperforms its MSEtrained counterpart.

Figure 4.2: RNTC-MPC architecture. Tracked obstacle positions and velocities are extrapolated over the MPC horizon and converted into a predicted SDF sequence. The stage-matched SDFs define the collision-avoidance constraints, while selected snapshots near the terminal stage form the conditioning input of the hypernetwork. The hypernetwork runs once per planning cycle and generates the main-network parameters. Inside the nonlinear program, the terminal constraint is the predicted terminal SDF minus the nonnegative main-network output, as in Equation (4.6). The solver evaluates this assembled function and its derivatives repeatedly.

Figure 7.1: Finite-horizon trajectories for the inverted pendulum, generated by (a) model predictive path integral (MPPI) sampling over the full control set and (b) the proposed vertex-restricted beam search. Both methods start from the same 160 random initial states, drawn as circles and colored by the worst constraint value mink c(xk) reached along the trajectory, so that red marks a constraint violation. The subsequent states are drawn as small arrows that point in the direction of motion. The black lines mark the constraint boundary and the purple dashed lines the boundary of the numerically computed maximal safe set. The vertex-restricted search keeps the pendulum inside the constraint set from almost every initial state in the numerically computed safe set, while the full-control sampler fails from many of them.

Figure 3.2: Architecture of the NTC-MPC local planner. From the current sensor data, an SDF is computed and used both as the geometric stage constraint of the MPC problem and as the conditioning input wk of the hypernetwork. The hypernetwork, a convolutional backbone with a fully connected head, outputs the parameters of the compact main network, which represents the estimated value function V̂Ψ( · | wk). The nonlinear program (NLP) solver queries the main network for the value and gradient of the terminal constraint at every optimizer iteration, while the hypernetwork is evaluated only once per planning cycle.

Figure 5.3: Architecture of the ORN-CBF safety filter. The discretized SDF wj computed from the observation oj is used twice, as the conditioning input of the hypernetwork, which generates the parameters Θ of the main network representing the nonnegative residual r̂Ψ, and as the input of the interpolant representing the observed constraint function c( · | oj). Barrier value and gradient are assembled by subtraction as in Equation (5.9), and the Lie derivatives Lf0ĥΨ and LgĥΨ parameterize the CBF-QP Equation (5.13) together with ĥΨ. The softplus output of the main network is not drawn as a separate stage. The hypernetwork runs once per observation update, and the main network and the interpolant are queried at control rate.

Figure 1.5: Organization of the dissertation. After the introduction and the preliminaries, Parts I and II group the technical chapters by controller interface, and within each part the development progresses from static to dynamic environments. Part III varies a third design choice, the origin of the reachability supervision. The concluding chapter compares the methods of the three parts.

The plots show the time evolution of the predicted terminal value V̂Ψ(xN |k | wk) and of the observed obstacle distance c(xk | ok), with the zero level marked by the dotted line. In this configuration, the obstacle distance of the baselines remains positive until shortly before the collision, while NTC-MPC begins to avoid the obstacle when its terminal value approaches zero, several seconds earlier.

This dissertation studies reachability-informed safety constraints across static and dynamic environments and across MPC and safety-filter interfaces.

Figure 3.3: Training procedure for the NTC model. Each SDF conditioning input w from the dataset is processed by the hypernetwork into the main-network parameters Θ(w), and all states of a state-space grid are propagated through the main network to predict the value function over the grid. HJ reachability analysis, using the same SDF as the constraint function c( · | w), provides the numerical target values V∞( · | w). The loss L compares predicted and target value functions, and its gradient updates the hypernetwork parameters Ψ. The main-network parameters are outputs of the hypernetwork rather than free variables. The figure shows a single training pair, so the batch and grid indices of Equation (3.7) are omitted.

(a) Safe-set intersection over union (IoU) over training epochs, with the residual models in green and the direct-regression models in orange, and the line pattern indicating the network size. The residual models start higher, converge roughly five times faster, and end higher. (b) Final IoU after 100 epochs. The residual models reach a higher IoU at every size, and the smallest residual model outperforms the largest direct-regression model.

The pairwise zero level sets (gray) surround the collision disk of each pedestrian (black) and are elongated along the direction in which that pedestrian moves relative to the robot, while the composite zero level set (green) traces a smooth outline around their union without touching the collision disks.

Figure 6.4: Block diagram of the CN-CBF safety filter. The robot state and the current obstacle-state estimates feed three parallel blocks. The batched CN-CBF evaluation of Figure 6.3 returns the composite barrier value and its gradients, the robot dynamics model supplies f0(x) and g(x), and the backward-difference estimator in Equation (6.16) supplies the obstacle state derivatives. Together they parameterize the CBF-QP Equation (6.18), which minimally modifies the nominal command unom.

The barrier value anticipates the encounter well before the distance becomes small and briefly becomes negative under model mismatch and measurement noise. The physical buffer contained in Rmin prevents a collision during this interval.

Figure 1.2: Unsafe states for a mobile robot avoiding a static obstacle and a dynamic obstacle crossing its path. The shaded regions are still collision-free, but neither full braking nor maximal steering to either side prevents collision. For the static obstacle, the region grows roughly with the braking distance. For the moving obstacle, it is additionally shaped by the relative motion. A controller that monitors only current distance (dashed trajectories) may enter this region, but a dynamics-aware controller (solid trajectory) evades while recovery remains possible.

Figure 3.1: Effect of the terminal constraint on an MPC local planner that approaches a static obstacle, shown at two consecutive planning steps. Each red-shaded region is a slice of the backward reachable tube (BRT) of the observed obstacle, that is, of the set X \ S⋆(ok) of states from which collision can no longer be avoided under the actuation limits. The slice depends on the heading, so a solid outline belongs to the current state and a dashed outline to the terminal state. In the lower row the dotted body marks the position at step k. Left: the terminal constraint is distance based, so every state predicted at step k keeps a nonnegative distance to the obstacle and the planner continues straight ahead. At step k + 1 the robot has entered the BRT, and every admissible input sequence collides at some later instant. Right: the reachability-based terminal constraint xN |k ∈ S⋆(ok) makes the planner steer away already at step k, so the robot remains outside the BRT one step later.

Figure 5.10: Representative quadrotor scenario. (a) Executed motion under the LQR nominal controller with the ORN-CBF safety filter among the ten cylindrical obstacles (gray), colored by time. The filter steers the quadrotor around the obstacles with which the goal-directed LQR would otherwise collide. (b) Evolution of the barrier value ĥΨ(x(t) | wj), which decreases toward zero during the avoidance maneuvers and remains positive throughout the run.

Green denotes successful runs and red denotes collisions. Figure 4.3: RNTC training procedure. Each obstacle trajectory is split at a reference instant. Selected snapshots before that instant form the conditioning input w of Equation (4.5), which the hypernetwork converts into the main-network parameters Θ(w). The generated main network produces a nonnegative residual on the state-space grid. The subsequent trajectory segment defines the time-varying failure set used to compute the numerical HJ target V ( · | w) at the reference instant. Subtracting the predicted residual from the reference-instant SDF yields the value-function estimate used in the training loss. The figure shows a single training pair, so the batch and grid indices of Equation (4.10) are omitted. Signal names match Figure 3.3.

Figure 4.1: Effect of the terminal constraint on an MPC local planner among moving obstacles, shown at two consecutive planning steps. The robot tracks the reference path to the right at constant speed and with a limited turning rate, while an obstacle crosses that path from the front left. Each red region collects the states from which a collision can no longer be avoided under the actuation limits. It extends along the obstacle velocity relative to the robot, so it is not aligned with the drawn velocity arrow, and the region at the terminal instant is the region at the current instant displaced and rotated according to the obstacle motion over the horizon. In the lower row the dotted outlines mark the positions at step k. At step k + 1 its state lies inside that region, where continued straight motion and both extreme steering maneuvers end in the predicted obstacle. Right: the terminal constraint xN |k ∈ SN |k of RNTC-MPC refers to the predicted geometry and is already active at step k, so the planner turns away and its plan remains feasible one step later.

(a) At tj, a previously unobserved obstacle lies beyond the boundary of the sensing window of half-width ρ. Neither the failure set F (grey) nor its BRT B∞(F) (red) is part of the observation oj. (b) Between two updates the robot travels at most vmax∆to, and the window is recentered at the new robot position. The new observation thus gains a band of that depth beyond its previous boundary (dashed) and now contains most of the obstacle. Under the boundary-appearance assumption, previously unseen obstacles can appear only inside this band, and hence at least ρ− vmax∆to away from the robot. Continued safety requires the state to lie outside B∞(F) at the instant at which the barrier is replaced.

Figure 5.4: Closed-loop arrangement of the ORN-CBF safety filter for a robot that operates on local observations. A nominal controller of arbitrary design issues the command unom. From the current observation oj, ORN-CBF generates the barrier candidate ĥΨ( · | wj) once per observation update, as detailed in Figure 5.3. The CBF-QP Equation (5.13) then evaluates this barrier at the measured state x at control rate, modifies the command minimally if needed, and forwards the filtered control u⋆ to the robot. The dashed arrows indicate that the nominal controller may use the same two signals, on which the filter places no requirement.

Figure 6.3: Structure of the CN-CBF barrier evaluation. The current obstacle states are stacked into a batch, combined with the robot state x into the batch of relative states zi = σ(x, qi), and propagated in parallel through the shared residual network r̂Θ and the closed-form pairwise constraint crel. Their difference yields the pairwise barrier values of Equation (6.8), which the smooth aggregation µβ reduces to the composite value in Equation (6.11). One reverse-mode differentiation pass through this graph returns all gradients in Equation (6.15).

papers.title: Learning Reachability-Based Safety Representations for Real-Time Robot Navigation in Unknown and Dynamic Environments
papers.tldr: The dissertation learns reachability-based safety representations offline so robots can perform real-time, dynamics-aware collision avoidance in unknown and dynamic environments.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are often pretrained via imitation learning, making reinforcement learning (RL) post-training important when deployment moves beyond demonstration coverage. Existing refinement paradigms expose a reliability--efficiency tension: model-free refinement avoids simulator bias but is interaction-intensive, whereas model-based refinement can exploit unreliable imagination even as its simulator adapts. We propose Model-Evolving Reinforcement Learning (MERL), a trust-calibrated framework that couples policy optimization with an online-updated simulator comprising a world model and a reward proxy head. Across stages, simulator reliability controls the imagined-data ratio and rollout horizon; within rollouts, chunk-level trust controls replay selection and optimization weight. For recursive imagination without exact grounded continuations, a residual predictor estimates trust without querying future ground truth. On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, MERL reaches 79.7% average success, improves high-threshold learning speed by 10.9% over the matched model-free control, and outperforms same-protocol external baselines across three training seeds. Fixed-data adaptation from 50 demonstrations per task achieves 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.
authors: Wenzhan Li, Yiran Qin, Heng Zhou, Huirui Wang, Yulan Guo, Ruimao Zhang
bullets: Addresses the efficiency–reliability trade-off between interaction-heavy model-free refinement and potentially biased model-based refinement.
Couples policy optimization with an online-updated world model and reward proxy, using simulator reliability to adjust imagined-data ratios and rollout horizons.
Uses chunk-level trust for replay selection and optimization weighting, with a residual predictor for recursive imagination without future ground-truth queries.
On perturbed LIBERO-PRO tasks, achieves 79.7% average success and 10.9% faster high-threshold learning than matched model-free control.
With 50 demonstrations per task, reaches 80.0% average success on two physical-robot tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of the MERL pipeline. At each online stage s, the policy collects grounded rollouts and updates an evolving simulator composed of a world model Wϕ and a reward proxy head Qψ . Calibration reuses stored grounded continuations with the same anchors and recorded actions; stage-level trust maps their measured errors to ρs and hs. A residual predictor refreshed after simulator update supplies no-oracle scores for unpaired recursive chunks and is frozen during imagination and policy optimization. Chunk-level trust then evaluates generated imagined chunks, assigns replay probabilities ps,i and optimization weights ws,i, and combines trusted imagined chunks with grounded rollouts for mixed policy optimization.

Figure 1: Paradigm evolution toward trust calibration. The columns illustrate design patterns represented by our matched refinement controls, from imitation and model-free RL to static and online-updated model-based RL. MERL uses simulator reliability to schedule, select, and weight rollouts before the subsequent mixed real–imagined policy optimization.

Figure 3: Learning dynamics, two-level trust, and real-robot task setups. Left: SR and S2T on Goal and Long. Right: trust diagnostics and AgileX PiPER X setups for Block-to-Box and Lid-to-Pot. All training axes count outer refinement stages. Panel (e) displays the horizon in action-chunk units hs/C ∈ [1, 4], with C = 8; panel (f) displays replay priority and trust weight against chunk error.
Figure 5: AgileX PiPER X task setups for fixed-data adaptation and closed-loop physical evaluation.

Figure 6: MERL real-robot deployment and simulator visualization on AgileX PiPER X. From top to bottom, rows show real Block-to-Box rollout, simulator-generated Block-to-Box continuation, real Lid-to-Pot rollout, and simulator-generated Lid-to-Pot continuation.

Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of simulator predictions. Rows show ground-truth future frames, predictions from the frozen simulator, and predictions from the evolving simulator under the same rollout condition. The evolving simulator produces visual continuations that remain closer to the ground truth over the prediction horizon.

papers.abstract: Deep reinforcement learning has shown strong potential for vision-based autonomous driving, but policies trained in simulation often suffer severe performance degradation when deployed in the real world. Existing sim-to-real methods commonly address this gap through image-transfer-based domain adaptation or policy-agnostic domain randomisation. However, the former requires laborious acquisition of target-domain data and is often limited to the deployment domain, whereas the latter introduces unguided perturbations that may not reflect the underlying sim-to-real discrepancy, leading to suboptimal transfer performance. To overcome these limitations, we propose XFD, an explainable artificial intelligence (XAI)-guided Fourier domain generalisation framework for pure-simulation sim-to-real reinforcement learning. The proposed framework extracts explainability attribution maps from simulated observations, and converts these attributions into policy-conditioned Fourier-domain interventions. By perturbing appearance-sensitive spectral components while preserving task-defining spatial structures, XFD constructs robustness-enhancing visual domains entirely within simulation. Subsequently, the proposed robust policy optimisation guides the policy towards attending to task-critical features while suppressing sensitivity to irrelevant visual information. Extensive experiments in simulation and zero-shot real-world deployment demonstrate that XFD consistently improves traveled distance and reward over standard policy and randomly domain-randomised baseline, especially on unseen maps with cluttered backgrounds. Attribution-based analysis further proves that the proposed policy preserves more consistent task-relevant visual evidence across simulation and real-world observations.
authors: Wei Yao, Chuyao Wang, Ziwei Wang, Nabil Aouf
bullets: Addresses severe sim-to-real degradation in vision-based autonomous-driving reinforcement learning.
Uses simulated-observation attribution maps to identify and perturb appearance-sensitive Fourier components while preserving task-relevant structure.

Simulation and zero-shot real-world experiments show improved travel distance and reward, particularly on unseen cluttered maps.

papers.abstract: Vision-based tactile sensors enable fine-grained perception for dexterous robotic manipulation, but current marker-based designs tightly couple surface texture and contact force signals within a single observation. Existing data-driven decoupling methods rely on serial mask-based inpainting, which suffers from mask-sizing dilemmas caused by physical indentation effects, error retention, and lack of real paired data for supervision. To address these challenges, we propose DeTac, a novel dual-branch generative framework that concurrently extracts clean shading and marker images from a single mixed tactile image. DeTac leverages full-image synthesis to naturally bypass mask dependency and introduces a cross-branch synergistic optimization that enables mutual supervision, effectively preventing error retention. Furthermore, we construct a strictly aligned, real-world paired tactile dataset using custom hardware to provide high-quality supervision. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DeTac achieves state-of-the-art decoupling accuracy, significantly facilitating downstream surface reconstruction and force estimation tasks while exhibiting cross-sensor generalization.
authors: Zhirui Zhang, Yunkai Tang, Jiahang Li, Fan Fei, Jinnuo Zhang, Kairan Ding, Jieji Ren, Yandong Guo, Boxin Shi
bullets: Addresses signal entanglement in marker-based vision-based tactile sensors and limitations of mask-based inpainting.

Introduces a strictly aligned real-world paired tactile dataset for supervised training.

papers.abstract: Humans expand their locomotion capability by wearing appropriate footwear, such as hiking boots for mountains or skates for ice. Footwear changes the ground-contact interface and enables traversal of otherwise difficult terrain. In contrast, locomotion controllers are typically trained for a fixed morphology, and their performance can degrade when shoes alter foot geometry, mass, and friction. We propose SHOES, a sample-efficient framework for adapting locomotion policies to footwear-induced morphology changes. SHOES freezes a simulation-trained nominal policy and fine-tunes only lightweight, identity-initialized modulation modules on the robot, preserving the initial behavior while enabling efficient hardware adaptation. We also introduce SafeBox, a workspace-aware waypoint sampler that constrains online adaptation within a user-defined workspace. The simulation results with a shoe-equipped Unitree Go2 show that SHOES substantially recovers locomotion performance after footwear-induced morphology changes using limited additional adaptation. Under the same adaptation budget, SHOES outperforms FiLM-only, Linear Adapter-only, and residual-RL baselines. Real-world experiments on a Unitree Go2 fitted with human shoes further evaluate the effectiveness of SHOES for hardware deployment.
authors: Kota Tsuruhara, Tsung-Yuan Chen, Kento Kawaharazuka
bullets: Addresses performance degradation caused by changes in foot geometry, mass, and friction from added footwear.

papers.abstract: Recent world action models draw on video generation priors to jointly predict future observations and robot actions. Adapting these priors to control requires determining how future predictions should guide policy learning. RAP-WAM combines predictive Rehearsal and Action Perturbations (RAP) with future-supervised queries and Coupled Action Projection for policy learning. Predictive rehearsal trains on model-generated inputs while retaining recorded targets, and accumulates recurring errors into a spatial prior. We perturb actions and measure changes in video predictions. Action-response-based spatiotemporal credit assignment combines these responses, prediction error, and the rehearsal prior to allocate visual supervision; spatially aggregating the responses determines supervision intensity across future action steps. No separate scoring network or deployment-time probe is required. The base learns from a video-pretrained backbone without intermediate pretraining on external embodied data. We evaluate the fixed base and its agent-refined, task-conditioned system. On 42 RoboDojo tasks, their average success rates are 12.85% and 15.62%, with Scores of 17.86 and 20.59. Across 15 real-robot tasks, the complete system achieves 89.00% task-macro-average success, exceeding the strongest of five baselines by 37.67 percentage points. Across 315 fixed-output simulation windows, 45.21% of response-top20 positions fall outside error-top20, revealing information beyond prediction error.
authors: Yuanpeng He, Ceyao Zhang, Fangjing Li, Kefei Zhu, Lijian Li, Yueheng Li, Tianjia He, Wenpin Jiao, Zhi Jin, Yaodong Yang, Yuanpei Chen
bullets: Addresses how future video predictions should guide policy learning in world-action models.

On 42 RoboDojo tasks, average success was 12.85% for the fixed base and 15.62% after agent refinement.

papers.abstract: Deploying robots in human-shared environments requires deciding not only how to navigate, but also when dedicated social signals are worth emitting. Classic observation-based inference can be misleading in such settings: confounding factors may bias the estimated relationship between a signal and the task outcome, leading to incorrect decisions. Causal inference provides a framework for disentangling these relationships by modelling the mechanisms linking observations, actions, and outcomes, and by estimating interventional effects after accounting for confounding paths. We study a human-robot interaction scenario in a corridor and use a causal model to estimate whether a social navigation signal causally improves transit success. We represent the interaction as a causal DAG involving robot action, pedestrian occupancy, available space, task outcome, and a controlled confounder (static obstacles). We compare the interventional estimate with the observational estimate obtained by conditioning only on the robot action, which does not explicitly model interventions. Our results show that accounting for confounding variables can reverse the conclusions drawn from naive observational analysis: the observational estimate wrongly suggests that the social signal is detrimental, whereas the causal estimate shows that it is beneficial. This discrepancy highlights how failing to account for confounding can lead to incorrect conclusions and demonstrates the importance of causal models for context-aware signalling decisions in social robot navigation.
authors: Francesco Baldo, Luca Castri, Gloria Beraldo, Nicola Bellotto
bullets: Studies when social signals are worth emitting in human-shared corridor navigation.

papers.abstract: Robot learning has undergone significant advancements in the domain of compliant control and robotic assembly. The development of novel methodologies has transcended the capacity to address discrete tasks, such as grasping or inserting, and has evolved to encompass the comprehensive construction of entire assemblies. Conventional benchmarks, which are predominantly focused on single tasks, are no longer adequate to address the complexity and interconnected nature of modern manufacturing processes. Consequently, the necessity for benchmarks to encompass a broader spectrum of assembly and subassembly steps is becoming apparent. In light of these developments, we propose LABIT, an industrial robotic assembly benchmark for long-horizon manipulation. This benchmark encompasses DIN-norm assembly tasks, including screwing, placing, inserting, and snapping, under both high and low tolerance conditions. The successive nature of these assembly steps implies that prior errors can influence subsequent manipulation. Consequently, this benchmark is particularly relevant for assessing the robustness of intelligent robotic systems. The proposed benchmarking protocols and novel performance metric, based on a taxonomy of assembly complexity in conjunction with the comprehensive list of parts and their corresponding CAD models, serve as essential tools for research and development in the field. To provide a baseline, we evaluate the benchmark using traditional force-position control and report reliability and score metrics per primitive, subtask, assembly category, and subassembly. Accompanying data is available at https://irp-hka.github.io/robotic-assembly-benchmark/.
authors: Constantin Schempp, Christian Friedrich, Luca Kofler, Laura Suhm
bullets: Covers DIN-norm operations including screwing, placing, inserting, and snapping.

papers.abstract: Generalist robot manipulation can benefit from pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) for semantic reasoning and video generation models (VGMs) for world modeling. However, existing unified models that directly fuse them through shared attention at multiple layers can make it harder to draw on their specialized capabilities. We introduce PINT, a unified model that coordinates semantic reasoning, world modeling, and action generation through a shared chunk-level Predictive Intent while preserving expert-specific pathways. PINT inserts learnable Intent Tokens into the VLM sequence to form this representation, conditioning both the VGM and an Action Expert (AE). It replaces only the VGM's prompt conditioning and retains the VGM at inference, where the AE reads its representations through one-way attention. Rather than prescribing what Predictive Intent should encode, PINT learns it jointly from the native prediction objectives of the VLM, VGM, and AE, which provide complementary views of the same upcoming task execution. Training uses two stages: Stage 1 freezes the VGM so that future video prediction shapes Predictive Intent with task-relevant future dynamics, while Stage 2 fixes the learned Intent and adapts the VGM and AE. Without embodied pretraining, PINT achieves strong in-distribution (ID) performance and substantially improves out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization, reaching 15.5% on RoboTwin 2.0-Hard compared with 1.8% for Fast-WAM and 3.2% for StarVLA, and 79.5% on LIBERO-Plus compared with 51.5% and 75.0%, respectively. Across five real-world bimanual tasks, PINT reaches 68% ID and 24% OOD success, compared with 35%/9% for pretrained Motus and 67%/35% for pretrained $\pi_{0.5}$.
authors: Xinyu Guo, Chao Jing, Li Yi, Xingyu Chen, Zhengxing Wu

papers.abstract: Multimodal model predictive control (MM-MPC) avoids local minima among moving obstacles by solving one optimal control problem (OCP) per combination of avoidance sides, so its computational cost grows exponentially with the number of decision-critical obstacles. We propose SideNet-MPC, which replaces this enumeration with a mode decision learned by imitating MM-MPC as an expert. A graph neural network is trained to predict the expert's minimum-cost mode, one avoidance side per obstacle. Its edges encode, for each obstacle pair, the gap predicted for the moment the vehicle first reaches either obstacle, so a neighbor that blocks a preferred passage can reverse the proposed side. The expert's selection rule compares its minimum-cost mode with the previously executed mode; SideNet-MPC keeps this rule and substitutes the network proposal for the minimum-cost mode. Hence at most two OCPs are solved per control period, and every applied input still comes from an OCP with control barrier function constraints rather than from the network. In $100$ seed-matched closed-loop Monte Carlo runs of mixed traffic, SideNet-MPC reaches $93\%$ of the expert's success rate and needs \SI{18.6}{ms} per control period on a single thread, 48\% less than the expert's \SI{35.5}{ms} on sixteen parallel threads. In a controlled gap sweep, its proposed side reverses in the same gap interval as the expert's, whereas proposers without pairwise edges, trained on the same data, never reverse and all deadlock at the blocked gates of a deterministic scene.
authors: Changyu Lee, Byung-Kwan Lee, Kanghoon Yoon
bullets: MM-MPC avoids local minima by enumerating avoidance-side combinations, but this cost grows exponentially with decision-critical obstacles.
A graph neural network predicts one avoidance side per obstacle, using pairwise gap information to account for blocked passages.
The controller preserves the expert’s mode-selection rule and solves at most two optimal control problems per control period.
In 100 seed-matched mixed-traffic runs, it achieved 93% of the expert’s success rate and reduced reported control time from 35.5 ms to 18.6 ms.
Pairwise graph edges enabled side reversals in the same gap interval as the expert; models without them deadlocked in the tested deterministic scene.

papers.abstract: Articulated object manipulation tasks such as opening doors, tightening bolts, and pulling drawers impose kinematic constraints on a robot end-effector's motion that neural policies may fail to satisfy. Unlike hybrid force-position control that strictly separates force and position control into orthogonal subspaces, impedance control modulates a mechanical impedance system in the form of a virtual inertia, damping, and stiffness. However, selecting task-appropriate impedance gains remains challenging for robot policies. In this paper, we address this problem for the case of manipulating articulated objects. Our constraint-decomposed impedance control method uses the sampling diversity of a generative policy to estimate the feasible motion directions in twist space. The key idea is to infer the feasible and constrained subspaces of twists from an ensemble of trajectories generated by the policy from the same observation. Principal component analysis (PCA) of the end-effector twists determines the feasible twist subspace, which is then used to form 6x6 impedance gain matrices. For many common articulated objects, the feasible twist subspace is independent of the object configuration, so the subspace and resulting gains are estimated once and held fixed during manipulation, minimizing computational overhead. For less common cases where this independence does not hold, we instead estimate a configuration-independent twist subspace of higher dimension that contains the local feasible subspaces, allowing the same fixed-gain strategy to be used. Experiments across simulated and real-world single- and multi-DoF objects show that the proposed method consistently reduces constraint-violating contact loads relative to isotropic impedance control while maintaining task execution.
authors: Kyungseo Park, Byeongdo Lim, Jungbin Lim, Minseok Choi, Frank C. Park
bullets: Targets manipulation tasks such as doors, bolts, and drawers, where end-effector motion must satisfy kinematic constraints.
Uses PCA over multiple policy-generated trajectories from the same observation to separate feasible and constrained twist directions.
Constructs 6×6 impedance gain matrices from the estimated feasible twist subspace.
For configuration-dependent constraints, uses a higher-dimensional, configuration-independent subspace to retain fixed gains and low computational overhead.
Simulated and real-world experiments on single- and multi-DoF objects reduce constraint-violating contact loads versus isotropic impedance while preserving task execution.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have advanced robotic manipulation by connecting visual perception and language instructions to action generation. However, many manipulation tasks depend on auditory cues that cannot be reliably inferred from visual observations and may need to be elicited through physical interaction. To address this gap, we present ListenVLA, an audio-conditioned VLA policy built on GR00T N1.7 for sound-guided manipulation. ListenVLA combines semantic audio embeddings with waveform-derived acoustic cues over a causal audio history and conditions continuous action generation through audio tokens and feature modulation. Moreover, we introduce an audio-action binding objective that uses context-matched demonstrations to link auditory differences to demonstrated action differences. The objective supervises short-horizon differences between flow-velocity predictions under different audio conditions, with shared pure-noise action inputs and fixed non-audio observations, alongside full-chunk action supervision. Furthermore, we develop LIBERO-Audio, an eight-task benchmark covering sound-based target selection, responses to auditory events, and physical interactions that reveal acoustic evidence. Experiments on LIBERO-Audio and three real-world manipulation tasks show excellent performance. Ablation studies support the contributions of binding supervision and audio modulation, while audio swap tests show that sound influences action predictions. Our code and videos are available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/listenvla-F18D
authors: Jiaqi Fan, Rui Xu, Jiakun Xia, Xuyu Fan, Shuailei Ma, Yuefeng Wang, Qing Wang, Jiarui Zhang, Yili Fu, Xu Li
bullets: Addresses manipulation tasks where relevant auditory information cannot be inferred visually and must sometimes be elicited through interaction.
Combines semantic audio embeddings and waveform-derived acoustic features with causal audio history to condition continuous action generation.
Introduces audio-action binding supervision using matched demonstrations and short-horizon differences in flow-velocity predictions.
Presents LIBERO-Audio, an eight-task benchmark spanning sound-based selection, auditory-event responses, and interactions that reveal acoustic evidence.
Reports strong results on LIBERO-Audio and three real-world tasks; ablations and audio-swap tests support the roles of binding supervision and audio modulation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. ListenVLA architecture and audio–action binding. (a) Three overlapping windows form the causal audio history. Frozen CLAP embeddings and waveform-derived acoustic cues supply window tokens and feed a temporal encoder. The resulting audio context supplies additional tokens and conditions AdaLN within the DiT (blue dashed path) and output FiLM before action decoding (orange dashed path). papers.abstract: Despite rapid progress, generalist robot policies remain brittle during execution. Reliable deployment therefore requires runtime monitoring that provides timely warnings of failure. Existing monitors commonly estimate risk from current observations or policy signals without explicitly predicting the future consequences of proposed actions. To anticipate such risks before action execution, we introduce ReAP, a future-aware runtime monitoring framework that combines visual failure recognition with action-conditioned failure prediction. Specifically, ReAP first trains a visual detector on successful and failed rollouts to learn a failure-relevant representation space and estimate current risk. An action-conditioned predictor then forecasts the resulting future representation in this space to estimate future failure risk. At runtime, the detector and predictor provide complementary signals for current-state failure recognition and future-aware risk assessment. Experiments across diverse robot policies in simulation and the real world demonstrate that ReAP effectively balances failure-detection accuracy and warning timeliness.
authors: Jingyuan Liu, Yunpeng Qing, Changxu Wei, Zhi Hou
bullets: Addresses the brittleness of generalist robot policies and the need for timely deployment warnings.
Learns a failure-relevant visual representation from successful and failed rollouts to estimate current risk.

Combines current-state detection with action-conditioned prediction to balance detection accuracy and warning timeliness.
Evaluated across diverse robot policies in simulation and the real world.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich insertion requires robots to combine visual alignment with tactile adjustment. However, existing visuotactile chunk-based policies collapse tactile feedback into a single generation-time fusion pathway, leaving persistent contact states, abrupt contact events, and future contact consequences implicitly modeled in a single representation. We present PACE (Phase-Aware Contact-Event Conditioning), a temporal-role tactile conditioning framework for chunk-based insertion policies. PACE organizes a shared tactile stream into three temporal roles: persistent contact states condition action-chunk generation, abrupt contact events correct the generated chunk, and contact-consequence prediction shapes action representations during training. This design preserves chunk-level action continuity while assigning distinct pathways to different temporal roles of contact feedback. Across five real-robot insertion tasks, PACE achieves an average success rate of 90.7%, outperforming vision-only and generation-time tactile-fusion baselines by over 44 percentage points; on the ManipulationNet benchmark, PACE maintains 88.7% success across six geometry-clearance configurations, including an industrial-grade 0.1-mm clearance. Ablations confirm the complementary contributions of the three temporal roles, mechanistic analyses show that PACE separates normal insertion progress from contact events requiring immediate correction, and cross-signal and cross-architecture experiments indicate that this temporal-role principle extends across different physical feedback signals and policy backbones. Videos and materials are available at https://pace-insertion.github.io/.
authors: Zhiyuan Chen, Shixiong Xu, Shuai Chen, Yangwei You
bullets: Targets the challenge of combining visual alignment with persistent and abrupt tactile contact during insertion.
Uses persistent contact states to condition action-chunk generation and abrupt contact events to correct generated chunks.
Trains contact-consequence prediction to shape action representations while preserving chunk-level action continuity.
Achieves 90.7% average success across five real-robot tasks and 88.7% across six ManipulationNet configurations, including 0.1-mm clearance.
Ablations and cross-architecture/signal studies support the complementary and transferable nature of the three temporal roles.

papers.abstract: Garment manipulation requires inferring both garment identity and complete configuration from partial, self-occluded observations. This creates a chicken-and-egg problem: completing a partial observation requires a garment-specific deformation prior, while identifying the garment requires a configuration that explains the observation. We introduce ClothAtlas, which jointly identifies garments and estimates their complete configurations from partial point clouds and a library of canonical meshes. A shared graph-conditioned flow-matching model samples configurations for each candidate mesh and ranks candidates by observation fit. The model accommodates different mesh shapes, vertex counts, and connectivities, allowing new garments to be added from canonical meshes alone without retraining. On held-out DexGarmentLab garments, ClothAtlas ranks the correct mesh first among 221 candidates for all 22 test garments from a single flat observation. From a single self-occluded observation, it identifies 15/22 garments, compared with 8/22 for a deterministic graph estimator. Persistent vertex identities support grasp-target localization on real garments, reducing mean error from 15.4 to 6.4 cm overall and from 17.0 to 8.3 cm on occluded targets compared with dense descriptor matching. Project page: https://clothatlas.github.io/
authors: Jens Lundell, Alberta Longhini, Lei Shu, Hemal Arora, Evan Robert, Carlota Par\'es-Morlans, Marcel B\"usching, M{\aa}rten Bj\"orkman, Jeannette Bohg

From self-occluded observations, identifies 15/22 garments versus 8/22 for a deterministic graph estimator.

papers.abstract: Flow Matching (FM) has recently emerged as a principled and efficient generative modeling framework for reinforcement learning (RL), enabling expressive, multimodal policy parameterizations via deterministic probability transport. Compared to diffusion-based policies that rely on stochastic denoising chains, FM uses sampling based on ordinary differential equations (ODEs), with learned velocity fields, which can substantially reduce inference latency and simplify the incorporation of RL objectives. As research in flow-based RL rapidly accelerates across offline continuous control, online fine-tuning, and foundation model alignment, the literature has become highly fragmented. In this survey, we provide a comprehensive taxonomy of flow-matching approaches in reinforcement learning. We organize the literature along two axes: the target distribution being modeled (e.g., action policies, value critics, transition dynamics) and the mechanism of RL signal integration (e.g., energy-weighted regression, flow-based policy gradients, and group relative policy optimization). Furthermore, we survey emerging frontiers such as discrete and non-Euclidean action spaces, provide a systematic comparative analysis against Gaussian and diffusion baselines, and outline critical open problems. Ultimately, this survey serves as a foundational roadmap for the next generation of generative reinforcement learning and alignment.
authors: Nabuat Zaman Nahim, Fairoz Nower Khan, Peizhong Ju
bullets: Flow matching enables expressive, multimodal RL policies through deterministic probability transport and ODE-based sampling.
The survey covers offline continuous control, online fine-tuning, and foundation-model alignment.
It classifies methods by modeled target distributions, including policies, value critics, and transition dynamics.
It also categorizes how RL signals are integrated, such as energy-weighted regression, flow-based policy gradients, and group relative policy optimization.
Emerging topics include discrete and non-Euclidean action spaces, alongside comparisons with Gaussian and diffusion-based approaches.

Figure 2: How flow matching is integrated with reinforcement learning. A common flow-policy backbone defines an expressive action generator through a learned velocity field and ODE sampler. In offline RL, the reinforcement signal typically enters at training time, most often by reweighting the flow-matching objective using value or energy estimates. In online RL, the signal enters through policy optimization using environment interaction, typically via stochasticized flows, pathwise gradients through the ODE, or group-based updates such as GRPO. Across both settings, additional stabilizers such as KL regularization, Wasserstein anchoring, clipping, and support constraints are often used.

Bottom left: training is simulationfree: one samples (x0, x1, t), constructs an interpolation point xt, and regresses the learned velocity field vθ(xt, t) toward the target conditional velocity ut. For the common linear optimal-transport path, the target velocity is simply x1−x0. Bottom right: after training, new samples are generated by integrating the learned ODE from base noise to the target distribution.
