papers.abstract: Audio Large Language Models (Audio LLMs) are embedded in agents for smart homes, vehicles, wearables, and embodied systems, where acoustic inputs can propagate from perception into persistent state and consequential execution. This setting extends security analysis beyond model behavior to the system conditions that determine how acoustic inputs can influence agent behavior and external actions. Existing surveys examine acoustic security, LLM-based agents, and edge deployment in isolation, leaving their security interactions in deployed Audio LLM-based agents insufficiently characterized. This survey introduces an Acoustic Sensing-to-Action (S2A) system model that traces these security implications along the path from acoustic sensing to external execution, while accounting for edge-cloud runtime and lifecycle transformation. We use the model to synthesize attacks, defenses, and evaluation methods across the acoustic, agent, and edge-system literature. The synthesis shows that security gaps can emerge within components and at the transitions between stages, where protections developed for one stage do not necessarily provide end-to-end assurance in the deployed system. These findings motivate security evaluation that follows acoustic influence from sensing to action across persistent state, system boundaries, and changing deployment conditions in real-world agents.
authors: Binhong Wang, Haidong Kang, Yanfeng Zhang, Hong-Ning Dai, Guo Yu, Shangce Gao
bullets: Focuses on smart homes, vehicles, wearables, and embodied systems where audio-driven decisions can have consequential effects.
Introduces an Acoustic Sensing-to-Action (S2A) model spanning acoustic sensing, agent processing, edge-cloud runtime, lifecycle changes, and external execution.
Synthesizes attacks, defenses, and evaluation methods across acoustic security, LLM-agent, and edge-system research.
Finds that vulnerabilities arise both within individual components and at transitions between stages, limiting the assurance of isolated protections.
Motivates end-to-end evaluation that tracks acoustic influence across persistent state, system boundaries, and changing deployment conditions.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are typically deployed as isolated single-agent policies. When several such agents share a workspace, they can coordinate implicitly, by observing one another, or explicitly, by exchanging messages, but it remains unclear when explicit communication becomes necessary. We introduce CoLA (Coordination via Learned Adapters), which keeps each agent's VLA backbone frozen and trains a lightweight message channel and a per-arm diffusion action head on top, with fully decentralised execution. Across three tasks that differ in how much each agent can observe, the channel matters only when information is private. On an occluded tray handover, where the box's colour marker is visible to one agent only, CoLA reaches 76.0% success versus 1.3% with messages zeroed throughout training. On two-arm and three-arm handover tasks, removing messages has no measurable effect with a shared overhead camera (90.6% vs. 88.3% at two arms; 63.5% vs. 60.0% at three), but lowers success on the two-arm task's wrist-only variant (74.8% vs. 64.3%). This architecture generalises across different VLA backbones as well. With a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ backbone on the same occluded tray task, CoLA matches the overall success rate of a LoRA-fine-tuned baseline (37.3% vs. 34.7%) using a fraction of the trainable parameters. When CoLA places the box, it selects the correct tray 71.8% of the time, whereas the independently fine-tuned baseline, whose placing arm never sees the marker, selects it at chance level (34.7% against 33.3%).
authors: Ahaskar Kashyap, Jiawen Zong, Boyu Ma, Chuhao Zhou, Jingliang Li, Stefano V. Albrecht, Jianfei Yang
bullets: Uses a trained message channel and per-arm diffusion action heads on frozen VLA backbones with decentralised execution.
Communication is valuable mainly under partial observability, such as an occluded handover where only one agent sees the box marker.
With shared overhead-camera views, disabling messages has little effect on two- and three-arm handover performance.
On a wrist-only variant, messages improve success from 64.3% to 74.8%; on the occluded tray task, success is 76.0% with messages versus 1.3% when removed during training.

papers.abstract: Words are increasingly becoming an interface for action: large language models (LLMs) can now invoke tools, operate devices, and make decisions that affect the physical world. However, current benchmarks largely evaluate LLMs through static text responses, offline tool calls, or simulated tasks, leaving open the question of how well they can act in real physical environments. We present a benchmark for measuring LLMs in closed-loop physical interaction, where models control a harness system connected to real-world components including robotic arms, cameras, and sensors. In each task, the model must issue instructions, receive physical feedback from the environment, interpret the resulting state, and adapt its next action accordingly. This setting evaluates capabilities beyond language understanding, including grounded perception, action planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, feedback-driven correction, and robustness to execution uncertainty. Through experiments with representative LLMs, we characterize their ability to translate linguistic reasoning into physical actions and identify common failure modes such as hallucinated state changes, poor recovery from unexpected outcomes, and unstable long-horizon plans. Our benchmark aims to provide a systematic foundation for evaluating LLMs as interactive agents that connect words, tools, and the physical world.
authors: Xinnan Dai, Kaiqi Yang, Yaxin Li, Cheng Luo, Wanli Li, Mingqing Xiao, Xinyang Jiang, Daoan Zhang, Kaitao Song, Fengze Liu, Zefan Cai, Caihua Shan
bullets: Addresses the gap between static language benchmarks and real-world embodied action.
Tests LLMs with robotic arms, cameras, sensors, and a harness system receiving physical feedback.
Measures grounded perception, planning, tool selection, spatial reasoning, correction, and robustness to uncertainty.
Experiments reveal failures including hallucinated state changes, weak recovery, and unstable long-horizon plans.
Provides a foundation for evaluating LLMs as agents connecting language, tools, and the physical world.

papers.abstract: Natural language specifications let non-expert users task robot teams, and large language models (LLMs) have recently proven effective at grounding such semantic specifications into plans for heterogeneous teams. Existing approaches assume missions that terminate and environments that, while unknown, do not change, but both assumptions fail in many emerging applications. For example, a disaster-response mission does not terminate, and its environment changes continuously as hazards spread and evacuees move. We identify three ways an LLM orchestrator breaks in this setting: its prompt grows without bound, its reasoning degrades as agents and targets accumulate, and it stops actively monitoring after covering the search space once. We build on the successful framework of grounded generative intelligence, and address each issue with a classical idea. A Markovian state summary, rebuilt from the semantic map at every invocation, replaces the growing interaction history. Partial delegation lets the orchestrator assign a subset of robots to an autonomous multi-agent protocol and reserve its reasoning for generating subtasks that require detailed parameters and careful ordering. Lastly, observation staleness, surfaced explicitly in the prompt, together with task-and event-triggered re-prompting, keeps the team vigilant. In a simulated urban search-and-rescue mission with spreading fire and moving evacuees, our framework rescues 98% of civilians versus 89% for the strongest baseline while using six times fewer tokens. Additional ablations isolate the contribution of each mechanism.
authors: Maria G. Mendoza, Victoria M. Tuck, Zachary Ravichandran, Shankar Sastry, George J. Pappas
bullets: Targets failures in persistent missions: unbounded prompts, degraded reasoning as complexity grows, and reduced monitoring after initial coverage.
Replaces interaction history with a Markovian state summary rebuilt from the semantic map at each invocation.
Partially delegates robot subsets to autonomous multi-agent protocols, reserving LLM reasoning for parameter-sensitive, ordered subtasks.
Uses explicit observation staleness and task/event-triggered re-prompting to maintain vigilance as conditions change.
In simulated urban search and rescue, rescued 98% of civilians versus 89% for the strongest baseline with six times fewer tokens; ablations assess each mechanism.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. System architecture. The mission statement, team specification, including task primitives and multi-agent protocols, and a partial semantic map are provided as inputs. The LLM is prompted with these inputs and the prompt information of Sec. IV-D to delegate a subset of the robots to the multi-agent protocols and generate subtasks for the rest according to the system needs. This plan is validated, and the LLM is provided feedback if there are issues. The actual task assignment is done symbolically with a linear program (LP) assignment. Multi-agent Protocols (green) are shown to be continuously operating with the self-loop or similar to tasks in that they have an endpoint. Asymmetric observations from all operations are constantly fused into the map. The feedback mechanism is triggered on task completion (solid lines) or on relevant map update events (dashed lines). Feedback on the map and observation age (orange) is compiled with a state summary of the history (blue) and provided in the new prompt to the LLM.

Fig. 5. The orchestrator reasoning about moving humans under partial information. Left: at k = 34 people are reported in r6 c0 and r7 c0, with an escort under way to r7 c0. Right: by k = 41 both regions have been re-observed clear and two civilians are reported in r6 c1. The orchestrator treats the re-observation as evidence the pickups are stale, cancels the escort, issues a local search around each vacated region to recover the missing group, and escorts the live report at r6 c1.

Fig. 7. Effect of exposing observation staleness to the orchestrator. With staleness in the prompt (green), the orchestrator sees max age = 202 and a median of 83, assigns all three aerial robots on coverage, and re-observes the region later in the run, recovering the last group of humans. Without it (blue), coverage looks complete (unobserved = 0), the mandatory-H constraint is dropped, aerial robots are released to other work, and the group is never found and the map is only covered once.

Fig. 6. Total tokens used across ablations. We show that for the same triggering mechanism, the stateless prompt (which does not re-send the prompt history) uses fewer overall tokens though more output tokens. These output tokens come from additional ”thinking” tokens the LLM needs.

papers.abstract: Traffic sign recognition plays a crucial role in the development of autonomous cars to reduce the accident rate and promote road safety. It has been a necessity to address traffic signs that are affected significantly by the environment as well as poor real-time performance for deep-learning state-of-the-art algorithms. In this paper, we introduce Real-Time Image Enhanced CNN ({\our}) for Traffic Sign Recognition. {\our} is a real-time, novel approach that tackles multiple, diverse traffic sign datasets, and out-performs the state-of-the-art architectures in terms of recognition rate and execution time. Experiments are conducted using the German Traffic Sign Benchmark (GTSRB), the Belgium Traffic Sign Classification (BTSC), and the Croatian Traffic Sign (rMASTIF) benchmark. Experimental results show that our approach has achieved the highest recognition rate for all Benchmarks, achieving a recognition accuracy of 99.75\% for GTSRB, 99.25\% for BTSC and 99.55\% for rMASTIF. In terms of latency and meeting the real-time constraint, the pre-processing time and inference time together do not exceed 1.3 ms per image. Not only have our proposed approach achieved remarkably high accuracy with real-time performance, but it also demonstrated robustness against traffic sign recognition challenges such as brightness and contrast variations in the environment.

papers.abstract: Beliefs in a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) are posterior distributions over the hidden state given the agent's history of actions and observations. They summarize everything the history says about the state, so planning in a POMDP is planning in a Markov decision process (MDP) over beliefs. Belief MDPs have continuous state spaces even for finite POMDPs, and exact planning in them is intractable in general. Planners must therefore approximate beliefs and estimate values. Monte Carlo planners do both inside a search tree, with an approximate belief at every node and a value estimate at every leaf. Approximations usually consist of sets of sampled states, with leaf values coming from rollouts, hand-designed bounds, or learned networks. Policies and values computed from these approximations are limited by their quality, and prior methods with learned networks rely on hand-chosen summaries of the sampled states. A belief representation should be computable from the parent node's representation through the POMDP's dynamics, let the search sample from it, and be learned so that it provides the information that policies and value functions need. We present Belief Embedding Tree Search (BETS), a Monte Carlo planner that meets these requirements by representing each node's belief with a generative distribution embedding (GDE) while updating it through the POMDP dynamics. BETS trains its belief model alongside its policy and value networks through experience, with the realized hidden state of the POMDP as the belief model's training target. We evaluate BETS on six configurations of RockSample, LightDark, and PocMan against BetaZero and three planners without learned components. BETS is competitive or leading on all six, while every baseline falls far behind on at least one. Where beliefs are highest-dimensional, it outperforms them by a large margin, even without search.
authors: Christopher Solinas, Radovan Halu\v{s}ka, Martin Schmid, Michael Buro, Nathan R. Sturtevant, Michael Bowling
bullets: POMDP beliefs are continuous posterior distributions, making exact planning generally intractable.
BETS represents each search-tree node’s belief with a generative distribution embedding (GDE).
The embedding is propagated through POMDP dynamics and supports sampling for Monte Carlo search.
Belief, policy, and value models are trained jointly from experience using the realized hidden state as the belief target.
Across six RockSample, LightDark, and PocMan configurations, BETS is competitive or leading and performs especially well in high-dimensional beliefs, including without search.

papers.abstract: Real-world Vision-Language Navigation (VLN) requires agents to act under partial observability, where map structure, semantic cues, and target locations may be incomplete or incorrectly inferred by foundation models. This paper presents a lightweight, training-free, and uncertainty-aware framework for cooperative multi-agent multi-target search in mapless environments. Instead of learning an end-to-end navigation policy, the framework separates high-level semantic reasoning from low-level execution through a scalable graph-optimization backbone. Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) serve only as hypothesis generators, proposing semantic zones, target-location cues, and possible navigable connections. These outputs are treated as uncertain priors and further refined using online observations and graph-context evidence. Cooperative navigation is then formulated as a rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear program with a lexicographic objective that first maximizes target-directed reward and then reduces travel distance, uncertain-edge use, and repeated visits. Experiments derived from 100 Matterport3D test cases show that the proposed framework improves target coverage and search efficiency over representative baseline methods, while shared information and joint planning enable more balanced workloads across agents. By operating on an abstract graph without relying on embodiment-specific policy parameters, the framework scales across varying numbers of agents and targets, generalizes to unseen environments, and accommodates different perception modules and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.
authors: Fan Pu, Keshu Wu, Jiwan Jiang, Shiyu Shen, Zhiwen Fan, Zhengzhong Tu, Jiachen Li, Yang Zhou
bullets: Addresses partial observability and unreliable foundation-model inferences in multi-target embodied search.
Uses MLLMs as hypothesis generators, then refines semantic zones, target cues, and connectivity with online observations and graph context.
Plans via rolling-horizon multi-agent mixed-integer linear programming with lexicographic priorities for target reward, shorter travel, fewer uncertain edges, and fewer revisits.
Experiments on 100 Matterport3D test cases report improved target coverage and search efficiency over representative baselines, with more balanced workloads.
Its abstract-graph design supports varying agent and target counts, perception modules, and low-level controllers without task-specific retraining.

papers.abstract: While asynchronous execution enables VLA models to operate in real-time environments by predicting the next chunk during execution, it inevitably introduces boundary misalignment with the committed action stream. Existing delay-aware solutions address this at the prohibitive cost of extensive retraining, architectural modifications, or fixed-prefix inpainting that inflates computation when low latency is vital. To address these problems, we propose FreeBar, a training-free real-time inference plugin that enables robust asynchronous execution with only marginal additional inference cost by casting chunk alignment in flow-based VLAs as barrier-guided action-space constraint. Specifically, FreeBar introduces a lightweight Control Barrier Function (CBF)-inspired consistency constraint between consecutive action chunks and solves the resulting correction in closed form, avoiding costly backpropagation through the VLA action head. By progressively tightening the consistency bound during generation, FreeBar aligns generated chunks with the committed execution stream while preserving early-stage generative and within-chunk future action flexibility,. Across Kinetix, RoboCasa, and diverse real-world robotic platforms with multiple VLA backbones, FreeBar improves success rates over naive asynchronous execution by 10%--15% on average, with larger gains in highly dynamic scenarios. It also preserves real-time computational efficiency, decreasing inference latency per action chunk over 45% than RTC. Additionally, as a universal plugin, FreeBar remains robust across distinct latency environments, base policies, and hyperparameter settings.
authors: Wenbo Yu, Jifan Li, Wenke Xia, Yuchen Li, Yizhuo Zhang, Pei Ren, Zhengping Che, Di hu
bullets: Addresses boundary misalignment between predicted action chunks and the committed execution stream.
Uses a lightweight Control Barrier Function-inspired constraint between consecutive chunks.
Computes corrections in closed form, avoiding backpropagation through the VLA action head.
Progressively tightens consistency during generation while preserving early and within-chunk action flexibility.
Improves success rates by 10%–15% on average and reduces per-chunk inference latency by over 45% versus RTC across simulated and real robotic settings.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents built on foundation models rely on an execution harness to organize observations, guide actions, and incorporate execution feedback into subsequent decisions. Failures can arise not only from limited model capabilities, but also from how the harness presents evidence and guides its use. These model-external mechanisms provide an adaptation target without updating model parameters, but task-specific interaction experience can be costly to collect. Task-level outcomes alone do not reveal whether relevant evidence was missing from the model input or was available but inadequately used. Moreover, these two aspects are coupled: effective action guidance may require evidence that the current context omits, while exposing that evidence alone does not ensure an appropriate response. We introduce EnactOpt, which uses limited execution feedback to jointly evolve reusable textual skills and context-construction code while keeping the underlying models and runtime fixed. It diagnoses adjacent decisions by relating action feedback to the actual model input and subsequent action. Structured episode summaries guide joint revisions through prompt-level edit operators, and candidate harnesses undergo compatibility checks and validation-based retention. Across VLABench, ALFWorld, and Embodied Agent Interface (EAI), EnactOpt improves task success by approximately 10-27 percentage points over the initial harnesses and outperforms the evaluated GEPA, TextGrad, and Trace2Skill baselines. These gains extend to task conditions not used for harness evolution or candidate selection. The results support a complementary route to embodied adaptation: turning limited execution experience into reusable behavioral improvements by jointly refining how evidence is presented and acted upon.
authors: ZhiYuan Feng, Zhuoshi Pan, Zhaolu Kang, Zhongxia Chen, Shuo Yang, Sen Ye, Heng Wang, Han Li

papers.abstract: Diffusion-based policies have recently emerged as a powerful paradigm for offline reinforcement learning, but their reliance on multi-step denoising introduces substantial computational overhead and requires backpropagation through time during training, limiting scalability and practical deployment. In this work, we propose \textbf{Instant Flow Q-Learning (InsQL)}, a single-step generative policy learning framework that retains the expressive capacity of diffusion models while eliminating iterative sampling and BPTT. InsQL builds on the flow-matching perspective of diffusion policies, but replaces marginal velocity parameterization with \emph{average-velocity} modeling and introduces a principled compositional mechanism, yielding a theoretically grounded objective that learns average velocity consistently across scales. This formulation provides a direct noise-to-action mapping and enables single-step action generation. InsQL further unifies compositional average-velocity modeling with behavior-regularized actor--critic optimization in a single framework, requiring only a single policy network and avoiding distillation, multi-stage procedures, and Jacobian computations during training. At inference time, actions are generated in a single forward pass and can be refined via value-guided candidate selection to improve performance. Extensive experiments on standard offline RL benchmarks and real-world robotic manipulation tasks show that InsQL matches or surpasses state-of-the-art diffusion-based methods while substantially reducing both training and inference time. Overall, these results establish compositional average-velocity modeling as an efficient and scalable alternative to multi-step generative policies for offline RL.
authors: Thanh Nguyen, Abu Hanif Muhammad Syarubany, Hwanhee Kim, Chang D. Yoo
bullets: Targets the high training and inference costs of diffusion-based offline RL policies caused by iterative denoising and backpropagation through time.
Uses average-velocity modeling with a compositional formulation to learn a direct noise-to-action mapping across scales.
Combines the generative policy with behavior-regularized actor–critic learning using one policy network, without distillation, multi-stage training, or Jacobian computations.
Generates actions in one forward pass, with optional value-guided candidate selection for refinement.
Experiments on offline RL benchmarks and robotic manipulation tasks show performance comparable to or better than diffusion-based methods while substantially reducing training and inference time.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Instant Flow Q-Learning (InsQL) overview. (a) Standard flow-matching (diffusion) policies learn an instantaneous marginal velocity field v(at, t, s) and generate actions by multi-step integration. (b) InsQL instead parameterizes the policy with an average-velocity field u(at, n, t, s) over finite intervals, enabling single-step action generation by directly mapping noise to action. (c) Velocity composition: long-interval average velocity (blue) is recursively composed from shorter-interval average velocities (green/red); in the infinitesimal limit, this recovers the marginal velocity used in FM. papers.abstract: Diffusion policies are increasingly used in robotic control and manipulation, vision-language-action models, and world-model-based agents. Their ability to represent multimodal action distributions offers rich opportunities for exploration in reinforcement learning (RL). However, optimizing diffusion policies with RL can reduce the behavioral diversity and further limit their exploration capability. In RL post-training, directly fine-tuning a pretrained policy may also disrupt its acquired capabilities, while action-space residuals may lack the expressive power for multimodal exploration. Together, these issues reveal a common challenge across online and offline-to-online diffusion RL: improving task performance while retaining the behavioral diversity and capabilities needed for continued adaptation. We introduce CFG-Policy, a unified, plug-and-play framework that separates exploration and exploitation into two generative policies and combines their score or velocity fields during sampling through classifier-free guidance. For online RL, a frozen exploration branch sustains behavioral diversity while an exploitation branch learns from task rewards; for offline-to-online RL, a pretrained exploitation branch remains frozen while a trainable branch steers the composed behavior. CFG-Policy preserves the underlying RL objectives and improves performance with QSM and QVPO on 5 MuJoCo tasks and with Flow-SDE+PPO on 4 RoboTwin manipulation tasks. Project page is at https://zhy-liu.github.io/cfg-policy-page.
authors: Shutong Ding, Zhaoyang Liu, Yimiao Zhou, Jingya Wang, Jiayuan Gu, Ye Shi
bullets: Addresses reduced exploration diversity and capability loss when fine-tuning diffusion policies with RL.

Supports online RL with a frozen exploration branch and offline-to-online RL with a frozen pretrained exploitation branch.
Integrates with QSM, QVPO, and Flow-SDE+PPO across MuJoCo and RoboTwin manipulation tasks.
Provides a unified, plug-and-play framework without changing the underlying RL objectives.

papers.abstract: Multi-finger hands contact objects at different times, so a global close command can overload early-contact fingers while others are still moving. Dense tactile arrays address this problem but add hardware, calibration, bandwidth, and computation. We present an edge-native pipeline that uses only built-in joint-angle and pre-use-calibrated actuator-load feedback to recognize the grasped object and predict an independent Stop event for each finger. Four samples and their first differences form a 4-by-20 contact-evolution window. At its core is a heterogeneous dual-expert architecture, termed DualExpert, that assigns complementary tasks to a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) and a Finger Graph Filter Network (FGFN). The TCN models short-term contact evolution and supplies all five Stop probabilities, while the FGFN encodes finger topology and contributes only to object classification. Fixed 0.7/0.3 class-probability fusion reaches 93.78\% trajectory-level classification accuracy on 225 held-out trials, improving the standalone TCN and FGFN by 4.00 and 2.22 percentage points, respectively. The TCN Stop path attains 95.25\% F1. The dataset contains 1,500 automatically collected trajectories from five object instances. In Flash deployment, mixed accelerator execution retains 93.78\% classification accuracy and 94.84\% Stop F1 with 2.890~ms mean inference time and 9.172~ms mean sample-to-stop latency. Across 50 physical trials, the system achieves 96.00\% recognition and 98.00\% grasp success while the complete embedded board draws approximately 0.80~W.
authors: Jiajian Zheng, Bin Zhang, Wen Fan, Yanan Liu
bullets: Addresses asynchronous multi-finger contact without dense tactile hardware, using pre-calibrated actuator-load and joint-angle signals.
Builds a 4×20 contact-evolution window from four samples and first differences.
DualExpert combines a TCN for temporal contact evolution and per-finger Stop prediction with an FGFN for finger-topology-aware object classification.
Fixed probability fusion achieves 93.78% trajectory-level classification accuracy and the TCN Stop path achieves 95.25% F1 on held-out trials.
Flash deployment maintains 93.78% classification accuracy and 94.84% Stop F1 with 2.890 ms inference, 9.172 ms sample-to-stop latency, and approximately 0.80 W board power.

papers.abstract: Robust motion planning and control for manipulators is the problem of guaranteeing safe execution and collision-free motion under disturbances. The Kinodynamic Motion Planning via Funnel Control (KDF) is a recently proposed planner that comes with robustness guarantees and is particularly attractive for collision-free control as it guarantees closed-loop evolution inside a funnel, i.e., a collision-free region around a nominal trajectory. Despite its attractive theoretical properties, the current approach for computing funnels is computationally demanding, which limits its expressiveness and performance. We address its current limitations by proposing a novel funnel planning and control solution. Our key tool to enable this is a neural Signed Configuration Distance Function (nSCDF) which allows us to estimate collision-free balls and gradients in a computationally efficient way. We use the nSCDF in our planner to compute a nominal trajectory, where path length and clearance are balanced. To track the trajectory with collision-avoidance guarantees, we design a funnel controller that exploits the geometric information from the nSCDF. From numerical experiments, we observe that our planner produces nominal paths $2$ times faster, while at the same time obtaining $20 \%$ shorter path length and $5$ times the clearance. Finally, we also observe improved motion performance and robustness properties when using the nSCDF for funnel control.
authors: Bernhard Wullt, Christos K. Verginis, Per Mattsson, Mikael Norrl\"of, Thomas B. Sch\"on
bullets: Targets the computational cost and limited expressiveness of Kinodynamic Motion Planning via Funnel Control (KDF).
Uses an nSCDF to efficiently estimate collision-free balls and gradients for planning and control.
Plans nominal trajectories that balance path length and obstacle clearance, then tracks them with a geometry-aware funnel controller.
Numerical experiments report paths computed 2× faster, with 20% shorter length and 5× greater clearance.
The approach also improves motion performance and robustness when the nSCDF is used for funnel control.

figures.caption: Fig. 5: Left: Illustration in world space, showing an example problem instance used in the experiments. The manipulator is 6 DOF colored black at a configuration along a collision-free path. The end-effector position is traced out along the path (blue curve). The start and goal configurations are colored transparent red and green, respectively. The obstacles are spheres (colored gray). Right: The learned configuration space representation of the world instance to the left, illustrated in the sub-space of the first three joints, i.e., main joints. The red, green and blue colored regions are the obstacle spaces for the main joints, wrist joints and self-collisions. The resulting path from our method is the black curve.

Fig. 3: All: A conceptual illustration of how the wrist configuration distance is computed for a 2 DOF arm, where qm is the main joint and qw is the wrist joint. The left plot is illustrated in the world space, the rest is illustrated in the configuration space. Left: The manipulator has two links (colored black). The main link is made transparent to emphasize that its collision with the obstacle is not considered. The obstacle is a disk (colored red). Its parameter vector is expressed in the base frame {0} as σ and in the wrist frame {w} as σlw. Computing the distance from the local wrist function results in a wrist movement (dashed blue arc) that moves the wrist to the obstacle boundary (transparent green). The distance or the movement does not include the main joint. Middle: Corresponding configuration space representation of the left plot. The configuration (red point); distance computed by the local wrist nSCDF (dashed blue line); the ground truth distance including the movement of the main joint (transparent red disk and green line). Right: To compute an estimate of the distance where the movement of the main joint is included, we discretize the space of the main joints (black points along the horizontal axis). For each grid point, we compute a distance, by forming the hypotenuse (red line) with the distance of the main joint (green line) and the wrist distance (blue line). This forms an estimated safe set (orange circle). From all estimates we take the smallest distance (blue circle).

Fig. 4: Illustrations in the configuration space. The SCDF, ψ, is illustrated as a colormap, with darker colors indicating lower distances. The zero-level contour, i.e., ∂Co, is represented by the solid purple curve. Left: Illustration of our medial-axis projection step. A discretized path (red points) is projected to points approximately on the medial axis (purple points), resulting in increased clearance. Middle: The projection steps result in a nonsmooth and distorted path. We solve a weighted shortest path problem by constructing a graph by using the points on the path as vertices. The edges are formed over intersecting balls (black lines). The weight function balances path length and clearance. Solving the problem results in an optimized path in the graph (red curve), which is continuously collision-free due to the intersection requirement of the resulting balls (red circles). Right: We smoothen the piece-wise linear path by solving a convex optimization problem. The key idea is to find a smooth path that is close to the original one (black curve). We do this by constructing collision-free capsules (transparent red) along the connecting line segments of the path. Each capsule is assigned a Bézier curve (colored curve within capsule). Continuity constraints are enforced with its neighboring curve. The closeness of the original path is controlled by the width of the capsules. Solving the optimization problem results in a smooth collision-free path.

Fig. 6: All: The vertical axis presents the integrated norm of the resulting jerk. Each data point is the average from 10 simulations in different funnels. If a run failed, then the average was not formed and no data point was added to the graph. The shaded region corresponds to ± one standard deviation. Funnel sizes: 0.10 rad (blue), 0.15 rad (orange) and with the nSCDF (green). Left: The horizontal axis represents different levels of model uncertainties. Right: The horizontal axis represents different amplitudes on the disturbance signal.

Fig. 1: Signed distance in the configuration space (brighter colors represent larger distance); the thick purple line (obstacle boundary) is the zero isoline. Our method computes a smooth trajectory (black curve) which balances path length and clearance. To track the trajectory, we develop a funnel controller such that the robot’s closed-loop trajectory (orange curve) stays within a funnel defined by the signed distance function (black circle and transparent red region).

Fig. 2: A conceptual illustration of the representation based on slices. The high-dimensional obstacle region (purple) is discretized into slices (dark purple), by forming the intersection with the hyperplanes (black). From a given query point (red point) we compute the distance to a slice (red line), by combining the normal plane distance (green line) and the in-plane distance to the slice boundary (blue line). The smallest distance from all the slices results in our estimate of the distance to the high-dimensional boundary.

papers.abstract: Multi-human cooperative object manipulation is a highly challenging topic in humanoid control. While existing methods can handle simple collaborative carrying tasks, they struggle with role-dependent, long-horizon, and sequential cooperative manipulation. To address this issue, we propose a hierarchical commander-executor framework that enables multiple agents to accomplish complex collaborative tasks in distinct ways. Specifically, a commander combines instructions and scene information for joint semantic and geometric planning. It then decomposes the task into role-specific subtasks and generates shared object-centric coordination plans, specifying execution timing, target positions, and manipulation actions for each agent. Conditioned on the commander's high-level strategy and each agent's local observations, the executor learns a low-level physics-based policy through a solo-to-cooperative curriculum to realize coordinated human-object interactions. The planned object trajectory provides a shared coordination target, while root positions and grasping instructions specify role-dependent execution cues. We evaluate our method on a variety of object manipulation tasks, demonstrating its ability to execute long-horizon tasks that combine different types of collaboration and to scale from two-agent to multi-agent cooperation. Extensive experiments further show that our approach achieves higher success rates compared to state-of-the-art methods. Code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/TJU-3DV/Co-Manipulation.
authors: Buzhen Huang, Xingchen Wu, Yuanwang Yang, Chenyi Xie, Kun Li
bullets: Targets collaborative manipulation tasks involving sequential actions, role specialization, and multiple agents.

The method reports higher success rates than state-of-the-art methods, though specific quantitative results are not provided.

papers.abstract: Humanoid Behavior Foundation Models (BFMs) can execute impressive motions, but downstream applications such as loco-manipulation demand high whole-body positional accuracy. Existing BFMs suffer from a systematic command-execution gap, where executed motions deviate from desired ones. We show that additional test-time compute can improve execution without retraining the BFM. First, we introduce Test-Time Command Optimization (TTCO), which adapts the input command to the specific BFM to produce an executed trajectory closer to the desired motion. TTCO finds such commands by sampling-based optimization through closed-loop simulations of the BFM and robot dynamics. Across three BFMs on the AMASS dataset, TTCO reduces mean global body-position error by 79-84% in simulation. Second, we analyze test-time compute scaling and derive an approximate compute-optimal strategy that can sustain performance gains as the compute budget increases. Third, TTCO can generate BFM-specific action labels from recorded robot trajectories without requiring the original teleoperation body-motion commands. Simulation and real-robot experiments show that these labels are effective for training high-level loco-manipulation policies. This method also supports reusing existing demonstrations across BFMs.
authors: Weiji Xie, Junsong Wu, Zibo Zhou, Yueru Chen, Xingyi Wang, Zhenhua Xiong, Weinan Zhang, Chenjia Bai

Derives an approximate compute-optimal scaling strategy to preserve gains with larger test-time budgets.
Generates BFM-specific action labels from recorded robot trajectories, validated in simulation and on a real robot for high-level policy training.

papers.abstract: Bilateral teleoperation with force feedback is becoming increasingly important, and the quality of external-torque estimation is critical to this process. However, manufacturer-provided disturbance-torque estimates on commercial robotic arms are often inaccurate, while the use of end-effector force/torque sensors adds cost and payload. We propose LETS, a physics-guided learning approach that assigns rigid-body dynamics to recursive Newton-Euler inverse dynamics and reserves learning for only the robot-specific residual. LETS uses only the robot's URDF model and joint feedback, deliberately excluding control commands and thereby decoupling external-torque estimation from control-command inputs. It trains on 12 minutes of free-motion data in under one minute, without requiring a dedicated end-effector six-axis force/torque sensor. In bilateral teleoperation, LETS achieves real-time external-torque estimation that enables stable force feedback. Its free-space error is 69% lower than the manufacturer-provided estimate, substantially reducing coupled oscillations between leader and follower; its contact error is 28% lower, yielding more accurate haptic feedback.

bullets: Addresses inaccurate manufacturer disturbance-torque estimates and the cost and payload of end-effector force/torque sensors.

papers.abstract: Test-time compute (TTC), which scores multiple candidate actions at inference time, is a powerful way to improve the execution performance of vision-language-action (VLA) models, but existing methods keep the policy frozen, so the gain must be recomputed at every execution. We propose Verify, Act, Distill, a framework that consolidates the gains of TTC into the VLA itself. A fixed verifier scores candidates generated by a flow-matching VLA, the weighted aggregate is executed, and the observations and aggregated chunks from successful adaptation episodes are distilled directly into LoRA parameters with the standard flow-matching loss. This reuses supervision that TTC has already produced during execution, without additional reinforcement learning or rollouts dedicated to teacher generation. On the 40 LIBERO tasks with a SmolVLA 5k checkpoint, distilling from only 10 episodes per task raises the mean success rate of verifier-free single-candidate generation from 54.1% to 70.6%, retaining about 74% of the improvement obtained by aggregating eight candidates. Applying the same aggregation to the distilled policy further raises the success rate from 76.4% to 82.3%, with a particularly large gain on LIBERO-Long (44.0% to 57.8%), and the single-candidate policy also improves on LIBERO-plus, which contains distribution shifts. These results show that using verification as a learning signal, rather than only as an execution-time selector, both retains the improvements of TTC and re-amplifies the effect of subsequent TTC.
authors: Kaneyoshi Hiratsuka, Satoshi Yamamori, Jun Morimoto
bullets: Existing TTC improves execution by selecting among candidates but requires recomputing this selection at every execution because the policy remains frozen.

The framework uses a fixed verifier to score flow-matching VLA candidates, executes their weighted aggregate, and distills successful episodes into LoRA parameters using the standard flow-matching loss.
It requires no additional reinforcement learning or teacher-generation rollouts, reusing supervision produced during TTC.
On 40 LIBERO tasks, distilling from 10 episodes per task raises verifier-free single-candidate success from 54.1% to 70.6%, retaining about 74% of eight-candidate aggregation’s improvement.
Applying aggregation after distillation further increases success from 76.4% to 82.3%, with gains also observed on LIBERO-Long and distribution-shifted LIBERO-plus.

papers.abstract: Cross-modal Thermal Geo-localization (TG) provides an illumination-robust positioning solution for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs) in Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS)-denied environments. However, existing thermal geo-localization methods mainly focus on near-nadir observations or depend on map-side elevation priors, limiting their applicability to continuous oblique thermal localization with only geo-referenced 2D satellite maps. To address this problem, we propose ScalLoc, a scale-aligned local-to-map localization framework for continuous oblique thermal UAV geo-localization. ScalLoc follows a reconstruction--refinement--anchoring--propagation design: it reconstructs local window geometry from thermal sequences, refines camera poses using track-based pose optimization, adaptively anchors each window to the satellite map, and propagates validated states to recover frame-level global trajectories. To support systematic evaluation, we construct Thermal-Oblique, a real thermal UAV sequence dataset containing 216 urban and rural day--night trajectories and 28,112 thermal frames with frame-level annotations. Extensive experiments demonstrate that ScalLoc reduces the mean localization error from 112.69 m to 26.97 m compared with the VGGT-only configuration, corresponding to a 76.07% reduction, and achieves the lowest frame-weighted mean position error among the compared methods. These results demonstrate the feasibility of continuous oblique thermal geo-localization using only lightweight 2D satellite maps, without requiring digital surface models or preconstructed 3D maps. Code and dataset are available at https://github.com/FloralHercules/ScalLoc.

papers.abstract: Action chunking improves temporal coherence in visuomotor imitation learning by jointly predicting sequences of future actions. However, many existing policies regenerate entire action chunks even when errors are localized, potentially replacing otherwise valid predictions. We introduce Contextual Masked Action Policy (CMAP), a visuomotor policy that refines continuous action chunks through history-conditioned local regeneration. Specifically, CMAP introduces a history-conditioned action tape that combines executed commands with masked future positions to produce coarse action predictions and per-step uncertainty scores. An uncertainty-guided span regeneration mechanism then selects a high-uncertainty contiguous span and reconstructs it using the executed history and retained future predictions as context. By jointly reconstructing neighboring actions, CMAP models local temporal dependencies while preserving all predictions outside the selected span. Extensive experiments on nine simulated and four real-world manipulation tasks demonstrate that CMAP achieves superior overall performance over several competitive baselines. Ablation studies validate the complementary contributions of its key components, while held-out trajectory analysis shows that local regeneration reduces prediction errors within selected spans.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation poses a stage-dependent sensory conflict: vision and proprioception are essential for localization and approach, when force is largely uninformative and potentially distracting, whereas force becomes critical after contact, when irrelevant visual details and correlated robot states may become shortcuts. We propose DEFT-VLA (Dual-Expert Force-specialized Training for Vision-Language-Action Manipulation), which retains the task-adapted base expert for vision-dominated non-contact behavior and introduces a force-aware contact expert for critical contact stages, localizing force-conditioned adaptation to where it is needed. We further introduce a contact-localized force-attending curriculum that applies force-attending post-training only to the contact expert, progressively restoring vision and masking state tokens to suppress shortcuts. Real-robot experiments on pipette tip attachment, bimanual pipette aspiration, and whiteboard wiping show that DEFT-VLA effectively exploits force feedback to improve contact-stage performance while maintaining strong non-contact behavior and robustness to held-out grasp heights. It improves overall task success by 20-40 percentage points over the strongest baseline on each task.
authors: Zan Huang, Yibo Qiu, Kan Ding, Xuanping Zhang, Ao Tian, Ronald X Xu, Mingzhai Sun

papers.abstract: Synthesizing believable 4D hand-object grasping sequences is important for character animation, extended reality, and embodied agents. Grasping requires a hand to approach, contact, and lift or manipulate an object coherently. Existing synthesis methods often model only the final static grasp or rely on additional conditions, such as language, target grasps, or object trajectories, to specify the interaction. We instead study the underconstrained problem of generating a complete grasping motion from a single initial hand-object state. Our framework decouples hand-motion generation from object-motion recovery. Given an object point cloud in the initial wrist frame and the initial parameterized hand configuration, conditional flow matching predicts a sequence-level contact map and a hand pose at each normalized sequence time. This time-indexed formulation avoids the error accumulation of autoregressive rollout while representing the complete motion. We then infer an attachment frame and recover rigid-object motion through training-free, contact-guided weighted registration. We evaluate on held-out DexYCB objects and unseen object geometries reconstructed from in-the-wild videos by Open-CHOIR. Compared with LatentHOI, our method produces smoother hand and object motion in every setting, matches or improves on its contact and penetration metrics in the wild under a shared initialization, and is about 30x faster per generated frame. In a 15-participant study, our motions were preferred in roughly two thirds of (forced-choice pairwise) comparisons. Precise contact closure on novel geometry, however, remains a key open challenge.
authors: Nga Kiu Kelly Ho, Yilin Liu, Hao Xu, Niloy J. Mitra
bullets: Addresses underconstrained grasp synthesis without language, target grasps, or object trajectories.
Predicts a time-indexed contact map and hand poses using conditional flow matching, avoiding autoregressive error accumulation.
Recovers rigid object motion via training-free, contact-guided weighted registration after estimating an attachment frame.
On held-out and in-the-wild objects, motion is smoother than LatentHOI, about 30× faster per frame, and preferred in roughly two thirds of user comparisons.
Precise contact closure on novel geometry remains an open challenge.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Method overview. Given an object point cloud P0 and an initial hand state h0, both expressed in the initial wrist frame, a contact flow samples a sequence-level contact-distance map ĉ (Sec. 4.1). Conditioned on ĉ, a pose flow generates the hand state ĥ(𝑡) independently at each queried motion time 𝑡, sharing one noise sample across the sequence (Sec. 4.2). A geometric stage then detects the attachment frame 𝑡att and propagates the object rigidly with the hand, yielding transforms {𝑇𝑘}, through contact-guided weighted registration (Sec. 4.3).

papers.abstract: We present a learning-based framework that enables a full-scale bipedal humanoid to sprint at over 7 m/s with motion-prior-guided gait and perform aggressive cornering at high speed with a pronounced trunk lean of up to $25^\circ$. Achieving this combination is challenging: above approximately 4 m/s, periodic foot impacts induce severe, high-frequency yaw-rate oscillations intrinsic to high-speed gaits. This high-frequency temporal structure corrupts the history of proprioceptive feedback that flat-MLP policies rely on, while rendering conventional yaw-rate tracking rewards counterproductive, as they fight against the robot's natural oscillatory dynamics. Moreover, a single style prior shared across skills cannot tell which skill is commanded and inherently compromises the low-speed skill fidelity. To overcome these limitations, we adopt a causal multi-head attention (MHA) module to explicitly model the high-frequency temporal feedback. In place of the oscillatory yaw rate, we design a heading-direction reward that supervises only the low-frequency velocity direction, allowing agile turning at high speed without suppressing natural gait oscillations. We further introduce skill-conditioned multi-adversarial-motion-prior (MAMP) discriminators that condition the style reward on the commanded skill. Ablation experiments confirm that each mechanism is essential: replacing structured temporal encoding with a flat-history MLP caps the top speed; reverting to yaw-rate tracking prevents high-speed turning; and a single shared discriminator makes in-place turning collapse into a quasi-static stance. Our framework bridges the gap between raw sprinting speed and reference-motion fidelity, demonstrating stable high-speed sprinting and aggressive cornering in both simulation and real-robot deployment.
authors: Huaxing Huang, Ruidong Li, Jinchao Han, Ziyang Dong, Wenhao Cui
bullets: High-speed foot impacts create yaw-rate oscillations that disrupt flat-history policies and make direct yaw-rate tracking counterproductive.
Causal multi-head attention captures high-frequency proprioceptive dynamics in the policy.
A heading-direction reward encourages turning while preserving natural gait oscillations.
Skill-conditioned multi-adversarial motion priors maintain distinct motion styles across sprinting and turning.
Ablations and simulation-to-real deployment demonstrate stable sprinting and aggressive cornering, including trunk lean up to 25°.

(3) The heading-direction reward supervises the low-frequency velocity direction at high speed, falling back to yaw-rate tracking below vmin. papers.abstract: Robust manipulation under uncertain object dynamics and geometry remains a core challenge in real-world robotics. Policies trained under fixed assumptions often degrade when object mass, friction, scale, or shape vary. Embedding-based adaptation methods such as Rapid Motor Adaptation (RMA) address this by conditioning actions on latent representations of environment dynamics inferred from interaction history. We investigate whether this paradigm scales from single arm settings to coordinated bimanual manipulation, where higher dimensional control, coupled contacts, and shared object forces introduce additional complexity. We evaluate bimanual RMA on three contact-rich ManiSkill tasks with randomized YCB object properties. Bimanual RMA, using observation-action history and dual wrist depth images, retains privileged policy performance on bimanual picking and lifting, while an otherwise matched stationary PPO policy without latent conditioning achieves low success; all methods remain limited on long-horizon stacking. We further demonstrate direct sim-to-real transfer on a dual Franka lifting task without real-world finetuning. Together, these results suggest that latent conditioning provides useful structure for scaling robust control to coordinated bimanual systems, while longer horizon tasks require additional temporal structure.
authors: Seung-Bin Joo, Alessandro Albini, Luca Wiehe, Perla Maiolino, Daniel Olmeda Reino, Jo\~ao F. Henriques

papers.abstract: Evaluating autonomous agents requires examining whether they can translate goals into coherent action across extended interactions. In persistent environments, this requires coordinating interdependent actions under incomplete observations, accounting for delayed effects, and adapting as earlier decisions shape subsequent opportunities. We introduce ASIWorld, a survival sandbox that combines persistent world and character state with character-scoped observations and a programmable asynchronous interface to study sustained goal execution. Agents pursue interdependent production and exploration tasks through direct actions or agent-authored programs that continue running between model calls. The evaluation assesses task success, the attainment of development achievements, and survival costs, complemented by an analysis of execution behavior. In an exploratory study of nine agent configurations using a common harness, eight complete the production task and six complete both tasks. Analyses of execution trajectories and performance across difficulty levels reveal different preparation, combat, and recovery behaviors among configurations with similar task outcomes. Incomplete preparation is associated with stalled progression, while configurations that complete the tasks differ in survival costs and the fulfillment of additional achievement criteria. These findings illustrate the value of assessing sustained goal execution through both task outcomes and the behaviors and costs associated with achieving them.

papers.abstract: End-to-end driving policies can achieve strong task performance while offering limited control over their driving style. Driving style describes how a vehicle accelerates, brakes, and maintains distance. Policies trained without explicit preference conditioning lack a direct mechanism for adjusting these behaviors at inference. We propose YOUDrive, a vision--language--action planner for continuous and composable driving-style control. Each teacher's behavior is distilled into a task vector, a learned parameter update that induces a style direction in the planner's representation. These directions can be scaled and combined at inference without retraining the backbone. Conditioned on these directions, a flow-matching decoder models a multimodal trajectory distribution and generates kinematically feasible motion alternatives. We introduce the Style Alignment Score (SAS) to describe human-referenced kinematic behavior after safety and task gating. On NAVSIM navtest, a single coefficient monotonically controls assertiveness across six teacher-derived personas, while PDMS remains above 0.90 across the tested individual and blended configurations, reaching 0.954. Further analyses reveal systematic policy-specific kinematics after controlling for scene context, whereas the evaluated discrete style labels provide limited additional explanatory power. Code, checkpoints, and the metric will be released.
authors: Guantian Zheng, Lidong Yu, Tianyu Gao, Jiaxing Chen, Jiashu Li, Chen Lv

papers.abstract: Camera-first agents must act on the visual world as it unfolds. We argue that the central obstacle for future camera-first agents is not recognition ability - multimodal models (vision-language and live/streaming alike) generalize well through language and remain the right tool for semantic reasoning - but time. Many visual targets are ephemeral: they appear, are query-relevant, and leave within a short window. Binding memory to the same end-to-end path as reasoning means that by the time a monolithic pipeline completes, the evidence is gone. We formalize this as Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) and a Perceptual Deadline Contract separating a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline, grounded in the bounded, passive nature of sensory and working memory. We propose a two-deadline architecture: an always-on, bounded, non-semantic fast path; an active remembering mechanism that commits a moment to durable memory before it is overwritten (event-driven in v1); and a deferred deliberation layer (multimodal model + tools). We instantiate the contract on real MOT17 track windows, a consistency check, and calibrate the single-path baseline from measured frontier-model latency: even a short answer takes 1.2-9.3 s, and an agentic identify-and-search longer. Answers can be late; evidence cannot be missed.
authors: Xiaofan Wu, Xi Zeng, Miaoxia Chen, Peishan Chen, Shuyan Li, Chen Wang, Jiyun Yao, Hanyong Zhong, Jiahao Zhu
bullets: The key bottleneck is timing, not visual recognition or semantic reasoning.
Ephemeral-Target Interaction (ETI) describes targets that appear and disappear before processing finishes.
A Perceptual Deadline Contract separates a hard memory deadline from a soft reasoning deadline.
The proposed architecture combines an always-on bounded fast path, active durable-memory capture, and deferred multimodal deliberation with tools.
Measured frontier-model latency suggests answers may take 1.2–9.3 seconds or longer, while evidence can disappear sooner.

papers.tldr: Camera-first agents should capture fleeting visual evidence immediately, then reason about it later, because semantic processing may outlast the moment an object is visible.

papers.abstract: Versatile quadruped locomotion depends on a tight coupling between what the robot perceives and what its body can execute. Yet existing visual controllers typically organize depth history using fixed temporal patterns, overlooking that the same temporal span corresponds to different spatial ranges as the robot's speed, posture, and gait phase change. Consequently, the same visual history may be insufficient in one motion state but outdated or misaligned in another. To address this limitation, we propose TempoLoco, a body-aware dynamic visual perception framework that organizes visual memory according to the robot's current locomotion state. TempoLoco learns multiple complementary temporal views from a long depth buffer, encodes them within a shared feature space, and dynamically aggregates them using proprioceptive history and multi-scale terrain evidence. This enables a single policy to align visual anticipation with the robot's current motion capabilities across complex terrains, including stairs, platforms, gaps, discrete obstacles, rough ground, and slopes. From the experiment analysis, TempoLoco achieves a 78.4% success rate, compared with 58.2% for the strongest fixed-history baseline and 62.1% for uniform multi-scale fusion. In separate capability evaluations, it completes 41/45 simulated trials across nine terrain types and 23/25 real-world trials on a Unitree B2 with a fixed arm, demonstrating robust and deployable locomotion through body-aware dynamic visual perception.
authors: Hao Zhang, Yuping Yan, Yitian Hong, Luying Feng, Tianhong Wang, Fengqi Dai, Wei Chen, Yaochu Jin
bullets: Fixed temporal visual histories can become spatially mismatched as speed, posture, and gait phase change.
TempoLoco learns multiple temporal views from a long depth buffer in a shared feature space.
Proprioceptive history and multi-scale terrain evidence dynamically select and fuse the most relevant views.
It achieves a 78.4% success rate versus 58.2% for the strongest fixed-history baseline and 62.1% for uniform multi-scale fusion.
The system completes 41/45 simulated trials and 23/25 real-world trials on a Unitree B2 across diverse terrains.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Detailed architecture of TempoLoco (actor path shown). At each 50-Hz policy step, a 37-slot depth FIFO and a five-step, 260-dimensional proprioceptive history are provided to the temporal-perception module. Four globally learned continuous strides construct complementary eight-frame histories; the displayed stride values are the initialization, and filled and hollow markers denote integer-slot and interpolated samples, respectively. A scaleshared visual encoder maps each history to a 128-dimensional feature, and a body-state-conditioned temporal gate computes online softmax fusion weights from proprioceptive history and all scale-specific visual features. The fused 128-dimensional visual representation is concatenated with proprioception to form the 388-dimensional actor input, which is processed by the four-expert locomotion MoE and the unchanged action-processing pipeline to produce 12 leg-joint targets. The actor and critic use independent temporal modules, and the critic appends 33 privileged dimensions only after temporal fusion. The lower panel shows deployment on the arm-equipped Unitree B2, with the arm fixed outside the locomotion action space.

Fig. 1. Overview of TempoLoco. Globally learned temporal strides construct complementary depth histories, which are dynamically aggregated by a body-state-conditioned gate using proprioceptive history and multi-scale terrain evidence. The resulting visual representation drives a single leg-control policy across diverse complex terrains. The strides remain fixed after training, whereas the fusion weights adapt online at every policy step. The mounted arm is fixed and excluded from the locomotion action space.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) commonly couple video and action experts through dense, layer-wise Mixture-of-Transformers (MoT) attention, exposing action prediction to irrelevant visual features while enforcing matched expert depths. This coupling hinders selective visual-feature use and introduces redundant computation. We introduce Bridge-of-Experts (BoE), instantiated as BridgeWAM, which aggregates visual, language, and proprioceptive priors through 32 Latent Bridge Queries (LBQs) into a shared, limited latent space. Joint video-action supervision lets action gradients guide the Video Expert toward representations better suited for action prediction, while the Action Expert learns to selectively retrieve task-relevant information through cross-attention. Decoupling expert depths and reusing LBQs during action denoising yield a 5.06B model with a 30-layer Video Expert and a two-layer Action Expert, achieving 98.25% success on LIBERO and 72.24% pooled success on LIBERO-Plus, demonstrating effective task execution and strong generalization with an ultralight action head. Ablations support joint representation adaptation and unified LBQ conditioning. Relative to Fast-WAM, BridgeWAM reduces single-sample inference FLOPs by 28.72% in simulation profiling and real-robot latency to 77.1 ms (a 2.47-fold speedup). Qualitative experimental results further indicate preferential attention to target objects and task destinations across perturbations.
authors: Jiaxin Fang, Ruitong Liu, Zeyu Lai, Xingyu Wang, Mingyuan Jia, Pingyue Sheng, Weikang Wan, Mengdi Xu, Yuxiang Gao
bullets: Replaces dense layer-wise video–action coupling with 32 Latent Bridge Queries that aggregate visual, language, and proprioceptive information.
Joint video–action supervision adapts visual representations for action prediction, while cross-attention retrieves task-relevant features.
Decouples expert depths and reuses bridge queries, enabling a deep 30-layer Video Expert with an ultralight two-layer Action Expert.
Achieves 98.25% success on LIBERO and 72.24% pooled success on LIBERO-Plus; reduces simulated single-sample FLOPs by 28.72% and reaches 77.1 ms real-robot latency.
Qualitative results suggest preferential attention to target objects and destinations under perturbations.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) combine action generation with future prediction, allowing predicted futures to support action evaluation and robot decision making. However, the future associated with a candidate action may contain action-induced and environment-driven changes. Directly evaluating the predicted future may not fully characterize the future change associated with the candidate action. For example, a candidate action that worsens a favorable environmental future may still yield a favorable outcome, while one that improves an unfavorable environmental future may still yield an unfavorable outcome. To analyze this issue, we formulate a Structural Causal Model (SCM) for action evaluation in WAMs. The SCM formalizes how action-induced and environment-driven changes jointly shape future evaluation, and reveals a backdoor path through which environmental evolution can also affect the future evaluation associated with a candidate action. Intervention and backdoor adjustment account for this path, providing a causal basis for characterizing the future change associated with each candidate action. Based on this analysis, we propose Causal Action-Gain World Action Model (CAG-WAM). For each candidate action, CAG-WAM predicts an action-conditioned future and an environmental future under the same current observation, and defines their evaluation difference as causal action gain (CAG) for characterizing the future change associated with the candidate action. During training, we incorporate CAG into Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) to guide robot policy learning. During inference, we evaluate the initial action with CAG and, when needed, revise it using predicted future information. Experiments on multiple benchmarks support the effectiveness of CAG-WAM.
authors: Peizheng Guo, Cheng Zhang, Xingyu Zhang, Changwen Zheng, Wenwen Qiang
bullets: WAMs can misjudge actions when predicted futures mix action-induced and environment-driven changes.
An SCM uses intervention and backdoor adjustment to isolate each candidate action’s future change.
CAG-WAM compares action-conditioned and environment-only futures to compute causal action gain (CAG).
CAG guides GRPO-based policy learning and supports inference-time action revision.
Experiments across multiple benchmarks support its effectiveness.

figures.caption: Figure 2: CAG-WAM Architecture. (a) Future-Conditioned Action Model generates action chunks from the current observation and task instruction, and can additionally incorporate future feedback for action revision. (b) Paired-Future World Model predicts action-conditioned and environmental futures under different action conditions and evaluates them using the same future evaluator.

Figure 3: Training and inference framework of CAG-WAM. (a) Training: candidate actions are evaluated by comparing their action-conditioned futures with the environmental future, and the resulting causal action gain is used as the policy-optimization advantage. (b) Inference: the initial action is evaluated using the same paired-future comparison; when its causal action gain falls below the revision threshold, future feedback is used for an additional action generation before execution.

Figure 1: Motivation and causal analysis. (a) Illustrative cases where the overall future evaluation may not fully reflect the future change associated with a candidate action. (b) Structural causal model of action evaluation, including the backdoor path At ← Ot → Et+1 → Ot+1 → Yt.

papers.abstract: Coupling a pretrained vision-language model (VLM) with a diffusion or flow-matching action expert has become the mainstream vision-language-action (VLA) paradigm for embodied policies, yet they remain unreliable once a task demands precise manipulation, e.g., submillimeter cable insertion. We attribute this weakness to a training objective that averages flow-matching errors across contexts and flow times, allocating little supervision to the few decisive moments determining task success. Along the generative path, inference integrates a locally supervised velocity field, so equally penalized errors at different flow times can affect the executed action unequally. Consequently, precision-task performance deteriorates as physical tolerance tightens by orders of magnitude. We call this supervision imbalance across contexts and flow times Flow-Time Starvation. The remedy is to jointly align supervision allocation and representation learning with context-dependent precision demand, enabling the policy to recognize when greater precision is needed. We instantiate this precision-forcing strategy as Precision-aware Reweighting and Internalization for Skilled Manipulation (PRISM), which scores precision demand offline, strengthens flow supervision where errors are consequential and action signals are visible, and internalizes that demand in the VLM condition representation. Simulation and real-robot experiments show that PRISM preserves or improves general-task performance while raising mean end-to-end success from 38.3% to 86.7% across drive connector insertion, bimanual connector mating, and screw tightening, substantially extending the precision boundary of existing embodied policies without new sensors or observation modalities.
authors: Chenghao Yue, Peiyan Li, Hao Wang, Lei Lv, Jiahao Chen, Huaping Liu, Yu Luo, Yuanlong Zhang

Simulation and real-robot experiments cover connector insertion, bimanual mating, and screw tightening.
Raises mean end-to-end success from 38.3% to 86.7% while preserving or improving general-task performance, without new sensors or modalities.

papers.abstract: Despite recent advances in Aerial Vision-and-Language Navigation (VLN), single Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) search-and-rescue in outdoor scenarios remains challenging due to partial observability, making cross-altitude collaboration a promising direction. However, existing collaborative navigation methods rely on precise target localization and rigid goal-dispatching paradigms, ignoring high-altitude observation uncertainty and suppressing low-altitude exploration autonomy. To address these issues, we introduce BGC-Nav, a training-free cross-altitude collaboration framework that enables robust navigation via Belief-Guided Coupling (BGC). Specifically, the high-altitude UAV maintains a Global Belief Memory encoding task-conditioned priors, which the low-altitude agent incorporates into decision-making via Local Exhaustion Memory (LEM), Local Attraction Augmentation (LAA), and Directional Belief Prior (DBP) as an advisory bias rather than a rigid command. Extensive experiments on ESARBench show that BGC-Nav consistently outperforms state-of-the-art single-agent and collaborative methods. Code is available at https://github.com/uestchjw/BGC-Nav.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D hand-object interaction (HOI) perception have opened new opportunities for learning dexterous robotic skills from human videos. However, existing dexterous imitation learning methods often rely on costly and manually teleoperated robot demonstrations, requiring substantial human effort. Therefore, we build DEXCAST, a framework that learns dexterous robotic hand control directly from monocular RGB-D videos by leveraging joint HOI reconstructions, without requiring any teleoperation. Furthermore, how to model high-dimensional robotic hand motion and extract temporal context to inform future action generation remains a key challenge. To this end, we propose a DexHand Motion Perception Module (DMPM) to capture inter-joint coordination and temporal dependencies in compact latent representations that condition our diffusion policy. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that DEXCAST achieves exceptional performance across diverse dexterous manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Vision-and-language navigation (VLN) agents are typically evaluated by whether they reach a target and how efficiently they follow an instructed route, yet these metrics provide little information about collision behavior. Moreover, continuous VLN evaluation commonly uses a sliding regime, where an agent can slide along obstacles after a collision, potentially masking the effect of unsafe actions on navigation performance. We introduce VLN-Safe, a benchmark for analyzing collision safety under two complementary evaluation regimes: sliding, reflecting common VLN evaluation practice, and blocking, where collision-inducing actions prevent forward motion and more directly expose their consequences. Across six published agents on R2R-CE, 38.5-56.8% of successful episodes contain contact under sliding, while switching to blocking decreases success rate by 11.7-36.1 percentage points. We further analyze signals for anticipating imminent collisions and find that depth geometry and recent movement history are more informative than policy-derived signals, while safe alternatives near the policy's preferred action are rarely available. Motivated by these findings, we introduce a training-free collision guard that vetoes risky forward actions, executes an escape maneuver, and returns control to the original policy. Under blocking, the guard reduces collision steps by 62-98% and improves success rate by 6.9-29.3 percentage points across five recurrent, topological, and vision-language-action agents. Under sliding, it leaves success rate unchanged while raising the share of collision-free successes by 4.1-12.4 points. These results reveal a substantial gap between task success and collision-safe navigation and show that lightweight collision-aware intervention can improve both safety and navigation performance.

papers.abstract: Continuous indoor-outdoor navigation connects destination-level reasoning with motion decisions that must respond to current observations. We present VbotNav-0, a cloud-edge dual-policy framework that links these processes through asynchronous policy-to-policy conditioning. The cloud policy produces subgoal guidance from visual history, navigation instructions, and route tokens; the edge policy combines available guidance with current RGB and LiDAR observations to generate local trajectories. This formulation allows the local perception-action loop to continue between cloud updates. A common route representation connects indoor paths and outdoor map routes, and the training recipe combines navigation demonstrations, corrective data, and grounded visual question answering (VQA). In the reported closed-loop evaluation of 258 episodes across 145 scenes, VbotNav-0 achieves 55.04% success rate and 55.03% success weighted by path length.
authors: Shiqi Tan, Yujun Zhang, Keyu Li, Shuaixi Pan, Siyu Zhou, Hailong Qin, Yinan Yu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of linking destination-level reasoning with observation-driven motion across indoor and outdoor environments.
Uses a cloud policy for subgoal guidance from visual history, instructions, and route tokens, while an edge policy generates trajectories from guidance, RGB, and LiDAR.
Asynchronous policy conditioning lets local perception and action continue between cloud updates.
A shared route representation connects indoor paths with outdoor map routes; training combines demonstrations, corrective data, and grounded VQA.

Lower left: System 1 fuses RGB semantics and geometry with LiDAR BEV features, compresses them with a Q-Former, and generates ten-point trajectories via a subgoal-conditioned flow-matching Transformer. The policies communicate asynchronously at nominal rates of 2 and 10 Hz. Right: Stage 1 combines mixed-source, multi-task SFT with DAgger; Stage 2 uses primarily real-robot data for trajectory-VAE learning and flow-matching-based local obstacle avoidance.
