papers.abstract: In this work, we aim to develop an embodied MLLM agent that understands and solves embodied tasks by learning, abstracting, and reusing transferrable and generalizable behavioral patterns. To this end, we propose StateSkill, a new skill representation for embodied agents, which introduces the concept of "finite-state machines" into skill modeling for effective and efficient skill construction and learning. The core idea of StateSkill is to model embodied interaction experiences as a finite-state machine, where a skill is organized around a set of task-progress states, state transitions, and state-conditioned guidance, enabling embodied agents to dynamically adjust their skills as the task progresses while keeping skill contexts compact and stage-relevant. We further develop StateSkill-Evolve, an experience-driven evolution mechanism that iteratively refines StateSkill through retrospective analysis of new successful and failed state-guided trajectories. Upon this, we introduce StateGRPO, which integrates StateSkill evolution and model optimization via state-conditioned GRPO into a unified iterative learning loop, enabling state-conditioned skills and model capabilities to co-evolve and reinforce each other. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed methods and trained model (i.e., StateSkill-Agent) across various embodied tasks.
authors: Changxu Wei, Jingyi Zhang, Zhiyu Zheng, Tianyi Lin, Yixian Zhang, Yunpeng Qing, Jingyuan Liu, Zhi Hou, Jiaxing Huang
bullets: Motivation: Embodied agents need transferable, generalizable behavioral patterns while keeping skill context efficient.

Experiments report effectiveness across various embodied tasks, though specific results and scope details are not provided.

papers.abstract: Navigating cluttered environments while carrying objects remains a challenging problem for quadruped robots. Compared with works that focused on load-aware locomotion adaptation to maintain gait stability, existing autonomous navigation systems generally ignore the influence of carried objects' geometries and use fixed footprint inflation, leading to overly conservative navigation. To fill this knowledge gap, we propose a two-phase load-aware navigation learning framework. In Phase 1, we train LOADNav, a load-aware navigation policy via reinforcement learning, enabling the robot to adapt its trajectory and clearance behavior according to the geometric size of the carried object. In Phase 2, we train CoGE, an online geometry predictor via imitation learning, which estimates unknown payload geometry from occasional contact events. We evaluate the framework in cluttered environments with loads of varying sizes and shapes. The results show that our navigation policy exhibits clear load-aware behaviors, and the online geometry predictor estimates object geometry from occasional contact events, refining its estimate and adapting the navigation behavior accordingly. Without requiring any prior knowledge of the payload, it narrows the gap to geometry-aware policies.
authors: Qi Yin, XiaoLi Zhang, Yangming Shi
bullets: Targets overly conservative navigation caused by fixed footprint inflation and ignored payload geometry.
LOADNav uses reinforcement learning to adapt trajectory and clearance behavior to the carried object's size.
CoGE uses imitation learning to infer unknown payload geometry from occasional robot–object contacts.
Experiments with varied load sizes and shapes show adaptive navigation and progressively refined geometry estimates.
Without prior payload knowledge, the method narrows the gap to geometry-aware policies.

papers.abstract: Test-time sampling promises to turn one action prediction into a set of distinct executable candidates that a verifier can choose among. Downstream fine-tuning works against that promise. A vision-language-action model trained to solve one task distribution concentrates its flow-matching decoder around the dominant demonstrated action, so repeated samples differ only marginally and the verifier receives many copies of one decision. We call this proposal contraction and identify it as a key constraint on test-time scaling: repeated samples can remain highly redundant as the candidate budget grows. Action Dynamic Sampling (ADS) alleviates the constraint on the proposal side, during training. At each training step, ADS integrates $K$ additional trajectories from the current policy under fresh base noise, scores each by the flow support along its path with a Hutchinson trace estimator, and corrects the policy's local action distribution toward this weighted set through a detached finite-set KL term. Training cost rises; deployment cost is unchanged. Across simulation and four physical-robot tasks, ADS raises proposal spread without the success penalty that Gaussian perturbation incurs, lifts oracle best-of-8 success on RoboCasa from 57.6% to 63.0%, improves fixed verifiers by 2.4 to 4.9 points in simulation, and raises TokenPB by up to 13.0 points on real-world manipulation.
authors: Chen Zhao, Zipeng Ye, Haitao Shen, Guanlin Li, Yuchen Xie, Jing Zhang
bullets: Problem: Fine-tuned VLA flow-matching policies contract around dominant demonstrated actions, producing redundant test-time candidates.
Method: Sample additional policy trajectories, weight them by flow support estimated with a Hutchinson trace estimator, and apply a detached finite-set KL correction.
Contribution: A training-time proposal-diversification method that increases candidate spread while avoiding the success degradation of Gaussian perturbations.
Results: Oracle best-of-8 RoboCasa success rises from 57.6% to 63.0%; fixed verifiers improve by 2.4–4.9 points in simulation and TokenPB by up to 13.0 points on physical-robot tasks.
Scope: ADS increases training cost, while deployment cost remains unchanged.

papers.abstract: During human-robot interaction, sight plays an important role. When the human sees a robot, they can observe the robot's actions and better predict the robot's future behaviors. Conversely, when the human cannot see the robot, they become uncertain about the robot's intent and plans. In this paper, we focus on the human's field of view. Existing human-aware planners either ignore this field of view and assume the human can observe the entire scene, or intentionally design their interactions so the robot is always visible to the human. By contrast, we enable robots to infer what the human has and has not seen during interaction, i.e., the human's field of view. We then apply this estimate as a vision-aware filter on the robot's actions. Given a nominal robot policy and a model of the interaction, we roll out the policy over a short horizon to see how the robot's state updates. We then reweight the actions based on how those actions impact the robot's predicted visibility: higher weights are assigned to actions that bring the robot into (or away from) the human's line of sight. In practice, our framework provides an online estimation and filtering process that repeatedly updates its understanding of the human's field of view and then locally perturbs robot actions based on the human's vision. We evaluate our vision-aware filter on robots that assist humans in collaborative cooking and coordinate with them in driving environments. Across simulations and a 12-participant user study, we find that our vision-aware filter changes both performance and preference: participants completed over three times as many subtasks with in-view assistance while cooking, and had fewer collisions with cars that purposely stayed out of their view while driving.
authors: Mengxue Fu, Ya-Chuan Hsu, Yinlong Dai, Erdem B{\i}y{\i}k, Dylan P. Losey
bullets: Addresses human–robot interaction settings where existing planners ignore the human’s field of view or keep the robot constantly visible.
Uses short-horizon rollouts of a nominal policy to estimate how candidate actions affect the robot’s predicted visibility.
Reweights and locally perturbs actions to bring the robot into or move it away from the human’s line of sight as appropriate.
Evaluated in collaborative cooking and driving simulations plus a 12-participant user study.
In cooking, participants completed over three times as many subtasks with in-view assistance; in driving, out-of-view behavior led to fewer collisions with cars.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of our vision-aware filter. The human (green) drives with an unknown field of view θ while robots (blue) control the surrounding traffic. Based on the human’s actions the robots infer the human’s current field of view (FOV). More formally, the robots maintain a belief bt(θ) over what the human can see. The robots then use this belief to modify the actions of a base policy. The robot’s base policy proposes candidate actions (e.g., speed up, slow down), and the robot leverages its model of the human and environment to roll out each candidate action and predict the time the robot will spend in the human’s vision under each FOV hypothesis (Cθ). The scores are weighted by the belief (C̄). The robot then applies these scores to adjust the action distribution of the base policy, modifying how the robot acts to account for the human’s FOV. Designers can tune whether this steers the robot into or away from the human’s line of sight. Here our approach is used to minimize visibility, driving other robots out of the human’s FOV.

Fig. 3. The user study interfaces. Top: Overcooked, where the participant sees only the region inside their FOV and selects among currently available high-level subtasks from the menu. Bottom: Highway, where the participant steers the ego vehicle and sees only vehicles inside their FOV.

Fig. 4. User study subjective ratings. Participants responded to a 7-point Likert scale survey after working with each filter type. Error bars show standard error, and an ⋆ denotes statistical significance (p < .05). We find that people preferred robots that used our vision-aware filter (the colored bars); the correct way to leverage that filter (in-view or out-of-view) depended on the domain.

Fig. 5. Forced choice comparison. Our 12 participants ranked the filter type from best to worst in both experimental domains. In Overcooked participants preferred in-view, while in Highway participants preferred out-of-view.

Fig. 2. Overcooked environment. Here we show the four kitchen layouts used in our simulation experiments. We visualize the start state for each option. From left to right: back bar, banquet pass, chefs table, and divider. Brick tiles are walls, which block the human’s line of sight; pane tiles are glass, which is impassable but see-through. Each kitchen contains meat, onion, and plate dispensers, a grill, a chopping board, a sink, and a serving window. The green-hat agent is the robot and the blue-hat agent is the human.

papers.abstract: Model-based reinforcement learning has shown superior sample efficiency by leveraging the learned latent dynamics either in the form of derivative-free planning/imagined rollout training or dynamics gradient-based policy updates. While these approaches achieve comparatively fast learning, they all suffer, to varying degrees, from issues of recurrent compounding errors, high inference-time latency, and instability in backward propagation through time (BPTT). In this work, we propose a model-based RL approach that uses the chunk world model as a differentiable training-time evaluator to optimize the chunk actor without recurrent model invocation. Through the collaborative chunk-wise prediction of the world model and policy, we can generate H-step hypothetical rollouts in a single forward pass and directly optimize value expansion, avoiding the costly and unstable BPTT. We evaluate our method on 19 challenging high-dimensional humanoid tasks from HumanoidBench and deploy our method to the real-world for quadruped bipedal walking. Project Website: https://song-wx.github.io/cmpo.github.io/
authors: Weixi Song, Donglin Wang, Yong-Lu Li
bullets: Targets compounding model errors, inference-time latency, and instability from backpropagation through time in model-based RL.
Uses collaborative chunk-wise prediction between the world model and policy to generate H-step hypothetical rollouts in a single forward pass.
Directly optimizes value expansion through the chunk world model during training, without recurrent model invocation.
Evaluated on 19 challenging high-dimensional humanoid tasks in HumanoidBench and deployed for real-world quadruped bipedal walking.

papers.abstract: Most existing approaches rely on video or motion-capture data for reinforcement learning (RL) training; however, all of these methods require an upper-level module to generate reference trajectories in real time. In object carrying tasks, the humanoid can only lift objects from designated locations along the reference trajectory, resulting in poor spatial generalization. Moreover, existing policies can only be evaluated inside a motion-capture studio. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{MOVER}, a multi-stage, Teacher-Assistant-Student, RL training framework for humanoid object carrying. We first collect data from videos and employ GENMO and GMR to retarget the video data, combining this with data augmentation techniques to generalize the data across objects of varying shapes and sizes. In the \textbf{first stage}, building upon the DeepMimic \cite{peng2018deepmimic} motion-training framework, we train the humanoid to transport objects from specified locations along designated trajectories. In the \textbf{second stage}, we relax the tracking of the reference motion and adjust the reward so that the humanoid learns to transport objects from different positions. In the \textbf{third stage}, we apply a Dagger-PPO distillation method to distill away the proprioceptive position observations and reference joint position of the humanoid. This allows the deployed policy to operate without relying on global position information from a motion-capture system; instead, the humanoid can directly perceive the object's pose from its onboard RGB-D camera to complete the carrying task. We design a series of simulation experiments to compare the success rates across stages (Stages 1 vs. 2) and before versus after distillation. We further transfer the policy to a real humanoid, successfully transporting objects at varying positions in a motion-capture-free setting.
bullets: Addresses poor spatial generalization and reliance on real-time reference trajectories and motion-capture systems in humanoid carrying.
Uses a three-stage Teacher-Assistant-Student RL framework based on retargeted human video, augmentation across object shapes and sizes, and progressive task relaxation.
Applies DAgger-PPO distillation to remove global position and reference-joint observations from the deployed policy.
Simulation experiments compare training stages and pre-/post-distillation performance.
Transfers successfully to a real humanoid that carries objects from varying positions without motion capture.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. The training pipeline of MOVER. In the first stage, the teacher model is trained using the full observation set. In the second stage, the reward function is adjusted and the teacher policy is resumed to obtain the assistant policy. In the third stage, distillation is performed using the Dagger-PPO algorithm, yielding the student policy. The student takes the object’s relative observations and the humanoid’s proprioception as input, and can be directly deployed on the real humanoid.

The network takes as input the object’s position and orientation relative to the humanoid, joint positions, target point, totaling 39 dimensions, and outputs the humanoid anchor reference orientation as a quaternion, totaling 4 dimensions. It comprises two lstm layers and is trained by minimizing the L2 distance between the predicted and ground-truth anchor reference quaternions.

papers.abstract: In multi-robot manipulation, an action's value depends on how teammates respond. We present \method{} (Cooperative Action--Response Belief Estimation), a framework for learning \emph{team-response beliefs} from local history. A predictive belief encoder represents the interaction and conditions a nominal action. Matched reactive and replay continuations separate each candidate's direct advantage from the utility contributed by teammate adaptation. A candidate-conditioned readout learns this response distribution alongside total advantage, and calibrated selection chooses an alternative or retains the nominal action. Our analysis characterizes when response changes the preferred action and how prediction and source errors limit the recoverable gain. With the representation, proposals, and data fixed, explicit response supervision improves candidate ranking and reduces selection regret relative to learning the same information through branch utilities. The benefit is concentrated in decisions where teammate adaptation changes the preferred action. Across RoboFactory, the MARS Control Track, and physical collaboration tasks, CARE achieves the highest average success among the evaluated policies, combining a capable nominal policy with selective coordination adjustments. Together, these results show that CARE turns predictions of teammate adaptation into effective decentralized action selection. Project page: https://jeong-zju.github.io/care/.

papers.abstract: Emerging strong Vision-Language Models (VLMs) have advanced navigation foundation models. However, these models still have unsatisfactory performance on goal-oriented navigation settings. In this paper, we first conduct a motivating study revealing that the key issue lies in the insufficient utilization of streaming observations and imprecise target localization. To tackle these challenges, we propose GG-Nav, a simple yet effective navigation framework that learns a structured chain-of-thought (CoT) mechanism via supervised fine-tuning to explicitly localize goal-relevant instances, accumulate grounding evidence, and support more reliable decision-making. Specifically, the structured CoT is designed with two key stages: (i) Observation-to-Evidence, which reasons over all intermediate frames between adjacent decision steps to retain useful goal-related evidence; and (ii) Evidence-to-Decision, which integrates the current observation with accumulated evidence to ground the target and support the generation of navigation actions or clarification questions. Extensive experiments show that GG-Nav outperforms the state-of-the-art methods in terms of success rates on the HM3D ObjectNav, VL-LN, and CoIN benchmarks by 3.1%, 16.6%, and 5.3%, respectively. Ablation studies further show that accumulating evidence from intermediate observations reduces evidence-missing failures by 11.6%, while explicit grounding reduces stopping errors by 49.4%. We also deploy GG-Nav on a Unitree Go2 robot, demonstrating its zero-shot generalization capability in unseen real-world environments.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot systems (MRS) offer significant advantages over single-robot platforms by enabling information sharing and coordination for different tasks in complex environments. However, reliable cooperation critically depends on inferring trust over both information sources and their reported hypotheses, particularly under partial observability and potential adversarial interference. Existing approaches frequently depend on pre-established trust relationships or side-channel information, which may not be available or reliable in realistic MRS deployments. This work introduces NeST-Bayes, a neural-symbolic framework that jointly infers robot and hypothesis trust using only inter-robot observation consistency, without requiring preassigned robot trust, reputation information, or side-channel identity signals. NeST-Bayes infers instantaneous trust evidence scores for robots and object hypotheses by reasoning over ego-centric relational graphs constructed from cross-robot observation consistency. These evidence scores are accumulated over time through Bayesian updates of Beta-distributed trust beliefs to maintain temporally consistent trust estimates. Extensive evaluations show that NeST-Bayes achieves the highest mean object precision and robot recall across all benchmark settings, and the highest robot precision and object recall in most settings, compared to trust-based methods. Under aggressive optimized attacks, it achieves 98.8\% robot precision with 93.8\% recall and 98.3\% object precision with 95.4\% recall. In an occlusion-rich Webots warehouse, it maintains 92.5\% robot precision with 92.0\% recall and 97.3\% object precision with 85.0\% recall. These results demonstrate joint improvements in the reliability and coverage of retained information.
authors: Ruiyang Wang, Hao-Lun Hsu, Haocheng Meng, Songqiao Xie, Miroslav Pajic
bullets: Addresses trust inference in partially observable, potentially adversarial multi-robot systems.

Reports strong robot and object precision-recall across benchmark settings, including under optimized attacks and warehouse occlusions.
Scope: trust is inferred solely from observation consistency, without preassigned trust, reputation, or side-channel identity signals.

papers.abstract: Microsurgical anastomosis is one of the most challenging and sophisticated procedures for surgical robotics, requiring accurate manipulation of surgical instruments within a limited space to achieve precise operations. Accurate surgical trajectory anticipation is essential for surgical scene understanding, intraoperative planning, robotic manipulation, and reliable behaviour analysis. However, existing approaches mainly focus on features extracted from surgical videos and historical trajectories, while overlooking rich semantic and motion information that can provide more discriminative multi-modal representations for complex surgical instrument-tissue interactions. In this work, we propose a cross-modal feature fusion framework for long-term 2D and 3D microsurgical anastomosis trajectory anticipation. The proposed framework consists of a multi-modal representation extractor and a cross-modal feature fusion network. Semantic recognition of surgical objects and consecutive motion estimation are incorporated as multi-modal visual cues, providing complementary spatial and temporal guidance for instrument-tissue interaction characterization. A coarse-to-fine progressive fusion strategy with a long-short-term memory mechanism is introduced to capture temporal dependencies step by step. The training and evaluation are conducted on our established robotic platform and a comprehensive dataset containing both phantom and ex-vivo surgical scenarios is constructed. Extensive quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework consistently outperforms existing methods and exhibits improved robustness across different surgical scenes, highlighting its potential for both intelligent robot-assisted and autonomous surgical systems.

papers.abstract: Autonomous Aerial Vehicle (AAV) trajectory planning requires real-time and accurate safety gradient guidance, especially in dynamic environments. Existing methods typically rely on static maps and dynamic obstacle tracking to construct gradient fields, imposing heavy computational burdens and yielding conservative trajectories. To address these limitations, we propose a two-stage Field-to-Planning (F2P) learning framework to provide accurate and efficient safety gradients for trajectory planning in dynamic environments. In the first stage, we introduce an Ego-centric Polar Occupancy (EPO) representation that naturally matches the geometry of the onboard camera frustum, while supporting unstructured scene modeling. Subsequently, we formulate a Temporal Polar Gradient Field (TPGF) via multi-kernel separable Gaussian convolution to provide unified safety gradients, without explicitly distinguishing between static and dynamic obstacles. To mitigate the inherent spatial ambiguity introduced by applying convolutions within the polar grid, we propose an ESDF-guided offline learning strategy that incorporates geometric priors into TPGF. In the second stage, we employ the calibrated TPGF to guide the trajectory planning policy in a self-supervised learning manner. Comparative results with other approaches demonstrate the superiority of our method. Extensive real-world experiments within various cluttered dynamic environments validate the real-time performance and robustness on resource-constrained onboard systems.

papers.abstract: A long-standing goal in robotics is to develop generalist robots that can perform tasks across a wide range of settings, flexibly specified with images and text. Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models offer a promising path toward this goal by training on large collections of robot demonstrations. However, while VLAs perform well in-distribution, they often fail under minor test-time shifts, such as changes in object positions, lighting, textures, and camera poses. To address this, we propose Quality Diversity for Diverse Environment Generation (Q-DEG), a method for improving VLA robustness by generating adversarial environments and fine-tuning the VLA on its own successful rollouts. Q-DEG uses Quality Diversity (QD) optimization to find a set of high-failure environments, while promoting diversity using policy embeddings extracted from the VLA. These environments expose vulnerabilities that can be mitigated through self-imitation fine-tuning, thereby improving the VLA's robustness. In simulation, we conduct experiments across three representative VLA models, and our results indicate that Q-DEG improves robustness to out-of-distribution (OOD) adversarial environments compared to the base VLA and VLAs fine-tuned using data collected from two red-teaming baselines. Furthermore, we demonstrate that improving VLA robustness through Q-DEG facilitates sim-to-real transfer. Our anonymous project website is at: https://qd-env.github.io/qdeg/.
authors: Shihan Zhao, Henry Chen, Ya-Chuan Hsu, Minjune Hwang, Siddharth Srikanth, Freddie Liang, Akanksha Saran, Aaquib Tabrez, Stefanos Nikolaidis, Daniel Seita

Experiments across three VLA models in simulation show improved robustness in OOD adversarial environments over base models and two red-teaming baselines.

papers.abstract: It is widely appreciated that robotic policies require long-term memory to perform complex tasks. However, directly conditioning policies on all past observations leaves policy learning susceptible to learning spurious shortcuts, and introduces large latency at policy deployment. As such, today's memory-augmented policies curate what to remember, either by retaining only recent frames, selected keyframes, or textual summaries, or by learning latent representations of the visual stream alone. In this work, we propose an alternative approach IMPRINT, a policy-agnostic latent memory framework that augments vision-language-action (VLA) models with multi-stream memory without explicitly constraining what the policy should remember. IMPRINT compresses different streams into a latent memory that is updated incrementally at inference, enabling low latency. To avoid shortcut learning, IMPRINT adopts a two-stage training procedure, first supervising memory to reconstruct multiple streams (observations, actions, proprioception) of past information, as well as estimate current task progress, followed by end-to-end finetuning, jointly with the policy, on action prediction. Across both simulation and real-world tasks demanding memory, IMPRINT improves average success over the base VLA by at least 26%, outperforming popular alternatives, and maintaining lowest inference latency among memory-augmented VLAs. Through careful ablations, we demonstrate the utility of incorporating diverse information streams into robotic memory, validating the advantages of foregoing history curation. Project website: https://yilin-wu98.github.io/imprint_website/.

papers.abstract: Successor-feature-based zero-shot reinforcement learning methods pre-train a task encoder and successor-feature predictor on offline, reward-free data, then recover a policy at test time by solving a closed-form linear regression over a small labeled dataset. We identify an underexplored limitation of this approach: when the task encoder produces dense representations, the inferred reward signal becomes diffuse across the state space, reducing the contrast between goal-relevant states and the background and providing a weaker signal for the policy to follow. We address this limitation by introducing an l1 sparsity penalty that concentrates reward-predictive structure into a smaller effective subspace of the task encoder's latent space. The penalty is applied only during training and requires no architectural change or modification to the closed-form inference procedure. We instantiate this approach as Sparse-TD-JEPA, a single-line of code addition based on Temporal-Difference Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (TD-JEPA) that significantly improved its performance in zero-shot reinforcement learning. We evaluate Sparse-TD-JEPA on 65 tasks across the DeepMind Control (DMC) Suite and OGBench, covering locomotion, navigation, trajectory stitching, puzzle solving, and robotic manipulation. Sparse-TD-JEPA improves over TD-JEPA in all 13 domain-level comparisons. On DMC, it increases the average return from 661 +- 6 to 714 +- 3. On OGBench, it increases the average success rate from 38.0 +- 0.8 to 48.4 +- 2.3, with improvements of 13.4-18.0 percentage points on the evaluated antmaze navigation and stitching domains. Overall, Sparse-TD-JEPA achieves the highest mean performance among established zero-shot baselines in nine of the 13 domains. Analysis further shows that sparsity produces a sharper and more task-informative inferred reward landscape.
authors: Duaa Nakshbandi, Zhiyu An, Wan Du
bullets: Dense task representations can diffuse inferred rewards across the state space, weakening goal-state contrast.
An L1 penalty concentrates reward-predictive information in a smaller latent subspace without changing the architecture or test-time closed-form inference.
Across 65 DMC Suite and OGBench tasks, Sparse-TD-JEPA improves over TD-JEPA in all 13 domain-level comparisons.
Average return rises from 661 ± 6 to 714 ± 3 on DMC; average success rate rises from 38.0 ± 0.8% to 48.4 ± 2.3% on OGBench.
The approach achieves the highest mean performance among established zero-shot baselines in 9 of 13 domains; analysis links gains to sharper, more task-informative reward landscapes.

papers.abstract: Retargeting human demonstrations into dynamically feasible dexterous hand trajectories requires resolving complex contact physics, yet current methods either omit physical constraints or rely on computationally expensive sampling-based optimization in simulation. Reinforcement learning has previously been used to achieve planning and control through contact dynamics; however, standard policies require object-specific training and fail to generalize across arbitrary geometries. This work reframes physics-based retargeting as a residual learning problem, where we demonstrate that zero-shot generalization across objects relies on structured state representations. Specifically, formulating the observation space to include a localized contact-error signal guiding each robot link to its target coordinate on the object surface enables a single, unified residual policy to successfully grasp novel, unseen object geometries. Rolling out this policy in simulation on a kinematic reference trajectory yields a physics-based retargeter, OATH. Operating at 0.4 seconds of compute per second of reference, OATH achieves 2.4x faster-than-real-time performance and a 60-350x reduction in computational cost compared to sampling-based methods. The system recovers 58% of held-out and 54% of unseen-object DexYCB trajectories while maintaining a sub-2 cm tracking error.
authors: Solvin Sigurdson, Prasanna Sriganesh, Juan Borbon, Joel Burdick, Dingqi Zhang, Jiuguang Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of producing dynamically feasible hand trajectories under complex contact physics without costly sampling-based optimization.
Uses a unified residual reinforcement-learning policy with structured observations that encode each robot link’s contact error relative to the object surface.
Generalizes zero-shot to novel object geometries, including held-out and unseen objects.
Runs at 0.4 seconds of compute per second of reference, achieving 2.4× faster-than-real-time performance and 60–350× lower computational cost than sampling-based methods.
Recovers 58% of held-out and 54% of unseen-object DexYCB trajectories with sub-2 cm tracking error.

papers.abstract: Dexterous robot hands can receive useful motion intent from teleoperation or learned policies, but successful execution also depends on contact decisions that these commands rarely specify. We introduce DexFLEX, a contact-aware foundation controller that turns upstream fingertip-motion drafts into contact-consistent joint commands. Instead of treating a draft as a trajectory to copy, DexFLEX treats it as evidence about intent: from the current tactile-proprioceptive state, it proposes feasible short-horizon motion chunks, predicts their contact consequences, and selects the candidate that best follows the command while preserving future contact stability. At inference time, a simple Draft-Dream-Select procedure combines pure-prior proposals for recovery with draft-seeded proposals for responsiveness, then decodes the selected motion into executable joint-space targets. Across degraded-command simulation, real-world shared control, and visuomotor policy learning, the same trained controller improves robustness without retraining, increasing real-world teleoperation success from 29.2% to 78.3% and reaching 46.7% policy-learning success, 3.5 times direct joint-action prediction, and 1.56 times prior-only correction. Videos are available at dex-flex.github.io.
authors: Weikang Wan, Zeyu Lai, Jianyu Hou, Yuchen Zhou, Jiawei Fu, Henrik I Christensen, Hao Su
bullets: Addresses the missing contact decisions in teleoperation and learned motion commands.
Uses tactile-proprioceptive state to propose short-horizon motion chunks and predict their contact consequences.
Draft-Dream-Select combines command-seeded proposals with prior-based recovery, then selects stable, command-following motions.
The same trained controller improves performance across simulation, shared-control, and visuomotor policy-learning settings.
Reported success rises from 29.2% to 78.3% in real-world teleoperation; policy-learning success reaches 46.7%.

papers.abstract: World-action models inherit broad visual and physical priors from video pre-training. However, standard within-video next-frame prediction allows them to rely on appearance shared between the context and future, rather than learning interactions that transfer across scenes and embodiments. We introduce WATCH, a cross-video pre-training that learns from task-paired human demonstrations collected across diverse environments. Conditioned on the video and actions of one demonstration, the model jointly predicts another demonstration's actions and future frames from its current observation. Predicting one demonstration from another encourages the model to learn task-relevant interactions that transfer across scenes and demonstrators. Our pre-training shows that these capabilities can be learned from readily scalable human-human pairs alone, without requiring matched human-robot demonstrations. Analyses before robot post-training show improved motion alignment across embodiments and better action and video prediction on unseen robots, with representations closer to those learned from robot pairs. After robot post-training, WATCH improves MimicDroid in-context success from 40.9% to 68.3% with Cosmos Policy and from 59.8% to 77.7% with Cosmos3, with the largest gains on the unseen levels. Gains persist under context-free post-training across robot embodiments. WATCH outperforms within-video pre-training and co-training baselines, supporting cross-video prediction as a scalable approach to learning transferable world-action representations.
authors: Jeongeun Park, Taekyung Kim, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun
bullets: Addresses the limitation of within-video prediction, which can rely on appearance overlap rather than transferable task interactions.
Uses cross-video pre-training on task-paired human-human demonstrations across diverse environments, without requiring human-robot pairs.
Jointly predicts the paired demonstration’s actions and future frames conditioned on the source video, actions, and target observation.
Improves motion alignment and action/video prediction on unseen robots before robot post-training.
Raises MimicDroid in-context success from 40.9% to 68.3% with Cosmos Policy and from 59.8% to 77.7% with Cosmos3; gains are largest on unseen levels and persist across embodiments.

papers.abstract: We present CoPlanVLM, which uses a Vision Language Model (VLM) to translate a single natural-language instruction and image into coordinated paths for a team of two robots. While VLMs offer a flexible, natural-language interface for commanding robot teams, their weak spatial reasoning has greatly limited VLM-based path planning. CoPlanVLM improves the VLM's spatial reasoning and path planning abilities through three components: (1) an image overlay marking both free space and obstacles, (2) task classification that selects the most appropriate low-level planner and reasoning prompt for each instruction, and (3) task-specific chain-of-thought reasoning that prompts the VLM to identify key objects, allocate roles, and verify routes are collision-free before committing to a plan. Together, these components enable the team to complete complex coordinated maneuvers requiring both robots and divide large tasks between robots to increase efficiency. CoPlanVLM also supports detailed maneuvers involving specific routes, loops, and coverage of large areas, as well as tasks requiring directional reasoning such as north/south or left/right. We validate CoPlanVLM in both Gazebo simulation and on physical Turtlebot 4 hardware. CoPlanVLM attains an average success rate of 84.4% compared to 50.0% for the closest baseline. On trials where both methods succeed, CoPlanVLM's paths are 27% shorter on average. Project code is available at https://github.com/AICPS/CoPlanVLM.
authors: David R. Martin, Jared Paquet, Mohammad Abdullah Al Faruque, Pramod Khargonekar, Kyle Volle, J. Humberto Ramos, Scott Nivison

Validated in Gazebo and on Turtlebot 4 hardware, achieving 84.4% average success versus 50.0% for the closest baseline.
When both methods succeed, its paths are 27% shorter on average.

papers.abstract: Latent world-model planning has shown promising results in goal-conditioned robotic manipulation, but remains challenging for long-horizon planning due to limited temporal guidance and inefficient action search. A distant visual goal provides little guidance for preparatory actions, while uninformed action sampling makes local optimization inefficient. We propose PILOT (Policy-Initialized Local Optimization with Temporal subgoals), which uses a video model to generate intermediate visual subgoals and a learned policy to initialize the cross-entropy method (CEM). CEM refines candidate action sequences toward each subgoal using an action-conditioned world model in a receding-horizon control loop. In our primary real-robot evaluation across four UR5e manipulation tasks, PILOT achieves 68.8% success, compared with 55.0% without policy initialization, 13.8% for policy-only execution, and 0.0% for direct final-goal planning. Simulation results show that these gains persist over longer horizons: PILOT exceeds direct execution of the same policy by 30 percentage points on long Push-T tasks and by 22 percentage points on LIBERO-10. Policy initialization also accelerates local optimization: on Push-T, CEM matches the cost reached by generic initialization after 10 iterations in only 4 iterations and reduces the final planning cost by 24.1% under the same sampling budget. These results show that combining temporal subgoals with policy-guided action search improves both long-horizon task execution and local planning efficiency. Videos are available on the webpage: https://pilot-planner.github.io/.

papers.abstract: Position tracking is a well-studied problem in Euclidean navigation, yet comparatively little attention has been given to navigation on general manifolds, where motion is governed by the underlying geometry of the space. In this work, we formalize the problem of manifold navigation as a velocity-driven tracking task and propose a coordinate-chart-based learning framework in which learning models operate entirely in a Euclidean representation. Predicted trajectories are mapped to the manifold via an immersion function prior to error computation, allowing geometric consistency to be evaluated without explicitly enforcing manifold constraints during learning. Within this framework, we focus on Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) for sequential position prediction on curved manifolds after comparisons with alternative recurrent architectures. We evaluate our GRU models, trained with pertinent custom loss functions, against both a standard MSE loss function and a naive vector-addition baseline. We evaluate our approach on both analytically (and numerically) defined manifolds, as well as a surface reconstructed from a LiDAR point cloud. Our results show that recurrent models can learn to approximate manifold-constrained dynamics from velocity sequences and consistently outperform Euclidean baselines. Our results demonstrate that certain custom loss functions significantly improve long-horizon prediction accuracy compared to conventional point-wise loss functions.

Focuses on GRUs and compares custom geometric losses with standard MSE and naive vector addition.
Evaluates on analytic/numerical manifolds and a LiDAR-reconstructed surface.
Custom loss functions improve long-horizon accuracy, while recurrent models outperform Euclidean baselines.

papers.abstract: Humans and animals do not learn vision from a fixed set of data: they move, interact, and learn from the visual consequences of their actions. Motivated by this developmental view, we study whether robots can improve visual learning by actively collecting experience through curiosity-driven interaction. We introduce DySCOVER, a self-supervised framework for active robot visual learning. A robot observes RGB frames, learns a visual autoencoder that encodes and reconstructs them, and trains a recurrent world model to predict the next visual latent state conditioned on the current state and action. The agent's policy is trained only with intrinsic rewards: reconstruction error encourages visually novel observations, while the world model's error encourages transitions whose consequences are not yet predictable. This prediction error biases the policy toward more intricate trajectories that enrich the agent's set of experiences with observations beyond those encouraged by visual novelty alone. Our experiments conducted with robotic arms as the embodied agents show that adding predictive curiosity improves the vision model over using visual curiosity alone. Across variations in initial conditions, experience capacity, embodiment, and scene content, adding predictive curiosity consistently improved visual learning. These results show that predictive curiosity can improve active visual learning beyond reconstruction-based curiosity alone.
authors: Stelios Zarifis, Panagiotis Filntisis, George Retsinas, Petros Maragos
bullets: Robots actively gather visual experience instead of learning from a fixed dataset.
A visual autoencoder reconstructs RGB observations, while a recurrent world model predicts future visual latents from states and actions.
Intrinsic rewards combine reconstruction error with prediction error to drive curiosity-based exploration.
Robot-arm experiments show predictive curiosity consistently improves visual learning over reconstruction-based curiosity alone.
The study evaluates varied initial conditions, experience capacities, embodiments, and scene contents.

papers.abstract: Diffusion models provide expressive trajectory priors for multi-robot motion planning (MRMP), but scaling them to large teams requires coordinating individual motions without expensive joint computation. We introduce Akule, a sparse interaction diffusion framework that augments a frozen single-robot prior with three learned modules: a reusable pairwise correction model $R_{\phi}$, a contextual selector $U_{\psi}$ that determines which corrections to evaluate, and a composer $G_{\omega}$ that combines their effects through context-dependent signed weights. This decomposition separates which interactions merit computation from how their effects should be combined into coordinated denoising updates. We train $R_{\phi}$ using matched pairwise trajectory optimizations, then learn $G_{\omega}$ and $U_{\psi}$ from physically optimized joint trajectories without requiring a prescribed ground-truth interaction graph. The resulting joint proposals are passed to a downstream search-based planner for validation and repair. Across diverse MRMP benchmarks, Akule achieves competitive planning success, complete-planner speedups of up to $25\times$, zero-shot population transfer, and successful planning with up to $256$ robots. Ablations further demonstrate that learned selection and composition reduce pre-repair conflicts and downstream repair effort relative to heuristic selection and uniform summation.
authors: Manav Vora, Gokul Puthumanaillam, Aditya Penumarti, Jane Shin, Melkior Ornik
bullets: Addresses the costly joint coordination problem in diffusion-based multi-robot motion planning.
Uses a frozen single-robot prior plus learned pairwise correction, interaction selection, and context-dependent composition modules.
Trains corrections from pairwise optimized trajectories and selection/composition from optimized joint trajectories without a predefined interaction graph.
Feeds generated joint proposals to a search-based planner for validation and repair.
Reports competitive success, up to 25× complete-planner speedups, zero-shot population transfer, and reduced conflicts and repair effort.

papers.abstract: An LLM-directed excavator can execute mechanically feasible motion whose destination or authority no longer matches the operator's approval. We propose execution-bound authorization for the approval--dispatch--execution interval. A one-use lease binds the action, generated motion, mission contract and admission tolerance; atomic dispatch rechecks current authority and measured joint drift. Periodic supervision detects revocation and requests a quintic stop with a carry-pitch endpoint, selected through sampled joint, stroke, flow and reference-acceleration checks. The framework connects exact motion identity to dispatch integrity and load-aware interruption. Evaluation combines a 672-case interface suite, four loaded digging cases in synchronous simulation, unloaded MuJoCo/Pinocchio transfers and two command-level LLM planners. The gateway admitted all 120 benign interface cases and produced zero unauthorized dispatches in the attack suite. Loaded dispatch-window tests produced zero unauthorized deposition. During simulated dump-phase revocation, maximum closed-site deposition decreased from 1.23 to 0.33\,m$^3$; loaded-slew stops used less than 75\% of nominal swing torque. These results demonstrate motion-bound authorization and quantify the retention and stopping behavior of supervised excavation skills.

papers.abstract: We introduce ClothCode, a unified generative framework for garment state estimation and action-conditioned dynamics prediction in a shared discrete configuration space. A material-aligned tokenizer encodes garment configuration as residual vector-quantized patch tokens, while task-specific Masked Generative Transformers predict these tokens through parallel confidence-guided refinement. Across three garment templates, ClothCode reduces mean displacement error by 26.6% for state estimation and 37.0% for dynamics prediction relative to the strongest baselines. Dynamics prediction requires only 16.7 ms per window, compared with 556.2 ms for diffusion. Integrated into the same model-predictive controller, ClothCode improves real-world folding and flattening success from 56.7% to 78.9%. Further results and videos are available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ClothCode-DE32
authors: Yingdong Ru, Lipeng Zhuang, Shiyu Fan, Zhuo He, Florent P. Audonnet, Gerardo Aragon Camarasa

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of our discrete generative framework for model-based garment manipulation. A garment configuration is encoded as a set of discrete patch tokens shared by two Masked Generative Transformers (MGTs). (1) The discrete garment representation captures local deformation states over fixed material patches. (2) For state estimation, an MGT iteratively predicts the complete token configuration from a partial point cloud. (3) For dynamics prediction, an action-conditioned MGT predicts future garment configurations for candidate actions, allowing MPC to select the trajectory with the lowest goal cost. (4) The resulting perception–prediction loop enables closed-loop garment manipulation on a real robot.

Fig. 2. Overview of ClothCode. ClothCode first learns a discrete representation of garment shape (top). Each mesh is divided into fixed patches that track the same material regions across deformations, encoded as two-level residual vector-quantization (RVQ) tokens, and reconstructed by a shared mesh decoder. This frozen representation provides a common prediction space for two tasks. For state estimation (bottom left), a masked transformer combines a partial point cloud with masked garment tokens to recover the complete garment configuration and its global position. For dynamics prediction (bottom right), a second masked transformer combines recent garment states with a candidate end-effector trajectory and jointly predicts the future garment sequence and its global motion. M denotes a masked token.

papers.abstract: Reward design remains a major bottleneck for reinforcement learning in robotic manipulation. Handcrafted dense rewards can compensate for the limited guidance provided by sparse rewards, but require substantial task-specific reward engineering. Learning rewards from videos provides a scalable, data-driven alternative to manual reward design. However, existing video-based rewards are often computed in entangled visual spaces where task-relevant state changes are confounded with extraneous visual variation. As a result, the learned reward may respond to visual distractors instead of actual task execution. To address this limitation, we propose DiTaR (Disentangling Task-Relevant Latent Dynamics for Reward Modeling), a framework for learning dense rewards from heterogeneous videos. DiTaR learns a continuous task-relevant representation from multi-frame video latents through an asymmetric two-stage procedure that suppresses task-irrelevant visual variation. In the task-relevant latent space, we train a history- and language-conditioned rectified-flow model to capture task dynamics and derive a directional dense reward from temporal changes in dynamics compatibility. Together, these components enable reward modeling directly over task-relevant dynamics rather than generic visual variation. DiTaR substantially improves policy learning on MetaWorld-v3 and ManiSkill over video-based reward baselines, and transfers to real-world offline RL through reward relabeling. Reward analyses further show that DiTaR provides more reliable rewards.

papers.abstract: Deformable-object manipulation requires accurate modeling of highly localized contact while maintaining simulation speeds suitable for interactive use. Uniformly fine tetrahedral meshes can resolve these interactions, but they introduce unnecessary degrees of freedom throughout the object. Coarse meshes are more efficient, yet they may under-resolve contact-induced deformation. We present a contact-adaptive mesh refinement framework that introduces spatial resolution only where it is most useful. The method uses geometric, elastic, and contact quantities already available from the deformable-body solver to score candidate edges. A fully GPU-parallel procedure then selects a conflict-free subset and updates both mesh topology and physical state directly within the simulation loop. We evaluate the approach on real deformable-object manipulation sequences. Adaptive refinement reduces simulation-to-real error, improves agreement with a fine-mesh reference, and remains substantially more efficient than uniformly fine simulation. These results show that local refinement can improve physical fidelity without incurring the cost of a globally fine discretization. The framework provides a practical basis for contact-rich simulation in interactive manipulation, sim-to-real modeling, and online physical digital twins.

papers.abstract: GPT-6 Astra provides robust embodied reasoning, but frequent external queries increase inference time and token costs. We equip a frozen $\pi_{0.5}$ policy with a lightweight CALL head that learns to predict when assistance is necessary. CALL reuses features from the standard policy forward pass and operates locally without consulting external models. Astra is activated solely for critical recovery events and returns control to $\pi_{0.5}$ upon stabilization. Evaluated across 40 LIBERO tasks (200 episodes), our system achieves a 97.5% success rate, outperforming the 95.5% baseline of pure $\pi_{0.5}$. In the Object, Goal, and Spatial suites, Astra executes only 5.49% of environment steps, consuming approximately 5,027 tokens per test episode. This selective intervention preserves the fast ordinary execution of $\pi_{0.5}$ while seamlessly integrating Astra's reasoning on demand. Our project page is available at https://kykgeek.github.io/Pi05_CALL_Astra/.

papers.abstract: Large language models can translate natural-language instructions into plausible manipulation plans, but robotic execution requires physically grounded decisions that respect robot embodiment, workspace geometry, reachability, collision constraints, and grasp feasibility. This paper presents a hardware-aware large language model-vision-language model (LLM-VLM) manipulation framework for a simulated Franka Research 3 robot in NVIDIA Isaac Sim. The framework separates symbolic reasoning from metric execution: an API-hosted LLM planner receives a structured scene summary and generates only symbolic task information, including the object to manipulate, target relation, approach preference, and objects to avoid. A local Qwen3-VL 8B VLM verifier supports semantic confirmation of ambiguous objects and open-container surrogates. Both the LLM planner and the VLM verifier are prohibited from generating robot coordinates, grasp poses, keepout dimensions, gripper commands, trajectory waypoints, or success labels. Instead, these decisions are handled by deterministic grounding and execution modules that use the robot model, scene geometry, MoveIt 2 collision checking, inverse kinematics, grasp validation, release verification, and final visual assessment. Execution feedback is returned only as symbolic context for replanning. The framework is evaluated through simulated digital-twin trials involving pickup, occluded-source access, keepout reasoning, relation placement, and sequential manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Embodied Audio-Visual Navigation (AVN) requires an agent to locate sound targets by jointly leveraging visual and auditory cues. While prior work has achieved notable success with static sound sources, real-world scenarios often involve moving targets, giving rise to the more challenging problem of \textbf{Dynamic Audio-Visual Navigation (D-AVN)}. Existing approaches largely rely on semantic auditory features, which limits generalization to unheard sound categories and hinders fine-grained spatial reasoning. To address these challenges, we propose a novel \textbf{Two-Stage Multi-modal Learning} framework for D-AVN. In the Physical Alignment stage, the proposed \textbf{Intensity-Calibrated Geometry Encoder (ICGE)} performs physics-informed alignment of sound intensity with visual geometry to capture category-agnostic spatial correspondence. In the Scene Aggregation stage, a Transformer-based \textbf{Cross-Modal Scene Aggregator (CMSA)} dynamically integrates multi-modal features to construct a robust state representation for policy learning. Extensive experiments on Replica and Matterport3D demonstrate that our method achieves state-of-the-art success rates, while significantly improving generalization and navigation efficiency in complex environments and under unheard sound scenarios.

papers.abstract: Multi-view perception is often treated as a safe design choice for robot manipulation: if one camera is useful, more cameras should be better. We revisit that assumption in tabletop bimanual manipulation by comparing policies trained with two large-field-of-view (FoV) wrist cameras against policies that additionally receive a head view, using controlled-variable experiments on a real bimanual platform. Across three tabletop tasks, adding a head view does not consistently improve task completion or execution quality: when the wrist cameras already observe the objects, grippers, and goal regions, wrist-only policies form a strong baseline. Restricting the wrist-camera FoV increases the potential value of a head view, but performance improves most reliably when the added view supplies concentrated, task-relevant information: region-of-interest (ROI) cropping yields more consistent head-view gains than the uncropped image, which is dominated by background and task-irrelevant regions. The data-scaling results further suggest an interaction between FoV and demonstration count: wide observations improve coverage but may require more data to stabilize, and they may reach a higher performance ceiling once enough demonstrations are available. These results suggest that camera design should be framed as a task-relevance and information-density problem rather than as a simple count of input views.
authors: Yuhui Duan, Shi Jin, Yuntian Wang, Jin Wang, Siao Liu, Wenchang Gao, Zhaxizhuoma, Yan Ding
bullets: Tests two wide-FoV wrist-camera policies against variants that also use a head view on three real tabletop bimanual tasks.
Wrist-only observations provide a strong baseline when they cover objects, grippers, and goal regions.
Restricting wrist-camera FoV increases the potential benefit of a head view.
ROI-cropped head views yield more consistent gains than uncropped views dominated by background.
FoV and demonstration count interact: wider views may need more data but can achieve a higher performance ceiling.

papers.abstract: Competitive humanoid table tennis requires two distinct abilities: executing a desired return and deciding where to return the ball. We separate these two problems, with the ball landing target serving as an interface between motor control and strategy. (1) We first train a whole-body motor policy conditioned on the desired landing target, which maps the target to an executable humanoid stroke through a model-based strike planner and a learned controller. (2) We then improve the motor policy through self-play in closed-loop rallies, where the robot learns to handle incoming balls generated by another player rather than only prescribed incoming balls. At this stage, the landing targets are still sampled without considering the opponent, so the policy improves its execution without learning game strategy. (3) Finally, we freeze the entire motor stack and train a stroke-level strategic policy to choose landing targets through competitive self-play. Motor self-play improves both landing accuracy and legal-return rate during rallies. More importantly, with the entire motor stack fixed, changing only the target-selection policy leads to large differences in game outcomes: the learned strategy wins 89%, 82%, and 73% of points against center, random, and away-from-opponent baselines, respectively. The learned strategy also changes where it sends the ball according to the opponent's position and the previous target, showing that self-play learns more than simply aiming at fixed "good" locations. On hardware, the same frozen execution stack and strategic interface support complete 11-point games against a recreational human opponent, including multi-stroke rallies with both forehand and backhand returns.
authors: Fanrong Dong, Ziyi Sun, Ziqi Han, Junhan Sun, Lei Ye, Zetong Jing, Hao Zhao, Shaoxun Liu, Rongrong Wang
bullets: A target landing point serves as the interface between whole-body motor control and game strategy.
A model-based strike planner and learned controller execute strokes conditioned on desired targets.
Closed-loop motor self-play improves landing accuracy and legal-return rates without learning opponent-aware strategy.
With the motor stack frozen, strategic self-play selects targets based on the opponent and prior target, substantially changing game outcomes.
The system completes 11-point hardware games against a recreational human, including multi-stroke forehand and backhand rallies.

(a) Target-conditioned motor training is followed by interaction-driven motor self-play; the resulting motor layer is then frozen for strategic self-play. (b) At each stroke event, the strategic policy selects a landing region whose induced continuous target conditions both the model-based planner and learned whole-body controller. Opponent position enters only the strategic policy, preserving the separation between tactical selection and motor execution.

Fig. 3. Target-conditioned execution in single-return and closed-loop rally evaluations. (a) Simulated landing distributions, per-target error and accuracy, and command–response curves characterize continuous landing-command realization. (b) Hardware trials evaluate the same interface across nine targets. (c) Under matched rally conditions, Stage I is compared with matched-budget prescribed continuation and interaction-driven self-play, both initialized from the same Stage-I checkpoint and trained with the same additional budget. Prescribed continuation retains the Stage-I incoming-ball distribution, whereas interaction-driven self-play uses rally-generated incoming states. The latter achieves higher target-landing accuracy and legal-return rate across rally depth. Curves show means over eight seeds; error bars denote ±1 SEM.

papers.abstract: Sampling-based model predictive control (SMPC) is increasingly practical for contact-rich manipulation because GPU-based physics simulators enable real-time evaluation of large numbers of non-differentiable contact rollouts. However, this computation budget is finite and can be spent in competing ways, including denser control exploration, representing dynamics or state uncertainty, replanning more frequently, or aligning the simulation better with the physical state. Yet, the resulting trade-offs are not well understood in real-world sim-to-real control. In this work, we address this question through a systematic study of how to allocate a fixed computation budget for SMPC in contact-rich manipulation. To enable controlled comparisons, we develop a GPU-based framework named Budget-Allocating Model Predictive Control (BAMPC), which runs on MuJoCo Warp and exposes dynamics uncertainty, state uncertainty, and temporal alignment as independent dimensions of the computation budget while using the same control stack in simulation and on a real robot. Across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, we find that the best budget allocation depends on the dominant sim-to-real error, with dynamics randomization not universally the most effective one.
authors: Magnus Dierking, Jo\~ao Carvalho, Vince Kurtz, Jan Peters, Nils Dengler, Georgia Chalvatzaki
bullets: SMPC budgets can be divided among control exploration, uncertainty representation, replanning frequency, and simulation–reality alignment.
The study introduces BAMPC, a GPU-based framework built on MuJoCo Warp for controlled budget comparisons.
BAMPC independently varies dynamics uncertainty, state uncertainty, and temporal alignment within one shared control stack.
Across three contact-rich manipulation tasks, optimal allocation varies with the primary sim-to-real error.
Dynamics randomization is not consistently the most effective use of computation.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of Budget-Allocating Model Predictive Control (BAMPC). A fixed real-time computation budget is allocated across control exploration, state uncertainty, dynamics uncertainty, and temporal alignment. Candidate controls are evaluated under multiple state and physics realizations using GPU-based MuJoCo Warp rollouts, aggregated into scalar costs, which are used by the sampling-based planner to produce the optimized spline control points. The same control stack is used in simulation and on the real robot.

Fig. 1: Under real-time constraints, SMPC frameworks have a finite simulation budget that must be allocated among competing uses, including control exploration, state uncertainty, dynamics uncertainty, and temporal alignment. The most effective allocation is task-dependent and should reflect the dominant source of sim-toreal error. BAMPC provides a common framework to expose and compare these choices across different tasks.
Fig. 3: Overview of the real-world contact-rich tasks used in our experiments.

Fig. 8: Balance-to-Track sensitivity to mass (top) and rollingfriction (bottom) mismatch at two parameter values and different replanning rates. Curves show mean accumulated pose error and one standard deviation over four seeds and four repeats. (c) In the lowfriction range, rolling is nearly non-dissipative and underestimating friction has little effect, whereas overestimating it introduces artificial dissipation and a corresponding model mismatch. This range is also readily identifiable from the observed rolling behavior. Missing mass results are caused by numerical instability, while large rollingfriction values are outside the physically plausible range for the rigid sphere. 18500/9000/2800 samples used at 5/10/20 Hz.

The panel titles give the true parameter values and the horizontal axes show the values used for planning. Shown are the mean and standard deviation over four initial states and four repeats. 75000/28000/13500 samples used at 2/5/10 Hz.

(b) Increasing the number of state realizations can improve performance. (c) An intermediate belief width performs best. papers.abstract: State-of-the-art perceptive humanoid locomotion is mostly built on retargeted motion capture, a generative motion prior, and a distillation stage. We report a complete system that does not require this pipeline for a humanoid to cross varied terrain. In its place, we provide a five-expert mixture routed by a terrain classifier over a sensed elevation grid, and target every foothold with a model-based planner, refined by six closed-form-gradient steps on an interpolated terrain-cost field instead of picked from a fixed grid. Driven through the same perception-to-actuation software a robot would run, inside a second, deployment-fidelity simulator, it crosses an $85$\,m five-segment waypoint course $18$ of $20$ times end-to-end ($90\%$, Wilson $95\%$ CI $70$--$97$) and succeeds $20/20$ on four of five segments scored alone, where an ablated configuration without the mixture and without refinement reaches $0\%$ on both the stair and the hurdle segment. The continuous refinement moves $72.4\%$ of foot placements across at least one grid-cell boundary, which produces real sub-grid correction. We also ran matched component studies to report what does not account for it: one expert equals five on the training distribution, four label-free routers collapse to near-uniform activation, and a self-supervised terrain embedding loses to the privileged label.
authors: Thanh Ly, Chien Le, Truong-Duy Dang, Duy M. H. Nguyen, Duy-Dung Le, Vien Anh Ngo, An T. Le
bullets: Replaces retargeted motion capture, generative priors, and distillation with five terrain-routed experts and model-based foothold planning.
Refines each foothold using six closed-form-gradient steps on an interpolated terrain-cost field, enabling sub-grid corrections.
Completes an 85 m, five-segment course in 18/20 trials (90%; Wilson 95% CI: 70–97%).
An ablated system without expert mixture or refinement achieves 0% on both stair and hurdle segments.
Component studies find that label-free routers and a self-supervised terrain embedding underperform the privileged terrain label.

papers.abstract: Frontier language models reliably refuse to explain how to cause physical harm. We ask whether this refusal survives when the same models control a robot. We introduce RoboHarm, a physical AI safety benchmark of harmful robot instructions, and test seven frontier models on it. We hold each model fixed and vary only the interface, from text to Code as Policies to vision agents that command end-effector poses or joint angles. In a MuJoCo simulation twin of a bimanual YAM arm robot, refusal falls from 73% of text requests to 18-25% once the model controls the robot, even when it is told what the objects are. On the physical robot, six models with end-effector control refused 18% of 612 trials against 19% in sim, and three with joint control refused 41% of 252 against 31%. GPT-5.6 Sol refused every text request and none of its trials on the real robot. Case studies of the robot transcripts show that models miss the hazard, name it without inferring its consequences, or act despite recognizing it, and their refusals often hinge on uncertainty about what an object is rather than on the harm of the action. Safety alignment learned in text thus fails to generalize to action, leaving current models with a poorly understood safety gap in the physical world.
authors: Edward Sun, Christopher Leet, Sravanthi Machcha, Achyutha Menon, Tzu Kit Chan, Yuchen Cui, Jay Chooi
bullets: Introduces RoboHarm, a benchmark for harmful robot instructions across text, code, vision, and robot-control interfaces.
Tests seven frontier models in MuJoCo simulations and on a physical bimanual robot while holding models fixed and varying only the interface.

Transcripts suggest failures arise from missed hazards, failure to infer consequences, or acting despite recognizing harm.
Refusals often depend on uncertainty about object identity rather than the harmfulness of the action itself.

papers.abstract: A longstanding goal for robot reinforcement learning (RL) is that robots learn from their own physical experience, as humans and animals do. A key obstacle to learning directly from physical experience, especially outside instrumented lab environments, is that the state of the world is usually unobservable to the learner and must be estimated from on-board sensing. Errors in that estimate corrupt both the policy input and potentially the reward signal. We study this challenge using the contact-rich task of a bipedal robot learning to score soccer goals. We estimate all key state variables on-board with an unscented Kalman filter (UKF) and no external instrumentation (e.g., motion capture or overhead cameras). Because the UKF may incorrectly estimate state when the ball is unobserved, we learn a new state representation with a recurrent state-space model (RSSM) that, critically, only corrects the RSSM's latent state when the ball is observed. Building on RLPD, we introduce RSSM-RLPD and apply it to the task of a NAO robot learning to dribble a soccer ball into a goal. We show that the robot learns to score from multiple starting positions after 30 minutes of real-world interaction, reaching 100% success against 0% for a feed-forward policy under the same training budget. We complement our physical robot experiments with a simulation study and show that RSSM-RLPD learns policies that achieve a higher success rate than behavior cloning, a feed-forward, and GRU baseline. Taken together, our results show that the addition of a learned state representation to existing on-robot learning methods enables RL from real-robot data even with a high degree of partial observability.
authors: Ryan Gao, Ashvin Anilkumar, Nicholas Corrado, William Cong, Josiah Hanna
bullets: The work addresses partial observability and onboard state-estimation errors in real-robot reinforcement learning.
A NAO robot uses an unscented Kalman filter without external instrumentation, augmented by an RSSM that updates its latent state only when the ball is observed.
The proposed RSSM-RLPD method learns to dribble and score from multiple starting positions after 30 minutes of real-world interaction.
The robot achieved 100% success, compared with 0% for a feed-forward policy under the same training budget.
Simulation results also show higher success than behavior cloning, feed-forward, and GRU baselines; the scope is demonstrated on soccer dribbling and complementary simulation experiments.

papers.abstract: Embodied Artificial Intelligence (AI) introduces cyber-physical risks because digital failures and attacks can cause physical harm. This survey organizes embodied AI safety through a four-layer reference architecture -- comprising the physical interaction, system and middleware, algorithm and decision, and cloud-edge and data layers -- and uses it to connect vulnerabilities, propagation paths, and safeguards across the system stack. It traces the evolution of safety paradigms and examines how faults and attacks cross architectural boundaries to produce physical consequences. Furthermore, the survey systematizes composite attack chains, outlines multi-layered defense strategies, and reviews representative embodied safety benchmarks. Ultimately, we advocate for unifying software alignment with rigorous hardware constraints to build trustworthy systems capable of operating safely within human-centric environments.
authors: Tuo Feng, Yue Zhang, Shiji Zhou, Zhaoxin Fan, Wenguan Wang, Xiaowei Chi, Tianyu Shen, Xiangtai Li, Xuesong Bai, Zheng Zhu, Sirui Han, Boyu Zhou, Zhaosong Wang, Shizhe Chen, Zilong Zheng, Chenjia Bai, Jiangmiao Pang, Yaodong Yang, Hao Zhao, Di Hu, Li Yi, Yan Huang, Qi Wu, Hanwang Zhang, Fei Gao, Shanghang Zhang, Hongsheng Li, Jianye Hao, Yuan Zhang, Yingjie Xia, Jian Shen, Cewu Lu, Hui Zhang, Kai Chen, Wenwu Yu, Badong Chen, Jungong Han, Yike Guo
bullets: Organizes safety across physical interaction; system and middleware; algorithm and decision; and cloud-edge and data layers.
Connects vulnerabilities, attack propagation paths, safeguards, and physical consequences across the system stack.
Systematizes composite attack chains and reviews multi-layer defense strategies and representative safety benchmarks.
Advocates combining software alignment with rigorous hardware constraints for trustworthy operation in human-centric environments.
papers.selection_reason: Survey of cross-layer safety in embodied AI.
papers.title: From bits to atoms: A survey of cross-layer safety in Embodied AI
papers.tldr: This survey presents a four-layer framework for analyzing and defending against cross-layer safety risks in Embodied AI that can turn digital failures into physical harm.

papers.abstract: Contact-rich manipulation requires a robot to be precise in free space to establish the intended contacts, and compliant once in contact to avoid excessive forces. Imitation learning has proven effective for simpler manipulation tasks, but the compliance underlying a demonstration is not directly observable and is therefore difficult to infer from demonstration data alone. We present a framework that makes compliance explicit at every stage. During data collection, the operator teleoperates the real robot while a synchronized digital twin visualizes the error between the commanded reference and the achieved pose, making the current compliance visible, and selects between two discrete compliance modes. To generalize across object poses, we combine Laplacian editing, which retargets trajectories efficiently but is not physics-consistent during contact, with simulation-based trajectory optimization, which enforces physical plausibility but offers no manual guidance. Finally, a residual reinforcement learning policy refines the interaction forces by adjusting the reference pose of the underlying admittance controller. We evaluate on three flipping and pushing tasks on a Franka FR3 based on a total of 7 demonstrations across tasks. Our method is successful on all 40 out-of-distribution trials, compared to 33/40 and 24/40 for two baselines, with our base policy alone reaching 35/40.
authors: Chunyu Jiang, Yichen Cai, Shuai Li, Wenbin Sun, Jo\~ao Carvalho, Kostas Daniilidis, Oleg Arenz, Cristiana de Farias, Jan Peters
bullets: Targets contact-rich tasks requiring precise free-space motion and safe, compliant contact.
Uses a synchronized digital twin and two discrete compliance modes to expose otherwise hidden compliance during teleoperation.
Combines Laplacian trajectory editing with simulation-based optimization to retarget demonstrations while maintaining physical plausibility.
Residual RL adjusts the admittance controller’s reference pose to refine interaction forces.
Across 40 out-of-distribution trials, the method succeeds in all trials, versus 35/40 for its base policy and 33/40 and 24/40 for two baselines.

(e) The system takes in the robot’s proprioception, stiffness of the admittance controller, external force feedback, and the object pose estimated by the digital twin to predict expected stiffness level and reference poses for implementing the task.
