papers.abstract: LiDAR-inertial odometry (LIO) is widely used for real-time localization and mapping, but its reliability can degrade substantially in subterranean environments affected by smoke, dust, and other airborne obscurants, whereas radar remains comparatively robust. This article presents a one-class temporal learning framework for LiDAR degradation detection and reliability-aware localization under such conditions. A broad set of degradation-sensitive cues, including spatial, cross-modal, geometric/motion, intensity, and measurement-recency features, is evaluated to characterize changes in LiDAR sensing quality. Their temporal evolution is modelled over sliding windows using an LSTM autoencoder trained exclusively on nominal operation, enabling deviations from healthy sensor behaviour to be detected without requiring labelled degradation data. The resulting LiDAR reliability estimate governs adaptive selection between LIO and radar inertial odometry (RIO), retaining LIO during reliable sensing and transferring localization authority to RIO when degradation is detected. The framework is evaluated using real-world ground robot data collected in GNSS-denied subterranean tunnels under nominal and dense-smoke conditions. Experimental results demonstrate degradation detection, adaptive modality switching, and continued localization output under severe LiDAR degradation. A feature family ablation study further shows that a reduced feature representation can improve degradation-aware localization performance in the evaluated dense-smoke scenarios, highlighting the importance of feature parsimony in one-class sensor degradation detection. The code will be released as open source to support reproducibility and further research.
authors: Moumita Mukherjee, Avijit Banerjee, Anton Koval, George Nikolakopoulo
bullets: Targets LiDAR reliability loss caused by airborne obscurants in GNSS-denied underground settings.
Uses spatial, cross-modal, geometric/motion, intensity, and recency cues modeled over time.
Trains an LSTM autoencoder only on nominal data, avoiding labeled degradation examples.
Controls switching between LIO and RIO, preserving LIO when healthy and transferring authority to radar when degraded.
Real-world tunnel experiments show degradation detection, adaptive switching, and continued localization under dense smoke; a reduced feature set improved performance in the evaluated scenarios.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Proposed reliability aware LMRIO framework. Asynchronous LiDAR, IMU, LIO, and RIO measurements are temporally synchronized and encoded into a Twelve dimensional degradation sensitive feature representation(fη). Consecutive normalized feature vectors(f̄η) form a temporal sequence processed by an LSTM autoencoder trained on nominal operation. Reconstruction errors are used to infer LiDAR degradation and adaptively select between LIO and RIO.
Fig. 1: Conceptual framework for LiDAR degradation-aware adaptive localization under airborne obscurants.

Fig. 4: Trajectory comparison across the four experimental scenarios. Under nominal conditions, LMRIO closely follows LIO for both the P-shaped and round-tunnel traversals (a,c). Under dense smoke, the P-shaped traversal exhibits severe LIO divergence following LiDAR degradation (b), while the roundtunnel traversal shows stale LiDAR-based localization (d). In both degraded cases, LMRIO selects RIO during unreliable LiDAR operation, preserving a continuous localization output.

Fig. 3: Localization trajectories and LiDAR maps for the P-shaped and round-tunnel traversals. Under nominal conditions, LMRIO closely follows the LIO estimate in both trajectories (a,c). In dense smoke, the P-shaped traversal exhibits pronounced LIO divergence as LiDAR quality deteriorates (b), while the round-tunnel traversal shows stale LiDAR measurements and loss of LiDAR-based localization updates (d). In both degraded cases, LMRIO switches to RIO during intervals identified as unreliable, maintaining a consistent localization output.

Fig. 5: Raw and smoothed LSTM-autoencoder reconstruction errors with the nominal threshold. Nominal traversals remain largely below the threshold despite transient fluctuations (a,c), whereas dense-smoke traversals show pronounced or sustained error growth associated with LiDAR degradation (b,d). The smoothed error drives learned degradation detection, while LiDAR recency is evaluated independently.

Fig. 6: Estimator-selection traces across the four experimental scenarios. LIO remains selected throughout nominal operation (a,c). Under dense smoke, the degradation detector triggers a transition to RIO in the P-shaped traversal (b), while the LiDAR-recency criterion activates RIO when measurements become stale in the round-tunnel traversal (d). The switching variables ∆LIO and ∆RIO indicate the active localization modality.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict a robot's actions together with the observations those actions will produce. However, the strongest models rely on video diffusion transformers that are far too computationally expensive for resource-constrained edge devices. We present SmolWAM, a latent WAM that we derive from the 2B-parameter Cosmos Policy by keeping its pretrained trunk and rebuilding its inference interface: single-frame visual latents, cached text features that preserve the trunk's attention sinks, 12 of 28 transformer blocks, and 1,008 tokens from which actions and future visual latents are read out in one rectified-flow step. Trained in 3.6 GPU-hours, SmolWAM succeeds in 95.5% of 400 LIBERO episodes at 57 ms and 2.3 TFLOP per 16-action chunk with 2.4 GiB of GPU memory, 11x faster than its teacher with 18.5x fewer FLOPs and 3.2x less memory, and its world head still forecasts scene motion.
authors: Timi Owolabi, Hikmah Olawore, Frances Adelakun, Ayotomiwa Oyewumi
bullets: Targets the high computational cost of video-diffusion world-action models on resource-constrained edge devices.
Rebuilds a pretrained 2B-parameter model’s inference interface using visual latents, cached text features, 12 transformer blocks, and a single rectified-flow step.
Achieves 95.5% success across 400 LIBERO episodes with 57 ms inference latency and 2.4 GiB of GPU memory.
Runs 11× faster than its teacher while using 18.5× fewer FLOPs and 3.2× less memory.
Its world head retains the ability to forecast scene motion.

papers.abstract: Cooperative multi-agent tasks often impose constraints on a shared objective or collective safety. A team level violation cost function can measure this constraint outcome, but does not distinguish which agents' actions most strongly influence that violation. We present SafeDiSTL, a constrained multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that allows for credit assignment even with joint constraint measurements. We use Signal Temporal Logic (STL) robustness to measure episode-level violation through running-maximum cost increments. Smooth full-episode robustness and differentiable dynamics provide action sensitivities, which allocate each cost increment across agents at the same decision time. These sensitivities account for delayed effects when weighting agents' shares of each cost increment. We study the framework in cooperative payload transport, connected navigation, and networked traffic control tasks. SafeDiSTL achieves 1.6-5.1x the safe-success rate in transport, improves navigation safe-success by 11.1%, and delivers 50-68% more throughput in traffic when compared to constrained baselines. Results demonstrate a strong improvement of the learned policy in dealing with shared constraint while retaining the performance of unconstrained policies.
authors: Hongrui Zheng, Aditya Singh, Rahul Mangharam
bullets: Addresses joint constraints whose team-level violation costs do not reveal which agents caused them.

Evaluated on payload transport, connected navigation, and networked traffic control.
Reports 1.6–5.1× higher safe-success in transport, 11.1% better navigation safe-success, and 50–68% higher traffic throughput than constrained baselines.

papers.abstract: Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse manipulation dynamics. We introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable latent action pre-training paradigm with two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM learns continuous latent actions by explaining frame-to-frame visual transitions in human videos and uses them as human-derived supervision, while LAPT-Scale-Policy trains a VLA policy through human-video latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM uses a continuous latent space to preserve fine-grained motion and interaction dynamics. We further combine perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals to improve transition-level supervision beyond pixel reconstruction. Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, LAPT-Scale-LAM provides implicit action supervision for policy pre-training, yielding consistent scaling gains and improving real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video scales from 1K to 5K hours. The learned policy also generalizes to unseen visual conditions.
authors: Zhiyuan Xiang, Peidong Liu, Mingyang Li, Jiawei Li, Wenhow Li, Wenbo Ding, Xiang Deng
bullets: Addresses the high cost of collecting robot interaction data and the lack of action labels in human videos.
Learns continuous latent actions from frame transitions using perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals.
Pre-trains a vision-language-action policy, aligns it to the target robot embodiment, and applies task-specific post-training.
Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, it improves real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% when annotated human video increases from 1K to 5K hours.
The resulting policy generalizes to unseen visual conditions.

The first row shows the groundtruth video, the second row shows decoder rollout using the ground-truth latent action encoded by LAPT-Scale-LAM, and the third row shows decoder rollout using the latent action predicted by the Stage-1 VLA policy.

papers.abstract: Standard Policy Gradient (PG) algorithms suffer from high estimation variance because they rely on Monte Carlo updates. While off-policy variance reduction mitigates this problem, establishing optimal sample complexity currently requires either restrictive assumptions, such as uniformly bounded importance weights, or impractical second-order operations. In this work, we introduce Loopless Variance-Reduced PG (LVR-PG), a unified theoretical framework that abstracts a class of first-order estimators that integrate recursive updates with defensive importance sampling, including known estimators such as PAGE-PG and STORM-PG. We prove that this algorithmic class achieves $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(\epsilon^{-2})$ last-iterate global convergence under weak gradient domination for general parametric policies. We establish this guarantee using purely first-order updates, with minimal assumptions and without gradient preconditioners. By extending state-of-the-art lower bounds to continuous parametric policies, we establish an $\Omega(\epsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity limit, confirming our framework is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors and horizon terms.
authors: Leonardo Cesani, Matteo Papini, Marcello Restelli
bullets: Addresses the high variance of Monte Carlo policy-gradient estimates and limitations of existing off-policy variance reduction methods.
Unifies recursive estimators with defensive importance sampling, including PAGE-PG and STORM-PG.
Proves last-iterate global convergence with approximately O(ε⁻²) sample complexity for general parametric policies under weak gradient domination.
Uses only first-order updates, without bounded importance weights or gradient preconditioners.
Extends lower bounds to continuous parametric policies, showing the rate is minimax-optimal up to logarithmic factors and horizon terms.

papers.abstract: Automating biological laboratories requires robots to perform dexterous tool interactions under realistic visual conditions while handling dynamic experimental phenomena, presenting significant challenges for robotic manipulation. To enable systematic evaluation under these conditions, we introduce AutoBio+, a simulation benchmark and framework for dexterous manipulation in realistic biological laboratory environments. AutoBio+ comprises 14 tasks across 4 robot embodiments, spanning functional tool use, precision manipulation, language-conditioned visual grounding, and instrument operation. We introduce controllable dynamic experimental phenomena, including flames, vapor, and bubbles, to capture the evolving visual conditions of laboratory procedures. To further enhance environmental realism, we develop a hybrid rendering pipeline that integrates interactive simulated foreground objects with Gaussian-splatting backgrounds reconstructed from 6 real laboratory scenes. For efficient large-scale data generation and evaluation, we further build a parallel simulation framework on top of mjlab, proposing Parallel Finite-State Machine (PFSM) and integrating batched rendering with decoupled trajectory replay for demonstration generation and model-independent closed-loop policy evaluation. Our evaluation reveals substantial variation in policy performance across tasks, exposing distinct strengths and weaknesses of current manipulation policies. Real-world experiments further demonstrate a reduced sim-to-real gap, supporting the validity of AutoBio+ for realistic manipulation evaluation. Supplementary materials are available at https://autobio-plus.github.io/AutoBioPlus.
authors: Xuanye Wu, Yue Shi, Yongcan Yang, Yiqun Wang, Zhaoqi Wan, Dayu Xia, Jiezhang Cao, Xiangfei Li, Yao Mu, Guangtao Zhai

Provides scalable evaluation through parallel finite-state machines, batched rendering, and decoupled trajectory replay.
Finds substantial task-dependent variation in policy performance, with real-world experiments indicating a reduced sim-to-real gap.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies issue sparse targets whose arrival at the robot controller is delayed and irregular, so a reasonable predicted action can still produce abrupt motion near people. Remedies are evaluated on different streams, delays and metrics. JitterVLA replays identical commands and arrival traces through alternative controllers, isolating the controller's effect. We apply it to synthetic reaches, hand trajectories from 20 people, three open VLA pipelines (838 episodes) and a physical UR3. Interpolation lowered modeled p99 jerk for every source, by 83% (615 to 106 m/s^3) on human motion with 200 ms delay, at a 2.0 cm tracking cost, and the effect replicated on 598 new episodes; jerk-limited generation lowered jerk further at a larger cost. Entropy-discontinuity associations had opposite, replicated signs in two pipelines, and entropy gating helped in one but not the other. On the UR3, interpolation lowered accelerometer-derived jerk by 3.0-14.0% in all six exploratory pairs, while a position-derived metric did not resolve the contrast. JitterVLA supports screening before human-centred studies; code and data will be released.
authors: Faith Ogunwoye, Didar Seyidov, Konstantin Gubernatorov, Dzmitry Tsetserukou
bullets: VLA commands arrive sparsely and irregularly, potentially causing abrupt motion near people.
The benchmark isolates controller effects by replaying the same commands and arrival traces across alternatives.
Interpolation reduced modeled p99 jerk by 83% on delayed human-motion traces, with a 2.0 cm tracking cost; jerk-limited generation reduced jerk further at greater cost.
Results across three VLA pipelines showed inconsistent links between entropy discontinuities and motion quality, and entropy gating helped only one pipeline.
On a physical UR3, interpolation reduced accelerometer-derived jerk in all six exploratory pairs, while a position-derived metric did not show the same contrast.

papers.abstract: Pre-trained robot policies, such as Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models, provide a strong foundation for generalist robotic manipulation, but adapting them to new tasks with only a few demonstrations remains challenging. Directly fine-tuning a pre-trained policy often achieves strong in-distribution performance, yet it can distort the representations learned during pre-training and weaken the model's generalization ability under out-of-distribution shifts. We propose Retrieval-Anchored Representation Alignment (RARA), a two-stage adaptation method, to address this issue. First, RARA retrieves representation features from pretraining with similar task intent and motion, and aligns the policy's representations of the target demonstrations with the pre-trained representations of the retrieved demonstrations. Second, RARA fine-tunes the policy on the target demonstrations while limiting how much its representations of the retrieved demonstrations change during fine-tuning. By reducing the representation mismatch before action learning and preserving pre-trained knowledge during adaptation, RARA limits unnecessary representation drift during fine-tuning. Experiments with Diffusion Policy and GR00T on 13 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboCasa, and on a real robot show that RARA improves the average success of fine-tuning by 9.5 points in-distribution and 13.6 points out-of-distribution, and outperforms all compared baselines. Project page: https://shua-kang.github.io/RARA_robot/
authors: Xuhui Kang, Sung-Wook Lee, Yan Zhuang, Tianle Zhong, Yen-Ling Kuo
bullets: Addresses representation drift and weakened out-of-distribution generalization when adapting pre-trained robot policies with few demonstrations.
Uses a two-stage process: retrieve similar pre-training features and align target representations, then fine-tune while constraining changes to retrieved representations.
Evaluated with Diffusion Policy and GR00T across 13 tasks in RoboTwin, RoboCasa, and on a real robot.
Improves average fine-tuning success by 9.5 points in-distribution and 13.6 points out-of-distribution, outperforming compared baselines.

papers.abstract: Humanoid tennis requires reactive whole-body coordination under rapidly changing ball dynamics, yet collecting task-specific motion-capture demonstrations that cover diverse approach states, contact locations, and timing conditions is costly. Inspired by how humans acquire new skills by combining reusable motor experience with task-specific demonstrations, we present ATHLETE, a framework for learning reactive humanoid tennis from generic locomotion data and ordinary tennis videos. ATHLETE combines LAFAN1 locomotion with video-derived striking motions and uses Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching (TGMM) to construct diverse task-conditioned whole-body references. These references are transformed into a reactive policy through physics-based teacher--student learning with online DAgger distillation, followed by PPO fine-tuning for the tennis task. The resulting policy responds directly to robot and ball observations without requiring reference-motion inputs at deployment. On a real humanoid robot, ATHLETE achieves forehand and backhand hit rates of $90.00\%$ and $86.67\%$, respectively, and enables multi-shot rallies with human players. These results demonstrate that ATHLETE can learn dynamic humanoid tennis skills from reusable locomotion data and video demonstrations. Result videos and code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/w/ATHLETE2027/.
authors: Zhihao Tian, Zifan Wang, Enzheng Zhu, Xun Yang, Jialong Qin, Mengbo Wang, Junwei Liang
bullets: Addresses the costly need for extensive task-specific motion-capture data covering diverse tennis states.
Uses Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching to build task-conditioned whole-body references from locomotion data and ordinary tennis videos.
Distills these references into a reactive physics-based policy with online DAgger, then fine-tunes it with PPO.
The deployed policy uses only robot and ball observations, without reference-motion inputs.
On a real humanoid, it achieves 90.00% forehand and 86.67% backhand hit rates and supports multi-shot rallies.

(3) We distill the teacher into a reactive student policy through online DAgger and privileged representation alignment. (4) We fine-tune the student using PPO with task-specific rewards and domain randomization to improve ball contact and return accuracy. (5) The resulting student policy is deployed on a humanoid robot to enable real-world tennis rallies with human players, using a motion-capture system for ball-state estimation.

papers.abstract: Anticipation of vessel trajectories is an essential task when navigating at sea. This applies to both human navigators and autonomous surface vessels. Trajectory forecasting enables sub-routines such as collision avoidance to assess the situation and react accordingly in time. This paper investigates Transformer and Performer models for trajectory prediction of surface vessels in confined waters. Using widely available position data from the Automatic Identification System (AIS), candidate models are trained and evaluated. Historical information on how other vessels have moved in the local area surrounding each agent is conveyed using positional heat maps. The heat maps are generated using Kernel Density Estimation (KDE) and encoded with a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) before entering the Transformer models. The models are trained with quantile loss to efficiently obtain a model-aware prediction interval, as this is crucial for timely collision avoidance. The proposed model architectures are shown to greatly outperform previous work while the inclusion of local heat maps enables the prediction of vessel movement that is not otherwise indicated from the previous positions.
bullets: Addresses vessel trajectory prediction in confined waters to support navigation and collision avoidance.
Combines historical AIS positions with local-vessel positional heat maps generated by KDE and encoded by a CNN.
Evaluates Transformer and Performer architectures trained with quantile loss to estimate model-aware prediction intervals.
Reports substantially better performance than previous work.
Local heat maps help predict movements not evident from an agent’s own past positions.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models offer a promising foundation for generalist robotic intelligence by predicting the consequences of actions. However, existing robotic datasets provide limited coverage of the diverse interaction dynamics required for generalizable world modeling. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer complementary interaction experience, yet the embodiment gap between human hands and robotic manipulators hinders effective cross-embodiment learning. Meanwhile, the predominance of successful demonstrations leaves failure dynamics substantially underrepresented, limiting the ability of world models to anticipate unsuccessful executions. To address these limitations, we introduce HF-WM, an action-conditioned world model that combines Human interaction learning with Failure-aware post-training. To bridge the embodiment gap, we develop a dual-branch framework that couples video generation with auxiliary pointflow prediction, using stabilized pointflow as a unified motion representation across human and robot interactions while suppressing egocentric camera motion. To improve failure modeling, we further perform Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training on perturbed actions derived from successful demonstrations, guided by action alignment and physical plausibility rewards, enabling the model to learn plausible failure dynamics without paired ground-truth videos. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HF-WM achieves state-of-the-art performance in action-conditioned video generation and exhibits strong utility for policy evaluation in downstream robotic tasks.
authors: Peiyan Tu, Cong Wang, Hanxin Zhu, Xin Jin, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Addresses limited interaction diversity, the human–robot embodiment gap, and the underrepresentation of failures in robot datasets.
Uses a dual-branch model combining action-conditioned video generation with auxiliary pointflow prediction.
Employs stabilized pointflow to represent motion across human and robot interactions while reducing egocentric camera-motion effects.
Applies GRPO post-training to perturbed actions, guided by action-alignment and physical-plausibility rewards, without paired failure videos.
Experiments report state-of-the-art action-conditioned video generation and strong utility for downstream robotic policy evaluation.

figures.caption: Figure 1 Overview of HF-WM architecture. HF-WM extends learning beyond successful robot demonstrations in two stages. Stage 1 uses a dual-branch architecture with stabilized pointflow supervision to learn interaction dynamics from egocentric human interactions (Sec. 3.2). Stage 2 applies GRPO to counterfactual action perturbations, guided by action alignment and physical plausibility rewards, to model failure dynamics without paired failure-video supervision (Sec. 3.3).

Figure 3 Qualitative comparison of action-conditioned video generation. Evaluated on both successful and failed execution samples, our method is compared against six models and achieves much better visual quality with precise action following.

Figure 2 Dual-branch architecture of HF-WM with stabilized pointflow. The auxiliary pointflow branch predicts interaction motion from intermediate video representations, while pointflow stabilization suppresses egocentric camera motion so that supervision is better focused on interaction-induced dynamics. The pointflow branch is used only during training and introduces no additional inference overhead.

papers.abstract: Runtime failure monitors for robot policies are typically evaluated by how accurately they distinguish failed from successful executions. Yet an accurate alarm may arrive too late for recovery, while an unnecessary intervention may disrupt an execution that would otherwise succeed. We introduce RESCUE, a counterfactual framework for evaluating whether a monitor's alarms enable useful interventions. By restoring simulator and policy states at execution checkpoints, RESCUE compares alternative actions, identifies the latest checkpoint satisfying a specified recovery criterion, and evaluates whether acting on alarms reduces expected task-completion cost. We evaluate RESCUE with OpenVLA-OFT and $\pi_{0.5}$ over LIBERO-Spatial and LIBERO-Plus using 128,340 counterfactual branches. Recoverability depends on the state--intervention pair rather than on robot state alone: at $\tau=0.5$, 14 of 66 OpenVLA-OFT/LIBERO-Plus failures contain a recoverable checkpoint under continuation, compared with 34 of 66 under continuation or scripted recovery, while recovery reduces recoverability in other conditions. On the primary strong-policy conditions, favourable detection scores do not establish lower intervention cost. Under the evaluated stop-and-reset model, even an idealised detector can afford only a 2.0--3.3% false-alarm rate before unnecessary resets outweigh the savings from stopping failures early. These results show that monitor value depends jointly on the intervention available and the workload in which it is deployed.
authors: David Ahmedt-Aristizabal, Abdelwahed Khamis, Mohammad Ali Armin, Lars Petersson
bullets: Motivation: alarms can be too late to enable recovery, or can disrupt executions that would have succeeded.
Method: restore simulator and policy states at checkpoints, compare counterfactual interventions, and find the latest recoverable checkpoint.
Contribution: a framework for measuring recoverability and intervention cost jointly with monitor performance.
Findings: recoverability depends on the state–intervention pair; favourable detection scores do not necessarily reduce intervention cost.
Scope/limitation: under the evaluated stop-and-reset model, ideal detectors tolerate only a 2.0–3.3% false-alarm rate before resets become counterproductive.

papers.abstract: Nonlinear model predictive control (NMPC) can be applied to large nonlinear systems with complex objectives while enforcing constraints, but the cost of solving the underlying optimization problems limits real-time application for systems with fast dynamics or many states. Neural networks can reduce this online cost by approximating the control law, but may violate constraints and typically require many precomputed optimizer solutions for training. The learning-based iterative solver for constrained optimization (LISCO) instead learns to predict primal-dual steps toward satisfaction of the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions through self-supervised training without precomputed solutions, but its dense, monolithic architecture grows with the prediction horizon. We remove this horizon dependence by exploiting the temporal structure of the problem in the solver architecture, which makes the network size independent of the horizon while leaving the training loss and the solver iteration unchanged. A closed-loop resampling strategy further aligns the training distribution with closed-loop operation at no additional sampling cost. On an economic NMPC benchmark of a CSTR cascade, the proposed solver scales to larger problems than monolithic LISCO and achieves median speedups of up to a factor of four over IPOPT. In closed loop, it achieves comparable control performance to IPOPT with no observed constraint violations.
bullets: Addresses the high online optimization cost of NMPC for large or fast nonlinear systems.
Uses a temporal-decomposition architecture to predict primal-dual KKT steps without network growth as the prediction horizon increases.
Retains LISCO’s self-supervised training and iterative solver procedure, requiring no precomputed optimizer solutions.
Adds closed-loop resampling to better match training data with deployment conditions without extra sampling cost.
On a CSTR cascade benchmark, scales to larger problems, reaches up to 4× median speedups over IPOPT, and achieves comparable closed-loop control with no observed constraint violations.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement Learning (RL) substantially improves planning performance in autonomous-driving Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. However, existing RL methods rely on scalar trajectory rewards that measure overall quality but fail to identify specific planning errors or provide actionable correction signals. In long-tail scenarios, errors in scene understanding, behavior selection, and trajectory execution are compressed into a single score. We observe that Reflective Guidance turns trajectory evaluation into explicit diagnoses and corrective instructions, substantially improving planning accuracy. Yet such guidance requires an initial prediction and its evaluation results, making it unavailable for direct single-pass inference. We propose Reflect-VLA, which treats Reflective Guidance as training-time privileged information and internalizes its planning benefits through Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation (Dual-OPSD). Unlike scalar-reward optimization, Dual-OPSD uses the driving score only to route student-generated trajectories. It distills dense token-level corrective distributions from the teacher for risky trajectories while applying self-imitation to preserve reliable ones. To provide reliable corrective distributions on student rollouts, the teacher is progressively constructed through Driving-Knowledge Pretraining, Planning-and-Refinement SFT, and Self-Refinement Rejection Sampling. At inference time, Reflect-VLA generates trajectories in a single pass without explicit guidance or iterative refinement. Experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 and Bench2Drive demonstrate competitive planning performance while reducing training time by over 90% compared with RL.
authors: Yuechen Luo, He Chong, Fang Li, Shaoqing Xu, Hexin Zhang, Ruiqi Zhang, Ziying Song, Lei Yang, Zhi-Xin Yang, Fuxi Wen
bullets: Scalar trajectory rewards provide limited, non-actionable feedback for specific planning errors, especially in long-tail scenarios.
Dual-Path On-Policy Self-Distillation uses driving scores to route student rollouts, distilling token-level corrections for risky trajectories and self-imitation for reliable ones.
A progressively built teacher supplies corrective guidance through knowledge pretraining, planning/refinement supervised fine-tuning, and self-refinement rejection sampling.
At inference, the model plans in a single pass without explicit reflection or iterative refinement.
Experiments on NAVSIM v1/v2 and Bench2Drive show competitive planning performance and over 90% lower training time than RL.

The results illustrate how Reflective Guidance shifts the teacher toward safer and more expert-aligned trajectory tokens, and how Dual-OPSD transfers these corrective preferences to the distilled student.

papers.abstract: Collective Autonomous Vehicle (AV) route choices in real-world traffic networks can create externalities for Human-Driven Vehicles (HDVs), as routes that benefit AVs may increase travel times for other road users. To address this, we introduce a social component, the marginal cost, to the selfish travel time AV reward. Marginal cost captures an AV's impact on other road users by comparing their travel times with those in a counterfactual simulation in which the AV is removed. We study AV route choice in mixed-autonomy traffic settings using Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning (MARL), where AVs learn routing policies through repeated interactions with the traffic environment. Experiments on the real-world networks of Ingolstadt and Provins show that incorporating marginal cost into the AV reward not only limits the increase in HDV travel times and shortens AV travel times relative to selfish AV routing, but also improves overall system performance. In Ingolstadt, selfish routing of 40\% AVs increases the travel times of other vehicles by 1.7\%, and this drops to 1.1\% when the social reward is included. Interestingly, not only does overall system performance improve, but the AVs are also better off when acting socially.This effect is consistent across tested cities, penetration rates, and replications, yet when the weight of the social component in the reward increases, the system fails to reach the desired performance. For a more scalable approach to social AV routing in mixed-autonomy traffic, we compute the marginal cost only for the AVs whose route choices most affect the traffic system. This reduces the number of counterfactual simulations and achieves similar performance at a significantly lower computational cost. Our results suggest that AV routing should go beyond selfish rewards and, for the benefit of all traffic participants, include a social component in its objective.
authors: Anastasia Psarou, Mikolaj Rams, Blazej Torbus, Rafal Kucharski
bullets: Selfish AV route choices can increase travel times for human-driven vehicles in mixed-autonomy traffic.
The method estimates each AV’s impact by comparing traffic with and without that AV in a counterfactual simulation.
Experiments on Ingolstadt and Provins show lower human-driver delays, shorter AV travel times, and better system performance with social rewards.
For 40% AV penetration in Ingolstadt, the human-driver travel-time increase falls from 1.7% to 1.1%.
Computing marginal costs only for the most influential AVs preserves similar performance at lower computational cost; excessive social-reward weighting can hurt performance.

papers.abstract: End-to-end planning in complex scenes must model diverse driving intentions and select the most appropriate trajectory using scene context and future risks. However, multi-query regression may collapse to one mode, while anchor-based and generative planners share a scaling bottleneck: small candidate sets limit maneuver coverage or discovery of high-quality trajectories, whereas large sets increase generation and scoring costs. We propose ManeuverFlow to generate trajectories for distinct intentions in one step and evaluate and refine them using current and future evidence. The model selects relevant maneuver modes, draws corresponding noise from the Gaussian mixture prior, and maps it to intention-specific trajectories through a maneuver-routed mixture-of-experts MeanFlow field. Current features and future features predicted by the world model are aggregated along each candidate path into trajectory-specific evidence for PDM-factor prediction. Using the same evidence, the refiner predicts local Frenet residuals for selected candidates; refined and retained candidates are then jointly re-scored for selection. With a lightweight TransFuser-style ResNet-34 backbone, ManeuverFlow achieves 90.6 PDMS and 90.1 EPDMS on NAVSIM v1/v2 navtest, respectively. On WorldEngine's recent 3DGS closed-loop benchmark, it attains the highest listed PDMS$^\ast$ scores of 75.19 and 74.58 under logged and IDM-controlled traffic, respectively. Code: https://github.com/wyh-autonomy/maneuverflow.
authors: Yuhao Wei, Yong Chen, Chen Yang, Yingchen Wang, Delin Ouyang, Lingfeng Qi, Qi Lan, Zhanhua Zhang, Jie Li, Guofa Li
bullets: Addresses mode collapse and the cost–coverage trade-off of small versus large candidate sets.
Uses maneuver-routed mixture-of-experts MeanFlow to map maneuver-specific Gaussian-mixture noise to trajectories.
Aggregates present and world-model-predicted future features along each path for trajectory-specific scoring.
Refines selected candidates with local Frenet residuals before joint re-scoring.
Reports strong performance on NAVSIM v1/v2 and the WorldEngine 3DGS closed-loop benchmark.

papers.abstract: Reliable real-time failure detection is critical for deploying learned robotic policies, yet defining failures explicitly is infeasible in open-world settings. This motivates failure detection from nominal demonstrations alone. Existing methods, however, struggle to balance robustness to benign variations with the ability to capture semantic and interaction-level errors. We introduce Robot-WATCHDOG, a self-supervised framework that models manipulation scenes as object-centric spatio-temporal graphs. Building on this representation, we investigate two complementary failure scores: Trajectory Projection and Correlation (TPC), a non-parametric measure of geometric deviation and relational consistency, and GnnT, a Graph Attention Network with a Transformer that predicts future object states. We evaluate both on a public benchmark and on a new dataset of semantically complex manipulation tasks, across six tasks and ten random seeds. Both scores outperform image-based failure detectors, particularly on semantic and interaction-level failures. TPC provides the strongest performance in AUPR and MCC on both dataset averages, with low variance across seeds. Qualitative results are made available at https://cea-list.github.io/Robot-WATCHDOG/.
authors: Quentin Rolland, Fabrice Mayran de Chamisso, Jean-Baptiste Mouret
bullets: Addresses open-world failure detection without requiring explicitly labeled failures.
Introduces two self-supervised scores: TPC for geometric and relational deviations, and GnnT for predicting future object states.
Evaluated on a public benchmark and a new semantically complex manipulation dataset spanning six tasks and ten random seeds.
Both methods outperform image-based detectors, especially for semantic and interaction-level failures.
TPC achieves the strongest average AUPR and MCC with low variance across seeds.

papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence is beginning to automate scientific discovery, yet physical robot-policy research still relies on scientists and engineers to interpret experimental failures and decide how controllers should be revised. We present EndoRSI (Endoscopic Recursive Self-Improvement), a human-governed, self-improving robotic research system in which the embedded EndoForge coding agent iteratively develops and refines endoscopic robot policies using evidence from physical experiments. Physical execution remains isolated within a safety-constrained runtime under human authorisation. In motorised endoscopy, validation evidence first caused the agent to reject an initial action representation, while subsequent physical experiments falsified an offline-supported insertion strategy by revealing hazardous closed-loop behaviour absent from the source data. Failed physical rollouts were then incorporated into policy revision; insertion success subsequently increased from 2/21 in the first generation to 17/21 in the fourth. The frozen final policy retained competence across visual and hardware shifts and was the best performing autonomous policy across six independent ex-vivo porcine specimens. These results show that physical robot interaction can serve as experimental evidence for agent-driven robot policy research.
authors: Chi Kit Ng, Yidong Zhang, Tianchun Wu, Siu Hing Lui, Hanlin Zhao, Huxin Gao, Hongliang Ren

papers.abstract: Translating language into humanoid motion requires coordinating body parts, determining motion duration, and producing references suitable for robot execution. We introduce PartiGen, a part-aware latent diffusion framework that incorporates anatomical structure into a shared whole-body motion representation. Part-specific attention processes anatomically masked frame features, and its outputs are fused to combine local limb information with whole-body context. Conditioned on text and motion history, the model generates motion primitives autoregressively. Forward-kinematics supervision encourages kinematic consistency, while a learned end-of-sequence predictor selects a frame-level endpoint after generation. On HumanML3D retargeted to the Unitree G1, PartiGen achieves a segment-level FID of 3.165, a 16.8% reduction over TextOp, and improves R@1 by 1.4 percentage points. In the duration study with 16-frame primitives, endpoint prediction reduces mean absolute duration error from 12.471 to 3.080 frames compared with a fixed-length cutoff. We further evaluate robot execution using a pretrained, frozen GRIT tracker: 409 of 500 generated references (81.8%) pass the posture-based stability screen in MuJoCo. Following simulation screening and manual selection, 26 of 27 attempted motions are judged successful on the real G1.

Given history motion h and future motion f , the BP-MVAE encodes motion into a shared latent vector z ∈ R128. Part-aware features are fused into this vector for whole-body reconstruction. (b) Stage 2: DA-LDM Training. Building on latent diffusion [Rombach et al., 2022], DA-LDM directly predicts the clean shared motion code (x0 parameterization), conditioned on the noisy latent, CLIP text embeddings [Radford et al., 2021], history motion h, and diffusion timestep. The predicted clean latent is decoded to generate future motion f̂ . (c) Endpoint Selection. EOS selects an endpoint after complete candidate generation. (d) MultiPart Instructions. papers.abstract: Existing real-world reinforcement learning methods improve robot policies by combining human corrections with autonomous rollouts. However, accumulated experience varies in its value for policy improvement, and even successful trajectories can contain inefficient or redundant behavior, motivating more selective experience reuse. To this end, we propose Evo-RL, an iterative reinforcement learning method that combines human interventions with advantage-guided experience selection. Evo-RL uses human corrections and experience with positive estimated advantages from successful trajectories to iteratively refine the policy. To support learning from these different experience sources, we introduce RW-RL-Dataset, which spans over 1,000 hours across four robot embodiments. On a real-world high-precision manipulation task, Evo-RL improves attempt success rate over RECAP by 30.46\%. Our code, model checkpoints, and dataset are publicly available.

Code, checkpoints, and dataset are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Tool-using agents increasingly require a common substrate for building, training, evaluating, distilling, and maintaining agentic systems, yet existing tooling typically addresses these stages in isolation. We present AgentTune, a source-available Python library that provides a unified framework for developing and optimizing tool-using agents. At its core, AgentTune introduces a two-tier EventLog representation that preserves agent trajectories while supporting consistent projections for training, evaluation, and auditing. Building on this substrate, the library provides a shared agent runtime, tool-calling reinforcement learning, agentic distillation, retrieval-augmented generation, decision workflows, evaluation utilities, and a designed path toward self-healing agents. These components are exposed through composable interfaces so that agent strategies, training methods, evaluation procedures, and recovery mechanisms can be combined without requiring separate representations or pipelines. We demonstrate the framework across agentic tasks including legal contract search and domain-specific applications, illustrating its use for trajectory-based optimization, tool-use evaluation, and cross-task agent development. AgentTune is released as a source-available library at https://github.com/Lexsi-Labs/AgentTune
authors: R E Zera Marveen Lyngkhoi, Abhivansh Gupta, Vidushee Vats, Ram Mohan Rao Kadiyala, Vinay Kumar Sankarapu, Pratinav Seth

Production (5) runs DECIDE workflows and the detect–classify–generate–retrain–gate cycle, whose audited failures and corrected trajectories return to Layer 3 as new training data. papers.abstract: Memory-dependent manipulation requires a policy to track execution state and recover visual evidence that is no longer observable. We propose dual-stream memory for vision-language-action policies, assigning these requirements to complementary representations. A task-agnostic Gated DeltaNet compresses history into one temporal token, supervised by progress prediction and action-conditioned feature reconstruction. A task-conditioned retriever retains frames above a fixed relevance threshold; linear multi-scale fusion encodes each frame into sixteen spatial tokens. We then freeze the temporal compressor and jointly optimize retrieval and policy learning. Across sixteen RoboMME tasks, the complete model achieves 49.22% mean success versus 44.51% for the published FrameSamp+Modul reference, improving fourteen tasks and all four suite means. On four real-robot tasks, mean success reaches 62.5% versus 37.5%, with the largest gains on repeated actions requiring execution-stage discrimination. These results support combining execution context with selective visual access, while failures under cup swaps expose persistent identity tracking as an unresolved requirement.

On 16 RoboMME tasks, mean success is 49.22% versus 44.51% for FrameSamp+Modul; real-robot mean success is 62.5% versus 37.5%.

papers.abstract: Actions specify what a robot should execute, but do not describe what those commands will achieve. Vision-language-action (VLA) policies nevertheless learn primarily by predicting action chunks from images, language, and state. We introduce Action--Future Coupled Effect Learning (AFCE), which makes a future-grounded physical Effect the policy's primary prediction target. An offline tokenizer constructs temporally ordered Effect tokens from demonstrated actions, realized robot responses, and sparse visual transitions. Reconstruction objectives encourage the representation to retain executable detail and observed physical change. A flow-matching VLA predicts Effects from current images, instruction, and robot state, while a state-conditioned decoder converts them into action chunks. Embodiment-specific interfaces allow single- and dual-arm tasks to share the Effect model. On DexJoCo, AFCE achieves $50.97\%$ overall success, improving over $\pi_{0.5}$ and UVT by 11.82 and 15.21 percentage points, respectively. It leads on all five bimanual tasks, highlighting the value of Effect supervision for coordinated dexterous manipulation. The project page is available at https://afceproject.github.io/AFCE-Web/.
authors: Min Lin, Bokai Zhou, Jianqi Lin, Kaiyuan Yang, Yicheng Chang, Junjie Yu, Xiaofan Liu, Jianhua Han, Rui Li, Shen Zhao, Xiaodan Liang
bullets: Targets future-grounded Effect tokens rather than actions alone.
Builds temporally ordered Effect tokens from demonstrations, robot responses, and sparse visual transitions.
Uses flow matching to predict Effects, then a state-conditioned decoder generates action chunks.
Supports shared Effect modeling across single- and dual-arm embodiments.
On DexJoCo, achieves 50.97% overall success and leads on all five bimanual tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Action–Future Coupled Effect Learning (AFCE). Stage I fuses demonstrated actions At, robot response ∆St, and visual transitions Vt into ordered Effect tokens E∗ t , supervised by action, state, and visual reconstruction. Stage II predicts the normalized target Z∗ t from current images, instruction, and robot state, then decodes an action chunk. The lower panel shows the shared Effect space with embodiment-specific interfaces. The dashed path denotes training targets; future evidence is not used at deployment.

Figure 1: Comparison of policy supervision paradigms. A standard VLA predicts actions directly; world-action models use future dynamics to support control; AFCE predicts an action-decodable Effect grounded in executed actions, robot response, and world change. Future evidence constructs training targets but is unavailable to the deployed policy.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) under partial observability typically re- lies on recurrent networks to encode temporal information, with the recurrent module trained jointly with the policy or value function. This raises a natural question: is learning the recurrent network actually necessary? In this paper, we investigate whether a frozen recurrent network can provide sufficient memory for solving par- tially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs). Motivated by the theoretical foundations of Reservoir Computing (RC) and Generalized Reservoir Computing (GRC), we study a simple archi- tecture that combines a fixed recurrent network with a trainable nonlinear output module. We evaluate this approach across tasks with varying memory demands, observation modalities, and action spaces. Surprisingly, frozen recurrent networks support recall over hundreds of steps and achieve competitive control performance across diverse POMDPs, while using less than half the number of trainable parameters required by their fully trainable counterparts. These results suggest that learning the recurrent memory module is not always necessary for solving POMDPs. Frozen recurrent networks therefore provide a simple, parameter-efficient, and sur- prisingly strong baseline for partially observable RL. Our source code is available at https://github.com/Aphlios/FRN-POMDP
authors: Zekang Wang, Zhe He, Gaojie Jin
bullets: Partially observable RL commonly trains recurrent memory jointly with policy or value functions.

They achieve competitive control performance while requiring less than half as many trainable parameters as fully trainable recurrent models.
The approach is proposed as a simple, parameter-efficient baseline, though its effectiveness is evaluated within the studied POMDP tasks.

papers.abstract: Autonomous landing of unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) on unmanned surface vehicle (USV) is difficult in high sea states. Existing hierarchical landing methods often infer future USV motion only implicitly from short observation histories, which limits their ability to adapt to severe and rapidly changing sea conditions. This paper presents a prediction-informed hierarchical control framework. A pretrained model is developed to explicitly predict the USV attitude during high-level landing decisions. The prediction helps identify suitable landing windows and choose the right touchdown time, while a conventional low-level flight controller maintains UAV stability and tracks motion commands. To evaluate the framework under realistic disturbances, a real-sim validation setup is constructed in which USV-motion data collected in real sea conditions are transferred to a MuJoCo USV. The experiments demonstrate the feasibility of using explicit attitude prediction to improve landing-window selection and support timing-aware UAV landing planning in rapidly varying marine environments.

Real-sea motion data transferred to a MuJoCo USV provide real-sim validation, demonstrating feasibility in realistic disturbances.

papers.abstract: Scaling robot manipulation policies requires large amounts of diverse, action-labeled data, yet collecting such data in the real world remains expensive and difficult to scale. Existing methods either depend on human teleoperation, rely on simulation with limited visual realism, or use human videos that lack embodiment-specific annotations. In this paper, we introduce Grounded-Dreamer, a framework for synthesizing physically grounded robot manipulation data with video world models while avoiding human teleoperation demonstrations. Grounded-Dreamer combines the visual realism of generative video models with simulator physics engines. Starting from a small set of real images depicting robot task initial states, our method automatically reconstructs task-relevant objects and camera geometry, aligns them in simulation, and collects physically valid trajectories. These trajectories are used to post-train both a video world model and an inverse dynamics model, enabling the generation of visually realistic robot manipulation videos and corresponding robot actions from real images. To filter physically implausible rollouts, Grounded-Dreamer replays generated trajectories in the reconstructed simulation and retains only those that successfully complete the tasks. The real-world robot policies are trained solely on the grounded synthetic trajectories without any human demonstrations. Empirical results in real-world tasks demonstrate that Grounded-Dreamer can synthesize physically grounded data and substantially facilitate policy learning without requiring human teleoperation effort.
authors: Feng Jiang, Shu Chen, Yuanfei Wang, Yuan Li, Zhenhao Shen, Jiaqi Liang, Yang Chen, Lei Wei, Chen Xie, Ruihai Wu
bullets: Addresses the cost and scalability limits of collecting real-world robot demonstrations.
Reconstructs task objects and camera geometry from a small set of real initial-state images, then aligns them in simulation.
Post-trains a video world model and inverse dynamics model to generate realistic manipulation videos and robot actions.
Filters synthetic rollouts by replaying them in simulation and retaining only task-successful trajectories.
Uses only grounded synthetic data to train real-world policies, which facilitates policy learning in real-world tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of Grounded-Dreamer. Our framework automates the generation of massive, high-fidelity robot data from a small number of real-world reference images. By combining generative world models with simulation-based verification, Grounded-Dreamer produces data that is both visually realistic and physically consistent. This simulation verification loop effectively filters out the physical hallucinations common in purely generative approaches, allowing robot policies to be trained directly on scalable synthetic data that transfers robustly to complex real-world scenarios.

Figure 2: The Grounded-Dreamer Pipeline. Given several real-world reference images, our pipeline first reconstructs physically aligned simulation scenes and objects. Within these environments, task data is automatically collected and processed with interaction-aware masking to fine-tune Cosmos-Predict 2.5 as the core data generation model. An image refinement model then synthesizes diverse initial frames by combining reconstructed assets with real scene backgrounds and object appearances. Conditioned on these frames, the generation model produces manipulation videos, which are converted into action trajectories using an Inverse Dynamics Model (IDM). Finally, all synthesized trajectories are replayed in simulation for closed-loop verification, filtering out physically inconsistent samples before policy training and real-world deployment.

papers.abstract: Collecting dexterous manipulation demonstrations for each robot hand requires repeated task-specific data acquisition. We ask whether one shared corpus of natural human demonstrations can instead serve as a reusable data interface for different dexterous hands, without collecting task demonstrations on each target robot. We present Human2Dex, a wrist-centric human demonstration interface that separates shared human observation and motion semantics from embodiment-specific execution. It aligns observations through local hand-appearance adaptation and a shared 21-point hand representation with consistent structural semantics across human and robot observations. It constructs executable supervision by retargeting fused human hand motion to each target hand, and introduces the Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation (GPIR) to express tracked objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket. The corpus is converted into separate training sets for Linker O6 and Wuji, while action labels, normalization, training, and diffusion-policy checkpoints remain hand-specific. Across six real-world tasks, Human2Dex achieves 109/120 (90.8%) successes on Linker O6 and 97/120 (80.8%) on Wuji. Across both hands, Human-Raw achieves 63/240 (26.3%) successes, whereas the complete Human2Dex configuration achieves 206/240 (85.8%). These results support the use of wrist-centric human demonstrations as a reusable interface across calibrated dexterous hands while retaining embodiment-specific policy learning. The project website is publicly available at https://human2dex.pages.dev/.
authors: Jiachen Zhang, Yuanyuan Li, Shaqi Luo
bullets: Addresses the need to repeatedly collect task demonstrations for each robot hand.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world action models (WAMs) have advanced robotic policy learning by building on pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) and video generative models (VGMs), respectively. Yet VLAs learn without explicit supervision from future world states, while WAMs that condition actions on predicted futures incur extra inference cost and let visual prediction errors propagate into actions. We present Forward Dynamics Models (FDM), a family of robotic action models that couples action and future world-state prediction through an action-to-future paradigm. Future prediction is conditioned on action features, never the reverse: end-to-end training lets ground-truth future states supervise the policy through these features, while prediction errors cannot propagate into actions. At inference, FDM skips future generation entirely, avoiding its computational cost. The paradigm is backbone-agnostic, and we instantiate it with both VLM and VGM backbones. Experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate the effectiveness of FDM across both backbone families, achieving a state-of-the-art 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and absolute gains of up to 13% over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.
authors: Zipei Ma, Junzhe Jiang, Jiahui Zhang, Juntong Zhang, Chun Gu, Bozhou Zhang, Jiankang Deng, Xiatian Zhu, Li Zhang
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit future-state supervision in VLAs and the inference cost and error propagation of WAMs.
Uses an action-to-future paradigm: predicted futures condition on action features, not vice versa.
End-to-end training lets future-state prediction supervise the policy without allowing prediction errors to affect actions.
Backbone-agnostic design is instantiated with both vision-language and video-generative backbones.
Demonstrates a 99.4% average success rate on LIBERO and up to 13% absolute gains over VLA and WAM methods on real-world tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Overview of our Forward Dynamics Models. The context expert encodes visual observations and the instruction to guide the action expert. During training, the generation expert predicts future states from context and action features; its loss backpropagates through these action features to complement action imitation. This asymmetric connection lets future supervision shape the policy while keeping action prediction independent of predicted futures. At inference, the action expert generates actions using the required context features, skipping future generation.

Figure 1: Architectural comparison of action prediction and future supervision. (a) VLA predicts actions directly from the current observation and instruction. (b) A future-conditioned WAM conditions action prediction on predicted future video, requiring future generation at inference. (c) FDM conditions future prediction on context and action features through action-to-future learning. During training, action imitation and future prediction are jointly optimized; the future loss backpropagates through action features to supervise the policy. At inference, FDM denoises action chunks using only the current observation and instruction, skipping the future-generation branch marked as training only while retaining context processing.

papers.abstract: Visual agents for symbolic graphics reasoning depend on executable world representations, yet continued improvement remains bottlenecked by ambiguous supervision from final renders. Recent agentic systems refine scenes through repeated interaction, but they lack mechanisms to recursively extract actionable evidence from execution traces, overlooking which proposed symbolic edits survived, disappeared, or interfered during program execution. To address this, we propose VETR (Verified Execution Trajectories for Refinement), a framework that enables agentic recursive self-improvement over executable world representations for symbolic graphics reasoning. Within each task, VETR retains aligned program/render records with bounded runtime observations and introduces an execution refiner that compiles observed writes and state changes into constrained alternative programs. The refiner validates their endpoints and preservation conditions against captured runtime state; the ordinary visual verifier then assesses goal relevance. Repair construction makes no additional language-model calls, but can require additional executions. Evaluations on BlenderGym (280 tasks) and BlenderBench (27 released tasks) with GPT-5.6-luna and Qwen3.8-27B show that VETR consistently outperforms existing refinement strategies, including BlenderAlchemy and VIGA. Controlled ablations evaluate the contributions of execution refinement and role-asymmetric evidence organization under fixed generator-interaction caps.
authors: Yingbo Ma, Kuangshi Ai, Gordon Dai, Chenglong Yu, Chaoli Wang, Hua Shen
bullets: Addresses ambiguous supervision from final renders by identifying which symbolic edits persist, vanish, or interfere during execution.
Maintains aligned program/render records with bounded runtime observations and compiles state changes into constrained alternative programs.
Validates repaired programs against runtime endpoints and preservation conditions, then uses visual verification for goal relevance.
Evaluated on BlenderGym and BlenderBench with two language models; consistently outperforms prior refinement strategies, including BlenderAlchemy and VIGA.
Ablations examine execution refinement and role-asymmetric evidence organization under fixed generator-interaction limits.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Conceptual overview of VETR. VETR refines scenes through execution-grounded evidence, bridging a scene program, its execution trace, and the realized 3D scene. Given a start and goal image, the system performs iterative updates guided by observed writes and realized bindings. This evidence-supported refinement targets viewpoint alignment, appearance (lighting/material) editing, and geometry and placement adjustments. Runtime checks test supported effects, while visual feedback guides subsequent proposals toward the goal.

papers.abstract: Autoregressive robot policies rely on action tokenizers to convert continuous action chunks into compact sequences of discrete prediction targets. Existing tokenizers can reconstruct action chunks from discrete codes, but often leave implicit what each individual token contributes to the reconstructed action. We introduce Residual Action Tokenization (ReAT), which gives each token an explicit role in refining the current action reconstruction. It uses the decoded reconstruction as feedback to construct the next token from the remaining action error. This closes the loop between encoding and decoding, making each new token responsive to the errors left by the actual decoded prefix. Across 19 manipulation tasks spanning three simulation benchmarks and real-world settings, 8-token ReAT policies outperform the evaluated baselines in task success; on LIBERO, even 4-token ReAT surpasses the evaluated 8-token action-tokenization baselines at half the token budget. These results suggest a path toward action tokenization that supports self-corrective policy learning, helping autoregressive policies learn to progressively refine their own action plans.

papers.abstract: People often learn how an unfamiliar object moves through a small exploratory push, using its response to guide their next motion. Inspired by this behavior, we study humanoids pushing carts whose mass and caster stiffness are initially unknown. Our object-centric framework closes online estimation, flow-based planning, and whole-body control into a loop, creating a tension: replacing the plan whenever the belief shifts disrupts the maneuver under way, while keeping it strands the robot on a path its evidence has ruled out. Belief-Overlap Partial Inversion (BOPI) scales revision to agreement, inverting the flow under the old belief only as far as the beliefs disagree before reconstructing under the new one. Across 18 simulated goals it lowers pooled final position and yaw error by roughly 33% and 47% against fixed-depth replanning, and on hardware it translates and turns a non-holonomic cart.

bullets: Addresses the trade-off between disruptive full replanning and continuing along invalidated plans.
Combines online object-property estimation, flow-based planning, and whole-body control.
Partially inverts the old plan only where old and new beliefs disagree, then reconstructs the remainder under the new belief.
Across 18 simulated goals, reduced pooled final position error by roughly 33% and yaw error by 47% versus fixed-depth replanning.
Hardware experiments demonstrated translation and turning of a non-holonomic cart.

papers.abstract: Third-person human videos offer a scalable alternative to task-specific reward engineering, teleoperation, and manually scripted demonstrations for humanoid loco-manipulation. Recent video-to-humanoid systems have shown that noisy human motion, object trajectories, and contacts can be extracted from unstructured videos and refined into deployable skills. However, a key gap remains for contact-rich imitation: the task is often defined by world-frame contacts whose poses, timing, and speed must survive embodiment mismatch and runtime scene changes. Towards this, we present VICAR (Video Imitation with Contact-Aware Retargeting), a pipeline for learning humanoid interactive skills from third-person human videos. The system first recovers human motion, reconstructs task-relevant obstacles from monocular video, and then retargets the motion to a humanoid while preserving global contact poses, motion speed, and collision clearance. Unlike retargeting methods that only remove penetration or preserve local interaction geometry, our formulation represents user-specified contact poses and collision clearance as high-priority Lagrangian penalty terms and optimizes the full motion to remain smooth through contact-rich transitions. The resulting motions are used to train a contact-conditioned motion generator whose inputs include movable contact points enabling runtime adaptation to new contact positions. We demonstrate the framework on ten diverse third-person video skills, including six table-tennis serves, three object-pickup tasks, and ladder climbing, and deploy the learned skills on hardware. These results suggest that contact-preserving retargeting is a practical step toward humanoids that learn useful interactive behavior by watching humans.
authors: Dvij Kalaria, Bike Zhang, S. Shankar Sastry
bullets: Addresses contact-rich imitation under embodiment mismatch and changing runtime scenes.
Recovers human motion and task-relevant obstacles from monocular video, then performs contact-aware humanoid retargeting.
Uses high-priority Lagrangian penalties for user-specified contact poses and collision clearance while optimizing smooth motion.
Trains a contact-conditioned motion generator with movable contact points for adapting to new contact positions.
Demonstrated on ten skills—including table-tennis serves, object pickup, and ladder climbing—with hardware deployment.

papers.abstract: Multi-robot coordination is essential in applications such as coverage, target tracking, and information gathering, where robots must jointly select actions to maximize team performance. Submodular maximization provides an effective framework for such coordination, and resilient variants further account for robot failures or adversarial removals. However, existing methods typically overlook the impact of robot loss on the communication network, which may disconnect the surviving team and prevent continued coordination. To address this issue, we introduce Resilient $k$-Connected Submodular Maximization, which jointly considers task performance, resilience, and communication connectivity. The resulting feasible family is not a matroid, preventing the direct application of classical curvature-greedy guarantees. We overcome this challenge through a Menger-based connectivity reduction, a connectivity-aware greedy algorithm with a feasibility-preserving fallback, and a new curvature-based analysis that captures the cost of enforcing connectivity through a single factor $\rho$. Our method achieves a worst-case post-failure objective within a factor of $[\max(1-\nu_f(\mathcal{I}),h(N,\beta))]^2 \rho \frac{1}{\kappa_f}(1-e^{-\kappa_f})$ of the optimal connectivity-respecting resilient assignment, while recovering the classical unconstrained guarantee in the appropriate limits. Experiments on multi-robot target tracking validate the proposed method and characterize the practical impact of connectivity constraints.
authors: Yoonjae Hwang, Hojune Kim, Ellen Novoseller, Guangyao Shi, Gaurav S. Sukhatme
bullets: Addresses the risk that robot loss disconnects the surviving communication network, halting coordination.
Introduces Resilient $k$-Connected Submodular Maximization, jointly modeling task performance, failure resilience, and communication connectivity.
Uses a Menger-based connectivity reduction, connectivity-aware greedy selection, and a feasibility-preserving fallback.
Provides curvature-based worst-case guarantees that account for connectivity costs through a factor $\rho$ and recover classical guarantees in limiting cases.
Experiments on multi-robot target tracking evaluate the method and the practical effects of connectivity constraints.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: The core structural conflict in multi-robot deployments. (Left) Aerial teams face adversarial attacks or failures removing up to β nodes. (Middle) Existing frameworks treat requirements in isolation, in which standard resilient maximization risks post-attack fragmentation, while standard connectivity assumes a failure-free environment. (Right) Our framework resolves this by achieving simultaneous adversarial resilience and (β+1)-vertex-connectivity, ensuring the surviving team remains structurally connected and performant.

papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) inherit powerful priors from pretrained video generation models, but their variational autoencoder (VAE) representations are optimized for visual reconstruction rather than manipulation. External visual representations can improve manipulation, but existing methods couple representation choices with different integration mechanisms, obscuring their individual effects. We systematically compare visual representations, five integration mechanisms, and feature combinations under controlled settings. Our study yields three main findings. First, strong general-purpose visual representations provide broader robustness gains and can match or outperform representations pretrained for specific visual capabilities. Second, channel-wise joint prediction achieves the highest average success rate; further analyses suggest that future-feature prediction and the action expert's effective use of added visual information contribute to its gains. Third, additional sources should be selected for the task-relevant information they contribute beyond existing representations, as the same source can help one combination but harm another. However, even the best evaluated composition provides a smaller additional gain than the initial improvement from adding a strong general-purpose representation to the VAE-only baseline. We instantiate the resulting Representation Recipe as R$^2$-WAM. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on RoboCasa GR1 Tabletop with an 84.7% success rate and reaches 92.8% on RoboTwin 2.0, improving over the VAE-only baselines by 5.9 and 2.2 percentage points, respectively. Taken together, these findings suggest that future work should prioritize stronger general-purpose visual representations and more effective mechanisms for integrating them into WAMs, with feature composition serving as a supplementary route to improvement.

papers.abstract: Continual learning requires models to accumulate past experience and transfer it to new tasks. Despite substantial research on continual learning, existing work remains largely confined to non-embodied settings, without extending to embodied environments. To address this gap, we introduce EmbodiedCLBench, the first benchmark in embodied simulation for evaluating the continual learning capability of self-evolving agents. With compositional generalization as the core evaluation principle, our benchmark evaluates whether agents can first learn from basic tasks and then recombine the acquired skills to solve complex, unseen advanced tasks. Based on EmbodiedCLBench, we conduct extensive experiments across multiple agent harnesses and learning methods, revealing consistent limitations and distinctive behaviors. Our results show that while advanced tasks can be hardly solved under zero-shot setting, the experience from basic tasks enables consistent improvement. Such benefit from the experience remains stable even if the task complexity increases. However, this improvement does not scale accordingly with the number of learning samples, and current agents cannot extract meaningful information from additional experience. Collectively, our findings highlight continual learning as a fundamental yet underexplored capability, and our benchmark offers valuable resources for designing effective self-evolving agents in embodied environments. Our code and dataset are available at https://pku-value-lab.github.io/EmbodiedCLBench-homepage.
authors: Jie Huang, Yanan Chen, Ruixun Liu, Kaichen He, Xinyi He, Rui Huang, Zilong Zheng, Zhenliang Zhang, Yiwu Zhong

papers.abstract: Learning-based methods have demonstrated strong performance in mapless robot navigation. However, a learned policy remains restricted to the embodiment on which it was trained. Many cross-embodiment navigation methods require time-consuming online training and can still underperform target-specific policies. In fact, demonstrations collected on a source embodiment already contain navigation experience that is potentially reusable for deriving a policy for each target embodiment, but the embodiment mismatch prevents these demonstrations from directly serving as valid supervision for the target. In this article, we present CeDR-Nav, a cross-embodiment demonstration recasting framework that trains a dedicated navigation policy for each target embodiment from existing source demonstrations without online data collection. Geometry-consistent scaling with per-demonstration validity assessment converts the source demonstrations into target training data, and a target-specific Gaussian mixture policy generates feasible avoidance maneuvers for each target embodiment. Extensive quantitative simulations and real-world deployments across multiple robot platforms demonstrate the effectiveness of CeDR-Nav, with an average success-rate gain of 13.8 percentage points over DRL-DCLP in cross-embodiment simulations and target-specific policy training completed within seconds.
authors: Xianghui Wang, Xinming Zhang, Yiwei Qian, Siwei Cheng, Shanze Wang, Dan Zhang, Wei Zhang

papers.abstract: Empowerment measures the capacity of an agent to actively control its environment. In this work, we explain the connection between skill learning and empowerment. While skill learning is not empowerment, we introduce a simple scalable recipe for empowerment maximization: empowerment corresponds to the number of executable skills from a state, so maximizing empowerment corresponds to reaching states that are good starting points for many skills. Our recipe applies to arbitrary underlying skill learning methods. Whereas most prior work on empowerment looks at tabular settings, this recipe enables us to study empowerment at a scale where we can realize theoretically-predicted but empirically-elusive properties of empowerment (e.g., gathering resources, environment modification, survival). Experiments show that empowerment maximization unlocks interesting emergent properties, such as building a house in Crafter. Website and code at \href{https://empowerment-geometry.github.io/scaling-empowerment/}{this https url}.
authors: Catherine Ji, Vivek Myers, Joshua Lin, Alexandra Wingate, Sergey Levine, Benjamin Eysenbach
bullets: Connects empowerment with skill learning while distinguishing the two concepts.
Defines empowerment operationally as the number of executable skills available from a state.
Proposes a simple recipe that works with arbitrary underlying skill-learning methods.
Scales empowerment studies beyond tabular environments to realize theoretically predicted behaviors.
Demonstrates emergent behaviors, including house building in Crafter.
