papers.abstract: Learning from Demonstrations (LfD) enables robots to learn object manipulation directly from human demonstrations. In contrast to resource-intensive and labor-intensive teleoperation, egocentric demonstrations are easy to collect, enabling scalable data collection. Manipulated objects are often partially occluded in everyday environments, yet prior egocentric demonstration-based methods that require no robots or specialized teaching devices do not explicitly address occlusions. To fill this gap, we propose EgoReveal, a framework that learns viewpoint-repositioning together with manipulation actions from egocentric human demonstrations to reposition the viewpoint and obtain target visibility under partial occlusions. EgoReveal instantiates this as two imitation policies: one predicts the future camera-arm pose sequence from the current view and camera-arm pose, and the other predicts the future control commands from object keypoints and a history of control commands. EgoReveal switches between the two based on target visibility. In experiments where the manipulated object is partially occluded initially, EgoReveal repositions the camera to obtain visibility and completes the task more reliably than fixed-camera baselines.
authors: Hiromu Kurihara, Kazutoshi Tanaka, Masashi Hatano, Tadashi Kozuno, Hideo Saito, Mariko Isogawa
bullets: Addresses partial object occlusions, which prior robot-free egocentric demonstration methods do not explicitly handle.
Uses two imitation policies: one predicts camera-arm repositioning, and the other predicts manipulation controls.
Switches between viewpoint repositioning and manipulation based on target visibility.
Experiments show more reliable task completion than fixed-camera baselines when objects are initially occluded.

papers.abstract: Embodied agents must translate multimodal observations and user requests into executable actions while adapting to product constraints, changing goals, and execution feedback. We present JoyInside-VLM-Agent, a ReAct-style multimodal agent developed through product-conditioned trajectory construction and staged policy learning for robotic platforms and smart hardware. A closed-loop sandbox generates multimodal interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, which are checked against execution outcomes and semantic criteria. Supervised fine-tuning and multi-teacher on-policy distillation precede reinforcement learning with DPER (Dual-Source Privileged On-Policy Self-Distillation with Token-Level Evidence Routing). DPER routes token-level evidence between a frozen privileged teacher and a privileged student sharing the rollout policy's parameters, modulating reward-derived token advantages while preserving their signs. Training rewards combine generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency. JoyInside-VLM-Agent achieves a BFCL v4 overall score of 77.44, exceeding the evaluated baselines; results on the other public benchmarks are mixed. On JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, the evaluated system, which includes domain-specific skill refinement, leads the baselines on all reported metrics. Two real-world quadruped case studies illustrate visually grounded search, replanning after execution failure, and explicit failure reporting.
authors: Gangyi Li, LuYao Wang, Jingfu Sun, Jingyi Yuan, Hang Liu, Hao Zong, Yujia Hu, Tingting Gao, Jianyong Wang, Xu Yang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting multimodal observations and changing user goals into executable actions under product constraints.
Builds closed-loop interaction trajectories covering goal revisions and failure recovery, validated by execution outcomes and semantic criteria.
Uses staged learning—supervised fine-tuning, multi-teacher on-policy distillation, and reinforcement learning with DPER token-level evidence routing.
Combines generative process evaluation, multi-judge rankings, and task-queue consistency for training rewards.

Scores 77.44 on BFCL v4 and leads reported metrics on JoyInside-Devices and JoyInside-Robotics, while results on other public benchmarks are mixed; quadruped case studies demonstrate search, replanning, and failure reporting.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified framework for visual understanding, language grounding, and robot control, yet anticipating how the scene will evolve beyond the current observation can provide additional information for control. Action supervision alone does not explicitly encourage such anticipation, while future-image prediction entangles task-relevant motion with largely static appearance. To address these limitations, we introduce Evo-World, a lightweight VLA model that augments policy learning with future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision, thereby providing a task-relevant predictive signal focused on motion rather than appearance. We further design the training procedure to preserve these predictive representations during policy learning, regulating representation diversity while decoupling representation learning from action optimization. Across simulation benchmarks, Evo-World demonstrates strong performance, achieving a tier-averaged success rate of 91.1% on Meta-World MT50 , with a 13.0% relative improvement over the non-predictive baseline. On real-world AgileX robots, Evo-World outperforms the evaluated baselines across single-arm and bimanual manipulation tasks while using only 0.87B parameters and delivering lower GPU memory usage and higher inference efficiency. These results demonstrate that future motion prediction through optical-flow supervision provides an effective and lightweight approach to enhancing the predictive capabilities of VLA models.
authors: Zile Zhong, Yuxin Du, Tao Lin, Haoxiao Wang, Wei Dai, Binhua Zuo, Bo Zhao
bullets: Addresses the limitation that action supervision does not explicitly teach VLAs to anticipate scene evolution.
Uses optical-flow-based future motion prediction to focus representations on task-relevant motion rather than static appearance.
Preserves predictive representations during policy learning by regulating representation diversity and decoupling representation learning from action optimization.
Achieves a 91.1% tier-averaged success rate on Meta-World MT50, a 13.0% relative gain over a non-predictive baseline.
Shows stronger performance than evaluated baselines on real-world single-arm and bimanual AgileX tasks with 0.87B parameters, lower GPU memory use, and higher inference efficiency.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models have shown strong promise in robotic manipulation, yet their post-training still predominantly relies on trajectory-level supervised imitation over robot demonstrations. While effective for learning feasible actions, this paradigm supervises policies to reproduce expert actions at each step, biasing them toward demonstration-specific action paths and providing limited guidance for recovering toward task-progress states once execution deviates from demonstrated trajectories. To address this limitation, we propose OGPO, an Offline Goal-conditioned Policy Optimization framework for recoverable VLA post-training. Instead of treating offline demonstrations merely as step-wise action labels, OGPO adaptively relabels trajectories with semantic key states and constructs goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize the policy for reaching these task-progress states. In this way, OGPO shifts VLA post-training from trajectory-level action imitation to key-state reachability learning, enabling policies to acquire a more robust ability to complete goal states from feasible off-demonstration states without requiring additional online interaction. Experiments on LIBERO and MetaWorld show that OGPO consistently improves VLA policy performance over standard supervised fine-tuning. Moreover, evaluations on LIBERO-Plus and our proposed LIBERO-ReAct, a mid-execution perturbation benchmark, further demonstrate that OGPO achieves stronger robustness and goal-directed recoverability under distribution shifts and recoverable off-demonstration states.
authors: Xule Gao, Xi Wang, Zehua Zang, Rui Wang, Changwen Zheng, Chuxiong Sun
bullets: Problem: Step-wise imitation can overfit to demonstration paths and offers limited guidance after execution deviates from them.
Method: Relabels offline trajectories with semantic key states and uses goal-conditioned process rewards to optimize key-state reachability.
Contribution: Shifts VLA post-training from trajectory imitation toward recoverable, goal-directed behavior from feasible off-demonstration states.
Results: Improves performance over standard supervised fine-tuning on LIBERO and MetaWorld, with stronger robustness under shifts and perturbations on LIBERO-Plus and LIBERO-ReAct.

papers.abstract: Agile and reliable navigation is a core capability for embodied robots navigating complex spatial constraints and dynamic interactions. However, a single policy often struggles to accommodate the distinct decision-making demands of diverse scenarios. We present TAME-Nav, an asymmetric Teacher-Student navigation framework built around a temporal soft mixture of experts (Soft-MoE). The Teacher combines clean observations with causally maintained dynamic-obstacle tracks to construct privileged representations, while the Student learns complementary navigation features from corrupted observation histories through temporal encoding, soft expert routing, and latent distillation. Procedural scenario generation and parallel task-level simulation broaden training coverage, while deployment-informed asymmetric domain randomization supports sim-to-real transfer. Across in-distribution and unseen compositional scenarios, TAME-Nav achieves higher success rates, lower collision rates, and higher navigation scores than representative baselines. On a real quadruped robot, it completes all twenty trials across local-trap escape and narrow-passage navigation with sudden dynamic obstacles, with only one minor contact.
authors: Lingjie Zhang, Jun Xue, Shanze Wang, Haoyu Xi, Xinming Zhang, Xiaoyu Shen, Wei Zhang
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of using one navigation policy across varied spatial constraints and dynamic interactions.
Uses an asymmetric Teacher–Student framework with temporal soft mixture-of-experts routing and latent distillation.
The Teacher uses clean observations and maintained dynamic-obstacle tracks; the Student learns from corrupted observation histories.
Procedural scenario generation, parallel simulation, and deployment-informed domain randomization support broad training and sim-to-real transfer.
Outperforms representative baselines in success, collision, and navigation scores; a real quadruped completed 20 trials with one minor contact.

papers.abstract: In the practical deployment of vision--language--action policies, handling long-tailed task distributions is a common challenge due to the highly imbalanced composition of robot demonstration datasets. To investigate this issue, we study the head-task action bias in shared robot policies, particularly focusing on its relationship with task-specific visual evidence. Our experimental analysis shows that, when the visual evidence required by a tail task is insufficient, the policy increasingly falls back on action patterns reinforced by data-rich head tasks, resulting in degraded performance on under-represented tasks. Motivated by this observation, we propose Evidence-Guided Counterfactual Learning, a training framework for long-tailed robot policies. Our method identifies decision-relevant visual evidence using instruction-related and action-related signals, and constructs counterfactual observations by removing the selected evidence. The resulting counterfactual predictions are used to strengthen the association among task instructions, visual evidence, and actions, with the supervision adaptively adjusted according to the number of demonstrations available for each task. The proposed framework requires neither additional training data nor region-level annotations and incurs no additional computation during deployment. Extensive experiments across simulated benchmarks, different VLA architectures, and real-world robot platforms demonstrate that our method robustly and consistently improves long-tailed robot policy learning, particularly for tail tasks, while maintaining reliable performance on head tasks.
authors: Weiwei Chen, Chenghao Xu, Meiling Yu, Xu Yang, Cheng Deng
bullets: Long-tailed demonstration data can cause shared policies to favor action patterns from data-rich head tasks, harming under-represented tail tasks.
The method identifies decision-relevant visual evidence from instruction- and action-related signals, then removes it to create counterfactual observations.
Counterfactual predictions reinforce links among task instructions, visual evidence, and actions, with supervision adjusted by task demonstration frequency.
It requires no additional data or region-level annotations and adds no deployment-time computation.
Experiments across simulated benchmarks, multiple VLA architectures, and real robots show improved tail-task learning while maintaining head-task performance.

papers.abstract: In maximum entropy and behavior-constrained reinforcement learning (RL), the optimal policy is given by a Boltzmann distribution. Generating samples from this distribution can be challenging, as it is often complex and multimodal. While flow policies trained with flow matching provide a powerful framework for representing such distributions, they traditionally rely on access to training data, which is generally unavailable in online RL. To address this limitation, we propose fixed-point flow matching (FFM), a data-free procedure for training and fine-tuning flow policies in RL. FFM leverages the target flow identity to formulate the actor update as a fixed-point iteration, utilizing a flow-matching-style regression objective where the critic's action gradients serve as regression targets. We show that the optimal policy is a fixed point of this iteration. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that FFM effectively fine-tunes pretrained flow policies in the offline-to-online setting and enables efficient and accurate training of flow policies from scratch in online RL. These results establish fixed-point flow matching as a principled approach for learning expressive flow-based policies without requiring training data.
authors: Denis Blessing, Onur Celik, Gerhard Neumann
bullets: Targets maximum-entropy and behavior-constrained RL, where optimal policies are complex Boltzmann distributions.
Uses a fixed-point iteration based on the target flow identity to update the actor.
Trains flow policies with a regression objective whose targets come from critic action gradients.
Supports fine-tuning pretrained flow policies offline-to-online and training them from scratch in online RL.
Experiments show effective and accurate learning, though the abstract does not specify numerical results or limitations.

figures.caption: Figure 3: Maximum Entropy Online RL. We have run FFM on all 20 MJX Playground tasks and on the four MJX humanoid tasks and present the aggregated results over all Playground tasks (left two panels) and the aggregated results over the humanoid tasks (right two panels). We have evaluated all methods on 10 seeds for every single environment (see Figure 4 and Figure 5 for results) and report the IQM with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals following Agarwal et al. (2021). FFM performs on par with the baselines on the Playground tasks (left two panels) but converges to the highest return much faster than TRUDI on the high-dimensional humanoid tasks. This result indicates that FFM’s benefits are most pronounced on high-dimensional tasks. Furthermore, we can boost FFM’s performance by leveraging its deterministic mapping properties and incorporating correlated exploration (FFM + OU), which leads to a significantly faster convergence to a similar return value as the best-performing baseline DIME (left two panels) (see Figure 15).

Figure 2: Per-domain aggregated offline-to-online success rate (mean over the five tasks and all seeds). Offline (≤ 1M) and online (> 1M) phases are shaded; FFM (ours) is drawn in bold with a ±1 standard-deviation band. Per-task curves and full tables are in Section E.3.

Figure 1: The FFM policy-improvement step. FFM repeats: (1) Clean actions X1 are generated from the current policy by integrating Equation (5) (forward only, no gradients); the grey curves are sampling trajectories. (2) Critic action gradients are required for the FFM regression target of Equation (12). (3) Fresh noise ε and the clean action X1 are used to sample a noised action Xt via Equation (3). (4) A flow-matching-style regression pulls vθ toward the FFM target. The optimal policy π⋆ ∝ eQ/λ is a fixed point of this loop.

Figure 4: Maximum Entropy Online RL: MJX Playground tasks. We plot the IQM per-task learning curves with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021) over 10 seeds. On most of the tasks, FFM performs similarly to or on par with baselines. However, we observe that there are some tasks such as AcrobotSwingupSparse, HopperHop, HopperStand, where FFM (and most of the baselines) perform badly, indicating that a more sophisticated exploration strategy is required. On a subset of the tasks, we have therefore run FFM with correlated exploration (FFM + OU), where we show the chosen τou hyperparameter on the respective plot. Please note that correlated exploration is only possible due to FFM’s deterministic mapping (Section 5) Correlated exploration can help improve performance, such as in HopperHop, or even more significantly in the HopperStand task. The aggregated results when using the correlated exploration curves whenever applicable are given in Figure 3 (left two panels).

Figure 13: Ablation. Deterministic evaluation (MJX Playground). We plot the IQM per-task learning curves with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021) over 10 seeds on each of the 20 MJX Playground tasks for X0 = 0 (deterministic) and X0 ∼ N (0, I) (stochastic) during evaluation. While most of the results indicate that there are not many differences, for FingerSpin, or WalkerRun, deterministic evaluation seems to improve performance.

Figure 7: Ablation. Geometric versus linear interpolant schedule (MJX Playground). We plot the IQM per-task learning curves with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021) over 10 seeds on the 20 MJX Playground tasks. The performance between the schedule types is the same for most tasks and differs only for some tasks such as FingerSpin or PendulumSwingup, which, however, lie within the confidence intervals. Therefore, there is no statistically clear result on which interpolant should be used for the Playground tasks.

Figure 5: Maximum Entropy Online RL: MJX Humanoid tasks. We plot the IQM per-task learning curves with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021) over 10 seeds. FFM converges faster to a similar performance level as TRUDI and performs significantly better than TRUDI on the T1JoystickRoughTerrain task. The high-dimensional humanoid tasks showcase FFM’s benefits more clearly.

Figure 11: Ablation. Action squashing mapping. We plot the IQM per-task learning curves with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021) over 10 seeds on the four MJX humanoid tasks for the tanh and erf squashing functions. The results indicate that FFM is insensitive to the choice of the squashing function.

Figure 15: Ablation. Correlated Exploration. On a subset of the MJX Playground tasks, we analyze the effect of correlated exploration by varying τou ∈ {1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32}, where we have run every curve on 10 seeds and report the IQM with 95% stratified bootstrapped confidence intervals (Agarwal et al., 2021). Correlated exploration can significantly boost FFM’s performance for the right choice of τou. For example, the HopperStand task is solved, while FFM without correlated exploration struggles on this task.

Figure 10: Ablation. Number of Integration Steps. papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language models (VLMs) already exhibit strong visual, spatial and reasoning capabilities relevant to robotic manipulation. The key challenge in turning pretrained VLMs into generalist manipulation policies is to expose these capabilities through an appropriate action interface. Vision-language-action (VLA) models provide a unified trainable policy, but typically introduce learned action tokens, action heads, or action experts whose semantics must be learned from robot data pretraining. In contrast, modular foundation-model-based manipulation methods can exploit pretrained VLM capabilities for zero-shot manipulation, but rely on external planning and control scaffolds that are not end-to-end trainable as a unified continuous-action policy. In this work, we introduce EASG, an Explicit Action-Space Grounding framework that bridges these two paradigms. By projecting a tool center point (TCP)-centered action frame into the wrist camera observation and expressing actions in the form of VLM's native textual generation interface, EASG makes the semantics of a continuous robot action space directly observable in the VLM's perceptual context. This allows pretrained VLMs to directly generate executable robot actions using their existing visual-spatial reasoning capabilities, without robot-action pretraining or additional action modules. Besides, the same action interface supports direct fine-tuning with robot trajectories, allowing the models to continuously improve beyond their manipulation capabilities unleashed by EASG. Overall, EASG enables zero-shot manipulation and generalization across object positions, categories, and robot embodiments, while supporting effective fine-tuning in the same continuous action space. These results demonstrate that, given an appropriate action interface, pretrained VLMs can themselves serve as native action models for robotic manipulation.
authors: Jingkun Yi, Shujie Zhang, Zirui Zhou, Haoxiao Wang, Haiyang Sun, Yuhang Dong, Xudong Xu, Xing Shen, Tao Zhang, Yong Liu, Jiangning Zhang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of exposing pretrained VLM reasoning capabilities through a unified continuous-action interface.
Projects a tool-center-point action frame into the wrist-camera view, making action semantics visible in the VLM’s perceptual context.
Represents robot actions through the VLM’s native textual generation interface, avoiding robot-action pretraining and extra action modules.
Supports both zero-shot manipulation and trajectory-based fine-tuning in the same continuous action space.
Enables generalization across object positions, categories, and robot embodiments, as described in the abstract.

papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn compact latent world models without pixel reconstruction. Existing JEPA pipelines typically train visual representations and action-conditioned dynamics before adding a control policy or solver. We introduce LeWAM, an end-to-end JEPA for control with: (1) a joint training objective over next latent state prediction and action flow matching, and (2) an isotropic Gaussian constraint on the latent state, enabling a single model to support direct policy execution and efficient planning by evaluating sampled actions with its learned latent dynamics. Compared with prior JEPAs in visual planning, LeWAM improves success rate from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks, and plans 32.3 times faster. On behavior cloning tasks in simulation and physical robots, LeWAM is also competitive with established methods. Interpretability analyses show that LeWAM learns control-relevant representations and action distributions effectively guiding test-time planning and control.
authors: Minghao Fu, Tavis Siebert, Eryk Halicki, Randall Balestriero
bullets: Addresses the separation of representation, dynamics, and control training in prior JEPA pipelines.
Jointly trains next-latent-state prediction with action flow matching under an isotropic Gaussian latent constraint.
Supports direct policy execution and test-time planning by scoring sampled actions through learned latent dynamics.
Improves visual-planning success from 28.6% to 89.7% on contact-rich tasks and from 10.9% to 46.2% on long-horizon tasks.
Plans 32.3× faster than prior JEPAs and remains competitive on simulated and physical-robot behavior cloning tasks.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies fail on memory tasks, behaviour that depends on events observed long before the current frame, because their training data is overwhelmingly Markov and mapping episodic memory directly to action chunks is hard. Yet the same policy, finetuned once to follow a privileged oracle's grounded-subgoal text, nearly solves these tasks: the difficulty lies entirely in mapping memory to a grounded symbolic subgoal. Existing work entrusts this stage to a single VLM that selects keyframes and reasons over raw frames, and falls far short of the oracle: key identities and dynamics are buried in noisy pixels, the reasoning spans hundreds of frames in an unbounded context, and hallucination corrupts the memory itself. We instead present GAMMA (Grounded multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit), which builds the stage as a collaborating two-agent memory system: a detector tool (SAM-3) for spatial grounding, a VLM writer that distils each replan window into one grounded text line, an append-only text memory bank, and a VLM reasoner that reads the bank and emits the next grounded subgoal at the oracle's cadence, wrapped in a propose-verify harness that admits, defers, corrects, or rejects every agent claim against mechanical visual evidence, at training-corpus construction and at deployment alike. On a sixteen-task memory-manipulation suite GAMMA recovers a large fraction of the oracle ceiling with the policy held fixed, reaching the ceiling on several tasks, and transfers with unchanged contracts to a second benchmark.
authors: Yudong Liu, Yueqian Lin, Zijia Tang, Yuxi Zheng, Yuan Li, Shuai Zhang, Yi Li, Taotao Jing, Shuangjun Liu, Dashan Gao, Ning Bi, Jingwei Sun, Yiran Chen, Hai Helen Li

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires maintaining a firm grasp while strictly avoiding both contact slip and structural damage to the object. Satisfying these inherent \textit{secure-and-gentle} grasping constraints is challenging for unknown objects. We present a novel online data-driven predictive control framework for safe dynamic robotic grasping of unknown objects. The proposed system features a pair of compact, single-channel tactile-sensing modules that characterize the gripper-object dynamic interaction in real time, entirely bypassing the need for prior knowledge or offline training. A finite-state-machine-based grasping force probing mechanism is developed to establish the initial grasping force and explicitly identify grasping force constraints. Through online dynamics learning, a Gaussian Process (GP) model captures gripper-object interaction dynamics. The model uncertainties are further used to form robust grasping constraints, which are embedded into a model predictive control scheme. We demonstrate error convergence in a probabilistic sense. The proposed control framework runs at 100~Hz in real time to dynamically manipulate and handle objects rather than static holding. Extensive experimental evaluations across diverse contact surface topologies and various types of objects validate superior performance and efficiency compared to baseline strategies. The proposed method is able to manipulate objects ranging from delicate items, such as raw tofu and marshmallows, to rough objects, such as rocks.
bullets: Uses compact single-channel tactile sensors to monitor gripper–object interactions in real time.

papers.abstract: Humans effortlessly react to the world; they adeptly return a tennis shot, catch a falling cup, step aside from a passing cart, or pass a box tossed during truck unloading. These everyday actions require anticipating a moving target and reflexively responding with the whole body within about a second. Such visual reactive whole-body control remains challenging for humanoids, which must (1) coordinate whole-body control, (2) react to object dynamics in real time, and (3) ground perception in egocentric vision. We study catching thrown boxes as a representative task that demands all three capabilities; existing systems cover only part of it, relying on end-effectors, motion capture, or marked objects. We present Reflex, a three-stage framework that learns these capabilities stage by stage while connecting them through a compact representation of object dynamics. First, a state-based policy learns whole-body catching with reinforcement learning. Second, the policy learns to infer the dynamics of a moving box from delayed and incomplete observations. Third, an egocentric RGB-D encoder learns to recover this dynamics representation directly from visual observations while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. This decomposition provides each capability with a direct training signal and makes visual learning substantially more scalable. In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is critical: removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and laterally offset throws. On a real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes with 65% and 40% success at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of human catchers' success at the same distances.

Human motion examples supply reference tracking and an AMP style reward. Stage 3 learns visual grounding by predicting the latent from RGB-D histories and camera ego-motion, using box-state supervision and DAgger rollouts. Because Stage 3 learns only the latent predictor, the visual controller reuses the PPO-trained decoder without modification.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly used for high-level multi-robot task planning, yet independently generated symbolic plans can become jointly infeasible after geometric grounding because of shared spatial and temporal constraints. We study execution-aware coordination of large-language-model (LLM) planners for multi-robot navigation. We compare a centralized architecture, in which one LLM jointly reasons over the robot team, with a decentralized multi-LLM architecture in which each robot independently proposes a task plan. A geometric verifier grounds the candidate plans into robot trajectories, detects predicted inter-robot conflicts, and converts conflict information into structured feedback for targeted replanning. This verifier-mediated architecture separates semantic task reasoning from execution-level feasibility while enabling iterative coordination among LLM planners. Experiments in CARLA and on Crazyflie aerial robots evaluate coordination performance as task complexity increases and characterize the trade-offs between centralized reasoning, decentralized verifier-mediated coordination, and physical executability.
authors: Vivek Khatana, Zijian Song, Naira Hovakimyan, Petros Voulgaris
bullets: Addresses the gap between independently generated symbolic plans and jointly feasible robot trajectories.
Compares centralized joint planning with decentralized, per-robot LLM planning.

Evaluates increasing task complexity in CARLA and with Crazyflie aerial robots, including physical executability trade-offs.

Predicted obstacle or inter-agent conflicts are converted into structured feedback and returned to the affected LLM planner for targeted replanning.

papers.abstract: Ego-trajectory prediction in urban roadway work zones remains an underexplored topic in autonomous-driving research, with limited dedicated data and systematic evaluation. Roadway work zones involve temporary changes in the lane layouts and connectivity of the roads, complicating interactions with surrounding vehicles and workers. These changes make future vehicle trajectories difficult to predict. To address these challenges, we collect WZDrive-Data, a multimodal dataset comprising 1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers, using a human-in-the-loop driving simulator with prerecorded worker animations and VR-controlled workers. Driver control and gaze signals are recorded from human participants, while vehicle trajectories and scene information are obtained from the simulator. Our proposed multimodal ego-trajectory predictor, WZDrive, achieves a mean minADE (K=6) of 1.09 m and minFDE (K=6) of 2.12 m. Compared with the best-performing state-of-the-art baseline for each metric in our benchmark, WZDrive reduces minADE (K=6) by 7.18% and minFDE (K=6) by 13.18%. This research addresses a gap in autonomous-driving research on urban work zones by combining human-in-the-loop data collection with multimodal learning from human driving signals and in the context of work zones.
authors: Shuo Zhang, Aman Sunesh, Semiha Ergan, Kaan Ozbay
bullets: Work zones introduce temporary lane changes and altered road connectivity, making vehicle-trajectory prediction difficult and underexplored.
The WZDrive-Data dataset contains 1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers, including vehicle, scene, control, and gaze signals.
The WZDrive predictor uses multimodal human-driving and scene information to forecast multiple possible ego trajectories.
It achieves minADE@6 of 1.09 m and minFDE@6 of 2.12 m, improving on the strongest benchmark baselines by 7.18% and 13.18%, respectively.
The study focuses on urban roadway work zones and relies on human-in-the-loop simulator data.

papers.abstract: Indoor navigation to task-relevant targets remains difficult when the target is small, occluded, or visually indistinct. Meanwhile, smart appliances, mobile devices, and IoT tags emit Wi-Fi signals during everyday communication, providing a pervasive but underused spatial cue. We study visual-Wi-Fi navigation, where a robot reaches a signal-emitting device in an unmapped environment using onboard visual observations and Wi-Fi packets overheard from the device, without connecting to the device or modifying infrastructure. Realizing this requires pose-dependent Wi-Fi observations during closed-loop policy learning and reliable spatial cues from bearing measurements corrupted by indoor multipath propagation on a moving robot. We present WiFiSpaces, which extends the Habitat embodied simulator with online ray-traced Wi-Fi sensing, rendering Wi-Fi observations for a robot-mounted antenna array at continuous poses during policy rollouts. On top of it, we build ViFiNav, a localization-aware navigation framework: an online source-localization algorithm exploits robot motion to disambiguate and robustly aggregate bearings from multiple viewpoints into a confidence-aware source estimate, and a learned policy fuses this evolving estimate with depth observations and learns to act on it as it is refined. Experiments show that exploiting robot motion is key to accurate source estimates, and that fine-tuning on ray-traced Wi-Fi observations in WiFiSpaces improves the success rate of ViFiNav. The policy transfers zero-shot to unseen scene datasets, and we deploy it on a real robot with a Wi-Fi sensor built from a commodity router, without any real-world training.
authors: Lihao Wang, Tianjian Xu, Tianmin Shu, Renjie Zhao
bullets: Addresses navigation to small, occluded, or visually indistinct devices using Wi-Fi signals as a spatial cue.
Introduces WiFiSpaces, a Habitat extension that simulates pose-dependent, ray-traced Wi-Fi observations during policy rollouts.

A learned policy fuses the evolving Wi-Fi estimate with depth observations for closed-loop navigation.
Improves with ray-traced Wi-Fi fine-tuning, transfers zero-shot to unseen scenes, and runs on a real robot without real-world training.

They form a closed loop: the policy’s motion selects the localizer’s viewpoints, and the policy is trained on the evolving estimate rather than on a fixed goal. The policy is trained with reinforcement learning (RL) in WIFISPACES, using a reward available only in simulation, and deployed zero-shot on a real robot.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to retain task-relevant history while revising conclusions no longer supported by physical evidence. Retaining observations alone does not specify which completed conditions should be withdrawn after a disturbance or which obligations require repair. We introduce REMM, Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation, a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor. REMM separates an append-only evidence history from revisable task state and explicitly links derived relations and completed conditions to their supporting facts. When accepted evidence changes a supporting fact, it withdraws dependent conclusions and schedules targeted recovery at verified skill boundaries without updating the executor. Across 51 physical trials, including operator-assisted runs, REMM improves mean recorded task progress over the strongest baseline from 57% to 91% in intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% in sequence recall. Complementary video diagnostics show improved grounding of retained history into the next instruction, including comparisons with $\pi_{0.5}$-compatible high-level planner adaptations. These results support revisable memory as a practical interface for continued manipulation without policy retraining. Project: https://revanthsenthil.github.io/remm/.
authors: Revanth Krishna Senthilkumaran, Ruwan Wickramarachchi, Alessandro Oltramari, Jonathan Francis

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) offer a promising route toward general-purpose robotics by transferring semantic knowledge from large-scale vision-language pretraining into language-conditioned control. However, most VLA evaluations emphasize aggregate manipulation success under changes in objects, instructions, or environments, leaving unclear how reliably these policies ground spatial descriptions in the physical scenes where they act. We therefore ask a sharper question: how reliably can current VLAs translate spatial descriptions into appropriate real-robot behavior? To investigate this, we introduce Spa-Bench, a real-robot benchmark that evaluates spatial grounding across six tabletop tasks covering Object State, Relative Size, Referential Description, Relational Placement, Ordinal Position, and Counting. Our primary evaluation compares in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) spatial configurations while retaining training support for the relevant objects, concepts, and actions, reducing object and motor unfamiliarity as alternative explanations for failure. Four diagnostic conditions further probe physical execution, sensitivity to wording, object-task associations, and recognition that no action is required. We release 4,092 episodes collected on the SO-101 robot arm: 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations and 2,892 real-robot evaluation rollouts from five state-of-the-art VLA policies. Across the three fully evaluated policies, success falls from 67.5-73.3% on ID spatial configurations to 40.7-52.0% on OOD spatial configurations, while matched direct instructions improve success by 28.3-40.0 percentage points. These results show that the evaluated VLAs can often execute the required manipulations but lack robust spatial grounding. Project materials, including videos, code, and benchmark data, are available at https://justintiensmith.github.io/Spa-Bench/.

papers.abstract: Non-prehensile manipulation with mobile robots has primarily targeted placement in coarse goal regions. Precision placement has been studied with manipulators on benchmarks such as Push-T, where an omnidirectional end effector can readily re-approach an object from any side. For a mobile robot, correcting the same placement errors may require wide repositioning maneuvers around the object. We formalize multi-object pushing with a mobile robot as a multi-target assignment problem at tight tolerances. We propose a diffusion planner with a causal factorization: each robot denoising step is followed by an object step conditioned on the current clean robot estimate. This factorization allows us to sample multiple object outcomes for a single robot plan, capturing the multi-modality of pushing. We also design a set of pushing-specific costs for mobile robots, used for both guidance and best-of-$N$ sampling at inference. On Push-T, our planner attains the highest success rate of the methods we compare, while having the lowest rate of implausible object motion. Across three multi-box pushing environments resembling warehouse scenarios, it raises the fraction of boxes placed by $21.5$ percentage points over an unguided baseline, and replans $1.8\times$ faster than a planner that denoises the two trajectories together. Lastly, we deploy the guided planner on a TurtleBot 3 Burger with object shapes absent from the training data, where it places $85.0\%$ of objects within tolerance against Diffusion Policy's $37.5\%$.
authors: Lance Pharand, Megnath Ramesh, Mark Chiu, Yash Vardhan Pant, Stephen L. Smith
bullets: Formulates tight-tolerance multi-object pushing as a multi-target assignment problem for mobile robots.
Uses causal diffusion: each robot denoising step is followed by an object step conditioned on the robot estimate, capturing multiple possible pushing outcomes.
Introduces pushing-specific costs for guidance and best-of-N trajectory selection.
Achieves the highest compared success rate and lowest implausible-motion rate on Push-T; improves box placement by 21.5 percentage points over an unguided baseline.
Replans 1.8× faster than joint trajectory denoising and places 85.0% of objects within tolerance on a TurtleBot 3 Burger with unseen shapes.

papers.abstract: Motion retargeting is a critical preprocessing step for transferring human motion data to humanoid robots. While existing methods are effective for single-character motions, interactions involving multiple characters and objects introduce additional contacts and spatial relationships that must be preserved. Retargeting is commonly formulated as a weighted multi-objective optimization problem, where conflicting objectives can require careful tuning of relative weights and can still compromise important motion characteristics. We introduce PriMoRetarget, a prioritized motion-retargeting framework that replaces relative objective weighting with an explicit priority hierarchy. Lower-priority updates are constrained to preserve higher-priority objectives, allowing critical characteristics such as foot placement and interaction contacts to take precedence over lower-priority pose objectives. The method is evaluated on four datasets spanning single-character motion, character-object manipulation, and character-character interactions. The resulting motions better preserve task-relevant interactions and provide reference trajectories that can be tracked more reliably than those produced by widely used retargeting methods.
authors: Nicholas Ioannidis, Dun Yang, Max Smith, Tue Vu, Ziyu Zhang, Shayegan Omidshafiei, Xue Bin Peng
bullets: Addresses motion-retargeting failures in multi-character and character-object interactions, where contacts and spatial relationships must be preserved.
Replaces manually tuned weighted objectives with prioritized optimization: lower-priority updates cannot compromise higher-priority objectives.
Prioritizes task-critical features such as foot placement and interaction contacts over lower-priority pose matching.
Evaluated across four datasets covering single-character motion, manipulation, and character-character interactions.
Produces motions that better preserve interactions and yield more reliably trackable reference trajectories than widely used retargeting methods.

papers.abstract: Recently, soft robotic procedures are being developed aiming at achieving targeted minimally invasive operations or drug administration in specific locations in the human body. Accordingly, specialized path-planning algorithms need to be investigated for the estimation of efficient paths that would protect the delicate tissue structures and simultaneously satisfy a set of requirements for the efficient navigation of the robot. In this context, we propose an image-based 3D pathplanning algorithm, which is an extension of the A* algorithm, for the navigation of a soft-growing robot inside the spinal subarachnoid space (SSS). The proposed algorithm is capable of estimating a safe pathway towards the goal location, while ensuring the establishment of anchor points that facilitate the efficient steering of the soft robot. The algorithm is evaluated using a highly detailed model of the SSS with respect to its capacity to satisfy the robot movement requirements and path efficiency.
authors: George Dimas, Panagiotis G. Kalozoumis, Panagiotis Vartholomeos, Dimitris K. Iakovidis
bullets: Targets minimally invasive procedures and drug delivery in delicate anatomical environments.
Plans paths while accounting for tissue protection and soft-robot navigation requirements.
Establishes anchor points to support effective steering of the growing robot.
Evaluated in a highly detailed spinal subarachnoid space model for movement feasibility and path efficiency.

papers.abstract: Humanoid and service robots operating in clut- tered human environments may encounter motion planning problems that are infeasible when all surrounding objects are treated as fixed obstacles. The Minimum Constraint Removal problem, which we refer to as MCR, addresses this situation by identifying the minimum number of constraints, such as movable objects, whose removal enables a collision-free path. However, computing an optimal MCR solution is NP-hard. In this work, we propose a graph-based heuristic pipeline that combines bidirectional feasible-set generation with fixed- length searches over reduced MCR graphs. We further derive an extended feasible-set generator for instances in which the candidates produced by the first generator do not contain a complete optimal removal set. Across six benchmarks, the evaluated pipeline matches the exact solution in three cases and, in the remaining cases, selects at most 31.25% more obstacles than the optimum, while being between 3.4 and 33.7 times faster than exact search. In one of the benchmarks, involving a manipulation task amidst clutter, selecting two rather than seven obstructing objects reduces the combined MCR, inverse- kinematics, and motion planning time from 84.72 s to 30.59 s. These results indicate that the proposed approach provides a practical compromise between computational efficiency and solution quality for motion planning among movable obstacles.
authors: Antony Thomas, Fulvio Mastrogiovanni, Marco Baglietto
bullets: Targets Minimum Constraint Removal (MCR), which is NP-hard in cluttered environments with movable obstacles.
Combines bidirectional feasible-set generation, fixed-length searches, and an extended generator for difficult instances.
Matches the exact solution on three of six benchmarks; other solutions remove at most 31.25% more obstacles than optimal.
Runs 3.4–33.7× faster than exact search and substantially reduces planning time in a cluttered manipulation example.

papers.abstract: Prior research on learning from humans often requires real human demonstrations. But advances in video generation models offer a new paradigm: we can now prompt these generators to make synthetic videos of the task. On the plus side, these synthetic videos take place in the robot's current environment, and do not require actual human teaching. However, while the generated videos appear to show plausible motions, they lack both physical consistency and robot grounding, and thus the robot cannot directly roll out the trajectory shown by the video. In this paper we seek to formalize the process of going from synthetic video generation to real-world robot trajectories for zero-shot manipulation tasks. We recognize that this problem is an instance of constrained optimization. The object trajectories extracted from the synthetic video provide an initial guess at the correct motion, and the robot must refine these trajectories (for instance, within a digital twin) while enforcing physical feasibility and semantic consistency. Our optimization-based formalism provides insights into the video generation properties necessary for success. Specifically, we show that the video generation must probabilistically seed the search within a semantic basin of attraction where the trajectory can be locally modified without losing its task alignment. Our analysis further reveals that state-of-the-art approaches can be viewed as instances of our unified formalism with key simplifications. In our experiments we remove these simplifications to more closely match the underlying optimization, leading to more robust zero-shot trajectories from synthetic videos and improving average task success by 34.1% compared to the best-performing baseline. See videos at our project website: https://collab.me.vt.edu/CASTER
authors: Yinlong Dai, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Dylan P. Losey
bullets: Synthetic videos avoid real human demonstrations and can depict tasks in the robot’s environment.
Video-derived object trajectories serve as initial guesses, which are refined under physical-feasibility and semantic-consistency constraints.
Success requires generated videos to seed trajectories within a task-aligned semantic basin of attraction.
The framework unifies existing approaches and removes simplifying assumptions to better match the underlying optimization.
Experiments report a 34.1% improvement in average task success over the best-performing baseline.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of CASTER. From the synthetic videos we extract the object trajectories, which then serve as initial guesses for trajectory optimization within the digital twin. (Bottom) The trajectories extracted from synthetic videos do not need to be perfect: instead, they must lie within a semantic basin of attraction where the optimization can locally modify the trajectory shape without removing its semantic meaning. (Bottom Right) We perform constrained optimization so that the robot’s actions in the digital twin cause the objects to move similarly to their video trajectories, while enforcing kinematic constraints so that the output can be directly executed by the real robot.

Fig. 1. Using video generation models at inference time to guide real-world robot trajectories. We bridge the gap between generation and deployment by developing an optimization-based formalism. Under this formalism the robot uses multiple synthetic videos to seed its search and identify task-critical features. By matching these features while enforcing semantic consistency and physical feasibility, we can transfer erroneous videos to successful zero-shot trajectories.

papers.abstract: Memory allows large language model (LLM) agents to use past experience, often stored as textual records, when responding to requests. For embodied agents that control robots, visual and spatial observations introduce a broader choice of memory modalities, affecting both the information available for subsequent tasks and the model inference costs of constructing and using memory. We introduce MeMoREval, a benchmark for studying this problem through a controlled experience-request protocol. Agents first experience a sequence of events without knowing the subsequent tasks, and subsequently they use memory to respond to information and action requests without receiving new observations. The benchmark comprises 53 tasks across four simulated indoor environments and measures task success alongside the inference costs of memory construction and use. Our reference evaluations reveal that storing frames outperforms storing generated descriptions at lower write-time inference cost for the primary model, while storing frames with scene graphs achieves the highest aggregate task success for every tested model. Extensions to accumulated experience, selective frame retention, and visual input to memory writers demonstrate how the benchmark accommodates further memory-design investigations. Two physical-robot demonstrations establish the feasibility of applying its protocol beyond simulation.
authors: Junxiang Wang, Yuchen Liu, Yi Wu, Guofei Chen, Nir Pechuk, Tao Chen, Zackory Erickson, Yuzhe Qin, Tianyu Li

The protocol also supports studies of experience accumulation, selective frame retention, visual memory writers, and physical-robot deployment.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have many degrees of freedom and contact surfaces, yet most loco-manipulation research restricts manipulation to the hands and avoids other body contacts with the environment. To extend manipulation beyond the hands, we present PanTact, a system that learns humanoid whole-body dexterity, the capability to manipulate with any suitable body surface, directly from robot-free human demonstrations. Our key idea is to use contact as manipulation-centric information that transfers across embodiments. Contact locations and timing specify the interactions needed to accomplish a task, while the robot chooses how to coordinate its body to realize them within its own physical constraints. Specifically, PanTact captures, learns, and executes whole-body contact via: 1) a wearable, robot-free data collection interface that augments egocentric vision and bimanual UMI grippers with whole-body modular contact patches to record body contact locations and states; 2) a visuomotor policy that mitigates the egocentric observation gap and predicts whole-body contact goals; and 3) contact-aware whole-body control formulations that realize active contact goals using suitable robot surfaces. We deploy PanTact on a Unitree G1 humanoid without additional body contact sensors, demonstrating whole-body dexterity involving body support, pushing, sweeping, and load-sharing. papers.abstract: Embodied coding agents construct robot policies from natural-language instructions by generating executable programs and refining them from execution feedback. This refinement assumes that execution feedback reveals whether the task succeeded and, after a failure, provides sufficient evidence to guide program revision. Aerial manipulation violates this assumption in two ways. Payload constraints restrict onboard camera coverage and leave task-critical outcomes outside the robot's view (partial observability), while strong dynamic coupling and limited control margins make physical interactions fragile (limited interaction robustness) and leave failure causes unresolved. Re-examining the same feedback cannot recover observations that were never collected or separate failure causes that the available evidence does not distinguish. To acquire this missing evidence, we introduce Active Feedback (AF), an active "View and Probe" framework. When execution feedback leaves unresolved questions, the agent synthesizes a separate diagnostic program that runs in simulation to inspect unseen outcomes from informative viewpoints (View) or test hypotheses about failure causes through targeted physical interactions (Probe). Across six simulated aerial manipulation tasks with 60 trials per condition, AF reduces false completion declarations from 25 to 5 and raises final task success from 31.7% to 75% compared with terminal feedback under the same coding-agent configuration and task-execution limit. Using shared robot APIs, task programs refined with AF in simulation run on a physical aerial manipulator without task-program source-code modification and complete multi-stage manipulation tasks in the real world. These results show that executable diagnosis fills gaps in execution feedback for embodied coding agents, improving both completion assessment and program refinement in aerial manipulation.
authors: Jaewoo Lee, Jeongyeon Seo, Sihyun Cho, Gyeongrak Choe, Yutong Wang, Bavin Saravanan, Jia-Bin Huang, Furong Huang, Sebastian Scherer, Guanya Shi, H. Jin Kim, Seungjae Lee, Dongjae Lee
bullets: Aerial manipulation suffers from partial observability and fragile physical interactions, making ordinary execution feedback insufficient for program refinement.

The approach is demonstrated within the scope of simulated evaluation and selected real-world aerial manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: EliteTable is a self-improving program-search algorithm guided by large language models (LLMs) that uses a fixed-capacity table of high-scoring solutions to guide new proposals, edits of existing solutions, and remixes of several solutions. Performance was evaluated across six Gymnasium control tasks, each with ten generations and fifty candidate slots per generation. Each task was evaluated across ten independently initialized searches. Candidate-score medians rose between the first and final generations in all six tasks, and selected-winner search-score medians rose in five. In CartPole-v1, the selected winner reached the search-score ceiling in the first generation of all ten searches. All ten paired held-out endpoints improved in four of the six tasks. BipedalWalker-v3 and CarRacing-v3 improved without reaching their reporting targets. Six of ten Acrobot-v1 searches declined on held-out episodes, and the median paired change was negative. The results document improvement during program search and the transfer of selected-winner gains to new episodes in some tasks. Comparisons and ablations are needed to establish EliteTable's relative performance and the contributions of its components.
bullets: Maintains a fixed-capacity table of strong solutions to guide new proposals, edits, and multi-solution remixes.

papers.abstract: Tactile feedback provides embodied agents with physical information beyond visual observations, enabling more reliable interaction with the real world. However, despite the rapid progress of vision-tactile-language-action (VTLA) policies, there remains a lack of unified benchmarks for evaluating tactile-enabled robot manipulation across simulation and the real world. To address this gap, we introduce OpenViTac, a visuo-tactile manipulation benchmark for evaluating robot policies across simulation and the real world. OpenViTac organizes contact-rich manipulation into four tactile-relevant capability dimensions and provides paired simulation-real-world settings for consistent evaluation of VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies. Building upon this benchmark, we investigate how different tactile representations and integration strategies affect the performance of pretrained VLA models. Correspondingly, we introduce OpenVTLA, a tactile augmentation framework that combines the best-performing representation and integration strategy. Furthermore, we leverage the paired benchmark setting to study sim-real co-training and analyze factors affecting cross-domain policy learning. Together, OpenViTac provides a unified platform for evaluating and advancing visuo-tactile robot manipulation.
bullets: Targets the lack of consistent benchmarks for tactile-enabled manipulation across simulation and reality.
Organizes contact-rich tasks into four tactile-relevant capability dimensions with paired sim-real settings.
Evaluates VLA, WAM, and VTLA policies, including different tactile representations and integration strategies.
Introduces OpenVTLA, a tactile augmentation framework based on the best-performing design choices.
Uses the paired benchmark to study sim-real co-training and factors influencing cross-domain policy learning.

papers.abstract: Mobile manipulators such as humanoid robots are increasingly deployed in dynamic, unstructured environments to perform dexterous manipulation tasks. However, end-to-end manipulation policies trained to imitate demonstration data collected from a single robot pose are brittle: even centimeter-scale deviations in robot pose at deployment can drive ego-centric observations and end-effector trajectories out of the training distribution, leading to sharp drops in performance. We introduce MobileVISTA, a data generation framework that transforms demonstrations captured at canonical poses into diverse, pose-perturbed training data by jointly (1) augmenting egocentric visual observations and (2) retargeting actions to compensate for base pose changes. Unlike prior methods, which assume a camera rigidly mounted off the actuated chain or non-trivial articulated robot geometry largely out of frame, MobileVISTA targets compatibility with egocentric platforms (e.g., humanoids) where the camera is both influenced by and must observe the robot's kinematic chain as it moves. We study MobileVISTA in simulated tasks spanning humanoid and bimanual embodiments, and on a real Galaxea R1 Pro. We find policies trained on MobileVISTA-augmented data demonstrate improved robustness to previously out-of-distribution poses encountered at test time, without additional demonstration collection or a trained generative model. Additionally, we find MobileVISTA's benefit is largest on tested humanoids, where the camera rides the actuated chain and the robot fills much of the frame. Additional videos and appendix can be found on our website: https://mobilevista.github.io
bullets: Addresses brittleness caused by training demonstrations collected from a single robot pose.
Jointly generates pose-perturbed egocentric observations and compensating action trajectories.
Designed for egocentric robots, including humanoids whose cameras move with and observe the actuated body.
Evaluated in simulated humanoid and bimanual tasks and on a real Galaxea R1 Pro.
Improves robustness to previously unseen test poses without collecting more demonstrations or training a generative model; gains are largest on tested humanoids.

papers.abstract: Behavioral cloning (BC), despite its simplicity, exhibits many counterintuitive phenomena in the real world. For example, the performance of BC often keeps increasing as the model overfits more to the dataset, and fully closed-loop policies often completely fail without action chunking. Unfortunately, properly studying these anecdotal phenomena ("behavioral cloning mysteries") is challenging: in the real world, datasets and experiments are costly and not fully controllable; in simulation with synthetic data, these phenomena are often not easily observed partly due to the discrepancy between scripted policies and human demonstrations. In this work, we propose OCBench, a robotic manipulation benchmark with controllable scripted policies that have similar properties to human demonstrations. We show that, by mimicking key properties of human demonstrations, OCBench reproduces many anecdotal BC-related phenomena in controlled settings. With its GPU-accelerated environments and scripted policies, we demonstrate how OCBench enables scientific studies of previously reported BC-related phenomena by analyzing and refuting various hypotheses. Project page: https://seohong.me/projects/ocbench
bullets: Behavioral cloning can show counterintuitive behavior, including improved performance under overfitting and closed-loop failures without action chunking.
Existing real-world studies are costly and difficult to control, while conventional synthetic simulations may not resemble human demonstrations.
OCBench uses GPU-accelerated environments and scripted policies designed to mimic key properties of human demonstrations.
The benchmark reproduces several reported BC phenomena and supports controlled analysis that evaluates and refutes proposed explanations.

papers.abstract: Task-oriented grasping (TOG) requires robots to grasp functional parts of objects (e.g., the handle of a mug for pouring), yet these affordance regions are frequently occluded in cluttered scenes. Active perception via next-best-view (NBV) planning can resolve such occlusions by moving the camera for more informative observations. However, existing NBV methods typically optimize viewpoints for grasping the target object as a whole without distinguishing which part is task-relevant. A naive adaptation, fully scanning the target object before predicting the affordance, wastes most of the viewpoint budget on task-irrelevant surfaces (e.g., the mug body for pouring). To address this, we propose ATAP, an Affordance-Targeted Active Perception framework that shifts viewpoint planning from exhaustive target scanning to targeted affordance verification. ATAP hypothesizes the occluded target geometry via a generative shape prior and predicts the affordance distribution over the imagined complete surface. In cluttered scenes, severe occlusion can make the location of the hidden affordance ambiguous, leaving multiple locations plausible given the partial observation. ATAP therefore introduces an uncertainty-aware viewpoint planner that jointly optimizes expected entropy reduction over these competing hypotheses and expected affordance verification gain from real observations. This process iterates until the affordance is sufficiently verified for grasp execution. Experiments in simulation and real-world cluttered scenes show that ATAP substantially improves the functional grasp success rate over fixed-view TOG baselines, and outperforms reconstruction-based active perception with over 57% fewer NBV steps.
bullets: Targets viewpoint planning at affordance regions rather than exhaustively scanning entire objects.
Uses a generative shape prior to imagine occluded geometry and infer possible affordance locations.
Selects views by balancing uncertainty reduction across hypotheses with expected affordance-verification gain.
Iterates perception and viewpoint planning until the affordance is sufficiently verified for grasp execution.
Improves functional grasp success over fixed-view baselines and uses over 57% fewer NBV steps than reconstruction-based active perception.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of ATAP. Given a language instruction and an RGB-D observation, ATAP completes the target geometry, predicts task-relevant affordances, and maintains multiple affordance-location hypotheses. The NBV planner selects targetcentered views by jointly considering affordance verification, hypothesis disambiguation, and motion cost. The loop continues until the affordance is sufficiently verified and the remaining ambiguity is low, or the viewpoint budget is exhausted, after which the verified affordance guides task-oriented grasping.

ATAP selects an active viewpoint that exposes the affordance region, enabling a successful TOG.

papers.abstract: As the number of autonomous robots continues to grow, safety becomes increasingly important. Control barrier functions (CBFs) provide a theoretically grounded framework for ensuring safety, but existing design methods often face limitations in effectiveness, scalability, or interpretability, and may result in overly conservative safe sets. In this paper, we propose \emph{VertexCBF}, a framework for learning neural CBFs in a scalable, systematic, and explainable way. We approximate the stationary Hamilton--Jacobi value function using a neural network trained via a combination of physics-informed and sparsely supervised learning. By exploiting control-affine dynamics and a convex polytope control set, under which the Hamiltonian is maximized at the control vertices, we efficiently generate supervision points via GPU-parallel vertex-restricted tree search, while a residual architecture guarantees that the learned CBF is never larger than the specified constraint function. We evaluate the method on 15 systems and compare it against relevant baselines, showing that it reliably recovers large safe sets where the baselines are conservative or fail completely. In addition, we perform a hardware experiment in which a mobile robot safely avoids pedestrians using a neural CBF trained with our method.
bullets: Addresses conservative, ineffective, or poorly scalable existing methods for designing control barrier functions.
Approximates the stationary Hamilton–Jacobi value function with a neural network using physics-informed and sparse supervision.
Uses GPU-parallel vertex-restricted tree search, enabled by control-affine dynamics and convex-polytope controls, to generate supervision efficiently.
A residual architecture ensures the learned CBF does not exceed the specified constraint function.
Across 15 systems and a mobile-robot pedestrian-avoidance experiment, the method recovers large safe sets and achieves safe hardware operation.

papers.selection_reason: Proposes VertexCBF for learning neural control barrier functions to ensure safety in mobile robot navigation.
papers.title: VertexCBF: Improving Neural Control Barrier Functions via Vertex-Restricted Control Search
papers.tldr: VertexCBF learns scalable, interpretable neural control barrier functions by restricting safety-related control search to polytope vertices, enabling larger safe sets and demonstrated hardware safety.

papers.abstract: Offline-to-online reinforcement learning reduces interaction cost for real-world robot learning but suffers from persistent value estimation instability. Existing methods address this through pessimistic regularization, lower-bound calibration, and architectural normalization, but an overlooked source of instability lies in the entropy formulation: the standard log-entropy term can become negative, destabilizing policy updates. We introduce SCQ (Sigmoid-Bounded Conservative Q-Learning), which replaces this term with a sigmoid-bounded formulation that stays strictly positive. SCQ retains conservative Q regularization and return-based lower-bound calibration, stabilizing policy optimization without sacrificing exploration. We evaluate SCQ on D4RL (Minari) benchmarks under both single-demonstration and standard dataset settings, as well as on simulation and real-world visual tasks. SCQ matches or exceeds baseline performance while exhibiting more stable training dynamics across state-based and visual benchmarks, and transfers to four real-robot platforms including manipulation, wheeled, quadruped, and humanoid systems. A direct clipping intervention that removes negative log-probability contributions, together with gradient-matched positive-score controls, indicates that positivity rather than a particular score shape alone drives much of the improvement. Project website: https://scq-rl.github.io.
bullets: Targets persistent value-estimation and policy-update instability in offline-to-online reinforcement learning.
Combines sigmoid-bounded entropy with conservative Q regularization and return-based lower-bound calibration.
Evaluated on D4RL/Minari, simulated and visual tasks, and four real-robot platforms.
Matches or exceeds baseline performance with more stable training across state-based and visual benchmarks.
Interventions suggest positivity of the entropy-related score, rather than its exact shape, drives much of the improvement.

Each panel reports five-seed means with ± one sample standard deviation for old log-probability entropy and SigEnt, using the same replay mixture, critic backup, and 1M-step budget. papers.selection_reason: Proposes SCQ, a reinforcement learning method for stabilizing robot policy learning, evaluated on real-world robotic platforms.

papers.tldr: SCQ stabilizes offline-to-online robot reinforcement learning by replacing potentially negative log-entropy with a strictly positive sigmoid-bounded formulation.

papers.abstract: Multimodal AI, powered by Large Language Models (LLMs) and Vision-Language Models (VLMs), is transforming assistive technologies by enabling simultaneous processing of visual and textual data. This advancement holds significant promise for over 43 million visually impaired and neuro-divergent individuals worldwide who face persistent challenges in navigating indoor and outdoor environments due to limited spatial awareness and insufficient environmental cues. Existing navigation aids often lack comprehensive 3D scene understanding, relying on constrained route-based strategies that hinder user autonomy. In this paper, we introduce a novel end-to-end framework that integrates LLMs, VLMs and digital twin technologies to deliver a spatially cognitive navigation support for visually impaired and neuro-divergent users. Our system captures video input via standard mobile phone cameras, and employs SLAM3R to generate dense 3D point clouds from monocular RGB sequences in real-time. Our custom post-processing algorithm ensures accurate point cloud alignment across multiple viewpoints without requiring predefined reference points. This enhances the capabilities of SpatialLM to produce structured 3D representations, including architectural elements and oriented object bounding boxes. The enriched spatial data is then processed by a locally deployed LLM, which interprets 3D contexts to generate detailed scene descriptions and precise distance measurements between users and surrounding objects. We evaluated our approach across diverse video scenarios featuring various perspectives, looped walking views and captured in multiple environments. The evaluation results demonstrate consistent accuracy in 3D scene interpretation and object localisation, underscoring the potential of our system as a transformative assistive navigation solution that combines advanced visual perception with spatial reasoning
bullets: Addresses the limited spatial awareness and environmental cues provided by conventional route-based navigation aids.
Uses monocular video, SLAM3R, and custom point-cloud alignment to construct dense, consistent 3D environments without predefined reference points.
Extends SpatialLM with structured representations of architectural elements and oriented object bounding boxes.
A locally deployed LLM converts 3D context into scene descriptions and user-to-object distance estimates.
Evaluation across varied viewpoints, walking sequences, and environments reports consistent 3D scene interpretation and object-localisation accuracy.

papers.abstract: This work evaluates the direct transfer of a co-evolved communication protocol from a 2D simulation to a 3D physical environment, without retraining the network weights. Two e-puck-type robots, controlled by a GRU network with residual connection, were evaluated in a food-seeking task with social signaling. The sensory and motor translation layer required three corrections for stable physical operation, including the calibration of a hunger term based on a measurable asymmetry in the trained residual weights. Even with these corrections, the transfer was partial and asymmetric: one agent reached the food source in one of thirty tested seeds, while the other did not reach it in any. Task success was measured by both agents reaching the food area. An additional experiment incorporating explicit directional information in the social channel produced observable changes in the trajectory of the receiving agent and improvements in several specific cases. However, these improvements were not enough to allow the second agent to reach the food source, suggesting that the limitation may not be explained solely by signal translation, but also by the ability to navigate under the new physical constraints. The results suggest that successful transfer of emergent communication may depend not only on preserving the signaling process itself, but also on preserving the ecological and navigational conditions under which the protocol evolved.
bullets: Direct transfer was tested without retraining GRU network weights on two e-puck-type robots in a food-seeking task.
Three sensory/motor translation corrections, including hunger-term calibration, were needed for stable physical operation.
Transfer was asymmetric: one agent reached the food in 1 of 30 seeds, while the other never reached it; joint task success was not achieved.
Adding explicit directional information changed the receiver’s trajectories and helped in some cases, but did not enable the second agent to reach the food.
Findings suggest communication transfer requires preserving not only signaling, but also the ecological and navigational conditions in which the protocol evolved.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models typically operate on RGB images produced by a fixed camera image signal processor (ISP), leaving the imaging pipeline outside the learning and evaluation loop. We systematically examine the consequences of this overlooked design choice across five fundamental ISP dimensions: gain, sensor noise, chromatic response, tonal response, and bit depth. Our analysis reveals that RAW-to-RGB processing materially shapes both action prediction and manipulation success, with different ISP dimensions exerting substantially different effects. Guided by these findings, we introduce RawVLA, a streaming neural ISP that adaptively renders RAW observations for frozen VLA policies while concentrating its capacity on the imaging factors relevant to embodied behavior. We further present RawVLA-Bench, a RAW-domain manipulation benchmark to expose image processing as an explicit evaluation variable across clean and adverse acquisition conditions. Experiments on RawVLA-Bench show that RawVLA preserves performance under standard conditions while substantially improving robustness under degraded imaging, establishing adaptive RAW processing as an effective interface between physical cameras and embodied policies.
bullets: Fixed RGB camera pipelines can significantly affect action prediction and manipulation success.
The study evaluates five ISP factors: gain, sensor noise, chromatic response, tonal response, and bit depth.
RawVLA is a streaming neural ISP that adaptively renders RAW observations for frozen VLA policies.
RawVLA-Bench evaluates RAW-domain manipulation under clean and adverse acquisition conditions.
Experiments show improved robustness to degraded imaging without sacrificing standard-condition performance.
