papers.abstract: Lifelong physical agents must reason over extended interactions where past events continue to shape the world long after they disappear from view. Beyond recalling what happened, agents must infer how history changes the current state and constrains future actions. Yet existing embodied and video-memory benchmarks largely focus on historical retrieval and summary, leaving such history-dependent causal reasoning underexplored. We introduce EMBER-Bench, an egocentric benchmark for cross-event causal reasoning in long-horizon embodied tasks, for which we newly created the task design, video recording, and data annotation. It contains 189 household tasks and 699 QA pairs, spanning task progress, failure recovery, external interventions, and compound long-horizon tasks with distant dependencies and prerequisites, with fine-grained event and causal-chain annotations. EMBER-Bench evaluates reasoning in both directions: next-action prediction selects the next action from history, and causal traceback, given that action, identifies the historical event that makes it necessary. Input ablations that add action logs or privileged cause-and-consequence annotations to the video indicate which kind of historical information models fail to use. Among the 16 evaluated models, the highest overall accuracy is 61.2%, compared with a mean of 98.3% across two human evaluators. At paired decision points, correct traceback is not associated with correct next-action prediction. Adding action logs yields a gain of 1.6 points, whereas cause-and-consequence annotations yield an additional gain of 13.0 points on top of that. These results suggest that extracting causal information from past events and converting it into constraints on current actions remains a key difficulty for long-horizon embodied agents. Project Page: https://zhaoalexgoat.github.io/EMBER-Bench/
authors: Aoyang Cai, Boning Zhao, Shaoxuan Xie, Dahui Gao, Huan Yang, Zhongyuan Wang, Zhiwei Yu, Guocai Yao
bullets: Introduces an egocentric benchmark with 189 household tasks and 699 QA pairs covering progress, recovery, interventions, and compound long-horizon dependencies.

Across 16 models, the best accuracy is 61.2%, versus 98.3% for two human evaluators.

Action logs improve accuracy by 1.6 points, while explicit cause-and-consequence annotations add a further 13.0 points, highlighting difficulty extracting causal structure from video.

papers.abstract: Floorplans provide compact and widely available geometric maps for indoor localization, but existing high-performing floorplan-based methods still convert them into dense scene-specific offline databases, tying accuracy, storage, and runtime to the sampling resolution of the discretized pose space. We present FreeLoc, an online RGB-based floorplan localization framework that treats the floorplan as a directly queryable geometric map. FreeLoc introduces an efficient online geometric querying and diffusion-aided refinement scheme, which retrieves plausible pose anchors through on-the-fly floorplan ray querying and refines them into accurate continuous pose estimates. For sequential localization, FreeLoc develops an online likelihood construction strategy that bridges single-frame localization and probabilistic temporal fusion by constructing likelihoods from coarse-sampled candidates and refined pose hypotheses, enabling histogram-filter-based temporal fusion without offline databases. Experiments demonstrate real-time online inference and state-of-the-art performance in both single-frame and sequential localization, while real-world results validate practical deployability in indoor robotic localization scenarios.
authors: Haocheng Peng, Boyang Zhou, Jiarui Hu, Xiyue Guo, Ziyang Zhang, Boming Zhao, Yifan Gao, Xiao Li, Hujun Bao, Zhaopeng Cui
bullets: Addresses the storage, runtime, and resolution dependence of dense offline pose databases used by floorplan localization methods.
Queries floorplan geometry on the fly to retrieve plausible pose anchors, then applies diffusion-aided refinement for continuous pose estimation.
Builds likelihoods from coarse candidates and refined hypotheses to support histogram-filter-based temporal fusion for sequential localization.
Demonstrates real-time inference, state-of-the-art single-frame and sequential localization, and practical indoor robotic deployment.
Scope: performance depends on available floorplan geometry and is evaluated for RGB-based indoor localization.

papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning controllers for underwater vehicles are usually trained against one physics representation and deployed against another, so reported performance does not always describe behavior outside training. This paper presents a pipeline-tracking architecture for a six-degree-of-freedom remotely operated vehicle (ROV) in which one Universal Scene Description (USD) scene supplies the real BlueROV2-Heavy mass, added-mass, damping, buoyancy, and thruster parameters to both halves of the system: a vectorized NumPy implementation of Fossen's marine-craft equations, and an interactive NVIDIA Isaac Sim deployment applying the identical equations as PhysX forces at every step. The Coriolis-centripetal term is the primary dynamics model in both branches; a controlled ablation on PPO and TRPO shows that including it does not destabilize either algorithm and modestly improves tracking, about 19 percent lower standoff RMS error for TRPO. Five reinforcement learning algorithms, PPO, soft actor-critic, TD3, DDPG, and TRPO, are trained against one environment, reward, and randomized evaluation harness through a checkpoint-compatibility layer scoring any policy with the same code. The pipeline is extended with six classical baselines, PID, sliding-mode, fuzzy logic, feedback linearization, model predictive control, and an adaptive neuro-fuzzy inference system, driven by the same guidance geometry and thruster allocation as the learned policies. Under Coriolis-enabled dynamics, PPO, TRPO, and feedback linearization reach the strongest combination of 100 percent success and competitive accuracy; PID, fuzzy control, and the neuro-fuzzy baseline also reach 100 percent success with looser tracking; DDPG and TD3 each show a specific, explainable failure mode rather than a general weakness of off-policy learning; and classical control remains a strong baseline against the best learned policies.
authors: Cheng Siong Chin, M. Venkateshkumar, Jianhua Zhang
bullets: Uses one USD scene to provide consistent BlueROV2-Heavy dynamics to both vectorized NumPy training and Isaac Sim deployment.
Evaluates PPO, SAC, TD3, DDPG, and TRPO alongside PID, sliding-mode, fuzzy, feedback-linearization, MPC, and neuro-fuzzy controllers.
A shared reward, environment, evaluation harness, and checkpoint interface supports cross-controller comparison.
Coriolis dynamics do not destabilize PPO or TRPO; TRPO achieves about 19% lower standoff RMS error in the ablation.
Under Coriolis-enabled dynamics, PPO, TRPO, and feedback linearization combine 100% success with strong tracking, while classical methods remain competitive.

papers.abstract: Level-$K$ reasoning generates a hierarchy of policies specialized to opponents with different reasoning levels. When an opponent's level is unknown, a common deployment rule estimates that level and selects the corresponding response. In a dynamic, partially-observed game, this selection is repeated, with each choice shaping subsequent states and observations. The response associated with the most likely opponent level need not maximize expected return from the current history. We formulate this deployment problem as dynamic orchestration of a fixed, pretrained policy library in a partially observable Markov game. We compare classification-based orchestrators (CBOs) trained using offline data or on-policy data aggregation with a reinforcement-learning-based orchestrator (RLBO) trained to maximize expected discounted return. In pursuit-evasion experiments, on-policy training improves classification and return, yet RLBO achieves higher return than the on-policy and offline CBOs. Given a pretrained library, RLBO also reaches performance comparable to a policy trained directly over the pursuers' action space with fewer training timesteps. These findings support treating a hierarchy of level-$K$ policies as a resource for orchestration, not a prescription for deployment.
authors: Addison Kalanther, Sanika Bharvirkar, Daniel Bostwick, Chinmay Maheshwari, Shankar Sastry
bullets: Problem: The most likely estimate of an unknown opponent’s reasoning level may not yield the best long-term response when selections alter future states and observations.
Method: Formulate policy selection as orchestration over a fixed pretrained policy library in a partially observable Markov game.
Comparison: Evaluate offline and on-policy classification-based orchestrators against a reinforcement-learning-based orchestrator optimized for expected discounted return.
Result: On-policy data improves classification and return, but RL-based orchestration achieves higher return than both classification-based approaches.
Scope: With a pretrained library, the RL orchestrator reaches performance comparable to direct policy learning using fewer training timesteps.

papers.abstract: Robot agents must connect their intended actions to observed outcomes while retaining the context needed to revise their choices over repeated attempts. Existing interfaces often leave these choices inside predefined tools or require agents to manage detailed execution code and its growing history. We introduce RobotUse, a robot agent harness that organizes computation, context, and decisions around specifying and revising physical actions. Agents visually select targets and poses, while the backend handles geometry, motion planning, and control. Subagents retain detailed interactions within each subgoal and return the information needed for subsequent decisions. Continual harnessing lets agents learn from execution by updating a persistent playbook. On RoboLab, RobotUse achieves 45% task success, outperforming CaP-X by 6.7 percentage points while maintaining compact decision contexts and reducing reliance on predefined action abstractions. Furthermore, we show that RobotUse learns from real-world execution despite imperfect feedback and transfers what it learns to subsequent tasks. Project page is available at https://robotuse-team.github.io/.
authors: Junhoo Lee (KAIST), Injun Baek (Seoul National University), Seungyeon Kim (Seoul National University), Suhyun Jeon (Seoul National University), Minkyu Kim (Seoul National University), Baekseung Kim (Seoul National University), Nojun Kwak (Seoul National University)
bullets: Addresses the challenge of connecting intended actions to observed outcomes without forcing agents to manage detailed execution histories.
Agents visually select targets and poses; the backend performs geometry processing, motion planning, and control.
Subagents retain detailed context within subgoals, while a persistent playbook supports continual learning from execution.
Achieves 45% task success on RoboLab, 6.7 percentage points above CaP-X, with compact decision contexts.
Demonstrates learning and transfer across subsequent real-world tasks despite imperfect feedback.

papers.abstract: Visually identical containers can conceal loads that require different handling decisions. We present TANav, which uses a brief nudge to measure push resistance for navigation under a site-defined handling boundary. TacPhys reads the force sequence, with optional RGB-D and kinematics, into a mass estimate for push authorization. A repeated-patrol planner weighs probe and route costs, requests a second contact when useful, and reuses observations across visits. In simulation, TacPhys approaches a resistance-only Bayes reference and reduces missed pushes from 28.7% to 5.5% relative to peak-force thresholding at comparable low-risk operating points. In repeated-patrol simulation, TANav recovers 90% of the oracle's path saving, more than halves human interventions relative to always-detour, and reduces boundary violations from 4.3% to 2.9% relative to RGB-D-only probing. On a quadruped manipulator with a Hall-array fingertip, offline zero-shot MAE is 0.28-1.07 kg on containers up to 2.82 kg. Force-rise calibration at 3 kg gives 93.5% pooled offline accuracy (86.4% on non-cube episodes); a separate raw-peak rule gives 15 of 20 correct online decisions on unseen boxes.
authors: Xianyao Li, Fang Xu, Ruitong Tian, Bowen Sun, Xiao Hu, Yang Ye, Jing Du
bullets: Visually identical containers may require different handling based on hidden loads and a site-defined push boundary.

A quadruped-manipulator test with a Hall-array fingertip reports offline mass-estimation and online decision results on unseen boxes.

papers.abstract: Real-time agents are often evaluated with the world paused, or with decision time rounded to whole ticks (tick conversion). Tick conversion predicts almost no loss for a learned decider whose hit accuracy falls by 14.8 percentage points (pp) on the same games in asynchronous play. We instead split the decider's gap to a zero-latency teacher into time and quality components. In ViZDoom, we train a small decider by imitating a scripted teacher, run the game on wall-clock time, and add a control in which the teacher waits for a call to the decider's server before deciding. On a Windows host, three preregistered studies put the time component at 6.5-8.7 pp and the quality component at 6.3-8.6 pp. On a Linux host that skips 0.08-0.09% of ticks, the time component disappeared (-0.1 pp; paired 95% bootstrap interval [-0.4, 0.0]) while the quality component remained (5.6 pp [3.7, 7.5]). Retraining on teacher-labelled states from the decider's own play (DAgger) improved it on new games on both hosts (2.6 pp [0.4, 4.9] and 3.1 pp [1.1, 5.2]), a preregistered partial success. Imposing one delay schedule on every arm in live play left a quality component of 5.8 pp [4.0, 7.5] on 100 new games, and retraining cut the decider's disagreement with the teacher on its own states from 22.7% to 14.9%. In a conveyor simulator with a 400 ms deadline, delay past it erased the quality component. A latency-matched control whose delays match the decider's shows which remedy to try.
authors: Chihoon Shin, Junyeong Lee, Kihyeok Jeong, Wonok Kwon
bullets: Tick-based evaluation can substantially underestimate real-time degradation: hit accuracy dropped 14.8 percentage points in asynchronous play.
On Windows, latency and decision quality contributed roughly equally; on Linux, skipped ticks removed the latency component while the quality gap persisted.
DAgger-style retraining on states encountered during the decider’s own play improved performance on new games on both hosts.
A uniform-delay live-play control confirmed a remaining quality gap, while retraining reduced teacher disagreement from 22.7% to 14.9%.
In a conveyor simulator, delays beyond a 400 ms deadline eliminated the quality component, illustrating that the appropriate remedy depends on the failure source.

papers.abstract: Three-dimensional perception is critical for robotic manipulation, particularly for high-precision tasks, as recovering metric depth and precise 3D object positions from monocular RGB observations is inherently ill-posed. However, many Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models rely solely on RGB observations for perception. Leveraging recent advances in foundation models for stereo matching, we introduce ExStereo, a stereo module that augments pre-trained 2D VLAs with 3D perception. ExStereo reconstructs scene geometry from stereo image pairs and renders multi-view observations as an explicit stereo representation for stereo feature extraction. The action tokens from the action expert selectively attend to the resulting stereo tokens through our proposed action-stereo cross-attention mechanism, enabling the policy to generate robot actions conditioned on 3D scene information. To learn robust 3D representations, we introduce a mid-training stage before task-specific post-training, using a self-supervised learning objective on large-scale stereo data. We validate our approach by fine-tuning two publicly available VLAs, $\pi_{0.5}$ and SmolVLA, and evaluate them in simulation and on a real-world bimanual PiPER platform. Across both settings, VLAs fine-tuned with ExStereo consistently outperform baselines, demonstrating the effectiveness of stereo perception for robotic manipulation. Our project website is at: https://exstereo-vla.github.io/ExStereo/.
authors: I-Chun Arthur Liu, Jason Chen, Gaurav S. Sukhatme, Daniel Seita
bullets: Addresses the ambiguity of estimating metric depth and 3D object positions from monocular RGB inputs.
Reconstructs scene geometry from stereo pairs and renders multi-view observations as an explicit representation for stereo feature extraction.
Uses action-stereo cross-attention so action tokens selectively incorporate stereo features when generating robot actions.
Adds self-supervised mid-training on large-scale stereo data before task-specific post-training.
Improves two VLAs, π₀.₅ and SmolVLA, over baselines in simulation and on a real-world bimanual PiPER platform.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: Overview of ExStereo. ExStereo enhances pre-trained VLA models by leveraging a stereo camera and a pre-trained, frozen stereo foundation model [12]. Given a stereo image pair, the stereo model predicts a disparity map, which is converted into a metric depth map and 3D point cloud using the camera intrinsics and stereo baseline. We render the point cloud from four orthogonal viewpoints (Top, Front, Left, and Right) using z-buffering. Each view is rasterized at a resolution of 128× 128 and contains depth, 3D coordinates, and a validity mask. The four views are horizontally tiled into a multi-view observation of size 128×512×5, then processed by a Vision Transformer (ViT) [5] to extract stereo tokens z. We leverage z for action generation through our proposed action-stereo cross-attention, where action tokens a′ query z to selectively retrieve relevant 3D visual features while leaving the VLA’s prefix sequence and VLM weights unchanged. To learn robust 3D representations, we introduce mid-training with masked autoencoding (MAE), where the VLA reconstructs randomly masked multi-view patches from a large-scale stereo dataset while learning action-relevant features from incomplete observations. During VLA post-training, the ViT and action-stereo cross-attention block are frozen to prevent overfitting to task-specific demonstrations, while the MAE decoder is discarded.

Fig. 4: Real-World Rollouts with Multi-View Observations. Examples of successful π0.5-ExStereo rollouts on two real-world tasks using the bimanual AgileX PiPER platform. Each column shows a trajectory over time, with each row containing the left stereo image and its corresponding multi-view observations (Top, Front, Left, Right) at a given timestep. The left column shows Close Fridge Door, in which the left arm closes the fridge door; the right column shows Lift Glass Bottles, in which both arms grasp and lift two glass bottles.

Fig. 1: ExStereo is a stereo module that enables 3D spatial perception in pretrained, off-the-shelf Vision-Language-Action models. Given a stereo image pair, it constructs four orthogonal views of the scene with metric 3D coordinates. papers.selection_reason: Augments 2D VLA policies with explicit stereo 3D perception and action-stereo cross-attention, directly relevant to embodied manipulation and spatial intelligence.
papers.title: ExStereo: Lifting 2D Vision-Language-Action Models to 3D with Explicit Stereo Representations
papers.tldr: ExStereo upgrades 2D vision-language-action models with explicit stereo-based 3D perception to improve precision in robotic manipulation.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon mobile manipulation requires a task plan and the motion that executes it. Generative planners trained on demonstration produce both in one pass, requiring neither a symbolic domain nor search. To date, however, they have relied on thousands of scripted demonstrations of fixed-base arms and executed open loop. This paper presents a hybrid flow matching planner: a single network generates the symbolic plan with masked discrete flow matching and the motion trajectory with continuous flow matching. Unlike prior generative planners, we aim to learn from a much smaller set of demonstrations and to execute the plan in closed loop. Two properties of the data compensate for the small dataset. A demonstration resumed from any of its intermediate actions is itself a demonstration, which multiplies the training samples and enables replanning after every action. Objects of the same kind are interchangeable, which turns demonstrations of one goal into demonstrations of every permuted goal. Our base implementation produces valid plans on 68% of held-out scenes; a training and generation scheme for the discrete plan raises this to 76%, and replanning after every action raises the task completion rate from 40% to 53% in a kinematic simulation. The planner matches the task completion rate of motion-only flow matching policies while additionally providing the symbolic plan, and it outperforms previous hybrid diffusion formulations on both task completion and plan validity. We validate the planner on a real mobile manipulator. Videos and project page: https://andreumatoses.github.io/research/hybrid-flow-planning
authors: Zuleika Redondo Garcia, Andreu Matoses Gimenez, Javier Alonso-Mora
bullets: Targets long-horizon mobile manipulation without requiring symbolic domains or search.
Uses masked discrete flow matching for symbolic plans and continuous flow matching for motion trajectories in one network.
Exploits intermediate-action restarts and interchangeable objects to expand supervision from a small demonstration set.
Achieves 76% valid plans and improves simulated task completion from 40% to 53% with action-level replanning.
Matches motion-only policies while also producing symbolic plans, outperforming prior hybrid diffusion methods; validated on a real mobile manipulator.

Its cross-attention reads the memory: one token per flow time (Fourier features) and one per observation component (an MLP), each with a type embedding. The token head gives pθ at every symbolic position and the velocity head vθ at every waypoint.

papers.selection_reason: Hybrid flow-matching planner for long-horizon mobile manipulation from demonstrations; directly relevant to learned robot manipulation and task-and-motion planning.
papers.title: Learning Task and Motion Plans from Real Demonstrations with Hybrid Flow Matching
papers.tldr: A hybrid flow-matching planner learns symbolic task plans and motion trajectories from few demonstrations, improving closed-loop mobile-manipulation performance through replanning.

papers.abstract: Latent world models enable robots to plan by predicting the consequences of actions. Planning long tasks with control-rate actions requires many prediction steps, which enlarges the search space and accumulates error. Skill-level actions shorten these sequences, but a symbolic skill vocabulary requires domain knowledge and labeled demonstrations. We construct skill-level actions from the inputs of a flow-matching policy trained on demonstrations segmented into complete skills. The policy maps a noise seed and an observation, optionally with a code or label, to a complete skill execution, so one execution is one world-model transition. On this mechanism we propose four action abstractions with increasing task knowledge: a compressed seed, two discrete codes learned from the demonstrations, and a symbolic label. We evaluate them with a common world-model training procedure and planning framework on simulated block rearrangement tasks that require up to 14 sequential skills. The symbolic label succeeds in over 90% of the tasks that require up to six skills and degrades beyond. Without any label, an object-centric learned code matches it on single-skill tasks and retains half to three quarters of its success on tasks of two to five skills. Ablations attribute much of the label's advantage to its planner knowing which actions are applicable, rather than to the label itself. Beyond six skills the search, not the world model, limits success. Project page: https://andreumatoses.github.io/research/flow-skill-wm
authors: Andreu Matoses Gimenez, Andrei-Carlo Papuc, Chris Pek, Javier Alonso-Mora
bullets: The approach replaces many control-rate predictions with one world-model transition per complete skill execution.
It compares four abstractions: compressed noise seeds, two learned discrete codes, and symbolic skill labels.
On simulated block rearrangement tasks, symbolic labels exceed 90% success for tasks requiring up to six skills, then degrade.
An object-centric learned code matches labels on single-skill tasks and retains roughly half to three-quarters of their success for two-to-five-skill tasks.
Ablations suggest labels help mainly by informing the planner which actions are applicable; beyond six skills, search—not model prediction—is the main bottleneck.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Skill-level world modeling and planning. (a) A flow policy generates a complete skill from the current observation, a noise seed, and an optional code or label. Each abstraction uses a separately trained policy with a common architecture. (b) The four action abstractions: a compressed seed, a learned code, an object-centric code, and a symbolic label with a continuous residual. The first three require no symbolic action labels. For the two learned-code abstractions, the seed is sampled at execution rather than selected by the planner. (c) A separately trained world model predicts the outcomes of candidate skill sequences in a learned representation of the scene. Candidates are proposed by enumeration, by learned models, or by symbolic rules, depending on the abstraction. The planner scores sequences by their predicted distance to the goal, executes the first selected skill, observes the resulting scene, and replans.

Fig. 7. The skill-level world model with the symbolic label solving the k=14 tower swap. Left: the start and goal observations (front camera), the planner’s only task specification. Right: one frame per executed skill, numbered by turn as in Fig. 6, with the skill performed and, in the corner, the residual â of that skill. The planner reaches the goal after 16 skills: it corrects two placements (turns 13 and 15) on the way. In this layout the staging moves of the optimal plan lower the imagined cost from the fourth action on, so the beam keeps them.

Fig. 6. Imagined cost of the plan the beam returns. (a) The tower swap of Fig. 7, one task: the cost of the chosen plan per turn, per abstraction. The star marks the turn at which the label reaches the goal. (b) Symbolic label on the problem set, k+5 turns: success against the imagined cost of the plan returned at the first turn, pooled over all 1400 tasks in log-spaced cost bins (grey, 95% Wilson interval) and per k at the median cost (dots). A low first-turn cost means the beam found a sequence the model believes reaches the goal, and success follows that cost rather than k.

Fig. 1. Planning over complete skills. The world model predicts the outcome of an entire skill in one step. Each planned action selects inputs to a flow policy, which generates 256 control steps. The planner evaluates candidate skill sequences using the world model, executes the first selected skill, and replans from the observed scene.

Fig. 5. Validity of the proposed candidates. The label and the two codes without the precondition knowledge in their proposal, dashed, colors as in Fig. 4; the label also loses its effects. Gray: a random valid label at each turn, without world model. All fall below Fig. 4, the label the most.
Fig. 4. Planning success versus task difficulty k (100 paired tasks per k, k+5 turns, Wilson 95% intervals). Success grows with the injected knowledge; every abstraction falls from k ≈ 7.

papers.selection_reason: Constructs skill-level latent action abstractions from flow-matching policies for long-horizon robot planning with world models; directly fits robot learning and latent action modeling.
papers.title: Flow Policies as Actions of Skill-Level World Models: Learned and Symbolic Abstractions for Long-Horizon Planning
papers.tldr: Flow-policy executions can serve as skill-level world-model actions, enabling long-horizon planning with learned or symbolic abstractions and reducing control-step search complexity.

papers.abstract: Modern models increasingly learn through black-box oracles such as humans, optimization solvers, and external tools that provide feedback without exposing their internal mechanisms. A common remedy is to learn an (action-)value function as a control variate. In this paper, we first observe that even an exact action-value function can be arbitrarily far from variance-optimal. We show that this gap arises because the value function minimizes the noise in each action's own gradient term, while an action can still affect the rest of the gradient estimator through shared parameters. A simple unbiased correction, at no extra oracle cost, can still reduce its variance by an arbitrarily large factor. Motivated by this, we then prove that the residual variance can be decomposed exactly by actions with no cross terms. This decomposition yields a closed-form variance-minimizing correction for neural-network parameters, which can be computed by a simple projection. Empirically, our correction consistently reduces the variance left by the value function and improves learning across all tasks. The source code for all experiments is available at https://github.com/Zihao-Kevin/black_box_opt.
authors: Zihao Zhao, Shuhan Zhang, Kai Wang
bullets: Exact action-value functions only minimize noise in each action’s own gradient term, ignoring effects through shared parameters.
The proposed unbiased correction requires no additional oracle calls and can yield arbitrarily large variance reductions.
Residual variance decomposes exactly by action without cross terms.
This decomposition gives a closed-form variance-minimizing correction for neural-network parameters via a simple projection.
Experiments report consistent variance reductions and improved learning across all evaluated tasks.

Figure 1: Variance across decisions in the LLM MCP task at different stages of training. The x-axis indexes the 4 decision slots, and the y-axis reports the corresponding variance on a log scale. Solid curves use the true reward table, while dotted curves use the fitted reward model.
Figure 3: More offline data improves the fitted reward model and strengthens variance reduction.

papers.selection_reason: Variance-optimal control variates for black-box feedback learning are transferable to improving robot/embodied policy learning.
papers.title: Variance-Optimal Control Variates for Learning with Black-box Feedback
papers.tldr: A value-function control variate can be far from variance-optimal in black-box-feedback learning, while a simple projection-based correction substantially reduces estimator variance and improves learning.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we develop a method that enables bimanual dexterous hands to manipulate articulated objects with a high success rate without suffering from an embodiment gap. We observe that the correlation between hand motions and object motions is dictated by the object rather than the hands and can be learned from human-object demonstrations. Based on this observation, we propose PatternDex, a method that learns this correlation and represents it as a token sequence, which we call an interaction pattern. From this pattern, PatternDex estimates the wrist motions and contact points that fit the target robot, and then trains a reinforcement learning policy that exploits these estimates as guidance. Since the guidance fits the target embodiment, the policy explores only the actions that the target robot can execute and thus achieves high success rates. PatternDex also requires only simple fine-tuning to train a new robot, since it can reuse the learned interaction pattern. We evaluate PatternDex with bimanual dexterous hands on human demonstrations from the ARCTIC dataset. PatternDex achieves, on average, a 92.8% success rate with Allegro hands, while the state-of-the-art baseline achieves 52.2%. Also, it achieves success rates above 70% with three other robot hands after fine-tuning alone. Furthermore, we verify that the learned policy transfers well to a real-world task of opening a microwave. Videos and additional results are available at https://patterndex.github.io/PatternDex/
authors: David Minkwan Kim, Runfa Blark Li, Beckham Po-Ju Lee, Nikolay Atanasov, Truong Nguyen
bullets: Learns hand–object motion correlations as tokenized interaction patterns determined by the articulated object.
Uses these patterns to estimate robot-compatible wrist motions and contact points for RL guidance.
Reduces the embodiment gap by restricting exploration to actions executable by the target robot.
Achieves a 92.8% average success rate with Allegro hands versus 52.2% for the reported baseline on ARCTIC demonstrations.
Transfers across three other robot hands with fine-tuning and to a real-world microwave-opening task.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: PatternDex Model. In the prediction stage (left), the guidance predictor G encodes the object trajectory Ot:t+H and the human wrist motions Wt:t+H into the interaction pattern PI . From PI and the robot hand description R, it then estimates the wrist motions Ŵt:t+H and the contact points Ĉt:t+H . In the guided policy learning stage (right), the policy trained with these estimates executes bimanual dexterous manipulation of articulated objects, such as opening a microwave with Allegro hands mounted on xArm6 arms.

Fig. 5: Sim-to-Real Experiment. (a) The wrist motions and contact points are estimated from a human demonstration video, and the guided policy is trained in the simulator with these estimates. The learned policy is then transferred to the real robot. (b) The real Allegro hand opens the microwave at steps 1, 50, and 100. The camera view and the front view are shown as insets in each snapshot.

Fig. 4: Qualitative results of the guided policy. (a) Guided by the estimated wrist motions and contact points shown in the top row, Allegro hands open the microwave, the laptop, and the notebook. (b) Shadow, Paxini, and XHand hands succeed on the same tasks with the interaction pattern transferred from the Allegro hand.

Fig. 3: Interaction pattern for opening the microwave. The object trajectory is shown with its articulation angle only (dashed orange). The human wrist motions (red for the left hand, blue for the right hand) change as the articulation angle increases, and the interaction pattern encodes this change. The light red and light blue curves are Allegro wrist motions estimated from the interaction pattern. They preserve the shape of the human wrist motions and are shifted back according to the size of Allegro, which shows that the estimated wrist motions are adjusted to the robot.

Pos., Rot., and Joint err. denote the position, rotation, and joint angle errors of the object. Contact err. denotes the average distance from the robot hand to the estimated contact points.

papers.selection_reason: Learns interaction patterns from human-object demonstrations to guide reinforcement learning for bimanual dexterous manipulation.
papers.title: PatternDex: Learning Interaction Patterns to Guide Reinforcement Learning of Bimanual Dexterous Manipulation of Articulated Objects
papers.tldr: PatternDex learns object-driven interaction patterns from human demonstrations to guide embodiment-aware reinforcement learning for successful bimanual dexterous manipulation.

papers.abstract: Force-aware manipulation typically relies on specialized force or tactile sensors. We show that force-aware manipulation can instead be achieved through visual force prediction from the deformation of a compliant Fin Ray gripper. Our approach trains two models. First, we train a visual force estimator on calibration data and use it to annotate task demonstrations with force estimates. Second, we train an action--force proposal policy on these force-augmented demonstrations to jointly generate candidate robot actions and their associated forces. At test time, we sample candidate actions and the forces they are expected to produce, then execute the action whose predicted force is closest to a target from the demonstrations. We evaluate our approach on berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion. Our results show that visual force prediction can guide inference-time action selection for contact-rich manipulation without requiring force or tactile sensors at deployment.
authors: Haonan Chen, Feiyang Wu, Yuxiang Ma, Mustafa Mete, Pengfei Ye, Junxuan Shen, Cheng Zhu, Aurora Ruggeri, Kelvin Cheung, Jiayuan Mao, Edward Adelson, Jiajun Wu, Robert D. Howe, Yilun Du
bullets: Replaces specialized force/tactile sensing with visual force prediction from a compliant gripper’s deformation.
Trains a visual force estimator to annotate demonstrations with estimated forces.
Learns an action–force proposal policy that generates candidate actions and predicted forces.
At test time, selects the action whose predicted force best matches a target force from demonstrations.
Evaluated on berry picking, empty-can grasping, in-hand reorientation, and plug insertion.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of visual force estimation and inference-time force search. (a) Visual force estimation converts a wrist-camera image into a masked Sobel edge representation and uses gφ to estimate the axial interaction force from the visible deformation of the compliant Fin Ray gripper. (b) During inference-time force search, the policy jointly samples candidate end-effector actions and force values. We execute the action from the sample whose generated force value most closely matches the target force.

Fig. 7. Representative successful rollouts of four force-sensitive manipulation tasks using force-based candidate selection. Each row shows a task sequence progressing from left to right. For empty soda can grasping and berry picking, the robot applies sufficient gripping force to lift and transfer the object without crushing it. During in-hand reorientation, the robot maintains contact while allowing the metal plate to pivot into an upright configuration. During plug insertion, the robot maintains sufficient contact friction to prevent slippage and fully inserts the plug into the socket.
Fig. 5. Manipulation success rates. Success rate (%) over 15 trials per task for single-sample policy inference and our force-search method, both using the same policy checkpoint.

Fig. 3. Hardware setups used in our experiments. (a) Visual force data collection setup, where an Intel RealSense D405 camera observes the deformation of the hand-held Fin Ray gripper and a six-axis F/T sensor records the ground-truth interaction force through 3D-printed contact fixtures. (b) The six-axis F/T sensor and 3D-printed contact fixtures used to record ground-truth interaction force during data collection. (c) Robotic manipulation platform used for policy evaluation, consisting of an ARX robotic arm equipped with wrist and side-view cameras.

Fig. 4. Force-estimation accuracy. (a) Reference load cell. (b) Force trajectories. (c) Estimated versus measured force (three episodes, 442 frames); dashed line: perfect agreement. Mean episode MAE: motor current, 4.20N; ViewForce, 0.91N (equal episode weights).

Fig. 1. Force-aware manipulation from visual gripper deformation. Humans naturally regulate force when handling fragile objects (left). We use wrist-camera observations of a compliant gripper (right, inset) to infer interaction force from visible deformation and enable gentle robotic manipulation without dedicated force or tactile sensing at deployment.

Fig. 8. Force Search. Distribution of 32 force predictions sampled from the policy for a held-out soda-can observation. The teal star marks the prediction selected by force search (4.45N). Points are offset vertically for readability.

papers.selection_reason: Learns force-aware manipulation from visual gripper deformation and uses force-guided action selection for contact-rich robot tasks.
papers.title: Robot Learning with Visual Predicted Force
papers.tldr: A vision-based system predicts gripper forces from Fin Ray deformation and uses them to select actions for contact-rich robot manipulation without deployment-time force or tactile sensors.

papers.abstract: A pedestrian with a phone could be shown where nearby people will be in the next few seconds, if the forecast stays on the ground while the phone moves, is calibrated, and needs only a monocular camera and visual-inertial odometry (VIO). We build and evaluate such a system. People are detected, lifted onto the floor by ray-plane intersection, tracked in a gravity-aligned metric frame, and forecast as per-step probability maps by a small U-Net trained with a negative log-likelihood (NLL) loss on bird's-eye (SDD) and first-person (EgoTraj-Bench) trajectories. On handheld ADVIO recordings, vertical VIO drift and the user's own changes of level silently rescale monocular ground positions (by 87% within 90 s on one clip; on another, all tracks are lost for the last 31% of the clip); keeping the camera's height above the floor constant under a low-pass-filtered altitude avoids this, though it lags on escalators. On the SDD and EgoTraj-Bench test splits, the final forecaster lowers the NLL at 4.8 s by 1.51 and 1.37 nats relative to a fitted constant-velocity Gaussian. Lacking ground truth for people in handheld video, we score forecasts against the tracker's own later raw measurements. In an internally pre-registered evaluation on seven held-out clips, the final forecaster's NLL is lower than the benchmark-fitted baseline's at 1.2, 2.4 and 4.8 s (by 0.17, 0.23 and 0.47 nats; 95% intervals over people exclude zero), but by less than half as much as on the development clips. Exploratory analyses cut both ways: resampling clips instead of people widens the intervals to include zero at 1.2 and 2.4 s, and once both forecasters are recalibrated on the development clips the network is significantly better only at 1.2 s; but two clips run with ADVIO's reference poses favour the network much more when re-run with the phone's own poses. We discuss what such self-consistency scores can and cannot show.
bullets: Detects people, projects them onto the floor, tracks them in a metric frame, and predicts per-step probability heat maps with a small U-Net.
A low-pass-filtered fixed camera-height constraint reduces severe monocular VIO height drift, though it lags during escalator motion.
On SDD and EgoTraj-Bench, the forecaster improves 4.8-second NLL over a constant-velocity Gaussian baseline.
On seven held-out handheld clips, it achieves lower self-consistency NLL at 1.2, 2.4, and 4.8 seconds, with smaller gains than on development clips.
Evaluation uses trackers’ later raw measurements rather than ground-truth pedestrian positions; results vary with resampling, recalibration, and pose source.

figures.caption: Figure 1: System overview. Per frame, people are detected, their feet are lifted onto the floor by intersecting pixel rays with a floor plane that follows the phone’s smoothed height (Section 3.3), and tracked in metres. A bird’s-eye map collects where tracked people walked and, at 2 Hz, image segmentation projected onto the floor (the RGB-to-map path is not drawn). Each confirmed track is re-forecast at up to 2.5 Hz as a probability distribution over the ground for 12 future steps of 0.4 s; the stored forecasts are re-projected into every new frame with the current camera pose.

Figure 3: The final forecaster on three held-out clips at the middle of each clip (t = 45 s); the clips and the time were fixed in the protocol before the runs, so the frames are not selected. Coloured regions on the floor are the 50 % highest-density regions of each person’s forecast, from 0.4 s ahead (yellow) through green and blue to 4.8 s ahead (magenta), drawn fainter where the forecast is spread out; the inset is the bird’s-eye view (30 m). At this instant advio-03 and advio-20 have nobody close by, and in advio-05 shop-window mannequins are detected as people and forecast. Forecasts of people whose position is uncertain by more than 0.6 m are not drawn (display only; 9 % of the scored forecasts). Selected frames with more people are in Figure 5. Frames from ADVIO (CC BY-NC 4.0); heads of detected people blurred and the run’s timing line removed.

Figure 2: Left four panels: change of the phone’s height over the 90 s clip according to ARKit, ADVIO’s reference poses (“GT”) and the phone’s barometer. advio-06: ARKit drifts upward by 1.23 m while the reference poses stay level (barometer +0.33 m, within its noise). advio-22: ARKit and the barometer agree on a descent of about 1.5–1.8 m along a sloping street that the reference poses do not show. advio-23: ARKit fails; the barometer indicates a descent of about 4 m that the reference poses do not show. advio-01 (held out): two escalator rides. Right: confirmed tracks on advio-22 in the development run of Tier A with the floor held at its first-frame height and with the floor following the phone (Section 3.3).

Figure 4: Choosing the weight w of the network’s own heat map against the physics rollout steered by the network’s goals, on validation data only: mean NLL over 1.2, 2.4 and 4.8 s, and coverage of the 90 % region at 4.8 s.

Figure 5: Frames selected by us after the runs from the final forecaster’s held-out videos, to show typical output with several people and two failure modes. (a, b) advio-02: forecasts of people walking towards and past the phone; near the camera the 4.8 s regions cover much of the floor. (c) advio-04: a person at the top of an escalator, whose forecast is drawn on the escalator steps. papers.title: Probabilistic Pedestrian Forecasts from a Handheld Phone: World-Frame Heat Maps, Visual-Inertial Height Drift, and Evaluation without Ground Truth

papers.abstract: Memory is essential for long-horizon robotic manipulation, where successful actions may depend on past events that are no longer recoverable from the current observation. As episodes grow longer, however, retaining the full history becomes increasingly costly, creating a fundamental scalability challenge for memory-augmented policies. Existing approaches address this challenge by either storing selected past observations in a bounded memory bank or compressing interaction history into a fixed-size parametric state through Test-Time Training (TTT). Yet these formulations do not explicitly distinguish between historical information that can already be recovered from the policy's current context and information that must persist beyond it. We introduce TTT-RM, which repurposes TTT as Residual Memory, using fast weights not to generically compress history but to complement a bounded memory bank by preserving task-relevant historical information that cannot be recovered from the policy's current context. Concretely, TTT-RM learns a history decoder that reconstructs historical representations from the current observation and retrieved memory. The resulting reconstruction residual captures what this context fails to explain and serves as the learning target for TTT. The TTT slow weights are optimized against this residual target so that online fast-weight updates learn to encode complementary historical information over time. The fast-weight state is then queried to produce a residual memory representation that conditions action generation. Extensive experiments on memory-intensive simulation benchmarks and real-world tasks show that TTT-RM consistently improves across multiple memory designs, outperforms diverse baselines, and supports sustained execution on a three-minute, eight-stage stowing task.
authors: Haoxuan Wang, Gengyu Zhang, Ramana Rao Kompella, Gaowen Liu, Yan Yan
bullets: Addresses the scalability challenge of remembering task-relevant events during long-horizon manipulation.
Uses a bounded memory bank plus a history decoder to identify unrecoverable information as a reconstruction residual.
Trains Test-Time Training fast weights online to encode this residual and conditions action generation on the resulting representation.
Experiments across simulation and real-world tasks show consistent improvements across memory designs and baselines.
Demonstrates sustained execution on a three-minute, eight-stage stowing task.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Real-world results. Our method consistently achieves better performance across all task stages.

Disabling residual supervision (λres = 0) can degrade performance, while moderate values yield the strongest results. (b) compares TTT-RM with a naive EM+TTT combination, showing that simply adding TTT to an EM-equipped policy provides limited benefit. (c) examines the effect of our three-stage training pipeline, with the full procedure achieving the best performance across both EM variants.

During training, the history decoder estimates what past information is recoverable from the existing policy context, and its reconstruction residual supervises Residual Memory. At inference, the decoder is removed, while Explicit Memory and Residual Memory jointly condition action generation.

(b) Test-Time Training instead compresses history into a fixed-size fast-weight state whose size does not grow with episode length. (c) TTT as Residual Memory. TTT is repurposed to preserve only the historical information not recoverable from the current observation and retrieved memory.

papers.tldr: TTT-RM augments bounded robot-policy memory with test-time-trained fast weights that retain only historical information missing from the current context.

papers.abstract: Diffusion and flow models provide expressive policy classes for online reinforcement learning (RL), enabling multimodal behaviors and improved performance. However, training these policies remains challenging: the critic specifies the desired policy as an unnormalized Boltzmann density but does not provide direct samples from it. Many existing methods rely on importance sampling to construct training signals, which can suffer from high variance, increasing computational cost and destabilizing training. We propose Score-Calibrated Flow (SCF), a simple and efficient algorithm for training generative models to sample from unnormalized densities without importance sampling or backpropagation through the sampling trajectory. We learn the desired flow by enforcing self-consistency, bypassing target posterior mean estimation. By jointly exploiting the prescribed target score and the structure of flow matching, we establish these self-consistency requirements as score-calibrated optimality conditions, first for the terminal density and then for the trainable velocity field. We prove that their unique solutions are, respectively, the target density and the ideal flow model that conditional flow matching (CFM) would recover if target samples were available. We formulate the velocity condition as a fixed-point equation and exploit its conditional-expectation structure to construct a stop-gradient objective for enforcing it. The resulting training procedure retains the scalable sample-interpolate-regress structure of CFM despite the absence of target samples, using endpoints generated by the current flow. For online RL, the critic gradient supplies the target score at the generated actions, yielding a direct approach to actor training. Experiments on RL benchmarks demonstrate that SCF matches or improves upon state-of-the-art generative-policy baselines, while substantially reducing training time.
authors: Zeyang Li, Yunan Wang, Risheek Garrepalli, Mohammad Ghavamzadeh, Navid Azizan
bullets: Addresses high-variance importance sampling when training diffusion or flow policies from unnormalized Boltzmann targets.
Uses target scores and flow-matching self-consistency to learn the desired terminal density and velocity field without target samples.
Implements a stop-gradient fixed-point objective with the scalable sample–interpolate–regress structure of conditional flow matching.
In online RL, critic gradients provide the target score for direct actor training.
Experiments on RL benchmarks report competitive or improved performance over generative-policy baselines with substantially lower training time.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) and world-action models (WAMs) often degrade under out-of-distribution task variations despite retaining partial task capability. To recover such capability, we propose RoboIRS, an inference-time internal representation steering method that uses successful and failed rollouts to train linear classifiers, select outcome-relevant intervention locations, and derive task-specific steering directions without updating policy parameters. On 15 simulation tasks with a frozen $\pi 0.5$ policy, RoboIRS improves the average success rate from 44.4% to 66.2%, outperforming alternative inference-time intervention baselines while adding little inference time. We further validate RoboIRS on real-robot manipulation using the same $\pi 0.5$ policy and demonstrate its applicability to a world-action model Cosmos Policy, where the average success rate improves from 35.4% to 55.4%. These results show that directly steering internal robot-policy representations can improve the performance of robot policies at inference time. Project website is available at https://rollingoat.github.io/roboirs/.
authors: Jiuzhou Lei, Chang Liu, Dayou Li, Zhiyuan Zhang, Xiao Liang, Yu She, Zhiwen Fan, Minghui Zheng
bullets: Targets degraded performance on out-of-distribution task variations while preserving existing policy capabilities.
Trains linear classifiers on successful and failed rollouts to identify outcome-relevant intervention locations and task-specific steering directions.
On 15 simulation tasks with a frozen π0.5 policy, raises average success from 44.4% to 66.2% with little added inference time.
Also improves real-robot manipulation and Cosmos Policy performance, raising Cosmos Policy’s average success from 35.4% to 55.4%.
Scope: evaluated on simulated and real-robot manipulation with π0.5 and on a world-action model; policy parameters remain frozen.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) policies commonly learn action chunks through a fixed left-to-right (LTR) factorization, although the same expert trajectory distribution admits many valid chain-rule factorizations. We identify factorization order as an overlooked regularization choice and introduce causally anchored permutation (CAP), which samples action reveal orders with a tunable chronological prefix. Its auxiliary objective trains one shared policy to predict actions from different known subsets of the same expert chunk, while deployment retains deterministic LTR control. We call this conditional-set augmentation: it creates multiple conditional prediction problems from one expert chunk without adding demonstrations. This discourages reliance on the single chronological prefix used by ordinary teacher forcing. Controlled experiments show that CAP consistently outperforms standard LTR training on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus, with the same advantage appearing in cross-dataset CALVIN evaluation. A diagnostic that measures the expected squared difference between a chunk's joint log likelihood under two reveal orders verifies that CAP training internalizes agreement across reveal orders. These findings position sampled subset-conditioned auxiliary objectives as a general recipe for constructing VLA regularizers, illustrated by an extension to diffusion action generators.
authors: Yanqiao Chen, Yuhan Rui, Dongsheng Hou, Zijie Nie, Yutong Wan, Qi Hao
bullets: Problem: Fixed left-to-right factorization may over-rely on a single chronological prefix during VLA training.
Method: Causally anchored permutation (CAP) samples reveal orders with a tunable chronological prefix and trains one policy on subset-conditioned predictions from each expert action chunk.
Contribution: Conditional-set augmentation generates multiple prediction objectives from each demonstration without requiring additional data.
Results: CAP consistently outperforms standard left-to-right training on LIBERO, LIBERO-Plus, and cross-dataset CALVIN evaluation.
Scope: The regularization recipe is also extended to diffusion action generators; a likelihood-agreement diagnostic supports its intended effect.

figures.caption: Figure 2: PERMVLA architecture. A pretrained VLM with a Perceiver-style resampler produces context tokens that condition a two-stream action decoder; the sampled reveal order enters only through the attention masks during training, while deployment always executes a chronological action prefix.

Figure 1: Overview of PERMVLA. Autoregressive VLA training conventionally factorizes each expert action chunk in chronological order, so every action slot is always predicted from the same teacher-forced prefix. PERMVLA treats this reveal order as a training-only degree of freedom: the same physical actions are supervised under multiple valid conditioning subsets, while the expert target, action identities, and chronological autoregressive deployment remain unchanged.

Figure 4: Loss construction in PERMVLA. Standard LTR training follows one physical-time factorization and sums teacher-forced per-slot likelihoods against the expert chunk. CAP samples factorization orders over the same physical action variables, illustrated here with K = 1; each order defines revealed subsets and a corresponding likelihood. Their Monte Carlo average is a training-only regularizer of the shared policy. The drawn losses are unnormalized within-chunk sums; Equations 3– 4 define the normalized objectives. Action indices denote fixed physical slots in both panels, and deployment retains deterministic physical-time LTR control.

Figure 5: Illustration of CAP’s theoretical interpretation. In the upper path, a reveal order z defines a normalized joint density qzθ(A | C); substituting this density into the mixed CAP risk Rmix (Equation 16) and minimizing it preserves the expert population target. In the lower path, a demonstrated action chunk creates a family of conditional prediction problems; these problems jointly constrain a finite-capacity model, so features that remain predictive across conditional sets receive repeated support, thereby forming CAP’s regularization mechanism.

papers.abstract: Actor-critic methods reuse past experience to improve sample efficiency. However, historical data are typically regarded as off-policy samples for the current policy-improvement update. This work introduces Regularized Dual Averaging Actor Critic (RDA2C), which assigns a distinct role to replay. In regularized dual averaging, the subsequent policy is determined by accumulated policy-improvement feedback, so historical advantage estimates contribute directly to the actor objective rather than solely to the most recent update. RDA2C stores state-action samples with critic-estimated advantage labels, fits a dual score model $Z_\theta$ to the aggregated dataset, and derives the current policy from the accumulated score model using the entropy mirror map. In this way, replay defines an empirical dual objective from which the policy is computed. To analyze RDA2C, we establish a finite-time value-gap decomposition, separating the regularized dual-averaging term from errors due to stale-replay supervised fitting, critic bias, finite-buffer variance, and replay coverage, and stating the assumptions under which each error is bounded. RDA2C accepts advantage labels from any critic. With GAE labels, RDA2C outperforms PPO on six of eight MuJoCo tasks and eight of twelve Atari games. RDA2C also outperforms AAPDA, the closest dual-averaging baseline, on six of eight MuJoCo tasks. With twin-$Q$ labels, RDA2C matches SAC at matched batch size and update frequency.
authors: Nianli Peng, Geoffrey J. Gordon, Kiant\'e Brantley
bullets: Reframes replay: historical advantage estimates directly shape future policy updates rather than serving only as off-policy samples.
Fits a dual score model to replayed state-action samples with critic-estimated advantage labels, then derives the policy through an entropy mirror map.
Provides a finite-time value-gap decomposition covering stale-replay fitting, critic bias, finite-buffer variance, and replay-coverage errors.
With GAE labels, RDA2C outperforms PPO on 6/8 MuJoCo and 8/12 Atari tasks, and outperforms AAPDA on 6/8 MuJoCo tasks.
With twin-Q labels, RDA2C matches SAC under matched batch size and update frequency.

papers.abstract: A vision--language--action (VLA) policy can complete complex tasks while ignoring the evidence that should determine its actions. An object held near the wrist camera can displace the instructed target. Language and action show the same pattern: a familiar noun can trigger the operation it was paired with in training even after the verb changes, and a gripper that closed on nothing may lift anyway. We call these dependencies modality shortcuts: regularities in successful demonstrations make visual, lexical, or motor cues sufficient to predict expert actions without the task evidence needed for the underlying decision. More demonstrations of the same kind can raise task success while leaving these shortcuts intact. We propose Perturbot which makes task-relevant evidence easier to use and shortcuts insufficient on their own: it applies task-preserving wrist-view perturbations, enriches instructions with decision-relevant captions, and adds random and failed trajectory segments relabeled with the behavior they contain. It complements scaling by changing what is scaled, and leaves inference unchanged. Moreover, we propose GroundingFscore, an offline score that diagnoses how severely a policy relies on modality shortcuts. Task success rate shows whether a policy improves, while GroundingFscore reveals whether the policy scales healthily, relying on task evidence rather than shortcuts. Together, Perturbot and GroundingFscore provide a training-and-evaluation framework for disentangling VLA decisions from shortcut priors while preserving responsiveness to task-relevant evidence.
authors: Mingyu Liu, Chonghao Sima, Tianjian Feng, Hanqing Wang, Cong Chen, Hao Chen, Chunhua Shen
bullets: VLA policies may succeed by exploiting modality shortcuts instead of evidence needed for the underlying task decision.
PerturbBot uses task-preserving wrist-view perturbations, decision-relevant instruction captions, and relabeled random or failed trajectory segments.
The method changes training while leaving inference unchanged, complementing model scaling by improving the data and signals being scaled.
GroundingFscore provides an offline measure of shortcut reliance alongside task success, helping assess whether scaling is healthy.
The framework aims to preserve responsiveness to task-relevant evidence while disentangling decisions from shortcut priors.

papers.title: PerturBot: Breaking Shortcut Priors in Vision-Language-Action Models with Perturbative Training

papers.abstract: Soft robots present significant modelling challenges due to their non-linearity, complex dynamics and potentially intricate geometries. These difficulties in accurate system identification and dynamics modelling limit their applications in precise robotics tasks. Prior modelling approaches typically suffer from trade-offs in accuracy, computational efficiency, or speed. The differentiable finite element method (FEM) offers a promising balance between these desiderata for soft robot modelling, and enables the use of gradients for efficient calibration and trajectory optimisation. In this paper, we propose an end-to-end differentiable FEM-based framework designed to streamline modelling and system identification for pneumatic soft robots, enabling the generation of reliable models for downstream tasks. The framework automates the conversion of computer-aided designs into voxelised tetrahedral viscoelastic FEM meshes that accurately represent the robot's geometry and actuation mechanism. By integrating easily acquired point cloud data with differentiable FEM, the framework achieves precise identification of material and dynamic actuation parameters using a minimal experimental setup. Additionally, the differentiable nature of the model facilitates trajectory optimisation by leveraging gradients from robot dynamics and contact interactions. We validate the framework by modelling a complex bellow-shaped pneumatic soft robot and demonstrate its efficacy in real-world motion planning tasks. Experimental results indicate high modelling accuracy, with a maximum positional error of less than 3 mm, and successful application in tasks such as path following and grasping.
authors: Shaohong Zhong, Yao Yao, Perla Maiolino, Ingmar Posner
bullets: Addresses the accuracy–efficiency trade-off in modelling nonlinear pneumatic soft robots.
Automatically converts CAD designs into voxelised tetrahedral viscoelastic FEM meshes representing geometry and actuation.
Uses differentiable FEM and point-cloud measurements to identify material and dynamic actuation parameters with minimal experiments.
Supports gradient-based trajectory optimisation involving robot dynamics and contact interactions.
Validated on a complex bellow-shaped robot with positional error below 3 mm, achieving path following and grasping.

papers.abstract: Hierarchical control architectures are widely used to decompose complex control problems into interacting control levels and are particularly important in robotics, where planning, whole-body motion, and lower-level control must be coordinated across different levels of abstraction and time scales. Their overall closed-loop performance, however, depends strongly on parameters distributed across the hierarchy, such that tuning controllers on different levels independently may neglect relevant cross-layer interactions. We propose a contextual Bayesian optimization framework for joint parameter learning in hierarchical control systems. Rather than modeling closed-loop performance only as a scalar black-box function, we retain separate observations of task performance, realization quality, and control effort. A correlated multi-output Gaussian process models these performance components, while their known aggregation into the overall closed-loop objective is evaluated analytically. The formulation exploits three complementary consequences of hierarchical control: informative performance quantities exposed by the hierarchy, coupling between parameters of different controller levels, and variations of these relations with operating conditions. We evaluate the approach for humanoid loco-manipulation, jointly tuning a centroidal predictive controller and a whole-body controller for physical box pushing under varying box mass. The proposed method achieves the lowest mean empirical regret during both training and adaptation among the considered baselines.
authors: Sebastian Hirt, Lukas Theiner, Jan Peters, Rolf Findeisen
bullets: Independent tuning can miss interactions between parameters at different control levels in hierarchical robotics systems.
The method uses a correlated multi-output Gaussian process and analytically combines predicted performance components into the overall objective.
It exploits hierarchy-exposed metrics, cross-level parameter coupling, and operating-condition-dependent relationships.
Evaluated on humanoid box pushing, it jointly tunes centroidal predictive and whole-body controllers under varying box mass.
It achieves the lowest mean empirical regret during training and adaptation among the evaluated baselines.

papers.abstract: Robots need to anticipate how their actions will change the world, since manipulation success hinges on the resulting contacts and object motions. However, existing Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies that predict future observations from shared features leave the forecast decoupled from the actions the policy will actually execute, and impose no physical constraints on how the scene may evolve. We introduce ForeAct3D, a framework for policy-grounded future world modeling within VLA policies. Learnable geometric queries decode depth, semantic segmentation, and camera pose from the policy representation into current and future semantic 3D scene states, and the future queries are conditioned on the policy-generated action chunk to ground the forecast in the planned interaction. A physical-consistency closure relates the two states through background staticity and instance-level rigidity, and anchors the wrist-camera pose to end-effector kinematics. These objectives shape the shared representation used for action generation during training, and no future prediction is required at inference. Without robot pretraining, ForeAct3D achieves 98.3\% average success on LIBERO and an average task length of 3.73 on CALVIN, outperforming its base policy on every suite. Ablations show that semantic 3D supervision, physical consistency, and action conditioning each improve manipulation performance, and that action conditioning substantially improves future object localization. Real-world experiments on spatial placement, object insertion, and sequential manipulation further raise average success from 6.7\% to 37.8\% over the base policy. The project page and code are available at https://github.com/anthonytao80-crypto/ForeAct3D.
authors: Zhe Tao, Feiran Wang, Gaowen Liu, Ramana Rao Kompella$, Yan Yan
bullets: Addresses forecasts that are decoupled from executed actions and lack physical constraints.
Uses geometric queries to predict depth, semantics, and camera pose for current and future 3D scene states.
Conditions future prediction on action chunks and enforces background staticity, object rigidity, and wrist-camera kinematics.
Future modeling shapes training representations but is not required during inference.
Improves simulation and real-world manipulation performance over the base policy, with gains supported by ablations.

papers.abstract: Agile flight in unknown, cluttered, and dynamic environments requires a planner that knows where and when danger will appear, not only that a trajectory is dangerous. One-stage learning-based planners trained with differentiable privileged costs are fast and expert-free, but the only signal reaching their encoder is a scalar trajectory cost with no spatial or temporal structure, so avoidance degrades into late reactive maneuvers. We present RiskFly, a one-stage planner that predicts risk in the same space in which it acts. A dual-stream observation pairs a short depth sequence with a frustum-aligned inverted spherical range-map sequence, whose angular cells match the end-state proposals one to one. An auxiliary head regresses a frustum-aligned spatio-temporal risk field, supervised by a privileged closest-point-of-approach (CPA) target. This self-predicted field is queried differentiably along the instantiated quintic trajectory at its own arrival times, and also enters the training objective, so representation supervision and planning gradients meet in a single space. Privileged signals are discarded at deployment, and the planner runs map-free from onboard depth and proprioception. Extensive simulation and zero-shot real-world flights on resource-constrained platforms show higher success rates at comparable end-to-end latency.
authors: Luxia Ai, Haopeng Chen, Yuchao Mei, Guohao Zhang, Wenbing Tao
bullets: Addresses late reactive avoidance in one-stage planners that receive only scalar trajectory costs.
Uses depth sequences plus frustum-aligned inverted spherical range maps whose angular cells correspond to end-state proposals.
Predicts a spatio-temporal risk field from privileged closest-point-of-approach targets and queries it along quintic trajectories at arrival times.
Privileged supervision is removed at deployment; the planner operates from onboard depth and proprioception without a map.
Simulation and zero-shot real-world flights show higher success rates at comparable end-to-end latency on resource-constrained platforms.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. System overview. A depth sequence Dt, a frustum-aligned range-map sequence Lt, the proprioceptive state ot and the goal direction are encoded on the shared V ×H frustum grid: a CoAtNet branch and a range-map CNN are concatenated, fused with the state by a 1×1 convolution, and aggregated by a per-cell TCN into G. A risk head regresses the spatio-temporal risk field R̂ ∈ [0, 1]V ×H×B indexed by bearing and arrival time, and a planning head regresses one scored terminal-state proposal per cell. During training, the ESDF and ground-truth actor states supply the CPA target for Lrf and the trajectory costs, while R̂ is queried along the instantiated trajectory at its own arrival times as Jrf. At inference the privileged modules are detached and r̄ij modulates proposal selection.

papers.abstract: Fusing radar, LiDAR, and camera enables robust perception in diverse and adverse conditions, but the fusion performance critically depends on accurate extrinsic calibration among the three sensors. In this paper, we address the problem of online target-less extrinsic calibration for the radar-LiDAR-camera system. Existing target-less methods are mostly designed for a single sensor pair, and composing the pairwise results does not guarantee consistency across the three sensors. Moreover, the sparse and noisy radar measurements make the radar-involving pairs unreliable. To tackle these challenges, we propose a joint calibration framework that constructs residuals for each sensor pair and optimizes the extrinsics of all pairs together to minimize the overall residual. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive radar noise filter that rejects spurious radar returns using a range-dependent margin, and a correspondence accumulation strategy that aggregates sparse radar correspondences over frames. We validate our method on an in-house radar-LiDAR-camera dataset covering diverse urban environments, where it reduces calibration errors across all sensor pairs over a state-of-the-art camera-LiDAR baseline.
authors: Gunhee Shin, Yunsoo Kim, Chanhyuk Lee, Wanhee Kim, Minwoo Lee, Sungwoo Han, Jeongwoo Woo, Hyuntai Chin, Minha Park, Hyun Myung
bullets: Addresses inconsistent pairwise calibration and unreliable radar-involving calibration.

Accumulates radar correspondences across frames to improve sparse measurements.
Validated in diverse urban environments, reducing errors across all sensor pairs relative to a camera-LiDAR baseline.

The correspondences are accumulated over frames, and the joint optimization estimates the extrinsics of all three sensor pairs.

papers.abstract: Multiple LiDAR-inertial odometry methods have been widely applied in robotic applications owing to their enhanced accuracy and reliability. However, adopting multiple LiDAR systems can be challenging due to the discrepancies in measurement noise across different LiDARs. Existing methods have typically overlooked the noise discrepancies, which can significantly affect accuracy. In this paper, we propose Noise-aware Multiple LiDAR-Inertial Odometry (NM-LIO) that addresses the noise discrepancies. We integrate a noise model to quantify the measurement noise of each LiDAR. Additionally, we estimate the uncertainty of the residuals based on the measurement noise, allowing the measurement model to capture the noise discrepancies. Our proposed method is evaluated on a public multiple LiDAR dataset and compared with state-of-the-art methods. The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method can accurately estimate the odometry in various environments by accounting for the noise discrepancies.
authors: Gunhee Shin, Seungjae Lee, Minho Oh, Dongkyu Lee, Jaeyoung Lee, Youngwoo Seo, Hyun Myung
bullets: Multiple LiDAR systems improve odometry reliability but suffer when their sensor-specific noise discrepancies are ignored.
NM-LIO uses a noise model to quantify measurement noise for each LiDAR.
It estimates residual uncertainty from these noise levels, enabling a noise-aware measurement model.
Evaluation on a public multiple-LiDAR dataset shows accurate odometry across various environments.
The abstract does not specify quantitative gains or detailed limitations.

(c) Third, motion compensation is performed to compensate for the motion distortion. (d) Fourth, the residual is computed to form the measurement model. (e) Finally, the state is iteratively updated until it converges.

papers.abstract: Designing effective reward functions in RL typically requires substantial expertise and trial and error. Recent work automates this process with LLM-based systems that generate and iteratively improve reward code using policy feedback. However, these methods are often hard to compare because they differ in implementation details, feedback assumptions, and evaluation environments. To address this, we introduce a Benchmark for Iterative Reward Design (BIRD) that expresses existing methods in a unified configuration and evaluation space. This lets us compare algorithms directly, ablate individual design choices, and prototype new components under matched feedback conditions and policy-training budgets. Across MuJoCo, Meta-World, Assistax, and HumanoidBench, we identify a small set of simple design choices that consistently improve performance. Combining these choices yields significantly better performance than the evaluated methods from prior work. Our results highlight the strength of simple baselines and motivate further study of when additional algorithmic complexity improves iterative reward design. Code is available at https://github.com/safety-research/bird.
authors: Logan Mondal Bhamidipaty, Lauren Robson, Linda Petrini, Shengrui Lyu, Kamal Ndousse
bullets: Addresses the difficulty of fairly comparing iterative reward-design algorithms due to differing implementations, feedback assumptions, and evaluation settings.
Introduces a unified configuration and evaluation framework supporting direct comparisons, ablations, and component prototyping under matched feedback and policy-training budgets.
Evaluates methods across MuJoCo, Meta-World, Assistax, and HumanoidBench.
Finds that combining consistently effective design choices outperforms the evaluated prior methods and underscores the strength of simple baselines.
Motivates further investigation into when added algorithmic complexity benefits iterative reward design.
